stem:
A 7-year-old boy weighing 22 kg is brought into John Hunter Hospital trauma bay after being hit by a car at low speed. Primary survey: airway patent, breathing equal but rapid, circulation tachycardic with weak peripheral pulses, conscious GCS 14. T 36.5, HR 156, RR 38, BP 86/52, capillary refill 4 seconds. He has bruising over the right lower abdomen, no obvious external bleeding, no long-bone deformity.

The trauma team leader requests the first fluid resuscitation order, and the registrar must distinguish between the paediatric trauma bolus volume and the paediatric medical sepsis bolus volume.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 156, RR 38, BP 86/52, CRT 4 sec, GCS 14, weight 22 kg.
data_table.Examination: Bruising RLQ, abdomen guarding, no peritonism yet, no external bleeding, no long-bone deformity.
data_table.Investigations: FAST scan pending; blood group + crossmatch sent; bedside lactate 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which volume and fluid type should be administered as the first bolus, recognising that the paediatric trauma cut-off differs from the paediatric sepsis cut-off?

options.text: 20 mL/kg crystalloid (440 mL) over 5-10 min - standard paediatric sepsis bolus
options.rationale: Paediatric TRAUMA bolus is smaller than the sepsis bolus to limit dilutional coagulopathy and re-bleeding from clot disruption. The Royal Children's / NSW trauma protocol gives 10 mL/kg crystalloid then early blood, not 20 mL/kg crystalloid loading. Sepsis bolus (20 mL/kg) is the wrong physiology for active haemorrhage. Source: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol; PHANTOM.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.text: 10 mL/kg crystalloid (220 mL) over 5-10 min then transition to packed red cells 10 mL/kg if persistent shock; activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol
options.rationale: AU paediatric trauma protocol (NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage; PHANTOM) recommends limited crystalloid (10 mL/kg) then early conversion to packed red cells (10 mL/kg) and FFP (10 mL/kg) in a 1:1 ratio after the first crystalloid bolus, plus activation of paediatric massive transfusion. Goal is permissive hypotension during damage-control resuscitation and avoidance of dilutional coagulopathy. The discriminator is recognising trauma (limit crystalloid, early blood) vs sepsis (crystalloid 20 mL/kg). Source: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol; ANZSBT.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.text: 40 mL/kg crystalloid (880 mL) over 30 min - aggressive volume resuscitation as per ATLS adult protocol
options.rationale: Adult ATLS recommendations no longer support 40 mL/kg aggressive crystalloid in trauma even in adults (dilutional coagulopathy + clot disruption + ARDS risk); paediatric protocols are even more restrictive. Source: ATLS-AU; NSW Pathway.

options.text: 20 mL/kg of 4% albumin colloid - colloid resuscitation for trauma
options.rationale: Crystalloid is first-line in AU paediatric trauma resuscitation (FEAST trial impact and AU practice). Colloid as primary trauma resus is not supported. Source: NSW Pathway.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

options.text: Withhold all fluids until CT abdomen confirms intra-abdominal injury and surgical control achieved
options.rationale: Withholding all fluid in compensated shock is unsafe; the goal is balanced damage-control resuscitation with limited crystalloid then early blood, not no fluid. Source: NSW Pathway.
source_refs: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

explanation.summary: Paediatric trauma resuscitation cut-offs differ from paediatric sepsis: trauma limits crystalloid (10 mL/kg) and transitions early to blood components to avoid dilutional coagulopathy and clot disruption (damage-control resuscitation); sepsis allows higher crystalloid (20 mL/kg per bolus, up to 40-60 mL/kg). This is the key cut-off difference. Activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol early when haemorrhagic shock is suspected. Tranexamic acid 15 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) within 3 hours of injury is the AU paediatric trauma standard. Permissive hypotension targets SBP 5th centile for age while damage control is achieved.
key_points: Paeds trauma bolus: 10 mL/kg crystalloid then early blood
Paeds sepsis bolus: 20 mL/kg crystalloid x2-3
Paediatric MTP: PRBC + FFP + platelets in 1:1:1 ratio
TXA 15 mg/kg IV (max 1 g) within 3 hours of injury
Permissive hypotension: target SBP 5th centile for age until damage control
explanation.pearls: Tachycardia is the earliest paediatric shock sign; hypotension is late and often preterminal. Capillary refill >2 seconds + tachycardia is enough to start resuscitation; do not wait for hypotension.

sources.label: NSW Health Paediatric Major Haemorrhage Protocol

subtopic_detail: Paediatric trauma vs sepsis fluid bolus discrimination

stem:
A 9-month-old girl is referred to paediatric cardiology at the John Hunter Children's Hospital for a murmur picked up at the 8-month vaccination visit. Birth was at term, weight 2.8 kg (10th centile), no antenatal concerns. She has fed well but feeds slowly. Her mother volunteers that she has the most outgoing personality of any baby in the family. Examination: weight on 5th centile (down from 10th at birth), interactive smile, prominent forehead and short upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth, small chin, mild infraorbital fullness.

Cardiac auscultation: harsh ejection systolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal edge with a thrill, transmitted to the carotids, no diastolic murmur. Femoral pulses present and equal. Mild generalised hypotonia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 36, BP arm 108/68 (right) and 96/62 (left), no postductal differential, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Dysmorphic facies (prominent forehead, upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth), small chin, mild hypotonia, harsh ESM with thrill at right upper sternal edge, normal femoral pulses.
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram pending. Random ionised calcium 1.42 mmol/L (high, ref 1.15-1.32). Random glucose 4.2 mmol/L. UEC otherwise normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely unifying diagnosis, and which targeted genetic test should be requested?

options.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21); request karyotype and atrioventricular septal defect echocardiography
options.rationale: Down syndrome facies are upslanting palpebral fissures, brachycephaly, single palmar crease, hypotonia - and the typical cardiac lesion is AVSD or VSD, not supravalvular AS. The described upturned nose and personality phenotype do not fit. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion); request FISH for 22q11.2 and cardiac imaging for conotruncal defects
options.rationale: 22q11.2 deletion has different facial features (long face, almond-shaped eyes, tubular nose, short philtrum) and typical conotruncal cardiac defects (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch), not supravalvular AS. Hypocalcaemia not hypercalcaemia. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene); request FISH for ELN deletion and cardiology assessment for supravalvular AS and peripheral pulmonary stenosis
options.rationale: Pattern recognition: elfin facies (prominent forehead, periorbital fullness, upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth, small chin), supravalvular aortic stenosis (right upper sternal edge ESM transmitted to carotids - NOT left as in valvular AS), idiopathic hypercalcaemia in infancy, mild intellectual disability with characteristically friendly disinhibited personality, mild generalised hypotonia. Williams syndrome from deletion of ~26 genes at 7q11.23 including ELN (elastin) which causes the vascular phenotype. FISH or microarray confirms. Cardiology surveillance for SVAS progression and PPS. Avoid IV calcium. Source: RCH CPG: Williams Syndrome; Australian Genetic Heart Disease Registry.

options.text: Noonan syndrome (PTPN11 mutation); request gene panel and ECG for pulmonary valve stenosis
options.rationale: Noonan has distinct features (hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, webbed neck, broad chest with widely spaced nipples) and typically pulmonary VALVE stenosis, not supravalvular AS. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation); request gene panel and echocardiogram for aortic root dilatation
options.rationale: Marfan presents with tall stature, arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, ectopia lentis - rarely in infancy with this presentation. Source: RCH CPG.

explanation.summary: Williams syndrome is a contiguous-gene deletion at 7q11.23. The discriminator constellation is: elfin facies + supravalvular AS (or peripheral pulmonary stenosis) + idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia + characteristic friendly cocktail-party personality + mild ID. Elastin (ELN) deletion explains the vascular phenotype (arterial wall fragility and stenoses). Surveillance includes annual cardiology, calcium monitoring (restrict vitamin D in infancy), school-age neurocognitive assessment, and hearing/vision. Compared with other syndromes that share one or two features, the combination is recognisable from this set.
key_points: Williams = 7q11.23 deletion (includes ELN)
Cardinal cardiac lesion: supravalvular AS - ESM at right upper sternal edge to carotids
Idiopathic hypercalcaemia infancy: restrict vitamin D, avoid IV calcium
Characteristic friendly outgoing personality + mild ID
Diagnosis confirmed by FISH for ELN or microarray
explanation.pearls: Supravalvular AS murmurs are louder over the RIGHT upper sternal edge with carotid transmission (lesion above the valve), unlike valvular AS which is loudest at the LEFT upper sternal edge. This bedside cue points to Williams in an infant with dysmorphism.

subtopic_detail: Williams syndrome constellation recognition + ELN deletion confirmation

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to a regional emergency department in Tamworth (Hunter New England LHD) after ingesting an unknown quantity of an over-the-counter medication that acts as a competitive, lipophilic antagonist at central and peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. There is no nicotinic activity. The agent crosses the blood-brain barrier readily. Onset was approximately 60 minutes ago. The grandparent who called the ambulance is unsure what was taken; the empty blister pack has been brought in but the label is unreadable.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, mumbling speech, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 148, BP 102/64, dry axillae, flushed dry skin, dilated minimally reactive pupils, bowel sounds absent, bladder palpable.
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L, paracetamol level <10 micromol/L, salicylate not detected, ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 88 ms QTc 440 ms.

lead_in: Based purely on the receptor mechanism described, which clinical feature is the single best discriminator from a sympathomimetic toxidrome?

options.text: Dry flushed skin with absent bowel sounds and urinary retention
options.rationale: Muscarinic antagonism blocks parasympathetic outflow to exocrine glands (anhidrosis with cutaneous vasodilation for heat loss producing flushing), gut smooth muscle (ileus), and detrusor (retention). Sympathomimetic toxidromes produce diaphoresis and active bowel sounds because cholinergic sweat innervation and gut activity are preserved.

options.text: Tachycardia with hypertension and mydriasis
options.rationale: Tachycardia and mydriasis occur in both toxidromes; hypertension is more sympathomimetic but is not discriminatory in early anticholinergic toxicity. Would be wrong (Source: eTG).

options.text: Hyperthermia with agitated delirium
options.rationale: Both toxidromes can produce hyperthermia and agitation; this is non-discriminating. Would be wrong (Source: Murray's Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Pinpoint pupils with bradycardia and bronchorrhoea
options.rationale: This is the cholinergic (muscarinic agonist) toxidrome, the opposite of what is described. Would be wrong (Source: eTG).

options.text: Hypotension with miosis and hyporeflexia
options.rationale: Describes opioid or sedative-hypnotic toxidrome, not a muscarinic mechanism. Would be wrong (Source: NSW PIC).

explanation.summary: Pure muscarinic antagonism produces a syndrome that copies sympathomimetic toxicity in vital signs and pupils but separates on exocrine and smooth muscle function. Sweat glands are anatomically sympathetic but pharmacologically cholinergic (muscarinic) so antimuscarinic toxicity produces anhidrosis with reflex flushing rather than diaphoresis. Gut and bladder are tonically parasympathetic so blockade produces ileus and retention rather than hyperactive bowel sounds. These four features are the bedside discriminator.
key_points: Anticholinergic = hot, dry, flushed, blind, mad, full bladder, gut stops
Sympathomimetic = hot, WET, agitated, normal bowel sounds
Sweat innervation is sympathetic anatomy but muscarinic pharmacology
QRS widening suggests sodium-channel blockade overlap (TCA, diphenhydramine)
Call NSW PIC 13 11 26 for paediatric ingestion advice
explanation.pearls: Common culprits in children: diphenhydramine, atropine eye drops, hyoscine patches, Datura/Brugmansia ingestion in older kids. Physostigmine (centrally acting AChE inhibitor) is reserved for severe agitated delirium; not first line in Australia.

subtopic_detail: Anticholinergic vs sympathomimetic toxidrome discrimination by mechanism

stem: A 12-month-old infant weighing 9.4 kg is brought to John Hunter Hospital paediatric ED 90 minutes after the parent inadvertently gave the child five doses of paracetamol 250 mg/5 mL suspension instead of paracetamol 120 mg/5 mL suspension, at the prescribed paediatric volume of 6 mL per dose, over the past 16 hours (one dose every 4 hours; the 5th dose was 90 minutes ago). The child is alert, well, afebrile, drinking, and has no abdominal pain or vomiting. No other agent was co-ingested. Pre-existing health is unremarkable. The parent has brought the bottle and the dosing syringe.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 28, BP 92/58, T 36.9 deg C, SpO2 99% room air.
data_table.Examination: Alert, hydrated, abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - clinician calculating total ingested dose to determine NAC eligibility.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management based on the calculated cumulative dose?

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting; cumulative dose below the staggered-ingestion treatment threshold
options.rationale: The calculation: 5 doses x 6 mL x 250 mg/5 mL = 5 x 300 mg = 1500 mg total over 16 hours = 1500 / 9.4 = 159.6 mg/kg. The Australian Poisons Information Centre threshold for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion in children is >150 mg/kg in any 24-hour period (or >100 mg/kg/day for >2 days). This child is above threshold; discharge is wrong. Source: Murray's Toxicology Handbook; NSW PIC.

options.text: Commence IV N-acetylcysteine using the 21-hour Prescott regimen and check paracetamol concentration and ALT now
options.rationale: Cumulative dose is 159.6 mg/kg in <24 hours (5 x 6 mL x 50 mg/mL = 1500 mg; 1500/9.4 = 159.6 mg/kg). This exceeds the 150 mg/kg/24h repeated supratherapeutic threshold. The nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion; treatment decision is based on dose plus ALT/paracetamol level. NAC is started empirically while bloods are awaited. The 21-hour Prescott regimen (150-50-100 mg/kg) is current Australian standard. Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre; Murray's Toxicology Handbook; eTG Toxicology.

options.text: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 4 hours post the most recent dose to decide NAC
options.rationale: The nomogram is invalid in staggered or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion - it was derived for single acute ingestions only. Source: NSW PIC.

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally to limit further absorption
options.rationale: Charcoal is useful only within 1-2 hours of an acute single ingestion, not for staggered ingestion of a now-mostly-absorbed dose. Source: eTG Toxicology.

options.text: Repeat paracetamol level at 24 hours post the most recent dose and decide on NAC then
options.rationale: Delaying NAC past 8 hours from ingestion significantly increases hepatotoxicity risk. Empirical NAC should start now and be discontinued only if labs clearly fall below treatment threshold. Source: NSW PIC.

explanation.summary: The discriminator is the unit-conversion trap: the family used a 250 mg/5 mL strength instead of 120 mg/5 mL, giving each 6 mL dose 300 mg of paracetamol rather than the intended 144 mg. Five doses over 16 hours = 1500 mg = 159.6 mg/kg in a 9.4 kg child. Australian staggered-ingestion threshold is 150 mg/kg/24h - this child is above. The Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to single acute ingestions; for staggered ingestion, decision is based on cumulative dose, ALT, and paracetamol level interpreted in clinical context.
key_points: Staggered paracetamol ingestion: nomogram does NOT apply
AU threshold for treatment in children: >150 mg/kg/24h or >100 mg/kg/day for >2 days
Paracetamol suspension strengths in AU: 120 mg/5 mL (infant) and 250 mg/5 mL (older child) - common dispensing error
Empirical NAC then de-escalate based on bloods is the safe pathway
Australian Prescott 21-hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
explanation.pearls: Always confirm the strength of liquid paediatric paracetamol with the parent and look at the bottle. Two-strength availability in Australia is a recurring source of accidental supratherapeutic ingestion.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy presents to a Tamworth paediatric ED with 24 hours of mild central chest discomfort, no syncope, no palpitations, no exertional symptoms. Exam normal, no pericardial rub, no murmur. ECG sinus rhythm, no ST changes, no PR depression. Troponin I 87 ng/L (upper limit of normal 14). He received his second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 booster 48 hours ago.

He has no past cardiac history, no family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death, no recent viral illness, no drug use, no stimulant medications. Echocardiogram requested.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 78, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air.
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds normal, no rub, no murmur, no peripheral oedema, chest non-tender.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus normal axis, no ischaemia or pericarditis. Troponin I 87 ng/L (ULN 14). CRP 12. FBC normal. Echocardiogram pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting; troponin rise is fully explained by recent vaccination and requires no investigation
options.rationale: While post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis is the leading differential, any troponin rise warrants echocardiography and cardiology review before discharge to exclude reduced LVEF or wall-motion abnormality. Source: NSW Health post-vaccine myocarditis guidance.

options.text: Admit for telemetry, complete echocardiography, repeat troponin at 6 hours, paediatric cardiology review, and recognise post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis as the most likely cause
options.rationale: Post-mRNA vaccine myocarditis is the most likely cause (young male, 1-5 days post second/booster dose, chest pain with troponin rise, normal pre-vaccine cardiac state). Confound elimination: ECG and FH excluded primary cardiomyopathy and ischaemic causes. Standard pathway is admission with telemetry, echo, repeat troponin, paediatric cardiology review. Course is usually self-limiting with NSAIDs or low-dose colchicine but ATAGI/NSW Health pathway is mandatory. Source: NSW Health Post-Vaccine Myocarditis Pathway; ATAGI Clinical Recommendations.

options.text: Commence empirical aspirin 300 mg orally and admit as suspected acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: ACS in a 16-year-old with no risk factors and a normal ECG is highly unlikely; aspirin loading is inappropriate. Source: eTG Cardiovascular.

options.text: Order CT coronary angiogram before any other intervention
options.rationale: CTCA is not first-line in adolescent myocarditis workup; echocardiography is. Cardiac MRI is the gold standard for post-vaccine myocarditis confirmation but is not the immediate next step in ED. Source: NSW Health Pathway.

options.text: Reassure and arrange outpatient stress test in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient deferral fails to exclude active myocarditis in the acute window when echocardiographic findings (segmental wall-motion abnormality, mild LVEF reduction) determine inpatient versus outpatient management. Source: NSW Health Pathway.

explanation.summary: The discriminator is recognising the confound: recent mRNA vaccine (24-72 h after second/booster dose, predominantly adolescent and young adult males) is the dominant cause of acute myopericarditis in this demographic since 2021. The reasoning trap is treating it as ACS or dismissing the troponin altogether. Standard Australian pathway is admit + telemetry + echo + repeat troponin + cardiology consult; cardiac MRI in 4-12 weeks confirms diagnosis. ATAGI maintains COVID-19 vaccine recommendations because benefit exceeds risk even when myocarditis is counted.
key_points: Post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis: 1-5 days post 2nd/booster, peaks day 2-3
Male adolescents and young adults at highest relative risk
Always exclude reduced LVEF before outpatient management
Cardiac MRI at 4-12 weeks confirms scar/oedema pattern
ATAGI recommends a temporary 6-12 month pause on further mRNA doses in confirmed cases
explanation.pearls: Differentiating cause-and-effect from confound is a recurring exam skill: post-transfusion bilirubin rise, post-vaccine serology positives, post-surgery troponin rise, post-statin CK rise. Always state the alternative diagnoses you excluded.

subtopic_detail: Post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis vs alternative myocardial injury

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to Maitland Hospital paediatric ED with 5 days of bloody diarrhoea, 24 hours of pallor, and 12 hours of reduced urine output. Her family returned 9 days ago from a 3-week farm-stay holiday on the NSW mid-north coast where the children regularly fed unpasteurised milk to orphan calves. Initial GP-ordered stool PCR is pending.

Today she appears pale, irritable, with abdominal tenderness but no peritonism. She has had no antibiotic exposure for this illness. There is no rash, no jaundice, no recent vaccinations, no medication exposure. Family history is unremarkable for renal or haematological disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4, HR 138, BP 105/72 (above the 95th centile for age), RR 26, SpO2 98%, weight 16 kg, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/h over 12 h.
data_table.Examination: Pallor, mild scleral icterus, generalised abdominal tenderness, no peritonism, no organomegaly, no rash, no peripheral oedema (yet).
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, WCC 14, blood film: schistocytes ++ and helmet cells. Reticulocytes elevated. Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline unknown, eGFR markedly reduced for age). LDH 1840 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, INR/aPTT normal, Coombs negative. Bilirubin 38 micromol/L (mostly unconjugated). Stool PCR pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis, and which clinical action is contraindicated?

options.text: Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura; commence prednisolone 2 mg/kg orally
options.rationale: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia, not the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + AKI triad described. Schistocytes on film exclude ITP. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: STEC-associated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (D+HUS); supportive management and avoid empirical antibiotics
options.rationale: Pattern: bloody diarrhoea + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, low haptoglobin, raised LDH, raised unconjugated bilirubin, Coombs negative) + thrombocytopaenia + AKI = classic STEC-HUS. Non-obvious cue is unpasteurised milk + calf contact at a farm-stay (STEC O157 reservoirs include cattle and unpasteurised dairy in Australia; multiple outbreaks). CONTRAINDICATED: empirical antibiotics (associated with increased Shiga toxin release and worsened HUS in some studies), antimotility agents, NSAIDs, platelet transfusion (paradoxical worsening). Management is supportive (careful IV fluids, monitoring for dialysis indication, blood transfusion if Hb critically low, plasma exchange in atypical HUS only). Eculizumab for atypical HUS, not STEC-HUS. Source: RCH CPG: HUS; eTG Paediatrics; CDNA STEC SoNG.

options.text: Acute leukaemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation; commence empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Coagulation profile is normal (INR/aPTT normal), excluding DIC. WCC is mildly elevated but no blast cells. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis post-infectious; commence furosemide and start ACE inhibitor
options.rationale: Post-infectious GN typically presents with hypertension, oedema, haematuria, mild proteinuria - not the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia pattern. ACE inhibitor in AKI worsens renal function. Source: RCH CPG.

options.text: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; commence prednisolone 2 mg/kg and IVIG
options.rationale: Coombs is NEGATIVE - rules out warm or cold AIHA. Pattern is microangiopathic (schistocytes, MAHA), not autoimmune. Source: RCH CPG.

explanation.summary: STEC-HUS (formerly D+HUS) is the dominant paediatric cause of acute kidney injury in Australia in children under 5. Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, AKI - usually 5-10 days after a prodrome of bloody diarrhoea. Mechanism: Shiga toxin from E. coli O157 (and other STEC strains) binds Gb3 glycosphingolipid on glomerular endothelium → endothelial swelling → microthrombi → mechanical RBC shear and platelet consumption. Antibiotics are contraindicated because Shiga toxin release is upregulated by bacterial stress response (multiple RCT-level signals of harm). Supportive care, blood transfusion when needed, dialysis if oligoanuric or hyperkalaemic. Notifiable to NSW Health public health unit.
key_points: Triad: MAHA + thrombocytopaenia + AKI after bloody diarrhoea prodrome
STEC sources: unpasteurised dairy, ground beef, petting farms, contaminated water
Antibiotics CONTRAINDICATED in suspected STEC-HUS
NSAIDs, antimotility agents, platelet transfusion all contraindicated
Notifiable disease - inform NSW Health public health unit
explanation.pearls: Atypical HUS (complement-mediated) presents without diarrhoea prodrome and is treated with eculizumab; STEC-HUS is supportive only. Always ask about farm visits, raw milk, and recent ground-beef consumption in paediatric AKI workup.

stem:
A 3-year-old boy weighing 14 kg is triaged at John Hunter Hospital paediatric ED at 0220 with 18 hours of fever, lethargy and decreased oral intake. Parents describe a non-blanching rash that developed in the last hour on both legs. He has not been immunised. Initial assessment: T 39.4, HR 178, RR 44, capillary refill 4 seconds peripherally and 3 seconds centrally, mottled extremities, BP 88/52, SpO2 96% room air.

He is drowsy but rousable, no neck stiffness on initial exam but obtunded enough to limit reliable testing. Blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L. The triage nurse is initiating the NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 178, RR 44, BP 88/52, SpO2 96% RA, CRT 4 sec peripheral, weight 14 kg.
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable, mottled extremities, non-blanching petechial rash both legs, dry mucous membranes, no obvious focus.
data_table.Investigations: Initial venous gas pending; bedside lactate 4.8 mmol/L; FBC, UEC, CRP, blood cultures, meningococcal PCR all sent.

lead_in: Within the NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway, what is the most appropriate fluid resuscitation and antibiotic decision for the first hour?

options.text: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes and reassess; defer antibiotics until lumbar puncture and CT brain are completed
options.rationale: Antibiotics must be given within the first hour of sepsis recognition and lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: 10-20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 5-10 minutes, reassess after each bolus to a usual maximum of 40-60 mL/kg, plus ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IV within 60 minutes
options.rationale: The current Australian paediatric sepsis approach uses 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each, given concerns from FEAST and subsequent NSW Health updates. Suspected meningococcaemia requires the meningitis-dose of ceftriaxone, which the Australian Medicines Handbook lists as 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) per dose. Inotropes (peripheral adrenaline 0.05-0.3 mcg/kg/min) are added after approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid without response. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway; AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: 40 mL/kg of 4% albumin as a single rapid push to address capillary leak, plus intravenous vancomycin and meropenem within 60 minutes
options.rationale: Isotonic crystalloid (not colloid) is first-line in paediatric sepsis, given as 10-20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment after each. Vancomycin plus meropenem is not first-line for community-acquired sepsis without specific resistance risk. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: Defer fluid resuscitation and commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.5 mcg/kg/min immediately as primary therapy before any crystalloid bolus
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation precedes inotropes in compensated paediatric septic shock; inotropes are added after approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid without response. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 60 minutes plus benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg intravenously, with immediate lumbar puncture during the bolus
options.rationale: Bolus over 60 minutes is too slow for resuscitation (target 5-10 minutes); lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until stability is restored. Benzylpenicillin alone is too narrow for empirical paediatric septic shock. (Source: NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway; eTG Paediatrics)

explanation.summary: The discriminator is recall of the current Australian paediatric sepsis pathway cut-offs: bolus volume 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid over 5-10 minutes with reassessment after each, antibiotic within 60 minutes, approximately 40 mL/kg of fluid before considering inotropes. For suspected meningococcaemia (non-blanching petechial rash, fever, unimmunised, shock features), the Australian Medicines Handbook ceftriaxone dose is 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) to ensure meningeal penetration; the 50 mg/kg dose is for non-meningitic sepsis. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. Public health notification within 24 hours for meningococcal disease.
key_points: Bolus 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid over 5-10 minutes, reassess after each
Approximately 40 mL/kg before escalating to inotropes
Antibiotic within 60 minutes of sepsis recognition
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) for suspected meningococcaemia or meningitis per AMH
Lactate above 4 plus tachycardia plus mottled extremities meets severe sepsis criteria
explanation.pearls: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock until cardiovascular stability is restored. Empirical antibiotics first; lumbar puncture later. Notify the public health unit for confirmed or suspected meningococcal disease.

subtopic_detail: NSW Health paediatric sepsis pathway cut-offs

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a previously well 2-year-old boy brought in at 0200 with 6 hours of barking cough and stridor. He has audible biphasic stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, pink mucosa, and is alert and interactive. He has been taking sips of water without difficulty. No drooling, no foreign-body history.

data_table.Examination: Audible biphasic stridor at rest; mild intercostal recession; chest otherwise clear; calm, no exhaustion
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed; clinical assessment only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose; observe until stridor at rest settles and oral intake adequate (typically 1-2 hours)
options.rationale: Mild-to-moderate croup (intermittent stridor at rest, mild recession, alert, well perfused) is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup. Observation is tied to clinical improvement, not a fixed clock; peak dexamethasone effect is 1-2 hours. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg; admit to short stay for 3 hours after the dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline plus 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup with marked recession, agitation, exhaustion, or hypoxia; using it for mild-to-moderate disease overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intubation in theatre by ENT and anaesthetics with transfer to the paediatric intensive care unit for ongoing respiratory support
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending respiratory failure with exhaustion, cyanosis, or altered consciousness, none of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg and ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg with admission for paediatric sepsis workup including blood cultures
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis would feature toxicity, drooling, and rapid progression; classic mild-to-moderate viral croup does not require antibiotics or sepsis workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms; reassess respiratory work and stridor at rest 20 minutes later in resus
options.rationale: Bronchodilators have no role in upper-airway obstruction from croup; they neither relieve stridor nor address subglottic oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by stridor (none, on exertion, at rest), work of breathing, mental state, and oxygenation. Mild-to-moderate croup features stridor at rest with mild recession but no agitation, pallor, or hypoxia. RCH gives a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild-to-moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening disease. Nebulised adrenaline (flat 5 mL of 1:1000) is added for severe disease, with a minimum 3-hour observation after the adrenaline because effects last 30 to 60 minutes. Observation after dexamethasone alone is tied to clinical resolution rather than a fixed clock.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild-to-moderate croup per RCH
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup
Observation after dexamethasone alone is to clinical resolution, not a fixed 4 hours
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose for severe disease, with 3-hour post-adrenaline observation
Antibiotics and bronchodilators have no role in viral croup
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone onset is 30 to 60 minutes and effect lasts 24 to 48 hours; oral, intramuscular, and nebulised routes are equivalent in efficacy.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis admission criteria and feeding support
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 6-week-old term infant in winter with 3 days of coryza and increasing work of breathing. Mum reports feeds have dropped from 100 to 40 mL every 3 hours over the last 24 hours, and the baby is becoming sweaty during feeds. There is no apnoea history. Older sibling has a viral URTI.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 91% RA (rises to 95% on 0.5 L/min nasal prong), BP 78/46
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession; tracheal tug; bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and wheeze; capillary refill 2 s; mucous membranes slightly dry
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; no bloods or chest x-ray; weight 4.6 kg (50th centile)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose; review at 1 hour
options.rationale: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids have no proven benefit in classic viral bronchiolitis under 12 months and are not recommended; supportive feeding and oxygen are the mainstays. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit; commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen to maintain SpO2 90% (RCH target); nasogastric feeds at two thirds maintenance
options.rationale: Sustained SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), feeding less than half normal volume, and increased work of breathing meet admission criteria; nasogastric or intravenous hydration plus titrated oxygen is the supportive standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with safety-net advice; review by general practitioner in 24 hours and red-flag information for parents
options.rationale: Hypoxia at rest below 92 percent, tachypnoea above 60 and reduced oral intake all argue against discharge; safety-net advice does not substitute for inpatient support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min from arrival; nil by mouth and intravenous maintenance fluids
options.rationale: High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen or persistent severe distress; routine first-line use does not change outcomes and overtreats. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg and gentamicin 7 mg/kg; chest x-ray and full septic workup including lumbar puncture
options.rationale: RSV-positive bronchiolitis with no toxic features does not require sepsis workup or empirical antibiotics; secondary bacterial pneumonia would warrant focal findings and rising inflammatory markers. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is supportive care only. Admission criteria are SpO2 persistently below 90% (RCH target), feeds less than half normal volume, severe work of breathing, apnoea or social risk. Nasogastric tube feeds at two thirds maintenance are preferred over IV fluids when tolerated. High-flow nasal cannula is a rescue therapy when low-flow oxygen and feeding support fail to maintain saturations or normalise work of breathing.
key_points: Bronchiolitis is supportive: oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), feeding support if intake under half
Bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics not routinely indicated
Nasogastric feeds at two thirds maintenance preferred to IV fluids
High-flow nasal cannula is rescue therapy, not first line
explanation.pearls: Apnoea risk is highest in infants under 6 weeks corrected age or with prematurity; admit for observation regardless of work of breathing.

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice phototherapy threshold and DAT
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term breastfed boy on the postnatal ward. The midwife noted increasing yellowing of the face and chest. The infant is feeding 8 times in 24 hours, settled, with normal stool and urine. Birth weight 3.6 kg, now 3.42 kg. Maternal blood group O Rhesus positive. Antenatal antibody screen was negative. The infant's serum bilirubin has just returned.

data_table.Examination: Mild jaundice to upper chest; no hepatosplenomegaly; tone normal; reflexes intact; well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 290 micromol/L total, conjugated 8; DAT positive; FBC Hb 198 g/L, reticulocytes 6%; blood group A Rh+

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and recheck serum bilirubin in 24 hours; advise increased feed frequency in the interim
options.rationale: DAT-positive ABO incompatibility with bilirubin 290 micromol/L at 60 hours crosses standard phototherapy thresholds; deferring 24 hours risks reaching exchange transfusion levels. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

options.text: Withhold breastfeeding and substitute formula for 24 hours; recheck serum bilirubin at the end of the formula trial
options.rationale: Withholding breastfeeding is not first line; haemolytic jaundice requires phototherapy not formula substitution, and breastfeeding should be supported throughout. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy and recheck serum bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours; ensure hydration with continued breastfeeding
options.rationale: Bilirubin 290 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with DAT-positive haemolysis crosses the RCH phototherapy threshold for a term infant; intensive phototherapy is initiated and bilirubin rechecked at 4 to 6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

options.text: Arrange immediate double-volume exchange transfusion; transfer to neonatal intensive care for line insertion
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion thresholds at 60 hours are above 450 micromol/L for a term low-risk neonate; intensive phototherapy is tried first and reassessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours; defer phototherapy pending response to immunoglobulin
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved as adjunct for haemolytic disease when bilirubin is rising despite intensive phototherapy or approaches exchange threshold; it does not replace initial phototherapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Jaundice in neonates)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice thresholds depend on postnatal age in hours, gestation and risk factors such as haemolysis or sepsis. DAT-positive ABO incompatibility places the infant in the high-risk category. RCH guidance uses age-in-hours nomograms; for a term infant at 60 hours, total bilirubin around 290 micromol/L crosses the phototherapy threshold. Intensive phototherapy is started and bilirubin is rechecked at 4 to 6 hours. IVIG is reserved for impending exchange.
key_points: Phototherapy thresholds depend on age in hours, gestation and risk factors
DAT-positive haemolysis lowers the threshold for treatment
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy
IVIG is adjunct, not first line
explanation.pearls: Exchange transfusion threshold at 60 hours in a term infant without high risk factors is above 450 micromol/L; bilirubin doubling above this needs urgent NICU transfer.

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 5-week-old term infant brought in by his parents with a documented temperature of 38.4 at home and irritability over 6 hours. He is alert in the cot, feeding well, with no respiratory or skin findings. His parents recall a recent viral illness in an older sibling. He has no risk factors for invasive group B Streptococcus and was discharged well at day 3.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.5, HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 98% RA, BP 78/44; capillary glucose 4.6
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused; anterior fontanelle soft; clear chest; soft abdomen; no rash; no focal source
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.2 (neutrophils 9.2), Hb 132, plt 320; CRP 32; urine collected by SPA pending; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally as required and general practitioner review in 24 hours; safety-net advice
options.rationale: Infants under 3 months with temperature 38 or above require admission and full septic workup regardless of clinical appearance; outpatient management is not standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Admit; observe without antibiotics or lumbar puncture pending 24-hour blood and urine culture results
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are mandatory in febrile infants under 3 months pending culture results, regardless of clinical wellness, because of bacteraemia and meningitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Admit; commence intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg; defer lumbar puncture pending repeat clinical assessment in 6 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover Listeria or Escherichia coli, the dominant causes in this age group; broader empirical cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit; perform lumbar puncture, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg, gentamicin 5 mg/kg and cefotaxime 50 mg/kg
options.rationale: Febrile infant 1 to 3 months requires full septic workup including lumbar puncture and immediate empirical cover for invasive bacterial infection including Listeria, group B Streptococcus and gram negatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform urine dipstick on bag urine only; commence oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily and discharge home with review
options.rationale: Bag-collected urine is unreliable for diagnosis under 12 months due to contamination; oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected invasive sepsis in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 3 months have a higher risk of occult invasive bacterial infection including meningitis even when clinically well-appearing. Standard Australian practice is to admit, obtain blood, urine (suprapubic aspirate or catheter) and CSF cultures, and start empirical antibiotics covering Listeria monocytogenes (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin), group B Streptococcus and gram-negative organisms (gentamicin plus a third-generation cephalosporin). De-escalation occurs at 36 to 48 hours based on cultures and clinical course.
key_points: Febrile infants under 3 months: full septic workup including LP
Empirical antibiotics cover Listeria, GBS and gram-negatives
Bag urine is unreliable below 12 months
De-escalate at 36 to 48 hours based on cultures
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime is preferred over ceftriaxone in neonates under 28 days due to risk of bilirubin displacement and biliary sludge; switch to ceftriaxone after 28 days.

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl with a 2-week history of polyuria and weight loss. Today she developed vomiting and is now drowsy but rousable, breathing deeply. She has no fever or sick contacts. The team weighs her at 26 kg. The first venous gas and ketones are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 142, RR 32 deep, BP 96/62, SpO2 99% RA, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul respiration; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 s; reduced skin turgor; clear chest; soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.10, bicarbonate 8, BSL 28, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8, Na 138 (corrected 142), K 4.2, urea 8.4, Cr 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin strategy in the first hour?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes as bolus; start IV insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately with the bolus
options.rationale: Insulin is started 1 hour after fluid resuscitation in paediatric DKA to reduce cerebral oedema risk; rapid concurrent infusion increases osmolar shift. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 1 hour; commence subcutaneous insulin glargine 0.3 unit/kg immediately for maintenance cover
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid for resuscitation increases cerebral oedema risk; long-acting subcutaneous insulin during active DKA is not first line and bypasses titration. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct acidosis; defer insulin until pH above 7.20
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in routine paediatric DKA: it is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk and worsens intracellular acidosis. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes as resuscitation bolus regardless of perfusion; reassess after 30 minutes only
options.rationale: Large rapid boluses without re-assessment are associated with cerebral oedema; standard is 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes only if shocked, with frequent re-assessment. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes for perfusion; start IV insulin 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour of fluid
options.rationale: Cautious 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline addresses perfusion, then ongoing deficit replacement is calculated and given over 48 hours; insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid resuscitation. (Source: ISPAD/APEG DKA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis with minimisation of cerebral oedema risk. Initial fluid resuscitation is conservative: 10 mL/kg of isotonic saline over 30 to 60 minutes only if signs of shock, with reassessment. Deficit replacement is calculated as 5 to 10 percent of body weight and given evenly over 48 hours. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid commencement. Bicarbonate is avoided. Potassium is added to maintenance fluid once urine output is established.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg isotonic saline only if shocked
Deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour starts 1 hour after fluid
Bicarbonate contraindicated in routine DKA
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema warning signs include headache, declining GCS, bradycardia and pupillary changes; treat with 2.7% saline 5 mL/kg or mannitol 1 g/kg over 15 minutes.

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar managing a 9-year-old girl with known asthma now in resus. She received three 12-puff burst-doses of salbutamol with spacer plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 60 minutes ago. She remains in marked respiratory distress, with subcostal recession and accessory muscle use, only managing single-word sentences. She has had no recent viral illness; her last hospitalisation was 8 months ago. There is no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 152, RR 38, SpO2 89% on 6 L/min mask, BP 108/68
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal recession; accessory muscle use; minimal air entry; widespread expiratory wheeze; alert
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.34, pCO2 38, lactate 2.4; capillary glucose 6.8; no CXR yet
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 12 puff x3 in 1 hour; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg; ipratropium 250 mcg x3

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes; continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol
options.rationale: After first-hour burst-dose salbutamol, ipratropium and systemic steroid have failed, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is the next step in severe paediatric asthma before further escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 1 hour; start maintenance aminophylline infusion immediately afterwards
options.rationale: Aminophylline is reserved for failure of magnesium and is used in ICU due to narrow therapeutic window; it is not the next step in standard escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) of 1 in 1000; repeat at 15-minute intervals as required
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline is used for anaphylaxis, not pure asthma exacerbations; routine use risks tachyarrhythmia without addressing bronchospasm better than nebulised beta-agonist. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg/kg and rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg; transfer to paediatric intensive care
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for exhaustion, hypercapnia or imminent arrest in severe asthma; the patient is still alert with normocapnia and IV magnesium has not been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: High-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min in 100% oxygen alone; cease bronchodilators and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Ceasing bronchodilators during active severe asthma is unsafe; high-flow nasal cannula is adjunctive support, not a substitute for pharmacological escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Severe paediatric asthma escalation follows a stepped pathway: oxygen, burst-dose salbutamol with ipratropium and oral or IV steroid in the first hour. If severity persists, IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is the standard next step. Aminophylline and IV salbutamol are reserved for ICU-level escalation. Intubation is for exhaustion, hypercapnia or arrest; ketamine RSI minimises bronchoconstriction.
key_points: First hour: oxygen, burst salbutamol/ipratropium, systemic steroid
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg is the standard second step
Aminophylline and IV salbutamol are ICU escalation
Intubation for exhaustion, rising pCO2 or arrest
explanation.pearls: A normal or rising pCO2 in severe asthma is a sign of failing respiratory effort and impending arrest; do not be reassured by a 'normal' venous gas.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease with coronary involvement
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-month-old boy with 7 days of fever to 39.5. He has mild conjunctival injection, one cracked lip, and a faint trunk rash. He has no cervical adenopathy and no peripheral changes. He is irritable but feeding. Blood tests and an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram are now available. The Kawasaki classic criteria are not all met.

data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis; cracked lower lip; faint truncal exanthem; no adenopathy; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 (neutrophils 14), Hb 96, platelets 580, CRP 165, ESR 78, albumin 28, ALT 92, Na 132; urine WCC raised; echo shows LAD Z score 3.1 with mild dilatation
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg PRN; ibuprofen ceased 2 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone for occult bacterial infection; defer further immune therapy pending blood cultures
options.rationale: Coronary involvement on echocardiography with fever 5 days or more and supportive laboratory criteria confirms incomplete Kawasaki; delaying immunoglobulin while awaiting cultures risks aneurysm progression. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus oral aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in 4 divided doses
options.rationale: Coronary artery Z score above 2.5 plus fever 5 days or more with supportive labs (CRP raised, albumin low, ALT raised, platelets high, sterile pyuria) meets American Heart Association incomplete Kawasaki criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin is first-line. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily alone; outpatient cardiology follow up in 2 weeks for repeat echocardiogram
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first line; the Kobayashi protocol adds steroid to IVIG in high-risk patients but does not replace it. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

options.text: Intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg single dose; cardiology review in 24 hours with repeat coronary artery measurement
options.rationale: Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-refractory Kawasaki disease; it is not first-line for newly diagnosed cases with coronary involvement. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

options.text: Oral aspirin 5 mg/kg daily alone as antiplatelet cover; repeat echocardiogram in 6 weeks to monitor coronary calibre
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin alone without IVIG fails to reduce coronary aneurysm risk; the 25 percent untreated aneurysm rate drops to under 5 percent with IVIG plus aspirin. (Source: AHA Kawasaki Scientific Statement)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when fever 5 days or more occurs with fewer than 4 classic features but coronary artery abnormality on echocardiography (Z score 2.5 or above) OR 3 or more supportive lab criteria. Supportive labs include CRP 30 or above, ESR 40 or above, anaemia for age, platelets 450 x10^9/L or above after day 7, albumin 30 g/L or below, ALT raised, and sterile pyuria. First-line treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in divided doses until afebrile for 48 hours, then low-dose aspirin. Steroids are added in Kobayashi-positive high-risk cases.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: 5 days fever + coronary echo OR 3 supportive labs
First-line: IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin
Steroids adjunctive in Kobayashi-positive cases
Infliximab reserved for IVIG-refractory disease
explanation.pearls: Untreated coronary aneurysm rate is 25 percent; IVIG within 10 days of fever onset reduces this to under 5 percent.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy with asthma at his routine 3-monthly clinic visit. He currently uses inhaled budesonide 100 micrograms twice daily with spacer and salbutamol as required. Over the past 3 months he has needed his salbutamol 3 to 4 times a week, woken at night with cough twice, and missed 2 days of school for an exacerbation managed by oral prednisolone. His inhaler technique is excellent on demonstration. There is no environmental trigger he can identify and no smoke exposure at home.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear today; no wheeze; growth on 50th centile; no eczema flare
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry FEV1 78% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.78, bronchodilator response +14%
data_table.Medications: Budesonide 100 mcg BD with spacer; salbutamol 100 mcg PRN; nil oral

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase inhaled budesonide to 200 micrograms twice daily; reinforce trigger avoidance and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Poor control on low-dose ICS in a child aged 6 to 11 with good technique warrants step-up to medium-dose ICS as the preferred next step before combination therapy. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Add montelukast 5 mg orally each evening; continue current inhaled budesonide and salbutamol
options.rationale: Montelukast is an add-on option but is less effective than increasing inhaled corticosteroid dose or adding a long-acting beta-agonist in this age group. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Switch budesonide to inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol combination 50/25 micrograms twice daily for combined therapy
options.rationale: Combination ICS/LABA is reserved for children aged 6 to 11 only after medium-dose ICS has failed; jumping directly from low-dose ICS to ICS/LABA is not the recommended step. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Cease budesonide and start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days; review at completion of course
options.rationale: Maintenance oral corticosteroids carry growth and adrenal suppression risk and are reserved for severe refractory asthma after specialist review, not for routine step-up. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Continue current regimen and provide written action plan; review only if further exacerbation requires hospital
options.rationale: Three to four reliever uses weekly, nocturnal cough and a recent steroid-requiring exacerbation define poorly controlled asthma; continuing without escalation accepts ongoing morbidity. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: Asthma control in children aged 6 to 11 is assessed over the previous 4 weeks: daytime symptoms more than twice a week, reliever use more than twice a week, any nocturnal waking, or any activity limitation indicates poor control. Step-up from low-dose ICS in this age group is to medium-dose ICS as the preferred option, with montelukast or LABA combinations reserved for failure of medium-dose ICS. Technique, adherence, trigger exposure and alternative diagnoses must be checked at every step.
key_points: Children 6 to 11 step-up: low-dose ICS to medium-dose ICS first
ICS/LABA combination reserved for failure of medium-dose ICS in this age group
Reassess control, technique, adherence and triggers at every step
Document a written action plan at every escalation
explanation.pearls: Budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily is the medium-dose threshold for children 6 to 11; fluticasone propionate equivalent is 200 micrograms twice daily.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose mother is worried that he looks pale and tires easily on outings. He drinks 800 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle since 9 months of age and eats little solid food, refusing meat and vegetables. He was born at term, breastfed for 4 months. He is otherwise well, with no jaundice, splenomegaly or recent infection. His growth has tracked the 25th centile. Bloods returned this morning.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no jaundice; soft abdomen, no organomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78, MCV 62, MCH 19, ferritin 7 microg/L, transferrin saturation 7%, CRP 2, reticulocytes 1.2%

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL/day and start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg elemental iron/kg daily; recheck in 1 month
options.rationale: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a toddler with excess cow's milk intake requires both dietary modification and elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg/kg/day; recheck FBC in 4 to 6 weeks to confirm response. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer to paediatric haematology for bone marrow examination; defer iron therapy pending specialist review
options.rationale: Classic microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and risk factors for iron deficiency does not require bone marrow examination; empirical iron with diet change and recheck is first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange same-day intravenous iron polymaltose infusion under sedation; admit for observation overnight
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance or non-adherence to oral iron after a trial; first-line is oral iron with dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells 10 mL/kg over 4 hours; admit for paediatric review and post-transfusion bloods
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise or Hb under 60 to 70 g/L in a sick child; this stable toddler does not meet criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Send haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia trait; defer iron therapy until results return
options.rationale: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is unreliable during iron deficiency and is deferred until iron repletion; ferritin under 12 with low transferrin saturation is diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in toddlers most commonly reflects excess cow's milk intake (which inhibits iron absorption and causes occult GI blood loss) and inadequate iron-rich solids. Workup shows microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin and transferrin saturation. First-line management is dietary advice (cow's milk under 500 mL/day, iron-rich solids including red meat or fortified cereals) plus oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day. Reassess Hb at 4 to 6 weeks; expect a 10 g/L rise.
key_points: Toddler iron deficiency: limit cow's milk to under 500 mL/day
Oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg elemental iron/kg/day first line
Expect 10 g/L Hb rise at 4 weeks of treatment
Defer haemoglobin electrophoresis until iron-replete
explanation.pearls: Continue oral iron for 3 months after Hb normalises to replete stores; ferritin should rise above 30 microg/L.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old infant in ED with 1 week of progressive paroxysmal cough, vomiting after coughing fits, and an apnoeic episode at home today. There is no fever. His 4-year-old sister has had a 3-week persistent cough recently labelled as a viral URTI. The infant has had no vaccinations yet; the family declined antenatal pertussis vaccination. Nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 168, RR 56, SpO2 92% RA (recovers between paroxysms), BP 78/46
data_table.Examination: Paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomit observed; chest otherwise clear
data_table.Investigations: Pertussis PCR positive; WCC 28 (lymphocyte predominant 18); CXR mild perihilar streaking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the infant and household contacts?

options.text: Treat the infant with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and reserve chemoprophylaxis for symptomatic household contacts only
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is contraindicated under 2 months due to kernicterus risk; symptom-based prophylaxis misses the asymptomatic infectious period. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Treat the infant with oral amoxicillin and offer prophylaxis only to household contacts under 6 months of age
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no role in pertussis; macrolides are first-line, and chemoprophylaxis extends to all close household contacts not just infants. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Manage the infant supportively without antibiotics; arrange vaccination of household contacts but no chemoprophylaxis
options.rationale: Antibiotics reduce infectivity even when started late and prevent ongoing transmission; vaccination alone is too slow to protect contacts within the incubation window. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Treat the infant with oral azithromycin and arrange azithromycin chemoprophylaxis for all close household contacts regardless of vaccination status
options.rationale: Azithromycin is first-line for pertussis treatment under 1 month and chemoprophylaxis is offered to all household contacts regardless of vaccination because vaccine effectiveness wanes and infants are at highest mortality risk. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Admit the infant for observation only; commence household antibiotics only if the older sibling tests positive on swab
options.rationale: Treating only the infant misses the household reservoir and waiting for sibling testing delays prophylaxis beyond the effective window of 21 days from index exposure. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months carries the highest mortality, often from apnoea or secondary pneumonia. Diagnosis is by nasopharyngeal PCR. Macrolides (azithromycin preferred under 1 month) reduce infectivity and shorten symptoms if started within 3 weeks of cough onset. Chemoprophylaxis with azithromycin is offered to all close household contacts regardless of vaccination, ideally within 14 to 21 days of first exposure, because waning vaccine immunity allows transmission even in vaccinated family members. Notification to public health is mandatory.
key_points: Pertussis PCR diagnosis; azithromycin first line under 1 month
All household contacts get azithromycin prophylaxis regardless of vaccination
Treatment within 21 days of cough reduces transmission
Notifiable disease; public health unit contact required
explanation.pearls: Azithromycin in neonates carries a small risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; counsel parents about projectile vomiting at 3 to 5 weeks of life.

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy with 12 hours of episodic inconsolable crying, drawing his legs up, and now passing a small amount of dark stool with mucus per rectum. He has had two episodes of bile-stained vomit. Between attacks he appears lethargic but is now pale and clammy. He is well perfused but the abdomen feels fullness in the right upper quadrant. There has been no recent viral illness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 99% RA, BP 92/58, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between paroxysms; soft abdomen with palpable RUQ sausage-shaped mass; PR exam shows blood-stained mucus
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal ultrasound shows target sign at the hepatic flexure; FBC and UEC unremarkable; lactate 1.4

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange same-admission air enema reduction by interventional radiology with paediatric surgical team in attendance
options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception in a stable child without peritonitis or perforation is reduced by air or contrast enema with surgical standby; success rate is around 80 to 95 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole; observe for 6 hours before deciding on intervention
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not reduce intussusception; delaying enema risks bowel ischaemia, perforation and the need for surgical resection. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparotomy and manual reduction with potential resection; no enema attempt
options.rationale: Surgical reduction is reserved for failure of pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction, peritonitis, perforation or shock; first attempt should be radiological in stable children. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting and arrange outpatient ultrasound in 24 hours if symptoms persist or worsen
options.rationale: Untreated intussusception progresses to ischaemia and perforation within hours; discharge of a confirmed case is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and trial of bowel rest for 12 hours; reimage if no improvement
options.rationale: Bowel rest does not reduce intussusception; mechanical reduction by enema is required and delay increases bowel-resection risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception typically presents in infants 3 months to 3 years with episodic crying, drawing up of legs, bile-stained vomiting and red-currant-jelly stool late in the course. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice, showing the target or doughnut sign. Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 95 percent of stable cases without peritonitis or perforation. Surgical management is reserved for failed reduction, signs of perforation, or shock. Recurrence after enema is 10 percent and usually occurs within 48 hours.
key_points: Ultrasound target sign confirms diagnosis
Air or contrast enema is first-line reduction in stable child
Surgery for failed enema, perforation or shock
Recurrence rate 10 percent, mostly within 48 hours
explanation.pearls: A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, Peyer patch hypertrophy, lymphoma) is more likely in children over 2 years or with recurrence and warrants further imaging.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old girl admitted 3 days ago with her first febrile urinary tract infection. The catheter specimen grew Escherichia coli sensitive to her current IV antibiotic. She defervesced within 36 hours and is now feeding well, with normal observations. The bladder ultrasound performed during admission showed mild left renal pelvis dilatation but no hydroureter. The team is preparing her discharge plan and follow up.

data_table.Examination: Well, alert, feeding normally; abdomen soft, no masses
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine: E. coli sensitive; bladder ultrasound: mild left pelvis dilatation, normal right; FBC and CRP normalised; UEC normal
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin and amoxicillin during admission; switching to oral cefalexin for discharge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further imaging plan?

options.text: Magnetic resonance urogram at 3 months to characterise the pelvis and rule out pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction in this child
options.rationale: MR urography is a second-line modality for selected complex anomalies and is not part of the RCH Melbourne post-UTI pathway after a typical first febrile UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Routine micturating cystourethrogram within 2 weeks for every infant after a first febrile UTI regardless of imaging findings shown
options.rationale: RCH Melbourne does not recommend routine MCUG after a first UTI; MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, dilatation on ultrasound, or atypical features. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring; no MCUG unless DMSA is abnormal or recurrent UTI develops
options.rationale: Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; the RCH CPG does not include routine DMSA in the post-UTI imaging cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No further imaging is required after this ultrasound; outpatient paediatric follow-up and parental advice for prompt presentation with any future fever
options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne CPG states that most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI once an acute renal tract ultrasound has excluded obstruction and significant dilatation; mild non-progressive pelvis change alone does not warrant DMSA or MCUG. Parents are counselled to present promptly for any future febrile illness. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Continuous prophylactic trimethoprim 2 mg/kg nocte for 12 months and no further imaging unless she becomes symptomatic again later
options.rationale: Long-term prophylaxis is reserved for proven high-grade reflux or recurrent UTI; first UTI without proven reflux is not an RCH-recommended indication. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne UTI CPG states most children do not require further imaging after a first UTI. A renal tract ultrasound during admission is appropriate for infants under 6 months without antenatal scans, for recurrent UTI, or when atypical features are present. The DMSA-at-4-to-6-months pathway is a NICE NG224 recommendation that RCH has not adopted. MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, ultrasound dilatation, or atypical features.
key_points: RCH Melbourne: no routine imaging after first typical UTI once acute renal tract ultrasound is normal or shows non-progressive minor change
DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE construct, not part of the RCH cascade
MCUG reserved for recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound
Long-term prophylaxis only for proven high-grade reflux or recurrent UTI
explanation.pearls: An atypical UTI per RCH is one with non-E. coli organism, septicaemia, raised creatinine, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, or failure to respond within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics.

stem: You are the GP working in a regional clinic when parents rush in carrying their 18-month-old boy who suddenly began choking on a peanut 2 minutes ago. The toddler is conscious, distressed, and making weak ineffective coughing sounds with audible stridor. He is making poor air entry on auscultation and his lips are starting to look dusky. He cannot vocalise. The nearest hospital with paediatric emergency capability is 25 minutes away by ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 168, RR 50, SpO2 86% on room air, BP not yet checked
data_table.Examination: Conscious, distressed, making feeble coughs with stridor; reduced air entry bilaterally; dusky lips
data_table.Investigations: Clinical assessment; no time for imaging

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Perform 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) immediately and call for senior assistance
options.rationale: Abdominal thrusts are reserved for children over 1 year as a second-line manoeuvre after back blows fail; primary use in a young toddler risks abdominal organ injury. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Encourage the child to keep coughing and call an ambulance; provide oxygen by mask while waiting for transport
options.rationale: Encouragement only applies when the cough is effective and the child can vocalise; an ineffective cough with stridor and desaturation requires immediate airway clearance manoeuvres. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Perform a blind finger sweep of the oropharynx to locate the foreign body before attempting back blows
options.rationale: Blind finger sweeps are contraindicated because they can push the object deeper or cause oedema; only remove if visible and easily graspable. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Give 5 back blows between the scapulae with the child head-down, followed by 5 chest thrusts if obstruction persists
options.rationale: Conscious infant or toddler with ineffective cough and airway obstruction is managed by alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are not used under 1 year due to liver injury risk and are second-line in older children. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Lay the child supine and commence chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute until ambulance arrives
options.rationale: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with compressions is started only after the child loses consciousness from obstruction; in a conscious child, airway-clearance manoeuvres are first. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

explanation.summary: ANZCOR guidance for foreign body airway obstruction depends on age and cough effectiveness. Effective cough (forceful, vocalising, conscious): encourage cough and observe. Ineffective cough (silent, stridor, cyanosis, decreasing consciousness) in conscious patient: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts in infants under 1 year; 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts in children over 1 year, with abdominal thrusts as second-line in older children. Unconscious patient: start CPR with chest compressions and inspect the airway during ventilation. Blind finger sweeps are contraindicated.
key_points: Effective cough: encourage and observe
Ineffective cough conscious: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts
Abdominal thrusts not used under 1 year
Unconscious: commence CPR and inspect airway during ventilation
explanation.pearls: After successful expulsion, all children with peanut or similar high-risk aspiration require bronchoscopy assessment because residual fragments cause delayed pneumonitis.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy whose parents are concerned about ongoing daytime soiling for 8 months. He passes small hard pellets every 3 to 4 days and has multiple episodes of liquid stool leakage into his underwear daily. He was toilet-trained at 3 years. He withholds and crosses his legs. His diet is poor in fibre. There is no blood, abdominal pain, weight loss or red-flag history. Abdominal examination is consistent with faecal loading.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa and suprapubic region; perianal skin normal; no anal fissure; gait and lower limb neurology normal
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no imaging indicated; growth on 50th centile
