lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Commence twice daily oral docusate 12.5 mg without disimpaction and review fibre intake over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Docusate alone is insufficient and skipping disimpaction means overflow soiling continues; without clearing the impacted mass, laxative titration fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (PEG 3350) over 3 to 7 days, followed by daily maintenance dosing and behavioural toilet program
options.rationale: Functional constipation with overflow soiling requires disimpaction first (high-dose macrogol over 3 to 7 days) followed by maintenance laxative plus a toilet-sitting program; treating the maintenance phase without disimpaction prolongs soiling. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer for anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease before any laxative intervention
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium passage and failure to thrive; a toilet-trained 6-year-old with classic functional pattern does not require biopsy as a first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Recommend daily phosphate enemas for 14 days as primary therapy and review symptoms at the end of the course
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas carry risks of hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia in children and are not first-line; oral macrogol is safer and equally effective for disimpaction. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric psychology for behavioural management of encopresis without medication for the first 3 months
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy alone fails when an impacted rectal mass causes ongoing overflow; pharmacological disimpaction and maintenance are needed together with the behavioural program. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with overflow soiling requires a two-phase approach: disimpaction followed by maintenance. Disimpaction uses high-dose oral macrogol (1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 to 7 days) until clear stools; maintenance uses lower-dose daily macrogol titrated to one soft stool daily. A behavioural toilet-sitting program (after meals for 5 to 10 minutes) and dietary advice (fibre, fluids) accompany medication. Red flags warranting further workup include delayed meconium passage, failure to thrive, abdominal distension, abnormal neurological findings or sacral dimple.
key_points: Disimpaction before maintenance to stop overflow
Macrogol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for disimpaction, lower dose for maintenance
Behavioural toilet program after meals essential
Maintenance for at least 6 months and weaned slowly
explanation.pearls: Maintenance laxatives are often required for many months; relapse rates exceed 50 percent if weaned within 6 months of symptom resolution.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-month-old boy at his routine health check. His parents report he has only 5 single words and does not combine them. He does not point to show interest, prefers to line up cars repetitively, and resists eye contact. He had no significant birth or perinatal history and his hearing screen at birth was normal. He has no regression of skills. His motor development is normal and he walks well. There is no family history of intellectual disability.

data_table.Examination: No dysmorphic features; growth 50th centile; gait and tone normal; no neurocutaneous stigmata; HEADSS not yet applicable
data_table.Investigations: Hearing screen at birth normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to speech pathology only and review in 6 months; defer paediatric review unless speech therapy alone fails to improve language
options.rationale: Isolated speech therapy without diagnostic assessment misses the broader social communication and restricted-repetitive behaviour phenotype and delays NDIS access. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.text: Reassure parents that boys develop language later and review at age 3 years if expressive language has not advanced over the next 9 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting beyond 2 years for language delay with social communication concerns delays diagnosis and access to NDIS-funded early intervention which has the strongest evidence under 5 years of age. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.text: Commence a 6-week trial of a Mediterranean-style diet and omega-3 supplementation and review behaviour and language at the end of trial
options.rationale: Dietary interventions including omega-3 have no robust evidence for autism management and delay access to evidence-based behavioural therapy. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.text: Order karyotype and Fragile X testing as the first investigation step before any specialist therapy referral or further developmental assessment
options.rationale: Genetic testing has a role in autism workup but is not the gatekeeper; multidisciplinary assessment and early intervention should commence in parallel, not wait for results. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

options.text: Refer for audiology assessment and to a developmental paediatrician for multidisciplinary autism assessment; arrange early intervention referral
options.rationale: Persistent receptive and expressive language delay with social communication concerns warrants audiology to exclude hearing loss and parallel referral for multidisciplinary autism assessment plus early intervention; delaying referral wastes the critical intervention window. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment)
source_refs: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

explanation.summary: Autism is a clinical diagnosis based on persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour or interests across multiple settings. Red flags by age 2 years include no two-word phrases, no joint attention, no pointing to show, lack of pretend play, lack of social reciprocity. Hearing assessment is mandatory to exclude hearing loss as a cause of language delay. Multidisciplinary diagnostic assessment, NDIS application and evidence-based early intervention (speech, OT, behavioural) should commence in parallel rather than sequentially.
key_points: Multidisciplinary assessment is gold standard for diagnosis
Hearing assessment mandatory to exclude hearing loss
Early intervention before age 5 has strongest evidence
NDIS funding from diagnosis supports intervention access
explanation.pearls: Under 9 years, NDIS access is available via the early childhood approach without a formal diagnosis if developmental delay is documented, accelerating intervention access.

sources.label: Australian National Guideline for Autism Assessment

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing an 18-month-old boy whose mother is worried about three episodes of him going limp and turning blue around his lips for around 20 seconds after he was scolded or denied something he wanted. Each episode ended with rapid recovery, no post-event drowsiness, no incontinence and no jerking movements observed. He is meeting all developmental milestones and is otherwise well. There is no family history of sudden death, syncope or seizures.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful; no dysmorphic features; cardiovascular and neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: FBC Hb 118, MCV 78, ferritin 24 microg/L; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure parents about the benign self-limiting nature of cyanotic breath-holding spells and provide simple first-aid safety advice
options.rationale: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are a benign reflex phenomenon peaking at 6 to 18 months with normal investigations; reassurance and basic safety advice are the primary management. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses with serum drug-level monitoring every three months in clinic
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants are not indicated for breath-holding spells which are reflex syncope not epileptic seizures; sodium valproate carries teratogenic and hepatotoxic risks unwarranted here. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

options.text: Arrange outpatient sleep-deprived EEG and 24-hour ambulatory video-EEG monitoring to exclude an underlying focal epilepsy syndrome
options.rationale: EEG is reserved for episodes with seizure features (jerking, prolonged unresponsiveness, post-ictal phase) which are absent here; routine EEG yields false positives in normal toddlers. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

options.text: Refer to paediatric cardiology for 24-hour Holter monitoring and exercise stress echocardiogram to exclude long QT syndrome
options.rationale: Cardiac referral is reserved for syncope with exertional or postural triggers, abnormal ECG or family history of sudden death; reflex triggers with normal ECG do not warrant escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg/day elemental iron for empirical supplementation despite ferritin within the normal reference range
options.rationale: Iron supplementation reduces spell frequency only when iron deficiency is present; this child has normal ferritin and supplementation risks constipation without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Apparent life-threatening event)

explanation.summary: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are reflex anoxic episodes triggered by frustration, anger or pain in toddlers aged 6 months to 4 years. The child cries, holds breath in expiration, becomes cyanotic and may lose consciousness for under 60 seconds with rapid full recovery. Distinguishing features from seizures include the consistent emotional trigger, absence of post-ictal phase and absence of stereotyped jerking. Iron deficiency anaemia worsens frequency, so checking ferritin is reasonable; supplementation only helps when deficiency is present. Reassurance with simple first-aid (lay child on side, avoid mouth interference, reinforce that spells are not harmful) is the cornerstone.
key_points: Reflex syncope triggered by emotion, not epilepsy
Check ferritin; treat only if deficient
EEG reserved for atypical features
Cardiac workup only if exertional trigger or family sudden death
explanation.pearls: Resolution by age 5 years occurs in over 90 percent; persistence beyond 6 years or new exertional triggers warrant cardiology review for long QT or catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.

subtopic_detail: Immediate antibiotic threshold in bilateral acute OM under 2 years
stem: A 15-month-old boy presents to your GP clinic with 24 hours of fever, irritability and right ear-tugging. He has no significant past medical history, is fully immunised, and is non-Aboriginal. He has no allergies. On examination he has a temperature of 38.7, both tympanic membranes bulging with reduced light reflex, and red middle ear effusion bilaterally. There is no mastoid tenderness and no facial weakness. He is alert and drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulging red tympanic membranes; no mastoid tenderness; no neck stiffness; well perfused; drinking 60 percent of usual

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents, advise paracetamol or ibuprofen for analgesia, and review in 48 hours if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for non-severe unilateral otitis media in children over 2 years with mild symptoms; under 2 years with bilateral disease meets the threshold for immediate antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin ear drops twice daily for 5 days as first-line treatment for acute otitis media
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics are for otitis externa or chronic discharging ears, not acute otitis media with intact tympanic membrane; oral amoxicillin is first-line. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours orally for 5 days plus regular paracetamol or ibuprofen analgesia
options.rationale: AU guidelines (RCH, eTG) recommend immediate oral amoxicillin in children under 2 years with bilateral acute otitis media, severe symptoms (severe pain, T 39 or above, vomiting), or systemic features. Dose 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days. Analgesia is essential. (Source: RCH CPG; eTG)

options.text: Prescribe cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily orally for 7 days as the first-line agent in childhood otitis media
options.rationale: Cefuroxime is reserved for amoxicillin failure or non-severe penicillin allergy; amoxicillin is first-line. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer to ENT for urgent tympanostomy tube placement given the bilateral nature of his presentation today
options.rationale: Tympanostomy referral is for recurrent (3 or more in 6 months or 4 or more in 12 months) or chronic OM with effusion lasting over 3 months, not a single acute episode. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in children is largely viral; bacterial cases involve S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Immediate antibiotics in Australia are reserved for under 6 months, under 2 years with bilateral disease, severe systemic features (T 39 or above, severe pain, vomiting), suppurative complications, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at higher risk of complications. Otherwise watchful waiting 48 hours with safety-netting. Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days is first-line. Augmentin reserved for treatment failure or recurrent. Analgesia is mandatory regardless of antibiotic decision.
key_points: Watchful wait OR immediate amoxicillin based on age, severity, risk group
Under 2 with bilateral disease = treat immediately
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days
Analgesia regardless of antibiotic decision
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children with acute otitis media have an 8-10 times higher rate of progression to chronic suppurative otitis media and hearing loss, so eTG recommends immediate antibiotic treatment for all acute OM in this population regardless of age or severity.

subtopic_detail: Supportive management thresholds in infant bronchiolitis
stem: A 10-month-old boy presents to your ED in late autumn with 3 days of coryza, rhinorrhoea, mild fever and 24 hours of wheezing and cough. His older sister had a cold last week. He has no prior wheeze, no atopy in the family, and is breastfed plus solid food. He is fully immunised. He has had no prior salbutamol use. He has 30 percent reduced feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 140, RR 50, SpO2 95 percent RA
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, widespread wheeze and bilateral fine crackles, mild dehydration with capillary refill 2 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer with reassessment of respiratory effort and oxygen saturation at 20 minutes
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not effective in children under 12 months with bronchiolitis (no smooth muscle to act on, no benefit shown in trials); RCH recommends against routine use. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Supportive care with feeds and oxygen monitoring; admit if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target) or feeds below 50 percent of normal
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis in infants is a supportive management diagnosis. RCH CPG recommends nasal saline, oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), NG or IV fluids if oral intake below 50 percent, and no routine salbutamol, steroids, adrenaline or antibiotics. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min as first-line therapy without trialling standard low-flow oxygen
options.rationale: HFNC is escalation for moderate-severe distress not maintained on standard low-flow; not routine first-line. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days to reduce airway inflammation and shorten time to discharge
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in bronchiolitis (no benefit shown in multiple large RCTs). (Source: RCH CPG; Cochrane)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 strength with continuous monitoring for 4 hours before reassessment
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline shows no benefit in routine bronchiolitis and may cause rebound; reserved for severe cases with failure of supportive measures. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months with viral lower respiratory tract symptoms. RSV is the commonest cause (60-70 percent). Management is supportive: gentle nasal saline, minimal handling, oxygen if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target), fluids via NG or IV if oral intake below 50 percent normal, and apnoea monitoring in younger infants. Salbutamol, corticosteroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are NOT routinely indicated. Escalation criteria: persistent hypoxia despite oxygen, exhaustion, recurrent apnoeas, severe distress.
key_points: Supportive care only - oxygen, feeds, observation
No salbutamol, no steroids, no adrenaline routinely
Admission if SpO2 below 92, feeds below 50 percent, apnoeas, severe distress
Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection
explanation.pearls: Apnoeas occur most commonly in infants under 6 weeks or preterm with bronchiolitis and may be the presenting feature even before respiratory distress is severe; cardiopulmonary monitoring is mandatory in this group regardless of initial SpO2.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to your GP clinic by his mother with 6 weeks of infrequent painful stools and recent soiling episodes. He passes a hard stool every 4-5 days and reports pain on defaecation. He is otherwise well, eats a variable diet, drinks plenty of water, and has not had recent illness. Growth is along the 50th centile, immunisations up to date. He has no red flags such as delayed meconium passage, blood per rectum, or anorexia.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant; perianal inspection normal; no anal fissure visible; growth on 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence Senna 5 mg nocte as a stimulant laxative without an initial disimpaction phase before maintenance
options.rationale: Stimulant laxatives can cause cramping pain and are second-line; osmotic laxative (PEG) is first-line in AU. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Order plain abdominal X-ray to confirm faecal loading and refer to paediatric gastroenterology outpatients
options.rationale: AXR is not routinely required; clinical diagnosis is reliable; specialist referral is reserved for red flags or failure of maintenance therapy. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for digital rectal examination under general anaesthetic for manual disimpaction
options.rationale: Manual disimpaction under GA is reserved for refractory cases failing oral disimpaction; oral PEG is first-line and effective in around 90 percent. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Commence macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at disimpaction dose for 3-7 days then maintenance dose
options.rationale: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes (Movicol Junior) is the first-line osmotic laxative in Australia for childhood functional constipation; disimpaction dose 1-1.5 sachets/kg/day for 3-7 days, then transition to maintenance 0.4-1 sachets/day adjusted to soft daily stool. (Source: RCH CPG; AMH)

options.text: Recommend dietary fibre, water and timed toileting routine alone with review of progress in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Lifestyle alone is insufficient when faecal impaction has occurred; impaction must be cleared before maintenance succeeds. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 95 percent of paediatric constipation. Red flags requiring further workup include delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours of life, growth failure, abdominal distension, vomiting, blood per rectum, abnormal neurological signs, or sacral dimple. Standard care involves two phases: disimpaction (oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes 1-1.5 sachets/kg/day for 3-7 days), then maintenance (PEG titrated to one soft stool daily, minimum 3-6 months). Lactulose is second-line. Behavioural training including timed toileting after meals and a stool diary support adherence.
key_points: Disimpaction THEN maintenance - both phases necessary
Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes (PEG) is first-line in Australia
Maintenance for minimum 3-6 months, often longer
Behavioural toileting routine integral to success
explanation.pearls: Approximately 50 percent of children with functional constipation relapse within 1 year of stopping maintenance laxatives, so plan a gradual wean over 2-3 months only after 6 months of soft daily stools without soiling; abrupt cessation predictably triggers re-impaction.

subtopic_detail: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia with cow's milk excess
stem: A 22-month-old girl is brought to your GP clinic for review of pallor. Her mother reports she drinks 750 mL of cow's milk per day from a bottle, eats variably, and refuses red meat. She is otherwise well, walks normally, and has met all developmental milestones. She is fully immunised. She has 5 episodes per day of upset and is described as fussy by her mother.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no koilonychia, no hepatosplenomegaly, weight on 50th centile, height on 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 64 fL, ferritin 7 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 6 percent, CRP under 5; coeliac serology negative; blood film microcytic hypochromic; reticulocyte count 1.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that the anaemia is mild and continue current diet with a routine review in 4 months
options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia at 22 months requires active treatment and dietary modification; untreated risks cognitive and developmental impact. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

options.text: Order serum lead level and refer urgently to paediatric haematology for further workup before treatment
options.rationale: Lead toxicity is rare in Australian children without risk factors; not standard initial workup. Iron deficiency is the typical cause of microcytic anaemia in this age. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Commence vitamin B12 1000 micrograms intramuscularly weekly for 4 weeks then 3-monthly maintenance
options.rationale: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic not microcytic anaemia; the FBC pattern points to iron deficiency. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Prescribe oral ferrous fumarate 100 mg daily without dietary advice or milk reduction during this visit
options.rationale: Iron supplementation without dietary modification is incomplete; cow's milk excess (over 500 mL/day) is a major driver and must be addressed. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Prescribe oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg daily, limit cow's milk to 500 mL/day, advise iron-rich foods, recheck in 8 weeks
options.rationale: RCH guidelines: oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg/day for 3 months, reduce cow's milk to below 500 mL/day, encourage iron-rich foods (red meat, fortified cereals, legumes), and recheck at 8 weeks expecting Hb rise of 10 g/L or more. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia affects 8-10 percent of Australian toddlers; risk factors include excessive cow's milk (over 500 mL/day), early cow's milk introduction before 12 months, low iron-containing solids, prolonged breastfeeding without iron supplementation, prematurity, and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background. Diagnostic markers: microcytic hypochromic anaemia, low ferritin (below 12 mcg/L), low transferrin saturation. Treatment: oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg/day for 3 months minimum, reduce cow's milk to below 500 mL/day, dietary modification, FBC and ferritin at 8 weeks. Iron deficiency without anaemia (low ferritin alone) still warrants treatment given developmental risk.
key_points: Most common cause of microcytic anaemia in toddlers
Cow's milk excess is the main modifiable factor
Oral iron 3 mg/kg/day elemental for 3 months
Recheck FBC at 8 weeks; Hb rise of 10 g/L or more confirms adequate response
explanation.pearls: Iron deficiency in the second year of life is associated with measurable IQ deficits up to 10 points and impaired motor development that may persist even after iron repletion; the window for prevention is more important than the rapidity of correction.

subtopic_detail: Empiric IV antibiotic regimen in febrile infant under 3 months
stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to your ED with 24 hours of fever (38.6 by parents), poor feeding, irritability, and a single episode of vomiting. He has no upper respiratory or other localising symptoms. He is fully immunised for age. On examination he is alert but irritable, with a temperature of 38.7, capillary refill 2 seconds, no rash, no meningism, and clear chest. His urine is collected by clean catch.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 165, RR 50, SpO2 99 percent RA, weight 5.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; no rash; anterior fontanelle soft; chest clear; no abdominal tenderness; perfusion adequate
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urine dipstick positive for leukocytes and nitrites; FBC, CRP, blood cultures, blood gas pending; LP being arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin empiric coverage following blood and urine cultures and lumbar puncture
options.rationale: In infants under 3 months with fever, the threshold for serious bacterial infection workup and empiric antibiotic cover is low; sepsis cannot be excluded clinically. The RCH approach is full septic screen (blood culture, urine catheter or SPA, LP) and empiric IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin, covering E. coli, Listeria, Group B strep, and other neonatal pathogens. (Source: RCH CPG; eTG)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 7 days as outpatient management with GP follow-up
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate in febrile infants under 3 months; sepsis evaluation and IV therapy are mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy at 50 mg/kg once daily without need for second agent
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone covers most enterics but does not reliably cover Listeria, which is important in this age group; AU empiric regimen includes benzylpenicillin or ampicillin for Listeria. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole orally as suitable empiric treatment for outpatient management of UTI
options.rationale: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is inappropriate for septic febrile infant; risks delayed source control and bilirubin displacement in neonates. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until urine culture is back at 48 hours and reassess clinically before commencing therapy
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics in a febrile young infant is dangerous; outcomes worsen markedly with each hour of delay. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Fever in infants under 3 months requires systematic evaluation because clinical signs are unreliable for identifying serious bacterial infection (SBI, around 10 percent prevalence). AU practice: full septic screen (blood cultures, urine via catheter or suprapubic aspirate, LP) and empiric IV antibiotics. Standard regimen IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (or amoxicillin plus gentamicin) covers E. coli, Group B Streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Add aciclovir if HSV suspected. Admit for at least 48 hours pending culture results.
key_points: Fever under 3 months - full septic screen plus empiric IV antibiotics
Empiric: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (covers Listeria plus neonatal pathogens)
Add aciclovir if HSV concern (vesicles, seizures, hepatitis)
Admit minimum 48 hours
explanation.pearls: Suprapubic aspirate is the gold standard urine collection in infants under 6 months when clean-catch is not feasible because bag samples have around a 25 percent contamination rate; ultrasound-guided SPA increases first-pass success to around 95 percent.

subtopic_detail: IVIG and aspirin for classic Kawasaki disease
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to your ED on day 6 of high spiking fevers up to 40, accompanied by a polymorphous rash on day 2, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis on day 3, a strawberry tongue with red cracked lips on day 4, and unilateral right cervical lymphadenopathy 2.5 cm. His feet became swollen yesterday with red palms. He is irritable and lethargic. He has been seen twice by his GP for viral illness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.8, HR 145, RR 32, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; cracked red lips and strawberry tongue; polymorphous rash trunk and limbs; right cervical lymphadenopathy 2.5 cm; oedema and erythema of palms and soles; no signs of meningism
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 18, neutrophils 13, platelets 580; CRP 198; ESR 78; Na 132; albumin 28; ALT 78; urinary sediment with 15 WCC; echocardiogram pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence amoxicillin and observe for clinical response over 48 hours before further investigations are arranged
options.rationale: This presentation meets full Kawasaki disease criteria (fever over 5 days plus four of five principal features); antibiotics alone risk progression to coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Treat as scarlet fever with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and observe response over the next 72 hours
options.rationale: Scarlet fever does not typically include conjunctivitis or extremity changes; testing for Kawasaki and treating now is essential. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin and arrange urgent echocardiogram
options.rationale: Kawasaki disease (fever 5 or more days plus 4 of 5: bilateral conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy) requires IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to under 5 percent; combined with aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses until afebrile, then 3-5 mg/kg/day until echo confirms no aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG; AHA 2017)

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as monotherapy without immunoglobulin or aspirin
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is reserved for IVIG-resistant cases as second-line; not first-line in Australia. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Reassure parents of viral exanthem, advise paracetamol, and arrange GP review of progress in 48 hours
options.rationale: Failure to recognise and treat KD risks coronary aneurysms; this child has multiple criteria for KD. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of young children (peak age under 5) with major sequelae being coronary artery aneurysms in 25 percent of untreated cases. Diagnostic criteria: fever 5 or more days PLUS 4 or more of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, red cracked lips), polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy. Atypical or incomplete KD requires lab criteria (CRP, ESR, anaemia, platelets over 450, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria). Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk to under 5 percent, plus high-dose aspirin transitioning to low-dose. Echocardiogram at baseline, 2 weeks and 6-8 weeks.
key_points: 5 day fever plus 4 of 5 criteria = classic Kawasaki
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days
Aspirin high-dose acutely, then low-dose for 6-8 weeks pending echo
Echo at baseline, 2 weeks, 6-8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Incomplete or atypical Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child under 6 months or over 5 years with 5 or more days of unexplained fever; coronary aneurysm risk is paradoxically highest in infants under 6 months despite often having fewer classic clinical criteria.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to your GP clinic with a 1-week history of a palpable purpuric rash on his buttocks and lower legs, abdominal pain, and 24 hours of left knee swelling. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. He is otherwise well, has a good appetite, and no haematuria reported by parents. Examination shows palpable non-blanching purpura on extensor surfaces of legs, mild ankle and knee swelling without joint effusion, and a soft non-tender abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura extensor lower limbs and buttocks; bilateral mild ankle swelling, painful left knee; soft non-tender abdomen with normal bowel sounds; no testicular involvement
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick clear (no blood, no protein); FBC normal platelets 380; coagulation normal; UEC normal; ASOT positive 380 U; throat swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Single review in 4 weeks with FBC and creatinine to confirm resolution of symptoms before discharge
options.rationale: Insufficient surveillance; nephritis can develop weeks to months after rash and is the major long-term morbidity. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 4 weeks, then fortnightly for 8 weeks, then 3-monthly to 12 months
options.rationale: AU paediatric guidelines (RCH) recommend urinalysis and BP weekly for first 4 weeks (when nephritis is most likely to manifest), fortnightly to 12 weeks, then 3-monthly to 12 months. Refer to paediatric nephrology if persistent proteinuria, haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, or rising creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP; KHA-CARI Paediatric)

options.text: Daily urinalysis at home with creatinine and proteinuria measurement performed monthly for 1 year
options.rationale: Daily home urinalysis is impractical and not evidence-based; structured schedule per guideline is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Renal biopsy at 6 weeks regardless of urinalysis findings as routine screening in this presentation
options.rationale: Renal biopsy is reserved for persistent significant proteinuria, declining renal function, or atypical features; not routine. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Single urinalysis and blood pressure check at 6 months in line with general practice protocols
options.rationale: Single late check misses early nephritis when intervention may matter; insufficient. (Source: RCH CPG)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the most common childhood vasculitis (peak 4-7 years), classically following upper respiratory infection. Tetrad: palpable purpura on dependent areas (universal), abdominal pain (60-80 percent), arthralgia or arthritis (60-80 percent), and renal involvement (20-50 percent). Renal involvement (nephritis with haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension) is the major long-term concern, occurring weeks to months after rash onset, and is the determinant of long-term outcome. Standard monitoring: urinalysis and BP weekly for 4 weeks, fortnightly to 12 weeks, 3-monthly to 12 months. Refer to nephrology if persistent proteinuria, raised BP, or rising creatinine.
key_points: Palpable purpura on dependent areas, post-infectious context
Renal involvement may develop weeks to months later - structured monitoring
Schedule: weekly 4w, fortnightly 12w, 3-monthly 12m
Steroids reduce abdominal pain duration but not nephritis incidence
explanation.pearls: Persistent proteinuria beyond 6 months from HSP onset, even at low levels, is the strongest predictor of long-term chronic kidney disease in adulthood and warrants paediatric nephrology referral for consideration of renal biopsy and immunosuppressive therapy.

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in shocked neonate - malrotation with midgut volvulus
stem: A 5-day-old term infant born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth (birth weight 3300 g) is brought to your tertiary neonatal ED with 6 hours of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and decreased feeding. The baby was breastfeeding well at home. He was discharged on day 1 of life. On arrival he is pale, peripherally cool, with capillary refill 4 seconds, and a distended tender abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.8, BP 56/35, HR 175, RR 65, SpO2 96 percent on room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Pale, peripherally shut down, tense distended abdomen with reduced bowel sounds; no obvious external mass; testes descended; no perianal abnormality
data_table.Investigations: BSL 2.4 mmol/L; ABG pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12, lactate 5.8; Hb 110, WCC 8.2, platelets 90; UEC: Na 132, K 5.8, urea 8.2, creatinine 56; CRP 18; clotted blood for cross-match sent; abdominal radiograph shows non-specific gas pattern with no obvious pneumatosis or free air; nasogastric aspirate is bile-stained

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate management priority?

options.text: Commence empiric intravenous gentamicin, ampicillin and metronidazole and observe the abdomen at frequent intervals while monitoring vital signs
options.rationale: Frequent observation in a shocked neonate with bilious vomiting is unsafe; volvulus may be present and demands immediate exploration. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics and arrange contrast upper gastrointestinal series within 2 hours to confirm diagnosis
options.rationale: Upper GI contrast study delays definitive surgical management in a shocked infant; bilious vomiting in neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise and warrants exploration; imaging is reserved for stable infants. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Insert nasogastric tube, commence intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and admit for clinical observation overnight
options.rationale: Conservative management with observation in a shocked infant with bilious vomiting risks bowel necrosis from volvulus; surgical consultation is the immediate priority. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg fluid bolus, commence broad-spectrum antibiotics, and arrange CT abdomen with contrast to clarify the cause
options.rationale: CT abdomen exposes the neonate to significant radiation and delays surgery; not first-line investigation in suspected midgut volvulus in a shocked infant. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Resuscitate with fluid and blood products, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and arrange immediate paediatric surgical consultation for laparotomy
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in any neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. In a shocked infant, imaging delays surgery; the standard of care is resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, immediate paediatric surgical consult and operative exploration without waiting for upper GI contrast. Delayed exploration risks total midgut infarction within 4-6 hours. (Source: RCH CPG; APSA; ANZNN)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in any neonate is a paediatric surgical emergency that must be assumed to be malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Volvulus produces midgut ischaemia from torsion around the superior mesenteric artery axis; total midgut infarction can occur within 4-6 hours. Stable infants undergo upper GI contrast study (definitive: abnormally positioned duodenojejunal flexure right of midline, corkscrew duodenum). Shocked or rapidly deteriorating infants go directly to laparotomy. Necrotising enterocolitis (typical in preterm, days 2-3 of life, pneumatosis on AXR) is a differential but the diagnostic approach in a shocked term neonate with bilious vomiting prioritises surgical exploration over imaging.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in neonate = volvulus until proven otherwise
Shocked infant = immediate laparotomy, no imaging delay
Stable infant = urgent upper GI contrast series
Window to prevent total midgut infarction: 4-6 hours
explanation.pearls: The Ladd procedure for malrotation involves derotating the volvulus anticlockwise, dividing Ladd's bands, broadening the mesentery, returning the small bowel to the right and colon to the left of the abdomen, and performing prophylactic appendicectomy because the appendix is left in the left upper quadrant.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

subtopic_detail: Empiric oral antibiotic for first febrile UTI in well toddler
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl in the short-stay unit with 24 hours of fever and reduced feeding. She is alert with no rash and tolerating sips. A clean-catch urine collected after meatal cleaning shows leucocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, and microscopy with 200 white cells per microlitre. Local antibiogram shows E. coli trimethoprim resistance of 28 percent and cefalexin resistance of 6 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent, BP 96/58
data_table.Examination: Alert, hydrated, soft non-tender abdomen, no flank tenderness, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine LE positive, nitrites positive, WCC 200/microL, urine culture pending; venous blood gas pH 7.38, lactate 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 7 days starting now in the short-stay unit
options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate has broader gram-negative cover than needed and higher rates of diarrhoea compared with the first-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until urine culture sensitivities are reported tomorrow morning before commencing any oral therapy
options.rationale: Delay in treatment of a confirmed febrile urinary tract infection increases the risk of renal scarring; empiric therapy is started after the urine sample is taken. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 4 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 7 days starting now as the empiric first-line oral antibiotic
options.rationale: Trimethoprim resistance of 28 percent locally exceeds the 20 percent ceiling for reliable empiric cover in febrile urinary tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days starting now as the first-line empirical oral antibiotic
options.rationale: Cefalexin is the RCH first-line oral agent for paediatric urinary tract infection. In children 12 months or older with febrile urinary tract infection the dose is 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily admit for 48 hours then switch to oral therapy guided by culture sensitivities
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is reserved for children who are unwell, vomiting, under 3 months, or unable to tolerate oral feeds; this child is well enough for oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Febrile urinary tract infection in young children is treated empirically after urine collection; the choice of oral agent depends on local resistance patterns and oral tolerance. RCH lists cefalexin as the first-line oral antibiotic for paediatric urinary tract infection: cystitis 20 mg/kg three times daily, pyelonephritis 25 mg/kg three times daily in children 12 months or older (25 mg/kg four times daily under 12 months). A 7-day course is standard for upper-tract urinary tract infection in well children. Trimethoprim is reserved for sensitivity-confirmed therapy or stepdown.
key_points: Empiric oral cefalexin first-line per RCH urinary tract infection guideline
12 months or older with pyelonephritis: 25 mg/kg three times daily
Intravenous therapy reserved for unwell, under 3 months, or vomiting
Trimethoprim only when local resistance is acceptable and sensitivities support it
Do not delay empirics for culture in a symptomatic confirmed urinary tract infection
explanation.pearls: Twice-daily cefalexin is not RCH dosing for paediatric urinary tract infection; the guideline consistently lists three times daily (or four times daily under 12 months in pyelonephritis).

subtopic_detail: Postexposure prophylaxis for household contacts of confirmed pertussis
stem: You are the GP registrar seeing a family after their 7-year-old son was diagnosed with PCR-confirmed pertussis 2 days ago. The household includes the index case, his 32-year-old mother who is 34 weeks pregnant, his 38-year-old father, an 8-week-old sister who is fully vaccinated for age, and a 4-year-old brother whose immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: All household members afebrile and asymptomatic at presentation today
data_table.Examination: Index case isolating at home with paroxysmal cough; other family members no respiratory symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Index case pertussis PCR positive 2 days ago; other family members no testing performed

lead_in: Which household members should receive antibiotic postexposure prophylaxis today?

options.text: Only the 8-week-old sister receives azithromycin while other contacts are observed at home
options.rationale: Selective prophylaxis to the infant alone leaves household transmission via the other contacts unaddressed during the infectious period. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

options.text: No prophylaxis is given because all household contacts are currently asymptomatic on review
options.rationale: Pertussis transmits from up to 6 days before cough onset; absence of symptoms in contacts does not exclude infection or transmission risk. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

options.text: Mother, 8-week-old sister, 4-year-old brother, and father all receive azithromycin
options.rationale: AU guidance recommends prophylaxis for all household contacts when a high-risk contact is present such as a young infant or a third-trimester pregnant woman. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

options.text: Only the mother and 8-week-old sister receive azithromycin while other contacts are observed
options.rationale: Restricting prophylaxis omits the father and 4-year-old brother who can transmit to both high-risk contacts within the household. (Source: CDNA SoNG Pertussis)

options.text: All household contacts receive trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole as the preferred first-line agent
options.rationale: Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is a second-line agent in pertussis prophylaxis reserved for macrolide-intolerant individuals over 2 months of age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis aims to interrupt household transmission and protect high-risk contacts. AU CDNA SoNG defines high-risk contacts as infants under 6 months, women in the last month of pregnancy, and unvaccinated childcare workers. When a high-risk contact is identified all household members receive prophylaxis regardless of immunisation status. Azithromycin is the macrolide of choice for infants over 1 month due to lower hypertrophic pyloric stenosis risk than erythromycin.
key_points: Azithromycin first-line for all ages including infants over 1 month
All household contacts treated if any high-risk contact present
High-risk: infant under 6 months, last month of pregnancy
Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole only if macrolide-intolerant and over 2 months
explanation.pearls: Maternal pertussis vaccination in pregnancy from 20 weeks provides passive protection but does not eliminate the need for household prophylaxis when a confirmed case is identified.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for moderate croup in ED
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy with a 12-hour history of barking cough, hoarseness, and intermittent stridor at rest. He is alert and accepts oral medications. There is no drooling, history of foreign body, or recent vaccinations missed. Local supply of dexamethasone oral solution is currently available.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 138, RR 36, SpO2 97 percent on air
data_table.Examination: Barking cough, stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, alert, normal air entry bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Westley croup score 4 (moderate); no investigations indicated for typical croup
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol given by parents 4 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as initial inhaled corticosteroid because oral intake is uncertain
options.rationale: Budesonide is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral steroid; this child is alert and accepting oral medications. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: AU practice supports a single oral dexamethasone dose of 0.15 mg/kg for moderate croup with onset of benefit within 30 to 60 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and observation pending resolution of stridor
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not treat the subglottic oedema responsible for croup and delays definitive steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 alone now without corticosteroid
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for severe distress as it acts for 1 to 2 hours and requires steroid co-administration to avoid rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose tried first because dexamethasone is unavailable
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is the preferred AU first-line agent due to longer half-life and single-dose efficacy; prednisolone is an alternative only if dexamethasone is unavailable. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is treated according to a severity score with oral dexamethasone the AU first-line for mild to moderate cases. Stridor at rest with mild recession indicates moderate severity warranting steroid and observation but not adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline is added for severe disease with marked recession, cyanosis, or altered mental state and always with concurrent steroid. Disposition depends on response at 4 hours after steroid: stable children can usually go home.
key_points: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose first-line
Adrenaline only for severe distress and always with steroid
Budesonide nebulised only if oral intake not possible
Discharge after 4 hours if no stridor at rest
explanation.pearls: Onset of benefit from oral dexamethasone in croup is 30 to 60 minutes with peak at 6 hours; this matches the typical 4-hour ED observation window before safe discharge.

subtopic_detail: IM adrenaline weight-band dosing and route in school-age child with anaphylaxis
stem: You are the ED registrar called to resuscitation as an 8-year-old boy arrives by ambulance after eating a peanut snack at school 20 minutes ago. He developed lip swelling, generalised urticaria, then dyspnoea and one episode of vomiting. Paramedics administered 300 micrograms intramuscular adrenaline 10 minutes ago via his school auto-injector. He weighs 32 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 154, RR 38, SpO2 91 percent on 6 L/min oxygen, BP 78/42
data_table.Examination: Widespread urticaria, perioral swelling, audible wheeze bilaterally, prolonged capillary refill, anxious
data_table.Investigations: Bedside venous gas pH 7.30, lactate 3.2
data_table.Medications: Adrenaline 300 micrograms IM 10 minutes ago (auto-injector); now 20 minutes since exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next adrenaline order while you secure IV access and prepare a fluid bolus?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 as the next adrenaline dose for upper airway oedema
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for stridor but does not address shock or lower airway anaphylaxis and does not replace systemic IM dosing. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 300 micrograms in the deltoid as a second dose for ongoing wheeze and hypotension
options.rationale: Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable during shock; intramuscular anterolateral thigh is the recommended route in anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms in the anterolateral thigh as the appropriate paediatric weight-band dose
options.rationale: The 150 microgram dose corresponds to children between 10 and 20 kg and underdoses a 32 kg child experiencing persistent severe anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg push as a single bolus over 30 seconds while preparing fluid
options.rationale: IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest risks malignant arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis and is reserved for refractory shock as an infusion. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms in the anterolateral thigh now and repeat at 5 minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: AU ASCIA guidance prescribes 10 micrograms/kg IM up to 500 micrograms with repeat dosing every 5 minutes for persistent severe anaphylaxis; in a 32 kg child the rounded dose is 300 micrograms IM. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis treatment in children is repeated IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh every 5 minutes for persistent severe features. The AU ASCIA weight bands prescribe 150 micrograms for 10 to 20 kg, 300 micrograms for 20 to 50 kg, and 500 micrograms for over 50 kg with simultaneous fluid resuscitation. Refractory shock after 2 or 3 IM doses prompts an adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 microgram/kg/min titrated to response with continuous cardiac monitoring. Antihistamines and steroids are not first-line in acute anaphylaxis.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg up to 500 micrograms every 5 minutes
Weight bands: 150 for 10-20 kg, 300 for 20-50 kg, 500 for over 50 kg
IV infusion only when refractory after 2-3 IM doses
Fluids 20 mL/kg crystalloid alongside adrenaline for shock
explanation.pearls: Persistent shock after 2 IM doses indicates impending refractory anaphylaxis; commence an adrenaline infusion early at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and call for senior airway support rather than escalating IM dose.

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic and LP timing in late onset suspected neonatal sepsis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12-day-old term boy brought in by his mother with poor feeding and reduced activity for 8 hours. He is now lethargic and grunting. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, breastfed, and discharged at 36 hours. He has not received any maternal antibiotics in labour. The local cefotaxime supply is unavailable due to a national shortage and ceftriaxone is being used as the substitute despite the patient being a term neonate without jaundice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 192, RR 68, SpO2 94 percent, BP 62/38, prolonged capillary refill
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, grunting, mottled, anterior fontanelle full, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.22 base excess -10, glucose 2.6, lactate 4.2, WCC 22, CRP 78, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next set of antimicrobial actions?

options.text: Commence IV cefazolin and gentamicin then add aciclovir if seizures or focal CNS signs develop later
options.rationale: Cefazolin lacks reliable CNS penetration; aciclovir is added empirically in any late-onset neonate with sepsis features even without seizures. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.text: Commence IV vancomycin and meropenem to cover resistant gram negatives and methicillin resistant staph
options.rationale: Broad cover with vancomycin and meropenem is reserved for nosocomial late-onset sepsis or proven resistance; community late-onset is treated with first-line regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin alone given a term neonate with cefotaxime unavailable on site
options.rationale: Late-onset sepsis with shock and full fontanelle requires meningitic third-generation cephalosporin cover not only beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.text: Start IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and ceftriaxone immediately then proceed to lumbar puncture when stabilised
options.rationale: Late-onset neonatal sepsis with septic shock requires immediate triple antimicrobial cover with meningitic ceftriaxone dose; LP is deferred until cardiovascular stability is achieved. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis; ANZCOR)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture first then commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin only after CSF is obtained
options.rationale: LP must not delay antibiotics in a shocked neonate; antibiotics are given immediately after blood cultures and LP is performed when safe. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

explanation.summary: Late-onset neonatal sepsis in a community setting is empirically covered with benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin and a third-generation cephalosporin at meningitic dose to cover group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria with CNS penetration. Aciclovir is added if features suggest possible HSV. Antibiotics must not be delayed for lumbar puncture in a haemodynamically unstable infant; the LP is performed when the patient is stabilised. Ceftriaxone may be used in term, non-jaundiced neonates over 1 week when cefotaxime is unavailable.
key_points: Late-onset community sepsis: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + cefotaxime or ceftriaxone
Add aciclovir empirically in late-onset neonatal sepsis with CNS features
Antibiotics first, LP when stable
Ceftriaxone acceptable substitute in term non-jaundiced neonates
explanation.pearls: Maternal HSV history is often absent in neonatal disseminated herpes; empiric aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours in a septic neonate has minimal downside and prevents catastrophic delay.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis in the neonate

subtopic_detail: Initial workup of weight faltering in 9-month-old without organic red flags
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 9-month-old boy whose weight has dropped from the 25th to the 3rd centile across the last three reviews. He was born at term, weighed 3.2 kg, and is exclusively breastfed with one daily solids tasting. His mother describes long unsettled feeds and reports she eats no extra protein. He smiles, transfers objects, and sits unsupported. There is no diarrhoea, vomiting, recurrent infection, or family history of coeliac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 124, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 6.4 kg (3rd centile, dropping), length 70 cm (25th), head circ 44 cm (25th)
data_table.Examination: Alert, no dysmorphism, no organomegaly, normal cardiac exam, soft non-distended abdomen, no rashes
data_table.Feeding: Breast feeds 6-8 times daily; offered pureed vegetable and rice cereal once daily; no formula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for paediatric admission and inpatient nasogastric supplemental feeding trial
options.rationale: Admission and NG feeds are reserved for severe weight faltering with dehydration, organic disease, or failed community escalation; this child is alert and developing normally. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

options.text: Arrange a structured feeding history with three-day diet diary and observe a feed
options.rationale: Detailed feeding assessment and observed feed remain the first-line evaluation for non-organic weight faltering before any investigation cascade. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

options.text: Order coeliac serology, full blood count, and renal function as the next investigation
options.rationale: Targeted bloods are reserved for children with red flags or no improvement after dietary and feeding optimisation; this child has none. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

options.text: Advise immediate cessation of breastfeeding and introduction of full-strength formula
options.rationale: There is no evidence-based reason to stop breastfeeding; mixed feeding decisions follow assessment, not precede it. (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure the mother that weight tracking on the 3rd centile is normal variation
options.rationale: Crossing two major centile lines downward warrants assessment rather than reassurance, even when development is preserved. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

explanation.summary: Weight faltering in infancy is most commonly multifactorial, with inadequate intake the leading cause when there are no organic red flags. Evaluation starts with a feeding history, three-day diet diary, and observation of a feed before laboratory testing. Investigations are guided by red flags such as diarrhoea, vomiting, recurrent infection, dysmorphism, or developmental regression. Solids should be established with iron-rich foods around six months in addition to milk feeds.
key_points: Crossing two centiles downward triggers structured assessment
Feeding observation and diet diary precede investigations
Coeliac and other serology reserved for red flags or non-response
NG feeds reserved for severe or unresponsive cases
explanation.pearls: An observed breastfeed in clinic typically lasts 10 to 40 minutes; transfer volumes under 60 mL in a 9 month old over a sustained feed flag low effective intake before any blood test is sent.

subtopic_detail: HPV vaccine routine schedule for 12-year-old at school-based program
stem: You are the school-based immunisation doctor reviewing a 12-year-old girl in Year 7 attending the routine school program. She is fit, well, has had no severe vaccine reactions, and is not immunocompromised. Her mother has consented in writing and asks whether she will need a second dose later this year or next.

data_table.Examination: Well, no acute illness, BMI on the 60th centile
data_table.Immunisations: Up to date with childhood schedule; never received HPV
data_table.Other: No pregnancy, no immunosuppression, no current febrile illness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate HPV immunisation plan?

options.text: Administer Gardasil 9 today and book a second dose at six months
options.rationale: The two-dose schedule was replaced in 2023 by a single-dose schedule for healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer Gardasil 9 today as a single dose with no further doses required
options.rationale: Healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years receive a single dose of Gardasil 9 under the AU schedule since 2023. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer vaccination until she turns 14 years to align with menarche cohort outcomes
options.rationale: There is no clinical reason to delay; immunogenicity and program uptake are highest in early Year 7. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer Gardasil 9 today and book three total doses across six months
options.rationale: Three doses are only required for moderately to severely immunocompromised adolescents, not healthy 12-year-olds. (Source: ATAGI; Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Decline routine vaccination and instead recommend cervical screening once eligible
options.rationale: Vaccination and screening are complementary; vaccination prevents most oncogenic HPV exposure that screening later detects. (Source: NCSP; Cancer Council Australia)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Immunisation Program moved to a single-dose Gardasil 9 schedule for healthy adolescents aged 9 to under 26 years in 2023. Three doses remain for those with moderate to severe immunocompromise. The program is delivered in Year 7 to maximise pre-exposure efficacy and uptake. Vaccination does not replace cervical screening, which begins at age 25 under the renewed National Cervical Screening Program.
key_points: Single-dose Gardasil 9 for healthy 9 to under 26 years
Three doses retained for moderate to severe immunocompromise
Delivered in Year 7 by school-based programs
Does not replace cervical screening from age 25
explanation.pearls: Gardasil 9 covers HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 and is the only HPV vaccine available on the Australian schedule since 2018.

subtopic_detail: Differentiating paraphimosis from physiological phimosis in 4-year-old boy
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy whose father retracted his foreskin during a bath two hours ago to clean underneath. The foreskin has not returned over the glans and the child is now crying with marked penile discomfort. There has been no trauma, fever, or urinary symptoms, and he passes urine without difficulty. The father describes the foreskin as previously non-retractable until tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/60, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Foreskin retracted behind a swollen, painful glans with a constricting band; glans pink, warm, non-dusky; no urinary retention
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear; no imaging performed
data_table.Past history: Otherwise well, immunisations up to date, no surgical history

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Reassure the family that the foreskin is non-retractable and arrange GP review
options.rationale: This is paraphimosis with an entrapped foreskin, which is a urological emergency rather than physiological phimosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

options.text: Apply topical lignocaine gel and attempt manual reduction with sustained glans compression
options.rationale: Topical anaesthesia with sustained glans compression to reduce oedema followed by manual reduction is the first-line management of paraphimosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

options.text: Refer to urology for elective circumcision booking and discharge with paracetamol
options.rationale: Definitive surgery is not the first step; the entrapment must be reduced urgently to avoid glans ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

options.text: Apply topical corticosteroid cream twice daily for six weeks and review in clinic
options.rationale: Topical steroid is treatment for symptomatic phimosis, not for an acute paraphimosis with entrapment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

options.text: Insert urinary catheter to relieve urinary retention and admit for intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: There is no retention or infection; catheterisation does not address the foreskin entrapment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin conditions)

explanation.summary: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans and creates a constricting band leading to oedema and risk of ischaemia. Initial management uses topical anaesthesia, sustained manual compression of the glans to reduce oedema, and gentle reduction. If reduction fails or the glans becomes dusky, urgent urology review for dorsal slit is required. This contrasts with physiological phimosis, where the foreskin is simply non-retractable in a well child without entrapment.
key_points: Paraphimosis is a urological emergency, not phimosis
First step: topical anaesthesia and manual reduction
Failed reduction or dusky glans needs urgent urology review
Never forcibly retract a physiologically tight foreskin
explanation.pearls: Most physiological phimosis resolves by age 10 without any intervention; only 1 percent of boys still have a non-retractile foreskin at age 16.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Suspected foreign body inhalation in toddler with focal wheeze and stable airway
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl who began coughing during a family dinner two hours ago. Her grandmother saw her chewing peanuts before the choking episode. She is now alert, tolerating sips, with mild intermittent cough but no stridor or cyanosis. On auscultation she has decreased air entry and end-expiratory wheeze localised to the right side.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 96 percent on air, BP 98/60
data_table.Examination: Sitting comfortably, no tripod posture, mild intercostal recession, focal right wheeze and reduced air entry
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray inspiration: subtle right hyperinflation; expiration film: persistent right hyperinflation with mediastinal shift to the left
data_table.Past history: Well child, full immunisation, no asthma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial salbutamol via spacer and review in two hours before any procedural plan
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not move a fixed obstructing foreign body and may delay definitive removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Refer urgently to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the definitive intervention for suspected airway foreign body with focal signs and air trapping. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Perform five back blows and five chest thrusts and admit for observation overnight
options.rationale: Back blows are part of basic life support for complete airway obstruction, not for a stable child with focal signs. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Order high-resolution chest CT to confirm radiolucent foreign body before any referral
options.rationale: CT may delay definitive bronchoscopy when the clinical picture and inspiration-expiration films already support a foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

options.text: Discharge home with chest physiotherapy advice and GP review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharge risks delayed pneumonia, atelectasis, and irreversible airway injury from a retained foreign body. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body inhalation)

explanation.summary: Suspected airway foreign body in a toddler with witnessed choking, focal wheeze, and unilateral air trapping on inspiration-expiration films is a definitive indication for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia. Bronchodilators, back blows, and CT all delay treatment. Children with peanut, seed, or hard food inhalation can present with a quiet asymptomatic phase before secondary pneumonia. Initial assessment focuses on whether the airway is patent and whether the child can phonate and cough effectively.
key_points: Witnessed choking with focal findings = bronchoscopy
Expiration film air trapping is a key radiological clue
Back blows only for complete obstruction in a basic life support sequence
Avoid bronchodilators or CT delays
explanation.pearls: Right main bronchus is the most common site for inhaled peanut in toddlers because of its more vertical orientation; ipsilateral air trapping on expiration film is the most sensitive radiographic sign.

subtopic_detail: Suspected button battery oesophageal ingestion in 2-year-old with delayed presentation
stem: You are the rural ED consultant reviewing a 2-year-old boy whose mother found him near a hearing-aid box six hours ago. He vomited once, refused dinner, and is now drooling with retrosternal discomfort. The nearest endoscopy service is at a tertiary hospital 90 minutes away by road retrieval. He has no stridor, intact saturation, and looks well perfused. The mother offered him milk to drink an hour ago; he kept it down.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 134, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent on air, BP 98/56
data_table.Examination: Drooling, refusing oral intake, mildly distressed; chest clear; no haemoptysis; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Chest and abdominal X-ray: 20 mm circular radiopaque object with double-rim halo lodged at the level of the thoracic inlet; no free air; no pneumomediastinum

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention before retrieval?

options.text: Administer 10 mL aliquots of oral honey every 10 minutes while awaiting retrieval transport
options.rationale: Oral honey within 12 hours of ingestion in a child over 12 months reduces oesophageal alkali injury severity pending endoscopic removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery; NCPP)

options.text: Withhold all oral intake and arrange immediate endoscopic removal at the local hospital
options.rationale: Local endoscopy is not available; oral nil by mouth alone offers no tissue protection during the transport delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery)

options.text: Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac to attempt expulsion before transfer to the tertiary centre
options.rationale: Induced vomiting risks aspiration, further mucosal injury, and is contraindicated for button battery ingestion. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 1 g/kg via cup to bind the battery contents before retrieval departure
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind battery alkali leakage and adds aspiration risk without altering tissue injury. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Insert a wide-bore nasogastric tube and attempt mechanical dislodgement of the battery toward the stomach
options.rationale: Blind NG manipulation risks oesophageal perforation and is not part of any current guideline. (Source: RCH CPG: Button battery)

explanation.summary: Oesophageal button battery is a time-critical emergency because alkali generation begins within two hours and full-thickness injury within four hours. Australian guidance supports oral honey 10 mL every 10 minutes in children older than 12 months presenting within 12 hours, awaiting endoscopic removal as the definitive treatment. Sucralfate suspension is an alternative in hospital. Imaging shows the characteristic double-rim halo on PA view and step-off on lateral, distinguishing battery from coin.
key_points: Time-critical: tissue injury within 2 to 4 hours
Honey 10 mL every 10 min if over 12 months and within 12 hours
Definitive treatment is endoscopic removal under anaesthesia
Never induce vomiting or attempt blind NG dislodgement
explanation.pearls: On PA chest X-ray a button battery shows a double-rim halo whereas a coin shows a single uniform edge; the lateral film shows a step-off at the negative pole that points to the side of greatest mucosal injury.

subtopic_detail: First-line investigation for global developmental delay with no syndromic features
stem: You are the paediatrician reviewing a 3-year-old boy referred for delay in all developmental domains. He is non-verbal, walks unsteadily, and has poor social engagement. There is no parental consanguinity, no regression, no seizures, and no dysmorphism. Hearing and vision testing are normal. Newborn screening was unremarkable and no metabolic decompensation history exists. Family is keen to identify a cause to guide reproductive counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 100, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 75th centile, height 70th centile, OFC 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Non-dysmorphic, normal cardiac and abdominal examination, normal genitalia, normal skin findings
data_table.Investigations: TSH, ferritin, creatine kinase, urine metabolic screen all normal; MRI brain not yet done

lead_in: What is the single best next investigation?

options.text: Karyotype with G-banding to screen for whole chromosome aneuploidy as a first step
options.rationale: Karyotype is reserved for suspected Down or Turner syndrome; it has lower yield than microarray for non-syndromic delay. (Source: RACP; HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.text: Chromosomal microarray as the first-tier genetic investigation for unexplained global delay
options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray is the first-line genetic test for unexplained global developmental delay or intellectual disability and detects copy number variants with about 15 percent yield. (Source: RACP; HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.text: MRI brain with contrast as the highest yield single investigation in this clinical setting
options.rationale: MRI is useful if there are focal neurological findings, microcephaly, regression, or seizures; otherwise yield is lower than microarray. (Source: RACP)

options.text: Whole exome sequencing as the first genetic test to bypass microarray triage entirely
options.rationale: Exome is a second-tier test in Australia after a normal microarray and fragile X, or when a specific syndrome is suspected. (Source: HGSA)
source_refs: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

options.text: EEG to exclude epileptic encephalopathy as the underlying cause of the delay
options.rationale: EEG is reserved for suspected seizures or regression; routine EEG is not part of the workup for global delay. (Source: RACP)

explanation.summary: Global developmental delay in a child without dysmorphism, regression, or seizures still has a high yield genetic basis. Chromosomal microarray is the first-tier genetic investigation in Australia, detecting clinically significant copy number variants in approximately 15 percent of unexplained cases. Fragile X testing is concurrent or sequential. Exome sequencing follows if first-tier testing is negative or if specific syndromic features emerge. Neuroimaging is reserved for focal neurological signs, microcephaly, regression, or seizures.
key_points: Microarray is first-tier for unexplained global delay
Fragile X testing is concurrent or sequential
Exome sequencing is second-tier after negative first-tier
Neuroimaging only if focal signs, microcephaly, regression, or seizures
explanation.pearls: Chromosomal microarray has a diagnostic yield of about 15 percent in non-syndromic global developmental delay versus about 3 percent for karyotype, which is why it has replaced karyotype as first-tier in Australian practice.

sources.label: HGSA: Genetic testing in developmental delay

subtopic_detail: Sentinel facial features in fetal alcohol spectrum disorder assessment
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 4-year-old boy referred by his kindergarten teacher for behavioural concerns and slow language.
