His birth mother has been open about ongoing alcohol use through the pregnancy. He is in long-term foster care. His foster mother reports impulsivity, poor emotion regulation, and difficulty following two-step instructions. Growth is below the 3rd centile for weight and length. There is no history of perinatal infection, head trauma, or seizures, and metabolic screening done at school entry was normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight 13.1 kg (<3rd centile), height 95 cm (<3rd centile), head circumference 47.5 cm (<3rd centile)
data_table.Facial findings: Short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border
data_table.Development: Receptive language 2 years 6 months, expressive language 2 years, gross motor age-appropriate
data_table.Hearing and vision: Audiology and ophthalmology screening normal in the last 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Send a chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing as the next investigation
options.rationale: Genetic testing is reserved for atypical features, additional dysmorphism, or when other syndromes are competing on the differential; the sentinel triad with confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure makes broad genetic testing low yield as the first step. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: Refer for multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment with standardised facial measurement
options.rationale: Australian diagnostic criteria require multidisciplinary assessment confirming three sentinel facial features and severe impairment in three or more neurodevelopmental domains, alongside documented prenatal exposure. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: Commence a 6-week trial of methylphenidate for presumed attentional and impulse difficulties
options.rationale: Stimulant trials may be considered after formal diagnosis and behavioural strategies have failed, not as a diagnostic shortcut in a 4-year-old with developmental concerns. (Source: RCH CPG: ADHD)

options.text: Arrange brain MRI to exclude a structural cause of the developmental delay
options.rationale: Routine MRI is not part of the diagnostic pathway when the clinical picture and prenatal exposure are typical; imaging is reserved for focal neurology or seizures. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

options.text: Reassure the family and re-review developmental progress in 6 months in clinic
options.rationale: Delaying assessment misses the early-intervention window that improves long-term outcomes when neurodevelopmental impairment is already evident. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

explanation.summary: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is diagnosed in Australia using the Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD, which requires either three sentinel facial features (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion) with confirmed or unknown prenatal alcohol exposure, OR severe neurodevelopmental impairment across three of ten domains with confirmed exposure. Multidisciplinary assessment is mandated. Early identification opens access to NDIS support, structured behavioural therapy, and educational accommodations. Stimulants may help comorbid attentional symptoms after diagnosis but are not the first response.
key_points: Three sentinel facial features plus exposure suffice for diagnosis of FASD with three sentinel features
Without all three facial features, severe impairment in 3 of 10 neurodevelopmental domains plus confirmed exposure is required
Growth restriction is supportive but not required for diagnosis
Multidisciplinary assessment is mandatory in the Australian framework
Early diagnosis unlocks NDIS and educational supports
explanation.pearls: Smooth philtrum and thin upper vermilion are scored against the University of Washington lip-philtrum guide, with rank 4 or 5 counting as a sentinel feature.

sources.label: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of FASD

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic pathway for suspected Hirschsprung disease in delayed meconium passage
stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a term male newborn on day 3 who has not passed meconium since birth and now has bilious vomiting after each feed. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 39 weeks. His abdomen is progressively distended, and a digital rectal examination produces a forceful expulsion of meconium and gas. He has not had any prior abdominal surgery. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis, and the newborn screening blood spot is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 158, RR 52, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Distended soft non-tender abdomen, visible bowel loops, no inguinal hernia, anus normally sited and patent
data_table.Hydration: Capillary refill 2 seconds, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 2.1 mmol/L; supine abdominal radiograph shows dilated bowel loops with paucity of rectal gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Proceed directly to laparotomy and intraoperative levelling biopsies under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgery is the definitive treatment after histological confirmation; proceeding without a confirmed diagnosis risks unnecessary laparotomy in alternative causes such as meconium plug or ileal atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

options.text: Request a water-soluble contrast enema to characterise the transition zone in colonic anatomy
options.rationale: Contrast enema is supportive but neonates often lack a mature transition zone; its sensitivity in the first weeks is limited and it does not establish histological diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

options.text: Arrange a suction rectal biopsy for histological assessment of ganglion cells
options.rationale: Suction rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells with hypertrophic nerve trunks is the definitive diagnostic test in neonates and can be done cot-side without anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

options.text: Trial high-dose oral lactulose and review the response over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Stool softeners do not address aganglionic obstruction and risk worsening proximal distension with enterocolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Hirschsprung disease)

options.text: Send sweat chloride testing to exclude meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis
options.rationale: Sweat testing is unreliable before 2 weeks of age and the explosive release of stool on rectal examination is classic for Hirschsprung rather than meconium ileus. (Source: RCH CPG: Cystic fibrosis)

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease presents in approximately 90 percent within the neonatal period with delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. The classic squirt sign on rectal examination is highly suggestive. Suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard. Contrast enema may identify a transition zone but is unreliable in neonates because the aganglionic segment has not yet hypertrophied proximally. Enterocolitis is the most dangerous early complication and warrants empiric antibiotics and rectal washouts.
key_points: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours is a red flag
Suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic test of choice
Histology shows absent ganglion cells with hypertrophic nerve trunks
Contrast enema sensitivity is limited in the neonatal period
Enterocolitis is the leading cause of mortality before surgery
explanation.pearls: Rectal biopsies must be taken at least 2 cm above the dentate line to avoid the physiologically hypoganglionic zone and a false-positive result.

subtopic_detail: Application of revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever in high-risk populations
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional Northern Territory hospital reviewing an 8-year-old Aboriginal girl with a 5-day history of migratory polyarthralgia and intermittent fevers. She had a sore throat 4 weeks ago that resolved without medical review. Her parents report she is no longer able to walk on the right knee. On examination she has a soft mid-systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender swelling of the right knee and left wrist.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 132, RR 24, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Investigations: ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP 92 mg/L, ASOT 800 IU/mL, ECG PR interval 180 ms (age-corrected upper limit), throat swab pending
data_table.Echocardiography: Pending; transthoracic study available later today
data_table.Skin findings: No subcutaneous nodules or erythema marginatum identified

lead_in: Which diagnostic conclusion is best supported by the available findings under the 2015 revised Jones criteria?

options.text: Definite acute rheumatic fever can be diagnosed on the current clinical and laboratory findings
options.rationale: In high-risk populations the revised Jones criteria allow polyarthralgia plus carditis (auscultatory mitral regurgitation murmur) as two major manifestations, with elevated ASOT confirming preceding streptococcal infection. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

options.text: Probable acute rheumatic fever is the most that can be assigned without echocardiography confirmation
options.rationale: Clinical carditis on auscultation contributes a major criterion even before echocardiogram, although echocardiography should still be obtained urgently for severity assessment. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

options.text: Possible acute rheumatic fever is the appropriate label until subcutaneous nodules develop on review
options.rationale: Subcutaneous nodules are uncommon and not required; the case already meets the high-risk threshold for definite disease. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

options.text: Reactive arthritis is the more likely diagnosis given the migratory pattern of joint symptoms
options.rationale: Reactive arthritis would not produce a new murmur or ESR over 60, both of which fulfil rheumatic fever criteria. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

options.text: Septic arthritis must be excluded by joint aspiration before any rheumatic fever diagnosis
options.rationale: Septic arthritis is monoarticular and severely tender with a single hot joint; the migratory polyarthropathy and systemic features here do not fit. (Source: RHDAustralia 3rd edition guideline)

explanation.summary: The 2015 revised Jones criteria split populations into low-risk and high-risk. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from northern Australia are categorised as high-risk, in whom polyarthralgia counts as a major criterion and monoarthritis (with high-grade fever and elevated inflammatory markers) can also count. Two major, or one major plus two minor, manifestations plus evidence of streptococcal infection fulfils definite disease. Echocardiography is mandatory for severity grading and may upgrade clinical carditis or detect subclinical carditis. Lifelong benzathine penicillin G is the keystone of secondary prevention.
key_points: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from northern Australia are high-risk for application of Jones criteria
High-risk thresholds count polyarthralgia and monoarthritis as major manifestations
Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (ASOT, anti-DNase B, swab) is required
Echocardiography is mandatory for severity and may detect subclinical carditis
Benzathine penicillin G every 21-28 days is the standard secondary prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: ESR over 60 mm/hr or CRP over 30 mg/L counts as a minor criterion in the high-risk threshold; together with raised temperature over 38 degrees this scenario also satisfies two minor criteria.

subtopic_detail: Stepwise escalation of atopic eczema flare beyond moisturiser and mild topical steroid
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a severe atopic eczema flare across the trunk and limbs. Her mother has applied liberal sorbolene and 1 percent hydrocortisone cream twice daily for 7 days with worsening lichenification and excoriation. There is no honey-coloured crusting, fever, or vesicular lesions. The family demonstrates good technique with moisturiser. Her sleep has been disturbed for 4 nights.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Skin examination: Diffuse erythema with lichenification at antecubital and popliteal fossae, excoriations, no pustules or oozing crust
data_table.Atopic background: Egg-allergy infancy, sibling with asthma, dust mite specific IgE strongly positive
data_table.Previous treatments: Sorbolene 3 times daily, 1 percent hydrocortisone twice daily for 7 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue 1 percent hydrocortisone twice daily and review the response again in 7 days
options.rationale: Mild steroid has failed after a full week; persisting risks ongoing skin damage and steroid phobia. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric dermatologist for ciclosporin or methotrexate consideration
options.rationale: Systemic immunosuppression is reserved for severe disease refractory to a moderate-potency topical steroid trial with wet wraps. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 5 days to settle the flare quickly
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids cause rebound flare on cessation and are not recommended for routine atopic eczema flares. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent once daily with wet-wrap bandages overnight
options.rationale: Moderate-potency steroid plus wet wraps is the recommended escalation for moderate to severe flares not controlled on mild steroid, with rapid response and good safety in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Switch to topical pimecrolimus twice daily as steroid-sparing maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Calcineurin inhibitors are indicated for sensitive areas or as steroid-sparing once a flare has settled; they are too slow as the primary flare treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

explanation.summary: Atopic eczema flares follow a stepwise approach: liberal emollients, low-potency topical corticosteroid, moderate-potency steroid with or without wet wraps, then specialist input for phototherapy or systemic therapy. Wet-wrap therapy uses a moist tubular layer over the steroid plus emollient to enhance penetration, cool the skin, and improve sleep. It is suitable for short courses of 3 to 5 nights. Steroid phobia is best addressed by demonstrating the fingertip unit and explaining that under-treatment causes more skin damage than appropriate steroid use.
key_points: Step up potency rather than persisting with an inadequate strength steroid
Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent is moderate-potency and once-daily
Wet wraps amplify steroid penetration and reduce excoriation
Oral corticosteroids cause rebound and are avoided in routine eczema
Calcineurin inhibitors are best for sensitive areas or maintenance
explanation.pearls: Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent applied once daily is approximately equivalent in potency to twice-daily betamethasone valerate 0.05 percent and is preferred in young children for the lower potency-to-effect ratio.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Atopic dermatitis

subtopic_detail: Renal monitoring and referral thresholds in Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy 4 weeks after a presentation with palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower limbs, abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle arthritis. He met clinical criteria for Henoch-Schonlein purpura and his skin and joint symptoms resolved within 10 days. His mother reports cola-coloured urine over the last 2 days. He is otherwise well, eating and drinking normally, with no oedema. The local emergency department sent a urine sample at the time of presentation that was negative for blood and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 96, RR 20, BP 122/78 mmHg (>95th centile for height)
data_table.Blood results: Creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 35), urea 9.1 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange a repeat urine dipstick and blood pressure check in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with rising creatinine and hypertension is not benign and demands urgent specialist input rather than community follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks and review in clinic in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Steroids alone do not reliably prevent progression of established nephritis and starting without renal biopsy planning misses the diagnostic step that guides therapy. (Source: KHA-CARI: HSP nephritis)

options.text: Start oral aspirin and discharge with a 2-week clinic review for joint symptoms
options.rationale: Aspirin does not address established nephritis and the joint symptoms have already resolved. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Order renal ultrasound and discharge with general practitioner urinalysis monitoring weekly
options.rationale: Ultrasound rarely changes management in HSP nephritis and weekly GP monitoring fails to act on already established nephrotic-range disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Refer immediately to paediatric nephrology for inpatient assessment and renal biopsy planning
options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypertension and an acute creatinine rise meets Australian criteria for urgent paediatric nephrology referral and biopsy to guide immunosuppression. (Source: KHA-CARI: HSP nephritis)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis is the most important long-term complication of HSP and can develop weeks after the rash and joint symptoms have resolved. All children require monthly urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring for 6 months because nephritis can develop late. Mild urinary abnormalities are followed; nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, acute kidney injury, or persistent moderate proteinuria warrant nephrology referral and biopsy. Treatment is guided by ISKDC histology grade and may include corticosteroids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide for crescentic disease.
key_points: Monthly urinalysis and BP for 6 months after HSP onset
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is urine protein creatinine ratio above 250 mg/mmol
Rising creatinine, nephrotic range proteinuria or hypertension trigger nephrology referral
Biopsy directs immunosuppressive intensity
Late onset of nephritis up to 6 months after rash is well-recognised
explanation.pearls: ISKDC grade 3 or higher crescentic HSP nephritis is the histological threshold above which Australian centres typically add mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide to prednisolone.

subtopic_detail: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy management ladder in infancy
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 5-month-old infant with a 6-week history of loose blood-streaked stools, eczema flare, and unsettled feeding. He is exclusively breastfed and his weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile. There has been no acute reaction to any food, no hives, no swelling, and no vomiting. The mother has tried eliminating dairy from her own diet for 1 week with partial improvement. Skin prick testing to cow milk is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 122, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 6.5 kg (25th centile, dropping), length 65 cm (25th centile), head circ 42 cm (25th centile)
data_table.Stool examination: Mucus and visible blood streaks, no diarrhoea
data_table.Examination: Mild eczema in antecubital fossae, soft non-tender abdomen, no perianal fissure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue maternal dairy exclusion strictly for at least 2 to 4 weeks with dietitian support
options.rationale: Non-IgE cow milk protein allergy in a breastfed infant is managed by complete maternal dairy elimination for a minimum 2 to 4 weeks before judging response, with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

options.text: Switch immediately to extensively hydrolysed formula and cease breastfeeding now
options.rationale: Cessation of breastfeeding is not required and is harmful when maternal elimination can be trialled successfully in non-IgE disease. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

options.text: Switch immediately to amino acid based formula given the bleeding per rectum
options.rationale: Amino acid formula is reserved for severe enteropathy, anaphylaxis history, or failure of extensively hydrolysed formula. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

options.text: Refer for paediatric gastroscopy and colonoscopy to exclude infantile inflammatory bowel disease
options.rationale: Inflammatory bowel disease is rare in this age group and the clinical picture fits non-IgE cow milk protein allergy; endoscopy is reserved for failure of elimination. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

options.text: Trial soy formula for 2 weeks and review symptoms in clinic at the end of the trial
options.rationale: Up to 30 percent of infants with cow milk protein allergy will also react to soy, so it is not a recommended first-line alternative. (Source: ASCIA: Cow milk allergy)

explanation.summary: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy commonly presents in the first 6 months with proctocolitis (blood-streaked mucousy stools in an otherwise well infant), enteropathy, or chronic GORD-like symptoms. Skin prick test is negative because it is non-IgE mediated. In breastfed infants, maternal cow milk exclusion is first line for at least 2 to 4 weeks with dietetic input and calcium plus vitamin D supplementation. If symptoms persist or the infant is formula-fed, extensively hydrolysed formula is next; amino acid formula is reserved for failure or severe disease. Cow milk should be reintroduced at 9 to 12 months to assess tolerance.
key_points: Non-IgE CMPA is diagnosed clinically; skin prick test is negative
Maternal dairy exclusion in breastfed infants is first line
Extensively hydrolysed formula is next when not breastfed
Amino acid formula is reserved for failure or severe disease
30 percent cross-react with soy; soy is not first line
explanation.pearls: Reintroduce cow milk at 9 to 12 months using the milk ladder to assess tolerance; up to 80 percent of children with non-IgE CMPA tolerate cow milk by age 3 years.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow milk protein allergy

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of incomplete (atypical) Kawasaki disease in infants
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy on day 6 of unexplained high fevers despite appropriate empiric ceftriaxone. He has a fine truncal rash, conjunctival injection without exudate, and red dry lips but no extremity changes, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and no oral cavity changes. Blood and urine cultures are sterile at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR is negative. Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 168, RR 38, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 12.1 x10^9/L, platelets 540 x10^9/L, ALT 85 U/L, albumin 27 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue empiric ceftriaxone for a further 48 hours and review for clinical change
options.rationale: Persisting bacterial therapy alone delays Kawasaki recognition and increases the risk of coronary aneurysm beyond day 10. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge with safety-net advice and arrange community paediatrician review in 1 week
options.rationale: Discharge before excluding Kawasaki disease in a febrile infant beyond day 5 is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Obtain echocardiography and treat with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin given supplemental criteria are met
options.rationale: Infants under 12 months with prolonged unexplained fever and at least 3 supplemental laboratory criteria (CRP >=30, ESR >=40, anaemia, platelets >=450 after day 7, albumin <=30, sterile pyuria, raised ALT) meet incomplete Kawasaki criteria and receive IVIG plus aspirin; echo guides surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 5 days as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not first line; adjunctive steroids are considered alongside IVIG in high-risk children, not as a stand-alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Order a chest computed tomography to investigate alternative infectious aetiologies
options.rationale: CT chest does not address the most likely diagnosis and exposes the infant to unnecessary radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is most likely in infants under 12 months and carries the highest coronary aneurysm risk if missed. Diagnosis requires fever for at least 5 days plus 2 or 3 of the classical criteria, with supplemental laboratory criteria substituting for absent clinical features. IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus aspirin (high or moderate dose) should be given by day 10 to minimise coronary risk. Echocardiography is performed at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks. High-risk infants may benefit from concomitant corticosteroid or infliximab.
key_points: Infants under 12 months often present incompletely and have the highest coronary risk
Supplemental criteria: CRP, ESR, albumin, anaemia, late platelet rise, pyuria, ALT
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin by day 10 is the standard treatment
Echocardiography at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks
Adjunct steroid or infliximab is considered in high-risk infants
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria in a febrile infant beyond day 5 is a classic Kawasaki clue and should not be misattributed to a partially-treated urinary tract infection.

sources.label: American Heart Association: Kawasaki disease scientific statement

subtopic_detail: Indications and timing of adenotonsillectomy in paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea
stem: You are the GP referred a 5-year-old girl by her preschool teacher for daytime inattention and morning headaches. Her parents describe loud nightly snoring with witnessed apnoeic pauses and restless sleep. She has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile for weight. There is no rhinitis, no recurrent tonsillitis, and no atopic history. She has tonsils that touch the uvula and a Mallampati class III oropharynx.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 96, RR 22, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 96 percent room air awake
data_table.Growth: Weight 16 kg (10th centile, falling), height 110 cm (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Mouth breathing, mild adenoidal facies, no inspiratory stridor, no rhinitis
data_table.Polysomnography (recent): Obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index 8.4 per hour, nadir SpO2 87 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ENT for adenotonsillectomy as the first-line treatment of moderate paediatric OSA
options.rationale: An obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index above 5 with tonsillar hypertrophy is moderate paediatric OSA and Australian guidelines support adenotonsillectomy as first-line surgical management. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

options.text: Trial intranasal mometasone for 6 weeks before any referral for surgical intervention
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid is reserved for mild OSA (OAHI 1 to 5) or as adjunct in persistent symptoms after surgery; it is not appropriate for moderate OSA. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

options.text: Commence trial of continuous positive airway pressure overnight while awaiting outpatient review
options.rationale: CPAP is the option when adenotonsillectomy is contraindicated, declined, or unsuccessful; it is not first-line in a typical child with tonsillar hypertrophy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

options.text: Order MRI airway to characterise the anatomy before any surgical referral is generated
options.rationale: Airway MRI is reserved for complex craniofacial syndromes or post-surgical persistent OSA, not initial assessment of typical adenotonsillar hypertrophy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

options.text: Reassure parents and arrange a sleep position trial with lateral positioning at night
options.rationale: Positional therapy is inadequate for moderate disease with daytime symptoms and growth faltering. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Paediatric OSA)

explanation.summary: Paediatric OSA is graded by the obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index: 1 to 5 mild, 5 to 10 moderate, above 10 severe. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the leading cause. Adenotonsillectomy is first-line for moderate and severe disease in otherwise well children, with cure rates of around 70 to 80 percent. Children with persistent symptoms after surgery, contraindications, or syndromic airways need CPAP. Untreated OSA causes daytime inattention, behavioural disturbance, growth faltering (from disrupted growth hormone secretion), enuresis, and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension.
key_points: OAHI 5 to 10 is moderate paediatric OSA
Adenotonsillectomy is first line in tonsillar hypertrophy
Intranasal steroid is for mild OSA, not moderate or severe
CPAP is second line after surgery failure or contraindication
Growth faltering can reverse after successful surgery
explanation.pearls: Children under 3 years, severe OSA, or significant comorbidity warrant overnight inpatient monitoring after adenotonsillectomy because of higher rates of respiratory complications.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called by the neonatal nurse about a term baby born at 39+5 weeks gestation, now 60 hours of age. The baby is appropriate weight for age (3.4 kg), exclusively breastfed, and has been admitted to the special care nursery for visible jaundice extending to the legs. The infant is feeding well, alert, with no neurological abnormality.

Mother is blood group O Rh positive; baby is group A Rh positive with positive direct Coombs test. Bloods show total serum bilirubin 410 micromol/L, unconjugated 390, conjugated 20, Hb 142 g/L, reticulocytes 5%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 44, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.9, weight 3.4 kg
data_table.Examination: Jaundice to legs (Kramer zone 4); alert; tone normal; no opisthotonus or high-pitched cry
data_table.Investigations: TSB 410 micromol/L (unconjugated 390, conjugated 20); Hb 142, retic 5%; DAT positive; baby A Rh+, mother O Rh+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home with general practitioner heel-prick total serum bilirubin re-check arranged within 24 hours of leaving the special care nursery
options.rationale: Bilirubin 410 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with positive DAT and ABO incompatibility approaches the exchange transfusion threshold; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

options.text: Stop breastfeeding completely and switch to exclusive infant formula feeding for the next 48 hours while keeping the infant in special care nursery
options.rationale: Brief formula supplementation may be considered in dehydration but ceasing breastfeeding is not first-line for hyperbilirubinaemia and does not lower bilirubin rapidly enough. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

options.text: Commence intensive multiple-bank phototherapy, ensure adequate hydration, and recheck the serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours without scavenger therapy
options.rationale: Intensive phototherapy and close re-check are appropriate, but at TSB 410 micromol/L at 60 hours of age with DAT-positive haemolysis, immediate exchange criteria are likely already met under Australian charts; preparation should be active rather than contingent. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

options.text: Start intensive multi-bank phototherapy, give IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg over 2 hours, ensure hydration, prepare for exchange transfusion via tertiary unit
options.rationale: Australian and NICE guidance recommend intensive phototherapy plus IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg for haemolytic disease when TSB approaches exchange thresholds, with active preparation for double-volume exchange in a tertiary unit if rapid response is not achieved. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

options.text: Administer oral phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg as hepatic enzyme induction therapy to enhance bilirubin clearance over the next 24-48 hour treatment period
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone enzyme induction is not standard acute management for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia in Australia and is not effective rapidly enough for this urgent presentation. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline Neonatal Jaundice 2022)

explanation.summary: ABO haemolytic disease with DAT-positive haemolysis in a term infant produces rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin. At 60 hours of age, total serum bilirubin 410 micromol/L approaches exchange transfusion thresholds on Australian nomograms. Management is intensive multi-bank phototherapy plus IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg in haemolytic disease, ensuring hydration, and active preparation for double-volume exchange transfusion in a tertiary neonatal unit if bilirubin does not fall or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy develop. Always plot age in hours against current bilirubin chart.
key_points: Plot bilirubin against postnatal age in hours, not days
Intensive multi-bank phototherapy first-line for severe hyperbilirubinaemia
IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg in DAT-positive haemolytic disease near exchange threshold
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy signs trigger immediate exchange
explanation.pearls: In a DAT-positive ABO haemolytic newborn at 60 hours with TSB approaching the exchange line, give IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg over 2 hours alongside intensive phototherapy rather than waiting for the next bilirubin to fail therapy - IVIG reduces exchange need substantially in isoimmune haemolysis.

sources.label: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days 2010 (updated)

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department reviewing an 11-month-old boy brought in by his parents with three episodes of inconsolable crying with leg-drawing each lasting around 8 minutes over the past four hours. Between episodes he is pale but responsive. He vomited bile-stained fluid once. His last bowel motion 90 minutes ago had a small amount of dark-red jelly-like material.

Examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, no peritonism, and capillary refill of 2 seconds. Abdominal ultrasound confirms ileocolic intussusception. There is no free air on AXR.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, BP 88/52, RR 36, SpO2 99%, Temp 37.4, weight 9.2 kg, CRT 2 s
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes; soft abdomen with palpable sausage mass RUQ; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: target sign at ileocaecal junction with no free fluid; FBC, UEC, glucose normal; lactate 1.4; AXR no free air or obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management step now?

options.text: Discharge home with detailed parental safety-netting advice and primary care review arranged within 12 hours of leaving the emergency department
options.rationale: Untreated intussusception progresses to bowel ischaemia, perforation and shock; observation off-site is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and observe for the next 24 hours before deciding on further imaging or operative interventions
options.rationale: Imaging has already confirmed the diagnosis; broad-spectrum antibiotics without reduction does not treat the obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

options.text: Resuscitate with isotonic IV fluid bolus 10-20 mL/kg, then transfer for air enema reduction by interventional radiology with paediatric surgery standby
options.rationale: Confirmed ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonitis is treated by air enema reduction in a tertiary or paediatric centre after resuscitation; paediatric surgery is on standby for perforation or failed reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

options.text: Proceed directly to operative laparotomy and surgical reduction without first attempting any non-operative pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction
options.rationale: Non-operative reduction by air enema succeeds in 80-90% of cases without perforation or peritonitis and is the first-line definitive management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

options.text: Trial a barium contrast enema with a delayed abdominal radiograph at 8 hours to confirm reduction before considering surgical intervention pathways
options.rationale: Air enema is preferred over barium because of lower perforation risk and cleaner imaging; barium delay is not part of current Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception 2020)

explanation.summary: Intussusception in a previously well infant or toddler presents with intermittent inconsolable crying with leg-drawing, vomiting, lethargy between episodes and the late sign of red-currant-jelly stool. Ultrasound confirms with the target or pseudo-kidney sign. After IV access and fluid resuscitation, definitive management is air (pneumatic) enema reduction performed by paediatric radiology with paediatric surgery on standby. Reduction is successful in 80-90% without perforation. Surgery is required for perforation, peritonitis, shock, failed reduction, or a pathological lead point.
key_points: Triad: intermittent inconsolable crying, vomiting, red-currant-jelly stool (late)
Ultrasound first-line for diagnosis (target / pseudo-kidney sign)
Air enema reduction first-line definitive treatment
Surgery for perforation, peritonitis, failed reduction or pathological lead point
explanation.pearls: In an 11-month-old with ileocolic intussusception confirmed on ultrasound and no perforation, transfer for air enema rather than barium - pneumatic reduction has a 80-90 percent success rate with lower perforation risk, and tertiary radiology can usually accommodate within hours.

sources.label: NSW Health Paediatric Clinical Practice Guideline Acute Abdominal Pain 2019

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in the ED reviewing a 7-week-old infant brought in by her mother with a 9-day history of progressively worsening cough. The infant has paroxysms of cough up to 12 per day, three episodes of apnoea overnight noted by the parents, and occasional cyanosis with coughing. She feeds intermittently. She has had her 6-week immunisations. Her older brother (4 years) had a coryzal illness with cough two weeks ago that has now resolved. On examination the chest is clear between paroxysms. NPA is sent for pertussis PCR. SpO2 between paroxysms is 96%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 50 between paroxysms, SpO2 96% between paroxysms, Temp 37.1, weight 4.6 kg
data_table.Examination: Vigorous baby between episodes; paroxysmal cough with cyanosis and three apnoeas overnight; chest clear; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 28 with lymphocytosis 22; CXR clear; pertussis NPA PCR pending

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate antimicrobial?

options.text: Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg orally three times daily for a 7-day course as the principal antimicrobial therapy in this case
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolides are the antimicrobial of choice in pertussis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019 - Pertussis)

options.text: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for a 5-day course as first-line antimicrobial in this young infant presentation
options.rationale: Azithromycin is first-line antimicrobial therapy for pertussis in infants under 1 month and is preferred over erythromycin because of lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the standard Australian regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

options.text: Erythromycin 10 mg/kg orally four times daily for a 14-day course as the first-line macrolide for young infant pertussis
options.rationale: Erythromycin in infants under 1 month carries increased risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; azithromycin is preferred. Even in older infants the shorter azithromycin course is favoured. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 8/40 mg/kg orally twice daily for 14 days as first-choice antimicrobial in this young infant pertussis case
options.rationale: TMP-SMX is an alternative in macrolide intolerance only and is contraindicated in infants under 2 months because of kernicterus risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg orally twice daily for a 7-day course as first-line antimicrobial therapy in this young infant pertussis presentation
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are not active against Bordetella pertussis and are not used for this indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in young infants is a notifiable disease in Australia and admission is required for infants under 6 months with apnoea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for 5 days is the first-line antimicrobial for pertussis in infants under 1 month and is preferred over erythromycin because of lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Macrolides reduce transmission but do not modify illness once the paroxysmal phase is established. Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts including unimmunised infants is indicated. The lymphocytosis is characteristic.
key_points: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day x 5 days - first line, especially under 1 month
Erythromycin in young infants risks hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Notifiable to public health
Admission for under-6-month-olds with apnoea or feeding compromise
explanation.pearls: In any infant under 1 month with suspected pertussis, prescribe azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days rather than erythromycin to avoid infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis - the absolute risk on erythromycin is increased about 10-fold.

stem:
A 5-week-old male infant is referred to your paediatric surgical unit with a two-week history of progressively worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds. He is hungry between feeds. Examination reveals a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis. He has dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 3 seconds, and depressed fontanelle. Weight has dropped from 4.0 kg to 3.6 kg over two weeks.

VBG shows pH 7.55, HCO3 38, base excess +14, Cl 86, Na 134, K 2.9. Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis with muscle thickness 4.5 mm and channel length 18 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 38, SpO2 99%, weight 3.6 kg (was 4.0 kg), CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, depressed fontanelle, palpable olive RUQ, visible peristalsis; lethargic but rousable
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.55, HCO3 38, BE +14, Cl 86, Na 134, K 2.9, glucose 4.2; ultrasound: muscle thickness 4.5 mm, channel 18 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Proceed directly to definitive pyloromyotomy operatively within the first hour of arrival to the paediatric surgical receiving unit
options.rationale: Surgery for pyloric stenosis is a semi-urgent rather than emergency procedure; the priority is correcting hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before anaesthesia to reduce apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

options.text: Commence 5% dextrose at a maintenance rate of 5 mL/kg/h with no sodium chloride or potassium electrolyte additives prescribed initially
options.rationale: Dextrose without sodium and chloride fails to correct the hypochloraemic alkalosis and worsens hyponatraemia risk; balanced sodium chloride containing fluid is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

options.text: Bolus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg, then 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose plus KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, book surgery when Cl >100 HCO3 <30
options.rationale: RCH guidance: 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus for hypoperfusion, then 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose and KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, with surgery once Cl >100 mmol/L and HCO3 <30 mmol/L because uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

options.text: Give 40 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline followed by intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic alkalosis prior to operative planning
options.rationale: Giving bicarbonate worsens existing metabolic alkalosis and is contraindicated; the alkalosis resolves with chloride and potassium replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

options.text: Place a nasogastric tube on free drainage and continue trial of small frequent oral feeds while awaiting elective surgical fixation in 24 hours
options.rationale: Continued oral feeds will worsen vomiting and electrolyte derangement; NPO with NG drainage and IV resuscitation is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis 2019)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3-6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds in a hungry infant. The metabolic derangement is hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss. Surgical correction is semi-urgent; the priority before anaesthesia is to correct hypoperfusion (20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus), then to replace chloride and potassium with 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose plus KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, with serial VBG and electrolytes until Cl >100, HCO3 <30 and K >3.5. Uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-anaesthetic apnoea.
key_points: Correct fluid and electrolyte derangement before surgery
Bolus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg if hypoperfused, then 0.45% saline + 5% dextrose + KCl at 1.5 x maintenance
Target Cl >100 mmol/L, HCO3 <30 mmol/L before theatre
Avoid bicarbonate; the alkalosis is the problem
explanation.pearls: Aim for serum chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy rather than rushing to theatre - uncorrected hypochloraemic alkalosis raises postoperative apnoea risk substantially and is the single most modifiable peri-operative variable.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline Paediatric IV fluids 2021

stem: A 6-year-old girl with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy presents to your tertiary paediatric ED via ambulance with a 2-hour history of fever 39.0 degrees and lethargy. She had vincristine 5 days ago. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter in situ. Capillary refill is 3 seconds, BP 88/52, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 98%. The line site is clean. She has no penicillin allergy. Her last neutrophil count three days ago was 0.4 x 10^9/L. Blood cultures are about to be drawn from line and peripherally.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 88/52, RR 28, SpO2 98%, Temp 39.0, weight 22 kg, CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, alert but tired; CVC site clean; no focal source on full examination
data_table.Investigations: Bloods drawn peripherally and from line; FBC pending; previous ANC 0.4 x 10^9/L three days ago
data_table.Medications: 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, recent vincristine; allopurinol; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis on Mondays and Tuesdays

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial regimen to commence within the first hour?

options.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after cultures, adding vancomycin only for haemodynamic instability, mucositis or proven line infection
options.rationale: Australian paediatric oncology febrile neutropenia protocols recommend piperacillin-tazobactam as first-line empiric monotherapy after cultures, with vancomycin added for shock, mucositis, MRSA risk or proven line infection. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 25 mg/kg three times daily with outpatient discharge and clinic review at 24 hours in haematology day unit
options.rationale: Outpatient oral antibiotics are reserved for selected low-risk febrile neutropenia in older children with predicted short neutropenia, not for a 6-year-old with haemodynamic compromise. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

options.text: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg intravenously once daily as empiric monotherapy throughout the first 48 hours of suspected febrile neutropenia in this child
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has limited Pseudomonas activity and is not recommended as monotherapy in febrile neutropenia in Australia; antipseudomonal beta-lactam is required. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

options.text: Meropenem 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours plus amikacin 15 mg/kg IV once daily as routine first-line empiric combination for all febrile neutropenia
options.rationale: Carbapenems are reserved for escalation, suspected ESBL or septic shock not responding to first-line therapy; routine empirical use risks resistance. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

options.text: Withhold all antibiotics until the central venous catheter is removed and the blood culture microbiology results have returned to clinical team
options.rationale: Withholding empiric antibiotics in suspected febrile neutropenia substantially increases mortality; empiric therapy must start within 60 minutes of presentation. (Source: COSA/eviQ Paediatric Febrile Neutropenia 2020)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia in paediatric oncology is a medical emergency. Australian COSA and eviQ guidance is to draw blood cultures (peripheral and from line) and start empiric antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV) within 60 minutes of presentation. Vancomycin is added for haemodynamic instability, severe mucositis, suspected line infection, MRSA colonisation, or proven Gram-positive isolate. Carbapenems are reserved for escalation. Source control of the central venous catheter is reassessed when there is persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy.
key_points: Door-to-antibiotic time within 60 minutes
First line: piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after cultures
Add vancomycin for shock, mucositis, line infection or MRSA risk
Escalate to carbapenem for clinical deterioration or resistant isolate
explanation.pearls: Aim for door-to-antibiotic time under 60 minutes with piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after blood cultures - every additional hour of delayed empiric antibiotic therapy is associated with measurable increases in paediatric febrile neutropenia mortality.

subtopic_detail: Perthes vs slipped upper femoral epiphysis
stem:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to your general practice by his mother with a 3-week history of intermittent right hip pain and a limp. He is in the 95th centile for weight at 78 kg and 50th for height. He has noticed his right foot turns outward when he walks, and he keeps the leg externally rotated when sitting. There is no fever, no recent illness, and no trauma.

Examination shows restricted internal rotation of the right hip with obligate external rotation when the hip is flexed (positive Drehmann sign). Bilateral AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs of both hips show mild posteromedial slippage of the right capital femoral epiphysis along the Klein line.

data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait with externally rotated right limb; restricted internal rotation right hip; obligate external rotation on hip flexion (positive Drehmann); no warmth or effusion
data_table.Investigations: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis: right capital femoral epiphysis posteromedially displaced relative to Klein line; left hip: equivocal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommend gradual weight loss and arrange clinic review with repeat plain radiographs of both hips in three months from today's primary care visit
options.rationale: SUFE is a surgical emergency; delaying definitive fixation risks progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

options.text: Commence ibuprofen analgesia and physiotherapy with planned outpatient orthopaedic review in six weeks once the symptoms have begun to improve
options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory and physiotherapy management is inappropriate for SUFE; mobilisation increases risk of further slip and AVN. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

options.text: Make him non-weight-bearing immediately, admit to paediatric orthopaedics, refer for urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation per RCH protocol
options.rationale: SUFE diagnosis on imaging requires immediate non-weight-bearing, admission and urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation to prevent progression and AVN; prophylactic contralateral fixation is considered for high-risk individuals. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

options.text: Order MRI of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis radiographically before referring on for orthopaedic surgical opinion and operative planning later
options.rationale: Plain radiographs already confirm the diagnosis; MRI is not required and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

options.text: Manage as Perthes disease with abduction bracing and physiotherapy with quarterly clinical and radiographic review by primary care general practitioner
options.rationale: Perthes typically presents in younger children (4-8 years) and has a different radiographic pattern; bracing is incorrect management for SUFE. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE 2019)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis classically presents in obese pre-adolescent males (10-14 years) with knee or thigh pain, antalgic gait and externally rotated lower limb. Drehmann sign (obligate external rotation when the hip is flexed) and disruption of the Klein line on AP pelvis x-ray are diagnostic. SUFE is a surgical emergency requiring non-weight-bearing on diagnosis, admission and urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation. Prophylactic contralateral fixation is considered for high-risk patients (endocrine disease, very young, very obese). Avascular necrosis risk rises with weight-bearing and instability.
key_points: Obese pre-adolescent male with externally rotated limb and limp
Drehmann sign and Klein line disruption are diagnostic
Non-weight-bearing immediately on diagnosis
Urgent in-situ single-screw fixation; consider prophylactic contralateral fixation
explanation.pearls: When SUFE is confirmed radiographically, instruct strict non-weight-bearing in the clinic that same visit and arrange same-day orthopaedic admission - the rate of avascular necrosis rises substantially with continued ambulation in an unstable slip.

sources.label: AOA Position Statement: Paediatric hip emergencies 2019

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the special care nursery to a previously well-appearing term male neonate born at 39 weeks who is now 60 hours of age. Over the past 12 hours he has become progressively lethargic, then irritable with hyperventilation, refusing feeds, with a brief tonic-clonic seizure 30 minutes ago. He has had no fever. There is no perinatal sepsis history.

There was no antenatal newborn screening result yet because the heel prick was taken at 48 hours. Bloods show NH3 540 micromol/L, respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.51, PaCO2 26, HCO3 22), glucose 4.1, lactate 2.0, anion gap 12, normal LFTs, normal coagulation, normal infection markers. There is no ketonuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 70 (hyperventilation), Temp 36.7, SpO2 99%, weight 3.4 kg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, hyperventilating, post-ictal; soft anterior fontanelle; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: NH3 540 micromol/L; ABG pH 7.51, PaCO2 26, HCO3 22, BE -1; glucose 4.1; lactate 2.0; anion gap 12; no ketosis; LFTs normal; coagulation normal; CRP <5; CSF acellular

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate emergency management?

options.text: Increase enteral protein intake aggressively to drive metabolic ammonia clearance via the residual ureagenesis catabolic pathway in this neonate
options.rationale: Protein loading worsens hyperammonaemia in urea cycle disorders by adding nitrogen substrate; protein must be stopped acutely. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

options.text: Withhold all treatment until a definitive enzymatic urea cycle diagnosis is confirmed by tertiary metabolic biochemistry and molecular genetic testing
options.rationale: Each hour at ammonia >500 micromol/L worsens neurodevelopmental outcome; empirical treatment must begin before diagnostic confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and gut decontamination with oral lactulose to reduce enteric ammoniagenesis and clear circulating ammonia
options.rationale: Lactulose has no role in inborn-error hyperammonaemia; this is a urea cycle disorder, not portosystemic shunting. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

options.text: Stop protein, give 10% dextrose with intralipid, sodium benzoate plus phenylbutyrate plus arginine scavengers, prepare haemodialysis if NH3 stays >400-500
options.rationale: Australian metabolic services manage acute hyperammonaemia by stopping protein, reversing catabolism with high-dose IV dextrose and lipid, giving ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, arginine) and triggering haemodialysis at ammonia 400-500 micromol/L or rising; this is the time-critical sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg as the principal pharmacological intervention to reverse acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in this neonatal presentation
options.rationale: Mannitol is reserved for raised intracranial pressure as adjunct in cerebral oedema and does not lower ammonia; it is not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia 2020)

explanation.summary: A previously well neonate who becomes encephalopathic on day two or three of life with hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis), no acidosis, no ketosis and ammonia greater than 200 micromol/L (often >500) is highly suspicious for a urea cycle disorder, most commonly ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency in males. Emergency management is to stop protein intake, reverse catabolism with high concentration IV dextrose with insulin if needed and intralipid, give ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, arginine) per state metabolic team protocol, and arrange emergency haemodialysis when ammonia exceeds 400-500 micromol/L or fails to fall. Neurodevelopmental outcome correlates closely with duration and peak of hyperammonaemia.
key_points: Urea cycle disorders present with encephalopathy + respiratory alkalosis + hyperammonaemia + no ketosis
Stop protein, reverse catabolism with high IV dextrose and lipid
Sodium benzoate + sodium phenylbutyrate + arginine as scavengers
Haemodialysis at NH3 >400-500 micromol/L or rising
explanation.pearls: Trigger haemodialysis at ammonia 400-500 micromol/L or any rising trend despite scavengers rather than waiting for clinical deterioration - neurodevelopmental outcome correlates more tightly with duration of NH3 above 200 micromol/L than peak level.

stem:
A 2-year-old previously well boy presents to your emergency department with one day of barking cough, hoarse voice and now severe inspiratory stridor at rest with marked sternal and intercostal recession. He is alert but anxious. The triage nurse reports oxygen saturations 93% on room air. He had a low-grade fever the day before. His vaccinations are up to date.

He has no drooling, has been drinking small volumes, and there is no neck swelling. The nurse asks what treatment to give immediately at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, BP not done, RR 42, SpO2 93% on RA, Temp 37.4
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest; marked recession; anxious; mild reduction in air entry both fields
data_table.Investigations: Westley score 8 (severe); clinical diagnosis; no bloods or imaging required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate initial management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with concurrent single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram while preparing escalation pathway with anaesthetics
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and recession warrants immediate nebulised adrenaline for rapid relief plus oral dexamethasone for sustained anti-inflammatory effect, with anaesthetic escalation pathway prepared. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram once and clinical observation for two hours without nebulised adrenaline because of stimulation and possible distress on application
options.rationale: In severe croup with stridor at rest, nebulised adrenaline is required for rapid airway relief; prednisolone alone is acceptable in mild croup but not for severe presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg per kilogram now for presumed epiglottitis and call ENT for direct laryngoscopy in the operating theatre without delay regardless of vaccination status
options.rationale: Croup, not epiglottitis, is the working diagnosis given barking cough, hoarse voice and stridor; Hib-vaccinated child without drooling makes epiglottitis very unlikely and antibiotics are not first-line therapy here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Heliox 70 of 30 with concurrent nebulised salbutamol as first-line therapy for severe upper airway obstruction in this preschool child without prior wheeze history
options.rationale: Salbutamol is for lower airway bronchospasm and has no role in croup; heliox is at most an adjunct after first-line adrenaline and corticosteroid have been administered. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Reassure parents and discharge home with humidified air at home as evidence-based first-line therapy for moderate to severe croup with safety-net advice about deterioration
options.rationale: Humidified air has no evidence of benefit in croup; severe presentations require admission, corticosteroid and adrenaline, not discharge home. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is a clinical diagnosis based on barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor. Severity is assessed using the Westley score or by clinical features such as stridor at rest, recession, oxygen saturation and conscious state. All severities receive a single dose of oral or intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram (or prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram in mild cases). Severe croup with stridor at rest, significant recession, or hypoxia requires nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 for rapid relief. Recurrence after adrenaline within 4 hours warrants admission for observation.
key_points: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; bloods and imaging not required
All severities get corticosteroid (dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram is standard)
Severe croup adds nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000
Observe for at least 4 hours after adrenaline for rebound
explanation.pearls: For severe croup with stridor at rest in a child under five, give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 immediately plus single dose oral or intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram and observe for 4 hours before discharge consideration.

subtopic_detail: Febrile UTI in infants under 3 months
stem: A 6-week-old infant girl is brought to your emergency department by her parents because of a tactile fever today, feeding refusal and increased sleepiness. She has not had any cough, coryza or rash. She was born at term, has been growing normally on the 50th centile, and was vaccinated at 6 weeks two days ago. On examination she has a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius rectally, is mildly irritable when handled and has no obvious focus of infection on careful examination including ears, throat and chest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 86/54, RR 48, SpO2 98% on RA, Temp 38.4 rectal
data_table.Examination: Mildly irritable; AF flat; no rash; no respiratory distress; no focus on examination
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4; CRP 38; venous pH 7.36, lactate 2.4; urine pending; chest X-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Send a bag urine sample for culture and discharge home with safety-net advice and paediatric follow-up at the local general practice clinic in 24 hours
options.rationale: Febrile infants under 3 months are at high risk of bacteraemia and meningitis and require admission and full septic workup; bag urine has high contamination rates and is not used. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.text: Admit, take blood cultures, lumbar puncture and a clean catch or suprapubic aspirate urine, then commence intravenous benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime empirically as a septic workup approach
options.rationale: Febrile infants under 3 months require full septic workup including blood cultures, lumbar puncture and catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine, with immediate empirical intravenous antibiotics pending cultures regardless of clinical appearance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.text: Reassure family that her recent vaccination explains the fever and observe for 4 hours without bloods, urine, lumbar puncture or empirical antibiotic therapy at the present time
options.rationale: Vaccine-associated fever does not explain fever above 38 degrees in a 6-week-old; serious bacterial infection must be excluded before attribution to vaccination. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.text: Perform a urinalysis only and treat as a presumed urinary tract infection with oral cefalexin for ten days while awaiting culture confirmation from the bag sample collected today
options.rationale: Empirical oral antibiotics for an infant under 3 months without lumbar puncture and blood cultures risks missing meningitis or bacteraemia; intravenous antibiotics in hospital are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

options.text: Order a chest X-ray and respiratory viral PCR only to identify the likely viral cause of the fever before deciding on the need for any antibiotic therapy in this infant
options.rationale: Identifying a viral cause does not eliminate the risk of serious bacterial infection in this age group; full septic workup and empirical antibiotics are still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

explanation.summary: All febrile infants under 3 months require admission for full septic workup including blood culture, lumbar puncture and catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine, with empirical intravenous antibiotic cover for likely pathogens (commonly benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime, plus aciclovir if HSV is suspected). Bag urine is unsuitable for diagnosis because of contamination. UTI is the single most common serious bacterial infection in this age group and meningitis must be actively excluded. Risk stratification (Rochester, Step-by-Step) may be applied to selected well-appearing infants but is not used to defer workup at this age.
key_points: All febrile infants under 3 months: admit, full septic workup, empirical IV antibiotics
Catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine; bag urine not used
Lumbar puncture mandatory before empirical antibiotics where feasible
Empirical cover: benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime
explanation.pearls: For any febrile (>=38.0) infant under 3 months, admit and complete blood culture plus lumbar puncture plus clean-catch or suprapubic aspirate urine before commencing empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime rather than discharging on oral antibiotics.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Febrile Infant Under 3 Months

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents to your emergency department on day 6 of an illness characterised by persistent fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash, oedema of the hands and feet and a unilateral 2.5 cm cervical lymph node. He is irritable and his bloods show CRP 124 mg per litre, WCC 18.4, platelets 540, ALT 78 and a normocytic anaemia. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Echocardiography has been requested and will occur within hours.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctival injection; strawberry tongue; cracked lips; polymorphous rash; oedema of hands and feet; 2.5 cm right cervical node
data_table.Investigations: CRP 124; WCC 18.4 with neutrophilia; platelets 540; ALT 78; Hb 96 (microcytic); urine sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Wait until day 10 of illness to confirm coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiography before commencing intravenous immunoglobulin therapy and aspirin antiplatelet therapy together
options.rationale: Delaying treatment until day 10 to await coronary artery aneurysm formation forfeits the window in which IVIG prevents aneurysms; treatment is recommended within 10 days of fever onset on clinical criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for presumed streptococcal toxic shock syndrome while awaiting blood cultures and discontinue if cultures are negative at 48 hours
options.rationale: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome presents with shock and a desquamating rash rather than the constellation of features here; failure to give IVIG within 10 days of fever onset increases coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours plus aspirin 30 to 50 mg per kilogram per day in four divided doses initially in hospital
options.rationale: Kawasaki disease meeting at least five of five principal features warrants intravenous immunoglobulin within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk, plus high-dose aspirin until afebrile and CRP normalises. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Treat with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg per kilogram daily for three days as first-line monotherapy without intravenous immunoglobulin in routine Kawasaki disease management
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are an adjunct for IVIG-resistant disease or high-risk Kawasaki, not a substitute for IVIG as first-line therapy in standard presentations. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Discharge with oral ibuprofen and paediatric outpatient review in three days if the fever persists beyond day 8 of illness with no other planned investigations or interventions today
options.rationale: Discharge of suspected Kawasaki disease delays IVIG and risks coronary aneurysm formation; admission and treatment within 10 days of fever onset is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis requiring fever for 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm). Untreated disease leads to coronary artery aneurysm in around 25% of children. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours within 10 days of fever onset reduces aneurysm risk to under 5%. High-dose aspirin is given until afebrile and inflammatory markers normalise, then continued at low antiplatelet dose for 6 to 8 weeks pending echocardiogram. Corticosteroids are added in high-risk or IVIG-resistant disease.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis: fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features
IVIG 2 g per kilogram within 10 days of fever onset
Aspirin 30 to 50 mg per kilogram per day until afebrile, then low-dose
Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: When fever has lasted 5 or more days with 4 of 5 Kawasaki features, give IVIG 2 g per kilogram plus aspirin within day 10 of fever onset rather than awaiting coronary aneurysm formation; this reduces aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to your paediatric clinic for follow-up of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) diagnosed three weeks ago by characteristic palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower limbs with mild abdominal pain. He has had no melaena, intussusception or arthritis. The previous review four days ago was unremarkable. Today his mother reports brown-coloured urine in the morning, ankle swelling and a blood pressure recorded at the local pharmacy as 132/86 mmHg. His urinalysis in your rooms shows haematuria 3+, proteinuria 3+ and red cell casts.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 134/88 (>95th centile), RR 18, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Faded purpura on lower limbs; mild bilateral ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 3+, protein 3+; RBC casts; Cr 78 (was 38); albumin 28; urine PCR 380 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase fluid intake and recheck urinalysis and renal function in two weeks with attendance at general practice if proteinuria worsens or new symptoms develop with no other intervention today
options.rationale: Severe HSP nephritis with hypertension and rising creatinine cannot wait two weeks for review; urgent nephrology referral is essential to prevent permanent renal injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Reassure family that haematuria after IgA vasculitis is universal and reviewing the urinalysis in three months is sufficient management without escalation of investigations today
options.rationale: Microscopic haematuria alone may be observed, but nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine reflect severe nephritis requiring urgent specialist involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram per day at the next routine general practice visit without specialist nephrology input or escalation of investigations today
options.rationale: Empirical corticosteroids without specialist guidance are inadequate for severe HSP nephritis; biopsy guides selection of pulsed corticosteroid plus other immunosuppressive agents. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric nephrologist for renal biopsy assessment and consideration of immunosuppressive therapy alongside renin-angiotensin system blockade for proteinuria
options.rationale: HSP nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and rising creatinine constitutes severe nephritis warranting paediatric nephrology referral, biopsy consideration and immunosuppressive therapy in selected cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence intravenous cyclophosphamide 750 mg per square metre as outpatient therapy in your general practice rooms today for the severe IgA vasculitis nephritic flare currently
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is an immunosuppressive option in crescentic HSP nephritis but only under specialist nephrology supervision after biopsy; it is not appropriate to commence in general practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (HSP) is the most common childhood vasculitis. Around 30 to 50% develop renal involvement, usually within four weeks of onset, ranging from isolated haematuria through to crescentic glomerulonephritis. All affected children require weekly urinalysis and blood pressure measurement for at least 6 weeks. Microscopic haematuria alone is observed. Persistent or significant proteinuria, hypertension or rising creatinine requires urgent paediatric nephrology referral and consideration of biopsy and immunosuppressive therapy. Long-term renal follow-up is required because hypertension and CKD can develop years later.
key_points: 30 to 50% of HSP develop renal involvement, usually within 4 weeks
All require weekly urinalysis and BP for at least 6 weeks
Proteinuria, hypertension or rising creatinine = urgent nephrology referral
Long-term follow-up because hypertension and CKD can develop years later
explanation.pearls: For HSP with urine PCR >250 mg/mmol, hypertension above the 95th centile, or rising creatinine, refer to paediatric nephrology within 48 hours rather than continuing observation, because crescentic disease can progress rapidly to end-stage kidney disease.

stem: A 5-month-old boy is referred to your paediatric inpatient team after a third hospital admission with severe pneumonia, this time with Pneumocystis jirovecii on bronchoalveolar lavage. He had oral candidiasis at 8 weeks, persistent watery diarrhoea since 3 months with documented failure to thrive crossing two major weight centiles downward, and chronic perianal excoriation. His maternal uncle died of overwhelming infection at 7 months. Vaccinations include BCG at birth, with no localised reaction at the BCG site. Lymphocyte counts on previous admissions have been persistently low.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 84/52, RR 56, SpO2 91% on 2 L NP, Temp 38.7
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; oral candidiasis; bibasal crackles; perianal excoriation
data_table.Investigations: Lymphocytes 0.4 (low for age); IgG 1.8 g/L (low); BAL Pneumocystis positive; CXR diffuse interstitial

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral itraconazole prophylaxis alone and arrange routine paediatric outpatient follow-up in six weeks without immunology referral or hospital admission for further investigation
options.rationale: Antifungal prophylaxis alone does not address the underlying immunodeficiency; immunology referral and definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplant planning are urgent. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.text: Continue co-trimoxazole, plan rotavirus catch-up vaccination this admission alongside MMR booster at 6 months and discharge once afebrile and feeding without further investigation
options.rationale: Rotavirus and MMR are live vaccines and are absolutely contraindicated in suspected SCID due to risk of disseminated vaccine-strain infection. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.text: Transfuse 10 mL per kilogram of non-irradiated packed red cells for an anticipated drop in haemoglobin during this acute respiratory illness without further immunology consultation today
