options.rationale: Non-irradiated blood in SCID can cause fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease; only irradiated CMV-negative blood products are used. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.text: Reassure the family that recurrent infections are normal at this age and continue routine immunisation schedule including BCG booster at 6 months of age in next month
options.rationale: Three serious infections including Pneumocystis pneumonia, failure to thrive, lymphopenia and family history are red flag features for primary immunodeficiency, not normal variation. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

options.text: Avoid live vaccines, place in protective isolation, withhold any non-irradiated blood products and refer urgently to a paediatric immunology centre for SCID confirmation and definitive treatment
options.rationale: The clinical and family pattern, lymphopenia, Pneumocystis pneumonia and BCG-without-reaction strongly suggest severe combined immunodeficiency; live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products risk graft-versus-host disease, and definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. (Source: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement)
source_refs: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement

explanation.summary: Severe combined immunodeficiency presents with severe and recurrent infections (especially Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, persistent thrush and chronic diarrhoea), failure to thrive and lymphopenia for age, often with positive family history of early infant death. BCG given at birth can disseminate without local reaction. Immediate management is protective isolation, avoidance of live vaccines, avoidance of non-irradiated and non-CMV-negative blood products, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and IVIG support, with urgent referral to a paediatric immunology centre for confirmation by lymphocyte subsets and genetic testing. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and is most effective before significant infection burden.
key_points: Red flags: Pneumocystis pneumonia, thrush after 2 months, lymphopenia, family history
BCG can disseminate without local reaction
Avoid live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products
Definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation
explanation.pearls: If a young infant has Pneumocystis pneumonia plus failure to thrive plus absolute lymphocyte count under 1.5 with positive family history, treat as SCID until disproven by placing in isolation, ordering only irradiated CMV-negative blood, withholding live vaccines and contacting paediatric immunology the same day for transplant pathway planning.

sources.label: ASCIA Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Position Statement
BMJ Best Practice: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency

stem:
A 9-year-old boy with a diagnosis of asthma attends a routine review at the general practice where you work as a registrar. He has been on budesonide-formoterol 100/6 micrograms two inhalations twice daily as maintenance for the past 12 months. He reports no daytime symptoms over the past three months, no night waking, and full participation in school sport without pre-exercise reliever.

His mother is keen to reduce his medication burden. He has had no oral corticosteroid courses in the past 18 months and no hospital presentations. His inhaler technique with a spacer is excellent and adherence has been confirmed by pharmacy refill data.

data_table.Examination: Weight 30 kg, chest clear, no nasal polyps, no eczema flare
data_table.Investigations: Office spirometry FEV1 105% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.88, bronchodilator response negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his asthma plan?

options.text: Switch to fluticasone propionate 250 micrograms twice daily and review symptoms in 3 months
options.rationale: Switching to a higher-equivalent-dose ICS as a single agent escalates total ICS exposure and is the opposite of step-down in a child with sustained control. Fluticasone 250 micrograms twice daily is a high paediatric dose by Australian conventions. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

options.text: Continue current dose unchanged for a further 6 months before reassessing step-down options
options.rationale: Prolonged continuation of an ICS-LABA in a child with sustained excellent control unnecessarily exposes him to growth velocity effects and adrenal suppression risk. After 3 months of stable control, step-down should be actively trialled rather than deferred. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

options.text: Cease budesonide-formoterol and prescribe salbutamol 100 micrograms as a reliever only when needed
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of preventer therapy in a child with confirmed asthma risks loss of control and exacerbation. SABA-only therapy is no longer recommended for any asthma above intermittent severity given the mortality signal in studies such as SABINA. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

options.text: Switch to montelukast 5 mg orally once daily as maintenance monotherapy and stop inhaled therapy
options.rationale: Montelukast is less effective than ICS for paediatric asthma control and carries a TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric adverse effects. It is not a recommended step-down from a well-tolerated ICS-LABA in a child with confirmed responsive disease. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

options.text: Reduce maintenance to budesonide-formoterol 100/6 micrograms one inhalation twice daily and review in 3 months
options.rationale: After at least 3 months of well-controlled asthma on a low-dose ICS-LABA, step-down by approximately 50% is appropriate, with review at 2 to 3 months to confirm sustained control. Halving the daily ICS dose while maintaining twice-daily dosing is the recommended step-down for paediatric stable asthma. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook - Children)

explanation.summary: Paediatric asthma maintenance should be stepped down once control has been sustained for at least 3 months on the current regimen. The typical approach is to halve the ICS dose while preserving the regimen architecture, then reassess at 2 to 3 months. Complete cessation of preventer therapy is reserved for children who have remained on the lowest dose with excellent control for at least 12 months. Spirometry, symptom diaries, and reliever frequency are all useful objective markers when titrating.
key_points: Step-down trialled after at least 3 months of sustained well-controlled asthma
Halve ICS dose rather than removing LABA partner first when on combination
Review at 2 to 3 months with spirometry and symptom assessment
Maintain a written asthma action plan throughout any step-down
explanation.pearls: In a child on low-dose ICS-LABA with sustained control for at least 3 months, the recommended step-down is to halve the ICS-LABA dose while keeping twice-daily dosing intact, then reassess at 3 months before considering further reduction.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - Asthma in Children
BMJ Best Practice - Asthma in Children

stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department where you are the registrar with two weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss. Today she has been vomiting and is drowsy but rousable. Capillary blood glucose reads HIGH on the ward meter. Capillary ketones are 4.8 mmol/L. She weighs 26 kg. Her father describes her as alert but exhausted. She has no significant past history and takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32 deep and sighing, Temp 36.5 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes dry, capillary refill 3 seconds, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid management in the first hour?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg intravenously over 30 minutes to correct the acidosis before any further fluid
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or pH below 6.9 with cardiovascular compromise. It paradoxically worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9% as a 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes, then commence insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: A 20 mL/kg rapid bolus exceeds the cautious volume recommended for paediatric DKA and is associated with increased cerebral oedema risk in this age group. Insulin is also typically commenced 1 to 2 hours after fluids are started, not concurrently with the initial bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Hartmann's solution at maintenance rate alone, without an initial bolus, while awaiting electrolyte results
options.rationale: A clinically dehydrated child with venous pH 7.18 and tachycardia requires an initial resuscitation bolus, not maintenance-only fluid. Waiting for further electrolytes to act would worsen her acidosis and perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.45% with 5% dextrose and 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at 1.5 times maintenance from the outset
options.rationale: Half-normal saline with dextrose is the typical rehydration fluid AFTER the initial resuscitation bolus and once glucose has fallen, not the first-hour resuscitation choice. Starting dextrose immediately at glucose 32 mmol/L is also inappropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9% as a 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, then reassess perfusion before further fluids
options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA guidance recommends a cautious initial resuscitation bolus of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes for a child with clinical dehydration but without shock, given the risk of cerebral oedema with aggressive fluid loading. Perfusion is reassessed before any further bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Initial management of paediatric DKA in Australia favours cautious fluid resuscitation due to the well-documented risk of cerebral oedema. A 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes is the standard initial step when there is clinical dehydration without shock. Insulin is commenced at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour around 1 to 2 hours after fluids begin to avoid rapid glucose drops. Potassium is added to ongoing fluids once urine output is established and serum potassium is known.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes in non-shocked paediatric DKA
Insulin infusion commenced 1 to 2 hours after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour
Bicarbonate restricted to life-threatening hyperkalaemia or pH below 6.9 with shock
Cerebral oedema risk peaks 4 to 12 hours into treatment, especially in new-onset diabetes under 5 years
explanation.pearls: In paediatric DKA the initial 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus is given over 30 to 60 minutes, not as a rapid push, and insulin is deliberately delayed by 1 to 2 hours to lower the risk of cerebral oedema.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines - DKA

stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric ward where you are the registrar with eight days of fever to 39.5 degrees C, persistent irritability, and refusal of feeds. He has a maculopapular rash on his trunk and conjunctival injection without exudate. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy and his oral mucosa is unremarkable. His mother reports a brief peeling at the fingertips noted yesterday. He has been treated with two courses of oral amoxicillin without improvement. There is no respiratory distress and no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 36, Temp 39.2 degrees C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: BCG scar site erythematous, mild perineal desquamation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 162 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, platelets 612 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 88 U/L, sterile pyuria on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin
options.rationale: Infants under 12 months frequently present with incomplete Kawasaki phenotype and have the highest risk of coronary artery aneurysm. With prolonged fever, BCG site reactivation, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia and thrombocytosis, treatment must not wait for full clinical criteria. Echocardiography defines baseline coronary status while immunoglobulin reduces aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Continue supportive care with paracetamol and reassess after a further 48 hours of observation
options.rationale: Coronary aneurysm risk rises sharply after day 10 of untreated fever in infants, and this child is on day 8 already. Watchful waiting in this high-risk demographic is dangerous when supportive laboratory features of incomplete Kawasaki are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Switch to intravenous ceftriaxone for occult bacterial infection and add doxycycline for atypical pathogens
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum antibiotics do not treat Kawasaki disease and delay definitive immunoglobulin therapy. Two courses of amoxicillin have already failed to defervesce; the laboratory pattern is inflammatory, not bacterial. Doxycycline is also contraindicated under 8 years for non-life-threatening indications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse therapy alone for inflammatory vasculitis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids may be added to immunoglobulin in selected high-risk Kawasaki cases but are not first-line monotherapy in Australia. Steroid-only treatment misses the proven aneurysm-protective effect of immunoglobulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid culture and commence empirical aciclovir intravenously
options.rationale: There are no features of meningoencephalitis, and the clinical and laboratory picture is dominated by systemic inflammation with mucocutaneous signs. Aciclovir and lumbar puncture do not address the leading diagnosis and delay immunoglobulin therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease must be considered in any infant with prolonged unexplained fever, even when only two or three classical features are present. Supportive laboratory criteria include CRP above 30, ESR above 40, platelets above 450, albumin below 30, ALT elevation, and sterile pyuria. BCG site reactivation is a highly suggestive sign in Australian infants. Treatment with immunoglobulin within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%.
key_points: Infants under 12 months have the highest coronary aneurysm risk and atypical phenotype
Five supportive labs convert a two-feature infant into a treatable incomplete Kawasaki case
Immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus high-dose aspirin is the Australian standard
BCG site reactivation is a useful Australian-specific clinical clue
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 12 months with fever for 5 or more days and 2 to 3 classical features, immunoglobulin 2 g/kg should be given within the first 10 days of fever to bring coronary aneurysm risk from around 25% down to under 5%.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement - Diagnosis Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease

subtopic_detail: Severe early jaundice with positive DAT
stem: You are the paediatric registrar covering the postnatal ward. A term male infant born at 39+4 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery is now 28 hours old and clinically jaundiced to the lower abdomen. His mother is blood group O Rh-positive, with anti-c antibodies detected at 28 weeks at a titre of 1:32. Cord blood at delivery showed haemoglobin 138 g/L and direct antiglobulin test positive. The infant is feeding eagerly. Birth weight was 3450 g and weight today is 3320 g. The transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 290 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 42, Temp 36.9 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, vigorous suck, no hepatosplenomegaly, scleral icterus to mid-trunk
data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 318 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, Hb 132 g/L, reticulocytes 8%, blood group A Rh-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with community midwife follow-up and a repeat bilirubin sample in 24 hours
options.rationale: Discharging a term infant with confirmed isoimmune haemolysis and bilirubin 318 micromol/L at 28 hours risks rapid kernicterus. The trajectory of antibody-driven haemolysis is unpredictable and demands inpatient management. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive multi-light phototherapy and prepare for possible exchange transfusion at this level
options.rationale: Serum bilirubin of 318 micromol/L at 28 hours of age in a term infant with confirmed isoimmune haemolysis crosses the intensive phototherapy threshold on the Australian gestational-age-adjusted graph and approaches the exchange line. Anti-c is a clinically significant antibody causing haemolytic disease similar in pattern to anti-D. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence single-bank conventional phototherapy and recheck the bilirubin at 24 hours
options.rationale: Conventional single-light therapy is insufficient when bilirubin is approaching the exchange threshold with active haemolysis. Intensive multi-light phototherapy delivers more irradiance and is appropriate for high-risk haemolytic jaundice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer oral phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg daily as a hepatic enzyme inducer and avoid phototherapy
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is not an accepted treatment for established neonatal haemolytic jaundice in Australia. The infant needs immediate light therapy and possibly exchange, not enzyme induction. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Withhold treatment and arrange repeat transcutaneous bilirubin in 6 hours before deciding on therapy
options.rationale: Once total serum bilirubin has confirmed a level crossing the phototherapy threshold in a high-risk infant, treatment must commence immediately. Transcutaneous values are unreliable above 250 micromol/L and after phototherapy starts. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Anti-c is a clinically significant non-D Rh antibody capable of causing severe haemolytic disease of the newborn. Cord DAT positivity, early jaundice within 24 to 36 hours, and rapid rise of bilirubin warrant intensive phototherapy and pre-emptive exchange preparation. The Australian phototherapy and exchange thresholds are age-in-hours and gestation-adjusted, with haemolysis lowering the trigger by approximately 35 micromol/L. Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg may also be considered as an adjunct in isoimmune haemolysis approaching exchange thresholds.
key_points: Anti-c can cause severe haemolytic disease equivalent in severity to anti-D
Phototherapy and exchange thresholds are lowered by approximately 35 micromol/L when haemolysis is confirmed
Intensive multi-light phototherapy delivers higher irradiance than single-bank
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg can reduce the need for exchange in isoimmune cases
explanation.pearls: In confirmed isoimmune haemolytic jaundice approaching the exchange line, intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 to 1 g/kg given alongside intensive phototherapy reduces the need for exchange transfusion by more than 50%.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-c in Pregnancy
NICE NG98 - Jaundice in Newborn Babies under 28 Days

stem: A 6-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department where you are the registrar after a single episode at home where she became limp and pale for around 20 seconds during a feed before returning to her normal state. She has fed and behaved normally since. She was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no fever, no respiratory symptoms, no preceding illness, and no family history of sudden infant death. Examination on arrival is normal. Her parents are very anxious but the child appears completely well on your assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 bpm, RR 38, Temp 36.8 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, normal tone, anterior fontanelle soft, chest clear, no rash, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L, paired pre-and-post-ductal saturations both 99%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and commence empirical intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: A well infant without fever, lethargy, or focus does not require empiric sepsis treatment based on a single brief episode. Routine LP and broad antibiotics are not part of BRUE evaluation. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

options.text: Discharge home with shared follow-up by the general practitioner within 24 hours and infant CPR education
options.rationale: Lower-risk BRUE discharge applies only to infants over 60 days who meet all low-risk criteria. This 6-week-old infant does not qualify regardless of how reassuring the current examination appears. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

options.text: Admit for at least 4 hours of monitored observation with paired saturation checks before discharge planning
options.rationale: Although her episode meets brief resolved unexplained event criteria, she is under 60 days old, which automatically places her in the higher-risk category and warrants a period of monitored observation. A 4-hour observation period with cardiorespiratory monitoring is the recommended minimum in Australian paediatric emergency protocols. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

options.text: Arrange outpatient electroencephalography and discharge home pending the test result in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient EEG without admission is not appropriate for an under-60-day infant with an unexplained event. The yield of unprovoked EEG is low and observation in the higher-risk group should be inpatient. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

options.text: Arrange immediate outpatient 24-hour Holter monitoring and discharge home with cardiology phone advice only
options.rationale: Holter monitoring is not the standard first investigation for BRUE in the absence of suspected arrhythmia or family history of long QT. The age-based higher-risk classification mandates inpatient monitoring, not outpatient cardiology. (Source: RCH CPG: BRUE)

explanation.summary: Brief resolved unexplained events are stratified into lower and higher risk based on age, gestation, episode features, and prior medical history. Lower-risk infants must be over 60 days, term, with a single episode under 1 minute, and no concerning history or examination. All infants under 60 days automatically fall into the higher-risk group regardless of how well they appear. Higher-risk infants warrant a period of monitored observation, paired saturations, glucose, ECG, and sometimes admission for further workup.
key_points: Age under 60 days is an automatic higher-risk criterion in BRUE
Lower-risk discharge requires age over 60 days, term gestation, single episode under 1 minute, normal exam, no prior BRUE
Higher-risk infants need monitored observation for at least 4 hours plus ECG and paired saturations
Family CPR education and clear safety-net advice are part of every BRUE disposition
explanation.pearls: Any infant under 60 days with a brief resolved unexplained event is automatically higher-risk by Australian and AAP definitions and needs at least 4 hours of monitored observation, regardless of how well they look in the emergency department.

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of coryza and an increasing wheeze. He has taken 60% of his usual feeds over the past 12 hours but is still having normal wet nappies. There is no fever and no history of choking. He was born at 38 weeks gestation and has had three previous episodes of viral wheeze. His father has asthma. On arrival he is alert and pink, with mild subcostal recession and a wet productive cough between feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 48, SpO2 91% room air, Temp 36.9
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession; bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze; CRT 2s; alert
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab pending; chest X-ray not performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Admit for supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 90% (RCH target)with small-volume oral or nasogastric feeds
options.rationale: AU paediatric guidance is to admit infants with bronchiolitis when SpO2 is below 90% (RCH target)in room air or feeding is below 50% of normal; oxygen is titrated to maintain SpO2 90% (RCH target)and hydration is supported by nasogastric or small-volume oral feeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess clinical response over the next 30 minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in infants under 12 months with bronchiolitis as the wheeze reflects small-airway oedema rather than smooth-muscle bronchospasm; trials show no meaningful response. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence inhaled fluticasone via spacer and review with the general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids have no role in acute bronchiolitis and do not modify illness duration; a primary-care review at 48 hours would also miss the existing hypoxia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Administer nebulised hypertonic 3% saline three times daily plus a short course of oral prednisolone
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline shows inconsistent benefit and is not part of routine AU paediatric care; oral corticosteroids do not alter outcomes in viral bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with oral amoxicillin to cover likely lower respiratory bacterial co-infection
options.rationale: Routine antibiotics are not indicated as bronchiolitis is viral; bacterial co-infection rates are low and discharge with hypoxia is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest cause of hospitalisation in infants under 12 months and is managed almost entirely with supportive care. AU paediatric guidance frames admission decisions around hypoxia, feeding adequacy, and work of breathing rather than imaging or laboratory testing. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis because the underlying pathology is mucosal oedema and debris rather than bronchospasm or bacterial infection. The shift in oxygen target from 94% to 90% (RCH target)in recent AU guidelines was driven by evidence that the lower threshold reduces length of stay without increasing safety events.
key_points: SpO2 90% (RCH target)in room air is the AU admission threshold for bronchiolitis
Feeding under 50% of usual or significant work of breathing also mandates admission
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics have no routine role
Nasogastric feeds and minimal handling are preferred over IV fluids when tolerated
explanation.pearls: RCH CPG sets bronchiolitis oxygen target at 90% (RCH target)and admits feeds below 50% of normal; bronchodilator trials add no value under 12 months.

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department in the early hours with a barking cough and inspiratory stridor that wakes him from sleep. The cough started 24 hours earlier with rhinorrhoea and a low-grade fever. He has otherwise been well, is fully vaccinated, and has had no choking or drooling. While in the cubicle he is settled on his mother's lap, taking sips of juice with no audible stridor at rest, and his voice sounds hoarse but normal in volume. He has had one previous episode 6 months ago which resolved without treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Barking cough on examination; no stridor at rest; mild intermittent suprasternal tug only when crying; air entry normal bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management at this point?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and prepare for paediatric retrieval team transfer
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor and recession at rest; this child is mild with no rest stridor. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg and observe for until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge
options.rationale: A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg per kg is recommended for all severities of croup, including mild, and reduces re-presentation; observation of around until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge confirms stability. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Reassure the parents and discharge home with humidified air advice and paracetamol as needed
options.rationale: Humidified air has no evidence base in croup; discharge without dexamethasone misses an opportunity to reduce illness duration and re-presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Take a lateral neck radiograph to exclude epiglottitis before initiating any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is not required to diagnose croup or exclude epiglottitis in a settled child; the clinical picture is diagnostic and imaging may distress and decompensate the airway. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin and review with the general practitioner the following morning for re-examination
options.rationale: Croup is viral and antibiotics are not indicated; this also omits dexamethasone which is the only proven therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Croup is a clinical diagnosis based on the barking cough and stridor in a young child following a viral prodrome. AU paediatric guidance recommends a single dose of oral dexamethasone for all severities, including mild, because it reduces symptom duration, return visits and need for adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline is added for moderate to severe disease, defined by stridor and recession at rest. Imaging is not required and may worsen distress.
key_points: Dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg per kg orally is given for all severity grades of croup
Mild croup is defined by no stridor and no recession at rest
Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate/severe croup or impending respiratory failure
Antibiotics have no role unless there is suspicion of bacterial tracheitis
explanation.pearls: AU paeds dose of dexamethasone in croup is 0.15 mg per kg orally as a single dose; observe until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge if mild.

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to her general practitioner with 24 hours of right-sided ear pain following a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection. She is non-Aboriginal, was breastfed for 6 months, and lives with parents who do not smoke. She has been more irritable but is drinking well and ate her dinner. She has had one previous episode of otitis media 14 months ago which resolved spontaneously. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is red, opaque, and bulging with poor mobility; the left is normal. There is no otorrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 38.1
data_table.Examination: Right TM erythematous, bulging, opaque; no perforation; no mastoid tenderness; alert and playful in waiting room
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management decision?

options.text: Prescribe immediate oral amoxicillin 30 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days due to the bulging tympanic membrane
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are indicated under 6 months or in higher-risk groups; in a well low-risk child over 2 years a watchful waiting strategy is recommended even when the membrane is bulging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence a delayed prescription of oral cefalexin to be filled if symptoms worsen within the next 6 hours
options.rationale: Cefalexin has poor middle-ear penetration and is not a recommended first-line agent for otitis media; the timeframe also undercuts watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Provide analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen and review in 48 hours, with antibiotics if no improvement
options.rationale: Analgesia and watchful waiting for 48 hours is recommended in low-risk children over 2 years without high-risk features; antibiotics are added only if symptoms persist or worsen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer the child to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of ventilation tube insertion immediately
options.rationale: Surgical referral applies to recurrent or chronic otitis media with effusion and hearing loss, not a first significant episode in 14 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe oral co-trimoxazole as covers respiratory pathogens including resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.rationale: Co-trimoxazole is not first-line for otitis media in Australia and has rising resistance among pneumococcal isolates; amoxicillin is preferred when antibiotics are indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in well children is largely self-limiting and AU antibiotic guidance favours analgesia plus watchful waiting unless high-risk features are present. Immediate antibiotics are warranted under 6 months of age, in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at risk of chronic suppurative otitis media, with bilateral disease under 2 years, otorrhoea, or systemic toxicity. The first-line oral antibiotic when needed is amoxicillin at high dose; second-line for true type-I penicillin allergy is azithromycin. Symptom resolution at 48 to 72 hours is the trigger to add or escalate therapy.
key_points: Watchful waiting is appropriate for low-risk children over 2 years without otorrhoea or systemic features
Immediate antibiotics for under 6 months, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation/otorrhoea, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children at risk
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily is first line when antibiotics are given
Analgesia is the most important short-term intervention
explanation.pearls: AMH and Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic endorse 48-hour watchful waiting in low-risk children over 2 years even with a bulging tympanic membrane.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is admitted with 6 days of fever to 39.5, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a polymorphous truncal rash, cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy of 1.8 cm. He received intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 12 hours and oral aspirin 5 mg per kg per day starting 36 hours ago. Despite this, his temperature has remained above 38 and his C-reactive protein has not improved on repeat testing. An echocardiogram performed before treatment showed mild dilation of the proximal left main coronary artery. He has no known immunodeficiency.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 38.7 (post-IVIG)
data_table.Examination: Persistent conjunctival injection; cracked lips; rash fading; cervical node 1.5 cm
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 (was 180), Hb 92, platelets 480, albumin 28, ALT 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue current aspirin dose and reassess clinically in 48 hours before considering further therapy
options.rationale: Persistent fever and CRP at 36 hours after IVIG defines IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease and warrants prompt second-line therapy as coronary aneurysm risk rises. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Switch aspirin from anti-inflammatory to antiplatelet dosing and continue observation for another 24 hours
options.rationale: Aspirin dose adjustment does not address IVIG resistance; second IVIG or corticosteroid is required to reduce ongoing vasculitis and aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically targeting toxic shock syndrome and septicaemia
options.rationale: Cultures should be drawn but the clinical picture meets Kawasaki criteria with documented coronary changes; antibiotics alone do not treat the underlying vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Administer a second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg and add intravenous methylprednisolone
options.rationale: IVIG resistance is defined as persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours after the first IVIG dose; the AU recommendation is a second IVIG dose at 2 g per kg with methylprednisolone, given the documented coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Switch aspirin to clopidogrel and commence oral prednisolone alone as a steroid-sparing maintenance regimen
options.rationale: Clopidogrel monotherapy is not appropriate and oral prednisolone alone does not match the second-line evidence base for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki with coronary involvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis with peak incidence in children under 5; untreated, around a quarter develop coronary artery aneurysms. The first-line therapy is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg given within day 10 of fever combined with aspirin. IVIG resistance, defined as persistent or recrudescent fever 36 hours after IVIG, occurs in 10 to 20% and significantly increases aneurysm risk; AU guidance recommends a second IVIG dose plus pulsed methylprednisolone in this scenario, with infliximab as third-line. Echocardiographic surveillance is repeated at 2 and 6 weeks regardless of initial findings.
key_points: IVIG resistance = persistent or recurrent fever 36 hours after first IVIG
Coronary artery involvement at baseline raises the threshold for prompt second-line therapy
Second-line = repeat IVIG 2 g/kg plus IV methylprednisolone in AU
Infliximab is reserved for third-line when steroids and repeat IVIG fail
explanation.pearls: Persistent fever beyond 36 hours after IVIG 2 g per kg in Kawasaki defines resistance and warrants repeat IVIG plus IV methylprednisolone in Australia.

stem: A 9-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents with 48 hours of polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, and rapid breathing. She is alert with sunken eyes and a dry tongue. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L. She weighs 30 kg. She has had no recent fluid intake. Her initial 10 mL per kg normal saline bolus has been completed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 134, BP 96/58, RR 36 (Kussmaul), SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes; mild abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28, pH 7.10, HCO3 8, ketones 5.6, K+ 4.2, Na+ 138; BSL on point-of-care confirms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid and insulin plan for the next phase?

options.text: Continue saline boluses at 20 mL per kg per hour until the heart rate normalises, then start insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour
options.rationale: Aggressive bolusing beyond initial resuscitation increases cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA; replacement fluid is calculated and given more slowly. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour immediately before any further fluid replacement
options.rationale: Insulin is started 1 to 2 hours after fluids in paediatric DKA to allow for circulating volume restoration and to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol per kg over 1 hour given the severity of the acidaemia on venous gas
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is associated with worsened cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA and is reserved for severe acidaemia with haemodynamic instability after appropriate fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Switch to 5% dextrose with potassium chloride 40 mmol per litre immediately and titrate to capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Dextrose is added only when blood glucose falls below 14 to 17 mmol/L; switching prematurely worsens hyperglycaemia and delays acidosis correction. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Replace a 5 to 7% deficit over 48 hours with 0.9% saline plus potassium and start insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units per kg per hour at 1 hour
options.rationale: AU paediatric DKA guidance replaces an assumed deficit (5 to 7% for moderate, up to 10% for severe) over 48 hours alongside maintenance using saline with potassium once urine output established; insulin starts at 0.05 to 0.1 units per kg per hour after 1 hour to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/ISPAD Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis against the catastrophic risk of cerebral oedema, which carries 20 to 25% mortality. Fluid resuscitation beyond an initial 10 mL per kg bolus is gradual: total deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours, with frequent neurological observations. Insulin is started after at least 1 hour of fluids at a low rate; bicarbonate, rapid sodium swings, and excessive fluid administration are independent risk factors for cerebral oedema. Dextrose is added when glucose falls toward 14 to 17 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin infusion without hypoglycaemia.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg only unless shocked; further boluses raise cerebral oedema risk
Deficit replaced over 48 hours, not 24, in paediatric DKA
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started 1 hour after fluids
Bicarbonate is generally avoided
explanation.pearls: AU paediatric DKA: 5 to 7% deficit replaced over 48 hours with saline+KCl; insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started after 1 hour, bicarbonate avoided.

stem:
A 5-year-old girl presents with her father to the general practitioner with 8 weeks of large, painful, hard bowel motions occurring once every 5 to 7 days. She has been soiling her underwear with small amounts of soft stool most days. She is otherwise well, fully toilet-trained for urine, and started prep this year. Her diet is varied but limited in fluids.

She has had no abdominal distension since infancy, normal growth, and no delayed passage of meconium. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa with no other findings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with palpable left iliac fossa faecal mass; no perianal abnormality; growth on 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gastroenterologist for rectal manometry to exclude Hirschsprung disease before any therapy
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease typically presents in infancy with delayed meconium and abdominal distension; manometry referral is not first-line for a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Recommend dietary fibre, increased fluids, and a daily fruit-juice trial without any laxatives initially
options.rationale: Diet alone is insufficient when impaction is present and overflow soiling is occurring; pharmacological disimpaction is required first. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe a single phosphate enema to disimpact and then review need for ongoing oral laxative therapy
options.rationale: Oral macrogol is preferred over enemas in children because of acceptability and equal efficacy; phosphate enemas have a small risk of electrolyte disturbance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence oral macrogol disimpaction regimen with escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days, then move to a maintenance dose
options.rationale: Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling is treated with oral macrogol disimpaction over 3 to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing, alongside toileting and behavioural advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Start senna 7.5 mg nightly for 6 weeks without disimpaction phase and review at the end of the course
options.rationale: Stimulant laxatives are used in addition to macrogol when response is poor; they are not first-line monotherapy and skipping disimpaction perpetuates overflow. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90% of paediatric chronic constipation and is managed with a disimpaction phase followed by maintenance. AU paediatric guidance recommends oral macrogol with electrolytes as first-line for both phases; disimpaction uses escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days then steps down to a maintenance dose titrated to one soft motion per day. Behavioural toileting after meals (using the gastrocolic reflex) and stool diaries support adherence. Red flags for organic causes (delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abdominal distension) prompt specialist referral.
key_points: Oral macrogol is first-line for disimpaction and maintenance
Overflow soiling indicates impaction and mandates disimpaction first
Senna is added as a second agent if macrogol alone is insufficient
Red flags for Hirschsprung include delayed meconium and infantile onset
explanation.pearls: Macrogol disimpaction at escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing is the AU first-line paediatric constipation strategy.

stem:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother after the mother found a written plan to take 30 paracetamol tablets the next day, alongside the cached tablets in her bedroom. The young woman is currently calm, articulate, and minimises the plan, saying it was a moment of frustration after an argument. She has been treated for moderate depression by her general practitioner for 4 months with limited response to sertraline 100 mg daily.

She lives with her mother who is supportive; her father has limited contact. She has had two emergency presentations in the past 6 months for superficial cutting; nothing has been ingested today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 110/68, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Composed; mood flat; no thought disorder; HEADSSS reveals social withdrawal and disordered sleep
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; paracetamol level not relevant (no ingestion); urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition plan?

options.text: Discharge home with safety planning, mother as primary supervisor, and outpatient psychology follow-up within 7 days
options.rationale: Active suicide plan with method, cached tablets, and limited treatment response is not adequately mitigated by community safety planning alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.text: Refer to school-based counselling and increase sertraline to 150 mg daily without acute admission
options.rationale: Increasing antidepressant dose without acute assessment misses the urgency of a planned ingestion and provides inadequate immediate safety. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.text: Admit only if she expresses ongoing intent within the next 2 hours during repeat interview by the registrar
options.rationale: Adolescents often minimise on direct questioning; basing admission on second-interview disclosure underestimates risk after a concrete plan with cached means. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.text: Discharge under a verbal contract of safety with the mother removing tablets at home and a phone call from CYMHS in 72 hours
options.rationale: Verbal contracts of safety lack evidence and are no longer recommended; phone follow-up after 72 hours does not address acute risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

options.text: Admit to a paediatric ward for safety, urgent child and youth mental health service review, and means restriction at home
options.rationale: Concrete plan, cached means, repeated self-harm and inadequate antidepressant response warrant inpatient admission for safety and urgent CYMHS review with collaborative means restriction planning before discharge. (Source: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

explanation.summary: Adolescent self-harm and suicidality is assessed across intent, plan, means, prior attempts, mental disorder, and protective factors. A specific plan with cached means, particularly paracetamol, and prior self-harm with limited treatment response confers high acute risk that exceeds community management. AU paediatric guidance supports inpatient admission with urgent specialist review (CAMHS/CYMHS) and concrete means-restriction. Safety contracts have no evidence base and have been replaced by collaborative safety planning involving the young person, family, and clinical team.
key_points: Cached method (especially paracetamol) raises acute risk substantially
Verbal safety contracts have no evidence and are not used
Inpatient admission is appropriate for high-risk plans with limited community supports
Means restriction is a core part of every disposition
explanation.pearls: Cached paracetamol with a written plan in an adolescent with prior self-harm meets RCH criteria for inpatient admission and urgent CYMHS review.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Self-harm in Children and Adolescents

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by his parents with 36 hours of watery diarrhoea (8 episodes) and 6 episodes of non-bilious vomiting, last vomit 90 minutes ago. He is alert but irritable and refuses solid food, though he accepted 50 mL of water at triage without further vomiting. There has been no blood in the stool, no fever above 38.5, and no travel.

Two children at his childcare centre have similar symptoms. He has had normal wet nappies but fewer in the past 12 hours. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and skin turgor is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 37.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and irritable, dry mouth, no sunken eyes, normal turgor, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; clinical assessment suggests 3 to 5% dehydration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration strategy?

options.text: Trial oral rehydration solution at 50 mL per kg over 4 hours given in small frequent sips with reassessment
options.rationale: Mild to moderate dehydration is managed with oral rehydration solution at 50 mL per kg over 4 hours in frequent small volumes; clinical reassessment guides escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a peripheral cannula and infuse 0.9% saline at 100 mL per kg over 6 hours empirically for dehydration
options.rationale: IV rehydration is reserved for failed oral or nasogastric trial, shock, persistent vomiting, or severe dehydration; jumping to IV violates the AU stepwise approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Commence a single intravenous bolus of 20 mL per kg 0.9% saline and recheck electrolytes in 2 hours
options.rationale: Bolusing without first trialling oral or nasogastric ORS in a non-shocked child is not the AU first step and exposes the child to cannulation unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Administer ondansetron orodispersible 4 mg and reassess feeding tolerance, then admit overnight irrespective of response
options.rationale: Ondansetron is reasonable for persistent vomiting, but routine admission irrespective of response is unnecessary if oral intake resumes; AU guidance favours discharge with ORS once tolerance returns. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Withhold fluids and food for 6 hours to rest the gut, then trial dilute apple juice as the first rehydration agent
options.rationale: Gut rest is not recommended in paediatric gastroenteritis; dilute apple juice has slightly higher relapse compared with structured ORS in moderate cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Acute viral gastroenteritis is one of the commonest paediatric ED presentations. AU paediatric guidance recommends oral rehydration solution as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration, delivered as small frequent volumes totalling around 50 mL per kg over 4 hours, with clinical reassessment. Nasogastric ORS is preferred over intravenous fluid if oral intake fails, as IV access is more invasive and not superior. Antiemetics are not routine; ondansetron is reasonable when vomiting prevents ORS uptake.
key_points: ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration
Nasogastric ORS precedes IV fluid in failed oral trials
Single dose ondansetron may rescue persistent vomiting
Gut rest and dilute juice are not routine
explanation.pearls: RCH CPG: 50 mL per kg ORS over 4 hours in frequent small volumes is the AU paediatric standard for mild to moderate dehydration.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy attends a follow-up appointment with his general practitioner after 6 months on inhaled fluticasone 50 mcg twice daily via spacer. Despite reliable adherence (verified by pharmacy refill records), he has needed his salbutamol reliever on 4 days a week and has been waking with cough twice a week. He has had two short courses of oral prednisolone in the past 3 months but no admissions.

There is no smoking in the household, his inhaler technique was reviewed last visit, and his weight and height are on the 50th centile. He has known house dust mite and grass pollen allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation; spacer technique reviewed and adequate; no eczema today
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; spirometry FEV1 82% predicted at last visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his preventer therapy?

options.text: Continue current fluticasone dose and add montelukast 5 mg nightly as a leukotriene receptor antagonist
options.rationale: Add-on LTRA is an option for partial control but the AU paediatric preferred next step in children with poor control on low-dose ICS is to increase ICS or add LABA above age 5. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.text: Increase fluticasone to 100 mcg twice daily and reassess control and inhaler technique in 4 to 6 weeks
options.rationale: In children with poor symptom control on low-dose ICS the AU preferred step is to double the ICS to medium dose with technique recheck and review at 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.text: Switch fluticasone to budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) in this age group
options.rationale: MART is established in adolescents and adults but not the AU preferred approach in children under 12; consider combination ICS-LABA in fixed dosing when escalation is needed. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.text: Stop fluticasone and trial a short course of oral prednisolone followed by environmental allergen avoidance only
options.rationale: Stopping preventer in poorly controlled asthma is unsafe; oral steroid courses do not replace ongoing preventer therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

options.text: Refer for omalizumab subcutaneous monthly therapy given his allergic phenotype and current symptom burden
options.rationale: Omalizumab is reserved for severe IgE-mediated asthma uncontrolled on high-dose ICS plus LABA in specialist clinics; this is premature at low-dose ICS. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

explanation.summary: Childhood asthma management follows a stepwise escalation guided by symptom frequency, reliever use, night waking and prior flares. Children under 12 starting at low-dose ICS who remain poorly controlled despite adherence and good technique are stepped up to medium-dose ICS (typically by doubling), with reassessment at 4 to 6 weeks. Add-on LTRA, fixed combination ICS-LABA, and biologics are subsequent options. Salbutamol use 3 or more days a week or night waking once a week or more indicates poor control.
key_points: Low-dose ICS to medium-dose ICS is the preferred first step in children
MART is not routinely used in children under 12 in Australia
Reliever use 3+ days/week or nocturnal cough = poor control
Always recheck technique and adherence before escalation
explanation.pearls: AU Asthma Handbook in children under 12: double low-dose ICS first before MART or biologics; review at 4 to 6 weeks.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma Handbook

stem: A previously well 6-year-old girl was diagnosed with Henoch Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) 10 days ago after a palpable purpuric rash on the lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle swelling. At initial review her urinalysis was negative, blood pressure was normotensive, and she had no haematuria or proteinuria. She has been managed at home with paracetamol and her family reports the rash is fading. She has returned today for follow-up and her urinalysis today shows blood 3+ and protein 2+. Her blood pressure is 118/78.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/78 (>95th centile for age and height), RR 20, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Fading purpura on lower limbs; soft non-tender abdomen; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 3+ protein 2+; urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPCR) pending; creatinine 38; albumin 36

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure the family the rash is resolving and review with urinalysis again in 4 weeks at the next scheduled visit
options.rationale: New significant haematuria and proteinuria with elevated blood pressure require urgent paediatric assessment, not routine follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg without specialist consultation and continue urinalysis weekly at home
options.rationale: Steroid initiation in HSP nephritis with proteinuria requires paediatric nephrology input on biopsy and treatment intensity; starting alone is not appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology for assessment including UPCR, eGFR estimation and consideration of biopsy
options.rationale: Persistent or new proteinuria with hypertension after HSP requires urgent paediatric nephrology referral; UPCR and eGFR guide need for renal biopsy and immunosuppression. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

options.text: Recommend an angiotensin receptor blocker via the general practitioner without specialist nephrology input now
options.rationale: RAAS blockade may be used for persistent proteinuria but only after specialist assessment, biopsy where indicated, and confirmation of injury pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

options.text: Admit for intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg per kg daily for three days irrespective of biopsy result
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for biopsy-proven severe crescentic nephritis or rapidly progressive disease, not initial assessment of significant urinalysis change. (Source: RCH CPG: HSP)

explanation.summary: Henoch Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) typically affects children under 10 with a triad of purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain; renal involvement develops in around a third and largely declares within 6 months. AU paediatric guidance is weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, fortnightly to 3 months, and monthly to 6 months. New or persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine triggers urgent paediatric nephrology referral for UPCR, eGFR, and biopsy consideration. Long-term proteinuria and hypertension are managed with RAAS blockade.
key_points: Surveillance urinalysis and BP for 6 months catches late nephritis
New proteinuria + hypertension = urgent nephrology referral
Biopsy indications include crescentic disease and persistent significant proteinuria
Routine steroids do not prevent nephritis
explanation.pearls: Urinalysis surveillance for 6 months and a urine protein:creatinine ratio above 100 mg per mmol prompt urgent paediatric nephrology referral in HSP.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department on day 4 of a sore throat originally treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin by his general practitioner 48 hours ago after a positive throat swab for group A Streptococcus. Over the past 12 hours his throat pain has become severe and predominantly right-sided; he has trouble swallowing his own saliva and his voice has become muffled.

He has no stridor, no drooling whilst sitting upright, and no neck stiffness. On examination, he has trismus opening only 2 cm, deviation of the uvula to the left, and a fluctuant bulge on the right superior tonsillar pole.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 38.6
data_table.Examination: Trismus 2 cm, uvula deviated to the left, fluctuant right superior tonsillar pole; no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound shows hypoechoic fluid collection 2.5 cm at right tonsillar pole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Switch from phenoxymethylpenicillin to oral clindamycin and continue review with the general practitioner tomorrow
options.rationale: Established peritonsillar abscess requires drainage in addition to antibiotics; antibiotics alone rarely resolve a fluctuant collection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT neck to confirm abscess before any drainage despite confirmatory ultrasound findings
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected deeper space involvement; ultrasound is already confirmatory and CT delays definitive drainage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent tonsillectomy under general anaesthesia within 24 hours as definitive management in adolescents
options.rationale: Acute tonsillectomy is not first-line; needle aspiration or incision and drainage with intravenous antibiotics is the AU first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently for needle aspiration or incision and drainage with intravenous benzylpenicillin and metronidazole
options.rationale: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) requires needle aspiration or incision and drainage by an ENT or experienced ED clinician, plus intravenous benzylpenicillin and metronidazole pending culture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence high-dose dexamethasone alone without drainage to reduce swelling and reassess at 24 hours
options.rationale: Steroids are an adjunct to drainage and antibiotics, not a substitute; relying on steroids alone risks airway compromise as the abscess enlarges. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a complication of bacterial tonsillitis classically presenting with trismus, muffled voice, severe unilateral throat pain and uvular deviation. AU first-line management combines drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus metronidazole to cover oral anaerobes, switching to oral therapy once afebrile. Dexamethasone may be added to reduce pain and swelling. Tonsillectomy is reserved for recurrent disease or as an acute Quinsy tonsillectomy in selected cases. Airway compromise (drooling, stridor) is the cue to mobilise anaesthesia and ENT immediately.
key_points: Trismus + muffled voice + uvular deviation = peritonsillar abscess
Drainage + IV benzylpenicillin + metronidazole is first-line
Steroids are adjunctive, not substitutive
CT neck is reserved for deeper space concerns
explanation.pearls: Quinsy: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6 hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg 8 hourly, with bedside drainage by experienced ED or ENT clinician.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the general practitioner with worsening eczema flares for 3 months affecting her flexures, face and trunk. Her parents are applying QV cream once daily but have stopped using hydrocortisone 1% after reading online about steroid concerns. She is itchy enough to wake at night and has new excoriations across the antecubital fossae. There is no oozing, no honey-coloured crusting, and no systemic upset. She is fully vaccinated and is otherwise growing well. There is a strong atopic family history including asthma and allergic rhinitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Apyrexial; growth 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema and lichenification in flexures; excoriations; no impetiginisation; no eyelid swelling
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate skin care plan?

options.text: Continue QV cream only and avoid all topical steroids; trial a hypoallergenic diet for 6 weeks instead
options.rationale: Dietary elimination is not first-line in eczema without IgE-confirmed food trigger and skipping topical steroid undertreats inflammation, perpetuating itch and infection risk. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

options.text: Switch hydrocortisone for a topical calcineurin inhibitor as first-line therapy for paediatric flexural eczema
options.rationale: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing agents; for flare control in a steroid-naive flexural eczema, an appropriate-potency topical corticosteroid is first. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

options.text: Wet-wrap a high-potency topical steroid (mometasone furoate) twice daily across all affected areas for 4 weeks
options.rationale: High-potency steroids and wet wraps are reserved for severe or refractory disease; an appropriate-potency step is preferred and wet wrap is short-term only. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

options.text: Commence oral antihistamine cetirizine nightly and topical antibiotic mupirocin to all eczematous skin
options.rationale: Antihistamines do not treat the underlying inflammation; topical antibiotics are reserved for impetiginised eczema, not routine flares. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

options.text: Educate family on regular emollients with methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% to affected areas once daily for 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: AU paediatric guidance recommends thick emollients applied liberally plus a moderate-potency topical steroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% once daily to the flare areas for 1 to 2 weeks, with education to address steroid phobia. (Source: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan)

explanation.summary: Paediatric atopic eczema is managed primarily with emollients applied liberally and topical corticosteroids matched to severity and site. Steroid phobia is a major barrier and education on safe potency-by-site (mild for face, moderate to potent for body), the fingertip unit, and duration is essential. Calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing for face/eyelids or maintenance. Bleach baths and intermittent proactive twice-weekly steroid application reduce flare recurrence in moderate disease. Systemic therapy and biologics are specialist domains.
key_points: Emollient + appropriate-potency steroid is first-line in flares
Moderate potency (methylprednisolone aceponate) suits non-facial flexural eczema
Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second-line steroid-sparing agents
Antihistamines and routine antibiotics have no flare-control role
explanation.pearls: ASCIA Eczema Action Plan supports methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% once daily for 1 to 2 weeks for moderate flexural flare, alongside generous emollient.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to a general practice clinic with pallor noted by her grandmother and reduced energy at playgroup over 6 weeks. She drinks 800 mL of cow's milk daily, eats limited solids (mainly white bread and pasta), and has no overt blood loss. She was born at term, exclusively breastfed for the first 4 months, and has been gaining weight on the 25th centile track.

She has had no recurrent infections, no jaundice, and there is no family history of haemoglobinopathy. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and palmar creases but no jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no jaundice; soft non-tender abdomen; no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 22 pg, ferritin 5 mcg/L, CRP 4, reticulocytes low; faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Empirical oral antibiotics for occult bacterial infection and recheck full blood count in 4 weeks before iron replacement
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of infection and a CRP of 4 is normal; antibiotics are not indicated and delay iron correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Recommend intramuscular iron polymaltose injection given likely poor oral adherence in toddlers under 2 years
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is reserved for failed oral therapy or malabsorption; oral elemental iron is first-line in most paediatric cases with dietary modification. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric haematology for bone marrow biopsy and haemoglobinopathy electrophoresis screen
options.rationale: Classic dietary iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with high milk intake and no red flags does not require haematology referral or marrow biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Start oral elemental iron 3 mg per kg daily, reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL daily, and recheck haemoglobin at 6 weeks
options.rationale: First-line treatment for paediatric iron deficiency anaemia is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg per kg daily combined with dietary advice to limit cow's milk below 500 mL per day; recheck haemoglobin and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells now as a one-off given the symptomatic anaemia, then commence ongoing oral supplementation
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise; this child is haemodynamically stable and responds to oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia frequently reflects excess cow's milk intake (over 600 mL daily reduces iron absorption and displaces iron-rich solids), low dietary iron, and ongoing physiological demand. AU paediatric guidance is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg per kg daily for 3 months alongside dietary modification (cow's milk under 500 mL per day, iron-rich foods, vitamin C-rich drinks); recheck haemoglobin and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks. Parenteral iron, transfusion and haematology referral are reserved for failures or red flags. Screening also covers maternal mental health and developmental milestones since chronic iron deficiency affects neurodevelopment.
key_points: Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg/day is first-line
Cow's milk under 500 mL/day reduces ongoing displacement of iron-rich solids
Recheck Hb and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks
Continue iron 3 months after Hb normalises to replete stores
explanation.pearls: RCH guidance: oral iron 3 to 6 mg per kg per day plus cow's milk under 500 mL per day; recheck Hb and ferritin at 4 to 6 weeks.

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with 4 weeks of gradually worsening left groin and knee pain after no specific injury. His parents note that he has started walking with the left foot turned outwards. He has gained 12 kg in the past year; his body mass index is now on the 97th centile. There is no fever, no rash, no morning stiffness, and no other joint involvement.

His mother has type 2 diabetes. On examination, his left leg is held in slight external rotation; passive hip flexion causes obligate external rotation; he can weight-bear with a limp but not stand on the left leg alone without pain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Left leg externally rotated; obligate external rotation on hip flexion; antalgic limp; no joint effusion of knee
data_table.Investigations: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis radiographs available; CRP 6, WCC 8.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy review in 1 week for an irritable hip diagnosis
options.rationale: Irritable hip rarely affects adolescents over 10 and typically resolves quickly; the obligate external rotation sign and risk profile make this presentation surgically urgent. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Recommend a low-impact exercise programme with weight loss advice and rheumatology review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Active orthopaedic pathology with mechanical signs needs prompt surgical evaluation rather than deferred rheumatology assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Order a bone scan to characterise the lesion before any orthopaedic referral or weight-bearing restrictions
options.rationale: Plain radiographs (AP and frog-leg lateral) are the imaging of choice; bone scan is not first-line and delays definitive surgical fixation. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Aspirate the hip under ultrasound guidance to exclude septic arthritis before further definitive imaging or referral
options.rationale: Aspiration is indicated for suspected septic arthritis; this presentation is not febrile, CRP is low, and the obligate external rotation sign supports a mechanical aetiology. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

options.text: Make the patient strictly non-weight-bearing, refer for urgent orthopaedic review with AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation in an overweight adolescent with chronic groin pain referred to the knee is slipped upper femoral epiphysis until proven otherwise; non-weight bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral with AP and frog-leg lateral views is the AU standard to prevent slip progression and avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: SUFE)

explanation.summary: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE) typically presents in obese adolescents between 10 and 15 years with chronic groin or referred knee pain and obligate external rotation on hip flexion. Bilateral disease occurs in up to 40% and risk factors include obesity and endocrine conditions (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency). Definitive management is urgent in situ pinning to prevent slip progression and avascular necrosis; the child is kept strictly non-weight bearing until surgery. Perthes disease affects younger children (4 to 10) and has a different radiographic pattern.
key_points: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an adolescent = SUFE until proven otherwise
Pain may refer to the knee and delay diagnosis
Make strictly non-weight bearing; urgent orthopaedic referral; AP + frog-leg lateral views
Up to 40% of cases are bilateral over time
explanation.pearls: Obligate external rotation in adolescent hip flexion is the cardinal SUFE sign; AP + frog-leg lateral X-rays confirm and surgery prevents progression.

stem:
A term-born baby boy is 72 hours old and reviewed on the postnatal ward by the paediatric registrar after the midwife noticed visible jaundice extending to the trunk. He is breastfed every 2 to 3 hours, has had appropriate wet nappies and has lost 6% of birth weight. He was born at 39+2 weeks, the pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother is O Rh positive.

The baby is alert, feeds vigorously, and has no organomegaly or pallor. There is no family history of haemolytic anaemia. His transcutaneous bilirubinometer reading is 285 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.9
data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundice to mid-trunk, no hepatosplenomegaly, vigorous feeding
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 295 micromol/L (transcutaneous 285); DAT negative; blood group O+; FBC normal; reticulocytes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy with a fibre-optic blanket or bank of lights and recheck serum bilirubin in 6 to 12 hours
options.rationale: Term infants at 72 hours with serum bilirubin around the phototherapy threshold on AU nomograms require intensive phototherapy and a repeat serum bilirubin within 6 to 12 hours to monitor response. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Recommend supplementary formula feeding to accelerate clearance and recheck bilirubin in 24 hours after observation
options.rationale: Routine formula supplementation is not first-line in breastfed infants; phototherapy is the intervention and continued breastfeeding is encouraged. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Discharge home with sunlight exposure advice and review with the general practitioner in 48 to 72 hours after discharge
options.rationale: Sunlight exposure is unsafe and ineffective; discharge near the phototherapy threshold without intervention risks acute bilirubin neurotoxicity. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Arrange exchange transfusion within 24 hours regardless of the rate of bilirubin rise and clinical response observed
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels above the exchange threshold or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; it is not first-line at this concentration. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Withhold any treatment and repeat serum bilirubin in 24 hours assuming physiological jaundice in a healthy infant
