options.rationale: Physiological jaundice peaks at days 3 to 5 but levels near the phototherapy threshold mandate intervention and serial monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is assessed against AU age-specific nomograms which plot serum bilirubin against postnatal hours; treatment lines are adjusted for gestational age and risk factors (haemolysis, sepsis, prematurity). Intensive phototherapy uses higher irradiance (>=30 microwatts per cm2 per nm) over a broad surface area and is monitored with repeat serum bilirubin at 6 to 12 hour intervals. Continued breastfeeding is encouraged; formula supplementation is reserved for inadequate feeding. Exchange transfusion remains the rescue therapy for severe hyperbilirubinaemia or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
key_points: Use AU nomograms plotting bilirubin against postnatal age in hours
Intensive phototherapy is the first-line intervention at threshold
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy
Repeat serum bilirubin every 6 to 12 hours during phototherapy
explanation.pearls: Serum bilirubin at threshold on the AU nomogram triggers intensive phototherapy plus repeat measurement at 6 to 12 hours; continue breastfeeding.

sources.label: NICE NG98 Jaundice in newborn babies

stem:
A previously well 5-month-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department by her parents with 24 hours of fever to 39 and one episode of vomiting. She is feeding 70% of normal and has decreased wet nappies overnight. She has no rash, no cough, no diarrhoea, no obvious focus on examination, and her ears, throat and chest are clear.

She has not received antibiotics recently. A clean catch urine collected by the midwife shows leucocyte esterase 3+ and nitrites 2+ on dipstick; microscopy shows pyuria. Blood cultures and urine culture have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 42, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 39.1
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; no rash; soft abdomen; clear chest; ears normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick LE 3+ nitrites 2+; microscopy pyuria and gram-negative rods; WCC 19; CRP 75; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days with general practitioner review in 48 hours after discharge
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI require intravenous antibiotic initiation in Australia until clinically stable and afebrile; oral monotherapy is unsafe at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Admit for intravenous gentamicin and intravenous benzylpenicillin or ampicillin pending sensitivities and clinical response
options.rationale: Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months requires admission and intravenous therapy; AU first-line is gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or ampicillin pending culture and sensitivity. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy for 7 days irrespective of culture results once initial blood culture is drawn
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved when first-line cover is inadequate or sepsis is severe; gentamicin and penicillin remain first-line for uncomplicated febrile UTI in young infants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim for 7 days with renal ultrasound at 6 weeks if symptoms persist beyond 5 days of therapy
options.rationale: Trimethoprim has significant resistance and is not first-line for febrile UTI in young infants; the AU pathway requires IV therapy at this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin for 5 days, encouraging increased fluid intake and follow-up urine culture in 1 week
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue levels for pyelonephritis; it is reserved for older children with uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Infants under 6 months with febrile urinary tract infection require admission for intravenous antibiotics in Australia due to the risk of bacteraemia and renal scarring. First-line cover is gentamicin (single daily dose) plus benzylpenicillin or ampicillin, transitioning to a narrow-spectrum oral agent once afebrile and sensitivities known, for a total course of 7 to 10 days. A renal tract ultrasound is recommended after the first febrile UTI under 6 months; further imaging (MCUG, DMSA) depends on the ultrasound findings and clinical course.
key_points: Febrile UTI under 6 months: admit for IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin/ampicillin
Ultrasound urinary tract after first febrile UTI in this age group
Switch to oral once afebrile and sensitivities known
Beware enteric gram-negative resistance to trimethoprim
explanation.pearls: AU first-line for febrile UTI under 6 months: IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin/ampicillin then oral switch on sensitivities for a 7 to 10 day total course.

stem: A 3-month-old boy with bronchiolitis admitted 18 hours ago to a metropolitan paediatric ward has deteriorated. He has been on high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L per kg per minute with FiO2 0.4 for 6 hours. Despite this his work of breathing has increased with marked subcostal and intercostal recession; he is now only intermittently rousable. His latest capillary blood gas shows pH 7.20, pCO2 9.1 kPa, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. He is being suctioned hourly and has stopped feeding orally. The treating registrar phones the local paediatric intensive care service.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188, RR 72, SpO2 92% on HFNC FiO2 0.4, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession; only intermittently rousable; sluggish capillary refill 3s
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.20 pCO2 9.1 kPa HCO3 22 lactate 2.4; chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with peri-hilar streaking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase HFNC flow to 3 L per kg per minute and continue current FiO2 with reassessment in 60 minutes before any other escalation
options.rationale: HFNC has clearly failed with rising CO2 and altered mental state; further uptitration delays definitive ventilatory support. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back for 30 minutes before any further respiratory support escalation step
options.rationale: Bronchodilators have no place in bronchiolitis and do not address the central failure of ventilation in this scenario. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Prepare for intubation and arrange paediatric intensive care retrieval team transfer to a tertiary paediatric ICU
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis with rising CO2, reduced mental state and HFNC failure has an indication for intubation and PICU transfer; AU paediatric retrieval services should be engaged early. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)

options.text: Commence non-invasive bilevel ventilation locally and continue oral feeds while awaiting tertiary paediatric ICU advice
options.rationale: BiPAP can be a bridge in some centres, but with reducing GCS and ongoing rise in CO2 a controlled intubation is preferred before deterioration. (Source: ANZICS Paediatric Respiratory Support Guidance)

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg per kg and start broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically for bacterial superinfection
options.rationale: Steroids do not modify bronchiolitis and empirical antibiotics are not indicated without a clear focus; the immediate problem is ventilatory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Severe bronchiolitis in infants is the commonest reason for paediatric ICU admission with viral illness. AU practice tiers respiratory support from oxygen via nasal prongs, to HFNC, to non-invasive ventilation (in selected sites), to intubation; HFNC failure markers include rising CO2, reducing GCS, increasing work of breathing, and tachycardia. Once HFNC failure is recognised, the treating team should escalate to PICU rather than uptitrate flow indefinitely. The paediatric retrieval service should be contacted early to facilitate inter-hospital transfer.
key_points: HFNC failure markers: rising CO2, reducing GCS, persistent tachypnoea and tachycardia
Escalation pathway is to NIV or intubation, not higher HFNC
Engage paediatric retrieval services early for inter-hospital transfer
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics have no role even in severe bronchiolitis
explanation.pearls: Rising pCO2 above 8 kPa with reducing GCS on HFNC in bronchiolitis is an indication for intubation and PICU transfer, not further HFNC uptitration.

subtopic_detail: Mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse
stem:
A 9-month-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of right thigh swelling. His mother reports that he fell from a low couch. He is not yet walking or pulling to stand and has had no previous fractures. On examination, there is bruising over the thigh, mild swelling, and pain on movement. Imaging shows a spiral fracture of the right femoral shaft.

The infant also has a 2 cm bruise on the left buttock and a torn frenulum. There is no other history offered, no medical illness, and the mother appears anxious but engaged. The treating intern is unsure what to do next.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 90/56, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Thigh swelling, bruising over thigh and buttock, torn frenulum, no other injuries on initial inspection
data_table.Investigations: Plain radiograph right femur: spiral fracture mid-shaft; FBC, coags, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother that accidental fractures are common in this age group and discharge with orthopaedic follow-up
options.rationale: Spiral femoral fractures in non-mobile infants are highly suspicious for inflicted injury; discharge without further safeguarding assessment is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Request a metabolic bone disease workup before initiating any safeguarding referral or specialist child protection assessment
options.rationale: Metabolic workup may be considered later but should not delay child protection processes; the clinical picture mandates immediate safeguarding action. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Discuss the fracture with the family for further explanation and consider safeguarding only if no plausible account emerges
options.rationale: The injury pattern in a non-mobile infant warrants immediate mandatory reporting and specialist child protection involvement, irrespective of subsequent family account. (Source: State Mandatory Reporting Legislation)

options.text: Notify child protection as mandated reporter and admit for skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy and child protection team consult
options.rationale: Spiral femur fracture in a non-mobile infant with additional bruising and torn frenulum is highly suspicious for non-accidental injury; the doctor is a mandatory reporter, the child requires admission with skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy review and child protection consultation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse; State Mandatory Reporting Legislation)

options.text: Apply a thomas splint, admit under orthopaedics for fracture management and arrange social work follow-up at discharge
options.rationale: Orthopaedic management alone misses the child protection imperative; admission must include safeguarding processes including skeletal survey and statutory notification. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Doctors in all Australian states and territories are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse. Spiral or metaphyseal fractures, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures of different ages, torn frenulum in non-mobile infants, and bruising in non-mobile infants are sentinel injuries that warrant immediate child protection involvement. Workup includes skeletal survey, head imaging (CT or MRI), ophthalmology fundoscopy, baseline coagulation studies, and consultation with the local child protection team. The threshold to report is reasonable suspicion, not proof.
key_points: Spiral femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant is a sentinel injury
Mandatory reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof
Workup: skeletal survey, head imaging, fundoscopy, coags
Specialist child protection team should be consulted early
explanation.pearls: Sentinel injuries (bruise/torn frenulum/spiral fracture in a non-mobile infant) trigger mandatory reporting AND a structured medical safeguarding workup.

stem:
A 3-week-old male infant is recalled to a tertiary paediatric centre after a positive newborn screening test for cystic fibrosis. He was born at term, was breastfed within the first hour and is now feeding well with appropriate weight gain. He has no respiratory symptoms, no steatorrhoea and no failure to thrive at this point. His parents are not known to each other to be carriers.

Genetic testing on the newborn screening dried blood spot shows two CFTR mutations: F508del and a class V splice-site mutation. The pulmonary nurse phones the on-call paediatric registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 42, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeding well, no respiratory distress, no abdominal distension, normal anal sphincter tone
data_table.Investigations: Immunoreactive trypsinogen elevated x2 screens; CFTR genotype F508del and class V splice-site mutation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming and initiating management?

options.text: Reassure parents that compound heterozygous mutations are usually mild and review with the general practitioner in 6 months
options.rationale: Confirmation of CFTR dysfunction is required regardless of mutation class; deferring to 6 months is unsafe and not consistent with the AU pathway. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

options.text: Arrange faecal elastase only and start pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy empirically without further confirmatory testing
options.rationale: PERT is initiated after demonstrating pancreatic insufficiency through faecal elastase plus clinical assessment; it is not the only step and does not confirm CF. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

options.text: Refer to the geneticist alone for counselling about carrier risk and defer all CF treatment until symptoms emerge later
options.rationale: Genetic counselling is essential but presymptomatic CF management is the AU standard; deferring care worsens outcomes. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

options.text: Reassure that two mutations meet diagnostic criteria; commence azithromycin prophylaxis and salt supplementation immediately
options.rationale: Two CFTR mutations support but do not yet replace a sweat test in the AU pathway; azithromycin prophylaxis is not initiated at 3 weeks. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

options.text: Refer to the tertiary paediatric CF service for confirmatory sweat chloride testing, formal multidisciplinary review and structured surveillance
options.rationale: Positive newborn screening with two CFTR mutations is confirmed by sweat chloride testing in an accredited CF centre, followed by tertiary multidisciplinary review including respiratory, gastroenterology, dietetics, physiotherapy, social work and genetic counselling. (Source: Royal Childrens Hospital CF Pathway)

explanation.summary: Newborn bloodspot screening for cystic fibrosis in Australia uses elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by reflex CFTR genotyping; positive screens are referred to a tertiary CF centre for confirmatory sweat chloride testing. Multidisciplinary care begins in the neonatal period with respiratory clearance education, nutritional review, pancreatic insufficiency screening (faecal elastase), and CFTR modulator eligibility assessment. The diagnosis is confirmed when sweat chloride exceeds 60 mmol per L; values of 30 to 59 prompt repeat testing and ongoing follow-up. Newborn diagnosis improves nutritional and pulmonary outcomes substantially.
key_points: Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L confirms CF in symptomatic and screen-positive infants
Two CFTR mutations support but do not replace sweat test confirmation
Tertiary multidisciplinary care starts in the neonatal period
Faecal elastase guides need for pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride above 60 mmol/L confirms CF diagnosis in the AU newborn screening pathway, with multidisciplinary tertiary care from the neonatal period.

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to a general practitioner by her mother with 6 weeks of progressive patchy hair loss on the scalp. The child attends a primary school where several other children have similar findings. On examination there is a 3 by 4 cm area of broken hair shafts, mild scaling, and a slightly tender posterior occipital lymph node.

There is no kerion formation, no honey-coloured crusting, and no widespread inflammation. She is otherwise well, fully vaccinated and growing along the 50th centile. She has no known immunodeficiency or recent antibiotic use.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Patchy alopecia 3 by 4 cm with broken hairs and fine scale; tender occipital lymph node; no kerion
data_table.Investigations: Mycology skin scraping and plucked hair sample sent; KOH preparation pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Commence oral griseofulvin or terbinafine and add an antifungal shampoo to reduce household spread, awaiting mycology
options.rationale: Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungal therapy (oral griseofulvin or terbinafine) for adequate hair-shaft penetration; an antifungal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) reduces spore shedding and household spread. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Apply topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for 6 weeks and recommend avoiding sharing brushes and pillows in the household
options.rationale: Topical antifungals alone do not penetrate the hair shaft and are inadequate as monotherapy for tinea capitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for 10 days for likely bacterial superinfection of the scalp before any antifungal therapy
options.rationale: There is no evidence of impetiginisation; antibiotics do not treat dermatophyte infection and delay definitive antifungal therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Recommend short-course oral prednisolone alongside topical betamethasone to suppress inflammation as initial measures
options.rationale: Steroids may worsen tinea capitis (tinea incognito) by suppressing inflammation without treating the dermatophyte. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Reassure the family the condition is self-limiting and review in 8 weeks with no specific treatment beyond emollient
options.rationale: Untreated tinea capitis progresses to scarring alopecia and continues to transmit; treatment is required to prevent permanent hair loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Tinea capitis in children is typically caused by Trichophyton or Microsporum species and presents with patchy alopecia, scaling, broken hair shafts and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by mycology of skin scraping and plucked hairs (more sensitive than scrape alone). Systemic therapy is required for hair-shaft penetration: oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks. Adjunctive antifungal shampoo reduces spore shedding and household transmission. Untreated disease may produce kerion (boggy inflammatory mass) or scarring alopecia.
key_points: Topical antifungals alone are inadequate for tinea capitis
Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks is the AU first-line
Antifungal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) reduces spread
Steroids alone risk tinea incognito
explanation.pearls: Tinea capitis requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 4 to 8 weeks plus antifungal shampoo; topical alone is inadequate for hair-shaft penetration.

stem:
An 8-year-old girl is brought by her parents to a general practitioner with 6 weeks of progressively worsening headaches. The headaches initially occurred once a week and now occur daily. They are worse in the morning and on coughing or straining, and she has vomited (without nausea) on three mornings this week. She has been clumsier than usual on the netball court.

There is no fever, no neck stiffness and no rash. On examination she has a mild right-sided lower facial weakness and dysmetria of the right hand. Her family history includes migraine in her mother.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Mild right facial weakness; right dysmetria; gait slightly wide-based; fundi reveal blurred disc margins
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 10 mg nightly as migraine prophylaxis and review at the general practice clinic in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Daily morning headaches with vomiting, focal neurology and papilloedema are red flags incompatible with primary headache; starting prophylaxis without imaging is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Refer urgently for same-day paediatric assessment with neuroimaging (preferably MRI) to evaluate for intracranial pathology
options.rationale: Progressive morning headache with vomiting, focal neurological deficit and papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure; AU paediatric guidance is urgent same-day specialist review and neuroimaging, preferring MRI over CT in stable patients. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Order an outpatient MRI brain and review the imaging in 7 to 10 days as next available radiology appointment
options.rationale: Outpatient delays of a week are unsafe for raised intracranial pressure red flags; same-day assessment is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Trial sumatriptan nasal spray during the next acute episode and review in the migraine clinic over coming weeks
options.rationale: Triptans are inappropriate when red flags suggest secondary headache; they neither diagnose nor treat the underlying lesion. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture today before any imaging to measure opening pressure and exclude meningitis or pseudotumour cerebri
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture before imaging is contraindicated in suspected mass lesion due to coning risk; imaging precedes LP when red flags are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Paediatric headache red flags that mandate urgent neuroimaging include progressive course, morning headache with vomiting, change in personality or school performance, focal neurological deficits, papilloedema, headache worsened by Valsalva, and headache in children under 3 years. MRI is preferred in stable patients due to better posterior fossa visualisation and no radiation; CT is reserved for acute deterioration or when MRI is unavailable. Lumbar puncture is deferred until imaging excludes a mass lesion.
key_points: Morning headache + vomiting + focal signs + papilloedema = same-day imaging
MRI is preferred unless acutely unstable or MRI unavailable
Avoid LP until imaging excludes a mass lesion
Outpatient imaging delays are unsafe in red-flag paediatric headache
explanation.pearls: RCH paediatric headache red flags: morning headache, vomiting, focal signs and papilloedema mandate same-day specialist review and imaging.

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department 8 minutes after eating her first taste of peanut butter at home. Her mother describes immediate facial flushing and lip swelling, then audible wheeze and one episode of vomiting in the car. The child has eczema and a family history of asthma but no previous food reaction. She weighs 10 kg. On arrival she is distressed, has generalised urticaria, peri-oral oedema, and audible expiratory wheeze with mild intercostal recession. She is alert and crying.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 44, SpO2 94% room air, BP 80/45, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; peri-oral oedema without tongue swelling; bilateral wheeze; CRT 3s; alert
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; allergy testing arranged out-patient after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Oral cetirizine 5 mg with planned clinical reassessment for any escalation in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Oral antihistamines treat cutaneous symptoms only and have no role as primary treatment in anaphylaxis; their use risks delaying adrenaline in a patient with airway and circulatory involvement. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as a bolus while preparing nebulised salbutamol therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no demonstrated effect on the acute phase of anaphylaxis and do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions; their administration must not precede intramuscular adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg of 1:1000 into the anterolateral mid-thigh and reassess promptly
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg up to 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh is the immediate treatment in paediatric anaphylaxis; a 10 to 20 kg child receives 0.15 mg, with repeat doses every 5 minutes if no response. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.15 mg with a concurrent intravenous bolus of 20 mL/kg normal saline
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline is no longer used in anaphylaxis because absorption is slow and unpredictable when peripheral vasoconstriction has occurred; intramuscular delivery into the thigh is essential. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask with oxygen 6 L/min before any parenteral therapy
options.rationale: Nebulised bronchodilators are adjuncts for residual bronchospasm after adrenaline but must never be primary treatment when angioedema, urticaria, and circulatory features confirm systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric anaphylaxis requires immediate intramuscular adrenaline at 10 micrograms/kg, drawn from a 1:1000 ampoule and delivered into the anterolateral mid-thigh through clothing if needed. For a 10 to 20 kg child the standard dose is 0.15 mg, escalating to 0.3 mg above 20 kg and 0.5 mg in adolescents and adults. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators are second-line adjuncts only. After the first dose the child should remain supine with the legs elevated if hypotensive; the dose can be repeated every 5 minutes for ongoing or recurrent symptoms.
key_points: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg is first-line in paediatric anaphylaxis
Subcutaneous and intravenous routes are NOT the standard initial route
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway or circulatory compromise
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no clinical response
explanation.pearls: For a 10 to 20 kg paediatric patient the ASCIA IM adrenaline dose is 0.15 mg from a 1:1000 ampoule into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed.

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is referred to a paediatric clinic by her general practitioner because her weight has crossed from the 50th centile at 6 months to below the 10th centile, while her height and head circumference have remained on the 25th centile. She walks well, says 10 words, and has reached her 18-month milestones. Her appetite has decreased and she now refuses bread, cereal, and pasta after several episodes of bloating.

Stools are bulky and pale 3 to 4 times per day. There is no history of vomiting, diarrhoeal illness, or recurrent infection. The family is well housed and food secure.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Thin child with mild abdominal distension; muscle bulk reduced in buttocks and thighs; no organomegaly; no rash; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart: weight crossed two major centiles down; height and head on track

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Coeliac screen with tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA, FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH, and urine culture
options.rationale: An 18 month old with weight faltering, bulky pale stools, and food avoidance after gluten introduction requires coeliac screening with tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA to exclude selective IgA deficiency, alongside baseline FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH, and urine culture to capture the common organic causes. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

options.text: Bone age radiograph, insulin-like growth factor 1, growth hormone provocation testing, and karyotype
options.rationale: Endocrine investigations are reserved for short stature with preserved weight or proportionate growth failure; in weight-led faltering growth with normal height and head, endocrine workup is low yield and delays nutrient-deficiency identification. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

options.text: Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to exclude an intracranial space-occupying lesion
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated when head circumference is abnormal or growth failure is paired with neurological signs; isolated weight crossing centiles with preserved head circumference does not warrant MRI. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

options.text: Chromosomal microarray and Fragile X analysis as first-line for syndromic short stature
options.rationale: Genetic testing is appropriate for proportionate short stature with dysmorphic features or developmental concern; this child has normal milestones and weight-led faltering growth, not syndromic short stature. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

options.text: Referral to a paediatric dietitian for food diary and high-energy supplement plan without further testing
options.rationale: Dietetic input is part of management once organic causes are excluded; commencing energy supplements before excluding coeliac or other malabsorption risks masking the diagnosis without resolving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering Growth)

explanation.summary: Weight-led faltering growth in a toddler with preserved height and head circumference points to inadequate intake or malabsorption rather than endocrine or neurological pathology. The history of bulky pale stools and post-gluten bloating raises coeliac disease as the leading organic differential, requiring tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA to avoid missing selective IgA deficiency. The first-line work-up also captures iron deficiency, renal causes, occult urinary infection, and thyroid dysfunction. Endocrine, genetic, and imaging investigations are reserved for short stature, dysmorphism, or neurological features.
key_points: Weight crossing two centiles down with bulky pale stools suggests malabsorption
Coeliac screen needs tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA
Baseline FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH and urine MCS capture common organic causes
Endocrine and genetic workup is for short stature or syndromic features, not weight-led faltering growth
explanation.pearls: Always order total IgA with tissue transglutaminase IgA; an isolated tissue transglutaminase IgA in IgA-deficient children is falsely negative and misses coeliac disease.

stem:
A 9-month-old previously well boy is brought to the emergency department with 12 hours of intermittent crying episodes during which he draws his knees to his chest and appears pale, followed by quiet drowsy periods. His mother reports one passage of stool that looked like raspberry jam this morning and two episodes of bilious vomiting. He has not fed since lunchtime.

On examination he is lethargic but rousable, with a sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant. There is no peritonitis. He weighs 9 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 36, SpO2 98% room air, BP 90/55, Temp 37.2
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable; CRT 3 s; soft abdomen with a sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation and proceed to image-guided air enema reduction with surgical standby
options.rationale: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonitis is treated with hydrostatic or pneumatic enema reduction after fluid resuscitation; success rates exceed 80 percent and surgical standby is required for failed reduction or perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Plan urgent laparotomy as first-line management because of bilious vomiting and the abdominal mass
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed enema reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point; primary laparotomy is unnecessary and exposes the child to avoidable risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Administer ondansetron and observe in the short stay unit with serial abdominal examinations
options.rationale: Observation alone allows progression to bowel ischaemia and perforation; the child has confirmed ileocolic intussusception that requires active reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone for likely bacterial gastroenteritis and reassess in 6 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not indicated for intussusception; treating presumed gastroenteritis misses the diagnosis and delays reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Perform a contrast meal and follow through study to confirm the diagnosis prior to definitive therapy
options.rationale: Ultrasound has confirmed the diagnosis; meal and follow through is not the diagnostic tool of choice and adds delay without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in infants between 3 months and 3 years presents with episodic colic, vomiting, redcurrant jelly stool, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass. Bedside ultrasound showing a target or doughnut sign confirms the diagnosis. After fluid resuscitation, image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction in the radiology suite with surgical standby is the standard of care, with surgery reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point. Bilious vomiting is common with prolonged intussusception and does not by itself mandate primary laparotomy.
key_points: Target sign on USS confirms ileocolic intussusception
First-line management is fluid resuscitation then pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction
Surgery is reserved for failed reduction, peritonitis, perforation, or a pathological lead point
Recurrence rate after enema reduction is 5 to 10 percent
explanation.pearls: Even infants with established bilious vomiting and lethargy can usually be reduced by air enema if there is no peritonism; primary laparotomy is the exception, not the rule.

stem: A 4-day-old term boy is referred by the midwife after his mother noticed two episodes of green vomit overnight. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, passed meconium at 12 hours, and had been breastfeeding well. On arrival to the neonatal review clinic he is alert and pink but mildly distressed. His abdomen is soft and minimally distended without peritonism. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and his vital signs are normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 48, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 36.8, BP 70/40
data_table.Examination: Alert and pink; mild abdominal distension; soft non-tender abdomen; normally placed anus; passing meconium
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, lactate 1.6; FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain supine abdominal radiograph and observe with hourly abdominal examinations in the paediatric unit
options.rationale: A plain abdominal film cannot reliably exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus; relying on it risks missing an evolving volvulus that progresses to bowel necrosis within hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise; an upper GI contrast study is the diagnostic investigation of choice and must be expedited as delay risks irreversible bowel ischaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Trial of a thickened amino acid based formula and dietitian review for cow's milk protein allergy
options.rationale: Cow's milk protein allergy does not present with bilious vomiting in the first week; trialling formula change delays the urgent diagnosis of a surgical cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Commence ondansetron and IV maintenance fluids and reassess in 12 hours in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Symptomatic antiemetic therapy without investigation is dangerous in any neonate with bilious vomiting; the diagnostic priority is to exclude volvulus by contrast study. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound to assess the superior mesenteric artery and vein relationship and bowel perfusion
options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound of the SMA and SMV relationship may suggest malrotation but is operator dependent and is not the primary investigation; an upper GI contrast study remains the standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until imaging proves otherwise. Even in a well-appearing infant the diagnosis is time critical because volvulus can cause irreversible bowel necrosis within hours. The diagnostic investigation of choice is an upper gastrointestinal contrast study, which demonstrates the duodenojejunal flexure position and any corkscrew appearance of the duodenum. Concurrent management is nil by mouth, nasogastric drainage, intravenous fluids, and immediate referral to paediatric surgery. Plain films and abdominal ultrasound are adjuncts that do not exclude the diagnosis.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in the newborn equals malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise
Upper GI contrast study is the primary investigation
Even a well infant needs urgent imaging because volvulus progresses quickly
Initial care includes NBM, NG drainage, IV fluids and paediatric surgical referral
explanation.pearls: Bile is green. A normal abdominal exam in a green-vomiting neonate does not exclude volvulus. Move directly to the contrast study, not the AXR.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bilious Vomiting in the Neonate

stem:
An 11-year-old girl with a 2-year history of migraine without aura attends a paediatric review with her mother. Headaches occur 4 to 5 times per month, last 6 hours each, and force her to lie down in a dark room. She has missed 6 days of school in the last term. Her abortive regimen is paracetamol with ibuprofen, taken at headache onset, which only partially helps.

She uses no triptans. There are no red flags on history or examination. Her mother has migraine. She is well in herself and her growth and development are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 110/68, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Normal general and neurological examination; no papilloedema; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; headache diary kept by mother showing 4 to 5 attacks per month

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue paracetamol and ibuprofen for acute attacks and review with a headache diary in 6 months
options.rationale: Attack frequency above 4 per month with school absence meets the threshold for prophylaxis in paediatric migraine; ongoing acute therapy alone underservices her. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Refer for urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any prophylactic agent is started
options.rationale: MRI is indicated for red flags such as new neurological signs, morning vomiting, occipital location with neck pain, or rapidly escalating severity; routine prophylaxis decisions do not require imaging in the absence of red flags. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 25 mg nocte and titrate the dose at 4 week intervals as tolerated
options.rationale: Amitriptyline at 25 mg in an 11 year old is an excessive starting dose with cardiac and anticholinergic risk; AU paediatric guidance favours pizotifen or propranolol first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Prescribe oral sumatriptan as routine PRN abortive therapy without any prophylactic medication
options.rationale: Triptans are appropriate adjunct abortive therapy in adolescents but do not address the frequency that drives school absence; prophylaxis is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

options.text: Commence pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte, optimise sleep, hydration, screen time, and review in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Paediatric migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4 or more attacks per month or significant school absence; pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte plus lifestyle measures is an Australian first-line option, with review at 8 weeks for response and adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)

explanation.summary: Prophylaxis is indicated in paediatric migraine when there are 4 or more attacks per month, significant school absence, or abortive failure. First-line options in Australia are pizotifen or propranolol, both started at low dose and titrated. Lifestyle interventions including regular sleep, hydration, meal timing, and screen-time review are essential adjuncts. Amitriptyline and topiramate are second-line and require closer monitoring for adverse effects. Imaging is reserved for red flags. Treatment success is measured by attack frequency, severity, and functional impact, not by symptom abolition alone.
key_points: Prophylaxis threshold in paediatric migraine is 4+ attacks per month or significant school absence
First-line agents are pizotifen and propranolol
Lifestyle measures are core, not optional adjuncts
MRI is for red flags only
explanation.pearls: Pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte titrated to 1.5 mg is a reasonable starting prophylactic in paediatric migraine; counsel about weight gain and somnolence.

stem: A 5-year-old previously well girl is brought to the emergency department after her parents noticed widespread pinpoint red spots and bruising for 24 hours. Two weeks ago she had a self-limiting febrile viral illness. There has been no nose bleed, no mucosal bleeding, and no haematuria. She is otherwise well and meeting milestones. On examination she is afebrile and well-appearing with diffuse petechiae over her trunk and limbs, scattered bruises, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Her platelet count is 8 x10^9/L with normal white cells, normal haemoglobin, and a normal blood film aside from large platelets.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7, BP 100/62
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing; widespread petechiae and bruises; no mucosal bleeding; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 125, WCC 7.5, platelets 8 x10^9/L; blood film shows large platelets, otherwise normal; CRP 4

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose to raise the platelet count rapidly
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for clinically significant bleeding or platelet counts below 20 with mucosal bleeding; this child has cutaneous signs only and a count of 8 alone does not mandate IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days with a planned haematology review at the end of the course
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are an alternative pharmacological treatment when intervention is needed but are not first-line in well-appearing children with cutaneous-only ITP. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Perform an urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude acute leukaemia before any therapy
options.rationale: Routine bone marrow examination is not required in typical paediatric ITP with isolated thrombocytopenia and normal red and white cells; it is reserved for atypical features or non-response to first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Observe with bleeding precautions, avoid contact sports, and review the next day with platelet count and clinical assessment
options.rationale: Paediatric ITP with cutaneous-only bleeding is managed conservatively because spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 80 percent within 6 months; treatment is reserved for clinically significant bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Transfuse a single adult unit of pooled platelets to raise the count above 50 x10^9/L for safety
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is ineffective in ITP because transfused platelets are also destroyed, and it is reserved for life-threatening bleeding only. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Acute immune thrombocytopenia in children typically follows a viral illness and presents with isolated thrombocytopenia and cutaneous bleeding signs in a well-looking child. Spontaneous remission occurs in approximately 80 percent within 6 months. Management is conservative when bleeding is cutaneous only, regardless of platelet count, with bleeding precautions and avoidance of contact sports. Indications for pharmacological therapy include mucosal or major bleeding, with IVIG, corticosteroids, or anti-D as first-line options. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. Bone marrow examination is required only with atypical features such as cytopenias in other lineages or non-response to first-line treatment.
key_points: Paediatric ITP with cutaneous-only bleeding is observed, not treated
Pharmacological treatment is reserved for mucosal or major bleeding
Platelet transfusion is ineffective except in life-threatening bleeding
Bone marrow is needed only for atypical features or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Platelet count alone does not drive treatment in paediatric ITP; bleeding severity does. A well child with petechiae and a count of 5 is still managed conservatively.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department 6 hours after falling from a horse onto his head. He vomited twice in transit and his Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 on arrival. Over the next 90 minutes his GCS has dropped to 11 with reduced verbal response and localising to pain. His right pupil is 4 mm and sluggish, while the left is 3 mm and reactive.

Blood pressure has risen from 110/65 to 140/55 and heart rate has fallen from 92 to 50. He has not yet been imaged. The retrieval team estimates 60 minutes to the nearest paediatric neurosurgical centre.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 50, RR 14 irregular, SpO2 97% on 6 L mask, BP 140/55, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5); right pupil 4 mm sluggish, left 3 mm reactive; localising to pain; no focal limb weakness yet
data_table.Investigations: CT head not yet performed; FBC, UEC, coags pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation, head-up 30 degrees, hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, urgent CT head and neurosurgery transfer
options.rationale: Falling GCS with anisocoria, the Cushing reflex of hypertension and bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity indicates raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation; standard care is RSI with head-up positioning, hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, and urgent imaging with definitive neurosurgical care. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude a treatable cause of altered conscious state before transfer
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in a patient with focal signs and likely raised intracranial pressure risks cerebral herniation and is absolutely contraindicated until imaging excludes mass effect. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone for likely bacterial meningitis after recent trauma
options.rationale: There is no fever, neck stiffness, rash, or history suggestive of meningitis; treating bacterial meningitis here delays the actual diagnosis of intracranial haemorrhage. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Hyperventilate to a target PaCO2 of 25 mmHg as the primary measure to lower intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Aggressive hyperventilation to low PaCO2 risks ischaemic injury through vasoconstriction; PaCO2 is normalised at 35 to 40 mmHg with brief targeted reduction only for impending herniation as a temporising measure. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg via a peripheral line without securing the airway first
options.rationale: Mannitol may be used for raised intracranial pressure but is not the immediate single intervention; airway protection precedes osmotherapy and hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred in paediatric protocols. (Source: RCH CPG: Head Injury)

explanation.summary: Raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation in a child after head injury is identified by the Cushing reflex of hypertension and bradycardia, irregular respiration, falling GCS, anisocoria, and focal signs. Immediate care is airway protection through rapid sequence intubation, head-up 30 degrees, and a hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, alongside expedited CT head and definitive neurosurgical care. Mannitol is an alternative osmotic agent but hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred in paediatric protocols. Hyperventilation is used only briefly as a temporising measure for herniation, and lumbar puncture is contraindicated.
key_points: Cushing reflex (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing) signals impending herniation
Airway protection precedes osmotherapy
Hypertonic saline is increasingly preferred over mannitol in paediatric protocols
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until imaging excludes mass effect
explanation.pearls: Head-up 30 degrees and 3 percent hypertonic saline 3 to 5 mL/kg is the immediate paediatric osmotherapy of choice; mannitol remains an alternative when sodium loading is contraindicated.

stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after his mother found him with an open bottle of her ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablets. She estimates 10 tablets may be missing, giving an exposure of approximately 65 mg/kg of elemental iron. He has vomited twice and passed one loose grey-coloured stool. He is alert and crying. He weighs 12 kg. An abdominal radiograph shows several radio-opaque tablets in the upper gastrointestinal tract.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, BP 100/65, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and crying; mildly distressed; soft tender epigastrium; CRT 2 s; no shock
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray: tablets visible in stomach; serum iron and venous gas sent at 4 hours post ingestion; UEC, FBC, LFTs pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally as soon as airway is protected for gastrointestinal decontamination
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind iron and adds no benefit while increasing aspiration risk; it has no role in iron poisoning. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

options.text: Administer empirical intravenous deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour before serum iron results are available
options.rationale: Deferoxamine is reserved for serum iron above 90 micromol/L taken 4 to 6 hours post ingestion, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis; empirical treatment is unnecessary in a well child with imaging visible tablets. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

options.text: Perform orogastric lavage with warm saline to clear the residual iron tablets from the stomach immediately
options.rationale: Gastric lavage is not routinely used in iron overdose and risks aspiration and oesophageal injury; whole-bowel irrigation is the preferred decontamination when tablets remain visible. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

options.text: Discharge home with safety advice because vomiting is a sign of likely self-decontamination and recovery
options.rationale: Iron ingestion above 40 mg/kg requires observation for 6 hours and a serum iron at 4 to 6 hours because the latent phase between gastrointestinal symptoms and shock can lull clinicians into a false reassurance. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

options.text: Commence polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation and serum iron at 4 hours, with deferoxamine if iron is above 90 micromol/L
options.rationale: With residual radio-opaque tablets and ingestion above 40 mg/kg of elemental iron, polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation clears the gut, while serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine, which is started for iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Iron)

explanation.summary: Iron poisoning has five recognised phases: gastrointestinal in the first 6 hours, a latent phase from 6 to 24 hours, shock and metabolic acidosis from 12 to 48 hours, hepatic injury, and late gastrointestinal scarring. Activated charcoal does not bind iron and is not used. Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is the preferred decontamination when radio-opaque tablets remain in the gut. Serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine therapy, with treatment initiated for serum iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, altered conscious state, or persistent acidosis. Even asymptomatic children with iron ingestion above 40 mg/kg require observation through the latent phase.
key_points: Activated charcoal does not bind iron
Whole-bowel irrigation is the decontamination of choice when tablets remain in the gut
Serum iron at 4 to 6 hours guides deferoxamine therapy
The latent phase from 6 to 24 hours masks deterioration; observe through it
explanation.pearls: A deferoxamine threshold of serum iron 90 micromol/L plus the trigger of shock or persistent acidosis covers nearly all cases; clinical state always trumps a borderline number.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to a paediatric clinic by his mother who has noticed a firm abdominal mass while bathing him over the last 2 weeks. She also reports irritability, weight loss, and easy bruising of the eyelids that she initially attributed to a fall. He has been febrile intermittently. On examination he is pale and miserable with a firm fixed left upper abdominal mass that crosses the midline, periorbital ecchymoses without trauma, and blanching subcutaneous nodules. His blood pressure is 100/65. Urinary catecholamines are elevated. An MIBG scan shows tracer avidity in the primary mass and in skull lesions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 100/65, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 37.6, weight 14 kg (50th centile previously, now 25th)
data_table.Examination: Pale and miserable; firm fixed left upper abdominal mass crossing midline; periorbital ecchymoses; blanching subcutaneous nodules
data_table.Investigations: Urinary catecholamines elevated; MIBG: tracer avidity in primary mass and skull lesions; FBC: pancytopenia

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plan urgent nephrectomy as definitive management for the abdominal mass and submit specimen for histology
options.rationale: The mass crosses the midline and shows MIBG-avid metastases with elevated catecholamines, consistent with neuroblastoma not Wilms tumour; primary nephrectomy is the wrong operation. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

options.text: Commence oral corticosteroids as a trial for likely autoimmune cytopenia with consequent ecchymoses
options.rationale: The combination of abdominal mass, MIBG-positive skull deposits, and elevated catecholamines indicates metastatic neuroblastoma; corticosteroid trial for autoimmune cytopenia is inappropriate and delays oncology care. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

options.text: Reassure the family that periorbital ecchymoses are likely traumatic and review again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Bilateral periorbital ecchymoses in the absence of clear trauma plus a fixed abdominal mass are red flags for metastatic neuroblastoma; reassurance and delay are unsafe. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric oncology for tissue diagnosis, full staging and risk-adapted multidisciplinary management
options.rationale: The presentation of a midline-crossing abdominal mass with bilateral periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), MIBG-avid skull metastases, and elevated catecholamines is metastatic neuroblastoma; urgent oncology referral for tissue diagnosis, staging, and risk-adapted treatment is the standard of care. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

options.text: Plan a renal biopsy under ultrasound guidance to confirm Wilms tumour before any further intervention
options.rationale: Wilms tumour does not typically cross the midline, lacks MIBG avidity, and does not produce catecholamines; renal biopsy targets the wrong diagnosis. (Source: eviQ Paediatric Neuroblastoma)

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and arises from sympathetic neural crest tissue. It typically presents in children under 5 years with an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour which usually remains confined to one side. Periorbital ecchymoses or so called raccoon eyes reflect orbital metastases, while subcutaneous blueberry muffin nodules and bone marrow involvement complete the syndrome. Urinary catecholamines and MIBG scintigraphy are diagnostic. Treatment depends on stage and risk stratification, including INSS stage, MYCN amplification, and age. Low-risk disease may regress spontaneously, while high-risk disease requires multimodal therapy including surgery, chemotherapy, autologous stem cell transplant, and immunotherapy with anti-GD2.
key_points: Neuroblastoma crosses midline; Wilms typically does not
Bilateral periorbital ecchymoses without trauma signal orbital metastasis
Urinary catecholamines plus MIBG scintigraphy clinch the diagnosis
Risk-adapted management is determined by stage, MYCN, and age
explanation.pearls: Bilateral racoon eyes without trauma in a toddler plus an abdominal mass crossing midline equals neuroblastoma until proven otherwise; do not biopsy the kidney.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is referred to the paediatric emergency department with two weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. Today he developed vomiting, abdominal pain, and laboured breathing. He weighs 22 kg. He is alert, oriented, with deep sighing respirations and acetone breath. He has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes and has no shock features clinically, though he is moderately dehydrated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 98% room air, BP 98/62, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul breathing; dry mucous membranes; CRT 2s; alert (GCS 15); no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28.4 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L; venous pH 7.10, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 9.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid management?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes then reassess for further boluses
options.rationale: Aggressive 20 mL/kg boluses in non-shocked paediatric DKA increase cerebral oedema risk; bolus volumes are reserved for circulatory shock and given as 10 mL/kg with reassessment. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes then maintenance plus deficit replacement over 48 hours
options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA protocols use a single 10 mL/kg bolus only when perfusion is impaired, then estimate dehydration at 7 to 8 percent and replace the deficit evenly over 48 hours alongside maintenance to minimise cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous Hartmann solution 30 mL/kg over an hour with intravenous insulin started immediately at induction
options.rationale: Large volume Hartmann boluses risk dilutional fall in osmolality and rapid bicarbonate correction with cerebral oedema; insulin started before intravascular volume restoration accelerates the osmotic shift. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Oral rehydration solution titrated to thirst with bedside ketone reassessment every two hours before any insulin
options.rationale: Oral rehydration is inadequate in vomiting children with significant acidosis; intravenous access and controlled deficit replacement with insulin infusion are mandatory. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes given the venous pH below 7.15 with normal saline alongside
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not indicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia or cardiac arrest; routine use worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG/RCH Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA fluid management balances volume restoration against cerebral oedema risk. A single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus is given only for circulatory compromise. Dehydration is estimated at 7 to 8 percent and replaced evenly over 48 hours alongside maintenance, with insulin started 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h. Bicarbonate is contraindicated outside arrest.
key_points: Bolus only for shock; single 10 mL/kg dose then reassess
Deficit replaced over 48 hours, not 24
Insulin starts 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h
Bicarbonate worsens outcomes in paediatric DKA
explanation.pearls: Australian APEG paediatric DKA protocol: 10 mL/kg saline bolus only if shocked, then maintenance plus 7 to 8 percent deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h starting 1 hour after fluids.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA

stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 02:00 with a 12-hour history of coryza and a barking cough. Over the last hour she has developed audible inspiratory stridor at rest and is visibly distressed. She weighs 14 kg and has no past medical history. Her vaccinations are up to date. She has not yet received any treatment in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 38, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 37.8
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest; suprasternal and intercostal recession; tracheal tug; agitated but rousable
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no imaging or bloods required

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose with reassessment of stridor severity after 30 minutes
options.rationale: Oral dexamethasone is correct for mild to moderate croup, but severe croup with stridor at rest plus retractions warrants concurrent nebulised adrenaline for rapid relief. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with concurrent oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and 3 hours (RCH minimum) observation
options.rationale: Stridor at rest with retractions defines severe croup; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid relief lasting 30 to 60 minutes and a single corticosteroid dose extends effect, with mandatory observation post-adrenaline for rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back to back with ipratropium 250 micrograms then admission to short-stay unit
options.rationale: Bronchodilators target lower airway bronchospasm and have no benefit in viral laryngotracheitis where the obstruction is subglottic oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg plus immediate ENT review with airway plan for theatre intubation
options.rationale: Empiric ceftriaxone with ENT is the pathway for suspected epiglottitis where the child is toxic, drooling, and sitting in tripod position; the barking cough and coryza here are typical viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Humidified oxygen via head box with a 30 minute trial of mist therapy before any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Cochrane reviews show humidified air provides no benefit in croup and delays effective treatment; severe croup mandates adrenaline and steroid without delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Severe croup is defined by stridor at rest plus retractions or agitation. Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL gives rapid relief within 10 minutes lasting around 60 minutes, and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg provides sustained corticosteroid effect. Children must be observed for 3 hours (RCH minimum) after-adrenaline because of potential rebound stridor before discharge can be considered.
key_points: Stridor at rest plus retractions = severe croup
Adrenaline acts in 10 minutes; effect wanes by 60 minutes
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO for severe disease
Observe 3 hours (RCH minimum) post-adrenaline for rebound
explanation.pearls: Severe croup: nebulised 1:1000 adrenaline 5 mL plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, observe 3 hours (RCH minimum) minimum because rebound stridor follows the 60-minute adrenaline window.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-day palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and an acutely swollen painful left knee. He had a coryzal illness two weeks ago. Today his urinalysis shows 1+ blood and no protein. His blood pressure is normal and his renal function is preserved. The family lives 90 minutes from the nearest paediatric centre and asks whether they need to remain admitted. The diagnosis has been discussed with the family.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura on lower limbs and buttocks; tender left knee with effusion; soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 1+, protein nil; Cr 38 micromol/L; FBC normal; platelets 312 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan for renal involvement?

options.text: Urine dipstick and blood pressure measurement weekly for one month then monthly to 6 months and at 12 months
options.rationale: Nephritis can present up to 6 months after initial rash even when urinalysis is initially normal; the recommended surveillance is weekly to 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months with a final review at 12 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Renal ultrasound now followed by routine paediatrician review in 6 weeks with paired urea and electrolytes
options.rationale: Renal ultrasound is not part of routine HSP surveillance and does not detect early nephritis; urinalysis and blood pressure are the screening tools that pick up significant proteinuria first. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Discharge with general practitioner urinalysis once at 4 weeks unless rash, joint, or abdominal symptoms recur
options.rationale: A single 4-week urinalysis misses the delayed nephritis window; up to 30 percent develop renal involvement within 6 months and weekly then monthly surveillance is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Empirical oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 weeks plus weekly urinalysis until rash resolves then discharge
options.rationale: Routine corticosteroids do not prevent nephritis or reduce long-term renal sequelae and are not justified solely to influence rash duration. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Urgent paediatric nephrology referral and percutaneous renal biopsy within 2 weeks regardless of progression
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistent significant proteinuria over 4 weeks, or rapidly deteriorating function; isolated microscopic haematuria does not warrant invasive investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Nephritis in HSP can present up to 6 months after the initial rash, and around one third of children develop urinary abnormalities. The Australian surveillance schedule includes weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, then monthly to 6 months, with a final review at 12 months. Persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or declining function trigger nephrology referral and potential biopsy.
key_points: Nephritis may appear up to 6 months after rash
Surveillance: weekly to 4 weeks, monthly to 6 months, then 12 months
Steroids do not prevent or treat nephritis prophylactically
Biopsy thresholds: nephrotic proteinuria, persistent significant proteinuria, or declining GFR
explanation.pearls: Even with normal initial urinalysis, HSP requires weekly BP and dipstick to 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months and review at 12 months because nephritis can present late.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerular Diseases

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to her general practice with 36 hours of left ear pain and fever to 38.4. She has had two previous self-limiting episodes of similar pain. She is otherwise well, eating and drinking, and clinically not toxic. Otoscopy shows a bulging, immobile, opaque red left tympanic membrane without perforation, with normal contralateral findings. She lives in metropolitan Sydney and has no chronic conditions. She is not from an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Left TM bulging, immobile, opaque, red; no perforation or discharge; right TM normal
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no swabs or imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4 hours plus oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days starting today
options.rationale: Routine immediate antibiotics are not first line in a non-toxic non-Indigenous child over 2 years with unilateral AOM and intact tympanic membrane; analgesia with 48-hour observation is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

options.text: Analgesia alone with paracetamol or ibuprofen and parental review in 48 hours if there is no clinical improvement
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines support a watchful-waiting approach with analgesia in well non-Indigenous children over 2 with unilateral AOM and intact tympanic membrane, reserving antibiotics for failure to improve at 48 hours, perforation, or systemic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days and topical ciprofloxacin drops to the affected ear
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after amoxicillin or perforation with discharge; first-line antibiotic when indicated is amoxicillin alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days with intranasal decongestants to reduce middle ear inflammation rapidly
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and decongestants have no demonstrated benefit in AOM and risk harm; analgesia is the cornerstone of supportive care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

options.text: Urgent ENT review and tympanocentesis to obtain middle ear fluid for microbiology and targeted therapy choice
options.rationale: Tympanocentesis is not routine and is reserved for atypical, recurrent, or complicated cases not responding to standard care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Otitis media)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media in well non-Indigenous Australian children over 2 years with unilateral disease and intact tympanic membrane is managed with analgesia and review at 48 hours. Antibiotics are reserved for children under 2, bilateral AOM, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, or failure to improve at 48 hours. When indicated the first-line agent is amoxicillin.
key_points: Watchful waiting suits non-toxic non-Indigenous unilateral AOM over 2
Amoxicillin first line when antibiotics indicated
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is second line for treatment failure or discharge
Antibiotics indicated in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children due to higher complication rates
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic Guidelines indications for immediate antibiotics in AOM: under 2 years, bilateral, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, immunocompromise, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background.

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents on day 6 of fever above 39 with persistent fever despite paracetamol. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm in diameter. He has erythematous palms with mild swelling. Streptococcal swab is negative and there is no contact with measles. Blood tests show neutrophilia, raised CRP, and thrombocytosis. He is reviewed in a paediatric inpatient unit. A baseline echocardiogram is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, BP 96/58, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 39.4
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection; red cracked lips; strawberry tongue; polymorphous rash; right cervical lymphadenopathy 2 cm; erythematous swollen palms
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (N 14.8), CRP 142 mg/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L; ASOT pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and discharge with paracetamol; review only if fever lasts beyond day 14 of illness presentation
options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 substantially increases coronary aneurysm risk; the priority is IVIG administration within the window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and oral roxithromycin for presumed group A streptococcal scarlet fever overlap
options.rationale: Scarlet fever does not produce conjunctivitis, mucositis, or palmar oedema; misdiagnosis delays IVIG and increases aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day in four divided doses without intravenous immunoglobulin and reassess at day 10
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is insufficient and does not reduce coronary aneurysm rates; IVIG is the disease-modifying treatment within the 10-day window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10 hours plus aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses
options.rationale: Five criteria of fever plus four of conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy confirm Kawasaki disease; IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm rate from 25 percent to under 5 percent, with adjunct aspirin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse alone with paracetamol around the clock for symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Adjunctive steroids are considered in high-risk or IVIG-resistant disease, not as monotherapy first line in straightforward Kawasaki within the IVIG window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by fever lasting 5 days or more with at least 4 of bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm. IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset cuts coronary aneurysm risk from around 25 percent to under 5 percent. High-dose aspirin is added until afebrile then reduced to antiplatelet dose. Baseline and follow-up echocardiograms are mandatory.
key_points: 5 days fever + 4 of 5 features confirms diagnosis
IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days dramatically reduces coronary aneurysm risk
Aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day initially then 3 to 5 mg/kg/day antiplatelet
Echocardiogram at baseline and follow-up 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Kawasaki disease key threshold: IVIG 2 g/kg within day 10 of fever drops coronary aneurysm rate from 25 percent to under 5 percent; aspirin is adjunct, not substitute.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

stem: An 18-month-old previously well boy presents after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting 18 minutes. The seizure terminated with intramuscular midazolam given by paramedics. He has a temperature of 39.1 and rhinorrhoea. He has fully regained his baseline neurological status over the past 2 hours. He has had one previous brief simple febrile seizure 4 months ago. Examination today shows no focal neurology, soft fontanelle, no neck stiffness, and no rash. He is feeding and interactive on the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, BP 92/56, Temp 39.1
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive; soft fontanelle; no neck stiffness; no rash; no focal neurology; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.8 mmol/L; venous gas normal; FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further investigation pathway?

options.text: Urgent CT brain followed by lumbar puncture and electroencephalogram performed during the same admission today
options.rationale: Routine CT and EEG are not indicated in a fully recovered well child with prolonged febrile seizure and no focal neurology, raised ICP signs, or persistent altered consciousness. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

options.text: Identify and treat the febrile source, observe for several hours, and discharge with safety-net advice if returned to baseline
options.rationale: A complex febrile seizure in a child who has fully returned to baseline without focal signs requires investigation of the febrile source and observation only; brain imaging and EEG are not routinely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

options.text: Lumbar puncture in all children under 24 months with any febrile seizure to exclude meningitis or encephalitis
