options.rationale: Universal LP in children under 24 months is no longer supported; LP is indicated when meningitis is clinically suspected, when the child has not returned to baseline, or when pretreatment with antibiotics could mask features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

options.text: Outpatient MRI brain plus electroencephalogram in 4 weeks and commence prophylactic sodium valproate today
options.rationale: Long-term anticonvulsant prophylaxis is not indicated for febrile seizures because the recurrence and subsequent epilepsy risk does not justify medication adverse effects. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

options.text: Admit to paediatric ICU for continuous EEG monitoring and 48 hours of intravenous antiepileptic loading therapy
options.rationale: ICU admission and EEG monitoring are not indicated after a self-terminating febrile seizure in a child who has returned to baseline; this overtreats a benign syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizures)

explanation.summary: Complex febrile seizures are those lasting more than 15 minutes, recurring within 24 hours, or focal. A well child who returns to baseline requires investigation of the febrile source and a period of observation, but routine imaging, EEG, and anticonvulsant prophylaxis are not indicated. LP and imaging are reserved for clinical suspicion of meningitis, altered consciousness, focal neurology, or signs of raised ICP. Recurrence risk after first febrile seizure is about 30 percent overall.
key_points: Complex = under 15 min, recurrent in 24 h, or focal
Investigate source of fever; do not routinely image
LP only if clinically suspicious for meningitis or not back to baseline
No role for anticonvulsant prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Complex febrile seizure with full recovery and no focal signs: investigate the fever source, observe, and discharge with safety-netting. No routine CT, EEG, or anticonvulsants.

sources.label: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile Seizures

stem: A 5-month-old previously well infant is admitted with a 3-day history of coryza, cough, and progressively worsening work of breathing. She weighs 7 kg. Standard low-flow nasal oxygen at 2 L/min over the past 2 hours has been insufficient to keep saturations stable above 92 percent and feeds have stopped. She remains alert and the bedside nurse asks for your guidance on the next step. The respiratory consultant has been notified. She has no congenital heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Moderate intercostal and subcostal recession; tracheal tug; widespread expiratory wheeze with bilateral crackles; alert but tiring
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; CXR not required routinely; nasopharyngeal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent 4-hourly with 100 percent oxygen via Hudson mask
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does not change duration of hospitalisation in bronchiolitis; rising oxygen requirement on low-flow nasal cannula indicates escalation to high-flow rather than nebuliser strategies. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back and reassess response after the third dose has been administered
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no demonstrated benefit in bronchiolitis under 12 months and is not recommended; the appropriate response is escalation of oxygen support. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh and prepare for emergent intubation now
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis, not bronchiolitis; intubation may be needed later but is not the immediate next step before non-invasive escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow humidified nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min FiO2 titrated to keep saturations above 92 percent
options.rationale: Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min is the recommended escalation when low-flow oxygen fails to maintain saturations above 92 percent in moderate bronchiolitis; the PARIS trial demonstrated reduced escalation to ICU compared with standard oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days and continue current oxygen support without further escalation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in bronchiolitis under 12 months and should not be used routinely; rising oxygen requirement signals escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants is managed primarily with supportive care: hydration via nasogastric or intravenous route as needed and oxygen titrated to maintain saturations above 92 percent. When low-flow oxygen is insufficient, heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min reduces escalation to ICU compared with standard oxygen (PARIS trial). Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline, and antibiotics are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Saturations target above 92 percent
HFNC 2 L/kg/min reduces ICU escalation (PARIS trial)
No role for salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics in typical bronchiolitis
Hydration: NG or IV when feeds dropping
explanation.pearls: PARIS trial: heated humidified HFNC at 2 L/kg/min reduces ICU escalation in infant bronchiolitis when low-flow oxygen fails; saturations target above 92 percent.

sources.label: PARIS trial - High-flow oxygen therapy in infants with bronchiolitis

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to your general practice with 8 months of infrequent, hard, painful bowel motions every 5 to 7 days, soiling episodes 3 days per week with overflow incontinence, and intermittent abdominal pain. On examination her abdomen is soft with a palpable suprapubic faecal mass and her bottom is fissured externally. Her growth is on the 50th centile.

There are no red flags for organic disease and her parents are anxious about a recent school review. Toilet training was uneventful and there has been no recent stressor.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 92/58, Temp 36.6, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Palpable suprapubic faecal mass; perianal fissure visible; normal lower limb neurology; normal sacral spine; thyroid clinically normal
data_table.Investigations: No further investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery now for outpatient anorectal manometry and possible Hirschsprung biopsy work-up
options.rationale: Hirschsprung presents in infancy with delayed meconium and tight rectum on PR; a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation and overflow soiling does not require surgical work-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Recommend daily lactulose 5 mL after meals plus a high-fibre diet and weekly bowel diary review
options.rationale: Maintenance therapy without disimpaction in a child with palpable faecal loading risks ongoing overflow soiling and does not address the impacted faecal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe stimulant senna 7.5 mg daily indefinitely with no disimpaction phase or behavioural toileting plan
options.rationale: Stimulant laxatives have a role as add-on therapy, but they should not be used as monotherapy in impacted constipation, and disimpaction with osmotic laxatives is the first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Schedule a sodium phosphate enema cycle weekly for 4 weeks in clinic before commencing oral therapy plans
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas carry hyperphosphataemia risk in children and are reserved for failed oral disimpaction; macrogol-based oral disimpaction is the standard first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence escalating macrogol disimpaction regimen over 3 to 7 days with maintenance dosing and behavioural toileting plan
options.rationale: Escalating macrogol (polyethylene glycol with electrolytes) is the recommended first-line disimpaction agent for paediatric functional constipation with faecal loading, with subsequent maintenance and behavioural toileting to prevent recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Paediatric functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction before maintenance. Escalating macrogol over 3 to 7 days is the first-line oral agent and avoids the risks of phosphate enemas. Maintenance dose macrogol is continued for months alongside scheduled toilet sits after meals, fibre and fluid optimisation, and reward systems. Stimulant laxatives are reserved for breakthrough. Red flags (delayed meconium, ribbon stools, sacral abnormality, faltering growth, abnormal lower limb neurology) warrant specialist work-up.
key_points: Disimpact first with escalating macrogol then maintain
Phosphate enemas carry hyperphosphataemia risk; avoid
Behavioural toileting after meals is essential
Red flags trigger specialist referral
explanation.pearls: Macrogol PEG with electrolytes escalating regimen is first-line disimpaction in paediatric functional constipation; do not skip disimpaction or overflow soiling will persist.

sources.label: NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN evidence-based recommendations on functional constipation

subtopic_detail: Neonatal hypoglycaemia screening in infant of diabetic mother
stem: A term male infant has just been born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes who was on a basal-bolus regimen requiring 76 units per day at term. Birth weight is 4380 g (above 90th centile). Apgars are 9 and 9 and the baby has fed briefly at the breast within 30 minutes of birth and is now asleep in skin-to-skin contact with mother. He is pink, well perfused, and asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98% in air, axillary T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Pink, alert when handled, normal tone, no jitteriness, no cyanosis, no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed since delivery 35 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this infant's management?

options.text: Check a true blood glucose at 2 hours of age after the second feed, before further feeding, and act on a threshold of 2.6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Australian NHMRC and Queensland Clinical Guideline schedules for IDM and large-for-gestational-age neonates screen at 2 hours after a feed (not earlier, as transient nadir at 1 hour is physiological), then before subsequent feeds with an operational threshold of 2.6 mmol/L. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Defer all glucose testing until 6 hours of age provided the baby remains asymptomatic and feeds three-hourly with no jitteriness
options.rationale: IDM and LGA neonates require glucose screening from 2 hours regardless of symptoms because severe asymptomatic hypoglycaemia is well documented in this population during the first 12 hours. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Check a true blood glucose immediately and again at 4 hours, treating any reading below 3.3 mmol/L with intravenous dextrose
options.rationale: Immediate screening captures a physiological postnatal nadir and the 3.3 mmol/L threshold is not the Australian operational cut-off; routine intravenous dextrose without enteral feed trial is excessive in an asymptomatic feeding IDM. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give 200 mg/kg of 40 percent buccal dextrose gel routinely at one hour of age regardless of the screening glucose value
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel is indicated when the screening glucose is below 2.6 mmol/L in an asymptomatic infant alongside a feed, not as universal prophylaxis irrespective of measured glucose. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Admit to special care nursery now for prophylactic 10 percent dextrose infusion at 60 mL/kg/day without further bedside glucose testing
options.rationale: Prophylactic intravenous dextrose is reserved for symptomatic infants or those failing to respond to enteral and buccal dextrose strategies; routine admission separates mother and baby unnecessarily in an asymptomatic IDM. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: IDMs, LGA, SGA and late-preterm infants are routinely screened for hypoglycaemia from 2 hours of age after a feed. The operational threshold in Australia is 2.6 mmol/L; below this in an asymptomatic infant, treat with feed plus 200 mg/kg buccal 40 percent dextrose gel and recheck in 30 minutes. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or persistent low readings escalate to IV dextrose. Earlier glucose checks pick up physiological nadir at 1 hour and prompt unnecessary escalation.
key_points: Risk groups: IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm, perinatal stress.
Screen at 2 h after first feed, then pre-feed during 12 to 24 h.
Threshold 2.6 mmol/L; gel 200 mg/kg + feed for asymptomatic.
IV 10 percent dextrose if symptomatic or refractory.
explanation.pearls: The 2.6 mmol/L threshold and 2-hour-after-feed timing are the most commonly missed numbers; buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg is given with a feed, never instead of it.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia in Neonates

subtopic_detail: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis diagnostic pathway
stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy presents with three days of progressively forceful non-bilious vomiting that now occurs after every breastfeed and reaches the foot of the cot. He remains hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting. He has lost 200 g since birth and last wet his nappy 8 hours ago. His mother had similar surgery as an infant. On examination he is alert with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and you palpate a firm mobile mass in the right upper quadrant during a test feed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.7, weight 3.9 kg
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, CRT 3s, no abdominal distension, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis after test feed, palpable olive RUQ
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.52, HCO3 33 mmol/L, Cl 88 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, Na 134 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound measuring pyloric muscle thickness and channel length against accepted paediatric thresholds
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory imaging in Australia; diagnostic thresholds are pyloric muscle thickness 3 mm or greater and channel length 15 mm or greater, with sensitivity above 95 percent and no radiation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study with barium swallow looking for a string sign at the pylorus
options.rationale: Contrast studies have been superseded by ultrasound in Australian paediatric centres because of radiation exposure and aspiration risk in a vomiting hypovolaemic infant; reserved for atypical presentations after a non-diagnostic ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy under general anaesthesia to visualise the pyloric channel and exclude mucosal pathology
options.rationale: Endoscopy is not indicated in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; it carries anaesthetic risk in a metabolically deranged infant and ultrasound is non-invasive and definitive. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Plain abdominal radiograph in supine and erect projections to identify the caterpillar sign and dilated stomach
options.rationale: Plain films are non-specific and neither confirm nor exclude pyloric stenosis; relying on them delays surgical referral and exposes the infant to ionising radiation unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Repeat test feed observation over 24 hours of inpatient admission with serial weight checks before any imaging
options.rationale: The presentation is already classic and biochemistry shows the typical hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; delaying imaging prolongs dehydration and surgical correction. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3 to 8 weeks with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting in a hungry feeder, palpable olive, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Ultrasound is the first-line confirmatory test in Australia using thresholds of muscle thickness at least 3 mm and channel length at least 15 mm. Management is resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline plus potassium to correct the alkalosis before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy. Family history (especially affected parent) increases risk substantially.
key_points: Classic 3-8 week age, hungry vomiter, projectile non-bilious.
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is biochemical hallmark.
Ultrasound thresholds: muscle 3+ mm, channel 15+ mm.
Resuscitate alkalosis before surgery; not a surgical emergency.
explanation.pearls: Surgical referral waits for the bicarbonate to fall below 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L; operating on uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea.

sources.label: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons paediatric resources

stem:
A 9-month-old previously well girl presents with 14 hours of episodic inconsolable screaming and drawing knees up, occurring every 20 minutes between which she is pale and listless. She vomited twice (one episode bile-stained) and passed dark red jelly-like stool in the nappy two hours ago. She is hydrated and alert between episodes, with a tender sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant.

There is no peritonism and no distension. Ultrasound performed in the emergency department shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, RR 28, SpO2 99% air, BP 92/58, T 36.9, weight 8.5 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert between paroxysms, soft non-distended abdomen, palpable RUQ mass, no peritonism, redcurrant jelly stool on PR
data_table.Investigations: USS: target sign RUQ, no free fluid, normal blood flow on Doppler. FBC normal, electrolytes normal, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole then re-evaluate in 4 hours to see whether the paroxysms settle
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not reduce an intussusception; perforation has not occurred and broad-spectrum cover is not the initial intervention in a confirmed ileocolic intussusception without sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Immediate laparotomy with manual reduction in theatre without any prior attempt at radiological reduction in the department
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed pneumatic reduction, perforation, peritonism, or shock; primary operation in a stable child denies an 80 to 90 percent chance of avoiding laparotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Barium contrast enema reduction in the radiology department with the family in the room throughout the procedure
options.rationale: Air contrast has replaced barium in Australian paediatric practice because air carries lower peritoneal contamination risk on perforation and higher reduction pressures are achievable safely. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Bowel rest with nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids for 24 hours awaiting spontaneous resolution before reimaging
options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction is uncommon and delay risks ischaemia, perforation, and increased need for bowel resection; non-operative reduction should not be delayed in a confirmed case. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Pneumatic (air contrast) reduction under fluoroscopic guidance with paediatric surgical team scrubbed for immediate laparotomy
options.rationale: Pneumatic (air contrast) reduction is the first-line definitive intervention in haemodynamically stable ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonism, with success rates of 80 to 90 percent and surgical backup mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in the 3 month to 3 year age range is managed by pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopy as the first-line definitive intervention when the child is haemodynamically stable, without peritonism, and without free air. Surgical team must be available for immediate laparotomy in case of perforation or failed reduction. Recurrence after pneumatic reduction occurs in approximately 10 percent and these are usually managed by repeat reduction. A pathological lead point (Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp) should be considered in children over 3 years or with recurrent episodes.
key_points: Pneumatic reduction is first-line for stable cases.
Contraindications: perforation, peritonism, shock.
Surgical backup essential during reduction.
Consider lead point in >3 y or recurrent cases.
explanation.pearls: Maximum air pressure for reduction is 120 mmHg under fluoroscopy; perforation rate is under 1 percent, and post-reduction the child stays for 24 hours observation.

subtopic_detail: Cystic fibrosis newborn screening positive workup
stem: A 4-week-old boy is referred by the state newborn bloodspot screening program. His day-3 immunoreactive trypsinogen was 122 micrograms per litre (well above the 99th centile cutoff of 99). Reflex molecular testing on the same bloodspot identified a single F508del CFTR variant. He was born at term, fed well from birth, and his parents are both healthy with no family history of cystic fibrosis. Examination today is unremarkable with appropriate weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.7, weight 4.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Pink, well perfused, no respiratory distress, no nasal polyps, soft abdomen, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screen: IRT 122 micrograms/L (cutoff 99), single F508del heterozygote on reflex panel
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K at birth, breastfed exclusively

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this infant's diagnostic workup?

options.text: Start oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation empirically while awaiting further testing
options.rationale: Pancreatic insufficiency is treated once confirmed by faecal elastase or weight faltering after diagnosis; empiric enzyme therapy in an asymptomatic infant pre-diagnosis is inappropriate. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

options.text: Full extended CFTR gene sequencing performed immediately, deferring all sweat chloride testing until the molecular results return
options.rationale: Sequencing is the second-tier test when sweat chloride is intermediate or when a single variant complicates classification; it is not the immediate next test ahead of sweat chloride. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure the parents that single-variant heterozygotes are healthy carriers and discharge without further testing
options.rationale: Australian newborn screening programs refer all infants with raised IRT and one or more CFTR variants for sweat testing because the bloodspot panel does not exhaustively detect every CF-causing variant. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

options.text: High-resolution chest computed tomography to assess for early bronchiectasis before any diagnostic biochemistry
options.rationale: Radiological imaging is not part of the diagnostic pathway in an asymptomatic newborn screen positive infant and carries radiation exposure with no diagnostic yield at this stage. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

options.text: Sweat chloride testing at a specialist cystic fibrosis centre using pilocarpine iontophoresis with paired bilateral collections
options.rationale: The gold standard confirmatory test after positive newborn screening is sweat chloride by pilocarpine iontophoresis at an accredited paediatric CF centre, with chloride 60 mmol/L or greater diagnostic, 30 to 59 intermediate, and under 30 normal in infants. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia: Diagnosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses raised IRT plus reflex CFTR variant detection; any infant with positive bloodspot screen is referred for sweat chloride testing at an accredited CF centre at 4 to 6 weeks of age. Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or greater confirms CF, 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate (CRMS/CFSPID, needing ongoing follow-up), and under 30 mmol/L excludes CF. Diagnosis triggers entry to a multidisciplinary paediatric CF service for surveillance, enzyme assessment, airway clearance education, and CFTR-modulator eligibility consideration.
key_points: Sweat chloride cutoffs: <30 normal, 30-59 intermediate, >=60 CF.
Test by pilocarpine iontophoresis at accredited centre.
Single variant after screen needs sweat test, not reassurance.
Multidisciplinary CF service for confirmed diagnoses.
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride should be paired (both arms) with at least 75 mg of sweat collected per arm; insufficient sweat is the commonest cause of an unsatisfactory test and warrants repeat at 4 to 6 weeks of age.

subtopic_detail: SUDI prevention safe sleep counselling for parents
stem: A 6-week-old healthy term infant attends with her parents for a routine immunisation visit. The parents are tired and report that the baby sleeps best on her tummy on the parental bed, swaddled with a soft cot bumper around her. The father smokes outside but not in the house. Mother breastfeeds at night and occasionally falls asleep with the baby on the couch. Both parents are well, the household has no siblings, and the family lives in a 2-bedroom apartment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.6, weight 5.1 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Pink, well, normal tone, normal cardiorespiratory examination, no concerning features
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated today
data_table.Medications: Vitamin D 400 IU daily (breastfed); routine vaccines today

lead_in: Which counselling point will most reduce this infant's risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy?

options.text: Continue tummy sleeping but only on a firm mattress with a thin sheet and remove the cot bumper from the sleep surface
options.rationale: Prone (tummy) sleeping is the single largest modifiable SUDI risk factor; supine sleeping cuts SUDI risk by more than half and is the strongest individual counselling point. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.text: Advise sleeping with the baby in the parents' bed as breastfeeding is easier and direct contact reduces SUDI risk in young infants
options.rationale: Bed-sharing (especially on couches, with sleep-deprived adults, smokers, or with soft bedding) increases SUDI risk; room-sharing on a separate sleep surface is the recommended arrangement. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.text: Recommend the father quit smoking entirely as smoke residue on clothing is the most modifiable SUDI risk in this family
options.rationale: Smoking exposure is an important SUDI risk factor and cessation is recommended, but in this family the most modifiable and highest-impact risks are prone sleeping and unsafe couch co-sleeping with maternal fatigue. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.text: Place the baby on her back to sleep every sleep, on her own safe sleep surface in the parents' room for at least the first 6 months
options.rationale: Supine sleep is the cornerstone of SUDI prevention and pairs with own-surface room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for at least 6 months in the Red Nose evidence-based recommendations. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

options.text: Use a wedge or anti-roll positioner to keep the baby on her side during sleep as this is the safest alternative to back sleeping
options.rationale: Side sleeping is unstable (baby can roll prone) and positioners themselves are SUDI hazards; Red Nose advises against any anti-roll or sleep-positioning device. (Source: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations)
source_refs: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations

explanation.summary: Red Nose Australia's six core safe-sleep messages are: sleep baby on back; head and face uncovered; smoke-free environment before and after birth; safe sleeping environment day and night; sleep baby in own safe sleep space in same room as parent or carer for the first 6 to 12 months; breastfeed if possible. Bed-sharing, particularly on couches with sleep-deprived parents and soft surfaces, dramatically increases SUDI risk. Positioners, bumpers, soft bedding, and loose blankets are hazards.
key_points: Supine sleep is highest-impact single intervention.
Room-share (not bed-share) for first 6-12 months.
Firm flat mattress, no bumpers/positioners/loose bedding.
Smoke-free environment, breastfeed if possible.
explanation.pearls: Use an Australian Standard AS/NZS 2172-compliant cot with a firm mattress, fitted sheet only, and feet-to-foot positioning; document safe sleep counselling at every well-baby check until 12 months.

sources.label: Red Nose Australia Safe Sleeping Recommendations
RACGP Guidelines for Preventive Activities in General Practice

subtopic_detail: Paediatric limp Kocher discrimination septic arthritis transient synovitis
stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with 36 hours of limp affecting the right leg. She had a coryzal illness one week ago. She is alert and walking but refuses to bear full weight on the right side. She is mildly distressed only when the right hip is examined; passive log roll provokes pain. There is no joint swelling or warmth, and no obvious limb deformity. She is tolerating oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% air, BP 100/62, T 38.6, weight 16.8 kg
data_table.Examination: Restricted internal rotation right hip, pain with log roll, no effusion or warmth at knee or ankle, no spinal tenderness, distal neurovascular intact
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L, ESR 42 mm/h; X-ray hip and pelvis normal; bedside ultrasound shows 4 mm right hip effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and review in 48 to 72 hours, presuming transient synovitis given the recent viral illness and the limited hip effusion
options.rationale: The Kocher count here is 3 of 4 (refusal to weight-bear, fever above 38.5, WCC above 12), giving a 93 percent probability of septic arthritis and requiring arthrocentesis rather than discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Trial 48 hours of bed rest with ibuprofen 10 mg/kg three times daily and reassess all Kocher criteria including repeat inflammatory markers
options.rationale: A pre-test probability over 90 percent does not justify watchful waiting; ibuprofen also blunts inflammatory markers and can mask deterioration before arthrocentesis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Request an urgent MRI of the right hip and spine before any joint aspiration or commencement of empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: MRI is helpful when osteomyelitis or pyomyositis is suspected and the joint is dry on ultrasound; here there is a visible effusion and aspiration takes priority because delayed treatment causes cartilage destruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Commence empiric oral cefalexin and arrange outpatient orthopaedic review in the next available clinic within 1 week
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for septic arthritis (which has a 90+ percent pre-test probability here) and a week of delay risks femoral head avascular necrosis; admission and arthrocentesis are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

options.text: Admit for urgent ultrasound-guided hip aspiration in theatre with paediatric orthopaedics and IV flucloxacillin after fluid sampling
options.rationale: With 3 of 4 Kocher predictors (refusal to weight-bear, fever above 38.5, raised WCC) plus a visible effusion, the probability of septic arthritis is over 90 percent; urgent arthrocentesis under image guidance with antibiotics after cultures is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

explanation.summary: Kocher criteria differentiate septic arthritis from transient synovitis in a child with hip pain: non-weight-bearing, temperature above 38.5, ESR above 40, WCC above 12 x10^9/L. The probability of septic arthritis is 3 percent (0 of 4), 40 percent (1 of 4), 62 percent (2 of 4), 93 percent (3 of 4), and 99 percent (4 of 4). Aspiration under image guidance is the diagnostic and therapeutic step; antibiotics (flucloxacillin in Australia, plus cefotaxime if under 3 months or risk of MRSA) are given immediately after cultures. CRP and Caird modifications add prognostic value.
key_points: Kocher 4 criteria: NWB, T>38.5, ESR>40, WCC>12.
3 of 4 = 93% probability of septic arthritis.
Aspiration before antibiotics where possible.
Empiric flucloxacillin IV; cefotaxime cover in young infants.
explanation.pearls: Hip aspiration in theatre under fluoroscopy or ultrasound prevents the false-negative of a dry tap; if pus is obtained, send for Gram, culture, cell count and crystals, and arrange surgical washout under the same anaesthetic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

subtopic_detail: Bacterial tracheitis recognition in croup that fails to respond to adrenaline
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to ED with worsening 'croup'. He had 3 days of viral upper respiratory illness with mild barking cough, then today rapidly deteriorated with high fever, severe stridor at rest, copious thick yellow secretions and a hoarse voice. He has had no benefit from two doses of nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000) given 30 minutes apart and 0.6 mg/kg oral dexamethasone given on arrival. He is now sitting forward, drooling, looking toxic and frightened. His parents have not refused any care.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 44, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, BP 96/56, T 39.5, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Toxic-looking, sitting forward, biphasic stridor, suprasternal and intercostal recession, hoarse voice, no rash, no obvious foreign body, copious purulent secretions
data_table.Investigations: Not yet - prioritising airway
data_table.Medications: Two doses nebulised adrenaline, oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, paracetamol given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000 and a second dose of dexamethasone, then reassess in 30 minutes for response
options.rationale: Failure of two doses of nebulised adrenaline plus dexamethasone in a toxic child with purulent secretions and high fever points away from viral croup; further croup therapy delays definitive airway management. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Obtain a lateral neck X-ray to look for a thumb-print sign of epiglottitis or steeple sign of croup before any airway intervention
options.rationale: Imaging in a child with imminent airway compromise delays definitive airway control and has no place ahead of expert intubation; airway team activation is the priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Perform an awake nasendoscopy at the bedside to inspect the supraglottis for swollen cherry-red epiglottis and exclude epiglottitis
options.rationale: Awake examination of the supraglottis in a distressed child with critical upper airway disease risks complete obstruction; airway inspection occurs after controlled anaesthesia in theatre. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Call anaesthesia, ENT and intensive care for theatre intubation, then send tracheal cultures and start intravenous flucloxacillin plus ceftriaxone
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis (a viral croup that does not respond to adrenaline, with toxicity, high fever, and purulent secretions) requires senior airway team-led controlled intubation in theatre, then tracheal toilet, microbiological sampling and empirical antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Administer high-flow nasal oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute and observe for 1 hour to allow steroid effect before considering intubation
options.rationale: HFNC does not relieve fixed upper airway obstruction from purulent secretions; waiting for steroid effect in a toxic deteriorating child risks loss of the airway. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

explanation.summary: Bacterial tracheitis classically follows a viral URTI with worsening croup that does not respond to nebulised adrenaline or steroids. The child is toxic, febrile, and has purulent tracheal secretions, distinguishing from viral croup (less toxic, dry barking cough) and epiglottitis (sudden onset, drooling, no cough). Management is airway team-led controlled intubation in theatre with simultaneous tracheal toilet, cultures, and intravenous flucloxacillin (Staph aureus is the dominant pathogen in Australia) plus ceftriaxone for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae cover.
key_points: Suspect when croup unresponsive to adrenaline + steroids.
Toxic child, high fever, purulent secretions.
Definitive airway in theatre with anaesthesia + ENT + ICU.
Empirical flucloxacillin + ceftriaxone IV.
explanation.pearls: Tracheal cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus in 50 percent of Australian cases; once intubated, mucus plugs need repeat bronchoscopic toilet and extubation usually proceeds at 3 to 7 days after resolution of secretions and fever.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis acute management
stem: An 8-year-old boy with homozygous HbSS sickle cell disease presents to ED with 6 hours of severe bilateral lower limb and back pain after a cold swimming session at school. His mother gave him paracetamol and ibuprofen at home with minimal effect. He has previously had three admissions for vaso-occlusive crises and is on regular hydroxyurea plus penicillin prophylaxis. He has no fever, cough or breathlessness. He scores his pain 9 of 10. He is alert and orientated, well perfused, with no focal neurology and clear chest examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 97% air, BP 108/64, T 36.8, weight 28 kg
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, tender thighs and lumbar region, no joint effusion, normal cardiorespiratory examination, no focal neurology, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (baseline 80), reticulocyte 8 percent, WCC 12.4 (baseline 10), platelets 360, CRP 6 mg/L; venous gas pH 7.39, lactate 1.4
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol and ibuprofen at home; usually hydroxyurea 20 mg/kg/day, phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg BD

lead_in: Within the first hour, what is the most appropriate analgesic and supportive plan?

options.text: Continue oral paracetamol and ibuprofen, then add oral oxycodone 0.1 mg/kg and reassess in 60 minutes after fluids and rest in a quiet bay
options.rationale: Oral analgesia has already failed in a child scoring 9 of 10 pain; sickle cell guidelines mandate strong opioid by intranasal or intravenous route within 30 minutes of arrival. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

options.text: Intranasal fentanyl while siting an intravenous cannula, then commence intravenous morphine titration with maintenance fluids and frequent reassessment
options.rationale: Australian sickle cell guidelines require strong opioid analgesia within 30 minutes (intranasal fentanyl bridge, then IV morphine titrated), warmth, oxygen if hypoxic, and intravenous maintenance fluids without overhydration, with regular reassessment of pain and respiratory status. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion through the haematology service to reduce HbS percentage and abort the vaso-occlusive crisis immediately
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke, multi-organ failure, or priapism; uncomplicated VOC is managed with analgesia, hydration and warmth. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

options.text: Bolus 20 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride to suppress sickling and reassess pain after rapid fluid loading is complete
options.rationale: Sickle vaso-occlusive crises are not a hypovolaemic state; large fluid boluses risk pulmonary oedema and acute chest syndrome and do not relieve pain. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

options.text: Administer intramuscular pethidine 1 mg/kg as a single dose to settle the pain rapidly while a cannula is being placed for fluids
options.rationale: Pethidine is contraindicated in sickle cell crises because its metabolite norpethidine accumulates and lowers seizure threshold; IM injections are also painful and slow onset compared with intranasal fentanyl. (Source: RCH CPG: Sickle Cell Disease)

explanation.summary: Vaso-occlusive crises require analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival: intranasal fentanyl 1.5 micrograms/kg as a bridge while siting IV access, then IV morphine titrated (typically 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg every 10 to 15 minutes), supported by maintenance fluids (avoid overhydration), warmth, oxygen if SpO2 below 95 percent, and continuous reassessment for acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms requiring exchange). Pethidine is contraindicated. Exchange transfusion is reserved for stroke, acute chest, multi-organ failure, or priapism.
key_points: Strong opioid within 30 minutes (intranasal fentanyl bridge to IV morphine).
Avoid pethidine - norpethidine lowers seizure threshold.
Maintenance fluids; avoid 20 mL/kg boluses.
Exchange transfusion only for chest, stroke, MOF, priapism.
explanation.pearls: Watch for the emergence of acute chest syndrome within 24 to 72 hours of admission: new infiltrate on CXR with fever, hypoxia, or chest pain triggers urgent haematology review for exchange transfusion.

subtopic_detail: Pertussis in young infant antibiotic choice
stem: A 5-week-old previously well girl presents with a 7-day history of coryza followed by paroxysms of coughing ending in cyanotic spells and post-tussive vomiting. She has had no inspiratory whoop. Her older brother had a persistent cough for several weeks. She has had no immunisations yet as she is approaching her 6-week vaccinations. She is feeding poorly between paroxysms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 92 percent room air during paroxysm, T 36.9, weight 4.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival haemorrhages, mild subcostal recession, otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 26 with lymphocytosis 18; pertussis PCR sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Inhaled salbutamol via spacer every 4 hours and oral prednisolone for 3 days to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Bronchodilators and steroids do not modify pertussis cough paroxysms; treatment is supportive plus a macrolide. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

options.text: Discharge home with reassurance as antibiotics do not alter the clinical course of pertussis
options.rationale: Antibiotics started in catarrhal or early paroxysmal phase shorten infectivity and may attenuate symptoms; infants under 6 months require admission regardless of treatment for apnoea monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

options.text: Admit and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg per kg daily for 5 days with cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Azithromycin is first-line for pertussis in infants under 1 month and over (10 mg/kg/day for 5 days); admission is mandatory under 6 months due to apnoea risk. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

options.text: Oral erythromycin 12.5 mg per kg every 6 hours for 14 days under outpatient daily review
options.rationale: Erythromycin in neonates carries increased risk of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; azithromycin is preferred under 1 month. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kg every 6 hours as empirical lower respiratory cover
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin has no useful activity against Bordetella pertussis; macrolide therapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Pertussis classically progresses through catarrhal (1 to 2 weeks), paroxysmal (2 to 8 weeks) and convalescent phases. Infants under 6 months are at risk of apnoea, pneumonia, seizures and death. Azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day for 5 days) is first-line under 1 month; clarithromycin or azithromycin from 1 month onward. Public health notification is mandatory. Postexposure prophylaxis for high-risk contacts (pregnancy 3rd trimester, household contacts of infant under 6 months) with the same macrolide. Promote maternal pertussis vaccination during each pregnancy from 20 weeks to prevent neonatal infection.
key_points: Infant under 6 months - admit for apnoea monitoring.
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg/day for 5 days under 1 month.
Erythromycin in neonates linked to pyloric stenosis.
Notifiable disease in Australia.
Maternal vaccination each pregnancy from 20 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Lymphocytosis greater than 50 percent of WCC in young infants with pertussis is associated with pulmonary hypertension and mortality - exchange transfusion or ECMO may be life-saving in severe cases.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with 2 weeks of nocturnal perianal itching that wakes him and his 9-year-old sister from sleep. His mother has seen small white moving threads at the anus in the early morning. The household includes both parents and the two children, all otherwise well with no abdominal pain or weight loss.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 92, normal growth
data_table.Examination: Perianal excoriation, no bleeding, abdominal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Sticky-tape test confirmed Enterobius eggs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Hygiene measures alone without medication including hand washing, short nails and washed linen
options.rationale: Hygiene alone rarely clears established infection within reasonable time; medication is needed to interrupt the cycle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

options.text: Single dose ivermectin to the index child only with second dose given two weeks later in clinic
options.rationale: Ivermectin is not first-line for threadworm; mebendazole to all household members is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

options.text: Three-day course of albendazole 400 mg daily to all household members in a single course
options.rationale: Mebendazole is the first-line agent in Australia; albendazole is an alternative when mebendazole is unavailable or contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

options.text: Single dose pyrantel pamoate 10 mg per kg to the index child only with hygiene measures alone
options.rationale: Treating only the index child leaves household reservoir; reinfection is highly likely without whole-household treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

options.text: Single dose mebendazole 100 mg to all household members and repeat the same dose in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Therapeutic guidelines recommend treating the entire household with single-dose mebendazole 100 mg repeated in 2 weeks to break the autoinfection cycle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Threadworm)

explanation.summary: Enterobius vermicularis (threadworm) is common in young children and spreads through household autoinfection. Classic presentation is perianal itch waking the child. Diagnosis is clinical or confirmed by sticky-tape test taken in the early morning. Australian first-line treatment is mebendazole 100 mg as single dose, repeated in 2 weeks, given to all household members regardless of symptoms. Adjuncts include hand hygiene, short fingernails, daily morning showers and hot washing of bed linen and night clothing for the 2 days after each treatment.
key_points: Treat entire household to break cycle.
Mebendazole 100 mg single dose then repeat at 2 weeks.
Hygiene: hand wash, short nails, morning shower, hot wash bedding.
Albendazole is alternative if mebendazole unavailable.
Reassure school - no need to exclude after treatment.
explanation.pearls: Mebendazole is not licensed in Australia for children under 6 months and has limited safety data under 1 year - in infants, consult Therapeutic Guidelines and consider pyrantel pamoate or topical petrolatum as alternatives.

subtopic_detail: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis first-line management
stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought in because he has never had a consistent dry night. He wets 5 to 7 nights per week and has had occasional brief dry spells of up to 1 week. He has no daytime urinary symptoms, no constipation, normal growth, and develops typically. His father had nocturnal enuresis until age 9. The child finds the wetting upsetting and his mother asks about treatment options.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/60, HR 78, BMI 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia, abdomen soft non-tender, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein and infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Intranasal desmopressin 20 mcg at bedtime with strict fluid restriction from 2 hours before sleep
options.rationale: Intranasal desmopressin is no longer recommended in Australia in children due to hyponatraemic seizures; oral melt is used when desmopressin is required, after alarm therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

options.text: Enuresis alarm therapy with parental supervision for a minimum of 8 weeks
options.rationale: Enuresis alarm is first-line for motivated children over 5 with primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis; lasting cure rates around 60 percent after 8 to 12 weeks of consistent use. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

options.text: Continue toilet training reminders and reward chart only without alarm or pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Reward charts alone have low success in established nocturnal enuresis; alarm therapy is superior when family-engaged treatment is sought. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

options.text: Imipramine 25 mg at bedtime as long-term pharmacological treatment for nightly wetting
options.rationale: Tricyclics are reserved for refractory cases due to overdose mortality and cardiotoxicity; not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

options.text: Referral for urodynamic studies and renal tract ultrasound before considering any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging and urodynamics are not indicated in primary monosymptomatic enuresis with normal examination; reserved for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTIs or abnormal findings. (Source: RCH CPG Nocturnal Enuresis)

explanation.summary: Primary nocturnal enuresis is involuntary wetting during sleep without a 6-month dry period, with no daytime symptoms. Treatment is offered from age 6 when child and family are motivated. Alarm therapy is first-line with 60 percent lasting cure rate after 8 to 12 weeks; relapses respond to a further course. Oral desmopressin is second-line for older children or short-term cover (school camps). Reward charts may complement alarm therapy. Look for constipation, daytime symptoms, snoring/OSA, behavioural concerns and diabetes if atypical features present.
key_points: Treat from age 6 with motivated family.
Alarm therapy first-line; 8 to 12 weeks minimum.
Oral desmopressin melt second-line.
Tricyclics reserved for refractory cases.
Screen for constipation, daytime symptoms, OSA, diabetes.
explanation.pearls: Desmopressin tablets/melt should be taken without fluids around the dose - children given desmopressin who drink large volumes overnight are at risk of severe hyponatraemic seizures, which is why the intranasal preparation was withdrawn.

subtopic_detail: Allergic rhinitis with sleep disturbance treatment escalation
stem: A 9-year-old girl with seasonal allergic rhinitis presents in spring with persistent rhinorrhoea, nasal blockage and itchy eyes. She wakes most nights with mouth breathing and is excessively tired at school. She has been using oral cetirizine 10 mg daily for 3 weeks without much improvement and has no other medical history.

data_table.Examination: Pale boggy nasal mucosa, conjunctival injection, no postnasal cobblestoning, tonsils 2+ symmetric
data_table.Investigations: Not required for diagnosis
data_table.Medications: Cetirizine 10 mg PO daily for 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Refer for sublingual immunotherapy as the next step before intensifying medical therapy further
options.rationale: Allergen immunotherapy is considered after maximal pharmacological therapy and confirmed allergen sensitisation; not the immediate next step. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

options.text: Switch cetirizine to a sedating antihistamine such as promethazine for nightly use only
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines impair learning and worsen daytime fatigue; non-sedating agents are preferred and addition of intranasal steroid is the priority. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

options.text: Add oral montelukast 5 mg nightly to the existing cetirizine for a 3-month treatment trial
options.rationale: Montelukast has modest efficacy and a TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects; reserved for cases unresponsive to topical corticosteroids. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

options.text: Add regular intranasal corticosteroid spray to the cetirizine for at least 4 weeks
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid is the most effective single agent for persistent allergic rhinitis and is recommended as add-on or first-line for moderate-severe disease in Australian guidance. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

options.text: Commence a 5-day course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily to break the cycle of symptoms
options.rationale: Oral steroids are reserved for severe refractory cases; routine use for moderate allergic rhinitis is inappropriate due to systemic side effects. (Source: ASCIA Allergic Rhinitis)

explanation.summary: Allergic rhinitis is classified by ARIA as intermittent or persistent and mild or moderate-severe. Mild intermittent responds to non-sedating oral antihistamines or saline rinses; moderate-severe persistent (sleep affected, school/work impact) requires regular intranasal corticosteroid as cornerstone therapy. Combination intranasal corticosteroid + intranasal antihistamine sprays improve speed of onset. Saline rinse before sprays improves drug delivery. Allergen immunotherapy is offered if pharmacotherapy fails or to modify long-term disease progression.
key_points: Moderate-severe persistent - regular intranasal corticosteroid.
Mild intermittent - non-sedating antihistamine or saline.
Combine antihistamine + steroid if single agent fails.
Avoid sedating antihistamines and oral steroids.
Immunotherapy after maximal pharmacotherapy failure.
explanation.pearls: Intranasal corticosteroid sprays work best when angled outward toward the lateral wall, not toward the septum - misdirected delivery causes septal irritation and epistaxis without improving symptoms.

stem: A 4-month-old breastfed boy presents with 6 weeks of frequent effortless regurgitation after most feeds. He gains weight along the 50th centile, feeds eagerly, and is otherwise well. There is no projectile vomiting, no blood, no bile, no back-arching during feeds and no respiratory symptoms. His mother is exhausted by laundry and is asking whether medication will help.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 36, T 36.7, weight 7.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Alert, smiling, soft abdomen, no abdominal distension, hydrated
data_table.Investigations: None required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch from breast to extensively hydrolysed formula and review the infant in 2 weeks time
options.rationale: Formula switch is reserved for suspected cows-milk protein allergy with red flags; not indicated in an exclusively breastfed thriving infant with no allergy features. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

options.text: Commence oral omeprazole 1 mg per kg once daily for an 8-week empirical treatment trial
options.rationale: PPIs are ineffective for uncomplicated reflux without oesophagitis and increase infection and fracture risk; not indicated in a well-thriving baby. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

options.text: Commence regular oral ranitidine 4 mg per kg twice daily as antacid for symptom control in this infant
options.rationale: Ranitidine has been withdrawn due to NDMA contamination; H2 blockers are no longer routine for uncomplicated reflux. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

options.text: Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for upper endoscopy and pH study before any conservative measures
options.rationale: Invasive investigation is reserved for red flags (poor growth, haematemesis, persistent respiratory or neurological symptoms); not for uncomplicated regurgitation. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

options.text: Parental reassurance and conservative measures including upright positioning after feeds
options.rationale: Uncomplicated infant gastro-oesophageal reflux is physiological and self-resolves by 12 to 14 months; reassurance and feeding-position advice are first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Gastro-oesophageal Reflux)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated infant gastro-oesophageal reflux is regurgitation without functional concern; it affects up to 40 percent of healthy infants and resolves spontaneously by 12 to 14 months. Reflux disease (GORD) involves complications: faltering growth, recurrent respiratory symptoms, oesophagitis, food refusal, distressed behaviour. Management is stepwise from parental reassurance, upright positioning, smaller more frequent feeds, thickened formula (not breastfed infants) through to acid suppression only if GORD is confirmed. Red flags (bilious vomiting, blood, bulging fontanelle, abdominal distension) demand urgent assessment for alternative diagnoses.
key_points: Uncomplicated reflux: reassurance, position upright after feeds.
PPIs and H2 blockers offer no benefit without GORD.
Thickened feeds OK for formula-fed infants.
GORD red flags: weight loss, recurrent wheeze, oesophagitis.
Bilious vomit, blood, bulging fontanelle - urgent assessment.
explanation.pearls: Sandifer syndrome (dystonic head/neck posturing during feeds) is a manifestation of GORD that mimics seizures - oesophageal pH/impedance monitoring rather than EEG is the appropriate first investigation.

stem: A 9-year-old girl living in a remote Northern Territory community presents with a 24-hour sore throat, fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius and difficulty swallowing solids. She has tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, large exudative tonsils and no cough. Her family has a history of acute rheumatic fever in an older sibling. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral exudative tonsils, tender anterior cervical nodes, no rash, no cough
data_table.Investigations: Throat swab taken for GAS culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management while awaiting throat swab results?

options.text: Single dose oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg now followed by symptomatic care alone
options.rationale: A single dose of phenoxymethylpenicillin is inadequate; either a 10-day oral course or single IM benzathine dose is required for streptococcal eradication. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 12 mg per kg daily for 5 days while awaiting the throat culture result
options.rationale: Macrolides are reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; resistance is rising and they are not first-line in this scenario. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

options.text: Single intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 900 mg now with single follow-up review
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin for sore throat in children at high risk of acute rheumatic fever (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background, remote community, family history). (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 25 mg per kg twice daily for 10 days starting today after sample collection
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg daily for 10 days is an alternative if IM benzathine penicillin is unavailable; adherence over 10 days is the challenge in remote settings, hence IM preferred. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

options.text: Watchful waiting with paracetamol for 48 hours before reconsidering antibiotic prescription
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate in low-risk populations but not for high-ARF-risk children where empirical antibiotics are recommended to prevent rheumatic fever. (Source: RHDAustralia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute sore throat management in Australia is stratified by ARF risk. High-risk groups include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, especially in northern Australia, those with personal or family history of ARF and people living in crowded conditions. In high-risk groups, all sore throats with GAS pharyngitis features are treated empirically. Single-dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is preferred for adherence; oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg BD for 10 days is an alternative. Low-risk populations may use Centor or FeverPAIN criteria with delayed prescription.
key_points: Risk-stratify by ARF risk.
High-risk: empirical IM benzathine penicillin G.
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days is alternative.
Macrolides for severe penicillin allergy.
Low-risk: Centor or FeverPAIN-guided delayed prescription.
explanation.pearls: Persistent throat carriage of group A streptococcus after appropriate treatment in a low-risk patient rarely needs eradication - it does not progress to invasive disease and adds antibiotic exposure without benefit.

subtopic_detail: Tetralogy of Fallot hypercyanotic spell first-line manoeuvre
stem: An 8-month-old boy known to have unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot is brought to the emergency department after a 10-minute episode of inconsolable crying, then deep cyanosis. He is now distressed, deeply blue and his mother says his murmur has become quieter. Cardiac surgery is planned in 2 weeks. He has no fever and no recent infections.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 56, SpO2 62 percent on room air, T 36.9
data_table.Examination: Marked central cyanosis, soft systolic murmur (previously harsh), no respiratory distress signs out of proportion
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 10 mcg per kg to support cardiac output during the spell
options.rationale: Adrenaline increases right ventricular outflow tract spasm by beta-agonism and worsens the spell; beta-blockade is the relevant pharmacology. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

options.text: Begin chest compressions and bag-mask ventilation as the first response to the deep cyanosis present
options.rationale: The child is not in cardiac arrest; aggressive resuscitation without addressing the shunt physiology will not resolve the spell. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

options.text: Commence inhaled nitric oxide via face mask to dilate the pulmonary vasculature immediately now
options.rationale: Pulmonary vasodilation is not the mechanism in tet spells; the problem is right ventricular outflow tract obstruction with shunt reversal. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

options.text: Provide intravenous frusemide 1 mg per kg to reduce preload and lung congestion in this child
options.rationale: Tet spells are not driven by pulmonary oedema; diuresis reduces preload and worsens the shunt. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

options.text: Place the child in the knee-to-chest position and give high-flow oxygen via face mask
options.rationale: Knee-to-chest increases systemic vascular resistance, reverses right-to-left shunting and is the immediate first step in a tet spell, with simultaneous high-flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic Heart Disease)

explanation.summary: A tet spell results from acute increase in right ventricular outflow tract obstruction combined with falling systemic vascular resistance, causing right-to-left shunting and profound hypoxia. Immediate management is to settle the child in knee-to-chest (or parental cuddling with knees flexed) plus high-flow oxygen. Pharmacological escalation includes morphine 0.1 mg/kg IM or IV to abolish hyperpnoea, IV phenylephrine to raise SVR, IV propranolol to relax the RVOT, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis and prompt referral for surgical or palliative shunting if recurrent. Quiet murmur indicates near-total RVOT obstruction.
key_points: Knee-to-chest + high-flow O2 are immediate first steps.
Morphine 0.1 mg/kg blunts hyperpnoea.
Phenylephrine raises SVR and reduces shunt.
Propranolol relaxes RVOT muscular obstruction.
Quieter murmur means worse spell.
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockade with propranolol is used both acutely (intravenously) and as outpatient prophylaxis (oral 1 to 2 mg/kg/day) in babies awaiting repair - schedule surgical repair before 6 months when spells start to recur to avoid long-term right ventricular damage.

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia salt-wasting crisis in newborn
stem: A 12-day-old breastfed boy is brought in by his parents after 3 days of poor feeding, lethargy and weight loss. He was born at term following an uneventful pregnancy. Examination shows hyperpigmented scrotal skin, weight 8 percent below birth weight, and obvious dehydration. Newborn screening for CAH was sent 9 days ago and result is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 56, BP 64/38, T 36.4, SpO2 96 percent
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, cool peripheries, normal male external genitalia with hyperpigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Na 121 mmol/L, K 6.9 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urea 8.4, creatinine 78, VBG pH 7.28

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate resuscitation step?

options.text: Withhold steroid until ACTH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone results return to confirm CAH diagnosis
options.rationale: Withholding steroid in a shocked baby with the classic biochemistry of salt-wasting CAH risks death; take samples and treat immediately. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Oral fludrocortisone 50 mcg now and admit for observation pending the newborn screening result
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for a shocked vomiting infant; intravenous hydrocortisone is required and fludrocortisone is started later when stable. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL per kg of 10 percent solution to stabilise the cardiac membrane
options.rationale: Calcium is indicated when hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes; the immediate priority is steroid replacement plus volume resuscitation, which itself corrects the potassium. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat plus 0.9 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose 20 mL per kg bolus
options.rationale: Acute adrenal crisis in suspected salt-wasting CAH requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (stress dose) and isotonic dextrose-containing fluid to correct shock, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia simultaneously. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent saline 5 mL per kg over 1 hour to rapidly correct the severe hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizures; rapid correction here risks osmotic demyelination and does not treat the underlying adrenal crisis. (Source: RCH CPG Adrenal Crisis)

explanation.summary: Classical salt-wasting CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency, most common) presents in the second week of life with vomiting, weight loss, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and shock. Males may not have ambiguous genitalia, making missed diagnosis at delivery common before newborn screen returns. Acute management is IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat (infant) plus IV 0.9 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose 20 mL/kg bolus, then stress-dose hydrocortisone infusion. Once stable, transition to oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone with sodium chloride supplementation. Genitogram, karyotype, ACTH, 17-OHP and renin sent on presentation.
key_points: Second week of life vomiting + weight loss - think CAH.
Biochemistry: low Na, high K, low glucose, metabolic acidosis.
IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat + saline-dextrose bolus.
Fludrocortisone and salt added once stable.
Send 17-OHP, ACTH, renin BEFORE first steroid dose.
explanation.pearls: Sick-day rules: triple the maintenance hydrocortisone dose during fever or vomiting and give IM hydrocortisone if oral dose cannot be retained - parents should be supplied with an emergency injection kit at diagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Down syndrome newborn cardiac screening pathway
stem: A term newborn male has clinical features of trisomy 21 on day 1: hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single transverse palmar creases bilaterally and a flat nasal bridge. He is feeding well and pulse oximetry congenital heart disease screen is normal. His chromosomal microarray result is pending and the parents ask about cardiac assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99 percent right hand and right foot, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur audible at left sternal edge; femoral pulses palpable equally bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Pulse oximetry CHD screen normal; chromosomal microarray pending
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K and hepatitis B vaccine given at birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cardiac investigation plan?

options.text: Chest radiograph and 12-lead electrocardiograph in the first month with cardiology review later
options.rationale: CXR and ECG cannot exclude septal defects; echocardiography is required. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

options.text: Formal transthoracic echocardiogram performed within the first 4 to 6 weeks of life
options.rationale: Around 45 percent of infants with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease and pulse oximetry screen misses non-cyanotic lesions like AVSD and VSD; transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in the first weeks of life. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

options.text: Pulse oximetry CHD screen alone with no further imaging while infant remains asymptomatic clinically
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry misses non-cyanotic CHD common in Down syndrome (AVSD, VSD, PDA); formal echocardiography is required. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

options.text: Cardiac MRI under general anaesthetic as the screening investigation of choice within 6 weeks
options.rationale: MRI is reserved for select complex lesions; echocardiography is the first-line non-invasive screen for CHD in Down syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

options.text: Defer cardiac imaging until the murmur is louder or symptoms emerge later in infancy
options.rationale: Awaiting symptoms risks irreversible pulmonary vascular disease in undiagnosed AVSD; early echocardiography is mandatory in trisomy 21. (Source: RCH CPG Down Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Down syndrome is associated with congenital heart disease in about 45 percent of children, atrioventricular septal defect being the most common, followed by VSD, ASD and PDA. Early echocardiography in the first 4 to 6 weeks identifies lesions before pulmonary vascular disease develops; surgical repair of AVSD is typically performed by 6 months. Other screening on the Down syndrome health check schedule includes hearing assessment at birth and 6 months, ophthalmology at 6 to 12 months, thyroid function annually, coeliac screen, atlantoaxial assessment before contact sport, sleep study if obstructive symptoms, and developmental surveillance.
key_points: About 45 percent CHD - AVSD most common.
Echocardiogram at 4 to 6 weeks regardless of pulse oximetry screen.
AVSD repair typically before 6 months.
Thyroid screening annually.
Atlantoaxial assessment before contact sports.
explanation.pearls: Atrioventricular septal defects in Down syndrome have early-onset pulmonary vascular disease compared with non-Down AVSD - elective repair is brought forward to 3 to 6 months to avoid Eisenmenger physiology.

sources.label: Down Syndrome Australia Health Care Guide

subtopic_detail: Persistent neonatal anuria suggesting posterior urethral valves
stem: A 3-day-old term male newborn has not passed urine since hospital discharge 24 hours after delivery and now appears irritable. His abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable bladder. Antenatal ultrasound at 32 weeks reported bilateral hydronephrosis but the parents declined further follow-up scans. His mother is otherwise well and birth was uncomplicated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 52, T 36.7, weight 3.2 kg (down 9 percent from birth weight)
data_table.Examination: Palpable bladder to umbilicus, no abdominal mass, normal external genitalia, dribbling urine stream when expressed
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, Na 132, K 6.4, bedside USS distended bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, dilated posterior urethra

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Suprapubic aspirate of urine for culture and discharge home with outpatient nephrology review
options.rationale: Aspiration alone does not relieve bladder outlet obstruction; ongoing obstruction continues to damage the kidneys and bladder. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

options.text: Fluid challenge with normal saline 20 mL per kg then reassess for spontaneous voiding within 4 hours
options.rationale: Volume loading without relieving obstruction risks bladder injury and worsening hydronephrosis; catheter decompression is required first. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 1 mg per kg to promote urine output before any imaging is performed
options.rationale: Frusemide does not relieve mechanical obstruction; outflow must be established first by catheterisation, and dehydration may worsen the picture. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

options.text: Urgent micturating cystourethrogram first before any other intervention to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: MCUG is required to confirm the diagnosis but only after the bladder is decompressed and the baby is stabilised; not the first step in an obstructed septic-risk neonate. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

options.text: Insert a small-bore urethral catheter and admit to neonatal unit with urology referral
options.rationale: Suspected posterior urethral valves are decompressed urgently with bladder catheterisation, then transferred for paediatric urological assessment and surgical valve ablation. (Source: RCH CPG Posterior Urethral Valves)

explanation.summary: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest cause of severe lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants. Antenatal findings include bilateral hydronephrosis, dilated bladder and keyhole sign of dilated posterior urethra. Postnatally, suspect in any boy with weak stream, palpable bladder or anuria. Immediate management is catheter decompression with a small feeding tube (urethral catheter balloons can lodge in dilated posterior urethra), correction of electrolytes and prophylactic antibiotics. Definitive surgery is cystoscopic valve ablation. Long-term complications include chronic kidney disease, bladder dysfunction and need for transplantation in around 30 percent.
key_points: Suspect in boy with weak stream + palpable bladder + AKI.
Catheter decompression first - use feeding tube without balloon.
Send creatinine, electrolytes, USS post-decompression.
Cystoscopic valve ablation is definitive.
Long-term CKD risk - lifelong urology and nephrology follow-up.
explanation.pearls: Post-obstructive diuresis is common after relief of bilateral obstruction - replace urine output 1:1 with 0.45 percent saline plus dextrose for 24 to 48 hours to prevent profound electrolyte and volume disturbance.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Paediatric Surgery

subtopic_detail: Croup - severity assessment and initial therapy
stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 23:00 with a 24-hour history of coryza, low-grade fever and a barking cough that has become harsher overnight. He has audible inspiratory stridor at rest but is comfortable on his mother's lap. He drinks half a cup of water without difficulty and his colour is normal. There is no drooling or tripod posture. He is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.0, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, no tracheal tug, alert, well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Bedside clinical assessment only - no investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses and oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg in the emergency department
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no role in croup as the obstruction is supraglottic; using it delays effective steroid therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and admission for observation overnight on continuous saturation monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous steroids are unnecessary because oral dexamethasone is rapidly absorbed and equally effective without cannulation distress. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and observation for until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) with discharge if stridor settles at rest
options.rationale: A single oral dose of dexamethasone is the standard Australian first-line treatment for mild to moderate croup with rapid onset of effect and durable benefit. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 immediately as the first intervention before any other treatment
