options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with marked stridor at rest, retractions and distress; it is not first-line for mild stridor. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Discharge home with advice and saline nasal drops alone given the child is feeding and is well perfused at presentation
options.rationale: Discharging without dexamethasone misses the opportunity to shorten symptoms and reduce return rates, even when the child is feeding well. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheitis with subglottic oedema causing barking cough and inspiratory stridor. Severity is graded by stridor at rest, retractions, oxygenation and mental status. A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg shortens duration and prevents readmission across the mild to moderate spectrum. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with significant respiratory distress; its effect lasts about 2 hours so observation for at least 4 hours after adrenaline is required. Discharge is safe if the child is stridor-free at rest, well hydrated and the parent can return easily.
key_points: Single oral dexamethasone for all mild and moderate croup.
Nebulised adrenaline for severe croup only.
Observe at least 4 hours after adrenaline before discharge.
No role for salbutamol in croup.
Avoid throat examination and IV access if not needed.
explanation.pearls: Choose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral over prednisolone 1 mg/kg even though both are used; dexamethasone has a longer half-life and is single-dose, reducing risk of bounce-back stridor.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic 2 weeks after diagnosis of IgA vasculitis. He presented with a palpable purpuric rash on his buttocks and lower limbs, periarticular swelling of both ankles and intermittent colicky abdominal pain. The rash and joint swelling have resolved and he is back at school. His mother has been doing weekly urinalysis as advised. The latest urinalysis dipstick today shows 2+ blood and 1+ protein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 92, BP 122/78 on a 130 cm 25 kg boy (above 95th centile)
data_table.Examination: No rash, no joint swelling, abdomen soft and non-tender, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 2+ blood 1+ protein, urine ACR 80 mg/mmol (normal <2.5), serum creatinine 58, eGFR 88, albumin 36

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and continue weekly home urinalysis only, expecting spontaneous resolution within the next 4 weeks because the rash has cleared
options.rationale: Significant proteinuria and hypertension above 95th centile require specialist review and further investigation rather than continued observation. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days then taper, planning empirical immunosuppression for nephritis without specialist input first
options.rationale: Empirical steroid therapy without paediatric nephrology assessment and consideration of biopsy is not standard initial management. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Stop further urinalysis monitoring and discharge from clinic because the active rash and arthritis have resolved, with return advice for abdominal pain or new rash
options.rationale: Significant proteinuria and elevated BP indicate renal involvement that requires ongoing nephrology surveillance, not discharge. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology with paired urine albumin to creatinine ratio, blood pressure confirmation and review for possible renal biopsy and treatment
options.rationale: Persistent significant proteinuria with hypertension warrants urgent paediatric nephrology referral for biopsy consideration and treatment to preserve kidney function. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence enalapril for blood pressure control and arrange routine outpatient nephrology review in 6 to 8 weeks for further monitoring
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are considered after nephrology assessment; delaying specialist review with significant proteinuria risks irreversible kidney damage. (Source: RCH CPG Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is a small vessel vasculitis of childhood with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and IgA glomerulonephritis. Renal involvement develops in about a third of cases, mostly within 4 to 6 weeks. Weekly home urinalysis is recommended for the first 4 weeks then less frequently for 6-12 months. Significant proteinuria (urine ACR above 30), nephrotic syndrome, hypertension or rising creatinine demand urgent nephrology referral for renal biopsy and treatment. Steroids do not prevent nephritis but reduce abdominal pain and arthritis duration in severe cases.
key_points: Monitor urinalysis weekly for 4 weeks then less frequently 6-12 months.
Refer if proteinuria ACR above 30, BP above 95th centile, or rising creatinine.
Nephritis can develop after rash and arthritis resolve.
Steroids reduce extra-renal symptoms but do not prevent nephritis.
Long-term renal follow-up needed for any nephritis.
explanation.pearls: Confirm hypertension with three separate readings using the correct paediatric cuff size and using the 95th centile threshold for age, height and sex from the AAP nomogram, not adult thresholds.

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease - diagnosis and IVIG timing
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents on the 6th day of a high fever that has not responded to paracetamol. He is irritable and refusing to feed. On examination he has bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a red cracked tongue, an inflamed pharynx without exudate, a polymorphous truncal rash, and a single tender 2 cm right cervical lymph node. His hands and feet are swollen and red. He is fully immunised and previously well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 138, BP 100/60, RR 28, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, swollen erythematous hands and feet, single right cervical node 2 cm
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18, neutrophils 14, CRP 168, platelets 540, ALT 76, urine 30 WBC per HPF, ESR 88, ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment after starting acute care assessment?

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for community-acquired bacterial sepsis pending blood culture and respiratory virus PCR results
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics treat infection but miss the Kawasaki diagnosis where IVIG within 10 days is critical to prevent coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day in divided doses and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days as outpatient therapy with weekly clinic review
options.rationale: Aspirin and steroids are adjuncts; IVIG within 10 days is the cornerstone of management to reduce coronary aneurysm risk to about 5 percent. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses after baseline echocardiography
options.rationale: IVIG 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 to about 5 percent. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Topical antiseptic mouthwash, oral analgesia and a 5-day course of oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg six-hourly for presumed cervical lymphadenitis with viral exanthem
options.rationale: Topical care and oral antibiotic for presumed bacterial adenitis miss the diagnosis and the time-critical window for IVIG before day 10. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as a single pulse dose followed by infliximab 5 mg/kg infusion as first-line immunosuppressive therapy
options.rationale: Steroid pulse and infliximab are second-line for IVIG-resistant disease, not first-line treatment for incomplete or complete Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by fever for at least 5 days plus 4 of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips, pharyngitis), polymorphous rash, peripheral changes (erythema, oedema, peeling) and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm. IVIG 2 g/kg given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to about 5 percent. High-dose aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day) is started during the acute phase, transitioning to antiplatelet 3-5 mg/kg/day once afebrile until echocardiography is reassuring. Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks tracks coronary changes.
key_points: Diagnosis: fever 5+ days plus 4 of the classical features.
IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm to 5 percent.
High-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose antiplatelet until echo clear.
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
Second IVIG dose or steroids/infliximab if persistent fever 36 h post-IVIG.
explanation.pearls: Incomplete Kawasaki disease (3 features plus fever) is more common in infants under 1 year - presentations may be subtle and CRP above 30 plus ESR above 40 plus other supportive features (anaemia, low albumin, ALT elevation, pyuria, platelets above 450) justify IVIG.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement Diagnosis Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease

stem: A 9-month-old previously well boy presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of intermittent episodes of inconsolable crying with drawing his legs up, followed by quiet pale periods. He has vomited twice in the last hour, and the most recent vomit was bile-stained. He passed a small amount of red jelly-like stool 30 minutes ago. He is normally fully breastfed and has had no fever today. His parents are anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 152, BP 90/56, RR 32, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Pale and quiet between episodes, abdomen soft, palpable sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass, no peritonism, normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118, WCC 11, U/E unremarkable, glucose 5.8, lactate 1.8, abdominal ultrasound shows target sign in right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of conservative management with bowel rest, intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression for 24 hours in the paediatric ward with serial examinations
options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction is uncommon and conservative management delays intervention and increases bowel ischaemia risk. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Immediate exploratory laparotomy and manual reduction with consideration of bowel resection if any necrotic segment is identified intraoperatively in theatre
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed enema reduction, perforation, peritonism or unstable patient; first-line reduction is non-operative. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Intravenous access, fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and image-guided air or contrast enema reduction in radiology with paediatric surgical standby
options.rationale: Hydrostatic or pneumatic enema reduction under radiological guidance is the standard first-line treatment for stable ileocolic intussusception. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Oral rehydration with electrolyte solution at home and outpatient surgical clinic review in 48 hours if symptoms persist or worsen with appropriate return advice
options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe; intussusception is a surgical emergency requiring inpatient resuscitation and prompt reduction. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Diagnostic gastroscopy and colonoscopy under anaesthesia to confirm the diagnosis and identify a pathological lead point before non-operative reduction is attempted
options.rationale: Endoscopy is not indicated; ultrasound has already confirmed the diagnosis and reduction takes priority over lead point investigation. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically presents in 6-36 month old children with episodic colicky pain, vomiting (initially non-bilious then bilious), redcurrant jelly stool (late sign) and a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows target or pseudokidney sign. Air or contrast enema reduction in radiology with surgical standby is the standard first-line treatment with success rates of 80-90 percent, contraindicated by peritonism, perforation, hypovolaemic shock or pneumatosis. Surgery is for failed reduction, perforation or pathological lead point. Recurrence is 5-10 percent, mostly within 24 hours.
key_points: Episodic pain, drawing up legs, redcurrant jelly stool, sausage-shaped mass.
Ultrasound confirms with target sign or pseudokidney sign.
Air or contrast enema is first-line for stable child.
Surgery if peritonism, perforation, failure of reduction or pathological lead point.
Recurrence 5-10 percent - admit overnight for observation.
explanation.pearls: In children over 2 years suspect pathological lead point (Meckel's diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma) and arrange follow-up imaging or surgical consultation even after successful enema reduction.

stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy is brought to the emergency department with a 1-week history of progressively worsening non-bilious vomiting after every feed that has become projectile. He is hungry between feeds but his weight has dropped 200 g over the past week. His mother has noted reduced wet nappies. The paediatric surgeon has confirmed pyloric stenosis on ultrasound and theatre is provisionally booked for the next morning.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 168, BP 78/46, RR 36, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, palpable olive in right epigastrium, visible gastric peristalsis after feed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 2.8, Cl 88, HCO3 36, pH 7.52, BE +10, glucose 4.4, creatinine 36, ultrasound pyloric muscle thickness 5 mm length 20 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Place nasogastric tube on free drainage, withhold oral feeds, give intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus then 0.9 percent saline with 20 mmol/L potassium maintenance until biochemistry corrects
options.rationale: Correction of hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with NaCl and potassium replacement is mandatory before anaesthesia; pyloric stenosis is a medical not surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Transfer directly to theatre for immediate Ramstedt pyloromyotomy in the next available slot, since dehydration will be most efficiently corrected by relieving the obstruction first
options.rationale: Anaesthesia with metabolic alkalosis causes hypoventilation and apnoea; biochemical correction must precede surgery. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Start a trial of small frequent feeds of thickened expressed breast milk in upright position before re-evaluating in 24 hours to see if symptoms improve with conservative measures
options.rationale: Feeding does not resolve mechanical pyloric obstruction; further vomiting worsens dehydration and electrolyte loss. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Administer intravenous ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg and observe for resolution of vomiting before deciding whether resuscitation or surgical pathway is the most appropriate option
options.rationale: Antiemetics do not treat mechanical obstruction; the diagnosis is confirmed and definitive management is fluid resuscitation then pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Commence intravenous dextrose 10 percent at maintenance rate alone without sodium chloride to address ongoing hypoglycaemia and weight loss before surgery is performed
options.rationale: Dextrose alone does not correct chloride and sodium deficits or replace gastric losses; volume and electrolyte replacement are the priorities. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically presents at 3-6 weeks in first-born males with projectile non-bilious vomiting, hunger between feeds, weight loss and a palpable olive. Ultrasound confirms with pyloric muscle thickness at least 3 mm and length at least 15 mm. Vomiting of gastric HCl causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria; this must be corrected before anaesthesia to prevent post-operative apnoea. Resuscitation uses 0.9 percent saline boluses then maintenance with added potassium once urine output established. Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative; feeding is reintroduced within hours postoperatively.
key_points: Projectile non-bilious vomiting in 3-6 week first-born male.
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is classic.
Correct biochemistry before anaesthesia to prevent apnoea.
Aim chloride above 100 and bicarbonate below 30 before theatre.
Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative; feed within hours.
explanation.pearls: Add potassium only after urine output is established (above 1 mL/kg/h) and never give as a stat bolus; standard maintenance fluid is 0.9 percent saline with 20-40 mmol/L KCl, never glucose-water alone in alkalosis.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Surgery Guidelines - Pyloric Stenosis

subtopic_detail: Cystic fibrosis newborn screening - positive result followup
stem: A 3-week-old well-appearing baby is brought in by her parents after they receive a phone call from the newborn screening program saying the test was positive for cystic fibrosis. The baby was term, weighed 3.4 kg at birth, has been gaining weight well on breastfeeding and is passing 6 wet nappies per day and stools 3 times per day. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. The parents are anxious and want to understand what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 142, RR 38, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Well, alert, normal tone, chest clear, abdomen soft, weight tracking 25th centile, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screening IRT 240 ng/mL (above 99th centile cut-off), CFTR gene panel pending, no symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange repeat blood spot newborn screening in 4 weeks if the baby remains well, given the positive screening test result on the initial sample today
options.rationale: Positive IRT plus pending CFTR genotyping requires definitive diagnostic confirmation, not repeat screening. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

options.text: Commence empirical pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy at 2000 lipase units per kg per feed with weekly clinic monitoring while diagnostic confirmation is pending
options.rationale: Treatment is not started until diagnosis is confirmed by sweat chloride; empirical therapy is inappropriate. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

options.text: Arrange an immediate plain chest x-ray to look for early lung disease and barium meal to exclude meconium ileus given the positive newborn screening test result
options.rationale: Imaging is not first-line in asymptomatic CF screen-positive infants; diagnostic confirmation by sweat chloride is required. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

options.text: Refer urgently to the local paediatric cystic fibrosis centre for diagnostic sweat chloride test and full CFTR mutation analysis with multidisciplinary team review
options.rationale: Sweat chloride is the gold standard diagnostic test for CF after positive newborn screening; CF centre referral coordinates testing, counselling and surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

options.text: Send a faecal elastase sample and stool fat estimation now to evaluate for pancreatic insufficiency before confirming the cystic fibrosis diagnosis with further specialist tests
options.rationale: Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic function but does not diagnose CF; sweat chloride is the diagnostic standard. (Source: RCH CPG Cystic Fibrosis)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) on day 2-3 dried blood spot, with elevated IRT (above 99th centile) prompting CFTR mutation panel. A positive screen requires confirmatory sweat chloride at a recognised CF centre by Gibson-Cooke method; chloride at least 60 mmol/L is diagnostic, 30-59 is intermediate (extended CFTR sequencing and clinical correlation needed), under 30 is normal. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary care (paediatrician, dietitian, physiotherapist, psychologist) improves growth, lung function and survival. Pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamins, airway clearance and CFTR modulators (in eligible mutations) are core treatments.
key_points: Newborn screening: IRT day 2-3 then CFTR panel if elevated.
Sweat chloride at CF centre is the definitive diagnostic test.
Chloride above 60 mmol/L diagnostic, 30-59 intermediate, under 30 normal.
CF centre coordinates multidisciplinary follow-up.
CFTR modulators (ivacaftor and combinations) transformed prognosis.
explanation.pearls: Suspect CF clinically even with a normal screen if meconium ileus, recurrent chest infections or failure to thrive develops - 1 in 20 CF cases are missed by screening due to rare mutations not on the panel.

sources.label: Australasian Cystic Fibrosis Standards of Care

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis - admission criteria and supportive management
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old, ex-37-week infant in ED with 3 days of coryza progressing to noisy breathing and reduced feeding. The parents report wet nappies have halved and the last feed was 80 mL of formula 5 hours ago, taken with several pauses for breath. The infant is alert when handled but tires. The mother smoked in pregnancy and there are no siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 162, RR 62, SpO2 93% in room air, BP 88/52, weight 6.3 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild tracheal tug and subcostal recession, fine bilateral crackles with scattered wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, anterior fontanelle flat
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate positive for RSV, capillary blood gas pH 7.35 pCO2 45 HCO3 22, blood glucose 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment in 20 minutes to determine whether bronchodilator therapy should continue regularly
options.rationale: Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; trials show no meaningful benefit and may cause tachycardia and desaturation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days alongside supportive care, given the wheeze component and family history of maternal smoking exposure
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in viral bronchiolitis even when wheeze is present; they do not shorten illness or reduce admission. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for observation with low-flow nasal cannula oxygen, nasogastric or small-volume oral feeds, and minimal handling with routine reassessment of work of breathing
options.rationale: SpO2 below 92%, feeding under 50% baseline and increased work of breathing meet admission criteria; supportive care with oxygen and assisted hydration is standard. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous amoxicillin and benzylpenicillin empirically while awaiting blood culture results, treating possible bacterial co-infection causing the respiratory distress
options.rationale: Bacterial co-infection is uncommon in confirmed RSV bronchiolitis without focal consolidation or marked fever; antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with parental advice on small frequent feeds, nasal saline drops, and return immediately for any apnoea, cyanosis or worsening work of breathing observed
options.rationale: Hypoxia, reduced feeding and increased work of breathing in a 4-month-old preclude discharge; this infant needs inpatient observation. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in infants under 12 months; investigations are not routinely required. Admission is guided by hypoxia (SpO2 persistently under 92%), feeding under 50% of normal, significant work of breathing, apnoea, or social risk. Therapy is supportive: minimal handling, oxygen if needed and nasogastric or intravenous fluids if feeding is poor. High-flow nasal cannula is escalated when standard oxygen fails. Salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline, adrenaline and antibiotics do not change outcomes in routine cases.
key_points: Admit if SpO2 under 92%, feeds under 50% or apnoea episodes.
Supportive care only - no bronchodilators or steroids.
Escalate to high-flow if work of breathing persists on low-flow.
RSV is the most common pathogen, but co-infection is rare.
Chest x-ray is not routine and may prompt unnecessary antibiotics.
explanation.pearls: Apnoea is the dominant deterioration in infants under 6 weeks or ex-premature; admit even with normal saturations if any apnoeic episode is reported by carers.

stem: You are the rural ED registrar called urgently to a 3-year-old brought in by ambulance with 6 hours of fever, irritability and a new spreading purpuric rash on the trunk and limbs. The child cries when handled and is mottled peripherally. The nearest tertiary paediatric hospital is 2 hours by retrieval helicopter. The parents report no prior immunisations because of religious objection. You have already secured intraosseous access in the right tibia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4, HR 178, RR 44, SpO2 96%, BP 78/40, capillary refill 4 seconds, weight 14 kg
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric lesions on trunk, thighs and forearms, neck stiffness present, Kernig sign positive, GCS 13
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 3.6, lactate 4.1, awaiting bloods, no LP performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture for cell count and culture before any antibiotic dose to maximise yield, then commence intravenous ceftriaxone after sample collection
options.rationale: LP is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal sepsis with shock or coagulopathy and must never delay antibiotics. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg now, give a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus reassessing after each, and activate paediatric retrieval immediately for transfer
options.rationale: Empirical ceftriaxone within the first hour and titrated fluid resuscitation with early retrieval are the time-critical priorities in suspected meningococcal septicaemia. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 1.2 g now while awaiting transfer team, withhold further fluid until blood pressure trend confirms the need for resuscitation
options.rationale: IV ceftriaxone is preferred where access exists and gives broader cover; withholding fluid in a shocked child with lactate 4 is dangerous. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg first to reduce neurological sequelae and then begin antibiotic therapy after the steroid dose has been administered
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not recommended in meningococcal disease and any role in pneumococcal meningitis requires steroid with or just before antibiotics, never delaying them. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Take blood cultures and meningococcal PCR before any antibiotic to preserve microbiological diagnosis, then start ceftriaxone once samples have left the bedside
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay for microbiology is unacceptable in suspected meningococcal sepsis; PCR remains positive after antibiotics are given. (Source: eTG Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Meningococcal septicaemia is a time-critical emergency where empirical antibiotics must be given as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, not delayed for investigations or lumbar puncture. Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg up to 2 g is the agent of choice; IM benzylpenicillin is the field alternative when no IV access exists. Fluid resuscitation should be cautious and reassessed after each bolus because of capillary leak and high risk of pulmonary oedema. Early activation of paediatric retrieval is critical in rural and remote sites. PCR remains positive for up to 72 hours after antibiotics.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour, never delayed by LP or imaging.
Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV is first line.
Reassess after every 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus for fluid overload.
Dexamethasone not used in meningococcal disease.
Notify public health for household chemoprophylaxis.
explanation.pearls: Single-dose ciprofloxacin 500 mg is preferred over rifampicin for adult household chemoprophylaxis because it is a single dose and avoids interactions with oral contraceptives.

subtopic_detail: Pyloric stenosis - acid-base disturbance and pre-operative resuscitation
stem: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 5-week-old male, the first-born of consanguineous parents, referred from the GP with 2 weeks of progressive non-bilious vomiting now described as forceful and projectile after every feed. The mother is anxious because feeds are taken hungrily yet weight has fallen below the 3rd centile. There is a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant after a test feed. He has not passed urine for 8 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 99%, BP 78/45, weight 3.9 kg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, visible left to right gastric peristalsis, anterior fontanelle depressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, Cl 88, HCO3 34, urea 9.8, creatinine 48, venous pH 7.52 pCO2 50, ultrasound pyloric muscle 4.5 mm thickness 18 mm length

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management before surgical referral for pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Proceed immediately to theatre for Ramstedt pyloromyotomy under general anaesthesia, correcting the electrolytes intraoperatively to avoid further delay to surgical cure
options.rationale: Pyloromyotomy is never an emergency; metabolic alkalosis must be corrected first to avoid post-anaesthetic apnoea from impaired respiratory drive. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of 4% albumin to restore intravascular volume rapidly then transition to half-normal saline with added potassium and dextrose for ongoing maintenance
options.rationale: Crystalloid is preferred over colloid for paediatric resuscitation; half-normal saline does not adequately replace chloride losses. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Commence intravenous Hartmann solution at 150 mL/kg/day with no potassium supplementation because the metabolic alkalosis will worsen with chloride poor crystalloid
options.rationale: Hartmann is relatively chloride poor and inadequate to correct the hypochloraemia driving the alkalosis; sodium chloride is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and restrict all fluid until vomiting settles to prevent further chloride loss and to allow spontaneous biochemical correction
options.rationale: Nil oral plus NG drainage without IV replacement worsens dehydration and electrolyte derangement; intravenous fluid is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at maintenance and add potassium chloride only after a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hour is documented
options.rationale: Resuscitation requires sodium chloride with dextrose to replace chloride and avoid hypoglycaemia, with potassium added safely once renal output is confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG Pyloric Stenosis)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid producing a characteristic hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. The kidney initially excretes bicarbonate then switches to a paradoxical aciduria once volume contraction dominates. Pyloromyotomy is a semi-elective procedure that should never proceed until pH is below 7.45, bicarbonate is below 28 and chloride is above 100, because residual alkalosis depresses central respiratory drive after anaesthesia. Resuscitation uses sodium chloride with dextrose; potassium is added after urine output is established. Ultrasound criteria for diagnosis are pyloric muscle thickness above 3 mm and channel length above 15 mm.
key_points: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is pathognomonic.
Correct biochemistry before surgery to avoid post-op apnoea.
Sodium chloride with dextrose is the resuscitation fluid.
Add potassium only after urine output 1 mL/kg/hour.
Ultrasound: muscle thickness above 3 mm, length above 15 mm.
explanation.pearls: Target pre-operative chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 28 mmol/L; if alkalosis persists despite saline, suspect inadequate volume replacement rather than ongoing vomiting alone.

subtopic_detail: Supraventricular tachycardia in infancy - acute termination
stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to the resuscitation bay for a 6-week-old breastfed infant brought in by ambulance with 4 hours of poor feeding, sweating during feeds and pallor. The infant was term, no antenatal concerns and immunisations up to date for age. The infant is alert but mottled. Cardiac monitoring shows a narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves and a fixed rate that does not vary with handling. IV access has been secured in an antecubital vein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 280, RR 60, SpO2 95%, BP 72/40, capillary refill 4 seconds, weight 4.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Pale, peripherally cool to mid-forearm, hepatomegaly 2 cm, no murmur audible at this rate, bilateral fine crackles at lung bases
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG narrow QRS at 280, no discernible P waves, axis normal; bedside glucose 4.0; venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a bag of crushed ice and water firmly to the central face for 15 to 30 seconds while continuous rhythm monitoring is observed for sinus rhythm restoration
options.rationale: Diving reflex with iced water to the face is first-line vagal manoeuvre in infants and terminates SVT in around 30% with minimal haemodynamic risk. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

options.text: Administer intravenous adenosine 0.1 mg/kg as a rapid push followed by a saline flush, with continuous rhythm strip and defibrillator pads on the chest ready
options.rationale: Adenosine is the correct pharmacological choice but vagal manoeuvres should be tried first in a stable infant before drug therapy. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

options.text: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 joule per kilogram under brief procedural sedation given the prolonged tachycardia and early signs of cardiogenic shock with poor perfusion
options.rationale: Synchronised cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamically unstable SVT or failure of vagal manoeuvres plus adenosine; this infant is still perfusing. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

options.text: Administer intravenous verapamil 0.1 mg/kg slow push with continuous ECG monitoring to slow conduction through the atrioventricular node and restore sinus rhythm
options.rationale: Verapamil is contraindicated under 1 year because of profound hypotension and cardiac arrest from negative inotropy. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone loading at 5 mg/kg over 30 minutes with continuous monitoring while preparing for transfer to a paediatric cardiac centre
options.rationale: Amiodarone is reserved for refractory or unstable arrhythmia after vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail; it is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG SVT)

explanation.summary: Infant SVT typically presents as a narrow complex tachycardia at 220 to 300 bpm with no rate variability and no visible P waves; the absence of beat-to-beat variation distinguishes it from sinus tachycardia. Acute management of a stable infant follows a stepped algorithm: vagal manoeuvres first (iced water bag to face is most effective in infants), then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg with rapid saline flush, doubling to 0.2 mg/kg, then synchronised cardioversion 1 J/kg if unstable or unresponsive. Verapamil is contraindicated under 12 months. Heart failure features such as hepatomegaly and crackles can develop after prolonged SVT but do not yet mandate cardioversion if perfusion is preserved.
key_points: Infant SVT rate usually 220 to 300, no rate variability.
Iced water diving reflex first, adenosine second.
Verapamil contraindicated under 1 year.
Cardioversion 1 J/kg if unstable or refractory.
Refer to paediatric cardiology after first episode.
explanation.pearls: Wolff-Parkinson-White accounts for around half of infant SVT; once converted, an ECG in sinus rhythm may show a delta wave and short PR indicating accessory pathway.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 12.2 Paediatric Advanced Life Support

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury - infant fracture work-up
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old infant brought in by mother and her new partner for irritability and reluctance to use the right arm since this morning. The mother reports the infant rolled off the change table 24 hours ago but acted normally afterwards. The partner is the primary daytime carer. Child protection records show no prior notifications. X-ray of the right arm shows a spiral fracture of the midshaft humerus. The infant is not yet rolling on developmental assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 150, RR 36, SpO2 99%, BP 86/52, weight 6.8 kg
data_table.Examination: Inconsolable when right arm handled, bruising over right upper arm and posterior thorax, small healing bruise on left cheek, fundoscopy not yet performed, anterior fontanelle soft, alert
data_table.Investigations: Right humerus spiral fracture midshaft, FBE and coagulation studies pending, CRP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a collar and cuff immobilisation, prescribe regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, and discharge home with orthopaedic outpatient review and safety net advice
options.rationale: Discharging an infant with a suspicious spiral fracture and unexplained bruising without child protection involvement is a serious safety breach. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

options.text: Arrange urgent bone profile including alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone, and refer for genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta before notifying authorities
options.rationale: Bone fragility work-up may be added but does not replace mandatory notification; child protection must be activated first. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

options.text: Apply a back slab for analgesia, take repeated histories from each parent separately to clarify the mechanism, then decide on imaging based on consistency of stories
options.rationale: Imaging and notification must not be delayed pending further history-taking; the fracture pattern is already inconsistent with the given mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit the infant under paediatrics for a full skeletal survey, head CT or MRI, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages, and mandatory notification to child protection
options.rationale: A spiral humeral fracture in a non-mobile infant with multiple bruises mandates admission for occult injury work-up and statutory child protection notification. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

options.text: Discuss with parents the differential of accidental injury and arrange community child health nurse follow-up within 48 hours, deferring notification pending nurse review
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting cannot be deferred to community follow-up; all clinicians are reporters when abuse is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Suspected physical abuse in infancy requires a structured response: admission, multidisciplinary work-up for occult injury, and statutory notification to child protection. Spiral or metaphyseal corner fractures, rib fractures, and any fracture in a non-mobile infant are high-specificity injuries for abuse. Skeletal survey is the imaging gold standard with repeat at 2 weeks to detect callus formation. Head imaging and ophthalmology assessment screen for occult intracranial injury and retinal haemorrhages of abusive head trauma. Bruising in a child under 4 months who is not yet cruising should always prompt a safeguarding assessment.
key_points: Bruise in a pre-mobile infant requires safeguarding work-up.
Skeletal survey with 2-week repeat is the imaging standard.
Head MRI and retinal review for occult abusive head trauma.
Mandatory notification by all clinicians where abuse is suspected.
Bone fragility work-up does not delay reporting.
explanation.pearls: Bruises in babies who don't cruise should not be ignored - the TEN-4-FACESp clinical decision rule identifies high-risk patterns: bruising on torso, ear, neck in under 4 years or any bruising in infants under 4 months.

sources.label: RACP Position Statement Child Abuse and Neglect

subtopic_detail: Periorbital versus orbital cellulitis - imaging and admission
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar assessing a 6-year-old with 3 days of right eyelid swelling and pain. The mother reports a recent upper respiratory infection. The child now refuses to open the right eye fully. On examination there is marked eyelid oedema with erythema, the eye appears proptosed by 3 mm compared with the left, and the child complains of pain on attempted upgaze with restricted abduction. The pupil is mid-sized and reactive but vision testing is difficult through swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 99%, BP 102/64, weight 22 kg
data_table.Examination: Right eyelid erythema and oedema, proptosis, restricted abduction with pain on upgaze, conjunctival chemosis, sinus tenderness over right maxilla
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 138, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home on oral cephalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily with ophthalmology outpatient review the following day given the absence of complete ophthalmoplegia in this child
options.rationale: Proptosis, restricted eye movement and pain on gaze meet criteria for orbital cellulitis; oral therapy and discharge are unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six hourly alone, with CT orbits and sinuses only if there is no clinical improvement after 48 hours of monotherapy
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone does not cover the sinus organisms that complicate orbital infection; imaging cannot be delayed in suspected orbital involvement. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.text: Admit for urgent contrast CT of orbits and paranasal sinuses, commence intravenous ceftriaxone with flucloxacillin or vancomycin, and request ENT and ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia indicate orbital cellulitis; urgent imaging defines abscess or subperiosteal collection and dictates whether surgical drainage is required. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy with ophthalmology review in the morning, repeat clinical examination in 4 hours, and arrange imaging only if vision deteriorates
options.rationale: Imaging should not be deferred when proptosis and gaze restriction are already present; delaying CT risks intracranial extension. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

options.text: Apply warm compresses, commence oral amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily, and arrange paediatric outpatient review within 24 hours with safety net advice
options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is appropriate only for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis without orbital signs. (Source: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis

explanation.summary: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum and presents with eyelid swelling and erythema but no proptosis, no pain on eye movement and preserved vision. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis extends behind the septum and causes proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement, chemosis and potentially reduced visual acuity or relative afferent pupil defect. Orbital cellulitis is a surgical emergency because subperiosteal abscess and intracranial extension are well-recognised complications. Contrast CT of orbits and sinuses is the imaging modality of choice; treatment is IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering sinus organisms with prompt ophthalmology and ENT involvement.
key_points: Proptosis or eye movement pain defines orbital cellulitis.
Urgent contrast CT orbits and sinuses, not delayed imaging.
Ceftriaxone with flucloxacillin or vancomycin as empirical cover.
Surgical drainage for abscess over 10 mm or vision threat.
Sinus disease is the most common source in children.
explanation.pearls: Reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupil defect signal optic nerve compromise from orbital pressure and require emergency surgical decompression regardless of antibiotic response.

sources.label: RCH CPG Periorbital and Orbital Cellulitis
eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler - management and counselling
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing an 18-month-old whose mother has noticed pallor and reduced energy for play over 6 weeks. Diet history reveals 900 mL of cow's milk daily taken from a bottle, limited intake of solids, and a strong preference for white bread and pasta. Birth history was unremarkable at term. Growth parameters are tracking along the 25th centile. Developmental milestones are age-appropriate. There is no history of pica or melaena. Family migrated from Eritrea 2 years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 99%, BP 92/56, weight 11 kg
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no koilonychia, cardiovascular examination normal with no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84, MCV 62, MCH 18, reticulocyte count 1.0%, ferritin 7, iron 4, transferrin saturation 6%, lead level pending, faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent paediatric haematology referral for haemoglobin electrophoresis and bone marrow examination given the markedly low MCV and migration history from northeast Africa
options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency; electrophoresis is added later only if iron repletion fails to correct anaemia. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Admit for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as oral absorption is unreliable in toddlers and intravenous therapy guarantees full repletion of iron stores in a single dose
options.rationale: IV iron is reserved for failed oral therapy, malabsorption or non-adherence; first-line is oral with dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Commence oral ferrous sulfate elixir 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily and counsel to reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL with iron rich solids and vitamin C sources
options.rationale: Oral iron with dietary modification including milk reduction below 500 mL is first-line therapy in nutritional iron deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Commence oral iron polymaltose 6 mg/kg of elemental iron three times daily with each meal for 12 weeks and review only after completion of the prescribed full course
options.rationale: Three times daily dosing is no more effective than once daily for iron deficiency in children and increases gastrointestinal side effects. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Transfuse one unit of packed red cells with furosemide cover, repeat full blood count after 24 hours, and commence oral iron supplementation once haemoglobin is above 100
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic anaemia under 70; this toddler is well-perfused. (Source: RCH CPG Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Nutritional iron deficiency anaemia is the most common haematological problem in Australian toddlers and peaks at 9 to 24 months. Excessive cow's milk intake above 500 to 600 mL daily is a key driver because milk is iron poor, displaces iron rich foods and causes microscopic enteric blood loss. First-line therapy is oral iron 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily with vitamin C sources to enhance absorption; once daily dosing is now preferred over divided dosing because it gives better fractional absorption and fewer side effects. Repeat haemoglobin and ferritin after 4 weeks; expect haemoglobin to rise by at least 10 g/L.
key_points: Limit cow's milk to under 500 mL daily after 12 months.
Oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg once daily is first line.
Vitamin C source with iron improves absorption.
Repeat Hb at 4 weeks; expect rise above 10 g/L.
Investigate alternative causes if no response after compliance.
explanation.pearls: Alternate-day iron dosing has equivalent absorption to daily and fewer side effects in adults; in toddlers the practical preference is still once daily because of palatability and parental compliance.

subtopic_detail: New presentation type 1 diabetes with DKA - initial fluid plan
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-year-old girl brought to ED with 5 days of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss and 12 hours of abdominal pain and vomiting. There is no past medical history. She is rousable but drowsy. The school nurse noticed her breath smelled fruity yesterday. There is no family history of diabetes. She has had no recent illness apart from this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 134, RR 32 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99%, BP 96/58, weight 28 kg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 28, ketones 6.2, venous gas pH 7.05 HCO3 6 pCO2 18, Na 132 K 5.4 Cl 100 urea 9.2 creatinine 88, urine ketones 4+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan over the first hour?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride as a rapid bolus over 15 minutes then commence insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour with hourly neurological observations recorded
options.rationale: Rapid bolus and early insulin both increase cerebral oedema risk; bolus is reserved for shock and insulin starts after 1 hour of fluid resuscitation. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.text: Give 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes then continue maintenance plus deficit replacement at a calculated rate, deferring insulin infusion until 1 hour of fluids has been delivered
options.rationale: Cautious 10 mL/kg bolus, gradual deficit replacement over 48 hours and delayed insulin start reduce cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.text: Commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour given the severe acidosis with pH 7.05, then begin sodium chloride maintenance and insulin infusion concurrently
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is harmful in paediatric DKA, causing paradoxical CSF acidosis and increased cerebral oedema; it is contraindicated unless life-threatening hyperkalaemia is present. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.text: Commence Hartmann solution at 1.5 times maintenance with insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour started immediately to halt ongoing ketogenesis without further delay to glycaemic control
options.rationale: Insulin must be delayed at least 1 hour after fluid resuscitation begins; immediate insulin worsens cerebral oedema risk. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

options.text: Give 30 mL/kg of 0.45% sodium chloride over 1 hour with added potassium 40 mmol/L from the outset, then halve the rate and start insulin once acidosis begins to resolve
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid increases free water and worsens cerebral oedema; isotonic sodium chloride is mandatory and rates this high are unsafe. (Source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA)
source_refs: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management balances correction of dehydration and acidosis against cerebral oedema risk, which carries 25% mortality. Bolus fluids are limited to 10 mL/kg unless overt shock; deficit assumed at 5 to 7% and replaced over 48 hours with isotonic fluid. Insulin starts at least 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour, never with a bolus. Potassium 40 mmol/L is added after serum potassium is known unless anuric. Bicarbonate is contraindicated. Watch for warning signs of cerebral oedema: headache, falling GCS, hypertension with bradycardia, cranial nerve palsy. Treat suspected oedema with mannitol or hypertonic saline and reduce fluid rate.
key_points: Limit bolus to 10 mL/kg, deficit over 48 hours.
Delay insulin start by at least 1 hour after fluids.
Never bolus insulin; infuse 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour.
Bicarbonate contraindicated except life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
Cerebral oedema warning: headache, falling GCS, hypertension with bradycardia.
explanation.pearls: Effective osmolality (2 x Na plus glucose) should fall by no more than 3 mOsm/kg/hour; faster correction is independently associated with cerebral oedema even with apparently appropriate fluids.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines Paediatric DKA

stem: You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term baby boy in the postnatal ward. Mother is blood group O Rh positive, baby is A Rh positive. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. The baby is breastfed but feeding has been hesitant. The midwives are concerned about increasing yellow tinge. The baby was born by uneventful vaginal birth at 39+5 weeks and weighed 3.4 kg. There is no perinatal infection risk. The mother is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99%, weight 3.25 kg (down 4.4% from birth)
data_table.Examination: Visibly jaundiced to chest, alert and responsive to handling, no hepatosplenomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft, primitive reflexes intact
data_table.Investigations: Total SBR 320 micromol/L, conjugated 10 micromol/L, Hb 158, reticulocytes 5%, blood group A Rh positive DAT positive (anti-A)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue exclusive breastfeeding with lactation support and repeat SBR in 12 hours, no phototherapy required as the value is below standard term thresholds for this age range
options.rationale: SBR 320 at 60 hours in a term infant with ABO incompatibility exceeds the phototherapy threshold; treatment is required now. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg as first-line therapy to reduce antibody-mediated red cell destruction and avoid the need for phototherapy or further escalation
options.rationale: IVIg is an adjunct considered only when intensive phototherapy fails or exchange transfusion is imminent in haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Arrange immediate exchange transfusion with double-volume calculation through an umbilical venous catheter to remove bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells without delay
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of intensive phototherapy or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, neither of which is present. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to expressed formula to confirm breast milk jaundice as the cause, then reintroduce breastfeeding once SBR has begun to fall
options.rationale: Breastfeeding interruption is not first-line; haemolysis is the driver here and lactation support with phototherapy is correct. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy with light source above and below, ensure adequate fluid intake by feeding or formula top-up if needed, and repeat SBR in 4 to 6 hours
options.rationale: SBR above the term phototherapy threshold with ABO haemolysis warrants intensive phototherapy with hydration optimisation and short-interval SBR monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is plotted on a gestational-age-specific nomogram to set phototherapy and exchange thresholds. ABO incompatibility lowers the treatment threshold because of ongoing haemolysis. Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or 20% of total is pathological and requires investigation for biliary atresia or sepsis. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) presents with lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, opisthotonus and a high-pitched cry. Intensive phototherapy reduces unconjugated bilirubin within hours; exchange transfusion is reserved for failure of intensive phototherapy or encephalopathy. Discharge follow-up should include a community SBR check within 24 to 48 hours when risk factors are present.
key_points: Use age-in-hours nomogram for phototherapy thresholds.
ABO incompatibility lowers treatment threshold.
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 needs separate work-up.
Exchange transfusion only for treatment failure or encephalopathy.
Adequate hydration is essential during phototherapy.
explanation.pearls: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological - haemolytic disease, sepsis or G6PD deficiency until proven otherwise - and never attributable to physiological or breast milk jaundice.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 6-year-old girl brought in by ambulance with an acute asthma exacerbation. She has a known background of mild-persistent asthma on a low-dose budesonide preventer and salbutamol as needed. Paramedics gave continuous nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium en route. On arrival 20 minutes ago she received oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and a further three back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers. She is now sitting forward, talking in short phrases, with persistent moderate work of breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 38, SpO2 92% on 6 L/min via nebuliser, BP 102/64, T 37.1°C
data_table.Examination: Tracheal tug, intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, air entry reduced at both bases, no focal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as a slow bolus and continue current nebulised therapy
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone has equivalent bioavailability and onset to IV hydrocortisone; she has already received an adequate corticosteroid dose, so switching steroid route is not the right escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh and observation for response
options.rationale: Adrenaline IM is reserved for anaphylaxis or near-arrest asthma where IV access is unavailable; this child has wheeze without urticaria, hypotension or angio-oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline 10 mg/kg loading dose over 60 minutes on the general paediatric ward
options.rationale: Aminophylline is a third-line option used only after IV magnesium has failed and is given in PICU because of arrhythmia risk; jumping to it now skips a safer escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Switch to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min FiO2 0.5 and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: HFNC does not deliver bronchodilator therapy and risks delaying definitive treatment in a child with rising pCO2; nebulised salbutamol via a tight-fitting mask remains the preferred delivery route during escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg infused over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral corticosteroid escalates to IV magnesium sulfate as the next step before intubation; the rising pCO2 with persistent hypoxia and lactate signals failing ventilation despite maximal nebulised therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Children with severe acute asthma who do not respond to back-to-back nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium and adequate systemic corticosteroid require escalation. The standard Australian paediatric escalation is intravenous magnesium sulfate, followed by IV salbutamol or aminophylline infusions in a high-dependency or PICU setting if magnesium fails. A rising pCO2 in a tiring child despite high-dose bronchodilator therapy is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure and mandates HDU or PICU transfer.
key_points: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is the standard next step after failed inhaled therapy plus systemic steroid in paediatric severe asthma.
Oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg has equivalent onset to IV hydrocortisone in children who tolerate oral therapy.
Rising pCO2 in an asthmatic child is a pre-terminal sign and demands HDU or PICU level care.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric severe asthma a venous pCO2 above 45 mmHg with persistent tachypnoea is the signal to give IV magnesium sulfate within 30 minutes and call the PICU.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 10-month-old boy at a follow-up visit two weeks after his first hospital admission for viral wheeze. His mother says the cough has resolved but he still has occasional noisy breathing when he gets a cold. There is no family history of atopy and he has no eczema. His father, who has well-controlled adult asthma, is asking whether the baby should start a preventer to stop further admissions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 99% on room air, T 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, normal work of breathing, clear chest, no eczema, growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Discharge summary: confirmed RSV positive, responded to oxygen and supportive care, no salbutamol response documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management advice?

options.text: Start a daily low-dose inhaled budesonide preventer via spacer for the next twelve weeks
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids in infants under 12 months with viral wheeze and no atopy do not reduce admission rates and expose the infant to potential growth effects without clear benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric respiratory physician for cystic fibrosis sweat testing
options.rationale: A single bronchiolitic admission with normal growth and no chronic cough does not raise concern for cystic fibrosis; newborn screening already reduces residual risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Prescribe a montelukast 4 mg granule sachet nightly during the winter respiratory virus season
options.rationale: Montelukast has only modest benefit in selected preschool wheezers older than 2 years and is not first-line in infants; behavioural and neuropsychiatric adverse effects further limit routine use. (Source: AMH; eTG: Respiratory)

options.text: Trial regular salbutamol 100 micrograms twice daily via spacer through the winter period
options.rationale: Regular salbutamol in infants without documented bronchodilator response is unhelpful and may mask deterioration; in this child salbutamol gave no benefit during admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Reassure the family, continue supportive care and review only if a further severe episode occurs
options.rationale: Under 12 months of age viral wheeze rarely represents atopic asthma and a documented poor salbutamol response confirms the bronchiolitis phenotype; routine preventers are not indicated and watchful waiting with safety-net advice is the standard approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Most wheeze in the first year of life is viral and not steroid-responsive, even when a parent has atopic asthma. Australian guidance reserves a preventer trial for children over 12 months with frequent episodes, interval symptoms or atopic features. Salbutamol responsiveness should be documented before chronic bronchodilator therapy is prescribed to infants. Parental anxiety is best managed with a written action plan and clear escalation triggers rather than empirical preventers.
key_points: Infant viral wheeze without atopy or salbutamol response does not justify a preventer trial.
Preventer trials become appropriate after 12 months when atopic features or interval symptoms appear.
Document bronchodilator response before prescribing regular salbutamol in any infant.
explanation.pearls: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce neither admissions nor symptom days in non-atopic infants under 12 months with isolated viral wheeze.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a 14-day-old term breastfed baby boy in the emergency department. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth with a normal antenatal course and was discharged home day 2 with a normal newborn examination. Over the last 12 hours his mother reports poor feeding, decreased wet nappies and an episode of mottling. He has had no contact with unwell siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188 bpm, RR 64, SpO2 96% on room air, axillary T 38.4°C, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, irritable on handling, mild jaundice, no rash, anterior fontanelle soft, no focal source
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pending; cultures from blood and urine taken; cerebrospinal fluid sample collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin at standard neonatal doses
options.rationale: Late-onset community-acquired sepsis in a previously well term neonate is empirically treated with cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin to cover Group B Streptococcus, Listeria and Gram-negatives including meningeal cover. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone at standard paediatric doses
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates under 28 days because of bilirubin displacement and a risk of kernicterus, particularly with concurrent calcium-containing fluids. (Source: AMH; eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin at standard neonatal doses
options.rationale: This combination targets early-onset sepsis pathogens but lacks reliable cover for community-acquired late-onset bacteraemia and meningitis; CNS penetration of gentamicin is poor. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem at standard paediatric doses
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum vancomycin and meropenem are reserved for hospital-acquired late-onset sepsis or suspected resistant organisms; community-acquired presentations do not need this breadth empirically. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin and oral acyclovir at standard neonatal doses
options.rationale: Acyclovir requires intravenous administration in suspected neonatal HSV and amoxicillin alone has inadequate Gram-negative cover; this combination undertreats both bacterial and viral targets. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Late-onset neonatal sepsis spans the period from 72 hours to 28 days of life. Empiric antibiotic choice in community-acquired disease must cover Group B Streptococcus, Listeria, Escherichia coli and other Gram-negatives, with adequate CNS penetration because meningitis cannot be excluded. The standard Australian neonatal regimen is intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin. Intravenous acyclovir should be added if vesicular rash, seizures, hepatitis or maternal HSV history exists.
key_points: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates under 28 days because of bilirubin displacement.
Cefotaxime is the cephalosporin of choice for neonatal sepsis with meningitis cover.
Add intravenous acyclovir if any HSV red flags are present in a sick neonate.
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin is first-line for community-acquired neonatal sepsis from day 3 to day 28 of life across Australian neonatal units.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on a tertiary inpatient ward managing a 9-year-old girl admitted four hours ago with new-onset diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis. She received a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus over 60 minutes and is now on a maintenance plus deficit infusion calculated for a 7% deficit replaced over 48 hours, alongside an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour.

Two hours into therapy the nurse calls you because the patient has developed a headache, has become increasingly drowsy and her heart rate has fallen from 130 to 78 bpm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 132/88, T 36.8°C, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Pupils 4 mm equal and sluggishly reactive, no focal weakness, fundi not seen
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 14.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.20 (improved from 6.98), K 4.0 mmol/L, Na corrected 138 mmol/L, ketones 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and add intravenous dextrose 10%
options.rationale: Glucose is falling appropriately and ketosis is improving; increasing insulin further does not address the deteriorating neurology and risks worsening cerebral water shifts. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 15 minutes and reduce fluid rate by one third
options.rationale: Bradycardia, falling GCS and hypertension after fluid initiation in paediatric DKA define clinical cerebral oedema; mannitol or hypertonic saline plus a fluid rate reduction is the standard emergent response without waiting for imaging. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Urgently transfer for non-contrast CT brain to confirm cerebral oedema before treatment
options.rationale: Cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA is a clinical diagnosis; imaging delays definitive therapy and adds no early sensitivity, although CT may follow once the child is stabilised. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Give a further 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus over 30 minutes for presumed hypovolaemia
options.rationale: A further bolus worsens cerebral oedema; the bradycardia here is a brainstem response to raised intracranial pressure, not hypovolaemic shock. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and continue maintenance fluids only for the next hour
options.rationale: Stopping insulin allows ketogenesis to resume and worsens acidosis without treating the cerebral oedema; insulin should continue alongside hyperosmolar therapy. (Source: ISPAD; APEG: Paediatric DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates approximately 1% of paediatric DKA episodes and carries 20 to 25% mortality. Risk peaks in younger children, first presentations, severe acidosis and high urea. Hyperosmolar therapy with intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg, combined with a one-third reduction in fluid rate, is initiated on clinical grounds. Headache, hypertension, bradycardia and falling conscious state form the Cushing triad equivalent in this setting.
key_points: Diagnose cerebral oedema clinically; do not wait for imaging.
Mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg are first-line.
Reduce IV fluid rate by one third and elevate the head of bed to 30 degrees.
explanation.pearls: Cushing triad in paediatric DKA - bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS - means give mannitol 0.5 g/kg now and cut the fluid rate by a third before imaging.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing a 4-year-old boy who has refused to weight-bear since waking this morning. His mother reports a mild upper respiratory illness over the last week that resolved spontaneously. He has not taken any medications. There is no history of trauma. He is reluctant to allow examination of the right hip but shows no swelling or erythema. He has a low-grade temperature on triage of 38.1°C.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, T 38.1°C, BP 102/64
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation, painful log roll, full passive range only achievable under analgesia
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 38 mg/L, ESR 42 mm/h, hip ultrasound shows a 5 mm joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia, weight-bearing as tolerated and review by general practitioner in 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: With three Kocher criteria positive the probability of septic arthritis is approximately 93% and outpatient management risks rapid joint destruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Admit for empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and ward reassessment in 24 hours without joint aspiration
options.rationale: Antibiotics given before aspiration reduce culture yield and delay diagnosis; aspiration must precede empirical antibiotics whenever septic arthritis is plausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Arrange urgent orthopaedic hip joint aspiration under image guidance for cell count, Gram stain and culture
options.rationale: Four Kocher criteria positive in this child (non-weight-bearing, fever 38.1°C, ESR over 40, WCC over 12 x10^9/L) gives a high pre-test probability of septic arthritis; aspiration is the definitive diagnostic step. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Order outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip prior to any invasive procedure or admission
options.rationale: MRI is helpful for osteomyelitis or atypical presentations but delays joint sampling in a probable septic hip; ultrasound has already confirmed an effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Prescribe oral ibuprofen with hourly observations and review in the short stay unit at 4 to 6 hours
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment risks masking deterioration in a child with four high-risk features; the priority is definitive sampling not analgesic monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria - inability to weight-bear, temperature over 38.5°C (often relaxed to 38°C in Australia), ESR over 40 mm/h and WCC over 12 x10^9/L - guide pretest probability of septic arthritis. Three or four positive criteria correspond to a 93 to 99% probability respectively. Joint aspiration provides immediate diagnostic yield via cell count, Gram stain and culture, and must precede empirical antibiotics whenever possible. Empiric flucloxacillin is then commenced; kingella kingae cover with cefazolin or addition of a second agent may be considered in children under 4 years.
key_points: Four Kocher criteria positive carries roughly 99% probability of septic arthritis.
Aspirate before antibiotics whenever feasible to maximise culture yield.
Empirical flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus; consider kingella kingae cover under 4 years.
explanation.pearls: A non-weight-bearing febrile child with CRP above 20 mg/L plus ultrasound effusion warrants same-day joint aspiration; transient synovitis remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to ED at midnight to see a 5-day-old term boy with three episodes of green vomiting since this afternoon. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth and discharged home day 2 with normal newborn examination. He has been exclusively breastfed and had passed meconium within 24 hours of birth. He fed reluctantly today and his abdomen has become mildly distended over the last hour. He has not had a wet nappy for the last 5 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 60, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.3°C, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, mildly distended soft abdomen, no palpable mass, no peritonism, anal patency normal
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.28, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound looking specifically for the whirlpool sign of the mesenteric vessels
options.rationale: Ultrasound is operator-dependent and only supportive; a negative scan does not exclude malrotation and must not delay the definitive contrast study. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study performed urgently within the next hour
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise; an urgent upper GI contrast study to confirm or exclude an abnormal duodenojejunal junction position is the definitive test before laparotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Plain supine and erect abdominal radiographs to look for free air or obstruction
options.rationale: Plain films are often normal in malrotation without established volvulus and cannot exclude the diagnosis; relying on them risks missing a surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Sweat chloride testing arranged through the paediatric metabolic team in the morning
options.rationale: Sweat testing investigates cystic fibrosis-related meconium ileus equivalents, which present earlier and without bilious vomiting; it does not address the surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

options.text: Contrast enema to exclude Hirschsprung disease as the cause of the obstructive symptoms
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease classically presents with delayed meconium passage and distal obstruction; bilious vomiting points to a proximal obstructive lesion, of which malrotation is the priority diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bilious vomiting)

explanation.summary: Bilious vomiting in any infant under 12 months is treated as midgut volvulus until imaging excludes it.
