Time-to-detorsion correlates directly with bowel survival, so the workup is compressed - nasogastric decompression, IV access, fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and an immediate paediatric surgical referral run in parallel with imaging. The upper GI contrast study showing a corkscrew or right-sided duodenojejunal junction confirms malrotation; whirlpool sign on ultrasound is supportive. Laparotomy and Ladd procedure are definitive.
key_points: Bilious vomiting in infants is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
Upper GI contrast study is the definitive imaging test.
Time-to-theatre directly determines bowel survival.
explanation.pearls: In a neonate with green vomiting, call paediatric surgery and book an upper GI contrast study before plain films or ultrasound delay the diagnosis.

sources.label: Paediatric Surgery: malrotation chapter (BMJ Best Practice)

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional hospital reviewing a 6-month-old formula-fed boy admitted overnight with five days of viral gastroenteritis. The community nurse reports the family had been adding extra scoops of formula powder to the bottles to keep him fed during the illness. He has been increasingly lethargic since this morning. He weighs 7.0 kg and his pre-illness clinic weight one week ago was 7.5 kg. He has not had a wet nappy for 8 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 36, SpO2 99% on room air, T 37.6°C, BP 80/52, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable, sunken eyes, doughy abdominal skin turgor, no rash, anterior fontanelle depressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 162 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.28

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate fluid plan for the next 48 hours?

options.text: Replace the 7% fluid deficit with sodium chloride 0.9% plus 5% glucose over 48 hours with sodium fall not exceeding 0.5 mmol/L per hour
options.rationale: Hypernatraemic dehydration requires slow correction with isotonic fluids over 48 to 72 hours; the deficit is replaced gradually so plasma sodium falls no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 12 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.45% then replace the deficit with the same fluid over 24 hours with electrolyte checks every 6 hours
options.rationale: Hypotonic resuscitation fluids drop plasma sodium too rapidly and risk cerebral oedema; the bolus strength should be isotonic and the correction phase prolonged. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9% then replace the deficit with 5% glucose over 24 hours with electrolyte checks every 6 hours
options.rationale: Pure glucose for maintenance after the bolus delivers free water too quickly and causes a precipitous sodium drop; correction must be paced over 48 hours minimum. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Administer oral rehydration solution at 10 mL/kg/hour and recheck sodium after 6 hours of trial of oral therapy
options.rationale: A lethargic child with capillary refill of 4 seconds and 7% volume loss requires intravenous resuscitation, although oral therapy is valuable once intravascular volume is restored. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Replace the deficit with sodium chloride 0.9% plus 5% glucose over 12 hours and reassess electrolytes every hour during correction
options.rationale: Rapid 12-hour correction predisposes to cerebral oedema and seizures despite using an isotonic fluid; rate of sodium fall not total volume is the safety variable. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration is most often caused by improperly mixed feeds, inadequate breastfeeding or large gastroenteritis losses without free water replacement. Rapid sodium correction draws water back into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema with herniation. The Australian paediatric standard replaces the deficit with isotonic sodium chloride plus dextrose over 48 to 72 hours, aiming to drop sodium no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day. Boluses are reserved for true shock.
key_points: Hypernatraemic deficit replacement runs over 48 to 72 hours not 24.
Plasma sodium must fall no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour.
Use isotonic fluids; hypotonic regimens accelerate dangerous sodium shifts.
explanation.pearls: Slow correction with sodium chloride 0.9% plus glucose 5% over 48 hours, capped at a 10 mmol/L sodium drop per day, prevents the cerebral oedema and seizures that follow rapid correction of hypernatraemic dehydration.

stem: You are the on-call paediatric registrar called by the neonatal screening service about a 12-day-old infant whose newborn screen returned a markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. The baby has been feeding poorly for 24 hours with three episodes of vomiting and a reduced wet-nappy count. On examination external genitalia show clitoromegaly with partial labial fusion. The infant looks pale and mottled and has lost 12% of birth weight since discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 192 bpm, RR 60, SpO2 96% on room air, T 36.3°C, BP 56/34, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, peripheral mottling, ambiguous genitalia, no palpable gonads, hyperpigmented areolae and scrotum-like rugae
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.1 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.22, 17-OHP markedly elevated on repeat

lead_in: Which combination of interventions should be initiated immediately?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 5 mg with oral fludrocortisone 50 micrograms and outpatient endocrinology phone review the next day
options.rationale: An unwell shocked infant in adrenal crisis cannot absorb oral therapy reliably; intravenous hydrocortisone with intravenous resuscitation is the correct route. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 0.5 mg stat with 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.45% bolus and routine endocrinology review next day
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is the wrong steroid in acute salt-wasting crisis; hypotonic fluids worsen hyponatraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat with 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% plus 10% glucose bolus and paediatric endocrinology referral
options.rationale: Salt-wasting CAH crisis requires immediate stress-dose hydrocortisone, isotonic volume resuscitation containing glucose to address hypoglycaemia, and urgent specialist involvement to guide ongoing replacement; fludrocortisone is added once enteral therapy is tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

options.text: Intravenous insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour with calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg over 10 minutes for the hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: The hyperkalaemia of salt-wasting CAH responds rapidly to volume and steroid replacement; insulin is unnecessary and risks profound hypoglycaemia in a glucose-2.1 mmol/L infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

options.text: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous immunoglobulin pending neonatal sepsis screening culture results
options.rationale: Although a septic workup is reasonable to add in parallel, the diagnosis of salt-wasting CAH is already supported by ambiguous genitalia, raised 17-OHP and the electrolyte pattern; immunoglobulin has no role. (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal crisis; APEG: CAH)

explanation.summary: Salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents around day 7 to 14 with vomiting, lethargy, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis. Female infants often have virilised genitalia; male infants have normal genitalia, which can delay recognition. Emergency management is intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone (25 mg in infants under 6 years), isotonic volume with glucose, and correction of hypoglycaemia. Long-term replacement combines hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and salt supplementation under endocrinology supervision.
key_points: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg is the stat dose in infants under 6 years with adrenal crisis.
Use isotonic fluids with glucose; avoid dexamethasone in acute crisis because of absent mineralocorticoid effect.
Hyperkalaemia of CAH usually resolves with volume and steroid, not insulin or beta-agonists.
explanation.pearls: Day 7 to 14 vomiting infant with sodium under 130 mmol/L and potassium over 6 mmol/L is salt-wasting CAH until proven otherwise; give intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg now.

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease counselling
stem: You are the GP seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother is worried she has chickenpox. Two days ago the child developed a low-grade fever and refused breakfast. This morning small grey-white blisters appeared on her palms, soles and the inside of her cheeks. Her older brother attends the same childcare centre. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and the girl is fully immunised including two doses of varicella vaccine. Mum asks when she can go back to childcare.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6°C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pinpoint vesicles on a non-erythematous base on hands, feet and buccal mucosa; trunk and face spared; alert and drinking small volumes
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding return to childcare?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh and observe response over 5 minutes
options.rationale: The Staying Healthy 5th edition advises exclusion of children with HFMD until the blisters have dried, with the child also clinically well; this aligns the duration to actual infectivity and clinical state rather than a fixed day count. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg infused over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring in HDU
options.rationale: HFMD is not on the standard national notifiable list and is managed by exclusion plus hygiene; PHU notification is only triggered in clusters of severe disease such as suspected EV71-associated brainstem encephalitis. (Source: CDNA Series of National Guidelines)

options.text: IV aminophylline 10 mg/kg load over 60 minutes on the general paediatric ward with telemetry only
options.rationale: HFMD does carry an exclusion period in Australian early childhood settings; absence of fever does not change the recommendation while the vesicles are still moist. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)

options.text: Switch to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min FiO2 0.5 and reassess at 30 minutes off bronchodilator
options.rationale: There is no mandated 21 day exclusion for HFMD; this length applies to no notifiable childhood infection currently listed in the NHMRC schedule. (Source: Staying Healthy 5th edition NHMRC)

options.text: Switch corticosteroid route to IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg slow bolus and continue current nebulisers
options.rationale: This is the rule for varicella, not for hand foot and mouth disease; the vesicles in HFMD do not crust like chickenpox and prolonged exclusion is not required. (Source: Staying Healthy: Preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease is a common coxsackievirus or enterovirus rash with grey-white vesicles on the palms, soles and oral mucosa. The Staying Healthy 5th edition recommends exclusion until the blisters have dried; there is no fixed day count and crusting is not part of the natural history. Hygiene measures and surface cleaning at the childcare centre are the main control strategies, with EV71 surveillance flagged separately for severe disease.
key_points: Exclude from childcare until blisters have dried, not until they have crusted.
There is no fixed day count for return; clinical wellness is required in addition.
Notification is only triggered in clusters with severe neurological involvement suggesting EV71.
explanation.pearls: If a child with HFMD develops ataxia, drowsiness or myoclonic jerks within the first 5 days, escalate urgently because enterovirus 71 brainstem encephalitis is a public health priority.

subtopic_detail: Scarlet fever and rheumatic fever prevention
stem: You are the rural GP seeing a 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community presenting with two days of sore throat, fever and a rough sandpaper-like rash that started on his neck and spread to his trunk. He has a strawberry tongue and tender anterior cervical nodes. He has no penicillin allergy and is well enough to be managed as an outpatient with reliable follow up through the community clinic. His mother is happy to give oral medication.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous oropharynx with tonsillar exudate, palpable petechial rash with sandpaper texture sparing the face, strawberry tongue, no joint swelling, no carditis
data_table.Investigations: Rapid throat swab unavailable; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for an abbreviated five-day course
options.rationale: Five days is enough to settle symptoms but is insufficient to eradicate Group A Streptococcus from the pharynx and so does not reliably prevent acute rheumatic fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg twice daily for a seven-day course with supportive care
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is an acceptable alternative when adherence to penicillin V dosing is a concern, but the AU rheumatic-fever prevention regimens specify a full ten-day duration, not seven. (Source: RHDAustralia guideline)
source_refs: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

options.text: Symptomatic care only with paracetamol and clinic review in 48 hours if not better
options.rationale: In a child from a high acute rheumatic fever risk group, withholding antibiotics is unsafe because rheumatic fever can follow even mild pharyngitis. (Source: RHDAustralia guideline)
source_refs: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

options.text: Oral roxithromycin 4 mg/kg twice daily for ten days with topical throat lozenges
options.rationale: Macrolides are reserved for documented penicillin hypersensitivity; in penicillin-tolerant patients they are not first-line because of increasing macrolide-resistant Group A Streptococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for a full ten-day course
options.rationale: In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children living in remote communities a full ten-day course of phenoxymethylpenicillin (or single dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin) is required to prevent acute rheumatic fever, even when symptoms resolve early. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever in an Aboriginal child from a remote community sits in the highest-risk group for acute rheumatic fever. The cornerstone of prevention is eradication of Group A Streptococcus from the pharynx with a full ten-day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin or a single dose of intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin. Shorter courses settle symptoms but leave organisms behind and do not prevent ARF. Macrolides are reserved for true penicillin allergy.
key_points: Phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for ten days is first-line.
Single dose IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is an alternative when adherence is uncertain.
Shorter courses settle symptoms but do not prevent rheumatic fever.
explanation.pearls: In any Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child with pharyngitis, treat group A streptococcal infection as a 10-day course or single benzathine dose; do not stop at 5 days even if the child is asymptomatic by day 3.

sources.label: RHDAustralia: Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD

stem: You are the paediatric outpatient registrar reviewing a 14-month-old boy referred by his GP for bow legs and delayed walking. He was exclusively breastfed until 12 months and was not given vitamin D supplements. He spends most of his day indoors and his mother veils for cultural reasons. The family lives in Melbourne and the child has darkly pigmented skin. He has no chronic illnesses, no diarrhoea, and his diet is now mostly cow's milk with very little meat or fortified cereal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7°C, HR 112, RR 24, weight on 25th centile, length on 10th centile
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, wrist widening, costochondral beading, valgus deformity of the lower limbs, hypotonia, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Calcium 1.95 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, ALP 1200 U/L, 25-OH vitamin D 18 nmol/L, PTH elevated, wrist X-ray: cupping and fraying of distal radius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily for three months without calcium supplementation
options.rationale: 1000 units daily is a maintenance dose; it is too low for established rickets, which requires a treatment dose for several weeks. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.text: Oral cholecalciferol 3000 IU daily for 12 weeks plus elemental calcium 500 mg daily
options.rationale: Treatment-dose vitamin D (1000 to 2000 units daily under 1 month, 3000 units daily 1-12 months, or 5000 units daily over 12 months) for 12 weeks, combined with adequate calcium intake, is the Australian guideline approach to symptomatic rickets. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for surgical correction of genu varum before further medical workup
options.rationale: Bow legs in nutritional rickets correct over months once vitamin D and calcium are repleted; surgery is not the first step. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.text: Single oral stoss dose of 300000 IU cholecalciferol with bloods rechecked at two weeks
options.rationale: High-dose stoss therapy has been associated with hypercalcaemia and is not the AU first-line approach; daily dosing is preferred where adherence allows. (Source: APEG vitamin D position statement)
source_refs: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg over 10 minutes and admit for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: IV calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany, prolonged QT); this child has mild biochemical hypocalcaemia and no acute cardiac or neuromuscular features. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypocalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets in Australia is most commonly seen in dark-skinned children with limited sunlight exposure, prolonged exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation, and low dietary calcium. Diagnosis combines hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, elevated ALP and PTH, low 25-OH vitamin D, plus radiographic metaphyseal cupping and fraying. Treatment is several weeks of cholecalciferol with adequate calcium intake; bony deformities correct over months without orthopaedic intervention.
key_points: Treatment dose cholecalciferol 1000 to 5000 units daily for 12 weeks depending on age.
Calcium 500 mg elemental daily is needed alongside vitamin D in established rickets.
ALP and 25-OH D are followed at 3 months to confirm response.
explanation.pearls: In suspected rickets, an ALP above 1000 U/L with a 25-OH vitamin D below 25 nmol/L is highly suggestive; check PTH to exclude renal forms.

sources.label: APEG: Vitamin D and health in children

stem: You are the GP seeing a 4-month-old formula-fed boy whose parents are worried about ongoing crying, regurgitation and intermittent loose mucousy stools, occasionally with streaks of fresh blood. Symptoms began at 6 weeks, around the time he switched from breast to standard cow milk formula. He has mild eczema on the cheeks. He is alert, playful and feeding well, but weight gain has slowed from the 50th centile to the 15th centile over six weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9°C, HR 130, RR 32, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-hydrated, mild facial eczema, soft non-tender abdomen, normal anal tone, no anal fissure
data_table.Investigations: Faecal occult blood positive, FBC normal, no eosinophilia, no skin prick or specific IgE testing performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to a lactose-free cow milk based formula and review symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Lactose-free formula still contains intact cow milk protein and does not treat protein-induced colitis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Refer for specific IgE testing to cow milk protein before any change of formula trial
options.rationale: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy is a clinical diagnosis with normal specific IgE; testing before a dietary trial delays treatment and is rarely diagnostic in this phenotype. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Switch to a soy-based infant formula and review symptoms in two weeks at the clinic
options.rationale: Up to one in three infants with cow milk protein allergy are also intolerant of soy protein; ASCIA does not recommend soy formula as a first-line substitute under 6 months. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Thicken current formula and start omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily before any formula change
options.rationale: Acid suppression treats reflux oesophagitis but does not address the immune-mediated colitis suggested by streaks of blood and slowing weight gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux)

options.text: Trial extensively hydrolysed casein formula for two to four weeks with clinical reassessment
options.rationale: Non-IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergy in a young infant with proctocolitis features is managed by a trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula; symptomatic improvement within two to four weeks supports the diagnosis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

explanation.summary: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy commonly presents in young formula-fed infants with crying, vomiting, mucousy bloody stools and faltering growth. Diagnosis is clinical: a 2 to 4 week trial of an extensively hydrolysed formula should resolve symptoms, with a planned milk challenge between 9 and 12 months. Soy formula is not first-line under 6 months because of cross-reactivity, and lactose-free formula does not remove the offending protein.
key_points: Extensively hydrolysed casein formula is first-line for proven or suspected non-IgE CMPA under 6 months.
Soy formula is avoided as first-line under 6 months due to cross-reactivity.
Specific IgE testing is normal in non-IgE phenotypes and should not gate the trial.
explanation.pearls: Blood-streaked mucous stools plus eczema and slowing weight gain in an infant just after the breast-to-formula switch is classic non-IgE cow milk protein allergy; expect symptoms to resolve within 2 to 4 weeks of extensively hydrolysed formula.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Infant feeding and allergy prevention

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 7-day-old term baby boy with three days of bilateral sticky eyes and increasing eyelid swelling. He was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 19-year-old mother whose antenatal STI screening was incomplete. The baby is feeding and gaining weight well, has no fever and no respiratory distress. Examination shows marked tarsal injection with mucopurulent discharge and mild eyelid oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9°C, HR 140, RR 44, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mucopurulent conjunctival discharge, no corneal involvement on fluorescein, no preauricular nodes, clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Eye swab for chlamydia PCR and bacterial culture obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial therapy while results are pending?

options.text: Saline eye toilet four times daily and clinical review in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: Watchful management without antimicrobials is appropriate for chemical conjunctivitis in the first 24 hours of life, not for a day-7 mucopurulent picture with high suspicion of chlamydia. (Source: STIs in gay men action group AU and Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg dose with saline eye toilet four times daily
options.rationale: Single-dose ceftriaxone is the regimen for suspected gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum (day 1 to 5, hyperacute purulent discharge); this presentation pattern is typical of chlamydia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol drops six times daily for seven days with saline eye toilet
options.rationale: Chloramphenicol drops cover bacterial conjunctivitis but do not eradicate chlamydia from the nasopharynx, leaving the baby at risk of pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks of age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg as a single dose with saline eye toilet four times daily
options.rationale: Azithromycin single dose is the standard for adult genital chlamydia but is not the AU regimen for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the 14-day erythromycin course also reduces pneumonitis risk and infantile pyloric stenosis risk is similar with either macrolide. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg per day in four divided doses for a total of 14 days
options.rationale: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis at day 5 to 14 of life is treated with systemic oral erythromycin for 14 days because topical therapy alone does not prevent later chlamydial pneumonitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis typically presents from day 5 to day 14 of life with mucopurulent discharge in a well-appearing baby. Systemic erythromycin for 14 days is the standard Australian regimen because topical therapy alone does not eradicate organisms from the nasopharynx and predisposes to chlamydial pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks. Maternal partner notification, infant pyloric stenosis counselling and contact tracing are integral parts of management.
key_points: Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 14 days is first-line.
Topical therapy alone is inadequate because of nasopharyngeal colonisation.
Counsel parents about the small risk of infantile pyloric stenosis with macrolides under 6 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Sticky eyes in a 1-2 week old baby with mucopurulent discharge and a well-appearing infant should be treated as chlamydia until PCR proves otherwise; do not stop at topical chloramphenicol.

sources.label: ASHM Sexually transmissible infections in primary care manual

stem: You are the rural GP seeing a 2-year-old girl who pulled a cup of freshly boiled tea onto her chest 30 minutes ago. The mother removed wet clothing and ran cool tap water for 20 minutes before driving in. The child is alert and crying intermittently but consolable. Examination shows a moist erythematous area with intact blisters across the anterior chest and right anterolateral abdomen. There is no facial, perineal or circumferential involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 130, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, cap refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Estimated 6% total body surface area partial-thickness scald to anterior chest and right flank, blistered with serous fluid, very painful to touch, no charring, no inhalational injury signs
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated in the field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV crystalloid by Parkland formula at 4 mL/kg per percent TBSA over the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Parkland-style fluid resuscitation is started for paediatric burns of at least 10% TBSA; a 6% scald is below that threshold but still warrants oral hydration and transfer. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

options.text: Burst blisters with a sterile needle, dress with paraffin gauze, observe in primary care
options.rationale: Deroofing intact blisters in the community is not advised; it increases pain, infection risk and contamination before burns-service assessment. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

options.text: Cling film cover, intranasal fentanyl 1.5 micrograms/kg, urgent paediatric burns transfer
options.rationale: ANZBA criteria require referral to a designated paediatric burns service for any partial-thickness burn over 5% TBSA in a child under 16; the AU pre-transfer cover is loose cling film (not circumferential), with effective analgesia. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management 4th edition)

options.text: Continue cool running water for a further 30 minutes and reassess depth and area after
options.rationale: Cooling beyond 20 minutes after a scald is not beneficial and increases hypothermia risk, particularly in a young child with a 6% surface area injury. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

options.text: Silver sulfadiazine cream, non-adherent dressing, oral paracetamol, review the next day
options.rationale: Silver sulfadiazine should not be applied before assessment by the receiving burns service because it stains the wound and complicates depth assessment; outpatient management of a 6% burn in a 2-year-old is also outside primary-care scope. (Source: ANZBA Burn Patient Management)

explanation.summary: ANZBA criteria mandate referral of any partial-thickness burn over 5% total body surface area in a child to a designated paediatric burns service, and any burn involving the face, hands, feet, perineum, joints or circumferential limb burns regardless of size. Pre-transfer wound care is cling film loosely applied, not circumferential, with strong analgesia; topical antimicrobials should be delayed until the receiving service has assessed depth. Parkland-style IV resuscitation is reserved for burns 10% or greater.
key_points: Refer any partial-thickness burn over 5% TBSA in a child.
Cling film loosely applied is the pre-transfer dressing of choice.
Parkland-style IV resuscitation begins at 10% TBSA, not at 5%.
explanation.pearls: In a child with a scald, calculate the burn area using the child's palmar surface (~1% TBSA) and use ANZBA criteria; never apply silver sulfadiazine before the burns unit has assessed depth.

stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl with 24 hours of profuse non-bilious vomiting and four watery stools over 12 hours. She has refused fluids for the last three hours and is tearful but consolable. Mum has been trying small sips of oral rehydration solution without success. She has no chronic illness, no surgical scars, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Capillary refill is two seconds and mucous membranes are slightly dry.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4°C, HR 132, RR 26, BP 96/60, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild dryness of mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds, soft abdomen, no peritonism, normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ketones 1.6 mmol/L, BSL 4.4 mmol/L; UEC not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert IV line and commence a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes now
options.rationale: IV fluid bolus is reserved for moderate-to-severe dehydration with haemodynamic compromise or failed oral rehydration after ondansetron; this child has only mild dehydration. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Nasogastric rehydration at 100 mL/kg oral rehydration solution given over four hours
options.rationale: NG rehydration is a reasonable option if oral fluids continue to fail after ondansetron, but it is not the first step in a child not yet trialled on ondansetron. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Send stool for viral PCR and bacterial culture before any further symptomatic treatment
options.rationale: Stool studies do not change acute management of typical viral gastroenteritis and are reserved for bloody diarrhoea, prolonged or atypical illness, or immunocompromise. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Single oral ondansetron 2 mg wafer followed by 30 minutes of patient oral rehydration
options.rationale: A single oral ondansetron dose (2 mg for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for over 15 kg) reduces vomiting and the need for IV fluids in mild-moderate dehydration; oral rehydration is then attempted before escalating. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Oral loperamide 50 micrograms/kg with each loose stool and discharge home with review
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are contraindicated in paediatric gastroenteritis because of toxic megacolon and CNS toxicity risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Mild to moderately dehydrated children with acute gastroenteritis who fail to keep down oral rehydration benefit from a single oral wafer dose of ondansetron, which roughly halves the rate of IV fluid escalation. If oral rehydration after ondansetron fails, NG rehydration is the next step, then IV fluids. Antimotility agents are not used in children and stool studies are reserved for atypical illness.
key_points: Ondansetron 2 mg wafer for 8-15 kg, 4 mg for over 15 kg, single dose.
Trial oral rehydration solution after ondansetron before considering IV or NG.
Avoid loperamide in children.
explanation.pearls: A single ondansetron wafer plus 30 minutes of patient oral rehydration prevents IV cannulation in roughly half of vomiting children with mild dehydration.

stem: You are the GP seeing the parents of a 3-year-old boy who for the last 6 weeks has woken about 90 minutes after sleep onset screaming, sweating, with dilated pupils and inconsolability. The episodes last 5 to 10 minutes, after which he settles into sleep. The next morning he has no memory of the event. He is meeting all developmental milestones, attends day care without concerns, and family history is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal between episodes
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, growth on the 50th centile, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated based on history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure parents, sleep hygiene advice, scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the usual time
options.rationale: Night terrors are a non-REM parasomnia that peaks at 3 to 7 years; reassurance, predictable bedtime routine and pre-emptive scheduled awakening for clustered episodes is first-line management, and most children outgrow them by adolescence. (Source: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.text: Refer to child psychiatry for assessment of an underlying primary anxiety disorder driver
options.rationale: Night terrors are not a manifestation of anxiety in toddlers and do not predict psychopathology; psychiatry referral is not indicated based on this history. (Source: RACGP HANDI)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.text: Sleep-deprived EEG to exclude frontal lobe nocturnal seizures before any other treatment
options.rationale: EEG is reserved for atypical features such as stereotyped movements, daytime symptoms, very brief episodes or episodes later in the night; a typical 3-year-old parasomnia in the first third of the night does not need investigation. (Source: RACGP HANDI)
source_refs: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

options.text: Commence low-dose melatonin 1 mg at bedtime and review clinical effect in four weeks time
options.rationale: Melatonin has weak evidence for sleep-onset insomnia in children, not for parasomnias, and is not the first-line approach for night terrors. (Source: AAP Clinical Report: Melatonin)

options.text: Prescribe oral clonazepam 0.05 mg/kg at bedtime for four weeks with monthly clinic review
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are reserved for severe, injury-causing parasomnias in older children after non-drug strategies have failed; routine use in a 3-year-old is not appropriate. (Source: AASM practice parameters)

explanation.summary: Night terrors are a non-REM parasomnia that occur in the first third of the night, peak between 3 and 7 years of age, and resolve spontaneously. Children appear awake but are unresponsive, have no recall, and should not be roused during the event. Management is reassurance, sleep hygiene and, for clustered episodes, scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the usual time. Investigations and pharmacotherapy are reserved for atypical or injurious episodes.
key_points: Typical onset 90 minutes after sleep, no recall, full recovery between episodes.
First-line management is reassurance and scheduled awakening.
Investigate only if features atypical (daytime, stereotyped, later in night).
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the expected terror, for two weeks, breaks the non-REM cycle and resolves clusters in most preschoolers.

sources.label: RACGP HANDI: Scheduled awakening for sleep terrors

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with two days of dark cola-coloured urine and puffy eyes on waking. Two weeks ago he had impetigo on his legs that resolved with topical mupirocin. He has had a brief headache today but no seizures or visual changes. He is otherwise well, normotensive in the GP rooms (BP 105/65), and his urine dipstick shows 3+ blood and 1+ protein.

Bloods show normal urea and creatinine but low C3, normal C4, and a positive ASOT. There is no rash, no joint pain and no oliguria.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 118/78 in clinic on repeat
data_table.Examination: Mild periorbital oedema, no peripheral oedema, no rash, chest clear, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ blood 1+ protein, urine microscopy red cell casts, Cr 50 micromol/L, urea 5 mmol/L, C3 0.4 g/L (low), C4 0.2 g/L (normal), ASOT positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Arrange urgent renal biopsy to define the histological subtype before any other management
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for atypical features such as persistent low C3 beyond 3 months, normal complement, nephrotic-range proteinuria, or progressive renal impairment; this child has classic PSGN. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Admit for blood pressure monitoring with salt restriction and short-acting nifedipine if needed
options.rationale: Children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are at risk of hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary oedema during the first 1 to 2 weeks; inpatient observation with salt restriction and short-acting antihypertensives like nifedipine is first-line if hypertension develops. (Source: KHA-CARI Adolescent and adult glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Reassure and discharge home on no specific therapy with weekly GP review for the next six weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient follow-up alone fails to capture the peak risk of hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary oedema in the first 1 to 2 weeks; admission for monitoring is safer. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Commence high-dose prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for four weeks and outpatient nephrology review
options.rationale: PSGN is a self-limiting illness; corticosteroids are not part of standard management and are reserved for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or proven crescentic disease on biopsy. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Commence oral phenoxymethylpenicillin to eradicate residual streptococcal carriage at home
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not alter the course of established PSGN; if active streptococcal infection persists in a household it is treated for the index case, not as part of PSGN management. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection by 1 to 3 weeks and presents with macroscopic haematuria, mild hypertension and periorbital oedema. Diagnosis is supported by low C3 with normal C4, evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASOT or anti-DNase B), and red-cell casts on microscopy. Management is supportive with admission for BP and fluid monitoring during the first 1 to 2 weeks; complement and urine should normalise by 8 to 12 weeks.
key_points: Low C3, normal C4, red cell casts, positive ASOT or anti-DNase B suggest PSGN.
Inpatient monitoring focuses on BP and pulmonary congestion in the first 1-2 weeks.
Biopsy is reserved for atypical or progressive presentations.
explanation.pearls: If C3 remains low at 12 weeks after presumed PSGN, switch the diagnosis to MPGN or lupus nephritis and refer for biopsy.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar consulted about a 14-year-old girl with six weeks of daily holocephalic headache that is worse on waking and on coughing. She has had two episodes of transient visual obscurations. Her BMI is 32. She started oral isotretinoin two months ago for severe acne. There is no fever, neck stiffness, focal neurology or recent head injury. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema and visual fields show enlarged blind spots.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no focal neurology, fundoscopy bilateral disc swelling, no nuchal rigidity
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and MR venogram: no mass, no venous sinus thrombosis, slit-like ventricles; lumbar puncture opening pressure 32 cm H2O lateral decubitus; CSF cells nil, protein 0.3 g/L, glucose normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and add propranolol 20 mg twice daily for migraine prophylaxis
options.rationale: Continuing the precipitant perpetuates the disease and the picture is not migraine; propranolol does not treat IIH. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and ophthalmology review with perimetry in two weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids cause rebound intracranial hypertension on withdrawal and risk weight gain in an obese adolescent; they are not first-line. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

options.text: Cease isotretinoin, start acetazolamide 500 mg twice daily, refer for serial automated perimetry
options.rationale: Stopping the precipitant (isotretinoin, tetracyclines, vitamin A excess), commencing acetazolamide and arranging serial automated perimetry is the standard AU adolescent management of idiopathic intracranial hypertension; surgical CSF diversion is for failing vision or medication-refractory disease. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Child Neurology Society IIH guidance)

options.text: Arrange therapeutic lumbar punctures every 48 hours to maintain a low CSF opening pressure
options.rationale: Serial therapeutic LPs are not the long-term management; they are uncomfortable and risky and have been replaced by acetazolamide and weight loss. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

options.text: Urgent neurosurgical referral for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion before any other therapy
options.rationale: Shunting (lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal) and optic-nerve sheath fenestration are reserved for vision loss despite optimal medical therapy. (Source: ANZCNS: Paediatric IIH)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension in adolescents is associated with obesity and certain drugs including isotretinoin, tetracyclines, growth hormone and excess vitamin A. Diagnostic criteria include papilloedema, normal neuroimaging including venogram, and elevated CSF opening pressure with normal constituents. Management is precipitant removal, acetazolamide and weight loss, with surgical options reserved for vision loss despite medical therapy.
key_points: Cease the precipitant drug before starting other therapy.
Acetazolamide is first-line pharmacotherapy.
Serial perimetry monitors visual function; surgery if vision loss progresses.
explanation.pearls: Any teenager on isotretinoin or doxycycline with a new daily headache needs fundoscopy at the first visit; missing papilloedema risks irreversible optic atrophy.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 13-year-old boy with three months of recurrent right-sided unilateral epistaxis, often requiring ED visits with packing. The episodes have become more frequent and are accompanied by progressive right-sided nasal obstruction. He has no easy bruising, no menorrhagia equivalent in family, and his bleeding screen at the last admission was normal. On anterior rhinoscopy you can see a smooth, lobulated, vascular-looking mass behind the right middle turbinate. He has no other red-flag symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Smooth lobulated reddish-purple mass posterior to right middle turbinate, no neck lymphadenopathy, no cranial nerve deficits, no proptosis
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coagulation screen normal; nasal endoscopy as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: In-office biopsy through the nasal cavity for histological diagnosis prior to any imaging
options.rationale: Direct biopsy of suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma can cause life-threatening haemorrhage; imaging confirms the diagnosis before any tissue sampling. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

options.text: Repeat full blood count and coagulation screen in two weeks before further investigation
options.rationale: The history of unilateral nasal mass plus progressive obstruction points to a structural lesion, not coagulopathy; further haematology testing will not capture this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

options.text: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the nasopharynx and skull base before any tissue biopsy is taken
options.rationale: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent male is a vascular tumour that bleeds catastrophically on biopsy; contrast MRI defines extent and intracranial spread, followed by preoperative angiography and embolisation. (Source: RANZCO and AAOHNS combined head and neck guidance)

options.text: Plain X-ray of the post-nasal space to estimate soft-tissue density before any cross-section
options.rationale: Plain films are insensitive for soft-tissue tumours of the post-nasal space and cannot define skull-base involvement. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

options.text: Empirical course of intranasal mometasone for six weeks before reimaging or specialist review
options.rationale: Steroid sprays treat allergic rhinitis, not a vascular nasopharyngeal mass, and delay definitive diagnosis. (Source: RANZCO/AAOHNS)

explanation.summary: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour of adolescent males that presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. A vascular nasopharyngeal mass should never be biopsied without imaging because of the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Contrast MRI defines extent and skull-base spread, followed by angiography, preoperative embolisation and endoscopic resection.
key_points: Adolescent male + unilateral epistaxis + nasal obstruction = consider JNA.
Image before any biopsy.
Pre-op angiography and embolisation reduces operative blood loss.
explanation.pearls: Never biopsy a smooth red mass behind the middle turbinate in an adolescent male without imaging first; embolise within 24 to 48 hours of resection to minimise revascularisation.

stem: You are the paediatric haematology registrar reviewing an 8-month-old boy of Greek heritage referred for progressive pallor, hepatosplenomegaly and faltering growth from 4 months of age. Newborn screening detected an elevated HbF and follow-up parental studies showed both parents to be beta-thalassaemia trait carriers. Confirmatory testing in the baby has shown two beta zero mutations on molecular genetic testing. He is now feeding poorly, listless and has hepatosplenomegaly extending 4 cm below the costal margins.

data_table.Examination: Marked pallor, mild scleral icterus, hepatomegaly 4 cm, splenomegaly 4 cm, frontal bossing, growth dropping across centiles
data_table.Investigations: Hb 58 g/L, MCV 62 fL, reticulocytes 10%, HbF 90% on HPLC, HbA absent, ferritin 80 micrograms/L, LDH elevated, bilirubin 35 micromol/L (unconjugated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence hydroxyurea 15 mg/kg daily to induce fetal haemoglobin and avoid regular transfusion
options.rationale: Hydroxyurea is established in sickle cell disease and used in some intermediate thalassaemias; it is not first-line in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major. (Source: HSANZ)

options.text: Commence oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review in six weeks before considering any transfusion
options.rationale: Folate alone does not correct the underlying defect; in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, folate is an adjunct, not a definitive treatment, and this child is already symptomatic. (Source: HSANZ)

options.text: Defer transfusion until haemoglobin falls below 50 g/L to limit cumulative iron loading risk
options.rationale: Withholding transfusion until profound anaemia leads to extramedullary haematopoiesis, severe skeletal changes and growth failure; modern regimens transfuse at pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L. (Source: HSANZ)

options.text: Start regular transfusion targeting pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L; chelate when ferritin rises
options.rationale: Confirmed beta-thalassaemia major with symptomatic anaemia, organomegaly and faltering growth meets criteria to start regular transfusion at a pre-transfusion Hb of 95 to 105 g/L; chelation is started later when ferritin rises. (Source: HSANZ: Thalassaemia in Australia)

options.text: Refer immediately for splenectomy as the primary measure to reduce transfusion requirements
options.rationale: Splenectomy is deferred until age over 5 years and reserved for excessive transfusion requirements, given infection and thrombosis risks. (Source: HSANZ)

explanation.summary: Beta-thalassaemia major presents in the second half of the first year as fetal haemoglobin production wanes, with progressive anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and faltering growth. Once the diagnosis is confirmed and the child is symptomatic, regular transfusion at pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and supports growth. Iron chelation is added when ferritin exceeds about 1000 micrograms/L, typically after 10 to 20 transfusions.
key_points: Start regular transfusion when symptoms, growth failure or organomegaly emerge.
Pre-transfusion target Hb 95 to 105 g/L.
Iron chelation begins around 10-20 transfusions or ferritin over 1000.
explanation.pearls: Curative haematopoietic stem cell transplant from an HLA-matched sibling should be discussed early in beta-thalassaemia major to capture the best-outcome window before iron overload.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old girl whose teacher and parents have noticed dozens of episodes per day where she stops, stares, blinks rapidly and is unresponsive for 5 to 10 seconds, then resumes activity. She has had no convulsive seizures, no postictal phase, and her development is normal. Hyperventilation in clinic for 3 minutes triggers a typical event. She has no family history of epilepsy and no behavioural concerns. The EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave with normal background.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, normal development
data_table.Investigations: EEG: 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave provoked by hyperventilation, normal awake and sleep background; MRI brain not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication?

options.text: Carbamazepine titrated to 15 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures and is contraindicated in idiopathic generalised epilepsies. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Lamotrigine titrated slowly over six weeks to 5 mg/kg per day as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is third-line for absence epilepsy; slow titration and lower response rates make it inferior to ethosuximide or valproate as initial therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sodium valproate titrated to 20 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Valproate is effective in childhood absence epilepsy but is second-line because of greater attentional side-effects in the CAE trial and the teratogenic risk that becomes relevant later in adolescence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Levetiracetam titrated to 40 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is not licensed for absence epilepsy in monotherapy and has lower efficacy than ethosuximide or valproate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide titrated to 15 to 40 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Ethosuximide is first-line for typical childhood absence epilepsy because it has superior efficacy and a better cognitive profile than valproate in childhood absence epilepsy (CAE) head-to-head trials. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology and Cochrane review of CAE)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy is an idiopathic generalised epilepsy that begins between 4 and 10 years with multiple daily brief unresponsive episodes triggered by hyperventilation, and a characteristic 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave EEG. Ethosuximide is the AU first-line monotherapy. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and tiagabine should be avoided because they can worsen absences. Most children remit before puberty.
key_points: Ethosuximide first-line, valproate second-line.
Avoid carbamazepine (worsens absences).
Hyperventilation provocation in clinic supports diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: If a child with apparent CAE has additional myoclonic jerks or GTCS, suspect juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and switch from ethosuximide to valproate or lamotrigine.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 4-year-old boy with three weeks of persistent night pain in both legs, increasing pallor and easy bruising. His mother brought him today because he is now refusing to walk in the mornings, and she noticed petechiae on his shins. He has had two low-grade fevers over the last week. There is no recent trauma, no joint swelling and no rash beyond the petechiae. He is otherwise alert and engages with you in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4°C, HR 130, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 95/58
data_table.Examination: Pallor, scattered petechiae on shins, palpable cervical and inguinal lymph nodes 1.5 cm, hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin, no joint swelling, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: Hb 70 g/L, WCC 24 x10^9/L with 70% blasts on film, platelets 18 x10^9/L, neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, LDH 1800 U/L, urate 0.55 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for suspected septic arthritis of the lower limbs before further workup
options.rationale: There is no joint swelling, warmth or limp localisation; the bicompartmental nightly pain in a child with pancytopenia points to marrow infiltration, not infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Commence empirical oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily and outpatient haematology in two weeks
options.rationale: Empirical steroids before tissue diagnosis can mask the marrow picture and delay accurate classification of the leukaemia subtype. (Source: eviQ)

options.text: Request outpatient FBC and bone biochemistry in one week with GP review of the results
options.rationale: The blood film already shows blasts; deferring action by a week risks tumour lysis, severe sepsis with neutropenia, or bleeding complications. (Source: eviQ)

options.text: Same-day paediatric oncology contact and direct transfer for tumour-lysis prophylaxis and marrow
options.rationale: Pancytopenia, peripheral blasts, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy and biochemical evidence of high cell turnover suggest acute leukaemia; immediate transfer for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (hyperhydration, allopurinol or rasburicase) and bone marrow assessment is mandatory. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL induction)

options.text: Commence oral ibuprofen for presumed growing pains and arrange GP review in one week
options.rationale: Night pain that wakes the child, with pallor, petechiae and hepatomegaly, is incompatible with benign growing pains and ibuprofen could worsen bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia commonly presents with bone pain, pallor, petechiae or bruising, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, and recurrent low-grade fevers. Pancytopenia with circulating blasts requires same-day discussion with paediatric oncology and admission for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (hyperhydration, urate-lowering therapy) and bone marrow biopsy. Empirical steroids before diagnosis should be avoided.
key_points: Night bone pain + pallor + petechiae = exclude leukaemia.
Same-day paediatric oncology contact; tumour-lysis prophylaxis is the first inpatient task.
Avoid empirical steroids before tissue diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Use the FBC, film and LDH to triage urgency: any child with night bone pain plus a circulating blast count needs same-day oncology contact, not a 'review in a week' plan.

stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to see a 24-hour-old term boy whose mother had an antenatal anomaly scan showing bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios in the third trimester. He has so far passed only a few drops of urine; the midwife reports a palpable distended bladder. He has mild respiratory distress on room air. There is no antenatal MRI; he was delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery in a regional centre with a paediatric service and access to telehealth subspecialty advice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 160, RR 64, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Examination: Distended bladder palpable to umbilicus, weak urinary stream when bladder pressed, no abdominal masses, no respiratory crackles
data_table.Investigations: Bedside bladder US confirms gross bladder distension and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis; Cr 110 micromol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, urine output last 12 h 0.5 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Pass a 6 Fr feeding tube to drain the bladder and arrange urgent paediatric urology transfer
options.rationale: Initial management of suspected posterior urethral valves is bladder drainage with a small feeding-tube catheter (Foleys may traumatise the prostatic urethra) followed by transfer for micturating cystourethrogram and cystoscopic valve ablation. (Source: APSA and ANZUNS paediatric urology guidance)

options.text: Defer any intervention and recheck serum creatinine and bladder volume in 24 hours time
options.rationale: Persistent obstruction worsens AKI, electrolyte derangement and bladder damage; drainage is required within hours. (Source: ANZUNS)

options.text: Commence IV furosemide 1 mg/kg now to maximise urine output before any catheter placement
options.rationale: Furosemide will not bypass a mechanical obstruction and can precipitate electrolyte derangement; the lesion is anatomical. (Source: ANZUNS)

options.text: Insert a 10 Fr Foley balloon catheter to maintain continuous drainage during transport in retrieval
options.rationale: A 10 Fr Foley balloon catheter can sit in the prostatic urethra and traumatise the valves; a fine feeding tube is preferred until cystoscopic assessment. (Source: ANZUNS)

options.text: Perform a single suprapubic aspiration only and discharge to outpatient urology follow up
options.rationale: A single aspiration does not provide ongoing drainage; an infant with PUV needs continuous bladder decompression and definitive surgical valve ablation. (Source: ANZUNS)

explanation.summary: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest cause of severe obstructive uropathy in newborn boys and typically present with antenatal hydronephrosis, oligohydramnios and a distended bladder with weak stream postnatally. Initial management is bladder drainage with a small feeding-tube catheter (Foley balloons can traumatise the prostatic urethra), followed by paediatric urology transfer for MCUG and cystoscopic ablation. Renal function should be monitored as nephrogenic damage may already be established.
key_points: Fine feeding-tube catheter for initial drainage, not a Foley.
Definitive treatment is cystoscopic valve ablation.
Renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia and bladder dysfunction may persist long-term.
explanation.pearls: Antenatal bilateral hydronephrosis + oligohydramnios + male fetus = plan for postnatal PUV; have a 6 Fr feeding tube ready at birth and paediatric urology on standby.

stem: You are the GP responding to a code-blue call at a community health centre. A 9-month-old girl was being fed grated apple and is now in obvious respiratory distress with an ineffective weak cough, marked stridor and central cyanosis. She has been unable to vocalise for 20 seconds. A nurse is supporting her in a head-down prone position on the resuscitator's forearm. She has no known allergies and is fully immunised. There are no signs of trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70 bpm, falling, SpO2 70%, RR ineffective, central cyanosis
data_table.Examination: Unable to cry or cough, marked indrawing, decreased air entry bilaterally, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate manoeuvre?

options.text: Perform a finger sweep across the oropharynx to remove any directly visualised foreign body
options.rationale: Blind finger sweeps may push the foreign body further into the airway; only remove a foreign body that you can directly visualise. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Commence chest compressions at the 30:2 ratio immediately because the heart rate is below 80
options.rationale: While bradycardia in choking is ominous, the immediate priority remains relief of the airway obstruction with back blows then chest thrusts; CPR commences only if the infant becomes unresponsive. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Perform five abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) just above the umbilicus in seated infant
options.rationale: Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year because they risk visceral and hepatic injury; chest thrusts are used instead after back blows. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Deliver up to five firm back blows between the scapulae in a head-down prone position
options.rationale: In an infant under 1 year with ineffective cough and obstruction, ANZCOR guidance is to deliver up to five back blows in a head-down prone position followed by up to five chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are contraindicated in infants. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

options.text: Administer 100% oxygen via tight-fitting non-rebreather mask and observe for spontaneous relief
options.rationale: Oxygen cannot reach the alveoli through a fully obstructed airway; mechanical relief of the obstruction is the priority. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4)

explanation.summary: ANZCOR Guideline 4 directs that an infant under 1 year with ineffective cough and severe airway obstruction receives up to five back blows in a head-down prone position, followed by up to five chest thrusts if obstruction persists. Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year. If the infant becomes unresponsive, commence infant CPR. Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps is the next step if available.
key_points: Back blows then chest thrusts in infants under 1 year.
Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated under 1 year.
Avoid blind finger sweeps.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia precedes arrest in airway obstruction; treat the obstruction first - oxygen will not bypass a complete mechanical block.

stem: You are the neonatology fellow planning autumn discharge for an ex-29-week preterm girl, now 6 months corrected age and 4.8 kg, with established bronchopulmonary dysplasia requiring 0.25 L/min home oxygen at discharge. Her family lives in regional Victoria. RSV season is about to start in 4 weeks. Her older brother attends day care and the family includes a 2-year-old cousin sharing the household. Her mother asks what can be done to reduce her risk of severe bronchiolitis this season.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7°C, HR 130, RR 48 on 0.25 L/min via nasal prongs, SpO2 95%
data_table.Examination: Weight 4.8 kg (3rd centile), mild intercostal recession, scattered fine inspiratory crackles, no acute respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Maternal antenatal RSV vaccination was not given (vaccine eligibility had not been reached before delivery), most recent chest X-ray: chronic interstitial changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prevention strategy?

options.text: Commence oral montelukast 4 mg nightly to reduce post-bronchiolitis wheeze across the season
options.rationale: Montelukast is not an RSV prophylactic and does not prevent severe RSV bronchiolitis admission. (Source: GINA Australia and Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Administer monthly intramuscular palivizumab for the duration of the local RSV season
options.rationale: Palivizumab is being replaced by single-dose nirsevimab in Australian jurisdictions because nirsevimab provides season-long protection in one dose. (Source: AIH)

options.text: Single weight-based intramuscular nirsevimab dose before the start of the RSV season
options.rationale: AU NIRP (immunisation handbook) recommends single-dose nirsevimab for high-risk infants under 2 years with chronic lung disease of prematurity or significant CHD entering their first or second RSV season, replacing monthly palivizumab in most jurisdictions. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook NIRP)

options.text: Standard hygiene and exposure-avoidance advice without any specific RSV pharmacoprophylaxis
options.rationale: Behavioural measures alone are insufficient in an infant with BPD on home oxygen; targeted monoclonal-antibody prophylaxis substantially reduces hospital admission. (Source: AIH)

options.text: Vaccinate the infant with the maternal recombinant RSV vaccine RSVpreF intramuscular dose
options.rationale: RSVpreF is a maternal vaccine given antenatally; it is not licensed for direct infant vaccination. (Source: AIH)

explanation.summary: Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody recommended in Australia for infants entering their first RSV season and for high-risk infants (chronic lung disease of prematurity, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease) entering their second RSV season. A single weight-based IM dose covers the entire season, replacing monthly palivizumab where funded. Maternal vaccination with RSVpreF is the alternative pathway for healthy term babies whose mothers were eligible antenatally.
key_points: Single-dose nirsevimab covers the whole RSV season.
Eligible: first season for all infants, second season for high-risk infants.
Maternal RSVpreF in pregnancy is an alternative for healthy term infants.
explanation.pearls: If maternal RSVpreF was given in pregnancy at 28-36 weeks, the term infant does not also need nirsevimab; if not, a single nirsevimab dose is the AU default.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in toddler with excessive cow milk intake
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose mother reports he tires easily on walks and is increasingly pale. He drinks about 750 mL of full-cream cow milk a day from a bottle and refuses meat, eggs and fortified cereal. He was exclusively breastfed until 10 months. Vaccinations are up to date. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no overt bleeding, no jaundice and no chronic illness. The blood film shows microcytic hypochromic red cells with anisocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 116, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, weight on 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival and palmar pallor; cardiovascular and abdominal examination otherwise normal; no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 64 fL, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP 2 mg/L, reticulocytes low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Trial a multivitamin syrup for six weeks before considering targeted iron treatment
options.rationale: Multivitamin syrups contain too little elemental iron to correct established deficiency anaemia; a therapeutic iron dose is needed alongside dietary change. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

options.text: Refer to paediatric haematology for an inpatient intravenous iron infusion
options.rationale: IV iron is reserved for failure of oral therapy, malabsorption or intolerance; uncomplicated nutritional deficiency responds to oral iron and dietary modification. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

options.text: Oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily and restrict cow milk to under 500 mL daily
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron for at least 3 months in nutritional iron deficiency, plus cow milk volume below 500 mL to reduce iron antagonism. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

options.text: Send haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia before commencing treatment
options.rationale: The very low ferritin and dietary history give an unambiguous nutritional diagnosis; electrophoresis is reserved if the anaemia fails to respond to iron replacement. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

options.text: Increase dietary iron alone and recheck the full blood count in eight weeks
options.rationale: Diet alone is too slow to correct symptomatic anaemia with Hb 84 g/L; oral iron replacement is required in addition to dietary advice. (Source: RCH CPG Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Excessive cow milk intake above 500 mL per day is a leading cause of toddler iron deficiency in Australia because milk displaces iron-rich foods and reduces non-haem iron absorption. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline recommends 3 mg/kg/day of elemental iron orally for at least 3 months, then a further 3 months once Hb normalises to replenish stores. A FBC and ferritin check at 4 to 6 weeks documents response. Dietary modification including red meat, iron-fortified cereals and vitamin C with meals is essential alongside supplementation.
key_points: Cow milk above 500 mL daily is a key dietary risk factor.
Elemental iron dose is 3 mg/kg once daily for three months.
Recheck FBC and ferritin at four to six weeks for response.
IV iron is reserved for oral failure, intolerance or malabsorption.
explanation.pearls: Expect a reticulocyte rise within 5 to 7 days and a Hb rise of about 10 g/L per month on oral iron; failure to respond after 4 weeks should prompt review of adherence, ongoing milk excess, or alternative diagnoses such as coeliac disease.

subtopic_detail: Atopic eczema stepped care in a toddler
stem: You are the GP seeing a 2-year-old girl with a 6-week history of dry itchy red flexural rashes at the antecubital and popliteal fossae, worse overnight and disturbing sleep. Her mother applies sorbolene cream twice a day. She has no infection signs and no oozing. Family history includes parental hay fever. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Vaccinations are up to date. There is no relevant medication history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Lichenified erythematous plaques at flexures with excoriations; no honey-crust, no vesicles, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Continue sorbolene only and review again in eight weeks without active treatment
options.rationale: Established lichenified eczema disturbing sleep needs active anti-inflammatory therapy; emollients alone are inadequate at this stage of the disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone 1% to the flexures twice daily plus a thick emollient liberally
options.rationale: Mild topical corticosteroid plus generous emollient is the stepped-care first-line for paediatric flexural atopic eczema, escalating potency if uncontrolled after a defined trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for 7 days alongside the existing sorbolene moisturiser
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for routine paediatric eczema due to rebound flare and adverse effects; topical therapy should be optimised first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

options.text: Start a daily non-sedating antihistamine without any change to topical treatment
options.rationale: Non-sedating antihistamines do not reduce eczema inflammation; the itch in eczema is histamine-independent and responds to topical steroid plus emollient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

options.text: Refer urgently to dermatology for ciclosporin without a trial of topical steroid first
options.rationale: Systemic immunomodulators are reserved for severe disease unresponsive to optimised topical therapy; a stepwise trial must be completed first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends a stepped-care approach to paediatric atopic eczema starting with generous emollient use plus a topical corticosteroid matched to severity and site. Mild potency steroids such as hydrocortisone 1% are appropriate for the face and flexures of young children, with stronger steroids reserved for thicker plaques or recalcitrant disease. A finger-tip unit guide helps families dose correctly. Antibiotic therapy is reserved for clinical infection rather than colonisation alone.
key_points: Use mild topical steroid for flexural toddler eczema.
Emollients applied liberally several times per day are essential.
Reserve systemic therapy for failure of optimised topical care.
Treat infected eczema with cefalexin or flucloxacillin if oozing or honey-crusted.
explanation.pearls: A single finger-tip unit (about 0.5 g) treats an area equal to two adult palms; under-dosing is the commonest reason for apparent topical steroid failure in toddler eczema.

subtopic_detail: Catch-up schedule for a partially vaccinated arrival
stem: You are the GP seeing a 14-month-old boy newly arrived from overseas. His written records confirm three doses of DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB at 2, 4 and 6 months, but no further immunisations. He is well, has no immunocompromise and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Mother asks what vaccines he should receive today to bring him up to schedule. Routine 12-month and 18-month doses are otherwise outstanding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5 °C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well thriving toddler; growth on 50th centile; cardiovascular and respiratory unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Not required prior to catch-up immunisation

lead_in: Which combination of vaccines should be administered today?

options.text: DTPa-IPV booster only today and defer all other vaccines to the next scheduled visit
options.rationale: Catch-up should bring multiple antigens up to schedule at one visit; deferring leaves the child unprotected against MMR, MenACWY and pneumococcal disease. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Defer immunisation until serology confirms current measles and varicella immune status
options.rationale: Catch-up schedules do not require pre-vaccination serology; serology delays protection and is not part of routine Australian practice. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine and varicella vaccine only today and review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Hepatitis A is not on the universal schedule for non-Aboriginal children; varicella alone misses MMR, meningococcal and pneumococcal protection that are now due. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: MMR plus meningococcal ACWY plus pneumococcal 13-valent at this visit using catch-up
options.rationale: These are the routine 12-month doses on the Australian schedule and are due now; the 18-month doses are given separately at the next planned visit. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Restart the schedule from infancy doses including DTPa, polio and hepatitis B today
options.rationale: Documented doses received overseas are accepted by the Australian Immunisation Handbook; restarting is unnecessary and causes vaccine wastage and overdosing. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: The Australian Immunisation Handbook provides catch-up schedules that respect previously documented doses while bringing children rapidly up to age-appropriate cover. At 12 months MMR, meningococcal ACWY and 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate are due, and 18-month doses include MMRV, DTPa and Hib. Serology before catch-up is not required. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, and those with medical risk conditions, receive additional doses such as hepatitis A and pneumococcal polysaccharide where indicated.
key_points: Accept documented overseas doses; do not restart the schedule.
At 12 months give MMR, MenACWY and PCV13.
Serology is not required prior to catch-up immunisation.
Use the Immunise Australia online catch-up calculator for complex histories.
explanation.pearls: All live parenteral vaccines including MMR, varicella and MMRV can be co-administered on the same day; if not given together they must be separated by at least 4 weeks to avoid blunting the immune response.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of ITP from HSP in school-age child with petechiae
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 5-year-old girl with two days of widespread bruising and mucosal bleeding from the gums. She had a viral upper respiratory illness two weeks ago. She has no fever, no joint swelling, no abdominal pain and no rash on the buttocks or legs. Examination shows scattered petechiae across the trunk and limbs with wet purpura on the buccal mucosa. Liver and spleen are not palpable. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 100/64
data_table.Examination: Wet purpura on buccal mucosa, scattered petechiae trunk and limbs; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, WCC 7.4, platelets 8 x10^9/L, blood film normal red and white cells, large platelets

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit and treat with intravenous immunoglobulin plus close inpatient bleeding observation
