options.rationale: Wet mucosal purpura with platelets under 10 x10^9/L is severe ITP with a real intracranial bleed risk; IVIG rapidly raises the platelet count and admission is mandatory. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

options.text: Discharge home with planned platelet recheck in one week and oral tranexamic acid
options.rationale: Wet purpura is a marker of severe bleeding risk; outpatient management is not appropriate until the platelet count has been raised and bleeding controlled. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day and review again in clinic in seven days
options.rationale: Steroids are an alternative but slower-acting therapy and bone marrow aspirate is needed before high-dose steroid to exclude leukaemia in atypical presentations. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

options.text: Order an urgent bone marrow aspirate prior to starting any specific drug therapy
options.rationale: Bone marrow examination is not required in a classic well child with isolated thrombocytopenia, normal blood film and no atypical features; it is reserved for atypical cases. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

options.text: Transfuse one adult unit of platelets immediately and admit for routine observation only
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding only because autoantibodies destroy transfused platelets rapidly; IVIG or steroid is the standard therapy. (Source: RCH CPG ITP)

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric ITP typically presents 1 to 4 weeks after a viral illness with isolated thrombocytopenia and an otherwise well child. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline reserves active therapy for wet purpura, severe mucosal bleeding or planned procedures; IVIG raises platelets within 24 to 48 hours. Bone marrow examination is needed only when features are atypical, when steroid is being considered without prior marrow review, or when the response is poor. HSP is excluded clinically by the absence of palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain.
key_points: Wet purpura plus platelets under 10 indicates severe ITP needing IVIG.
Platelet transfusion is reserved for catastrophic bleeding only.
Bone marrow is not required for classic acute paediatric ITP.
HSP is distinguished by palpable purpura on lower limbs and buttocks.
explanation.pearls: IVIG 0.8 g/kg as a single dose typically raises platelets above 50 x10^9/L within 48 hours; if no rise occurs by day 3, recheck the diagnosis with a bone marrow aspirate before further immunosuppression.

subtopic_detail: Undescended testis referral timing in a 9-month-old
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 9-month-old boy at his routine check. His mother says the right testis has never been visible in the scrotum. On examination, the right testis is palpable high in the inguinal canal and cannot be manipulated into the scrotum. The left testis is normally positioned. He was born at term and is otherwise well, with no abnormal genitalia, no hernia and no syndromic features. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right testis high in inguinal canal, non-retractable; left testis normal; phallus normal; no inguinal hernia
data_table.Investigations: Imaging not indicated; karyotype not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure parents and review the testicular position again at his 24-month visit
options.rationale: Spontaneous descent after 6 months is uncommon and delayed surgery worsens fertility and increases later malignancy risk; review at 24 months is too late. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery so that orchidopexy can be planned before 18 months of age
options.rationale: Persistent undescended testis after 6 months warrants surgical referral so that orchidopexy is performed before 18 months to preserve spermatogenesis and reduce malignancy risk. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

options.text: Arrange a scrotal and inguinal ultrasound to confirm the position prior to any referral
options.rationale: Imaging does not change management for a palpable testis and adds delay; surgical referral is based on clinical findings alone. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

options.text: Commence intramuscular human chorionic gonadotropin to encourage descent before surgery
options.rationale: Hormonal induction with hCG is not part of standard Australian care because of poor efficacy and adverse effects; surgical orchidopexy is the recommended approach. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

options.text: Send karyotype and androgen receptor studies before deciding on any specific surgery
options.rationale: Endocrine and genetic studies are reserved for bilateral non-palpable testes or ambiguous genitalia, not a single palpable undescended testis with normal phallus. (Source: RCH CPG Undescended testis)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends orchidopexy between 6 and 18 months for an undescended testis because surgery before 18 months improves long-term fertility and reduces malignancy risk. Spontaneous descent is uncommon after 6 months, so referral at the 6 to 12-month check should not be delayed. Imaging adds no value for a palpable testis. Endocrine workup is reserved for bilateral non-palpable testes or any sign of disorders of sex development.
key_points: Refer to paediatric surgery once persistence is clear after 6 months.
Operate before 18 months to preserve fertility.
Imaging does not change management for a palpable testis.
Bilateral non-palpable testes warrant endocrine and genetic evaluation.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral non-palpable testes in a newborn are a disorder-of-sex-development emergency until proven otherwise; obtain electrolytes, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and karyotype before assigning sex of rearing.

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease recognition and IVIG timing
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy with 6 days of high fevers above 39 °C unresponsive to paracetamol. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, dry cracked lips and a single tender enlarged cervical lymph node. A polymorphous truncal rash appeared yesterday. He has no peripheral oedema and no peeling. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and he is fully immunised. Throat swab and blood cultures are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 156, RR 32, SpO2 98% room air, BP 96/58
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, anterior cervical node 1.5 cm tender, polymorphous trunk rash; no peripheral oedema or peeling
data_table.Investigations: CRP 110 mg/L, ESR 80 mm/h, platelets 540 x10^9/L, ALT 78, albumin 28 g/L, urine WCC 30 x10^6/L sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and review in 48 hours if the fever persists today
options.rationale: Delayed treatment beyond day 10 of illness markedly increases coronary aneurysm rate; IVIG must be given promptly when the criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Treat with intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
options.rationale: Scalded skin syndrome presents with positive Nikolsky sign and fragile skin, not non-purulent conjunctivitis, cervical adenopathy and oral changes; the picture fits Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial cervical lymphadenitis and observe
options.rationale: Isolated bacterial adenitis does not produce the multisystem pattern of conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash and sterile pyuria; antibiotics alone will not prevent coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin and arrange echocardiogram
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when fever above 5 days plus supportive features and elevated inflammatory markers are present; IVIG within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Start high-dose prednisolone first-line and defer IVIG until clinical response is reviewed
options.rationale: First-line therapy in Australia is IVIG plus aspirin; corticosteroids are added for high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases, not as monotherapy. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed when at least 5 days of fever and 2 to 3 classic features are accompanied by supportive laboratory findings such as raised CRP and ESR, thrombocytosis, anaemia, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia or sterile pyuria. Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk from about 25 percent to under 5 percent if given before day 10 of illness. An echocardiogram should be performed at diagnosis and again at 6 to 8 weeks. Steroids are reserved for high-risk or treatment-resistant disease.
key_points: Treat suspected incomplete Kawasaki with IVIG plus aspirin promptly.
Aim to treat before day 10 of fever to minimise coronary risk.
Repeat echocardiogram at 6 to 8 weeks regardless of initial findings.
Sterile pyuria is a useful supportive feature in incomplete cases.
explanation.pearls: Persistent fever 36 hours after the first IVIG dose defines IVIG resistance and warrants a second IVIG infusion plus consideration of methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg or infliximab in conjunction with paediatric cardiology.

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent cyanotic neonatal cardiac lesion presentation
stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to the postnatal ward at hour 36 of life. A term male is increasingly cyanosed and lethargic. He passed initial pulse oximetry screening. He now has central cyanosis, weak pulses in all four limbs and a hyperdynamic precordium without murmur. Pre-ductal SpO2 is 65% and post-ductal SpO2 is 64% in air, unchanged on 100% oxygen for 10 minutes. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.18, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, base excess -12, normal glucose.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 °C, HR 178, RR 70, SpO2 65% pre-ductal, 64% post-ductal, BP 56/34 mean 41
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, weak pulses all four limbs, no murmur, hepatomegaly 2 cm; no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal QRS axis; CXR mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, oligaemic lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 10 nanograms/kg/min and call cardiology
options.rationale: Failed hyperoxia with cyanosis in the first 48 hours indicates a duct-dependent cyanotic lesion; prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency until definitive diagnosis and surgery. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

options.text: Increase FiO2 to 100% by nasal high flow and admit to special care nursery for monitoring
options.rationale: Persistent cyanosis on 100% FiO2 over 10 minutes is the failed hyperoxia test diagnostic of cyanotic congenital heart disease; oxygen alone will not address the lesion. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

options.text: Treat for presumed early-onset sepsis with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin only
options.rationale: Sepsis can mimic this presentation but failed hyperoxia and metabolic acidosis with hepatomegaly suggest a duct-dependent lesion that needs immediate prostaglandin therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the lactic acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate does not treat the underlying ductal-dependent circulation; restoring ductal patency with prostaglandin corrects perfusion and resolves acidosis. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

options.text: Commence dobutamine 5 micrograms/kg/min as inotropic support before any other measure
options.rationale: Inotropes do not restore ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow and may worsen the shunt; prostaglandin E1 is the priority intervention with cardiology input. (Source: RCH CPG Cyanotic neonate)

explanation.summary: A neonate with cyanosis and failed hyperoxia in the first 48 hours of life has duct-dependent congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Prostaglandin E1 reopens or maintains the ductus arteriosus and restores pulmonary or systemic blood flow until echocardiography defines anatomy and surgical or catheter intervention is arranged. Side effects to anticipate during prostaglandin therapy include apnoea, hypotension and fever. Septic workup and broad spectrum antibiotics may be added because sepsis can mimic duct-dependent collapse.
key_points: Failed hyperoxia means SpO2 stays under 85% on 100% oxygen.
Start prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanograms/kg/min and titrate.
Anticipate apnoea, hypotension and fever as side effects.
Echocardiography defines the lesion and guides intervention.
explanation.pearls: Prostaglandin E1 causes apnoea in about 10 to 15 percent of neonates; have a clinician at the bedside able to intubate before starting infusion, particularly during interhospital retrieval.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a metropolitan tertiary centre admitting a 13-year-old girl with severe restrictive eating disorder who has not eaten for 10 days and has lost 14 kg over 6 months. She is alert but profoundly fatigued. She weighs 32 kg with a height of 158 cm (BMI 12.8 kg/m2). She has bradycardia and hypothermia. The dietitian asks for your prescription before commencing feeding via nasogastric tube.

The team plans to use a polymeric formula at 20 kcal/kg/day initially. Her admission electrolytes are at the lower end of normal but no oral or intravenous supplementation has yet been given.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, Temp 35.4 degrees C, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Severe wasting, lanugo, cold peripheries, normal capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.84 mmol/L, magnesium 0.72 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, ALT 92 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention before commencing enteral feeds?

options.text: Withhold all feeds for 48 hours while correcting electrolytes intravenously and observing on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Prolonged starvation worsens cardiac and metabolic instability. Cautious feeding with concurrent prophylaxis is preferred over further fasting, which increases mortality in this cohort. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous thiamine 100 mg followed by oral phosphate and magnesium supplementation, then start feeds
options.rationale: In severe malnutrition with prolonged starvation, prophylactic thiamine before any carbohydrate load prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, and pre-emptive electrolyte replacement covers the anticipated refeeding shifts even when baseline levels are within normal range. Australian eating disorder guidelines recommend this prophylactic bundle for high-risk refeeding before commencing nutrition. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Commence enteral feeds at 40 kcal/kg/day immediately to address weight loss and reassess electrolytes daily
options.rationale: Starting at 40 kcal/kg/day in a severely malnourished adolescent without prophylaxis precipitates classical refeeding syndrome with phosphate, magnesium, and potassium crashes. Australian guidelines advise starting low and advancing cautiously with prophylactic micronutrients. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Give a single intravenous bolus of dextrose 10% 5 mL/kg to raise glucose before nasogastric feeding commences
options.rationale: A rapid carbohydrate load in a thiamine-deplete malnourished patient is a recognised trigger for both Wernicke encephalopathy and acute refeeding syndrome. Thiamine and electrolyte cover must precede any carbohydrate. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous parenteral nutrition rather than enteral feeds to reduce the refeeding metabolic shift
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition does not lower refeeding risk and carries additional line and metabolic complications. Cautious enteral nutrition with prophylactic thiamine and electrolytes is the Australian standard. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Refeeding Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises from the abrupt intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium driven by insulin release when carbohydrate is reintroduced after prolonged starvation. Adolescents with severe restrictive eating disorders and weight loss exceeding 15% are at highest risk. Prophylaxis with thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily and replacement of phosphate, magnesium, and potassium before and during early feeding prevents the cardiac, neurological, and respiratory complications. Initial feed volume is started low (around 20 kcal/kg/day) and titrated up over 7 to 10 days with daily electrolyte checks.
key_points: Refeeding risk highest with weight loss above 15%, prolonged starvation, or BMI under 14
Thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily before any carbohydrate load prevents Wernicke encephalopathy
Phosphate, magnesium, and potassium replaced prophylactically even when baseline levels appear normal
Initial feed at around 20 kcal/kg/day advancing over 7 to 10 days with daily electrolytes
explanation.pearls: Thiamine must precede any glucose or feed in severe malnutrition: a single intravenous bolus of dextrose into a thiamine-deplete adolescent can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours.

sources.label: NICE NG69 - Eating Disorders Recognition and Treatment

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called urgently to the special care nursery. A 3-day-old term male infant has become progressively lethargic with poor feeding over 18 hours and now has tachypnoea without respiratory distress and intermittent posturing. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He fed eagerly for the first 36 hours then deteriorated. Birth weight was 3380 g. A septic screen has been sent and cultures are pending. The mother had a sister who died in the neonatal period of unknown cause.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 78, Temp 36.6 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, intermittent extensor posturing, mild hepatomegaly, anterior fontanelle full
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.49, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, ammonia 420 micromol/L, ALT 38 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Stop protein-containing feeds, commence intravenous dextrose with intralipid, and arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Plasma ammonia above 400 micromol/L in a neonate with encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency consistent with a urea cycle disorder or organic acidaemia, with respiratory alkalosis driven by central ammonia toxicity. Immediate protein withdrawal, anabolic dextrose support, and dialysis are required to halt neurotoxicity. Family history of neonatal death increases the prior probability of an inborn error. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

options.text: Increase enteral feeds with a high-protein neonatal formula to support growth and metabolic recovery
options.rationale: Protein loading in a neonate with hyperammonaemia accelerates ammonia generation and worsens encephalopathy. Protein must be withdrawn for 24 to 48 hours while ammonia falls. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir for presumed neonatal herpes encephalitis and await CSF results
options.rationale: Aciclovir is appropriate empirically when HSV encephalitis is suspected, but the combination of normal CRP, profound hyperammonaemia, respiratory alkalosis, and family history strongly indicates an inborn error. Treatment of the metabolic emergency cannot be deferred for an HSV workup. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct acidosis and continue current feeds
options.rationale: The blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis - bicarbonate is contraindicated and worsens the alkalaemia. The therapeutic priority is ammonia removal and anabolic support. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

options.text: Commence phenobarbitone for presumed neonatal seizures and observe in the nursery overnight
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone treats clinical seizures but does not address the underlying hyperammonaemia, which is the primary driver of neurological injury. Without ammonia clearance, irreversible neurotoxicity progresses within hours. (Source: HGSA - Metabolic Emergency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Neonatal hyperammonaemia is a metabolic emergency typically due to urea cycle disorders or organic acidaemias. The classical pattern is a previously well term neonate who deteriorates 24 to 72 hours after feeding establishes, with lethargy, tachypnoea, and respiratory alkalosis from central ammonia stimulation. Plasma ammonia above 200 micromol/L in a sick neonate prompts urgent metabolic workup and treatment, and above 400 micromol/L triggers preparation for renal replacement therapy. The therapeutic bundle is stop protein, give anabolic dextrose with intralipid, give scavenger drugs (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate) where available, and dialyse.
key_points: Urea cycle disorders present with respiratory alkalosis; organic acidaemias with metabolic acidosis and anion gap
Ammonia above 400 micromol/L mandates urgent haemodialysis
Protein must be stopped within 24 to 48 hours; anabolic IV dextrose plus intralipid supports caloric needs
Family history of unexplained neonatal death is a strong clue for inherited metabolic disease
explanation.pearls: A previously well term neonate who deteriorates after 36 hours of successful feeding with respiratory alkalosis and ammonia above 200 micromol/L should be assumed to have a urea cycle disorder until proven otherwise, with dialysis prep at ammonia 400 micromol/L.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Suspected Inborn Error of Metabolism

stem:
You are the emergency registrar at a regional Queensland hospital during a 41 degrees C heatwave. A 15-year-old boy is brought in by ambulance after collapsing 90 minutes into a school cross-country event. He has been confused since collapse. He is now obtunded with hot dry skin despite cold packs applied in transit. Bystander first-aid included spraying him with water and fanning.

He has no known medical conditions. Weight is 60 kg. Estimated time since collapse is 35 minutes. Core (rectal) temperature has been recorded as 41.6 degrees C.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, RR 32, Temp 41.6 degrees C rectal, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: GCS 9 (E2 V3 M4), hot skin, capillary refill 4 seconds, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, CK 12500 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate cooling strategy?

options.text: Iced gastric lavage via nasogastric tube as the primary cooling strategy in the resuscitation cubicle
options.rationale: Gastric lavage achieves much slower cooling than immersion and carries aspiration risk in an obtunded patient. It is at best an adjunct, never a primary strategy. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

options.text: Tepid sponging with continuous fanning while administering intravenous paracetamol 1 g and dantrolene
options.rationale: Tepid sponging cools too slowly to prevent multi-organ injury in exertional heatstroke. Antipyretics do not work in heatstroke because the hypothalamic set-point is normal, and dantrolene has no proven role outside malignant hyperthermia. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

options.text: Cold-water immersion to bring core temperature to 39 degrees C as rapidly as possible while supporting airway and circulation
options.rationale: In exertional heatstroke, every minute above 40 degrees C drives multi-organ injury, and cold-water immersion is the most rapid cooling method, lowering core temperature by approximately 0.2 degrees C per minute. Cooling targets cessation at 39 degrees C to avoid rebound hypothermia. Airway and circulation are supported in parallel rather than sequentially. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

options.text: Cooled intravenous saline 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes as the primary cooling method with target normothermia
options.rationale: Cooled IV fluids contribute only modest cooling rates compared with immersion. Aggressive fluid loading also risks pulmonary oedema in an adolescent with normal cardiac function and threatens cooling target overshoot. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

options.text: Defer aggressive cooling until intubation is performed and central venous access is established
options.rationale: Cooling must commence immediately; mortality rises with every minute above 40 degrees C. Intubation and central access proceed in parallel with cold-water immersion, not before it. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 9.3.4 - Heat-Induced Illness)

explanation.summary: Exertional heatstroke is defined by core temperature above 40 degrees C with central nervous system dysfunction occurring during physical exertion. Mortality rises sharply for every minute spent above 40 degrees C, so the maxim is cool first, transport second. Cold-water immersion is the gold standard with cooling rates of approximately 0.2 degrees C per minute. Adjunct measures (cooled IV fluids, evaporative cooling, ice packs to groin and axillae) are added if immersion is not immediately available. Complications include rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, and ARDS.
key_points: Exertional heatstroke: core above 40 degrees C plus CNS dysfunction during exertion
Cold-water immersion cools at around 0.2 degrees C per minute, faster than any other method
Stop active cooling at 39 degrees C to avoid rebound hypothermia
Rhabdomyolysis, AKI and DIC are predictable complications and require admission to a high-acuity unit
explanation.pearls: Antipyretics like paracetamol do not work in heatstroke because the hypothalamic set-point is normal and the elevated core temperature is from environmental load, not endogenous fever - the only effective treatment is rapid external cooling, ideally cold-water immersion.

sources.label: Sports Medicine Australia - Hot Weather Guidelines

stem: You are the emergency department resident assessing a 4-month-old boy brought in with a 3-day coryzal illness and worsening cough. He has taken only half his usual feeds for the last 12 hours and has not had a wet nappy for 8 hours. He was born at term with no comorbidities. His 3-year-old sister had a cold last week. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. No vaccines are overdue.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 168, RR 62, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, fine crackles bilaterally with wheeze, mild head bobbing, alert and tracking carers
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab pending; routine bloods and chest x-ray not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask with reassessment of respiratory work in 20 minutes after the dose
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not improve outcomes in viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months and is not recommended in the Australian paediatric pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose with planned review in the department in 4 hours from administration
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids do not shorten bronchiolitis or reduce admission length and are not recommended by Australian guidelines. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit to the paediatric ward for standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 at least 90% with nasogastric feeding
options.rationale: RCH targets SpO2 of at least 90% in uncomplicated bronchiolitis and uses standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen first-line when SpO2 falls below this on room air. Feeding under 50% triggers nasogastric support. High-flow oxygen is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90% and no clinical improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence humidified nasal high-flow oxygen at 2 L/kg/min immediately as the initial respiratory support before any low-flow trial
options.rationale: RCH reserves high-flow nasal cannula therapy for failure of standard low-flow oxygen, defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% after at least 2 hours of low-flow oxygen with no respiratory improvement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone with admission for monitoring of presumed bacterial co-infection in this infant
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of bacterial co-infection and empirical antibiotics are not part of the bronchiolitis pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months driven by viral lower respiratory tract infection. The Royal Children's Hospital guideline targets SpO2 of at least 90% (not 92%) and admits for sustained SpO2 below 90%, severe work of breathing, feeding under 50% of normal, apnoea, or social concerns. Standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen is the first-line respiratory support; high-flow nasal cannula therapy is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90% and no improvement. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not part of the standard pathway.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target is at least 90% in uncomplicated bronchiolitis
Standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen is the first-line respiratory support
High-flow is reserved for failure of low-flow after at least 2 hours with persistent SpO2 below 90%
Feeding under 50% triggers nasogastric support
Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics are not routine
explanation.pearls: RSV-positive infants under 3 months and those born before 32 weeks are at highest risk of apnoea; admit even if SpO2 appears adequate, because apnoea may be the first sign of severe disease in this group.

stem: You are the after-hours emergency department registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy brought in with one day of coryza and a barking cough that started this evening. He has stridor audible at rest and mild intercostal recession but is interactive, smiling at his parents and has good colour. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. There are no immunisation gaps and no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 130, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor at rest with mild intercostal recession, no cyanosis, no agitation, alert and interactive
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via mask and reassess respiratory effort in 20 minutes
options.rationale: Salbutamol treats lower airway bronchospasm rather than the upper airway narrowing of croup and does not relieve stridor. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mL/kg of 1 in 1000 and prepare for paediatric intubation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is indicated for severe croup with marked respiratory distress or impending failure, not moderate disease with preserved alertness. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg now and admit for intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever and toxic appearance; this child is well between cough bouts and antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and observe in the department for 4 hours
options.rationale: Moderate croup with stridor at rest but no severe distress is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone and 4-hour observation; most children improve and are safely discharged. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation in theatre with ENT and anaesthetics teams on standby
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending or actual respiratory failure with cyanosis, exhaustion or reduced responsiveness, none of which is present. (Source: RCH CPG Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded clinically as mild (stridor with activity), moderate (stridor at rest with mild recession) or severe (stridor at rest with marked distress or altered mental state). Australian first-line treatment for moderate croup is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg followed by 4-hour observation. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease and bridges the time to dexamethasone onset. Antibiotics, bronchodilators and intubation are not used in uncomplicated viral croup.
key_points: Stridor at rest without severe distress defines moderate croup.
Single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first-line.
Observe for 4 hours after steroid and discharge if stable.
Reserve adrenaline for severe croup or impending failure.
explanation.pearls: Rebound at 4 to 6 hours after a single adrenaline dose is well described; never discharge a child who needed nebulised adrenaline without 4 hours of clear observation after administration, regardless of how well they look immediately afterwards.

stem: You are the GP reviewing an 18-month-old girl brought in by her mother with a 2-day history of fever and irritability, now refusing to lie flat and tugging at both ears. She is otherwise well, immunisations are up to date, and the family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She has no eczema, no rash, and no recorded penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 150, RR 30, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes red and bulging with absent light reflex; neck supple; chest clear; no rash; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus paracetamol for analgesia
options.rationale: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years with high fever and severe pain warrants immediate amoxicillin; 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is the Therapeutic Guidelines recommendation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Watchful waiting with paracetamol and review by phone in 48 hours if no improvement
options.rationale: Watchful waiting suits unilateral mild disease in children over 2 years, not bilateral disease with high fever in a child under 2. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol ear drops for both ears with daily fluids and analgesia
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic drops have no role in middle-ear infection through an intact tympanic membrane; they target external otitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral pseudoephedrine for 7 days with paracetamol and ibuprofen alternating for pain
options.rationale: Decongestants do not reduce middle-ear effusion or shorten illness and carry significant adverse effects in young children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for 3 days with delayed antibiotic prescription if needed
options.rationale: Systemic steroids are not part of acute otitis media management in Australian guidelines and may mask deterioration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend immediate antibiotic therapy for acute otitis media in children with bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, systemic illness, immunosuppression or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background. Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure at 48 to 72 hours. Adequate analgesia with paracetamol and ibuprofen is core to management irrespective of antibiotic decision. Watchful waiting suits uncomplicated unilateral disease in older children.
key_points: Children under 2 with bilateral disease need antibiotics now.
Amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line.
Analgesia is essential regardless of antibiotic choice.
Switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate if no improvement at 48-72 h.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent acute otitis media (three or more episodes in 6 months or four in 12 months) prompts ENT referral for grommet consideration; mastoiditis presents with post-auricular swelling, tenderness and downward-and-outward displacement of the pinna and warrants urgent admission.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 3-year-old girl brought by her mother with a 3-month history of hard infrequent stools every 5 to 7 days, soiling episodes and stool withholding posture during the day. There are no red flags: no blood per rectum, no abdominal distension, normal growth, normal back and anus on examination, and no delayed meconium at birth. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal for age
data_table.Examination: Soft palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant; normal anus and back; normal lower limb neurology; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Lactulose 1 mL/kg twice daily as the sole pharmacological treatment for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Lactulose is acceptable but Australian guidelines now recommend macrogol 3350 first-line because of higher disimpaction success and better palatability. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes disimpaction regimen followed by daily maintenance dosing
options.rationale: Macrogol disimpaction with up to 8 sachets per day for up to 7 days followed by maintenance is the first-line Australian regimen for functional constipation with faecal loading. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Daily oral senna alone with dietary fibre advice and toilet sitting after meals
options.rationale: Stimulants are added if osmotics alone fail; routine first-line use can cause cramping and is not standard for initial therapy. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for examination under anaesthetic and inpatient bowel washout
options.rationale: Surgical referral is reserved for organic causes such as Hirschsprung disease or anorectal malformation; none of these features are present here. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

options.text: Daily PR phosphate enemas for one week and then dietary fibre advice alone
options.rationale: Routine PR therapy is invasive, traumatising for young children and not first-line for typical functional constipation in well children. (Source: RCH CPG Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal loading is the commonest paediatric bowel complaint in Australia. Royal Children's Hospital and RACGP advice favour macrogol 3350 first-line for both disimpaction and maintenance. Disimpaction uses escalating sachet doses for up to 7 days, then maintenance is titrated to achieve one soft stool per day. Long-term success depends on toileting routine, reward charts and continued maintenance for at least 6 months after symptom resolution.
key_points: Macrogol 3350 is first-line for disimpaction and maintenance.
Disimpaction escalates over 7 days; maintenance follows.
Maintain therapy for at least 6 months after symptoms resolve.
Reserve surgery referral for organic red flags.
explanation.pearls: Beware of stopping macrogol the moment stools normalise; relapse rates are high without 6 months of maintenance, and many families need explicit permission to keep dosing once everything looks better.

subtopic_detail: Household pertussis chemoprophylaxis with infant under 6 months
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 32-year-old mother with 3 weeks of paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting. Pertussis PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab is positive. She lives with her 6-week-old infant who received the 6-week DTPa-IPV-Hib-HepB dose 3 days ago, a healthy 4-year-old who is up to date with vaccines, and her partner who had Tdap 12 years ago. None are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Mother: HR 76, BP 118/74, SpO2 98% room air; infant examined separately and well
data_table.Examination: Mother coughs intermittently during consultation; infant is feeding well with no apnoea, no cough and no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Maternal pertussis PCR positive; infant pertussis PCR not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure plan for the household?

options.text: Treat the mother with azithromycin and provide red flag advice only to the other household members
options.rationale: Pertussis spreads readily within households; chemoprophylaxis is indicated for all contacts when an infant under 6 months lives in the home regardless of vaccination status. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Vaccinate the 6-week-old with an accelerated DTPa dose and the adults with Tdap boosters
options.rationale: Vaccination does not provide rapid post-exposure protection; chemoprophylaxis is required for vulnerable contacts within the household. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Test the 4-year-old and partner with PCR first and treat only those who return a positive result
options.rationale: Pre-test triage delays prophylaxis and risks transmission to the infant during the 24- to 48-hour wait for swab results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer chemoprophylaxis pending the public health unit's instructions on close contacts
options.rationale: Public health notification is mandatory, but commencing prophylaxis should not wait; treatment of contacts within 21 days of exposure to an infant is time-critical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Give azithromycin chemoprophylaxis to the infant, sibling and adults alongside treating the mother
options.rationale: When an infant under 6 months lives in the household, azithromycin chemoprophylaxis is given to all close household contacts to prevent severe and fatal infant pertussis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pertussis remains a serious risk in young infants, with mortality concentrated in those under 6 months. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines indicate chemoprophylaxis for all close household contacts when an infant under 6 months lives in the home, irrespective of vaccination status. Azithromycin is first-line because of short course and good compliance. The index case is notifiable and the public health unit will trace wider contacts, but treatment should not be delayed for notification.
key_points: Index case requires treatment and notification.
All household contacts get prophylaxis when an infant under 6 months lives in the home.
Azithromycin is the first-line chemoprophylaxis agent.
Vaccination alone does not protect close contacts in time.
explanation.pearls: Infants under 6 months can present with apnoea before cough, especially if exposed to a coughing adult at home; admit for monitoring at the threshold of any apnoea, cyanosis or feeding change even if pertussis PCR has not yet returned.

stem: You are the GP in a regional clinic seeing a 14-year-old girl brought urgently by her mother. She is drowsy after 8 hours of fever, severe headache and one episode of vomiting. In the last 30 minutes a non-blanching petechial rash has appeared on her trunk and limbs. The nearest emergency department is 90 minutes away by road. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She has no documented antibiotic allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 130, RR 28, BP 92/56, SpO2 96% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching petechial rash on trunk and limbs; warm peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; mild neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L; lactate not available; venous access not yet established

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action in your clinic?

options.text: Administer intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg now and arrange urgent retrieval transfer
options.rationale: Suspected meningococcaemia in a community setting warrants immediate intramuscular benzylpenicillin while awaiting transfer; intramuscular is acceptable when intravenous access is not yet available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for paramedic arrival to gain intravenous access before any antibiotic is given
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcaemia worsens mortality; intramuscular benzylpenicillin should be given immediately when intravenous access is not yet established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and arrange retrieval transfer without antibiotic
options.rationale: Steroid alone has no role and antibiotic delay is dangerous; dexamethasone in meningitis is given with or shortly after the first antibiotic dose in hospital. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis to the family and transfer the patient
options.rationale: Prophylaxis for contacts is given once the index case is stabilised; it does not treat the index patient and must not delay her own antibiotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Transfer the patient to hospital without any antibiotic to avoid blood culture contamination
options.rationale: Pre-hospital antibiotic improves survival in meningococcaemia and outweighs the modest reduction in culture yield; cultures can still be taken on arrival. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected meningococcal disease in the community is a time-critical diagnosis. Australian guidelines indicate immediate intramuscular or intravenous benzylpenicillin if there is any delay establishing intravenous access. Survival correlates inversely with time to first antibiotic dose. After the first dose, urgent retrieval and supportive resuscitation with fluids and oxygen are arranged. Public health notification and ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for close contacts follow once the index case is stabilised.
key_points: Intramuscular benzylpenicillin in clinic if no intravenous access.
Do not delay first antibiotic dose for transfer or imaging.
Notify the public health unit on the same day.
Ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for household and kissing contacts.
explanation.pearls: Petechiae are a late sign; in early meningococcaemia the leg pain, cold mottled peripheries, and prolonged capillary refill precede the rash by hours and are the cues to act on suspicion alone.

subtopic_detail: Episodic viral wheeze in preschooler without maintenance ICS
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 2-year-old boy whose mother reports this is his fourth wheeze episode this winter, each triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection. Between episodes he is symptom-free, has no nocturnal cough and no exercise limitation. He has no eczema, no allergic rhinitis and no family history of atopy. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has had no oral steroid courses to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, HR 130, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild expiratory wheeze bilaterally with minimal recession; alert and feeding well; no nasal flare; symmetric air entry
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry not feasible at this age; chest x-ray not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence daily inhaled fluticasone 100 microgram twice daily via spacer for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Maintenance inhaled corticosteroids do not reduce viral-only wheeze episodes in preschoolers without atopic features and risk growth and adrenal effects. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Add daily oral montelukast and continue salbutamol as needed for symptom relief
options.rationale: Daily montelukast is not first-line for episodic viral wheeze and carries a black-box neuropsychiatric warning that limits use in young children. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Salbutamol via spacer as needed during episodes without maintenance inhaled corticosteroid
options.rationale: Episodic viral wheeze in a young preschooler without atopic features is managed with as-needed salbutamol via spacer; maintenance inhaled steroid is reserved for multi-trigger or atopic phenotypes. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Refer for allergy skin prick testing before any decision on inhaled treatment is made
options.rationale: Skin prick testing is reserved for suspected allergic asthma or multi-trigger phenotypes and is not needed for typical episodic viral wheeze. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe a 5-day course of oral prednisolone now and review again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Oral steroids are reserved for moderate to severe acute wheeze; routine prophylactic courses are not recommended in mild episodic viral wheeze. (Source: National Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze is divided into episodic viral and multi-trigger phenotypes. Episodic viral wheeze without atopic background is managed with as-needed salbutamol via spacer during exacerbations and red flag advice. Maintenance inhaled corticosteroid is reserved for multi-trigger wheeze, persistent inter-episode symptoms or strong atopic background. Oral steroids in this age group are restricted to moderate or severe acute exacerbations.
key_points: Salbutamol via spacer is first-line during viral wheeze episodes.
Maintenance inhaled steroid only if multi-trigger or atopic.
Avoid oral steroid for mild episodic viral wheeze.
Review phenotype if episodes become more frequent.
explanation.pearls: A spacer with a face mask delivers more drug to the small airways than a nebuliser in a wriggly toddler; switching from nebuliser to spacer often improves practical response and reduces tachycardia from systemic absorption.

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis of the hip discrimination from transient synovitis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old boy with 2 days of right hip pain, refusal to weight bear and progressive limp. He has had a low-grade temperature and looks unwell at triage. He has no recent trauma, no preceding viral illness and no rash. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 100/60, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Refusal to weight bear, hip held in flexion and external rotation, severe pain on log-roll and any internal rotation; no rash, no other joint involvement
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 95 mg/L, ESR 52 mm/h, blood culture pending; hip ultrasound shows joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with oral cefalexin and review in primary care in 48 hours if not better
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient care will fail to clear an established septic joint and risk femoral head osteonecrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours and start treatment only if the effusion has grown
options.rationale: Serial imaging delays definitive treatment; the four Kocher criteria together give a very high probability of septic arthritis and warrant urgent joint aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Trial of weight bearing with regular ibuprofen and outpatient orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in a well child; the combination of fever, raised inflammatory markers and refusal to weight bear makes this unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin without joint aspiration and reassess in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics before joint aspiration reduce culture yield and delay the source-control surgery that is required for septic arthritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent hip aspiration in theatre with washout and empirical intravenous flucloxacillin
options.rationale: Four positive Kocher criteria (fever above 38.5, refusal to bear weight, WCC above 12, ESR above 40) give over 95 percent probability of septic arthritis; aspiration, washout and intravenous antibiotics are the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG Septic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: The Kocher criteria stratify the probability of septic arthritis of the hip in a child with limp: fever above 38.5, refusal to weight bear, WCC above 12 and ESR above 40. With all four present probability exceeds 95 percent. Australian practice favours urgent surgical aspiration and washout with empirical intravenous flucloxacillin pending cultures. Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion in a well, afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers and rapid improvement on rest.
key_points: Four Kocher criteria give over 95 percent probability of septic arthritis.
Aspiration in theatre obtains cultures and decompresses the joint.
Empirical flucloxacillin covers the commonest organisms.
Transient synovitis requires normal inflammatory markers.
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is now the commonest cause of culture-positive septic arthritis in children under 4 in Australia and is fastidious; if Gram stain is negative and the child is under 4, ask the laboratory to inoculate paediatric blood culture bottles with the joint aspirate to improve yield.

stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing an 11-year-old girl with four weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. She has had no vomiting and is alert and well perfused. Her family has no history of diabetes. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Her mother is keen to take her home if it is safe.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 92, BP 110/68, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well perfused, no acetone breath, no Kussmaul breathing, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: BSL 22 mmol/L, capillary ketones 1.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 58 micromol/L, HbA1c 11.6%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline and commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with hourly capillary glucose monitoring
options.rationale: An insulin infusion is the diabetic ketoacidosis pathway and is not indicated when venous pH and bicarbonate are normal and ketones are only mildly elevated; it carries unnecessary risk of hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes Mellitus)

options.text: Admit for intravenous maintenance fluids and oral fluids only with insulin deferred until capillary ketones have cleared below 0.6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Withholding insulin in new-onset hyperglycaemia perpetuates ketogenesis and lipolysis and will worsen the metabolic picture; insulin is the definitive treatment for hyperglycaemia with ketosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

options.text: Admit under the paediatric diabetes team for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin initiation, structured education and a written sick-day plan before discharge
options.rationale: New-onset hyperglycaemia without acidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin and inpatient education by a paediatric diabetes service; this is the Australian standard and prevents readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge on metformin 500 mg twice daily with outpatient paediatric endocrinology review and home glucose monitoring within one week
options.rationale: Metformin is not appropriate for new-onset type 1 diabetes; the clinical picture of rapid weight loss and ketones points to insulin deficiency, and oral hypoglycaemics will not arrest progression to ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

options.text: Start subcutaneous long-acting insulin glargine alone with discharge home and outpatient diabetes review arranged for 48 hours later
options.rationale: Basal insulin alone will not cover prandial glycaemic excursions and ketosis, and discharging without structured education and a sick-day plan risks early readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis. (Source: APEG Type 1 Diabetes Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Around a third of paediatric type 1 diabetes presentations occur without ketoacidosis. These children still require hospital admission for insulin initiation because the underlying insulin deficiency will progress without treatment. Inpatient education by the paediatric diabetes team covers dose adjustment, hypoglycaemia recognition, ketone monitoring and sick-day rules. Discharge without these supports is a leading cause of early readmission with diabetic ketoacidosis.
key_points: Diabetic ketoacidosis is defined by venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 with ketones above 3.0 mmol/L
Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin is the initial regimen for non-ketoacidotic presentations in Australia
Inpatient diabetes education is part of initial management, not an optional add-on
Metformin and oral hypoglycaemics have no role in type 1 diabetes initiation
A documented sick-day plan with ketone testing thresholds is required before discharge
explanation.pearls: Capillary ketones above 0.6 mmol/L with a glucose above 14 mmol/L on a sick day triggers extra rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours under the APEG sick-day rule.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose parents are concerned that he is pale and tires easily. He drinks around 900 mL of cow's milk daily, refuses meat and prefers crackers. He was born at term and is otherwise well. There is no history of jaundice, dark urine or recent infection. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no scleral icterus, no hepatosplenomegaly, soft systolic flow murmur
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 19 pg, RDW 17.5%, platelets 480 x10^9/L, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP 3 mg/L, reticulocyte count 0.7%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange transfusion of packed red cells in the paediatric day unit and refer to paediatric haematology for further evaluation
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia or haemoglobin below 70 g/L with cardiovascular compromise; this child is haemodynamically stable and responds to oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily, reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL/day and review with full blood count in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Excess cow's milk intake displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss; oral iron with dietary modification corrects iron deficiency anaemia and the haemoglobin should rise by at least 10 g/L within a month. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Order haemoglobin electrophoresis, direct antiglobulin test and serum lactate dehydrogenase before starting any treatment to exclude haemoglobinopathy
options.rationale: The ferritin, microcytosis and dietary history are diagnostic of iron deficiency in this context; further haematology workup is reserved for failure to respond to a trial of oral iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer for an intravenous iron infusion in the outpatient setting now and continue current dietary intake while awaiting the appointment
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, oral iron intolerance or treatment failure; first-line therapy in a well toddler is oral iron with dietary adjustment. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Reassure the family that the findings reflect a physiological dietary phase and review in three months without starting any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: A ferritin under 12 micrograms/L with microcytic anaemia is not physiological and untreated iron deficiency in toddlers causes long-term neurodevelopmental harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers, driven by excessive cow's milk intake and selective eating. Oral elemental iron at 3 mg/kg once daily with dietary modification corrects the deficit in the majority of well children. A rise in haemoglobin of at least 10 g/L by four weeks confirms response; failure to respond prompts review for malabsorption, ongoing blood loss or alternative diagnoses. Persistent iron deficiency in this age group is associated with cognitive and motor delay.
key_points: Cow's milk above 500 mL daily in toddlers displaces dietary iron and causes occult enteric blood loss
Ferritin under 12 micrograms/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency in children when the C-reactive protein is normal
Oral iron once daily improves absorption versus divided dosing because of hepcidin kinetics
Reticulocytosis at 7 to 10 days confirms early response and haemoglobin rise at 4 weeks confirms cure
Intravenous iron is second line and reserved for treatment failure or intolerance
explanation.pearls: Once-daily oral iron given on alternate days may improve fractional absorption versus thrice-daily dosing because hepcidin remains elevated for 24 hours after each dose.

subtopic_detail: Moderate atopic eczema flare topical step-up
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a one-week flare of itchy, weeping eczema on her cheeks and antecubital fossae. She has been using a daily soap substitute and 1% hydrocortisone for two weeks without improvement. There is no honey-coloured crust, no fever and no spreading erythema. She is otherwise well and has no allergies. The parents are reluctant to use stronger topical steroids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Erythematous, weeping eczema on face and flexures, lichenification at popliteal fossae, no pustules or crusting, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Continue 1% hydrocortisone twice daily indefinitely with daily bleach baths and refer to a paediatric dermatologist for biologic therapy assessment
options.rationale: Failure of 1% hydrocortisone in a moderate flare warrants topical step-up rather than indefinite continuation; biologics are reserved for severe disease refractory to standard topical care. (Source: ACD Atopic Dermatitis Position Statement)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for five days and review in clinic at the end of the course before tapering the dose
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids cause rebound flares on cessation and are not used for atopic eczema in children outside specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily empirically for ten days and continue current topical regimen unchanged
options.rationale: There is no honey-coloured crust, pustule or systemic feature to suggest staphylococcal superinfection; antibiotics will not address the underlying inflammatory flare. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment once daily for two weeks, continue emollients and soap substitutes and review at the end of the course
options.rationale: A moderate-potency topical corticosteroid is the next step when low-potency steroid fails; a defined two-week course with emollients restores skin barrier function and matches Australian dermatology advice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Trial topical pimecrolimus 1% cream twice daily without any topical corticosteroid for a fortnight and review the response in clinic at that point
options.rationale: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second line for steroid-sparing maintenance or for sensitive sites such as eyelids, not for inducing remission in an actively weeping flare. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Atopic eczema management is a stepped ladder anchored on emollients and soap substitutes, with topical corticosteroid potency matched to flare severity. Hydrocortisone 1% is sufficient for mild flares on the face; moderate body or flexural flares need a moderate-potency steroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate. A short defined course of stronger steroid is safer and more effective than prolonged low-potency steroid. Parental steroid phobia is a major driver of undertreatment and persistent flare.
key_points: Topical corticosteroid potency should match flare severity, not patient age in isolation
Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% is a moderate-potency steroid safe for short courses in children
Antibiotics are added only when bacterial superinfection is clinically suspected
Topical calcineurin inhibitors are second line, particularly for sensitive sites or maintenance
Systemic corticosteroids are avoided because of rebound flares on withdrawal
explanation.pearls: The fingertip unit covers one adult fingertip from the distal interphalangeal joint to the tip and treats an area equal to two adult palms; this gives parents a reproducible dosing measure.

subtopic_detail: Urinary tract infection empirical antibiotic in a young child
stem: You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 14-month-old girl with 2 days of fever and irritability. She is feeding poorly but is alert and tracking carers. There is no cough, coryza or rash. She has no allergies and has had no recent antibiotics. A clean-catch urine sample has been collected. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 158, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, clear chest, soft abdomen, no rash, ears and throat normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood trace, protein 1+. Urine microscopy and culture pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical management while awaiting urine culture?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days while awaiting culture and review at the end of the course with the GP
options.rationale: Cefalexin is the RCH first-line empirical oral antibiotic for paediatric urinary tract infection; for a child 12 months or older with febrile urinary tract infection the dose is 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days. She is alert and tolerating oral intake so oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous gentamicin pending the urine culture result and reassess for an oral switch at 48 hours of treatment
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is reserved for infants under 3 months, suspected pyelonephritis with sepsis, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral antibiotics; this child is well perfused and tolerating oral intake. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Start oral trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole at standard paediatric dosing for 7 days and arrange follow-up with the GP at the end of the course
options.rationale: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is reasonable only once urine culture sensitivities confirm susceptibility; it is not RCH first-line empirical therapy because of background community Escherichia coli resistance. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin alone at standard paediatric dosing for 5 days with planned follow-up with the GP at the end of the antibiotic course
options.rationale: Amoxicillin alone has unacceptably high resistance among community Escherichia coli isolates in Australia and is not first-line empirical therapy for paediatric urinary tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange a repeat urine specimen at the GP in 48 hours with antibiotics deferred until microscopy and culture return positive results
options.rationale: A positive nitrite and leucocyte dipstick in a febrile child under 2 years is sufficient to commence empirical antibiotics; deferring treatment risks progression to pyelonephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: Febrile urinary tract infection in young children is treated empirically once a clean-catch urine sample has been collected, because untreated infection risks renal scarring. The RCH urinary tract infection guideline lists oral cefalexin as first-line empirical therapy: 20 mg/kg/dose three times daily for cystitis, and 25 mg/kg three times daily for pyelonephritis in children 12 months or older (25 mg/kg four times daily under 12 months). Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is only used once sensitivities confirm susceptibility. Intravenous gentamicin is reserved for infants under 3 months, sepsis, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral antibiotics.
key_points: Cefalexin is first-line empirical oral therapy for paediatric urinary tract infection per RCH
Pyelonephritis dose in 12 months or older: 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days
Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole only after sensitivities confirm susceptibility
Amoxicillin alone is not used because of community E. coli resistance
Intravenous antibiotics are reserved for under-3-month infants, sepsis, or oral intolerance
explanation.pearls: Recurrent febrile urinary tract infections or abnormal initial ultrasound trigger paediatric nephrology referral; the RCH cascade does not include routine DMSA or routine micturating cystourethrogram.

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura with abdominal pain and normal renal function
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 6-year-old boy who has had a non-blanching palpable purpuric rash over his buttocks and lower legs for five days. He now has colicky periumbilical pain and one episode of bile-stained vomiting. He has had a cold two weeks before this presentation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no oedema and is passing normal urine volumes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 110, BP 102/64, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower limbs, swollen tender ankles, soft abdomen with periumbilical tenderness, no peritonism, no scrotal swelling
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 1+, no nitrites or leucocytes. Urine protein:creatinine 32 mg/mmol. Creatinine 32 micromol/L, albumin 38 g/L. FBC and CRP normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows thickened proximal small bowel without intussusception.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for emergent laparotomy because of bile-stained vomiting and abdominal pain in a child with palpable purpura
options.rationale: Bowel wall oedema from the vasculitis can mimic obstruction, but the ultrasound excludes intussusception and there is no peritonism; laparotomy is not indicated without surgical findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for three days and admit to the paediatric intensive care unit for monitoring
options.rationale: Pulse intravenous methylprednisolone is reserved for severe nephritis with crescents or rapidly progressive renal failure; this child has only mild proteinuria and no acute kidney injury. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP Nephritis Guideline)

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a self-limiting illness and discharge home with simple analgesia and outpatient follow-up arranged in six weeks
options.rationale: Significant abdominal pain warrants admission for analgesia, hydration and observation for intussusception; ongoing renal surveillance is also required to detect late nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

options.text: Initiate oral cyclophosphamide and azathioprine in conjunction with prednisolone and refer to paediatric nephrology for outpatient review within one week
options.rationale: Cytotoxic therapy is reserved for biopsy-proven severe nephritis; it is not indicated for abdominal pain with mild proteinuria. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP Nephritis Guideline)

options.text: Admit for analgesia, intravenous fluids and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for two weeks with weekly urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring for six months
options.rationale: Significant abdominal pain in vasculitis is shortened by oral corticosteroids without changing renal outcomes; weekly surveillance for nephritis is required because renal involvement may emerge over the following 6 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is an immunoglobulin A small-vessel vasculitis that follows an upper respiratory infection in school-aged children. The classical tetrad is palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and renal involvement. Significant abdominal pain warrants admission for analgesia and observation for intussusception, which is typically ileoileal in this disease. Corticosteroids shorten the abdominal pain but do not alter the renal trajectory; long-term surveillance is mandated because nephritis can emerge over months.
key_points: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower limbs with arthralgia is highly suggestive of HSP
Intussusception in HSP is typically ileoileal rather than ileocolic and may be missed by enema
Significant abdominal pain is shortened by oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg daily
Steroids do not prevent or alter the course of HSP nephritis
Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 6 months is required to detect late nephritis
explanation.pearls: Renal involvement may appear up to 6 months after the initial rash, so surveillance with urinalysis and blood pressure is continued even after symptoms resolve.

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease treatment within ten days of fever onset
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old boy on day 6 of fever above 39 °C. He has a polymorphous truncal rash, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue and a unilateral cervical lymph node measuring 1.7 cm. His hands and feet are erythematous and swollen. He has had no diarrhoea and his immunisations are current. Throat swab for group A streptococcus is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 156, BP 95/58, RR 26, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Polymorphous rash, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, 1.7 cm right cervical node, swollen hands and feet, no peeling yet
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, platelets 540 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis: sterile pyuria. Throat swab negative. Echocardiogram requested.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg daily for ten days and review for clinical response and rash resolution at the end of the antibiotic course
options.rationale: The clinical picture and a negative throat swab do not support streptococcal infection; antibiotics will not address the underlying vasculitis or prevent coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Reassure the family that this is likely a viral exanthem with reactive cervical lymphadenitis and discharge home with simple antipyretic advice and review
options.rationale: Five days of fever plus four of the five clinical criteria meet the threshold for Kawasaki disease and inflammatory markers support active vasculitis; discharge risks untreated coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Order an echocardiogram first and defer all systemic treatment until coronary artery dimensions are formally confirmed by the paediatric cardiology service
options.rationale: Treatment is not contingent on echocardiographic findings; delaying intravenous immunoglobulin past day 10 increases the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Admit for intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily, with echocardiography arranged within the admission
options.rationale: He meets clinical criteria for complete Kawasaki disease; intravenous immunoglobulin within the first 10 days of fever plus low-dose aspirin reduces coronary artery aneurysm rates from approximately 25% to under 5%. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily monotherapy and arrange outpatient paediatric rheumatology follow-up within five working days of presentation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are an adjunct considered for IVIG resistance or high-risk patients, not as monotherapy; standard initial treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in Australian children. The diagnosis requires at least 5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 clinical features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus aspirin within the first 10 days of fever reduces coronary artery aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%. Sterile pyuria, raised transaminases and low albumin support the diagnosis even when classical features are partial.
key_points: Five days of fever plus 4 of 5 clinical criteria establishes complete Kawasaki disease
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus aspirin reduces aneurysm rates from around 25% to under 5%
Treatment within the first 10 days of fever is the key prognostic determinant for coronary outcomes
Sterile pyuria, raised liver enzymes and low albumin are supportive features
Refractory disease at 36 hours after IVIG triggers a second dose plus corticosteroid escalation
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive corticosteroids are considered up front for children with predicted IVIG resistance based on the Kobayashi or Sano scores in Japanese cohorts, although routine use in Australian children remains case-by-case.

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice with ABO incompatibility and phototherapy threshold
stem: You are the neonatal resident reviewing a 38-hour-old term boy who appears jaundiced down to his upper thighs. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery to a healthy mother whose blood group is O Rh-positive. The baby's blood group is A Rh-positive. He is breastfeeding 3 to 4 hourly with good attachment. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.
