data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, vigorous suck, well perfused, jaundiced to upper thighs, no scalp haematoma, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 305 micromol/L (conjugated 12 micromol/L), Hb 158 g/L, reticulocytes 5%, direct antiglobulin test weakly positive, blood group A Rh-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue routine breastfeeding without phototherapy or specific intervention and arrange a community midwife review at 72 hours of life for jaundice
options.rationale: His bilirubin sits well above the Australian phototherapy threshold for a well term baby at 38 hours, and ABO incompatibility raises the risk of rapid bilirubin acceleration; observation alone is unsafe. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Switch the infant to formula feeding for 24 hours, withhold breastfeeding and reassess the bilirubin trend after one full day of replacement feeds only
options.rationale: Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not indicated for haemolytic jaundice; supplementation may be considered for hydration but the underlying ABO incompatibility still requires phototherapy. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy, continue breastfeeding with supplementation if intake is inadequate and recheck bilirubin and haematocrit in 4 to 6 hours
options.rationale: His bilirubin exceeds the phototherapy line on the term low-risk nomogram at 38 hours, and the positive direct antiglobulin test with ABO mismatch is a risk factor for rapid rise; intensive phototherapy with hydration is standard. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Arrange immediate double-volume exchange transfusion in the neonatal intensive care unit as the initial intervention for haemolytic neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin levels above the exchange line, signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy or rapid rise on intensive phototherapy; the first step is intensive phototherapy. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg now and recheck the total bilirubin in six hours before deciding on additional phototherapy
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is an adjunct considered only when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy and approaches the exchange transfusion line, not as an initial intervention. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice plotted against postnatal hours on the Australian phototherapy nomogram is the basis of management decisions. ABO incompatibility with a positive direct antiglobulin test is an acceleration risk and lowers the threshold for intensive phototherapy. Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels above the exchange line, signs of bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction or failure of intensive phototherapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin reduces the need for exchange transfusion in isoimmune disease when bilirubin is climbing toward the exchange line.
key_points: Bilirubin must always be plotted against postnatal hours on a treatment nomogram
ABO incompatibility with positive direct antiglobulin test is a risk factor for rapid haemolysis
Intensive phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for failure or extreme levels
Intravenous immunoglobulin is adjunctive in isoimmune haemolytic disease at high bilirubin levels
Hydration with breast or expressed milk is continued throughout phototherapy whenever possible
explanation.pearls: A rise of more than 8.5 micromol/L per hour or failure to respond to intensive phototherapy is the trigger to consider intravenous immunoglobulin and prepare for exchange transfusion.

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile convulsion in a toddler
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 22-month-old boy who had a single 90 second generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home during a fever from a viral upper respiratory illness. He is now fully alert, feeding and interacting normally. He has had no previous seizures and his development is age appropriate. His older sister had two similar episodes as a toddler. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 140, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, no neck stiffness, no rash, ENT shows red bulging tympanic membranes bilaterally, soft abdomen, normal neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L; no further investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent outpatient electroencephalogram and brain MRI within two weeks and refer to the paediatric neurology clinic
options.rationale: EEG and neuroimaging are not indicated for a first simple febrile convulsion with normal neurological examination and recovery; they yield no useful prognostic information in this setting. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

options.text: Discharge home with parental education on febrile convulsion recurrence, fever management and clear ambulance call criteria for prolonged events
options.rationale: A simple febrile convulsion in a developmentally normal child needs no investigation; parental reassurance, recurrence counselling and an ambulance plan for seizures lasting over five minutes is the entire required management. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

options.text: Commence regular oral sodium valproate prophylaxis 10 mg/kg twice daily for six months given the positive family history and review in clinic
options.rationale: Continuous antiepileptic prophylaxis is not used for simple febrile convulsions because the modest reduction in recurrence does not outweigh the medication risks. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

options.text: Admit overnight for cardiorespiratory monitoring and intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg pending blood culture and lumbar puncture results
options.rationale: Empiric antibiotics and lumbar puncture are not warranted in a well child with a clear viral source and no meningism; reflexive sepsis workup is overtreatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

options.text: Prescribe rectal diazepam 5 mg for the parents to administer at the onset of every future fever to prevent recurrence and review in clinic
options.rationale: Intermittent prophylactic benzodiazepines at fever onset do not reliably prevent febrile convulsions and risk sedation that can confound assessment of a sick child. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Seizures)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile convulsions are generalised seizures under 15 minutes that occur once in 24 hours in a developmentally normal child aged 6 months to 5 years during a febrile illness. They do not require investigation, neuroimaging or prophylaxis. Recurrence occurs in roughly a third of children, usually within a year, and the risk of later epilepsy is only slightly above the population baseline. Family education on first-aid positioning and a clear ambulance threshold at five minutes is the core intervention.
key_points: A simple febrile convulsion is generalised, under 15 minutes, and occurs once in 24 hours in a well child
Neuroimaging and electroencephalogram have no role in simple febrile convulsions
Recurrence is around 30% and the risk of later epilepsy is only marginally raised
Continuous antiepileptic prophylaxis is not recommended
Ambulance should be called for any febrile convulsion lasting over 5 minutes
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg can be supplied for at-home rescue only when a child has a documented prolonged febrile convulsion over 5 minutes.

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in a toddler
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 20-month-old non-Aboriginal girl with 24 hours of fever, irritability and ear pulling. She has had no previous ear infections and immunisations are up to date. She has no penicillin allergy. There is no ear discharge and she has been drinking but not eating. The parents are keen to avoid unnecessary medications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 °C, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous with loss of light reflex, left tympanic membrane normal, no mastoid tenderness, oropharynx unremarkable, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days and arrange review if symptoms worsen or persist beyond 48 hours
options.rationale: Children under 2 years with unilateral acute otitis media and systemic features benefit from immediate amoxicillin per Australian guidelines; the higher dose covers intermediate-resistance pneumococcus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange watchful waiting with paracetamol and ibuprofen analgesia for 48 hours before deciding whether to commence antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reserved for children over 2 years with mild unilateral disease; under 2 years with systemic features Australian guidelines advise immediate antibiotic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily for seven days as a broader-spectrum alternative given the bulging tympanic membrane
options.rationale: Cefalexin has poor pneumococcal cover compared with amoxicillin and is not the first-line agent for acute otitis media in non-allergic children. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to the emergency department for intravenous benzylpenicillin and ENT review to exclude evolving mastoiditis given the high fever
options.rationale: Without mastoid tenderness, post-auricular swelling, or systemic toxicity, mastoiditis is unlikely and outpatient oral therapy is appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin ear drops twice daily for seven days plus oral paracetamol and ibuprofen for analgesia at home
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics are used for otitis externa or grommet-related discharge; they do not penetrate an intact tympanic membrane to treat acute otitis media. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media is the most common bacterial infection of childhood. Australian guidelines advise immediate antibiotics for children under 2 years with bilateral disease or with unilateral disease plus systemic features, for any child with ear discharge from acute perforation, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. Other children with mild disease may be observed for 48 hours with analgesia. High-dose oral amoxicillin remains first line.
key_points: Immediate antibiotics for under 2 years with unilateral disease and systemic features
High-dose amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days is first line in non-allergic children
Cefalexin and macrolides have inferior pneumococcal coverage
Topical antibiotics do not penetrate an intact tympanic membrane
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children receive immediate antibiotics at all ages because of perforation risk
explanation.pearls: Australian guidelines advise switching to amoxicillin-clavulanate if there is no improvement at 48 to 72 hours on high-dose amoxicillin.

stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 10-week-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by ambulance with three days of coryza and worsening cough. He is breastfeeding only every five hours instead of every three. He has had no apnoeas reported by the parents. His older sibling has the same illness. Birth was at term and there is no congenital cardiac history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 158, RR 62, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, audible wheeze, widespread fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds, normal fontanelle, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate respiratory syncytial virus positive; chest x-ray not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with parental education on feeding cues and warning signs and arrange general practice review the following morning
options.rationale: Reduced feeding to under half normal and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air meet admission thresholds for bronchiolitis in Australia; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for nasogastric or intravenous hydration with supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain saturations above 92% and ongoing observation
options.rationale: Admission criteria are met by tachypnoea over 60, hypoxia under 92% on room air and feeding under half normal; supportive care with hydration and oxygen is the mainstay of bronchiolitis management. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess after 20 minutes before deciding on further management of his work of breathing
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis under 12 months because bronchospasm is not the predominant pathology; routine bronchodilator use is discouraged. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg now and arrange a chest x-ray to assess for bacterial complication before deciding on admission
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in viral bronchiolitis and routine chest x-ray adds radiation without changing management in classical disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start empiric oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days to cover bacterial superinfection and arrange paediatric clinic review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Routine antibiotics are not indicated in classical bronchiolitis with a known viral cause and no focal consolidation or persistent fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the most common reason for hospital admission in Australian infants under one year. Management is supportive: oxygen for hypoxia, nasogastric or intravenous fluids for reduced feeding, and observation for apnoea. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and chest x-rays are not part of routine care. Admission thresholds include oxygen saturation under 92%, tachypnoea over 60, feeding under half normal, parental concern, apnoea, and high social risk.
key_points: Admission criteria include SpO2 under 92%, feeding under half normal, apnoea or moderate respiratory distress
Salbutamol, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated
Nasogastric fluids are preferred over intravenous when tolerated
High-flow nasal oxygen is reserved for those failing standard oxygen
Apnoea risk is greatest in infants under 6 weeks of age
explanation.pearls: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min reduces escalation to intensive care in moderately severe bronchiolitis but is reserved for failure of standard oxygen, not first-line.

subtopic_detail: Chronic functional constipation in a school-aged child
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with six months of hard stools every five to seven days associated with abdominal pain and recent soiling episodes at school. He has no rectal bleeding, no weight loss and growth tracks along the 50th centile. There is no family history of inflammatory bowel disease. He drinks little water and has a fussy diet. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa, normal perianal inspection, anal wink present, normal lower limb tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange abdominal x-ray and serum coeliac antibodies and refer to paediatric gastroenterology before starting any laxative therapy
options.rationale: Functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis when red flags are absent; imaging and routine coeliac serology add cost without benefit and delay disimpaction. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence oral macrogol 3350 disimpaction over three days followed by maintenance dosing, with toileting program and dietary advice
options.rationale: First-line management of paediatric functional constipation is oral macrogol disimpaction followed by maintenance, combined with a scheduled toileting routine; rectal interventions are second line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe a sodium phosphate enema in clinic now and review for further enemas if the impaction does not clear within 48 hours of disimpaction
options.rationale: Rectal enemas are reserved for failure of oral macrogol disimpaction; they are invasive and risk electrolyte disturbance in children. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Trial dietary fibre supplementation and increased oral fluids alone for four weeks without pharmacological laxatives before reassessment in clinic
options.rationale: Dietary and behavioural measures alone are insufficient once impaction has formed; macrogol is required to clear retained faecal mass before maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Start oral senna 7.5 mg nightly as monotherapy and review in two weeks to assess soiling frequency and frequency of bowel motions
options.rationale: Stimulant laxatives are added to macrogol if response is inadequate; they are not first-line monotherapy in paediatric chronic constipation. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90% of paediatric constipation. Treatment proceeds in two stages: disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol over three to seven days, followed by ongoing maintenance for at least three months after a normal bowel pattern is established. A scheduled post-meal toileting program, age-appropriate dietary fibre, adequate fluids and reward charts support the medication. Red flags requiring further investigation include onset before 4 weeks of age, failure to pass meconium, ribbon stools, severe failure to thrive, abnormal neurological exam or sacral abnormalities.
key_points: Disimpaction with oral macrogol precedes maintenance therapy
Maintenance laxatives continue for at least three months after a normal bowel pattern returns
Rectal enemas are reserved for failure of oral disimpaction
Imaging and bloods are not required when no red flags are present
Toileting routine after meals leverages the gastrocolic reflex
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 disimpaction dose escalates over three days from 4 sachets per day to 8 sachets per day for children 5 to 11 years.

subtopic_detail: Severe croup with stridor at rest
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old boy with two days of barking cough and worsening stridor for the last three hours. He has biphasic stridor at rest and obvious sternal recession. He is anxious and clinging to his mother but maintains eye contact. He has no drooling and is fully immunised. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.1 °C, HR 152, RR 44, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Loud biphasic stridor at rest, marked sternal and intercostal recession, hoarse voice, no drooling, no trismus, chest air entry reduced bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Bedside observation only; no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in 5 mL saline plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe for at least four hours
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession requires nebulised adrenaline for immediate relief plus dexamethasone for sustained effect; the four-hour observation captures the rebound at one to two hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose and discharge home with parental education about returning if stridor recurs at rest
options.rationale: Low-dose oral dexamethasone alone is appropriate for mild croup without rest stridor; severe croup with rest stridor and recession needs nebulised adrenaline and extended observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Arrange urgent lateral neck x-ray and intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg pending findings before deciding on airway management with anaesthetics
options.rationale: There is no drooling, trismus or toxic appearance to suggest epiglottitis; imaging delays adrenaline and exposes the child to upset that risks airway decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Trial inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess after 20 minutes before deciding whether to administer corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Salbutamol targets lower airway bronchospasm and has no role in upper airway oedema of croup; relying on it delays effective treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intubate immediately in the resuscitation bay with rapid sequence induction and admit to paediatric intensive care for ongoing ventilatory support
options.rationale: Most severe croup responds to nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone; primary intubation is reserved for impending failure unresponsive to medical therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by clinical features rather than oxygen saturation, which often remains preserved until late. Mild croup has barking cough without stridor at rest, moderate croup has stridor at rest with minimal recession, and severe croup has stridor at rest with marked recession and distress. All severities receive corticosteroid because it reduces return visits and shortens illness duration. Nebulised adrenaline gives rapid relief in moderate to severe disease, with onset in 10 minutes and effect lasting up to two hours, so observation for at least three to four hours catches rebound.
key_points: Severity is clinical, not based on oxygen saturation
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally is used in moderate and severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline is added for stridor at rest with significant recession
Observe at least 3 to 3 hours (RCH minimum) after adrenaline for rebound
Avoid distressing the child to prevent acute airway compromise
explanation.pearls: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.5 mL/kg up to 5 mL acts in under 10 minutes but rebounds within 2 hours, hence the mandatory observation window.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old non-Aboriginal boy with a one-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and three days of vomiting. He has lost 3 kg and is breathing deeply at rest. He has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes. He is alert and oriented, capillary refill is three seconds and mucous membranes are dry. His weight today is 25 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 132, BP 102/64, RR 30, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Deep Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, GCS 15, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: BSL 26 mmol/L, capillary ketones 5.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.18, HCO3 9 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.1 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, corrected sodium 136 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid prescription for the first hour?

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes followed by deficit plus maintenance calculated over 48 hours with potassium added
options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA guidelines use a single 10 mL/kg bolus followed by deficit replacement over 48 hours; this approach minimises rapid osmolar shifts that precipitate cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 20 minutes repeated until perfusion improves followed by maintenance fluids at twice the normal rate
options.rationale: Large repeated boluses and accelerated maintenance increase the risk of cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA; current Australian practice restricts bolus to 10 mL/kg unless shocked. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous 8.4% sodium bicarbonate infusion at 2 mmol/kg over the first hour to correct the acidosis before fluids and insulin
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA because it worsens intracellular acidosis and increases cerebral oedema risk without changing outcome. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately and withhold all crystalloid fluids until the blood glucose has fallen below 14 mmol/L
options.rationale: Insulin without preceding fluid resuscitation worsens dehydration and precipitates hypokalaemia; fluid is started first and insulin is added after the first hour. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give 5% dextrose in 0.45% sodium chloride at twice maintenance rate immediately to provide glucose substrate and prevent further ketogenesis before insulin
options.rationale: Dextrose-containing fluid is added later when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L; initial resuscitation uses isotonic crystalloid to restore intravascular volume. (Source: APEG Paediatric DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric DKA and is linked to rapid fluid shifts. Australian APEG and RCH guidelines therefore standardise resuscitation to a single 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus unless the child is in shock, followed by calculated deficit replacement spread over 48 hours and maintenance using a two-bag system with potassium. Insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour begins after the first hour of fluids. Bicarbonate, large repeated boluses and accelerated correction are explicitly avoided.
key_points: Initial bolus is 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline unless shocked
Deficit is replaced over 48 hours, not 24
Insulin starts at least one hour after fluid resuscitation begins
Bicarbonate is not used in paediatric DKA
Cerebral oedema risk peaks 4 to 12 hours after treatment start
explanation.pearls: A sudden headache, altered conscious state or bradycardia after starting therapy mandates immediate 3% saline 5 mL/kg bolus and reduction of fluid rate for suspected cerebral oedema.

subtopic_detail: Unexplained bruising in a non-mobile infant
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 5-month-old non-Aboriginal infant brought to the emergency department by her mother for unsettled crying. She is not yet rolling. While undressing her you notice two purple bruises over the left mandible and one over the right pinna. Her mother says she has not noticed them and gives no clear mechanism. The child is otherwise alert and feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 100% room air
data_table.Examination: Two 1 cm purple bruises over left mandible, one over right pinna, anterior fontanelle soft, no torn frenulum, no skeletal tenderness, normal neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: FBE, coagulation studies, LFTs and lipase pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for skeletal survey, head CT, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages, and immediate child protection notification to the relevant state authority
options.rationale: Bruising in a non-mobile infant or in protected sites such as ears and mandible is a sentinel injury and requires admission, full non-accidental injury workup and statutory child protection notification. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Discharge home with safety netting advice once coagulation studies return normal, and arrange general practitioner review in 48 hours for ongoing assessment
options.rationale: Normal coagulation does not exclude inflicted injury; the location and mechanism profile mandate workup and notification regardless of laboratory results. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Reassure the mother that bruising in this distribution is common in infants and arrange paediatric outpatient review within one week for reassessment
options.rationale: Bruising in non-mobile infants is rare and never normal; reassurance is unsafe and misses a sentinel injury that predicts escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Request a urine drug screen and a metabolic bone disease panel to exclude inherited causes before notifying any external agencies of suspected harm
options.rationale: Delaying notification while awaiting metabolic workup is not safe; mandatory reporting is triggered by suspicion alone and proceeds in parallel with investigation. (Source: RACGP Child Protection Resource)

options.text: Refer to the social work team for community follow-up only and arrange return for repeat examination in two weeks if any further bruises appear at home
options.rationale: Community follow-up alone for an infant with a sentinel injury risks serious further harm; statutory notification and acute admission are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, or bruising in protected sites such as ears, mandible, neck, torso, buttocks or genitalia at any age, is a sentinel injury for non-accidental injury. The rule "those who don't cruise rarely bruise" highlights how rare any bruise is before independent mobility. Investigation includes skeletal survey, neuroimaging, retinal exam, coagulation studies and consideration of metabolic bone disease. Statutory mandatory reporting to child protection is triggered by suspicion and is independent of investigation results.
key_points: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is concerning until proven otherwise
Bruising of ears, mandible, neck and torso is high specificity for inflicted injury
Skeletal survey plus neuroimaging plus retinal review forms the standard workup
Mandatory reporting is triggered by suspicion, not confirmation
A normal coagulation panel does not exclude inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: Up to 30% of children later confirmed as physically abused have a recognised sentinel injury in the preceding weeks that was not reported, so escalation of any single suspicious bruise is the inflection point for prevention.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by his parents for tactile fever and reduced feeding for 12 hours. He was born at term, breastfed and previously well. He has no rash and no cough. His mother had a negative group B Streptococcus screen at 36 weeks and labour was uncomplicated. He has not received any antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C rectal, HR 168, RR 52, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Pink, perfused, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no rash, normal tone, no focus of infection identified on full undressed examination
data_table.Investigations: Pending - FBE, blood culture, urine via catheter, lumbar puncture, CRP, viral PCR

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home on oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with general practice review in 24 hours and clear advice about returning for warning signs
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics in a febrile infant under 3 months are inadequate cover for occult bacteraemia or meningitis and the infant requires admission with parenteral therapy and full workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Admit for full septic screen including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending culture results
options.rationale: Australian guidelines mandate full sepsis evaluation including lumbar puncture and empiric intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for any febrile infant under 3 months without a clear viral focus. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Perform urinalysis and chest x-ray only, and observe for four hours in the short stay unit before deciding on antibiotics if no source is identified
options.rationale: A limited workup misses occult meningitis and bacteraemia in this age group; the full septic screen plus empiric antibiotics is the standard of care under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Admit for observation without antibiotics until blood culture or urine culture results are available, given that the infant currently looks well clinically
options.rationale: Delaying empiric antibiotics in a young febrile infant is unsafe because clinical appearance is a poor predictor of serious bacterial infection at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg monotherapy and admit for observation without performing a lumbar puncture in a well-appearing infant
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone misses Listeria cover required under 3 months, and lumbar puncture is part of the standard workup in this age group regardless of clinical appearance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Febrile infants under 90 days have a significantly higher rate of serious bacterial infection than older children and clinical appearance is unreliable. Australian guidelines mandate a full septic screen including urine collected by catheter or supra-pubic aspirate, blood culture, lumbar puncture, FBE, CRP and consideration of viral PCR. Empiric intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers Listeria, group B Streptococcus and E coli, the most common pathogens at this age. Cefotaxime is added if meningitis is suspected.
key_points: Under 90 days, clinical appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection
Full septic workup includes blood culture, urine, and lumbar puncture
First-line empiric therapy is intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
Cefotaxime replaces ceftriaxone in neonates because of bilirubin displacement
Viral PCR may shorten antibiotic course if positive and infant clinically improves
explanation.pearls: Cefotaxime is preferred over ceftriaxone in the first 28 days of life because ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin and risks kernicterus.

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease recognition and IVIG window
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old non-Aboriginal boy on day 6 of fever. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips with a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, and a single left cervical lymph node measuring 17 mm. His hands and feet are swollen and erythematous. He is irritable but not septic. His mother is asking when his fever will resolve.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 °C, HR 158, RR 32, SpO2 98% room air, BP 95/55 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, fissured lips, indurated palms and soles, polymorphous trunk rash, one left cervical node 17 mm, no meningism, chest clear, no murmur, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.5 x10^9/L (neutrophils 13.2), platelets 555 x10^9/L, CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis 25 WBC/HPF sterile, throat swab negative for group A strep

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial cervical lymphadenitis with systemic features and review cultures at 48 hours
options.rationale: A solitary 17 mm node with multisystem mucocutaneous findings and sterile pyuria does not fit bacterial adenitis; antibiotic delay risks coronary aneurysm formation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours and oral aspirin, and arrange a baseline transthoracic echocardiogram
options.rationale: Five days of fever plus four of five principal criteria meet the diagnostic threshold; IVIG given before day 10 of illness reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk from roughly 25% to under 5%. Baseline echocardiography establishes a comparator for coronary surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Send paired viral PCR including adenovirus and measles, withhold treatment, and review in 48 hours once the viral panel results have been formally reported
options.rationale: A 48-hour observation period beyond day 6 of fever wastes the IVIG efficacy window; viral mimics rarely produce this combination of mucosal, extremity and laboratory findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as initial monotherapy and review in the general paediatric clinic within three days
options.rationale: Australian first-line treatment is IVIG plus aspirin; corticosteroid monotherapy is not standard initial therapy and is reserved for IVIG-resistant or high-risk subgroups. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Reassure that this is viral exanthem with reactive adenopathy, prescribe regular paracetamol and oral fluids, and review in primary care in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: Discharge would miss the IVIG window; the constellation of findings beyond five days of fever meets clinical Kawasaki disease criteria and mandates inpatient treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically when fever lasts five or more days with at least four of five principal features (conjunctivitis, oral changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy over 15 mm). Untreated, coronary artery aneurysms develop in around 25% of children. IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin given before day 10 reduces this to under 5%. Baseline echocardiography and follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks track coronary involvement.
key_points: Diagnosis requires fever 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 principal features in classic Kawasaki disease
IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin should be given before day 10 of illness
Coronary aneurysm risk falls from around 25% to under 5% with timely IVIG
Baseline echocardiogram is performed at diagnosis with follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks
Incomplete Kawasaki disease may be treated on fewer criteria if inflammatory markers and supportive features are present
explanation.pearls: Children under 12 months often present with incomplete Kawasaki disease and have the highest coronary aneurysm risk; CRP over 30 mg/L plus albumin under 30 g/L lowers the diagnostic threshold to 2 of 5 criteria.

stem: You are the special care nursery resident reviewing a 60-hour-old term non-Aboriginal infant born at 39+2 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth. The midwives noted yellow sclerae and the transcutaneous bilirubinometer reads above the screening threshold. The mother is blood group O Rh-positive; cord blood was not sent. The baby is breastfeeding 6 times in 24 hours and has lost 7% of birth weight. There is no cephalohaematoma and no family history of haemolytic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 144, RR 46, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundice to mid-thigh, no plethora, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal tone and Moro, suck coordinated
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 320 micromol/L (gestation-and-age threshold for phototherapy 290; exchange 430), conjugated fraction 6 micromol/L, FBC Hb 175 g/L reticulocytes 4%, blood group O Rh-positive, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion under intensive care given the rising bilirubin trajectory and risk of acute bilirubin encephalopathy
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold or for signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy; this baby is well below exchange. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Withhold phototherapy, supplement with formula top-ups of 30 mL every three hours, and repeat the bilirubin in 12 hours before deciding treatment
options.rationale: Routine formula top-ups are not indicated when feeding is adequate and weight loss is under 10%; this delay risks crossing the exchange threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy, continue frequent breastfeeding with lactation support, and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours to confirm a downward trend
options.rationale: Serum bilirubin sits above the phototherapy threshold for this gestation and age; intensive phototherapy with ongoing breastfeeding is first-line and a 6-hour repeat captures rebound or treatment failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin infusion to slow ongoing haemolysis and arrange transfer to the neonatal intensive care nursery for cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: IVIG is used for proven isoimmune haemolytic disease with a rapidly rising bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test is negative and there is no evidence of haemolysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Discharge home with parental education on jaundice warning signs and arrange routine community midwife review at 5 days of life for a repeat bilirubin
options.rationale: Discharge with a bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold risks bilirubin neurotoxicity; treatment is required before community follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Australian neonatal jaundice management uses gestation-and-age-specific phototherapy and exchange thresholds plotted against postnatal hours. Term infants with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia above the phototherapy line need intensive phototherapy and continued breastfeeding. A repeat bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours assesses response and excludes ongoing rise toward exchange. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia above 20% or 20 micromol/L always prompts a separate cholestasis workup.
key_points: Phototherapy and exchange thresholds vary by gestation and hours of age in Australian nomograms
Intensive phototherapy plus continued breastfeeding is first-line above the phototherapy line
Repeat serum bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours to confirm downward trend
Negative direct antiglobulin test plus normal haemoglobin and reticulocytes argues against isoimmune haemolysis
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and prompts cholestasis workup
explanation.pearls: A conjugated bilirubin over 20 micromol/L or over 20% of total in any jaundiced infant at any age mandates same-day investigation for biliary atresia because Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes deteriorate sharply after 60 days of life.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric anaphylaxis intramuscular adrenaline dose band
stem: You are the emergency department resident called to a 4-year-old non-Aboriginal boy who collapsed at a family meal where he was unknowingly given cashew. Within 10 minutes he developed urticaria, lip swelling and audible wheeze. He has known anaphylaxis to peanut. His EpiPen Jr was administered by his father 3 minutes before arrival. On arrival he remains wheezy with a hoarse cry and is sleepy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 156, RR 36, SpO2 90% room air rising to 96% on 8 L/min via face mask, BP 78/40 mmHg, weight estimated 16 kg by Broselow tape
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, marked lip and tongue swelling, audible stridor and biphasic wheeze, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 13 (eyes 3, verbal 4, motor 6)
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.6 mmol/L; no further investigations yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intramuscular promethazine 0.5 mg/kg, give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000, and arrange urgent ENT review for the stridor
options.rationale: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory features; nebulised adrenaline is adjunctive for upper airway oedema only and never replaces IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.30 mL into the lateral thigh, give 200 mg hydrocortisone IV, and continue 8 L oxygen via face mask
options.rationale: 0.30 mL of 1:1000 is the adult dose, twice the band for a 16 kg child; hydrocortisone has no role in acute resuscitation and delays definitive measures. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg bolus once intravenous access is established, sit him upright and prepare nebulised salbutamol
options.rationale: IV adrenaline bolus risks severe hypertension and arrhythmia in an unmonitored child; an IV infusion at 0.1 to 1 micrograms/kg/min is the correct escalation, not a bolus. Upright posture worsens distributive shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.15 mL into the lateral thigh, lay him flat with legs elevated, and prepare a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
options.rationale: Persistent anaphylaxis after one EpiPen Jr requires a repeat dose; the paediatric weight-band for under 20 kg is 0.15 mg (0.15 mL of 1:1000) IM. Supine positioning with legs elevated and crystalloid expansion treats distributive shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Withhold further adrenaline as one dose has been given, administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back-to-back, and reassess after the bronchodilator has been delivered
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension and airway features mandates repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes until resolved; withholding risks death from distributive shock or airway obstruction. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with prompt intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 dosed by weight band, with supine posture for hypotension and crystalloid resuscitation. ASCIA dosing is 0.15 mg (0.15 mL) for 7.5 to 20 kg, 0.3 mg (0.3 mL) for over 20 kg, repeating every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not save the airway or restore blood pressure and must not delay adrenaline. After two doses persistent shock requires an adrenaline infusion in a monitored setting.
key_points: IM adrenaline 1:1000 lateral thigh is first-line by weight band: 0.15 mg under 20 kg, 0.3 mg over 20 kg
Repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist or recur
Lay the patient flat with legs elevated for hypotension; never sit upright with shock
Crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus for hypotension that does not respond to first adrenaline
Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and never replace adrenaline
explanation.pearls: Two or more IM adrenaline doses or any persistent hypotension is the threshold to start an adrenaline infusion at 0.1 to 1 micrograms/kg/min and call retrieval if the child is in a non-tertiary centre.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old non-Aboriginal infant with a 9-day history of coryza now followed by 3 days of paroxysmal coughing spells ending in cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no inspiratory whoop. He has had one apnoeic episode of 25 seconds witnessed by his mother. His older brother had a bronchitic illness 3 weeks ago. The mother declined pertussis vaccination in pregnancy; the infant has not yet received his 6-week immunisations. The household includes a 28-week pregnant aunt.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 168, RR 56 between coughs, SpO2 91% room air, 96% on 1 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Alert between coughs, mild subcostal recession, chest clear between paroxysms, no focal crackles or wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: WCC 32 x10^9/L with absolute lymphocytosis 22 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal PCR pending for Bordetella pertussis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with reassurance pending the nasopharyngeal PCR result, withhold antibiotics until the test confirms a positive result, and review in 48 hours in the general paediatric clinic
options.rationale: Treatment should be empiric for infants with clinically compatible pertussis; awaiting PCR delays therapy that reduces transmission and may worsen the apnoea risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days with parental education on cough monitoring and ambulance criteria for cyanotic episodes
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no useful activity against Bordetella pertussis; an infant with witnessed apnoea cannot be safely managed at home. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit, commence oral erythromycin ethyl succinate 40 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 7 days, and continue intravenous fluid maintenance until feeding improves
options.rationale: Erythromycin in infants under one month carries a recognised pyloric stenosis risk and is poorly tolerated; azithromycin is preferred in this age group in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours, and arrange a lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis as a cause of the apnoea
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin does not cover pertussis; the lymphocytosis, paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting fit pertussis far better than meningitis and a lumbar puncture is not justified here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit to a monitored bed, commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days, and arrange household contact post-exposure prophylaxis through public health
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with suspected pertussis and apnoea require admission for monitoring; azithromycin is first-line in this age group and reduces transmission. Household contacts including the pregnant aunt warrant prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in infants under 6 months presents with apnoea, paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting, often without the classic whoop. Admission for cardiorespiratory monitoring is standard, and azithromycin is the preferred macrolide because erythromycin in neonates increases pyloric stenosis risk. Household contacts including pregnant women and other infants require post-exposure prophylaxis. Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks of every pregnancy is the most effective prevention.
key_points: Infants under 6 months with pertussis often present without the classic whoop
Apnoea, lymphocytosis and post-tussive vomiting are the key clues
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days is the first-line antibiotic in young infants
Erythromycin in neonates is associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Maternal pertussis vaccination at 20 to 32 weeks is the most effective infant prevention
explanation.pearls: A peripheral white cell count over 20 x10^9/L with marked lymphocytosis (over 50% lymphocytes) in an infant with paroxysmal cough has a high positive predictive value for pertussis and is associated with severe disease and pulmonary hypertension.

subtopic_detail: Reye-like syndrome in a child given aspirin during varicella
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old non-Aboriginal girl admitted with 24 hours of incessant vomiting, irritability and increasing somnolence. Five days earlier she developed a vesicular rash that her grandmother managed with regular oral aspirin 300 mg every 4 hours obtained from an overseas pharmacy. She has no other medical conditions and her immunisations are otherwise up to date. There is no fever, no diarrhoea and no recent travel. Her mother brought her in because she became confused and combative an hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132, RR 28 with intermittent yawning, SpO2 98% room air, BP 108/60 mmHg, capillary glucose 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Crusted varicella lesions on trunk and scalp, GCS 11 (eyes 2, verbal 4, motor 5) with hyperreflexia and brisk plantars, no neck stiffness, no focal deficit, liver edge palpable 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: ALT 1180 U/L, AST 1420 U/L, ammonia 165 micromol/L (normal under 50), INR 2.4, bilirubin 22 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, paracetamol level not detected, salicylate 1.8 mmol/L, CT brain shows diffuse cerebral oedema without focal lesion

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Administer N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg loading dose, withhold dextrose to avoid hyperglycaemia, and transfer to a ward bed for further serial liver function monitoring
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity and has unproven benefit here; withholding dextrose in hypoglycaemia worsens cerebral oedema and a ward bed is unsafe with GCS 11. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

options.text: Cease aspirin, escalate to paediatric intensive care for intracranial pressure management with intravenous 10% dextrose, hypertonic saline and head-of-bed elevation
options.rationale: The clinical picture is Reye-like encephalopathy from salicylate exposure during varicella: hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia, transaminitis without jaundice and cerebral oedema. Aspirin must stop, dextrose corrects hypoglycaemia, hypertonic saline lowers intracranial pressure, and PICU manages the airway and pressure monitoring. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 500 mg/m2 every 8 hours and intravenous ceftriaxone, perform a lumbar puncture once cerebral imaging is clear, and admit to the ward
options.rationale: There is no fever or meningism, varicella lesions are crusted and CT shows diffuse oedema without focal lesion making encephalitis unlikely; lumbar puncture risks coning with raised intracranial pressure. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg via nasogastric tube, give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to alkalinise the urine, and arrange transfer for haemodialysis of salicylate
options.rationale: Charcoal is not indicated 5 days after the last dose; urinary alkalinisation is for acute salicylate poisoning, not for Reye-like mitochondrial injury at a level of 1.8 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Withhold all medications, observe in the short stay unit overnight, and arrange a metabolic screen including urine organic acids before deciding further management
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with raised intracranial pressure, hypoglycaemia and INR 2.4 is unsafe; an inherited metabolic disorder is in the differential but does not change the immediate resuscitation priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Liver Failure)

explanation.summary: Reye syndrome is a mitochondrial encephalopathy classically triggered by aspirin during viral illness, particularly varicella and influenza. The picture is hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and cerebral oedema, but jaundice is characteristically absent. Mortality is high and treatment is supportive: cease the inciting drug, correct glucose, lower intracranial pressure with hypertonic saline and PICU-level care. Inherited fatty acid oxidation disorders such as MCAD deficiency can mimic Reye and should be excluded once stable.
key_points: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with raised ALT and AST but normal or near-normal bilirubin is the Reye picture
Aspirin during viral illness, especially varicella and influenza, is the classic trigger in children
Hypoglycaemia and cerebral oedema dominate the early presentation
Treatment is supportive: stop aspirin, give dextrose, hypertonic saline and PICU care
Inherited metabolic disorders such as MCAD deficiency mimic Reye and require post-stabilisation workup
explanation.pearls: Aspirin is contraindicated under 16 years of age in Australia outside Kawasaki disease and specific cardiology indications; any child presenting with encephalopathy after a viral illness needs salicylate, paracetamol and ammonia levels in the first hour.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old non-Aboriginal boy 2 weeks after admission for Henoch-Schonlein purpura with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs and severe abdominal pain that resolved on a short steroid course. His joint swelling and skin lesions have resolved. He is otherwise well and eating normally. His parents want to know what follow-up is needed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 108/68 mmHg (above the 95th centile for height and age)
data_table.Examination: Fading post-inflammatory pigmentation on buttocks and lower legs, no active purpura, no joint swelling, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 2+ protein 1+, urine protein:creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (normal under 20), serum creatinine 38 micromol/L, albumin 36 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents, plan routine urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for 12 months, and refer to paediatric nephrology for ongoing assessment
options.rationale: Persistent haematuria with proteinuria above 20 mg/mmol and hypertension after HSP defines significant nephritis that requires paediatric nephrology review and 12-month surveillance per RCH guidance. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Discharge to primary care with no further follow-up given the rash has resolved and the patient is otherwise clinically well at this stage
options.rationale: Up to a third of HSP nephritis develops within 6 weeks; discharge without urinalysis surveillance misses progressive renal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and arrange urgent renal biopsy on the inpatient ward to confirm the diagnosis and grade severity
options.rationale: Routine prednisolone does not prevent or treat established HSP nephritis with this level of proteinuria and is not indicated without nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressive disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Arrange a routine review in 6 months and rely on parental observation for blood pressure changes or new rash with no scheduled urinalysis testing in the interim
options.rationale: Parental observation cannot detect persistent microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria; structured urinalysis at defined intervals is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein Purpura)

options.text: Commence amlodipine 2.5 mg daily for the elevated blood pressure and review the urinalysis result in 6 weeks at the general practice clinic for further plan
options.rationale: Specific antihypertensive choice and dose in HSP nephritis should be decided by paediatric nephrology after biopsy decisions; ACE inhibitors are preferred when proteinuria is the driver. (Source: KHA-CARI Paediatric Nephrology Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HSP is a small-vessel IgA vasculitis where extra-renal features usually resolve in weeks but nephritis can develop or worsen over the following 6 months. Australian practice is structured urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 12 months from diagnosis. Nephrology referral is triggered by persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or rising creatinine. Renal biopsy and immunosuppression are reserved for severe or rapidly progressive nephritis.
key_points: HSP nephritis can develop or worsen for up to 6 months after the rash resolves
Structured urinalysis and BP at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 12 months is standard surveillance
Refer to paediatric nephrology for persistent proteinuria, hypertension or raised creatinine
Routine corticosteroids do not prevent or treat established HSP nephritis
ACE inhibitors are the preferred antihypertensive when proteinuria is present, started under specialist guidance
explanation.pearls: Sustained proteinuria over 6 months or any nephrotic-range proteinuria in HSP triggers same-day nephrology referral because biopsy-proven crescentic disease has the highest long-term risk of chronic kidney disease.

subtopic_detail: Acute gastroenteritis in a toddler with mild dehydration
stem: You are the paediatric emergency resident reviewing a 14-month-old non-Aboriginal girl with 36 hours of watery non-bloody diarrhoea and three episodes of vomiting earlier in the day. She has been refusing breastfeeds but accepts sips of water. She lives at home with vaccinated siblings, attended childcare in the last week, and had her rotavirus immunisations on schedule. She is alert, plays in mother's lap and has cried tears during examination. Her parents are worried about her not eating solids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill 2 seconds, weight 9.2 kg (down from 9.7 kg one week ago at the child health nurse visit)
data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, mucous membranes mildly dry, eyes not sunken, anterior fontanelle closed, abdomen soft non-tender, bowel sounds active, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L, urinalysis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer single-dose ondansetron 2 mg orally, observe for 30 minutes, then commence oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for the first hour
options.rationale: Ondansetron is reserved for children who cannot retain oral fluids due to vomiting; this child has not vomited in the past several hours and tolerates sips. The bolus rate suggested is also faster than guideline. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a peripheral cannula and commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at maintenance plus deficit replacement over 24 hours
options.rationale: IV fluids are second-line after failed oral or nasogastric rehydration in mild dehydration; first-attempt cannulation is unnecessarily invasive when oral fluid is tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Commence oral rehydration solution at 50 mL/kg over 4 hours given in 5 mL aliquots every 5 minutes, continue breastfeeding, and review at 4 hours
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend oral rehydration as first-line for mild to moderate dehydration with 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, continuing breastfeeding throughout. Review at 4 hours assesses fluid intake and tolerance. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and commence rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours given the failure of breastfeeding and the recent weight loss noted
options.rationale: NG rehydration is appropriate when oral feeding fails despite encouragement; this child has not yet been trialled on oral rehydration solution in titrated aliquots. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Prescribe loperamide 0.2 mg/kg as a single dose to reduce stool losses and discharge home with parental advice to push high-sugar fluids such as apple juice
options.rationale: Antidiarrhoeals are contraindicated in young children due to ileus and toxic megacolon risk; high-sugar fluids worsen osmotic diarrhoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

explanation.summary: Australian gastroenteritis management starts with structured oral rehydration solution given in small frequent aliquots, with breastfeeding continued. Mild to moderate dehydration is treated with 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance. Ondansetron and nasogastric rehydration are reserved for failure of oral therapy. Intravenous fluids are second-line for severe dehydration or failure of enteral routes. Antidiarrhoeals are not used in children.
key_points: Oral rehydration solution 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration
Continue breastfeeding throughout rehydration
Ondansetron is reserved for children unable to tolerate oral fluids due to vomiting
Nasogastric or intravenous fluids escalate when oral fails or dehydration is severe
Loperamide and other antidiarrhoeals are contraindicated in children
explanation.pearls: Bloody diarrhoea, prolonged duration over 10 days, or recent travel triggers a stool culture and PCR including shiga-toxin producing E. coli, because empirical antibiotics in E. coli O157 increase haemolytic uraemic syndrome risk.

subtopic_detail: Positive newborn screen with raised immunoreactive trypsinogen
stem: You are the paediatric registrar at the regional CF service called by a community midwife about a 12-day-old non-Aboriginal infant whose newborn screening card returned a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen with two CFTR mutations identified on the second-tier panel. The infant is asymptomatic, breastfeeding well and has regained birth weight. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. The parents have just been told there is a problem with the screening test and are anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well-perfused, chest clear, abdomen soft with normal stools, no nasal polyps, no failure to thrive
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screening IRT raised, CFTR genotype Phe508del / G551D, confirmatory tests not yet performed

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Refer to the general paediatric clinic in 6 weeks for routine review, with no specific cystic fibrosis testing planned until symptoms appear or weight gain falters in early infancy
options.rationale: A 6-week non-CF-specific review misses the early-intervention window; sweat testing within the first weeks of life is the Australian standard after a positive screen. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.text: Reassure the parents that the raised immunoreactive trypsinogen is a common false positive and arrange a repeat newborn screening card in 4 weeks before further action
options.rationale: Two pathogenic CFTR mutations on the second-tier panel makes false positivity extremely unlikely; delay risks pancreatic insufficiency presenting as failure to thrive. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.text: Commence pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy 2000 units lipase per 120 mL feed and arrange a chest X-ray plus high-resolution CT within the week to assess for bronchiectasis
options.rationale: Pancreatic enzymes are started after sweat test confirmation and evidence of fat malabsorption; routine chest imaging in an asymptomatic neonate is not indicated. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.text: Arrange urgent referral to the tertiary paediatric cystic fibrosis clinic for sweat chloride testing and structured family counselling within 1 week
options.rationale: Two CFTR mutations on the newborn screen still require sweat chloride confirmation and multidisciplinary CF clinic linkage; early diagnosis improves nutritional and respiratory outcomes. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement)
source_refs: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

options.text: Initiate oral azithromycin 5 mg/kg three times weekly for prophylaxis against Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation and order nasal swab surveillance every 6 weeks
options.rationale: Azithromycin and surveillance swabs are introduced later in CF care under specialist guidance; they are not the first step at diagnosis confirmation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Australian newborn screening uses raised immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by a second-tier CFTR genotype panel; two mutations strongly suggest cystic fibrosis but sweat chloride remains the confirmatory test. Early referral to a tertiary CF clinic enables sweat testing, family counselling, dietitian and physiotherapy linkage and surveillance microbiology. Pancreatic enzyme replacement and CFTR modulator decisions occur after confirmation. Time to diagnosis matters: early intervention improves growth and lung function.
key_points: IRT plus two CFTR mutations on newborn screening is highly suggestive but not diagnostic
Sweat chloride over 60 mmol/L confirms cystic fibrosis
Urgent referral to a tertiary CF clinic with multidisciplinary team is the next step
Pancreatic enzymes start after confirmation and evidence of malabsorption
CFTR modulators such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor are increasingly used from young ages in eligible genotypes
explanation.pearls: Sweat chloride values of 30 to 59 mmol/L are equivocal in infants under 6 months and require repeat testing and CF specialist input; values 60 mmol/L and above confirm diagnosis even with only one or no identified CFTR mutation.

sources.label: Cystic Fibrosis Australia Newborn Screening Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis severity and respiratory support escalation
stem: You are the paediatric resident on the inpatient ward reviewing a 7-week-old term infant on day 4 of a coryzal illness. He is breastfeeding only 40% of usual volumes and has had two episodes of brief apnoea overnight without colour change. He has no risk factors for chronic lung disease and is fully immunised for age. The night nursing team have escalated because of increasing work of breathing despite low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 92% on 1 L nasal prongs, BP 78/48 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, tracheal tug, widespread fine inspiratory crackles, mild expiratory wheeze, alert but tiring, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for RSV, capillary blood gas pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to SpO2 at least 90%, start nasogastric feeds, and reassess after 2 hours before escalation
options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG specifies standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%, with HFNC reserved for persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after a minimum 2-hour low-flow trial. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes plus nebulised hypertonic saline 3% three times daily to reduce mucus plugging
options.rationale: The RCH CPG advises against routine salbutamol and nebulised hypertonic saline in bronchiolitis as neither alters disease course. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Switch directly to humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 above 92% without a low-flow trial first
options.rationale: The RCH CPG reserves HFNC for failure of low-flow oxygen defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after at least 2 hours; bypassing the low-flow trial is not RCH-aligned. The 92% target is a NICE figure, not the RCH 90% target. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Arrange immediate rapid sequence intubation and ventilation in PICU given the apnoeic episodes and the rising capillary blood gas carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of escalating non-invasive support; the RCH ladder is low-flow first, then HFNC if low-flow fails, then PICU input for further escalation. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and liaise with paediatric retrieval and intensive care services immediately on arrival
options.rationale: Would be correct only after a documented failure of low-flow oxygen (persistent SpO2 below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours); HFNC is not the RCH first-line respiratory support. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Bronchiolitis CPG places standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen as the first-line respiratory support, titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%. HFNC is reserved for failure of low-flow oxygen, defined as persistent SpO2 below 90% or no respiratory improvement after a minimum 2-hour low-flow trial. Salbutamol, nebulised hypertonic saline, and corticosteroids are not routinely recommended.
key_points: RCH SpO2 target in bronchiolitis: at least 90%
First-line respiratory support: low-flow nasal prong oxygen
HFNC reserved for low-flow failure (SpO2 persistently below 90% or no improvement after at least 2 hours)
Salbutamol, hypertonic saline, corticosteroids not routinely used
explanation.pearls: The 92% SpO2 target is a NICE figure; the RCH CPG explicitly uses 90% and notes that brief desaturations below 90% alone are not an indication to start supplemental oxygen.

subtopic_detail: Moderate-severe croup nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 16-month-old non-Aboriginal boy brought in at 02:00 with a 24-hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing. He has stridor at rest and moderate sternal recession but remains pink in air. His mother says he has had similar but milder episodes twice before that settled at home. He is fully immunised and has no chronic conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, HR 158, RR 42, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate sternal and intercostal recession, hoarse cry, alert and consolable on mother's lap, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed; bedside Westley croup score 6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose, give paracetamol for fever and discharge home with safety-net advice if symptoms have settled within four hours of observation
options.rationale: Stridor at rest with moderate recession is at least moderate croup; corticosteroid alone without nebulised adrenaline misses the rapid airway benefit and discharge at four hours is too early after adrenaline-eligible disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Commence nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back, add ipratropium bromide and reassess in 30 minutes for response to bronchodilator therapy and need for paediatric admission
options.rationale: Bronchodilators target lower airway smooth muscle and have no role in supraglottic-subglottic oedema of croup. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with oxygen and concurrent oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, then observe in the department for 3 hours (RCH minimum) with attention to recurrence of stridor at rest
options.rationale: Moderate-severe croup with stridor at rest mandates nebulised adrenaline plus a single dexamethasone dose; the benefit of adrenaline wanes by 2 hours so a 3 hours (RCH minimum) observation window screens for rebound. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Take lateral neck radiograph and arrange urgent ENT review for direct laryngoscopy in theatre because of recurrent stridor and possible foreign body or epiglottitis given his age and presentation
options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive treatment and provokes distress; classic prodrome, barking cough and absence of drooling or toxic appearance argue against epiglottitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Provide humidified oxygen via face mask, position on parent's lap and reassess every 15 minutes for spontaneous improvement before considering any pharmacological intervention or admission to the ward
options.rationale: Humidified air alone is no longer recommended and delays effective therapy that meaningfully reduces stridor and admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded by stridor and recession; stridor at rest with moderate recession defines moderate-severe disease and triggers nebulised adrenaline plus a single dose of dexamethasone. Adrenaline acts within 30 minutes and effects wane by 2 hours, so observation for 3 hours (RCH minimum) after the dose detects rebound stridor. Dexamethasone benefits all severities of croup and reduces re-presentation. Humidified air, antibiotics and bronchodilators are not recommended in viral croup. Children who remain stridor-free at rest after 3 hours (RCH minimum) can be discharged with safety-net advice.
key_points: Stridor at rest defines moderate-severe croup
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL acts within 30 minutes and wanes by 2 hours
Single oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg covers all severities
3 hours (RCH minimum) after adrenaline to detect rebound
Avoid lateral neck X-ray in suspected epiglottitis-resembling presentations
explanation.pearls: Recurrent or atypical croup under 6 months or over 6 years warrants ENT review for subglottic stenosis or anatomical narrowing; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose is non-inferior to 0.6 mg/kg in mild croup at the lower dose.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 5-month-old girl who has been admitted with her first febrile urinary tract infection. She responded to intravenous cefotaxime within 24 hours, defervesced and is now feeding well; there are no atypical features. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefalexin and trimethoprim. Antenatal anomaly scans were complete and normal, and her parents have no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, BP 88/52 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable bladder or flank mass, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Mid-stream clean catch urine: leucocytes 250/microL, nitrites positive, culture E. coli over 100 x10^6 CFU/L cefotaxime sensitive; FBC, UEC and CRP within paediatric reference ranges after treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan from here?

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound during this admission and a micturating cystourethrogram if hydronephrosis or scarring is demonstrated on the scan
options.rationale: The RCH urinary tract infection guideline reserves ultrasound during the acute illness for atypical urinary tract infection; with normal antenatal scans and a typical responsive first urinary tract infection at 5 months it is not routinely required. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: No additional imaging is required after this typical first urinary tract infection; counsel the family on prompt presentation for any future febrile illness
options.rationale: Royal Children's Hospital guidance states that most children do not require any imaging after a first urinary tract infection; ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection, and a renal tract ultrasound is only mandatory for infants under 6 months when antenatal monitoring was incomplete or there is recurrence.
