(Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Arrange a DMSA renogram within 4 weeks and a micturating cystourethrogram for all infants under 12 months after a first febrile urinary tract infection regardless of severity
options.rationale: DMSA and routine micturating cystourethrogram are part of the NICE algorithm and are not in the RCH cascade after a single uncomplicated treatment-responsive first urinary tract infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection; NICE NG224)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the urinary tract during this admission to exclude calculus and complex anomaly given the young age of the infant and high colony count
options.rationale: Computed tomography is not first-line imaging in paediatric urinary tract infection because of radiation exposure; ultrasound is the appropriate modality when imaging is indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

options.text: Commence long-term low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg nocte and defer renal tract imaging until age 2 years unless a further breakthrough urinary tract infection develops
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is reserved for recurrent urinary tract infection or significant reflux and is not used routinely after an uncomplicated first urinary tract infection in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary Tract Infection)

explanation.summary: After a typical first febrile urinary tract infection in an infant with a good response to treatment and a normal antenatal renal tract on anomaly scanning, the RCH guideline does not mandate any imaging. Imaging during the acute illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection (seriously unwell, poor urine flow, non-E. coli organism, raised creatinine, sepsis, or no response within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics). Infants under 6 months without complete antenatal monitoring, or those with recurrence, get a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound. Routine DMSA and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE constructs not adopted by RCH.
key_points: Most children need no imaging after a first urinary tract infection per RCH
Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection
Under-6-month infants with absent antenatal scans or recurrence get a renal tract ultrasound
Routine DMSA and micturating cystourethrogram are NICE-based and not in RCH cascade
Computed tomography is not first-line in paediatric urinary tract infection
explanation.pearls: Atypical urinary tract infection criteria that escalate imaging: seriously unwell appearance, poor urine flow, non-E. coli organism, raised creatinine, sepsis, or failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics within 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Suspected meningococcal sepsis lumbar puncture timing
stem: You are the night paediatric registrar at a tertiary children's hospital. A 22-month-old non-Aboriginal boy has been transferred by retrieval after 8 hours of fever and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash on the trunk and limbs. He was alert in the field but is now drowsy, with rising oxygen requirements and prolonged capillary refill despite 40 mL/kg of crystalloid given pre-transfer. The retrieval team has commenced ceftriaxone empirically and asks what investigation pathway you want pursued on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 188, RR 48, SpO2 92% on 6 L Hudson, BP 78/40 mmHg, capillary refill 5 seconds, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric rash on trunk and limbs with new lesions in the last hour, mottled peripheries, cool extremities, no neck stiffness, fontanelle closed, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.18, lactate 6.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, FBC WCC 22 x10^9/L platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, CRP 220 mg/L, blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for lumbar puncture?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture in the emergency department before any further fluid resuscitation to obtain cerebrospinal fluid before any further antibiotic doses alter culture yield and direct narrow-spectrum therapy
options.rationale: Shock, coagulopathy and rapidly progressive purpura are contraindications to immediate LP in suspected meningococcal disease; blood and skin biopsy PCR retain diagnostic yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture immediately after intubation and a second bolus of crystalloid, sending samples for cell count culture and meningococcal polymerase chain reaction before any further antibiotic doses
options.rationale: Intubation does not remove the LP contraindications of coagulopathy and shock; antibiotics should not be delayed for any LP in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer lumbar puncture for at least 24 hours and arrange a non-contrast computed tomography of the brain before any lumbar puncture is attempted, irrespective of haemodynamic and coagulation status at that point
options.rationale: Routine CT before LP does not exclude raised intracranial pressure and adds delay without changing the immediate threshold for LP. (Source: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s)
source_refs: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s

options.text: Defer lumbar puncture, continue empirical ceftriaxone, send blood for meningococcal polymerase chain reaction and serology and consider lumbar puncture later only once shock coagulopathy and rapidly evolving rash have resolved
options.rationale: Shock, coagulopathy (INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0), rapidly evolving purpura and GCS under 13 are all contraindications to LP; PCR on blood and skin biopsy plus blood culture obtains the microbiological diagnosis without delay. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal disease)

options.text: Defer lumbar puncture but discontinue ceftriaxone, switch to vancomycin and aciclovir empirically and recommence ceftriaxone only after blood polymerase chain reaction and culture results are available within 24 hours
options.rationale: Empirical ceftriaxone is the cornerstone of paediatric meningococcal sepsis therapy; switching to vancomycin plus aciclovir is not indicated in this clinical pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal disease when there is shock, coagulopathy, rapidly evolving purpura, focal neurology, GCS under 13 or signs of raised intracranial pressure. Antibiotics should never be delayed for an LP in a deteriorating child. Blood culture, blood meningococcal PCR and skin lesion PCR have high yield in invasive meningococcal disease without requiring CSF. LP can be performed later once the child has stabilised and contraindications have resolved.
key_points: Shock, coagulopathy, GCS under 13 and rapidly evolving purpura contraindicate LP
Empirical ceftriaxone must not be delayed for any LP
Blood and skin PCR retain meningococcal diagnostic yield
Routine CT before LP does not reliably exclude raised ICP
LP can be deferred and performed once contraindications resolve
explanation.pearls: In paediatric meningococcal sepsis, fluid resuscitation past 40 mL/kg without haemodynamic response is the trigger for intubation, vasopressor support and admission to intensive care; dexamethasone is not given when the dominant picture is sepsis without proven bacterial meningitis.

sources.label: NICE NG143 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease in under 16s

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury workup in an infant
stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-month-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by his father for being unsettled. On examination the child has a spiral fracture of the left humerus, multiple bruises of varying ages on the trunk and back and a small frenular tear. The father's explanation is that the baby rolled off the lounge yesterday and was crying intermittently. The infant is otherwise developmentally appropriate and feeds normally. He is medically stable and analgesia has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 148, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, BP 86/50 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Spiral fracture left humerus on radiograph, three trunk bruises of varying ages, frenular tear, no external head injury or seizure activity, anterior fontanelle soft, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT, coagulation profile within paediatric reference ranges, left humerus radiograph confirms spiral fracture, no other imaging performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate investigation pathway?

options.text: Admit for analgesia and arrange a full skeletal survey, fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist, non-contrast head computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging and make a mandatory report to the child protection authority
options.rationale: Spiral long-bone fractures, frenular tear and unexplained multi-age bruising in a non-mobile infant mandate full child protection workup including skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and a statutory report. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)
source_refs: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

options.text: Splint the humeral fracture, organise outpatient orthopaedic follow-up within 1 week and discharge home with social work liaison through the general paediatric clinic the following morning
options.rationale: Discharge home in suspected non-accidental injury before completing the workup and statutory report places the child at ongoing risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Arrange a head computed tomography scan only, defer skeletal survey and ophthalmology until the family have given informed consent and discuss further investigation with the consultant paediatrician in the morning
options.rationale: Limiting imaging and deferring statutory reporting until family consent is obtained breaches mandatory reporting obligations and risks missed occult injury. (Source: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management)
source_refs: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

options.text: Send extensive bone profile vitamin D and copper studies before any skeletal survey to first exclude metabolic bone disease as a cause of the spiral fracture, then reconsider child protection reporting in 48 hours
options.rationale: Metabolic bone disease is exceptionally rare and should not delay the standard non-accidental injury workup or mandatory reporting in this clinical pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Arrange a full skeletal survey now but defer fundoscopy and head imaging until the infant develops neurological signs such as seizures, vomiting, lethargy or focal weakness on serial paediatric review
options.rationale: Occult abusive head trauma occurs without external signs; fundoscopy and neuroimaging are part of the routine workup, not symptom-triggered. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Suspected non-accidental injury in a pre-mobile infant requires a structured workup including skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy by ophthalmology, baseline bloods and a statutory report. Frenular tears, posterior trunk bruising and spiral long-bone fractures in non-mobile infants are sentinel injuries with a high yield for occult injury. Mandatory reporting obligations apply to all medical practitioners in every Australian jurisdiction. Care planning and discharge decisions are made jointly with the child protection authority and not by the treating team alone.
key_points: Frenular tear, posterior bruising and spiral fracture in a non-mobile infant are sentinel for abuse
Workup is skeletal survey, neuroimaging, fundoscopy and baseline bloods
Mandatory reporting to the state child protection authority is required
Metabolic bone disease evaluation does not delay protective action
Discharge planning is joint with child protection
explanation.pearls: A skeletal survey repeat at 11-14 days improves yield for healing rib and metaphyseal fractures that are occult on the first set; classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures are highly specific for non-accidental injury.

sources.label: RACGP: Child Abuse Identification and Management

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid management at presentation
stem: You are the paediatric registrar receiving a 9-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. She has been brought in by her parents after a day of vomiting and increasing drowsiness. She is breathing deeply with a fruity odour to her breath and is moderately dehydrated. There is no clinical evidence of cerebral oedema. Her weight today is 28 kg. The endocrinology consultant has confirmed first-presentation type 1 diabetes complicated by DKA and asks you to write up the initial fluid plan.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 132, RR 32 deep Kussmaul, SpO2 99% room air, BP 102/64 mmHg, GCS 14, capillary refill 3 seconds, weight 28 kg
data_table.Examination: Reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, mild acetone breath, alert and orientated, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28.4 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, venous gas pH 7.10 pCO2 19 mmHg HCO3 6 mmol/L base excess minus 22, Na 132 corrected 137 mmol/L, K 4.5 mmol/L, urea 9.0 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?

options.text: Bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes and immediately commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour with hourly neurological observations and electrolyte checks
options.rationale: Rapid 20 mL/kg boluses and immediate insulin (before 1 hour of fluid replacement) increase the risk of paediatric cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

options.text: Give 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at maintenance plus 10% deficit replacement over 24 hours and commence intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour at the same time as fluids start
options.rationale: Insulin should not start until at least 1 hour of intravenous fluids has been delivered in paediatric DKA. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

options.text: Give 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes, then commence 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance plus 5-7% deficit over 48 hours and start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour after 1 hour
options.rationale: Paediatric DKA replacement uses cautious boluses (10 mL/kg) and a 48-hour deficit-plus-maintenance approach with insulin started after 1 hour and at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour to minimise cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg of Hartmann's compound sodium lactate over 60 minutes followed by maintenance fluids without potassium and review for insulin commencement when the venous gas has normalised on subsequent venous blood gas
options.rationale: Potassium replacement starts with the initial maintenance bag once urine output is present; awaiting gas normalisation prolongs ketosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give 8.4% sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the acidosis before commencing any insulin infusion and use total body water deficit calculation to dictate replacement rate over 12 hours
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA and a 12-hour rapid correction increases cerebral oedema risk. (Source: APEG paediatric DKA guideline)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management is built around cautious volume restoration and slow correction over 48 hours to reduce the risk of cerebral oedema. Initial boluses are typically 10 mL/kg unless there is shock, with the deficit estimated at 5-7% and replaced together with maintenance over 48 hours. Insulin is started after at least 1 hour of fluid at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour. Potassium is added once urine output is established. Bicarbonate is avoided.
key_points: Initial bolus 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline unless shocked
Replace 5-7% deficit plus maintenance over 48 hours
Insulin 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour starting after 1 hour of fluids
Potassium added with first maintenance bag once urine output is present
Avoid bicarbonate; monitor for cerebral oedema with hourly neuro obs
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA include age under 5 years, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis (pH under 7.1), bicarbonate therapy and rapid fluid administration over 50 mL/kg in the first 4 hours.

subtopic_detail: Suspected airway foreign body in a toddler
stem: You are the paediatric emergency registrar reviewing an 18-month-old non-Aboriginal boy brought in with sudden onset of coughing and stridor while playing in the lounge room. His grandmother thinks he may have put a peanut in his mouth shortly before the episode. He is now alert, breathing spontaneously and stable but has persistent inspiratory stridor and intermittent coughing. There is no cyanosis and he is maintaining oxygen saturation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 142, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Awake, alert and consolable on mother's lap, intermittent strong cough, audible inspiratory stridor at rest, mild subcostal recession, breath sounds slightly reduced on right, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: No imaging yet performed; bedside cardiorespiratory monitoring in place

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts immediately because the persistent inspiratory stridor confirms complete airway obstruction warranting basic life support manoeuvres before any expert airway help arrives
options.rationale: Effective coughing and ongoing stridor indicate partial obstruction; back blows and thrusts risk converting partial to complete obstruction. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 4 Airway)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for presumed viral croup and observe in the short stay unit for 4 hours before any specialist referral or further investigation
options.rationale: Sudden onset while eating and asymmetric breath sounds suggest foreign body, not viral croup, and bronchodilators or steroids do not address aspiration. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

options.text: Arrange an inspiratory and expiratory chest radiograph and review again only after the imaging is reported by a paediatric radiologist before deciding whether ENT or theatre referral is required
options.rationale: Normal radiographs do not exclude foreign body aspiration; ENT referral should not be deferred for imaging in an evolving airway presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

options.text: Commence direct laryngoscopy in the emergency department to retrieve the suspected peanut promptly under topical anaesthesia rather than transfer the child to the operating theatre with anaesthetic and ENT support
options.rationale: Awake direct laryngoscopy in a stridorous toddler risks complete obstruction; rigid bronchoscopy by ENT in theatre with anaesthetic support is the standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

options.text: Keep the child calm in the parent's arms with supplemental oxygen as tolerated, fast for theatre, contact ENT and anaesthetics urgently for rigid bronchoscopy and avoid distressing procedures or instrumentation
options.rationale: Partial airway obstruction from a suspected foreign body is managed by minimising distress, keeping the child upright in the parent's lap and arranging urgent rigid bronchoscopy under anaesthetic with ENT. (Source: RCH CPG: Inhaled foreign body)

explanation.summary: Suspected foreign body aspiration in a child with effective cough or stridor at rest is partial airway obstruction and is managed by minimising distress, supplemental oxygen as tolerated and urgent rigid bronchoscopy under anaesthetic. Back blows and chest thrusts are reserved for the child with ineffective cough or unconsciousness. Plain radiographs are insensitive for organic foreign bodies and should not delay ENT referral. Inhaled peanut is the commonest organic foreign body in toddlers.
key_points: Partial airway obstruction is managed by keeping the child calm with parents
Rigid bronchoscopy by ENT in theatre is the standard intervention
Back blows and thrusts are for ineffective cough or unconscious patients
Plain X-ray can be normal in radiolucent foreign bodies
Bronchodilators and corticosteroids do not treat foreign body aspiration
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric breath sounds, persistent unilateral wheeze or new-onset chronic cough in a toddler with a witnessed choking event are red flags for retained foreign body even with a normal radiograph; bronchoscopy under anaesthetic is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

subtopic_detail: Faltering growth in an exclusively breastfed infant
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 5-month-old exclusively breastfed non-Aboriginal infant whose weight has dropped from the 50th centile at birth to below the 3rd centile today, crossing two major centile lines over 8 weeks. His mother describes good attachment with feeds approximately every 3 hours but reports that he has slow weight gain at recent maternal child health nurse visits. There are no concerning features in the history and developmental milestones are appropriate for age.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, BP 86/52 mmHg, weight 5.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, normal tone and posture, soft anterior fontanelle, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiac and respiratory examination, abdomen soft non-tender with no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart shows downward crossing of 2 centile lines over 8 weeks, no bloods or imaging performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange admission for nasogastric supplemental feeds while a paediatric metabolic workup including amino acids, acylcarnitine profile and very long chain fatty acids is performed and reviewed by metabolic specialists
options.rationale: Inpatient metabolic workup is reserved for atypical features or no response to standard feeding interventions; first-line management focuses on feeding optimisation and a stepped outpatient workup. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)

options.text: Arrange a structured feeding history and observed feed with lactation support, a stool history for malabsorption, a focused examination and baseline investigations including FBC iron studies UEC LFT TFT urinalysis and coeliac serology
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends a structured feeding assessment, observed feed and baseline screen (FBC, iron, UEC, LFT, TFT, urinalysis, coeliac) before escalating to inpatient or specialist workup in non-organic faltering growth. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)

options.text: Refer immediately to a paediatric gastroenterologist for an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, jejunal biopsy and stool elastase to evaluate for malabsorption due to coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis or eosinophilic enteropathy
options.rationale: Endoscopy and stool elastase are second-line tests after a baseline screen and feeding assessment have failed to identify a cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Faltering growth)

options.text: Recommend immediate introduction of cow's milk formula every 3 hours alongside continued breastfeeding and review weight gain in 2 weeks regardless of the maternal preference for exclusive breastfeeding
options.rationale: Formula top-ups are introduced only after a structured feeding assessment confirms inadequate breastmilk transfer; routine introduction overrides maternal preference and undermines lactation. (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure the mother that the centile chart drop reflects genetic potential and adequate exclusive breastfeeding and arrange a routine weight review at the maternal child health nurse appointment in 4 weeks' time
options.rationale: Crossing 2 or more centile lines is faltering growth and warrants structured assessment; reassurance without further evaluation misses treatable causes. (Source: RACGP Red Book Faltering Growth)

explanation.summary: Crossing 2 or more major centile lines in infancy meets the definition of faltering growth and warrants stepped assessment in primary care. The first step is a structured feeding history, observed feed with lactation support, a comprehensive examination and a baseline investigation panel. Inpatient or specialist evaluation is reserved for severe deficit, red flags or failure to respond. Reassurance without assessment risks missing breastfeeding difficulties, coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis or other treatable causes.
key_points: Crossing 2 major centiles defines faltering growth
First-line is feeding assessment and outpatient baseline screen
Baseline screen: FBC, iron, UEC, LFT, TFT, urinalysis, coeliac
Lactation support precedes formula top-up in breastfeeding infants
Specialist referral is for red flags or failed first-line management
explanation.pearls: Red flags that bypass the staged outpatient workup and trigger admission include weight under 70% of expected, severe undernutrition signs, suspected child protection concerns, dysmorphic features or atypical examination findings.

subtopic_detail: Functional chronic constipation Movicol disimpaction and maintenance
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 4-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a 14-month history of infrequent painful bowel motions, with stool frequency of 1 to 2 per week, frequent staining of underwear with small amounts of liquid stool between hard motions, and observed stool-withholding behaviour. There is a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain. She has met all developmental milestones, is fully toilet trained for urine, and has no symptoms of urinary tract infection. Examination shows a palpable suprapubic mass consistent with faecal loading, normal anal position and tone, no sacral dimple, and normal lower limb neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 104, BP not routinely measured at age 4, weight 17 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Palpable suprapubic faecal mass, normal anal exam, no anal fissures, normal perineum and sacrum, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging required for diagnosis of functional constipation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase dietary fibre to 18 grams daily through fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, encourage 1.5 litres of fluid intake per day, and reassess at 4 weeks before considering any pharmacological intervention or specific oral stool-softening therapy
options.rationale: Dietary advice alone in the presence of demonstrable faecal impaction is insufficient; disimpaction with osmotic laxatives is recommended first to break the cycle. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric gastroenterology for anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung's disease given the duration of symptoms and presence of overflow soiling at the age of presentation
options.rationale: Hirschsprung's disease typically presents in infancy with delayed meconium passage; functional constipation does not require biopsy unless red flags are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Administer paraffin oil 5 mL orally twice daily and arrange daily glycerine suppositories for 7 days followed by ongoing rectal interventions if dietary modifications fail to soften stool after this initial disimpaction phase of intensive treatment
options.rationale: Oral disimpaction with high-dose polyethylene glycol is preferred over invasive rectal interventions in children, which can be traumatic and worsen stool-withholding behaviour. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Disimpact with high-dose polyethylene glycol 3350 with electrolytes (Movicol Junior) 4 sachets daily, increasing to 8 sachets daily as needed for 3 to 7 days until impaction clears, then transition to maintenance Movicol 1 to 2 sachets daily with toileting routines and parent education
options.rationale: RCH guidance recommends oral disimpaction with high-dose Movicol Junior (escalating regimen until impaction clears) followed by maintenance therapy with sustained Movicol for 3+ months alongside behavioural toileting program. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe lactulose 5 mL twice daily for 3 months as the only intervention required for functional childhood constipation alongside oral fluid encouragement and gradual increase in dietary fibre over the next month
options.rationale: Disimpaction must precede maintenance; lactulose alone without disimpaction or behavioural intervention in the setting of faecal impaction is inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation in children is the cause of over 90% of presentations. Diagnosis is clinical (Rome IV criteria: 2+ of 2 or fewer defecations per week, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard motions, large diameter stools, faecal mass on exam, soiling in toilet-trained child). Red flags suggesting organic cause include delayed meconium past 48 hours, failure to thrive, fever, vomiting, abnormal anal exam or neurology, sacral abnormalities. Management is disimpaction with oral PEG (Movicol Junior, escalating doses), then maintenance for at least 3 months, plus toileting behavioural program. Avoid rectal interventions where possible.
key_points: Functional constipation: clinical diagnosis (Rome IV), 90% of cases
Red flags: delayed meconium, FTT, abnormal anal exam, neurology
Disimpaction: Movicol Junior 4-8 sachets daily over 3-7 days
Maintenance: Movicol 1-2 sachets daily for at least 3 months
Behavioural: regular toileting after meals, reward charts
explanation.pearls: Premature cessation of maintenance laxatives in the first 6 months is the single most common cause of relapse; counsel families that hard-stool memories take months to fade and that staying on maintenance through a painless interval is the actual treatment, not just a dose.

sources.label: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schonlein purpura with renal involvement and timing of follow-up
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy in the emergency department with a 5-day history of a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent colicky abdominal pain for 3 days, and now a swollen painful right ankle. He has been previously well, fully immunised, no recent medication, and had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago.

He is haemodynamically stable. On examination there is a typical non-blanching palpable purpuric rash on the lower limbs and buttocks, a swollen tender right ankle, mild abdominal tenderness without peritonism, and normal genitalia.

data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura buttocks/lower limbs, right ankle swollen tender, abdomen mildly tender, no peritonism, normal scrotum
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WBC 9.4, Hb 124, plt 320; UEC normal; urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 1+, no casts; urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol; BP 102/64

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit for IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks and arrange urgent renal biopsy because of the proteinuria and microscopic haematuria at presentation
options.rationale: ACR 18 mg/mmol with blood 2+ is not nephrotic-range and does not warrant biopsy or pulsed steroids; HSP nephritis is monitored with urine and BP at follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

options.text: Discharge home with simple analgesia, supportive care, and a structured follow-up schedule of weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 2 months and then 3-monthly checks for 12 months to detect delayed HSP nephritis
options.rationale: Typical HSP with mild renal findings is managed with home follow-up; serial urinalysis and BP are recommended weekly for 1-2 months then 3-6 monthly for at least 12 months to detect delayed nephritis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

options.text: Admit for observation with intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically until a complete septic workup including blood cultures, CSF and lumbar puncture confirms or excludes meningococcal sepsis
options.rationale: Palpable purpura in HSP is a vasculitic eruption not meningococcal sepsis; the child is well, afebrile with characteristic distribution. Septic workup and broad antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

options.text: Admit for monitoring and arrange abdominal ultrasound urgently to exclude intussusception given the abdominal pain, before reassessment to determine outpatient management at the end of the admission period
options.rationale: HSP can cause intussusception (typically ileoileal) but it is not the most likely cause of mild abdominal pain in this child; routine US is not indicated unless pain is severe, persistent or there is bilious vomiting or PR bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days for arthralgia and abdominal pain without altering renal follow-up plan, on the basis that early steroids prevent progression to chronic HSP nephritis
options.rationale: Steroids do not prevent or alter incidence of HSP nephritis; they are reserved for severe symptoms (significant abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, severe arthralgia, established nephritis with crescents). (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis))

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the commonest small-vessel vasculitis of childhood. Diagnosis is clinical: palpable purpura with at least one of arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, biopsy-proven IgA deposition or renal involvement. Renal involvement (microscopic haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, nephritis) occurs in 20 to 40% and is the major long-term morbidity. Most cases self-resolve. Monitoring: urinalysis and BP weekly for 1-2 months, then 3-monthly for 12 months. Refer to nephrology if nephrotic-range proteinuria (UPCR over 200 mg/mmol or ACR over 250 mg/mmol), persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension, eGFR decline or significant haematuria/casts. Steroids do not prevent nephritis but are used for severe symptoms.
key_points: HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis/abd pain/IgA biopsy/renal involvement
Renal involvement in 20-40%; major long-term morbidity
Monitoring: urinalysis + BP weekly for 1-2 months then 3-monthly for 12 months
Steroids: severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, established nephritis
Refer nephrology: nephrotic-range, persistent significant proteinuria, hypertension, eGFR decline
explanation.pearls: Scrotal involvement in HSP can mimic testicular torsion; bedside ultrasound showing scrotal wall oedema with normal testicular Doppler flow supports HSP scrotal involvement and avoids unnecessary surgical exploration.

sources.label: Royal College of Paediatrics: HSP guideline

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice phototherapy threshold and risk-factor adjustment
stem:
You are the paediatric resident in the postnatal ward reviewing a 3-day-old term female neonate (40+2 weeks at birth, birthweight 3350 g) brought to the special care nursery because of yellowing of the skin extending to the trunk. She is breastfeeding 8 times per day, has wet nappies and is alert and active. Born by uncomplicated SVD. Mother's blood group A positive, infant's blood group B positive, direct Coombs negative.

Total serum bilirubin taken at 72 hours of age is 290 micromol/L (unconjugated 282), conjugated 8. The mother is Rh negative and received antenatal anti-D appropriately.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 142, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice cephalocaudally to the chest, alert and active, normal tone, no cephalohaematoma or bruising, normal cardiac and respiratory exam
data_table.Investigations: TSB 290 micromol/L at 72 hours, conjugated 8, unconjugated 282, Hb 168 g/L, reticulocytes 4%, Coombs negative, blood group B+, maternal A+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure mother that the bilirubin level is below the phototherapy threshold for a term well infant at 72 hours, advise on continued breastfeeding 8 to 12 times a day and arrange repeat bilirubin level at 96 hours
options.rationale: TSB 290 at 72 hours in a term infant crosses the phototherapy threshold per AAP/RCH nomograms; deferral risks further rise toward exchange-transfusion territory. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange urgent exchange transfusion because the bilirubin level of 290 micromol/L is in the kernicterus risk zone in a 72-hour-old infant and immediate dual-volume exchange transfusion is mandated to prevent neurological injury
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion threshold in a term infant at 72 hours is around 425 micromol/L (AAP) with no risk factors; 290 is below exchange threshold and warrants phototherapy first. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Investigate further with thyroid function, urine for reducing substances and G6PD screen given the elevated bilirubin and risk of metabolic causes before starting phototherapy because the level is unusual for breastfeeding-related jaundice
options.rationale: Breastfeeding-related jaundice and ABO setoff are reasonable considerations; investigations are useful but should not delay initiation of phototherapy at this level. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg over 4 hours because of the presence of ABO blood group setoff between mother (A) and infant (B) and the rising bilirubin trajectory, before considering phototherapy
options.rationale: IVIG is used for isoimmune haemolytic disease (Rh or ABO) with positive Coombs and rising bilirubin despite phototherapy approaching exchange threshold; Coombs is negative here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive (multi-light) phototherapy with monitoring of bilirubin in 6 hours, support continued breastfeeding with potential top-ups if hydration is suboptimal, and review for risk factors that would lower the threshold
options.rationale: TSB 290 at 72 hours crosses the phototherapy threshold for a term infant without risk factors; intensive phototherapy, ongoing feeding support and repeat TSB in 6 hours are recommended. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice is common; in term well infants without haemolysis the AAP/RCH 2022 nomogram thresholds for phototherapy at 72 hours are approximately 290 to 300 micromol/L (with thresholds adjusted lower with risk factors: gestational age under 38 weeks, isoimmune haemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, sepsis, significant lethargy or temperature instability). Exchange transfusion thresholds at 72 hours are around 425 micromol/L for term infants without risk factors. Phototherapy is given with intensive blue spectrum, feeding maintained, repeat TSB in 4 to 6 hours. Investigate prolonged jaundice (over 14 days term, 21 days preterm) for cholestasis, infection, hypothyroidism, metabolic causes.
key_points: Term well 72h: phototherapy at TSB approx 290-300 micromol/L
Adjust lower with risk factors: gestation under 38wk, haemolysis, G6PD, sepsis
Exchange transfusion term 72h: TSB approx 425 micromol/L
IVIG: Coombs-positive haemolysis approaching exchange
Investigate prolonged jaundice over 14 days term
explanation.pearls: Visual estimation of jaundice severity is unreliable past the umbilicus; always confirm with TSB or transcutaneous bilirubinometer (TcB) and plot on age-in-hours nomogram - the trajectory matters more than the static number.

sources.label: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperbilirubinemia in Newborn Infant 2022

subtopic_detail: Preschool viral-induced wheeze first-line bronchodilator and steroid evidence
stem: You are the emergency department paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old boy with the third episode in 6 months of wheeze, cough and increased work of breathing during a coryzal illness. He responded to salbutamol via spacer at home this morning but has worsened over the day with persistent wheeze and tachypnoea. His first wheeze episode was at 8 months. There is no atopic history (no eczema, no food allergy), no parental asthma, and no inhaled smoke exposure. He has met all developmental milestones and growth is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 152, RR 48, SpO2 92% room air, BP not routine
data_table.Examination: Moderate work of breathing with subcostal recession, audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, air entry symmetrical with widespread polyphonic wheeze, alert, mildly distressed
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or chest X-ray indicated routinely; NPS not required

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Administer back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses with high-flow oxygen, add nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms every 20 minutes and arrange admission for IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg every 6 hours
options.rationale: Salbutamol via spacer (6 puffs at this size) is preferred over nebuliser; oral prednisolone is preferred over IV in moderate exacerbation tolerating oral; routine ipratropium is reserved for severe disease. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Discharge home with an oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days, salbutamol via spacer 6 puffs every 4 hours as required, with safety-net advice and review at 24 hours by GP for ongoing management of the acute episode
options.rationale: SpO2 92% with moderate work of breathing requires in-department observation with bronchodilator and oxygen titration before considering discharge; not an immediate discharge candidate. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Administer salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for 3 doses with oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 94%, give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose, and reassess after the third salbutamol round before deciding admission
options.rationale: Moderate preschool wheeze responds to salbutamol via spacer (6 puffs) every 20 minutes for 3 doses; oral prednisolone in modest episodes in children with a clear viral-induced wheeze pattern who present to ED is now supported in Australian guidance. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence inhaled fluticasone propionate 100 micrograms twice daily as a preventer from today given the recurrent wheeze episodes and review symptom control in 4 weeks before adjusting therapy or stepping up to combination inhaler
options.rationale: ICS preventer in pure viral-induced preschool wheeze without interval symptoms or atopy has limited benefit; initiation should be considered after 3+ episodes when guided by phenotype, and not as the acute ED intervention. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with oxygen as is given for moderate-severe croup, on the basis that the wheeze could reflect upper airway involvement that has been mislabelled as lower airway disease
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is for stridor in croup, not for lower-airway wheeze; this is not appropriate for viral-induced wheeze. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia))
source_refs: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze (under 5 years) is heterogeneous - episodic viral-induced wheeze (no interval symptoms, no atopy) versus multi-trigger wheeze (likely asthma trajectory, often atopic). Acute moderate exacerbation: salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer (12 puffs for over 6 years) every 20 minutes for 3 doses with oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 over 94%. Oral prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg up to 50 mg) for moderate/severe exacerbations is recommended in Australian guidance even for preschool age presenting to ED. Ipratropium adds benefit in severe/life-threatening. ICS preventer use in pure viral-induced wheeze is debated; consider after 3+ episodes in a year, family history of asthma, or interval symptoms. Spacer technique is critical.
key_points: Acute moderate preschool wheeze: salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer q20min x3
Oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg (max 50 mg) for moderate/severe exacerbation
Ipratropium: add for severe/life-threatening
Spacer with mask under 4 years, mouthpiece from 4-5 years
ICS preventer: consider after 3+ episodes, atopy or interval symptoms
explanation.pearls: An infant under 12 months with a first wheeze illness is bronchiolitis not asthma until proven otherwise; reaching for salbutamol there is not evidence-based, but in a toddler with recurrent wheeze responding to bronchodilator, the phenotype tips toward asthma even before formal diagnosis.

sources.label: Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia)

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in infant of diabetic mother
stem: You are the paediatric registrar on the postnatal ward reviewing a 2-hour-old term male infant born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks weighing 4.3 kg to a woman with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes. He had skin-to-skin contact and an attempt at breastfeeding at one hour of age but latched only briefly. The midwife performed a routine pre-feed blood glucose at 2 hours which is 1.8 mmol/L on a calibrated cot-side meter. The infant is alert, pink, breathing at 48/min with no recession, and has a normal cardiovascular and neurological examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 48, SpO2 97% in air, T 36.9 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Vigorous, well-perfused, normal tone and reflexes, anterior fontanelle soft, no jitteriness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside BGL 1.8 mmol/L (laboratory confirmation pending)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this glucose is a normal physiological postnatal nadir in an infant of a diabetic mother and arrange a routine recheck only with the next scheduled three-hourly feed in approximately one hour
options.rationale: A BGL under 2.0 mmol/L in any at-risk infant always triggers active management and a 30-minute recheck after feeding, not passive observation until the next routine feed time. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Transfer the infant to the special care nursery immediately for insertion of a peripheral intravenous cannula and commencement of 10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day with hourly capillary glucose monitoring until two consecutive readings exceed 2.6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Intravenous 10% dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia, BGL under 1.0 mmol/L, or persistent BGL under 2.6 mmol/L after feed plus buccal gel; an asymptomatic 1.8 mmol/L at first measurement is treated with feed first. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Administer 200 mg/kg of 40% dextrose gel to the buccal mucosa now without offering an oral feed and recheck the capillary blood glucose 30 minutes later before deciding on any further escalation of management or further dextrose
options.rationale: Buccal 40% dextrose gel is used in combination with a feed, not instead of one, and only after the first low BGL persists or as second-line for the next low reading per the Sugar Babies and Queensland pathway. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Encourage an immediate breastfeed or expressed-breast-milk top-up of 5 mL/kg and recheck the blood glucose 30 minutes after the feed before considering buccal dextrose gel or intravenous glucose escalation
options.rationale: ASID and Queensland Health newborn hypoglycaemia pathways treat an asymptomatic BGL of 1.0 to 2.5 mmol/L with an immediate feed of 5 mL/kg expressed colostrum or formula and a recheck 30 minutes after; persistent levels below 2.6 mmol/L then trigger 40% dextrose gel and senior review. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Send a critical sample for plasma glucose, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids before any intervention because the most likely cause is congenital hyperinsulinism rather than transitional neonatal hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: A critical hypoglycaemia screen is appropriate when BGL stays below 2.6 mmol/L despite adequate feeds at over 48 hours of age, not at the first reading at 2 hours of life in an infant of a diabetic mother. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Newborn hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of diabetic mothers are at high risk of transient hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia from in-utero glucose exposure. Australian pathways treat asymptomatic BGL between 1.0 and 2.5 mmol/L with a 5 mL/kg feed of expressed breast milk or formula and a 30-minute recheck. Persistent low levels then trigger 40% dextrose gel (200 mg/kg = 0.5 mL/kg) plus a feed. Intravenous 10% dextrose is for symptomatic infants, BGL under 1.0, or failure of feed plus gel. The target threshold for treatment in the first 48 hours is 2.6 mmol/L.
key_points: IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm are at-risk groups requiring screening
Treatment threshold first 48h: BGL under 2.6 mmol/L
First line: feed 5 mL/kg EBM or formula, recheck 30 min
Second line: 200 mg/kg of 40% dextrose gel buccally plus feed
IV 10% dextrose if symptomatic, under 1.0 mmol/L, or persistent failure
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dose is 0.5 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) given with a feed, not instead of one - this single dose has reduced NICU admission in the Sugar Babies trial.

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup with stridor at rest and mild recession
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 22-month-old boy brought in by his mother at 0200 with a 1-day history of coryza followed by a sudden barking cough and noisy breathing on waking from sleep. He is upset and crying intermittently. On examination he has audible inspiratory stridor at rest, mild suprasternal and intercostal recession but no tracheal tug, and is well perfused with a respiratory rate of 36 and oxygen saturations of 97% in air. He has not had previous croup episodes and has no congenital airway concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degrees C, HR 138, RR 36, SpO2 97% in air, CRT 1 second
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest, mild recession, voice hoarse but cry strong, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed (clinical diagnosis)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone now and observe the child for at least four hours after the dose to assess clinical response before considering discharge home with a written croup advice sheet for the family
options.rationale: RCH and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as first-line for moderate croup with at-least 4 hours of observation; nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe disease with marked recession or tracheal tug. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 via mask immediately and arrange for paediatric high-dependency admission with continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours regardless of the response to the initial nebulised dose
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with marked sternal recession, tracheal tug or hypoxia; mild recession with stridor at rest is moderate and treated with steroid alone in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Take a nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viral PCR, perform a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray to look for the steeple sign and withhold any pharmacological treatment until imaging and laboratory results have returned
options.rationale: Croup is a clinical diagnosis and routine imaging or viral PCR delays treatment without changing management; steroids should be given promptly on clinical grounds alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Administer high-flow humidified oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and a single intramuscular dose of 50 mg/kg ceftriaxone empirically pending the result of a paired blood culture and full blood count
options.rationale: Croup is viral so antibiotics are not indicated; humidified oxygen is unhelpful in an infant with saturations of 97% and may distress the child further. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

options.text: Discharge home immediately with written advice on steam-bath therapy and indications to return, without any pharmacological intervention because the child is comfortably saturating well and the stridor will likely settle overnight
options.rationale: Even mild croup benefits from a single dose of oral dexamethasone to reduce relapse and re-presentation; discharge without steroid is suboptimal in stridor-at-rest disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis))

explanation.summary: Moderate croup is defined as stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession. First-line treatment is single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (or prednisolone 1 mg/kg if dexamethasone unavailable). Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) is added for severe disease with marked recession, tracheal tug, agitation or hypoxia. Children are observed for at least 4 hours post-steroid (or 4 hours post-last-adrenaline) before discharge. Antibiotics, imaging and routine humidification are not recommended.
key_points: Croup severity: mild (barking cough, no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest, mild recession), severe (marked recession, tracheal tug, agitation)
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for all moderate or severe croup
Add nebulised adrenaline for severe croup
Observe 4 hours post-treatment before discharge
Croup is a clinical diagnosis - no routine imaging
explanation.pearls: A child with croup who becomes drooling, very still and toxic should raise suspicion of bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis - call ENT/anaesthetics for theatre intubation before any throat examination.

subtopic_detail: Febrile infant under 3 months with possible UTI
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan tertiary emergency department reviewing a 7-week-old previously well term male infant brought in by his parents with a 12-hour history of poor feeding, fussiness and a measured rectal temperature of 38.6 degrees C at home. On examination he is irritable but consolable, well perfused with a capillary refill of under 2 seconds, has a soft fontanelle and no focal source of infection on full examination including ENT, chest, abdomen and skin. He has had no recent antibiotics and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degrees C, HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 99% air, CRT under 2 sec
data_table.Examination: Irritable but consolable, no rash, fontanelle soft, no meningism, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Bedside cap gas: pH 7.38, BE -1, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound and a micturating cystourethrogram before starting any antibiotic therapy because vesicoureteric reflux is the most likely underlying diagnosis in a male infant with fever
options.rationale: Imaging is not done before empirical antibiotics; renal tract US in confirmed UTI is arranged later per KHA-CARI and RCH timelines. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Collect a clean-catch bag urine specimen for microscopy and culture and discharge home on oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with a planned review by the general practitioner within 24 hours of presentation
options.rationale: Bag urine has a high contamination rate and is not acceptable for diagnosing UTI in infants; oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inappropriate for any febrile infant under 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Reassure the parents that the child is well appearing with a normal lactate and observation alone in the emergency department for 4 hours with paracetamol is sufficient before discharge home without antibiotics or urine collection
options.rationale: Well-appearance is unreliable in infants under 3 months and serious bacterial infection prevalence is 5 to 10 percent; observation alone is inadequate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Send urine collected by clean catch only for dipstick analysis and start oral amoxicillin clavulanate if the dipstick is positive for leucocyte esterase or nitrites, deferring blood tests unless the child clinically deteriorates
options.rationale: Urine dipstick is unreliable in young infants and oral antibiotics are not first-line; full septic workup and IV antibiotics are mandated. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Obtain a catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine sample plus blood culture and full septic workup including lumbar puncture, then commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin pending results in a paediatric inpatient setting
options.rationale: RCH and the Therapeutic Guidelines treat a febrile infant under 3 months as full septic workup including catheter urine, blood culture, LP and empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (cefotaxime if LP delayed) regardless of well appearance. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: Any febrile infant under 3 months of age requires a full septic workup. RCH defines this as urinalysis and culture by catheter or suprapubic aspirate, blood culture, FBC, CRP, and lumbar puncture (unless contraindicated). Empirical IV benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin covers Group B streptococcus, Listeria and Gram negatives; cefotaxime replaces gentamicin if meningitis suspected. The infant is admitted pending cultures. Well-appearance does not exclude serious bacterial infection in this age group.
key_points: Under 1 month: always full septic workup plus admit on empirical IV antibiotics
1-3 months: full septic workup unless very well and low-risk per Rochester/Step-by-Step
Empirical IV penicillin plus gentamicin (cefotaxime if meningitis suspected)
Urine: catheter or SPA only, not bag
Renal tract US after confirmed UTI in infants under 6 months
explanation.pearls: Listeria monocytogenes covers the rationale for adding ampicillin/amoxicillin to gentamicin in neonates - it is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric anaphylaxis dose, route and observation
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a busy emergency department called to triage to assess a 6-year-old girl who developed lip swelling, generalised urticaria and a hoarse voice within 10 minutes of eating a cashew from a snack bag at her brother's birthday party 25 minutes ago. She has a history of mild asthma controlled with a salbutamol inhaler used twice in the last year, no known allergies and no chronic medication. On arrival she is anxious, has audible inspiratory stridor, wheeze on auscultation, widespread urticaria and is centrally well perfused.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 36, SpO2 94% in air, BP 92/56 mmHg, T 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Audible stridor, bilateral wheeze, widespread urticaria, mild peri-orbital oedema, alert
data_table.Investigations: Bedside observations as above; weight estimated at 22 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Administer 10 mg of intramuscular promethazine and 200 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone as first-line therapy and observe for two hours of clinical improvement before re-evaluating the need for further pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and never replace adrenaline for any feature of anaphylaxis; delaying IM adrenaline increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous adrenaline 1 mcg/kg as a slow push followed by a continuous infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min, intubate immediately for the stridor and admit her directly to the paediatric intensive care unit for ongoing airway management
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses with persistent shock and senior clinician supervision; first-line is always IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1000 adrenaline by intramuscular injection into the mid anterolateral thigh now, lay her supine with legs elevated, give high-flow oxygen and observe for at least 4 hours after symptoms resolve before considering discharge
options.rationale: ASCIA action plan: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (max 0.5 mg) into the mid anterolateral thigh, with supine positioning, high flow oxygen and a minimum 4-hour observation after symptom resolution before discharge with an adrenaline autoinjector and follow up. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give 10 puffs of inhaled salbutamol via spacer and 5 mL nebulised adrenaline 1:1000, then reassess in 15 minutes and only proceed to intramuscular adrenaline if wheeze and stridor have not resolved with these inhaled therapies
options.rationale: Inhaled salbutamol treats wheeze but not airway oedema or hypotension; nebulised adrenaline is for severe upper airway oedema as an adjunct only, never replacing IM adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer an immediate 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously and observe blood pressure response before deciding whether intramuscular adrenaline is required, given that the systolic blood pressure remains above 90 mmHg
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed by any combination of skin, airway or breathing involvement after exposure regardless of blood pressure; IM adrenaline is given immediately rather than awaiting hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed when there is any acute onset of typical skin or mucosal change PLUS either respiratory or cardiovascular involvement, or any hypotension after a known allergen. First-line treatment is IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (10 mcg/kg, max 0.5 mg) into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes as needed. Supine positioning, high flow oxygen and IV fluid 20 mL/kg if hypotensive complete the bundle. Observation for at least 4 hours post symptom resolution is required, with adrenaline autoinjector script, action plan and allergy referral on discharge.
key_points: IM adrenaline first - always first - 0.01 mg/kg 1:1000 IM mid anterolateral thigh, max 0.5 mg
Repeat IM adrenaline every 5 minutes if no response
Supine with legs elevated unless pregnant (left lateral) or vomiting (lateral)
Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only
Observe at least 4 hours post symptom resolution
explanation.pearls: For a 22 kg child the IM dose is 0.22 mg, but ASCIA pre-calibrates by age band: 0.15 mg for under 20 kg, 0.30 mg for 20 to 50 kg and 0.5 mg for over 50 kg - the band is appropriate here despite slight under-dose.

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease meeting full criteria at day 6
stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old boy who has been febrile for six days with temperatures above 39 degrees C unresponsive to paracetamol. His parents describe a polymorphous truncal rash since day three, red cracked lips since day four and bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection that started yesterday. On examination today he has a tender 2 cm right cervical lymph node, swollen erythematous palms and soles, and pronounced strawberry tongue. He is irritable but well perfused and has no source of bacterial infection on workup.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 degrees C, HR 152, RR 30, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, dry fissured lips, strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, oedema of hands and feet, single 2 cm right cervical node
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 12.5), Hb 102 g/L, platelets 462 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, sterile pyuria on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Defer all definitive treatment until day 10 of fever to allow further inflammatory markers, echocardiogram and rheumatology consultation to confirm the diagnosis before committing the child to systemic immunoglobulin therapy and antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Delaying treatment beyond day 10 of fever loses the window of maximal IVIG efficacy in preventing coronary aneurysm; treat as soon as Kawasaki criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Treat empirically with intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and toxic shock pending blood culture results, with serial daily examination for any new desquamation or hypotension over the coming 48 hours of admission
options.rationale: The combination of fever for 6 days plus 4 of 5 principal criteria fulfils Kawasaki disease; staphylococcal scalded skin would not give bilateral conjunctivitis and strawberry tongue with this lymph node pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus oral aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, and arrange an inpatient baseline transthoracic echocardiogram to assess for coronary artery aneurysms during this admission
options.rationale: Single dose IVIG 2 g/kg infused over 8 to 12 hours plus high or moderate dose aspirin started within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25 percent to under 5 percent; baseline echo establishes coronary z-scores. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days as initial monotherapy without intravenous immunoglobulin and review the need for adjunctive aspirin once the inflammatory markers begin to fall on serial testing
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is not first line; high-risk Kawasaki may receive IVIG plus steroid combination (Kobayashi-style risk stratification), but never steroid without IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Start oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/day alone without intravenous immunoglobulin and arrange outpatient transthoracic echocardiogram in 6 to 8 weeks because the platelet count is already markedly elevated suggesting late convalescent phase
options.rationale: Low-dose aspirin is the maintenance antiplatelet dose used after fever resolves; the acute high-inflammation phase always requires IVIG plus moderate-to-high dose aspirin until day 14 or 48 hours afebrile. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically by fever for at least 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, mucosal changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), extremity changes (palmar/plantar erythema or oedema, periungual desquamation), polymorphous rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy of at least 1.5 cm. Treatment with single-dose IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm rates from 25 percent to under 5 percent. Aspirin is dosed at 30 to 50 mg/kg/day until 48 hours afebrile, then 3 to 5 mg/kg/day until echo follow up at 6 to 8 weeks.
key_points: Diagnose by 5+ days fever plus 4 of 5 criteria (or incomplete KD by criteria plus echo)
Treat within 10 days of fever onset: IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin
Baseline echo, repeat at 6 to 8 weeks
Steroid added upfront for high-risk (Kobayashi score) or IVIG resistance
Long-term cardiology follow up if z-score abnormal
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria, raised CRP, anaemia of inflammation and a normal-to-rising platelet count by week 2 are supportive markers used in incomplete KD scoring.

sources.label: American Heart Association: Kawasaki disease scientific statement

subtopic_detail: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts in a child
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old girl referred from her GP with a 3-week history of progressive pallor, recurrent low-grade fevers, easy bruising on her shins and a new petechial rash on her trunk noticed by her mother yesterday. She has been more tired than usual at preschool and has refused to walk to the car last week, complaining of left thigh ache. On examination she is pale, has scattered petechiae and small ecchymoses, a soft 3 cm spleen tip palpable, and mild bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 degrees C, HR 122, RR 24, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, scattered petechiae and bruises, soft spleen tip 3 cm, no hepatomegaly, no testicular masses, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Hb 64 g/L, MCV 84 fL, WCC 28.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 0.6, blasts 22.0 x10^9/L), platelets 22 x10^9/L, LDH 1820 U/L, urate 0.48 mmol/L, K 4.4, phosphate 1.62, calcium corrected 2.18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm splenomegaly and exclude an intra-abdominal lymphoma mass, plus a peripheral lymph node excisional biopsy for histopathology before considering systemic chemotherapy or transfer
options.rationale: Excisional lymph node biopsy is appropriate for suspected lymphoma without circulating blasts; here marrow examination is faster and definitive. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

options.text: Admit to a regional paediatric ward for transfusion of one adult unit of packed red blood cells and one adult therapeutic dose of platelets, then refer to the haematology outpatient clinic for a bone marrow biopsy within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Transfusion without first taking diagnostic marrow may confound flow cytometry; outpatient delay risks progressive cytopenia and tumour lysis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for presumed febrile neutropenia and oral fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis, and arrange a CT chest abdomen and pelvis to look for a sanctuary site of infection or occult abscess
options.rationale: Although febrile neutropenia management is needed if a fever spikes, the immediate priority is diagnosis with bone marrow aspirate and tumour lysis prophylaxis; abx are not first-line in stable apyrexial neutropenia. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

options.text: Transfer urgently to a tertiary paediatric oncology unit for bone marrow aspirate and trephine plus immunophenotyping and cytogenetics, and commence intravenous hyperhydration with allopurinol or rasburicase for tumour lysis prophylaxis en route
options.rationale: Circulating blasts on film with pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and raised LDH require urgent transfer for diagnostic bone marrow plus tumour lysis prophylaxis given the WCC and urate; ALL is the most likely diagnosis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

options.text: Send blood for Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and parvovirus B19 serology and a peripheral blood film for atypical lymphocytes, and review again in 48 hours once infective causes of pancytopenia have been excluded by these results
options.rationale: Viral serology has a place but never delays urgent tertiary referral when circulating blasts and a leukaemoid white cell count are present. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL - Induction)

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the most common childhood malignancy, typically presenting between 2 and 5 years with marrow failure (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms. Circulating blasts on film are diagnostic until proven otherwise. Tumour lysis risk increases with WCC over 50, raised LDH, urate over 0.45 mmol/L and bulky disease; intravenous hyperhydration at twice maintenance plus allopurinol (or rasburicase if very high risk) is started before induction. Tertiary transfer for marrow aspirate, immunophenotyping and minimal residual disease assessment guides risk-stratified chemotherapy.
key_points: Triad: marrow failure + organomegaly + bone pain in pre-school child
Film: circulating blasts trigger urgent transfer
Tumour lysis: hydrate twice-maintenance plus allopurinol or rasburicase
Avoid transfusion before diagnostic marrow if possible
Australian protocols via eviQ; cure rate over 90 percent in standard-risk B-ALL
explanation.pearls: Mediastinal mass on chest X-ray in T-cell ALL can compress trachea or great vessels; lying flat for procedures becomes hazardous and dictates early imaging.

sources.label: Children's Cancer and Leukaemia Group: ALL guidance

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis with significant proteinuria requiring biopsy decision
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-year-old boy who was diagnosed in your clinic five weeks ago with IgA vasculitis based on a palpable purpuric rash over his lower limbs and buttocks, bilateral ankle arthralgia and intermittent peri-umbilical pain. The rash has now resolved. You arranged weekly urine dipstick and blood pressure at his GP. Today his GP rings because his urinalysis shows 3+ protein with 2+ blood and his blood pressure is 130/86 mmHg seated. He looks well, is afebrile and has no oedema on examination today in your clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 130/86 mmHg (above the 95th centile for age, sex, height), HR 84, T 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Faded post-inflammatory pigmentation on lower limbs, no fresh purpura, no oedema, abdomen soft, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 220 mg/mmol, urine RBC 60/high power field, dysmorphic, Hb 124 g/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR 95, albumin 36 g/L, complement C3 and C4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that microscopic haematuria and mild proteinuria are expected after Henoch-Schonlein purpura and may persist for over a year without need for intervention, and continue weekly urinalysis monitoring with the general practitioner
options.rationale: Trace haematuria alone may resolve, but PCR over 100 mg/mmol with hypertension represents progressive nephritis that requires nephrology input rather than continued primary care monitoring. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.text: Refer to a paediatric nephrologist for an urgent renal biopsy and consideration of oral prednisolone or pulse methylprednisolone with adjunctive ACE inhibitor and blood pressure control as guided by biopsy ISKDC class
options.rationale: Persistent heavy proteinuria (PCR over 250 mg/mmol or nephrotic-range) with hypertension at 4 weeks after IgA vasculitis onset triggers nephrology referral for biopsy; ISKDC class II to V guides steroid plus immunosuppression decisions. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.text: Start a 4-week course of oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day without nephrology referral and aim to taper over a further 4 weeks while continuing community-based monitoring of urinalysis and blood pressure throughout the taper
options.rationale: Empirical steroid without biopsy classification is not first-line for HSP nephritis at this severity; KDIGO and RCH guide biopsy-stratified therapy rather than blind community steroid courses. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.text: Commence oral cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate mofetil empirically as combination therapy and arrange repeat urine protein creatinine ratio in 4 weeks to demonstrate biochemical response before deciding on need for renal biopsy
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is considered only after biopsy demonstrates crescentic or class IV-V disease and after steroid trial; empirical use is inappropriate. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

options.text: Test antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-GBM antibody and serum cryoglobulins urgently and treat as ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis with plasma exchange and rituximab pending these confirmatory serological results
options.rationale: Clinical picture of preceding palpable purpura with normal complement is classical IgA vasculitis nephritis, not ANCA-associated vasculitis; serology should be confirmatory but not delay biopsy referral. (Source: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis)
source_refs: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is a small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis of children with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis. Renal involvement determines long-term prognosis. Australian and KDIGO pathways monitor blood pressure and urinalysis weekly for 4 weeks then monthly to 6 months. Indications for nephrology referral and biopsy include nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistent PCR over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, raised creatinine or AKI, or atypical features. Biopsy ISKDC class guides treatment: class II-IIIA may have RAAS blockade alone; IIIB+ get steroids; class IV-V and crescentic disease often need pulse methylprednisolone plus cyclophosphamide or MMF.
key_points: Monitor urine and BP weekly for 4 weeks, then monthly to 6 months after diagnosis
PCR over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, AKI or nephrotic syndrome trigger nephrology referral
Biopsy stratifies treatment per ISKDC class
RAAS blockade is the cornerstone of proteinuria control
Long-term follow up because late progression to CKD can occur
explanation.pearls: Normal complement is the rule in IgA vasculitis nephritis - low complement should redirect workup toward post-infectious glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis instead.

sources.label: KDIGO 2021: Glomerular Diseases - IgA Vasculitis Nephritis

subtopic_detail: Mitochondrial disease presenting as developmental regression with lactic acidosis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar consulted on a 16-month-old boy admitted with two days of vomiting and decreased oral intake after a febrile illness.
