He was born at term, breastfed and weaned uneventfully but his parents now describe loss of words he previously had, loss of ability to walk in the last month and intermittent eye movement abnormalities. On examination he is thin but not dehydrated, has truncal hypotonia, brisk reflexes, an upgoing right plantar response and a left ptosis. There is no organomegaly. He has had no surgeries and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Examination: Hypotonia, brisk reflexes, left ptosis, intermittent dysconjugate eye movements, no organomegaly, weight on 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 4.0, K 3.8, Na 136, anion gap 22; CK 220 U/L; LFTs ALT 78 AST 102; ammonia 92 micromol/L; MRI brain shows symmetric bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem T2 hyperintensities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send blood and urine for very-long-chain fatty acids and white-cell enzyme analysis for late-infantile metachromatic leukodystrophy, and discharge home pending results because the child is haemodynamically stable and feeding adequately
options.rationale: MLD is a leukodystrophy with white matter lesions, not symmetric grey-matter basal ganglia pattern; discharge before treatment risks metabolic decompensation with intercurrent illness. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.text: Treat empirically as autoimmune encephalitis with intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day for 5 days followed by intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg, and arrange anti-NMDA and anti-MOG antibody testing on serum and cerebrospinal fluid
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is unlikely with symmetric metabolic-pattern lesions on MRI and persistent lactic acidosis; the clinical and imaging pattern points to mitochondrial disease. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.text: Manage as severe gastroenteritis with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% at 1.5 times maintenance plus ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg orally and continue ad lib oral feeding once vomiting subsides without further metabolic workup or imaging review
options.rationale: Gastroenteritis would not produce a persistent lactic acidosis with developmental regression, ptosis and basal ganglia lesions; the presentation is metabolic. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.text: Start sodium valproate orally as empirical treatment for suspected refractory partial seizures presenting as dysconjugate eye movements, and arrange outpatient electroencephalography with sleep deprivation within the next fortnight
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in suspected mitochondrial disease (especially POLG-related) due to risk of fatal hepatotoxicity; ictal-eye movements should not be empirically treated this way. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

options.text: Refer urgently to a metabolic genetics service for whole-exome sequencing and mitochondrial DNA testing, commence high-dose riboflavin, thiamine and coenzyme Q10 cofactor therapy, and avoid sodium valproate, metformin and aminoglycosides during admission
options.rationale: Symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem T2 lesions with lactic acidosis and a hypotonic regression suggest Leigh syndrome or mitochondrial disease; tertiary referral, mitochondrial cofactor cocktail and avoidance of mitochondrial-toxic drugs are recommended pending genetic diagnosis. (Source: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline)
source_refs: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial disease presents at any age but in infancy and toddlers classically features developmental regression, hypotonia, lactic acidosis, multisystem involvement (cardiomyopathy, deafness, retinopathy, hepatic and renal tubular dysfunction) and characteristic MRI patterns. Leigh syndrome shows symmetric T2 hyperintensities in basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebellum with raised brain or CSF lactate. Initial management is referral to tertiary metabolic genetics, mitochondrial cofactor support (riboflavin, thiamine, coenzyme Q10, biotin, levocarnitine) and strict avoidance of mitochondrial toxins including sodium valproate, metformin, linezolid, aminoglycosides and propofol infusions. Genetic diagnosis via mitochondrial DNA panel plus nuclear gene exome sequencing guides prognosis and family counselling.
key_points: Symmetric basal ganglia lesions + lactic acidosis + regression = Leigh syndrome until proven otherwise
Cofactor cocktail: riboflavin, thiamine, CoQ10, levocarnitine, biotin
Avoid valproate (fatal hepatotoxicity in POLG), metformin, aminoglycosides
Genetic confirmation by mtDNA panel + nuclear WES
Multidisciplinary care: neurology, cardiology, ophthalmology, audiology, dietetics
explanation.pearls: POLG mutations cause Alpers syndrome and are exquisitely sensitive to sodium valproate, which can precipitate fulminant hepatic failure - a key reason mitochondrial disease must be excluded before valproate in early-life epilepsy.

sources.label: HUMAN: Genetics and Metabolic - Mitochondrial disease guideline

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 5-month-old previously well term girl on day 3 of coryza, cough and fast breathing. She is taking around 60% of her usual breastfeed volumes, has not vomited, and her last wet nappy was 3 hours ago. Initial observations showed mild subcostal recession with SpO2 92% in air; after suction of clear nasal secretions and a 90 mL breastfeed she is alert, smiling, with no recession at rest and SpO2 of 95% in air for 30 minutes.

The mother is calm, has a working car, lives 25 minutes from the hospital, has a clear plan to seek review, and there is good GP follow-up the next morning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 95% in air (after suction and feed), T 37.6 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild wheeze with prolonged expiration, no chest wall recession at rest, good air entry, no focal crackles, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: Bedside nasopharyngeal aspirate viral PCR pending; no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her for a chest x-ray and intravenous benzylpenicillin until viral nasopharyngeal aspirate PCR results return, given the fever and the possibility of an early bacterial lower respiratory tract co-infection
options.rationale: Routine chest imaging and empirical antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated bronchiolitis without focal signs or persistent high fever; both increase harm without altering outcomes in this clinical picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with a written bronchiolitis action plan, simple analgesia for fever, advice on feed volumes and red-flag symptoms, and review by her general practitioner within 24 hours
options.rationale: She meets discharge criteria: SpO2 at or above 92% in air sustained for at least 30 minutes, mild work of breathing, feeding above 50% of baseline, no apnoeas, reliable carer and access to review; an action plan with red-flag advice and short-interval GP review is standard practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit her to the paediatric ward for nasogastric feeding at two-thirds maintenance and continuous pulse oximetry monitoring for at least 24 hours regardless of her current observations and ongoing feeding
options.rationale: Routine nasogastric feeding is reserved for infants taking under 50% of usual oral intake or in respiratory distress that precludes safe oral feeding, neither of which applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge her home only after a 4-hour high-flow nasal cannula trial at 2 L/kg/min in the ED short stay unit to confirm she does not develop any escalating oxygen requirement before going home
options.rationale: High-flow nasal cannula is an escalation therapy for infants with persistent hypoxia or severe work of breathing despite low-flow oxygen, not a pre-discharge screening test for a stable, normoxic infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit her for a trial of nebulised hypertonic 3% saline every 6 hours and a single inhaled salbutamol challenge to assess for any bronchodilator-responsive component of her wheeze before discharge
options.rationale: Nebulised hypertonic saline and trial salbutamol are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis management in infants under 12 months and do not change the disposition decision in a stable child meeting discharge criteria. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Disposition in bronchiolitis is driven by sustained SpO2, work of breathing, feeding adequacy, apnoeas and carer factors rather than by interventions of unproven benefit. This infant meets all RCH discharge criteria after simple suction and a feed. Hypertonic saline, bronchodilators, antibiotics and routine imaging are not indicated. Safe discharge requires a clear action plan and short-interval review.
key_points: Discharge thresholds: SpO2 at or above 92% in air sustained 30 minutes, feeds at or above 50% baseline, no apnoea, mild work of breathing
Hypertonic saline and salbutamol are not recommended in routine bronchiolitis under 12 months
Antibiotics and chest x-ray only with focal signs, persistent high fever or severe disease
Carer reliability, distance to care, and follow-up plan are part of the disposition decision
explanation.pearls: If SpO2 sits at 92% in air after suction and feed in an otherwise well infant with reliable carers, discharge with a written action plan and GP review within 24 hours is correct - admitting to escalate to high-flow is over-treatment.

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 26-month-old non-Aboriginal boy with no significant past history brought in by his mother after 24 hours of irritability, ear-tugging and fever to 38.6 degrees C. He is otherwise feeding reasonably, drinking, has been playing intermittently between paracetamol doses and has had no vomiting. He is fully immunised including 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, attends day care 3 days per week and has had no previous ear infections.

Otoscopy shows a bulging, opaque right tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks and no perforation or discharge; the left ear is normal. There is no mastoid tenderness, neck stiffness, facial weakness, or coexisting bacterial focus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 28, SpO2 99% in air, T 38.6 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging and opaque with loss of light reflex; left TM normal; no mastoid swelling; oropharynx mildly erythematous; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management of his ear?

options.text: Provide regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, written safety-net advice, and arrange routine review at 48 hours with antibiotics only if symptoms have worsened or have not improved at that review point
options.rationale: In a previously well, fully immunised non-Aboriginal child over 6 months with uncomplicated acute otitis media, watchful waiting with analgesia and 48-hour review is the preferred initial approach reserving antibiotics for failure to improve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days and refer urgently to ear, nose and throat outpatients for a discussion of grommet insertion if any further episodes occur
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is second-line if there has been recent amoxicillin or non-response, and grommet referral is for recurrent or persistent disease, not a first uncomplicated episode in a previously well child. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days now and review only if he develops persistent fever, ear discharge or new symptoms over the next week of treatment
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are reserved for under-6-months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, or systemic illness; none apply to this otherwise well child meeting watchful-waiting criteria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.text: Arrange same-day ENT outpatient review and tympanocentesis for microbiological sampling and an audiology assessment before any decision is made about whether antibiotics or analgesia alone is most appropriate
options.rationale: Routine tympanocentesis and same-day ENT review are not indicated in uncomplicated first-episode acute otitis media; analgesia and 48-hour reassessment guide management at primary care level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

options.text: Refer him to the local emergency department for intravenous ceftriaxone, blood cultures and a lumbar puncture given the fever, irritability and unilateral bulging tympanic membrane on otoscopy today
options.rationale: He has no features of meningitis, sepsis or mastoiditis: a well child with a bulging tympanic membrane and low-grade fever does not require parenteral antibiotics, blood cultures or lumbar puncture. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance supports watchful waiting in non-Aboriginal children over 6 months with uncomplicated, non-severe acute otitis media. Analgesia alone and review at 48 hours is the first step; antibiotics are reserved for at-risk groups, bilateral disease under 2 years, perforation with discharge, severe systemic illness, or failure to improve. Immediate amoxicillin would be appropriate in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children given the high rate of complicated otitis. Choosing parenteral antibiotics or ENT review is overreach in this clinical picture.
key_points: Watchful waiting with analgesia and 48-hour review for uncomplicated AOM in non-Aboriginal children over 6 months
Antibiotics from outset: under 6 months, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child, perforation with discharge, severe illness, or bilateral disease under 2 years
First-line antibiotic: amoxicillin; amoxicillin-clavulanate if non-response or recent amoxicillin
Tympanocentesis or parenteral antibiotics only if complicated (mastoiditis, sepsis, intracranial involvement)
explanation.pearls: In a non-Aboriginal, fully immunised, well-looking child over 6 months with first-episode unilateral AOM, regular paracetamol plus ibuprofen and 48-hour review beats amoxicillin from the door - antibiotics in this group reduce pain by less than a day and the number needed to treat is high.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Acute otitis media

stem:
You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy with a known diagnosis of mild persistent asthma on a low-dose inhaled fluticasone preventer who presented with a 6-hour exacerbation triggered by an upper respiratory infection. On arrival he had moderate work of breathing with tracheal tug and SpO2 of 93% in air. He has received salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer at 20-minute intervals for three doses, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer for three doses, and a single oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg dose 2 hours ago.

He is now alert, talking in full sentences, with no recession, has just eaten and drunk, and is keen to go home; his salbutamol interval has been stretched to 3-hourly with no return of recession.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 97% in air, T 37.4 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild scattered wheeze at end-expiration, no recession, full air entry bilaterally, no chest pain, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or bloods required; salbutamol response sustained at 3-hourly dosing across two cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue 1-hourly salbutamol by spacer for a further 6 hours in the short stay unit and only consider discharge once the salbutamol interval can be stretched to at least every 6 hours during the day
options.rationale: A salbutamol interval of 3 to 4 hours sustained with stable observations is the accepted discharge threshold; insisting on a 6-hourly interval before discharge is more conservative than guidelines and prolongs ED length of stay without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Add a single oral montelukast 5 mg dose now, then a 5-day course at home in addition to his existing preventer, and discharge once 4 hours have elapsed from the last salbutamol given today
options.rationale: Routine addition of montelukast is not recommended for an acute exacerbation; preventer step-up is determined at outpatient review, not driven by a single ED episode in a child already on appropriate preventer therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes and admit him to the paediatric high-dependency unit for ongoing monitoring of his magnesium level and his cardiac rhythm overnight
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium is for severe or life-threatening exacerbations failing to respond to first-line therapy; this child has clinically improved and has no indication for magnesium or HDU admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Admit him to the paediatric ward for continuous pulse oximetry overnight and a 24-hour observation period before stepping down salbutamol given the duration of the symptoms and the upper respiratory tract trigger
options.rationale: Sustained 3-hourly salbutamol with stable saturations and minimal work of breathing supports safe discharge; admission for routine overnight observation in this scenario is overuse of inpatient resources. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

options.text: Discharge home with a written asthma action plan, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for a further 2 days, ongoing inhaled fluticasone preventer, and review by his GP within 48 to 72 hours of discharge
options.rationale: He meets discharge criteria: SpO2 above 94% in air, salbutamol stretched to at least 3-hourly with sustained response, no recession, and tolerating oral intake; a 3-day prednisolone course, written action plan and short-interval review complete the package. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

explanation.summary: Paediatric asthma discharge requires SpO2 above 94% in air, salbutamol stretched to at least 3-hourly with sustained effect, minimal work of breathing and tolerating oral intake. Discharge is paired with oral steroid completion, ongoing preventer, a written action plan and short-interval GP review. Admission, IV magnesium and montelukast are reserved for ongoing severity or unresolved features, not as routine. Over-prolonged ED stays add cost without clinical gain.
key_points: Discharge criteria: SpO2 above 94% air, salbutamol every 3 to 4 hours sustained, no recession, oral intake tolerated
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for total 3 days in exacerbations needing systemic steroid
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is for severe or life-threatening attacks failing first-line therapy
Asthma action plan and GP review within 48 to 72 hours are mandatory on discharge
explanation.pearls: Stretching salbutamol to 3-hourly with no recession and SpO2 above 94% in air is the practical gate for safe discharge; do not wait for 6-hourly intervals or order IV magnesium for a child who is clinically improved.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma management handbook

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 22-month-old developmentally normal girl 90 minutes after a single 2-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure that occurred at home during the rapid rise of a viral upper respiratory illness. The seizure self-terminated before paramedics arrived; she had a brief postictal drowsiness, then woke spontaneously and is now alert, smiling, playing and breastfeeding well. Examination identifies an obvious viral source with clear coryza and erythematous pharynx and reveals no focal neurological signs, no neck stiffness, no rash, and no significant past medical or family history other than a maternal aunt who had two febrile seizures in childhood with normal subsequent development.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 26, SpO2 99% in air, T 39.1 degrees C (after one dose of paracetamol), capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, age-appropriate interaction, normal tone and reflexes, normal cranial nerves, soft anterior fontanelle, no rash, no neck stiffness, clear viral coryza
data_table.Investigations: No bloods, lumbar puncture, imaging or EEG performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid microscopy, glucose and protein, blood cultures and commence empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone given the height of the fever today
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture after a simple febrile seizure is reserved for children under 6 months, those with persistent altered mental state, meningism, or who are partially treated with antibiotics; none of these apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Admit her overnight for a 24-hour continuous video electroencephalogram and a paediatric neurology consultation to exclude an underlying focal epilepsy syndrome before discharging her home tomorrow
options.rationale: Inpatient video EEG and admission are not warranted after a single simple febrile seizure; her clinical picture and family history do not raise concern for an underlying epilepsy syndrome requiring inpatient workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Reassure the parents, give written advice on febrile seizure recurrence and basic first-aid recovery position management, discuss antipyretic use for comfort, and discharge home with GP follow-up
options.rationale: She has a simple febrile seizure with a clear viral focus and a normal neurological examination; routine investigations and admission are not indicated and a structured parental education and safety-net discharge is correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Commence regular sodium valproate as a maintenance anti-seizure medication for the next 6 months given the family history of febrile seizures in a first-degree relative and the height of the documented fever
options.rationale: Maintenance anti-seizure medication after simple febrile seizures does not reduce future febrile or unprovoked seizures and carries significant adverse effects; it is not recommended for prevention after a first event. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain scan today, an outpatient electroencephalogram within a week and outpatient paediatric neurology review before any decision is made about discharge home this afternoon
options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging and EEG are not indicated after a single simple febrile seizure in a developmentally normal child with a normal neurological examination and an obvious infective source. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures last under 15 minutes, are generalised, and are not followed by focal neurology or recurrence within 24 hours. In a developmentally normal child older than 6 months with an identifiable febrile source and a normal examination, routine workup is not required. Counselling covers recurrence risk (about 30%), reassurance that simple febrile seizures do not cause brain injury or developmental harm, basic first-aid, and that antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. Maintenance anti-seizure medication after simple febrile seizures is not recommended.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure: under 15 minutes, generalised, not recurrent within 24 hours, normal neuro exam
Recurrence risk around 30%, higher with first event under 18 months or low fever threshold
Lumbar puncture if under 6 months, meningism, partially treated with antibiotics or persistent altered mental state
No role for maintenance anti-seizure medication or routine EEG/imaging after simple febrile seizure
explanation.pearls: Antipyretics provide comfort but do not reduce the risk of seizure recurrence; written parental advice on duration, recovery position, and when to call for help is the highest-yield intervention you offer at discharge.

subtopic_detail: Intussusception recognition and air enema indication
stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar called to ED to review an 11-month-old boy with 18 hours of intermittent severe screaming attacks, drawing his knees up and going pale, each lasting 5 minutes and recurring every 20 to 30 minutes. He has vomited four times in the last 6 hours (now bilious), refused his last two feeds, and passed a small amount of dark blood mixed with mucus per rectum on the way to hospital.

On examination he is sleepy between episodes but rousable, has a soft non-distended abdomen with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, and his peripheries are well perfused. He has had no surgery or foreign-body ingestion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 36, SpO2 98% in air, T 37.2 degrees C, BP 96/58, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sleepy between episodes, mildly dehydrated, abdomen soft with right upper quadrant sausage mass, no peritonism, blood-stained mucus on PR
data_table.Investigations: Urgent abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign 3.5 cm diameter at the ileocolic junction, no free fluid, no perforation; venous gas pH 7.34, lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit him for nil by mouth, intravenous maintenance fluids and serial abdominal examinations over the next 12 hours, repeating the ultrasound only if his symptoms have not spontaneously settled in that period
options.rationale: Watchful waiting risks bowel ischaemia and perforation; ultrasound-confirmed intussusception with classic clinical features warrants prompt air enema reduction rather than observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula, commence a 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus, place a nasogastric tube on free drainage, give intravenous antibiotics and proceed to a radiologist-led air enema reduction with surgical standby
options.rationale: Confirmed ileocolic intussusception without perforation or peritonism is managed with resuscitation, decompression, intravenous antibiotic cover and image-guided air enema reduction performed with surgical standby in case of perforation or failed reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Transfer him directly to the operating theatre for an immediate diagnostic laparoscopy and manual reduction with possible bowel resection given the bilious vomiting and the blood per rectum noted on the way to hospital
options.rationale: Primary operative reduction is reserved for failed enema reduction, peritonism, perforation or shock; he has none of these and a non-operative air enema is the first-line therapy with high success rates. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Order a non-contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to confirm the ultrasound finding and exclude a lead point before proceeding with any decision about enema reduction or surgical referral
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the diagnostic modality of choice in paediatric intussusception with high sensitivity and specificity; routine CT adds ionising radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Give a stat dose of intramuscular morphine for the colicky pain and observe him in the short stay unit for 4 hours, expecting many ileocolic intussusceptions to reduce spontaneously without intervention
options.rationale: Spontaneous reduction is unreliable and delays risk ischaemic complications; analgesia is appropriate but does not replace urgent air enema or surgical reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Classic intussusception in an infant under 2 years presents with paroxysmal pain, vomiting (often bilious late), and redcurrant jelly stool; ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign. Without peritonism, perforation or shock, management is resuscitation, decompression, intravenous antibiotic cover, and image-guided air enema reduction with surgical standby. Operative reduction is reserved for failed enema, peritonism, perforation, or shock. CT adds nothing in classic ileocolic disease and should be avoided.
key_points: Air enema reduction success rate approaches 80 to 90% in uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception
Absolute contraindications to enema: perforation, peritonism, shock; relative: persistent ileus, lead point identified
Bilious vomiting in an infant should always prompt urgent surgical assessment
Recurrence after air enema reduction occurs in around 10%, usually within 48 hours, and a second air enema is acceptable if no peritonism
explanation.pearls: Surgical standby during the air enema is non-negotiable: if perforation occurs during reduction or the enema fails, operative reduction must follow within minutes - book the radiologist and theatre in parallel, not sequentially.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Surgical - Paediatric abdominal emergencies

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan ED reviewing a non-ambulant 8-month-old boy brought in by his mother and her current partner. The history is that he 'rolled off the couch' onto a carpeted floor 4 hours ago. On examination you find a 2 cm fluctuant boggy swelling over the right parietal scalp, three small ovoid bruises over the left upper arm in a grip distribution, a torn upper labial frenulum, and a small healing burn on the dorsum of the left hand.

He is interactive but quiet; his fontanelle is soft. The partner cannot describe the incident in detail. The mother appears anxious. The infant has not previously been seen at this hospital and the family is not known to child protection services.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 38, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.8 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Right parietal boggy swelling 2 cm, three ovoid bruises left upper arm with grip pattern, torn upper labial frenulum, healing dorsal hand burn 1 cm, no spinal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside neurological examination intact; no investigations performed at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit him for a non-contrast CT brain, a skeletal survey within 24 hours, dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology, paediatric child protection team consultation, and notify the statutory child protection agency before discharge
options.rationale: Multiple sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant (torn frenulum, patterned bruising, scalp haematoma, healing burn) mandate a structured non-accidental injury workup and statutory child protection notification under all Australian mandatory reporting frameworks. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Order a non-contrast CT brain only and discharge home with the mother once the scan is reported as normal, deferring the skeletal survey and child protection consultation to outpatient paediatric follow-up next week
options.rationale: A normal CT brain does not exclude abusive injury or skeletal fractures; skeletal survey, fundoscopy and inpatient child protection team review are part of the recognised package of investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange social work involvement and a community child health nurse home visit within 7 days, and ask the mother to bring him back to ED only if he develops new bruises or any signs of head injury such as vomiting
options.rationale: Community escalation alone is insufficient when sentinel injuries are present; the threshold for inpatient workup and statutory notification is met and cannot be delegated to outpatient services. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Discharge him home with the mother after a discussion about home safety, provide written safety advice on supervised tummy time off raised surfaces, and arrange GP review within a week to recheck the scalp haematoma and the healing burn
options.rationale: Discharge without statutory notification or imaging in a non-ambulant infant with multiple sentinel injuries breaches mandatory reporting obligations and risks repeat injury including life-threatening abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Take a more detailed history from the mother and partner separately and re-examine in 4 hours; if the explanation reconciles with the injuries, discharge with GP follow-up, otherwise consider further investigation later
options.rationale: Sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant require workup and notification regardless of how plausibly the history is rephrased; pre-judging plausibility before completing investigation and notification is unsafe practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries in a non-ambulant infant - bruising in patterned distributions, torn frenulum, scalp haematoma, burns - have a high specificity for inflicted injury. The RCH and statewide child protection pathways require admission for structured workup (CT brain, skeletal survey within 24 hours, dilated fundoscopy, coagulation screen) alongside specialist consultation and statutory notification. Mandatory reporting obligations apply to all Australian medical practitioners; you do not need certainty, only a reasonable suspicion. Failing to act risks fatal recurrence.
key_points: Bruising in a non-ambulant infant is highly suspicious for inflicted injury until proven otherwise
Recognised sentinel injuries: torn frenulum, ear bruising, patterned bruises, burns, scalp haematoma in non-ambulant infant
Workup: CT brain, skeletal survey at 0 and at 11 to 14 days, fundoscopy, coagulation, LFTs, amylase/lipase
Mandatory reporting in all Australian jurisdictions; reasonable suspicion is the threshold, not proof
explanation.pearls: Bruises in those who do not cruise are a red flag - in a non-ambulant infant, a single unexplained bruise warrants the full sentinel injury workup, and any combination as here mandates inpatient admission and statutory notification before discharge.

sources.label: AIFS: Mandatory reporting of child abuse and neglect

subtopic_detail: Mycoplasma pneumoniae atypical pneumonia in school-aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 9-year-old girl with 10 days of dry cough that has progressed to a paroxysmal cough productive of clear sputum and 4 days of fever to 38.5 degrees C, gradually worsening despite oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily prescribed by her GP on day 4. She has bilateral mild widespread crackles and scattered fine wheeze, no focal consolidation on examination, and is well perfused, alert and tolerating oral fluids.

Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy peribronchial infiltrates without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Two of her classmates have had similar prolonged coughs recently and her dry cough has continued to disrupt her sleep at night.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, RR 24, SpO2 96% in air, T 38.4 degrees C, BP 102/64, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral crackles, scattered fine wheeze, no focal consolidation, no respiratory distress, no extrapulmonary rash, oropharynx clear
data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral patchy peribronchial infiltrates, no lobar consolidation, no effusion; WCC 9.5 x10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in antimicrobial management?

options.text: Cease the amoxicillin and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1 followed by 5 mg/kg daily for a further 4 days, with safety-net advice about return precautions and a planned GP review at 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: The clinical picture (prolonged dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, lack of response to amoxicillin in a school-aged child) fits Mycoplasma pneumoniae; oral azithromycin is recommended first-line atypical cover in Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.text: Add oral doxycycline 2 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days in addition to her current amoxicillin to broaden cover to atypical pathogens while preserving pneumococcal cover until the cough resolves clinically
options.rationale: Doxycycline is avoided under 8 years in Australia outside specific scenarios (and azithromycin is the standard atypical cover in this age group); dual therapy with amoxicillin is unnecessary when the picture clearly fits atypical pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.text: Stop antibiotics altogether and arrange a chest CT angiogram with intravenous contrast to exclude pulmonary embolism, foreign body or interstitial lung disease as the explanation for the persistent cough
options.rationale: There is a coherent infective explanation with classmate clustering, atypical clinical pattern and a typical chest x-ray; advanced imaging is not indicated as the next investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Increase the oral amoxicillin to 45 mg/kg three times daily for a further 7 days to extend the bacterial cover for partially treated typical pneumococcal pneumonia given her improvement plateau and the recent classmate outbreaks
options.rationale: Amoxicillin lacks activity against Mycoplasma pneumoniae and dose escalation will not cover the most likely pathogen in this age and clinical pattern; escalating beta-lactam dosing is the wrong axis of change here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

options.text: Admit her for intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg six-hourly for at least 48 hours and arrange a CT chest if she has not defervesced clinically by 48 hours into the intravenous treatment course
options.rationale: She is well-perfused, normoxic and tolerating oral fluids; she does not meet admission criteria and intravenous beta-lactam does not cover Mycoplasma pneumoniae. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae becomes the dominant pneumonia pathogen in school-aged children and adolescents and presents with a protracted dry cough, low-grade fever, bilateral interstitial changes on chest x-ray, and characteristically poor response to beta-lactam antibiotics. First-line treatment in Australia is oral azithromycin (10 mg/kg day 1, then 5 mg/kg daily for 4 days). Doxycycline is generally avoided under 8 years; intravenous therapy or admission are reserved for hypoxia, severe respiratory distress, dehydration, complications or failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Mycoplasma pneumoniae predominates in pneumonia from school-age onward
Classic features: prolonged dry cough, low-grade fever, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, classmate clustering
First-line: azithromycin 10 mg/kg day 1 then 5 mg/kg daily for 4 days (5-day total course)
Doxycycline reserved for over-8s; amoxicillin lacks Mycoplasma activity and should not be escalated for atypical pneumonia
explanation.pearls: If a school-aged child fails amoxicillin at 48 to 72 hours with bilateral interstitial changes and ongoing dry cough, switch to azithromycin first rather than escalating beta-lactam dose or jumping to intravenous therapy.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Community-acquired pneumonia paediatric

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 2-year-old girl with a 12-hour history of harsh barking cough preceded by a coryzal prodrome. On assessment now, she has a barking cough, mild stridor only when distressed or crying, no stridor at rest, no chest wall recession, normal mental state, and is interactive with her parents while sitting on her mother's lap.

She has had no exposure to a foreign body, immunisations are up to date including Hib, and she has no past history of asthma or recurrent wheeze. Her older brother had viral croup two weeks ago. The Westley croup score is 1 and she has been observed for 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, BP 95/55
data_table.Examination: Barking cough on examination, no stridor at rest, no recession, alert and interactive, oropharynx unremarkable, chest auscultation clear, no drooling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 immediately followed by oral dexamethasone and observe in the short stay unit for at least four hours before reconsidering disposition with paediatric review
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest or significant recession; using it in mild croup risks rebound and unnecessary admission for observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg now as a one-off and discharge home with written parental advice to return for stridor at rest, drooling, severe distress or any deterioration
options.rationale: Mild croup with no stridor at rest is managed with a single dose of oral dexamethasone and discharge with safety netting, since corticosteroid shortens illness duration and reduces representations. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Admit for nebulised budesonide every four hours and supplemental oxygen as required with paediatric inpatient observation overnight on the children's ward for serial respiratory assessment by the nursing staff
options.rationale: Inpatient nebulised budesonide every four hours is not standard for mild croup, where a single dose of oral dexamethasone with discharge is preferred and oxygen is not indicated given SpO2 99%. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Reassure the family, provide humidified room air at home and paracetamol as required without corticosteroid, with no need for routine review unless the child develops obvious respiratory distress or worsening symptoms
options.rationale: Humidified air is not effective for croup and corticosteroid should still be given even for mild disease because it shortens duration and reduces representation. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone and intramuscular ceftriaxone for possible bacterial tracheitis, then admit to the short stay unit overnight with ENT review and serial airway assessment given the persistent stridor on exertion
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by toxic appearance, high fever and copious purulent secretions, none of which are present here; routine antibiotics and IV steroid are not warranted. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Mild croup is defined by a barking cough with no stridor at rest and no respiratory distress (Westley score 0-2). The Australian standard of care is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg with discharge home and clear written safety-netting advice. Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate or severe croup with stridor at rest or significant work of breathing. Humidified air is not evidence-based and corticosteroid should still be given even in mild disease.
key_points: Mild croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose plus discharge with safety net
Moderate or severe croup: add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and observe minimum 4 hours
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic child with high fever and copious purulent secretions, not classic croup
explanation.pearls: RCH uses dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose for mild croup; prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 days is an alternative when dexamethasone is unavailable, but dexamethasone has better evidence for reducing return visits.

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease IVIG within 10 days plus high-dose aspirin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy admitted on day 6 of persistent fever to 39.5 degrees not responding to paracetamol or ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, a strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash that is not vesicular, a single right cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm, and early peri-ungual desquamation around the fingertips of the right hand noted today.

There has been no exposure to new medications. Echocardiography is being arranged for today and bloods are pending. He was previously well, fully immunised, with no travel and no sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.5, HR 152, RR 30, BP 96/58, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, polymorphous trunk rash, right cervical node 1.8 cm, early fingertip desquamation, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2, neutrophil 14, platelets 580, Hb 102, CRP 145, ESR 78, ALT 65, albumin 28, urine WCC 25 sterile, throat swab negative, ASOT not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day divided four times daily until afebrile then low-dose aspirin to follow-up echocardiography at 6 weeks for coronary artery assessment
options.rationale: Kawasaki disease meeting four of five principal clinical criteria with fever beyond 5 days mandates IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: High-dose aspirin 30 mg/kg/day divided four times daily as monotherapy and observation in hospital with daily echocardiography while monitoring for spontaneous defervescence prior to commencing intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
options.rationale: Aspirin alone does not reduce coronary aneurysm risk; IVIG plus aspirin must be commenced together within 10 days of fever onset for maximum cardioprotection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg daily for three days as first-line therapy for refractory Kawasaki disease with planned IVIG at 48 hours if no clinical response is observed and serial inflammatory marker measurement
options.rationale: Initial high-dose steroid is reserved for high-risk patients in some protocols (e.g., Kobayashi score) but is not standard first-line in Australia; IVIG plus aspirin remains the standard first dose. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Supportive care with paracetamol for fever, oral fluid encouragement and outpatient cardiology follow-up in four weeks with repeat echocardiography to assess for coronary changes and consideration of IVIG only if symptoms persist beyond 14 days
options.rationale: Delay beyond 10 days of fever onset substantially increases the risk of coronary aneurysm; this is unsafe under-treatment of an established Kawasaki diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics with ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly for an occult bacterial focus and pending blood culture results before considering immunomodulatory therapy
options.rationale: The clinical picture is diagnostic for Kawasaki disease rather than bacterial sepsis or scarlet fever; antibiotics are not the answer and delay of IVIG is harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis based on fever for at least 5 days plus four of five principal clinical criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oromucosal changes, extremity changes including desquamation, and cervical lymphadenopathy at least 1.5 cm). Treatment with a single IVIG dose 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to under 5%. Echocardiography at diagnosis, at 2 weeks and at 6-8 weeks is standard.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg + high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk
Aspirin is not coronary-protective by itself; IVIG is the key intervention
Echocardiography at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks
explanation.pearls: If IVIG-resistant fever persists at 36 hours after the first dose, a second dose of IVIG 2 g/kg is given; infliximab and corticosteroid are options in refractory cases per cardiology and rheumatology input.

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA initial fluid resuscitation without cerebral oedema
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department assessing an 8-year-old girl with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with two weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and 24 hours of vomiting and lethargy. She is alert (GCS 15), has dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 3 seconds and is tachycardic but not shocked. Her weight today is 28 kg.

There are no focal neurological signs, the headache score is 0, and she has had no recent insulin (this is a new diagnosis). The PICU has been informed but admission to the children's ward is planned with one-hourly observation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 130, BP 95/60, RR 22 with deep breathing, SpO2 99% room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, normal cardiovascular exam, deep sighing respirations, no focal neurology, weight 28 kg
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 28.4, ketones 5.6, VBG pH 7.18 HCO3 9 pCO2 22, Na 134, K 5.0, urea 9.2, Cr 78, urine ketones ++++, HbA1c 11.8%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?

options.text: Give 0.9 percent saline 10 mL/kg bolus over 60 minutes then commence calculated fluid as maintenance plus 5-7 percent dehydration replaced over 48 hours, and start IV insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour 1 hour after fluids begin
options.rationale: Australian paediatric DKA protocols use a single 10 mL/kg bolus (no shock) and 48-hour deficit replacement at 5-7 percent to minimise cerebral oedema risk, with insulin infusion starting after fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give 0.9 percent saline 20 mL/kg bolus rapidly over 10-15 minutes followed by a second 20 mL/kg bolus if perfusion has not normalised, and commence IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg before transitioning to infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: Large rapid boluses (20 mL/kg) and an insulin bolus increase cerebral oedema risk in paediatric DKA and should be avoided unless the child is in true hypovolaemic shock. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Commence IV 0.45 percent saline at twice maintenance without any initial bolus, and start IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately, with hourly capillary glucose and 2-hourly venous gas monitoring until acidosis resolves
options.rationale: Half-normal saline is not the appropriate initial fluid choice in paediatric DKA and skipping an initial bolus delays restoration of perfusion in a tachycardic, dry-mucous-membrane patient. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the metabolic acidosis prior to other interventions, with 0.9 percent saline running concurrently and IV insulin commenced once the pH has improved above 7.20 on repeat gas
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely indicated in paediatric DKA and is associated with worsened outcomes including cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

options.text: Commence IV 5 percent dextrose with potassium 40 mmol/L at maintenance rate from the outset to prevent hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia, with IV insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour and target serum glucose between 6 and 10 mmol/L
options.rationale: Initial fluid should be 0.9 percent saline without dextrose; dextrose is added once glucose falls to ~14-15 mmol/L to allow continued insulin infusion to clear ketones. (Source: APEG/RCH CPG: Diabetic Ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA management in Australia follows APEG/ISPAD guidance: assess for shock (rare), give a single 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline if not shocked, then replace assumed 5-7% deficit over 48 hours alongside maintenance. Insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour is started 1 hour after fluids commence; no insulin bolus. Bicarbonate is not used routinely. Dextrose is added once glucose approaches 14-15 mmol/L. Frequent neuro observations are essential to detect cerebral oedema.
key_points: Initial bolus: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline (20 mL/kg only if shocked)
Insulin: 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr starting 1 hour after fluids; no bolus
Bicarbonate not routine; monitor for cerebral oedema (headache, GCS drop)
explanation.pearls: Cerebral oedema features include headache, vomiting, GCS deterioration, bradycardia and hypertension; treat with 3% saline or mannitol immediately and reduce fluid rate.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA

subtopic_detail: Phototherapy threshold for late preterm infant at day 5 using age- and gestation-adjusted nomogram
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-day-old male infant born at 35 weeks and 1 day gestation by uncomplicated vaginal birth, now exclusively breastfed at home. He has had 9 percent weight loss from birth weight, dry mucous membranes and reduced wet nappies. He has visible jaundice extending to the lower legs. He is alert with normal tone. Mother's blood group is A positive (same as the baby), DCT is negative, and there is no family history of haemolytic disease, no bruising or cephalohaematoma. He had no jaundice on day-2 review by community midwife.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 148, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air, weight 2480 g (birth 2725 g, 9% loss)
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice to lower legs, dry mucous membranes, alert, normal tone, no organomegaly, no cephalohaematoma or bruising, normal stool and urine output reported
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 280 micromol/L, direct 18, Hb 168, reticulocytes 3%, DCT negative, blood group A+ (same as mother), CRP <5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy using overhead and underneath lights with infant naked except for nappy and eye protection, with feeding support to address lactation and 6-hourly serum bilirubin to monitor response and aim for cessation criteria
options.rationale: At 35-week gestation and day 5, a TSB of 280 micromol/L crosses the phototherapy line on the age- and gestation-adjusted nomogram, requiring phototherapy plus feeding optimisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion at the tertiary unit with planned admission to the neonatal intensive care unit and pre-procedure cross-match for two units of compatible blood from the transfusion service
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin well above the exchange line or for acute bilirubin encephalopathy; this value sits at the phototherapy line, not exchange. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Reassure the family that the jaundice is physiological breastfeeding jaundice given the normal DCT and absent haemolysis, encourage continued exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation and review in the community in 48 hours
options.rationale: TSB at the phototherapy threshold in a late preterm infant warrants active treatment rather than watchful waiting; physiological labelling does not negate the need for phototherapy at threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Replace breastfeeding with formula feeds via cup feeding for 48 hours and recheck TSB at 24 hours without commencing phototherapy, as adequate caloric intake will usually resolve the bilirubin elevation without need for light therapy
options.rationale: Cessation of breastfeeding is not first-line; feeding support to optimise breastfeeding is preferred while phototherapy is delivered, since stopping breastfeeding has its own harms. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer IV immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg over 4 hours and commence phototherapy concurrently, with serial TSB monitoring and DCT recheck within 24 hours to look for evidence of late-onset isoimmune haemolysis missed on initial testing
options.rationale: IVIG is for confirmed isoimmune haemolytic disease (e.g., DCT positive Rh or ABO incompatibility) where bilirubin rises rapidly despite phototherapy; not indicated here with negative DCT. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Phototherapy thresholds depend on gestational age, postnatal age in hours and risk factors for neurotoxicity, using nomograms such as those in RCH CPG or AAP. Late preterm infants (35-36 weeks) have lower thresholds than term infants because of greater bilirubin neurotoxicity risk. At 5 days postnatal age and 35 weeks gestation, TSB around 280 micromol/L meets the phototherapy threshold. Feeding optimisation is integral, as inadequate intake worsens jaundice via enterohepatic recirculation.
key_points: Phototherapy threshold = nomogram value at gestational + postnatal age
Late preterm thresholds are lower than term thresholds
Optimise feeding alongside phototherapy; stopping breastfeeding rarely needed
explanation.pearls: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy clinical features (lethargy, hypertonia, opisthotonos, high-pitched cry) mandate immediate exchange transfusion regardless of TSB value.

subtopic_detail: Repeat IM adrenaline at adult dose for school-age child with refractory anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with known peanut allergy who accidentally ate a peanut butter biscuit at a party 10 minutes ago. He has developed urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting once, a hoarse voice, audible expiratory wheeze, and a feeling of throat tightness. His parent administered his prescribed EpiPen Jr (150 mcg adrenaline) into the lateral thigh 5 minutes ago at home with no clear improvement before transfer.

On arrival in the resuscitation cubicle he remains distressed, tachypnoeic and his oxygen saturation has fallen on room air. Weight at his last GP visit was 24 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 140, RR 36, BP 92/56, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Diffuse urticaria, lip and tongue swelling, hoarse voice, audible expiratory wheeze, mild intercostal recession, alert but distressed, weight 24 kg
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.6, ECG sinus tachycardia, no IV access yet established, allergy passport documents peanut as known allergen, prior adrenaline auto-injector at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Repeat the EpiPen Jr 150 mcg IM into the opposite lateral thigh, reassess in 5 minutes and consider escalation only if no response, while preparing intravenous access and high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: At 6 years of age and 24 kg, the appropriate adrenaline dose has moved from the 150 mcg auto-injector to 300 mcg IM (1:1000 0.3 mL); repeating the junior dose underdoses. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Administer 0.3 mL of 1:1000 adrenaline (300 mcg) IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh, apply high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, position the patient supine with legs elevated, and obtain IV access for fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: For a school-age child of 24 kg the standard IM adrenaline dose is 300 mcg (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if needed; positioning and oxygen are concurrent. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Administer IV adrenaline 50 mcg bolus immediately under cardiac monitoring as the initial parenteral dose given the failure of the prehospital intramuscular dose to control the patient's airway and respiratory features
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis under continuous cardiac monitoring after multiple IM doses have failed; it is not the next step here. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask and IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as primary therapy for the bronchospasm component, with adrenaline reserved as backup if there is no improvement over the next 10 minutes
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the first-line therapy in anaphylaxis; salbutamol and hydrocortisone are adjuncts but never primary, and delaying adrenaline worsens outcomes. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Administer oral promethazine 10 mg and ranitidine 75 mg as combined H1 and H2 antihistamine therapy with reassessment after 20 minutes, plus consideration of a single dose of IM prednisolone 1 mg/kg as additional steroid
options.rationale: Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway compromise or shock in anaphylaxis; adrenaline is the only first-line drug. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 1:1000 into the mid-anterolateral thigh as first-line therapy; doses are 0.1 mL (10 kg or less), 0.15 mL (10-20 kg, EpiPen Jr), 0.3 mL (20-50 kg, EpiPen) and 0.5 mL (over 50 kg). Repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Concurrent oxygen, supine positioning with legs elevated, and IV fluid resuscitation are essential. Salbutamol, antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only.
key_points: First-line: IM adrenaline 1:1000 mid-anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min
Doses by weight: 10 kg = 0.1 mL; 20 kg = 0.15 mL; over 20 kg = 0.3 mL; over 50 kg = 0.5 mL
Adjuncts (steroid, antihistamine, salbutamol) never replace adrenaline
explanation.pearls: Refractory anaphylaxis after 2-3 IM doses warrants IV adrenaline infusion under cardiac monitoring with anaesthetic/ED senior input; biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% and warrant observation.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: 3-monthly slit-lamp screening in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA
stem: You are the paediatric rheumatology registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl with a 6-week history of intermittent painless right knee swelling and mild morning stiffness in the same joint. She has no fever, rash, mouth ulcers, weight loss, or systemic features. Examination shows a swollen non-tender right knee with reduced flexion, no other joints involved, and no enthesitis. Inflammatory markers are mildly elevated, ANA is positive at 1:320, RF and HLA-B27 are negative, and FBC is normal. Oligoarticular JIA has been diagnosed and an intra-articular triamcinolone injection has been planned. The family asks what additional screening their daughter requires.

data_table.Examination: Swollen non-tender right knee with reduced flexion, no other joints involved, no rash, no enthesitis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: ANA 1:320 positive, RF negative, HLA-B27 negative, ESR 32, CRP 18, FBC normal, MRI knee shows synovitis with effusion, no slit-lamp examination done yet

lead_in: What additional screening should be recommended?

options.text: Annual review by an ophthalmologist with formal visual acuity testing and fundoscopy alone, with patient and family education to seek earlier review if any visual symptoms such as redness, pain, or photophobia occur in either eye
options.rationale: Annual screening is insufficient frequency for high-risk patients (ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in young girls); chronic anterior uveitis is typically asymptomatic until visual loss has occurred. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Testing for HLA-B27 has already been performed and was negative so further specific eye screening is not indicated, with reassurance that uveitis only complicates HLA-B27-positive enthesitis-related JIA
options.rationale: HLA-B27 is associated with acute symptomatic uveitis (enthesitis-related arthritis) but the highest absolute risk of chronic asymptomatic uveitis is in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Six-monthly review by an orthopaedic surgeon for joint protection advice and assessment of leg-length discrepancy, with no requirement for additional eye review beyond standard school vision screening at age five
options.rationale: Orthopaedic review may be appropriate for monitoring leg-length discrepancy from chronic knee inflammation but does not address the high uveitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Three-monthly slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist to screen for chronic anterior uveitis, given that ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in young girls is the highest-risk category and uveitis is typically asymptomatic until visual loss occurs
options.rationale: ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in girls under 7 carries the highest risk of chronic asymptomatic anterior uveitis; 3-monthly slit-lamp screening is standard during the first years after diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Reassure the family that screening for uveitis is only required if the patient develops symptoms of redness, pain or visual loss, given the low risk in oligoarticular JIA compared with polyarticular and systemic onset disease
options.rationale: Chronic anterior uveitis in oligoarticular JIA is characteristically asymptomatic; waiting for symptoms allows synechiae, cataract, glaucoma and visual loss to occur. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis is the most important extra-articular complication of JIA. The highest risk is in young (under 7), ANA-positive, oligoarticular JIA - up to 30 percent develop uveitis within the first 4 years. Screening frequency is determined by age at diagnosis, subtype and ANA status. For high-risk children, 3-monthly slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist is recommended for the first 4 years, then 6-monthly, then annually. Uveitis is typically asymptomatic; early detection prevents synechiae, cataract, glaucoma and visual loss.
key_points: Highest uveitis risk: ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in girls under 7
3-monthly slit-lamp for first 4 years in high-risk category
Symptoms are absent until complications develop; screen don't wait
explanation.pearls: First-line uveitis treatment is topical steroid and mydriatic; refractory cases require methotrexate or adalimumab via paediatric rheumatology coordination with ophthalmology.

subtopic_detail: Observation only for paediatric ITP without major bleeding
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old previously well girl referred by the GP with 5 days of widespread petechiae and easy bruising, and a viral URTI 2 weeks ago. Examination shows widespread petechiae and ecchymoses but no mucosal bleeding, no haematuria, no haematochezia, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy and no bony tenderness. She is alert, playing happily, and has had no head trauma. The blood film shows isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red and white cell morphology and no blasts. Acute immune thrombocytopenia is diagnosed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 102, BP 96/60, SpO2 99% room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and ecchymoses, no mucosal bleeding, no haematuria, no haematochezia, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bony tenderness, playful
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12, Hb 130, WCC 7.0 with normal differential, blood film isolated thrombocytopenia with no blasts, reticulocytes normal, coagulation profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single dose of IVIG 0.8 g/kg over 6 hours as initial therapy because the platelet count is below 20 and the risk of intracranial haemorrhage is high enough to warrant first-line pharmacological intervention regardless of bleeding status
options.rationale: IVIG is reserved for major bleeding or planned surgery; platelet count alone (even below 20) is not an indication for pharmacological treatment in paediatric ITP. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days as a first-line treatment for paediatric immune thrombocytopenia, with tapering over the subsequent week and repeat platelet count at 1 week to assess response to corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Prednisolone is used for major bleeding or where treatment is required; it is not first-line for an asymptomatic well child with no bleeding even at platelet counts below 20. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Bone marrow examination before any management decision is made in order to exclude acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting with isolated thrombocytopenia, with treatment guided by bone marrow findings and haematologist input
options.rationale: Bone marrow examination is required only if atypical features (lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, abnormal blood film, abnormal red or white cell lines), none of which are present. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Single dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as inpatient therapy and admission for observation, with planned IVIG addition if no platelet response within 24 hours and haematology consultation for ongoing management
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for severe bleeding or refractory ITP; it is over-treatment of a well child without bleeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Observation only with no pharmacological treatment, written advice to avoid contact sport and NSAIDs, family education on signs of significant bleeding requiring re-presentation, and repeat platelet count by the GP in 1 week
options.rationale: Asymptomatic paediatric ITP without major bleeding is managed by observation; platelet count alone is not an indication for pharmacological therapy, and most acute cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Immune Thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Acute paediatric immune thrombocytopenia is a clinical diagnosis after viral illness with isolated thrombocytopenia and otherwise normal blood film. Treatment is guided by bleeding severity, NOT platelet count. Asymptomatic children without major bleeding are managed by observation with safety advice (avoid contact sport, NSAIDs, anticoagulants); most resolve spontaneously within 3 months. IVIG, anti-D, or prednisolone are reserved for major bleeding or planned procedures. Bone marrow examination is needed only when atypical features raise concern for malignancy.
key_points: Treat the bleeding, not the platelet count; observation if asymptomatic
Bone marrow only if atypical features (anaemia, abnormal WCC, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly)
Most acute paediatric ITP resolves within 3 months
explanation.pearls: Intracranial haemorrhage in paediatric ITP is very rare (<1%) even at very low platelet counts; head trauma, NSAIDs and anticoagulants are the main avoidable precipitants.

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease versus herpangina and HSV stomatitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old previously well boy with 2 days of fever to 38.5 and refusal to eat due to mouth pain. Examination demonstrates multiple small grey-white vesicles on the palms of both hands (approximately 8 lesions), soles of both feet, and shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa and tongue, with no rash on the trunk and no truncal vesicles.

His 5-year-old sister had a similar mild illness 1 week ago that resolved spontaneously. He is well-hydrated, alert, interactive with his parents, and there is no neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash on the buttocks or perineum, and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Small grey-white vesicles on palms and soles (about 8 on hands), shallow oral ulcers on buccal mucosa and tongue, no truncal rash, mucous membranes moist, no lymphadenopathy, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: No bloods taken; bedside glucose 5.4; no swabs sent; family confirms no recent travel; immunisations including MMR up to date

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.text: Primary herpes simplex stomatitis with widespread painful vesicles and ulcers in the mouth, with oral aciclovir 80 mg/kg/day in divided doses for 5-7 days, paracetamol-based analgesia, and exclusion from childcare until oral lesions have crusted
options.rationale: Primary HSV stomatitis typically causes larger painful gingivostomatitis with peri-oral involvement; absence of peripheral hand and foot vesicles makes HSV unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.text: Varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox) with vesicular eruption progressing from face and trunk centrifugally, with supportive care, anti-pruritic management, and exclusion from childcare for at least 5 days after the rash has appeared
options.rationale: Varicella has a typical centripetal vesicular truncal rash with lesions at multiple stages and posterior pharynx ulcers; peripheral hand and foot distribution with sparing of the trunk is not consistent with varicella. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.text: Hand foot and mouth disease caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71 with supportive care, adequate analgesia, oral fluid encouragement, and exclusion from childcare until vesicles have crusted (usually 7-10 days), with no antiviral therapy required
options.rationale: Hand foot and mouth disease is a clinical diagnosis based on oral ulcers plus peripheral hand and foot vesicles in a well child; management is supportive with childcare exclusion until vesicles crust. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.text: Herpangina from coxsackievirus group A presenting with isolated posterior pharyngeal vesicles and ulcers with high fever, with supportive analgesia and oral hydration, antiviral therapy is not warranted, and exclusion from school until resolution
options.rationale: Herpangina is limited to the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars without peripheral vesicles; this patient has peripheral hand and foot vesicles consistent with hand foot and mouth disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome with mucocutaneous involvement requiring urgent admission, cessation of any culprit medication, fluid and electrolyte management, ophthalmology and dermatology input, and dermatology-directed biopsy of representative skin lesions
options.rationale: Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents with multiple mucosal involvement plus target lesions and skin denudation in a systemically unwell child, none of which are present here; this child is well. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is caused most commonly by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71 (EV71 implicated in more severe and rare neurological complications). Clinical features are fever, painful oral ulcers (anywhere in the mouth, often anterior), and a vesicular rash on hands, feet and sometimes buttocks. Management is supportive with adequate analgesia and oral fluid encouragement. Children should be excluded from childcare until vesicles have crusted (usually 7-10 days). Adequate hand hygiene reduces household transmission.
key_points: Triad: fever + oral ulcers + peripheral vesicles (hands and feet)
Coxsackievirus A16 most common; EV71 occasionally causes severe disease
Supportive care only; exclude from childcare until vesicles crust
explanation.pearls: Watch for atypical EV71 disease (myocarditis, brainstem encephalitis, neurogenic pulmonary oedema) - red flags include high persistent fever, hyperhydrosis, myoclonus and listlessness.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

subtopic_detail: Moderate bronchiolitis HFNC and feeding strategy in infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old previously well term infant on day 3 of a coryzal illness now presenting with increased work of breathing and reduced feeds. He has had no apnoeas, is taking around 40% of his usual feed volumes, has had wet nappies 4 hours ago, and his older sibling is unwell with a viral upper respiratory tract infection.

He has no past wheeze, no atopy, no congenital heart disease and was not premature. Nasopharyngeal swab is pending. Trial of suctioning has provided only transient improvement and he remains in moderate respiratory distress on room air after observation in the ward over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 89% room air, BP 86/52
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, scattered fine inspiratory crackles bilaterally, occasional expiratory wheeze, alert but irritable, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Nasal swab pending; VBG pH 7.34 pCO2 50 lactate 1.4; no chest X-ray done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back and reassess in 20 minutes; if no improvement, give a single dose of oral prednisolone and admit overnight
