options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease presents earlier (often delayed meconium and failure to thrive); a 4-year-old with normal growth, soiling and a fissure has functional constipation. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Administer a phosphate enema in the clinic then commence lactulose for maintenance therapy at home
options.rationale: Oral macrogol is preferred over rectal disimpaction in children because it is less distressing and equally effective; phosphate enemas risk hyperphosphataemia in small children. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Arrange abdominal X-ray to quantify faecal loading and base disimpaction decisions on the radiographic score
options.rationale: Plain abdominal X-ray is not recommended in routine functional constipation; clinical assessment guides therapy and X-ray adds radiation without altering management. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at a disimpaction dose for up to 7 days then transition to maintenance
options.rationale: Australian paediatric guidance favours oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes for both disimpaction (escalating dose for up to 7 days) and maintenance in functional constipation, with ongoing behavioural toileting. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Recommend dietary fibre and increased fluid intake alone for 4 weeks before considering laxative therapy
options.rationale: Dietary advice alone rarely clears impaction and prolongs symptoms; macrogol with electrolytes is first-line alongside behavioural and dietary measures. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with faecal impaction in a preschool-aged child is treated with oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at a disimpaction dose for up to 7 days, then maintenance dose for several months alongside toilet sit routines and behavioural interventions. Rectal therapies are reserved for failed oral disimpaction. Imaging is rarely required.
key_points: Oral macrogol with electrolytes is first-line for both disimpaction and maintenance
Maintenance is continued for months past resolution to avoid relapse and re-impaction
Red flags (delayed meconium, faltering growth, perianal disease) prompt secondary review
explanation.pearls: Anal fissures from passing hard stools maintain the withholding cycle; topical local anaesthetic and stool softening together break the loop.

sources.label: NICE NG: Constipation in children and young people

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to ED with a 5-day history of palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain and bilateral ankle pain. Today he has had two episodes of dark cola-coloured urine. He had a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. His mother says urine output is reduced. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.1 degrees Celsius, HR 104, RR 22, BP 132/88 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower legs, abdomen soft with mild tenderness, no peritonism, ankles swollen but full range, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ blood, 2+ protein with red cell casts; urine protein-creatinine ratio 180 mg/mmol; creatinine 78 micromol/L; urea 9 mmol/L; platelets 380 x10^9/L; coags normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and initial management?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and outpatient urinalysis weekly because skin and joint signs predominate
options.rationale: Hypertension and nephritic-nephrotic urinary findings exceed simple HSP and mandate admission; outpatient management is reserved for isolated rash with normal BP and urinalysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

options.text: Admit for blood pressure control, monitoring of renal function and paediatric nephrology consultation
options.rationale: Macroscopic haematuria with hypertension and nephrotic-range proteinuria in HSP signals significant nephritis requiring inpatient monitoring, antihypertensive therapy, and early nephrology input. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg in the emergency department and discharge with follow-up in a week
options.rationale: Steroids may help abdominal pain or arthritis but do not prevent or treat established nephritis; severe nephritis requires admission, BP control, and nephrology input. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

options.text: Request abdominal ultrasound to exclude intussusception then discharge if no lead point is identified
options.rationale: Intussusception screening is reasonable with severe abdominal pain in HSP but does not address the dominant problem of nephritis with hypertension. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

options.text: Commence empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for suspected post-infectious glomerulonephritis
options.rationale: The rash, joint involvement, abdominal pain and timing make HSP nephritis the unifying diagnosis; broad-spectrum antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of sepsis. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura)

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura with macroscopic haematuria, hypertension and nephrotic-range proteinuria represents severe nephritis. Australian practice is admission for blood pressure control, serial renal function and urinalysis, and early paediatric nephrology consultation. Children with isolated rash and arthralgia, normal BP and bland urine can be managed as outpatients with weekly urinalysis for 6 months.
key_points: BP above the 95th centile with red-cell casts in HSP warrants admission
Steroids treat pain and arthritis but do not prevent or modify HSP nephritis
All HSP children need 6 months of urinalysis and BP monitoring to detect late nephritis
explanation.pearls: Renal biopsy is considered when nephrotic-range proteinuria persists beyond 4 weeks or creatinine rises; ACE inhibitor therapy is started for persistent proteinuria above 100 mg/mmol creatinine ratio.

stem: An 11-year-old girl presents to ED with 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg weight loss. She has no vomiting, abdominal pain or tachypnoea. She walks into the cubicle. A fingerprick capillary BSL is 22 mmol/L. You are deciding the initial inpatient plan as the paediatric registrar. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 18, BP 108/64 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, mildly dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft, no Kussmaul breathing, no acetone on breath
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.35, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 1.6 mmol/L, BGL 22 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 60 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Admit and commence a subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin regimen with diabetes education and oral fluids
options.rationale: Normal venous pH, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L and beta-hydroxybutyrate under 3 mmol/L exclude DKA; new T1DM without ketoacidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration and structured education. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/h with 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance rates
options.rationale: Insulin infusion is reserved for DKA or unable to tolerate oral intake; in mild hyperglycaemia without acidosis it adds risk of hypoglycaemia without benefit. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)

options.text: Administer a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus then commence DKA protocol with two-bag system
options.rationale: She does not meet DKA criteria; aggressive resuscitation in well-perfused euglycaemic-ketosis risks cerebral oedema and is not warranted. (Source: APEG/ADS DKA)

options.text: Discharge after diabetes nurse contact and commence metformin pending outpatient endocrinology review
options.rationale: Metformin is not first-line for type 1 diabetes; insulin is required from diagnosis. New T1DM mandates inpatient education and insulin initiation. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)

options.text: Trial oral rehydration in the short-stay unit and re-measure ketones at 4 hours before deciding on insulin
options.rationale: Insulin should not be delayed in new T1DM; without insulin ketosis will worsen and DKA may develop overnight. (Source: APEG/ADS New Onset T1DM)

explanation.summary: New onset type 1 diabetes without ketoacidosis is managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, oral hydration and structured inpatient education in Australian paediatric practice. DKA criteria require venous pH under 7.30 or bicarbonate under 18 mmol/L plus ketonaemia. Intravenous insulin and DKA protocols are reserved for those meeting these biochemical criteria or who cannot tolerate oral intake. Cerebral oedema risk increases with aggressive fluid resuscitation in mildly ill children, making the distinction important.
key_points: DKA requires pH under 7.30 OR bicarbonate under 18 mmol/L AND ketones 3 mmol/L or higher
Subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin is first-line for new T1DM without DKA
Metformin has no role in initial type 1 diabetes management
explanation.pearls: Typical starting total daily dose is 0.5 to 0.75 unit/kg/day split as 50% basal, 50% bolus with carbohydrate-counting and correction doses titrated to BSL targets.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is recovering from his second culture-confirmed febrile UTI in 6 months, both with E. coli. His first UTI at 18 months was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and he had a normal renal tract ultrasound at the time. Today he is afebrile after 24 hours of oral co-trimoxazole. His mother asks what additional imaging is needed.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 110, RR 24, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well, abdomen soft non-tender, no renal angle tenderness, growth on 50th centile, no spinal anomaly

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: Commence long-term low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis and defer all imaging unless a further symptomatic infection occurs in the future
options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne pathway reserves prophylaxis for proven high-grade reflux or frequent recurrence and does not defer imaging review in recurrent UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange an urgent inpatient micturating cystourethrogram to assess for vesico-ureteric reflux before discharge from this admission
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive and is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound; it is not the RCH first step after a second uncomplicated febrile UTI. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Repeat renal tract ultrasound and refer to paediatric nephrology for recurrent UTI; no routine DMSA scan in the RCH pathway
options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound for recurrent UTI together with paediatric specialist referral; DMSA is part of the NICE NG224 algorithm and is not part of the RCH cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange a contrast-enhanced CT KUB to characterise the renal cortex and to exclude any obstructive uropathy in this child
options.rationale: CT delivers significant ionising radiation and has no routine role in screening children for scarring or reflux. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring after this second febrile UTI episode
options.rationale: Would be correct only when following NICE NG224 rather than the local RCH Melbourne pathway; the RCH CPG does not include routine DMSA in the recurrent UTI cascade. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: After a second febrile UTI in a child under 3 years, the RCH Melbourne CPG recommends a non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and paediatric specialist referral. DMSA at 4 to 6 months is a NICE NG224 recommendation and is not part of the RCH algorithm. MCUG is reserved for atypical infection or abnormal renal tract ultrasound.
key_points: RCH Melbourne recurrent-UTI imaging: non-urgent renal tract ultrasound and specialist referral
DMSA is a NICE construct not adopted by RCH
MCUG reserved for atypical infection or abnormal ultrasound
Prophylaxis only for proven high-grade reflux or frequent recurrence
explanation.pearls: The RCH bottom-up strategy of ultrasound plus clinical follow-up reduces invasive imaging without missing significant uropathy.

sources.label: NICE NG: Urinary tract infection in under 16s

stem: A 2-day-old male term neonate is brought back to a regional hospital with poor feeding and cyanosis. He was born by uncomplicated NVD with Apgars 9 and 10 and discharged at 18 hours. His mother reports he has become progressively bluer over the morning, particularly with crying. Pre-ductal SpO2 is 78% and post-ductal SpO2 is 78%; both fail to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen by Hudson mask. Cardiac auscultation reveals a single second heart sound and no murmur. The paediatric retrieval team is 2 hours away.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 168, RR 60, SpO2 78% pre and post-ductal, BP 64/40 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed even on 100% oxygen, peripheries warm with brisk capillary refill, abdomen soft, liver edge 1 cm below costal margin, no audible murmur, single loud S2
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, BSL 3.2 mmol/L; CXR shows narrow mediastinum with mildly increased pulmonary vascularity

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step before retrieval arrives?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min and monitor for apnoea
options.rationale: Failure of SpO2 to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen with single S2 and narrow mediastinum suggests duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition with intact septum being a key consideration); prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and is life-saving while awaiting retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Continue 100% oxygen via Hudson mask and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram before any treatment
options.rationale: Oxygen alone is insufficient in duct-dependent lesions and may further close the ductus; treatment should not await imaging when failure of hyperoxia is documented. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Intubate, ventilate with 100% oxygen and commence dopamine infusion at 10 microgram/kg/min
options.rationale: Without ductal patency, dopamine will not raise systemic oxygenation; high FiO2 may accelerate ductal closure and worsen cyanosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence intravenous adenosine 100 microgram/kg as a rapid bolus for suspected supraventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: Heart rate 168 in a neonate is appropriate for distress and not SVT; adenosine has no role in cyanotic congenital heart disease without arrhythmia. (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation)

options.text: Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for sepsis and defer cardiac assessment until cultures return
options.rationale: Sepsis is in the differential but the hyperoxia test result and cardiac signs point to duct-dependent cardiac lesion; delaying prostaglandin while awaiting cultures risks ductal closure and circulatory collapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: A neonate with central cyanosis that fails to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen, single second heart sound and narrow mediastinum on CXR has duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease until proven otherwise. Intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 50 nanogram/kg/min is started immediately to maintain ductal patency while awaiting paediatric cardiac retrieval. Apnoea, hypotension and fever are recognised side effects requiring monitoring.
key_points: Hyperoxia test failure (SpO2 under 85% in 100% O2) suggests cyanotic congenital heart disease
Prostaglandin E1 10 nanogram/kg/min maintains ductal patency and is started before imaging
Apnoea is a key adverse effect; have intubation ready when starting prostaglandin
explanation.pearls: Pre and post-ductal saturations equal at 78% with the single S2 fits transposition of the great arteries with intact septum; the patient depends on shunting at atrial and ductal level until balloon atrial septostomy or arterial switch surgery.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

stem: A 30-month-old boy is brought to his GP with 36 hours of right ear pain and fever to 38.6 degrees Celsius. He has been miserable but is feeding well and is alert between febrile episodes. He has had one prior episode of unilateral acute otitis media 8 months ago that resolved with observation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 26, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous with reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; no otorrhoea; left tympanic membrane normal; chest clear; throat unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic analgesia with regular paracetamol and review in 48 hours if not improving
options.rationale: Australian guidelines support watchful waiting in children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe acute otitis media; antibiotics are added if not improving at 48 hours or worsening. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days commenced immediately today
options.rationale: Immediate antibiotics are indicated for bilateral AOM under 2 years, otorrhoea, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, severe illness or systemic toxicity; this child meets none of those criteria. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days commenced now
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for treatment failure after 48-72 hours of amoxicillin or for recurrent AOM, not for initial therapy of straightforward unilateral disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Oral cefuroxime axetil 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as a cephalosporin alternative
options.rationale: Oral cephalosporins are reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy and are not first-line in AOM; their pneumococcal pharmacokinetics are inferior to amoxicillin. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute otitis media)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as a single dose given the risk of mastoiditis
options.rationale: Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is reserved for children vomiting all oral antibiotics or with non-severe penicillin allergy when oral options are inappropriate; it is not first-line in well children. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Watchful waiting with safety-net analgesia is supported in children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe AOM in Australian guidelines. Immediate antibiotics are reserved for children under 2 with bilateral disease, otorrhoea, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, or systemic toxicity. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and cephalosporins have specific second-line indications.
key_points: Children over 2 years with unilateral non-severe AOM can be safely observed for 48 hours
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for AOM treatment failure or recurrent disease
Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is reserved for those unable to tolerate oral antibiotics
explanation.pearls: The most reliable AOM antibiotic indications in Australia are bilateral disease under 2 years, otorrhoea at any age, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity and systemic toxicity.

stem: An 18-month-old girl presents to her GP with a 2-day history of fever to 38.4 degrees Celsius, oral pain and a rash on her hands and feet. She is still drinking water and dilute juice but has refused solids for 24 hours. She attends family day care 3 days per week. Her vaccinations are up to date and she is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air; wet nappies in last 4 hours
data_table.Examination: Multiple shallow grey ulcers on tongue and buccal mucosa; vesicles on palms and soles and around perioral skin; no neck stiffness; chest clear; abdomen soft

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days targeting herpes simplex replication
options.rationale: Aciclovir has no role in enteroviral hand foot and mouth disease; it is reserved for herpes simplex stomatitis which typically causes ulcers on the anterior tongue and gingiva without acral vesicles. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.text: Symptomatic analgesia with paracetamol, oral fluids, and day care exclusion until blisters dry
options.rationale: Hand foot and mouth disease is self-limiting; management is analgesia and hydration, with day care exclusion until all vesicles have dried as per NCIRS recommendations. (Source: NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days targeting bacterial pharyngitis as cause
options.rationale: Bacterial pharyngitis would not produce vesicles on the hands and feet; antibiotics are not indicated for the enteroviral exanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.text: Topical viscous lignocaine 2% to the oral ulcers four times daily as topical analgesia
options.rationale: Topical lignocaine carries a risk of seizures and methaemoglobinaemia in young children and is not recommended in this age group for HFM. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

options.text: Oral nystatin 100,000 units four times daily as antifungal mouth therapy for oral ulcers
options.rationale: Oral candida produces white plaques rather than ulcers and acral vesicles; nystatin is not indicated in the enteroviral exanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease

explanation.summary: Hand foot and mouth disease is a self-limiting enteroviral illness with oral ulcers and acral vesicles. Management is analgesia, hydration and day care exclusion until all vesicles have dried. Topical lignocaine should be avoided in young children due to seizure and methaemoglobinaemia risk. Antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals are not indicated.
key_points: Hand foot mouth disease is supportive only with analgesia and hydration
Day care exclusion is required until all vesicles have dried per NCIRS
Topical lignocaine is unsafe in young children for oral ulcer pain
explanation.pearls: Watch for dehydration as the main complication; admit if a child cannot maintain oral intake or develops neurological signs suggesting rare enteroviral encephalitis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Hand, foot and mouth disease
NCIRS: Enteroviruses and hand, foot and mouth disease

stem: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of fever and reduced feeding. There are no respiratory symptoms and no rash. She is the first child of well parents, was born at term and has had no prior infections. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. A catheter specimen of urine shows leucocytes and nitrites with bacteria on microscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.4 degrees Celsius, HR 170, RR 40, SpO2 98% in room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; anterior fontanelle soft; chest clear; abdomen soft with no mass; nappy area normal
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine: leucocytes 4+, nitrites positive, bacteria 3+; bloods: WCC 18, CRP 75, creatinine 30; blood culture pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 4 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days at home with GP review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI require initial parenteral therapy due to the risk of bacteraemia and pyelonephritis; oral therapy alone is inappropriate at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days as outpatient management today
options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is not appropriate for febrile UTI under 6 months; admission for IV antibiotics is required while culture and sensitivities return. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily and IV benzylpenicillin while culture results return
options.rationale: Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months requires admission for empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin per Australian paediatric guidance; transition to oral therapy follows clinical improvement and sensitivities. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children

options.text: Discharge with a single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and outpatient follow-up tomorrow
options.rationale: Single-dose IM ceftriaxone with outpatient follow-up is not the standard Australian approach in young infants and risks under-treatment of bacteraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Discharge with oral amoxicillin and arrange an outpatient renal tract ultrasound next week
options.rationale: Discharge on oral amoxicillin alone is unsafe in a young infant with febrile UTI; renal tract imaging is appropriate after acute treatment but is not the initial step. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Febrile UTI in infants under 6 months is managed with admission for empirical IV gentamicin and a beta-lactam in Australia, given the risk of bacteraemia and pyelonephritis. Oral therapy alone, single-dose IM ceftriaxone, and outpatient discharge are inappropriate at this age. Renal tract imaging is arranged after acute treatment.
key_points: Infants under 6 months with febrile UTI need admission for IV antibiotics
Empirical regimen is IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin
Outpatient oral therapy is inappropriate due to bacteraemia risk at this age
explanation.pearls: After first febrile UTI in any child under 6 months, arrange renal tract ultrasound; consider DMSA at 4-6 months and MCUG only if there is high recurrence or imaging abnormality.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: Urinary tract infection in children

stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes at home in the setting of fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius. He has had 24 hours of cough and rhinorrhoea. He has no prior seizures and his development is normal. He is now alert though sleepy. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.8 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air, capillary glucose 5.2
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, no focal neurology, anterior fontanelle closed and not bulging, no neck stiffness, no petechial rash, ENT normal, chest clear

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for lumbar puncture given age under 24 months and a seizure in the setting of fever
options.rationale: LP is no longer recommended on age alone in a well, alert, fully vaccinated child with a simple febrile seizure; it is reserved for signs of meningitis or atypical features. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Commence daily prophylactic sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day to prevent further febrile seizures
options.rationale: Daily anti-seizure medication is not recommended for simple febrile seizures; the benign natural history and the side effects of valproate outweigh any small reduction in recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient EEG within 1 week to characterise the seizure type before discharge
options.rationale: EEG is not routinely indicated for a simple febrile seizure; it does not predict recurrence or epilepsy and is reserved for atypical or complex features. (Source: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children)
source_refs: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children

options.text: Reassure the family, advise antipyretics for comfort, and provide written first-aid seizure advice
options.rationale: Simple febrile seizures are benign with a low risk of epilepsy; management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort (which do not prevent recurrence) and written seizure first-aid advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

options.text: Prescribe buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg for parents to use if any future seizure exceeds 5 minutes
options.rationale: Rescue benzodiazepines are reserved for children with prolonged or recurrent complex febrile seizures, not after a single simple febrile seizure of 2 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile seizure)

explanation.summary: Simple febrile seizures are brief generalised tonic-clonic events in well children aged 6 months to 5 years and carry a benign prognosis. Management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort and written first-aid advice. Lumbar puncture is reserved for suspected meningitis. Daily anti-seizure medication and routine EEG are not indicated.
key_points: Simple febrile seizure is brief, generalised, single in 24 hours, in a well child
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent febrile seizure recurrence
LP, EEG and daily anticonvulsants are not routinely indicated
explanation.pearls: Buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg is reserved for children with previous febrile status epilepticus or known epilepsy, not after a first simple febrile seizure.

sources.label: NSW Health: Febrile convulsions in children

stem: A 5-year-old boy (20 kg) with known peanut allergy collapsed at a birthday party 15 minutes ago after eating a satay skewer. The ambulance crew gave intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg in the lateral thigh en route and again 5 minutes later on arrival in the emergency department. IV access has been established. He remains audibly stridorous with widespread urticaria.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 38, SpO2 90% on 8 L oxygen via mask, BP 65/35, HR 165, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor and expiratory wheeze, generalised urticaria, perioral angioedema, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Medications: Two IM adrenaline 0.15 mg doses given 5 minutes apart; IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus commenced

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Third intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg dose with a second IV crystalloid bolus of 20 mL/kg
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends that anaphylaxis failing to improve after 2 IM adrenaline doses is escalated to a controlled IV adrenaline infusion rather than further IM doses, due to absorption variability in shock. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and oral cetirizine 5 mg as adjunct anti-inflammatory therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines are second-line adjuncts and do not reverse airway compromise or shock; they are not the immediate priority in refractory anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in 5 mL of saline for ongoing upper airway swelling and stridor
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for upper airway oedema but does not address systemic hypotension; an IV adrenaline infusion is preferred when refractory shock coexists. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis)

options.text: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg using the adult dose to overcome refractory severe symptoms
options.rationale: Adult-dose IM adrenaline is not weight-appropriate in a 20 kg child; further IM dosing is not the recommended escalation when 2 doses have failed. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

options.text: Commence IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated and continue IV fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: When anaphylaxis is refractory after 2 IM adrenaline doses, ASCIA recommends a controlled IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response with ongoing fluid resuscitation. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
source_refs: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis refractory to 2 doses of IM adrenaline is managed with an IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response, in addition to continued fluid resuscitation and airway support. Corticosteroids, antihistamines and nebulised adrenaline are adjuncts rather than primary therapy. Adult dosing and further IM doses are not recommended in refractory paediatric shock.
key_points: IV adrenaline infusion is indicated when anaphylaxis fails to respond to 2 IM doses
Starting rate is 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to clinical response in monitored settings
Fluid resuscitation continues alongside vasoactive escalation
explanation.pearls: Always seek airway expertise early in refractory anaphylaxis; angioedema can progress rapidly and a small calibre paediatric airway is at risk during ongoing resuscitation.

sources.label: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis Guidelines

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP with 6 months of hard infrequent stools every 4 to 5 days and recent daily faecal soiling of his underwear. He has crampy abdominal pain that improves after stooling. He passed meconium at 18 hours of age, growth percentiles are appropriate for age and the lumbosacral spine is normal. He has been on lactulose 5 mL twice daily for 8 weeks without improvement.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with palpable suprapubic faecal mass; perianal inspection normal with no fissure or anteriorly displaced anus; normal lower limb tone, reflexes and gait
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart: height and weight tracking 50th centile; no plain abdominal x-ray performed

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence outpatient high-dose macrogol 3350 with electrolytes disimpaction regimen over 3 days
options.rationale: Functional constipation with overflow soiling and palpable faecal mass is managed with disimpaction followed by maintenance laxatives; high-dose macrogol with electrolytes outpatient over 3 days is first-line per RCH and NICE. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for assessment for Hirschsprung disease and anorectal manometry
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease is unlikely given timely meconium passage, appropriate growth and absence of red flags; surgical referral is not indicated as the initial step. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people)
source_refs: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.text: Admit for nasogastric polyethylene glycol lavage given outpatient laxative failure to date
options.rationale: Inpatient nasogastric PEG lavage is reserved for failure of outpatient disimpaction; an adequate disimpaction regimen has not yet been trialled. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Add a daily sodium picosulfate stimulant to current lactulose for ongoing chronic management
options.rationale: Adding a stimulant without first disimpacting the rectal faecal mass will not relieve overflow soiling and risks ongoing cramping; disimpaction must precede maintenance therapy. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people)
source_refs: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

options.text: Order plain abdominal x-ray to confirm faecal loading before changing management today
options.rationale: Plain abdominal x-ray is not routinely required when faecal loading is clinically evident and adds radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation with overflow soiling in a child without red flags is managed with outpatient disimpaction using high-dose macrogol with electrolytes over 3 days, followed by maintenance laxatives and behavioural measures. Inpatient lavage is reserved for outpatient failure. Surgical referral and routine imaging are not indicated when red flags are absent.
key_points: Disimpaction precedes maintenance therapy in functional constipation with overflow
High-dose macrogol with electrolytes over 3 days is the standard outpatient regimen
Red flag features prompt referral but routine imaging is not required
explanation.pearls: Educate that maintenance laxatives are continued for at least 6 months, with toileting routines after meals to use the gastrocolic reflex; weaning is gradual after several months of regular soft stools.

sources.label: NICE CG99: Constipation in children and young people

subtopic_detail: Infantile spasms recognition and initial therapy
stem: A previously well 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 2-week history of recurrent brief episodes of sudden symmetric flexion of her head, arms and legs, occurring in clusters of 10 to 30 events shortly after waking. Her parents have captured several events on video. Over the same period her parents report loss of social smiling and reduced engagement compared with her baseline. She is afebrile and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Alert but quiet, no focal neurology, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference 50th centile; no neurocutaneous stigmata on inspection of skin
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.8; videos reviewed show characteristic flexor spasms in clusters with brief crying after each cluster

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents that these are benign myoclonic jerks of infancy and require no investigation
options.rationale: Loss of developmental skills with clustered flexor spasms is highly suggestive of infantile epileptic spasms syndrome rather than benign myoclonus of infancy and requires urgent assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Arrange urgent neurology referral and EEG within 24 to 48 hours and start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily
options.rationale: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome requires urgent EEG looking for hypsarrhythmia and prompt first-line therapy with prednisolone or vigabatrin (vigabatrin if tuberous sclerosis); delayed treatment worsens developmental outcome. (Source: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

options.text: Trial oral phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg daily and review response in clinic at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is not effective for infantile spasms; first-line therapy is hormonal (prednisolone or ACTH) or vigabatrin, with rapid review for response. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Order outpatient MRI brain at 4 weeks and review with results before treatment
options.rationale: Treatment must not be delayed for MRI; commencing first-line therapy promptly while imaging is arranged optimises developmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 20 mg/kg daily and review in 2 weeks for clinical response
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is not first-line for infantile spasms; hormonal therapy and vigabatrin have higher response rates and faster resolution of hypsarrhythmia. (Source: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

explanation.summary: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West syndrome) presents with clusters of flexor spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Prompt first-line treatment with hormonal therapy (prednisolone or ACTH) or vigabatrin within days improves developmental outcome. Sodium valproate and phenobarbitone are not first-line. Treatment is not delayed for MRI.
key_points: Clustered flexor spasms with developmental regression is the West syndrome triad
First-line therapy is prednisolone or ACTH; vigabatrin if tuberous sclerosis
Delay to treatment worsens neurodevelopmental outcome
explanation.pearls: Look for ash-leaf macules and other neurocutaneous stigmata; tuberous sclerosis with infantile spasms is preferentially treated with vigabatrin.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of Physicians: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

subtopic_detail: Neonatal HSV central nervous system disease
stem: An 18-day-old term neonate is brought to the emergency department with 24 hours of lethargy, poor feeding, fever to 38.4 degrees Celsius and clusters of vesicles on the scalp at the site of a fetal scalp electrode. The mother had primary genital herpes at 36 weeks of gestation and was on suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks. He was born by spontaneous vaginal birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 180, RR 60, SpO2 96% in room air, capillary glucose 3.6
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, decreased tone, anterior fontanelle full but not bulging, scalp vesicles in clusters on a red base; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Blood culture pending; CSF: WCC 50 (mononuclear), protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 2.4; CSF HSV-2 PCR positive; surface viral swabs pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: IV cefotaxime 50 mg/kg eight-hourly for 14 days as empirical bacterial meningitis cover only
options.rationale: Empirical bacterial cover does not treat HSV; in any neonate with CSF HSV PCR positive disease, IV aciclovir is mandatory and prolonged. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: Oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 14 days as outpatient management with review
options.rationale: Oral aciclovir has inadequate bioavailability and CNS penetration in neonatal HSV; IV therapy for 21 days is required for disseminated or CNS disease. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg eight-hourly for 21 days with ophthalmology and neurology review
options.rationale: Neonatal HSV with CNS or disseminated involvement is treated with IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 21 days, with ophthalmology assessment and a repeat CSF PCR at the end of therapy to confirm clearance. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and IV amoxicillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly for 10 days
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates due to bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation; HSV CNS disease additionally requires IV aciclovir. (Source: RCH CPG: Herpes simplex virus)

options.text: IV ganciclovir 6 mg/kg twice daily for 21 days targeting cytomegalovirus disease
options.rationale: Ganciclovir is reserved for congenital CMV disease; it is not the agent for HSV-2 neonatal CNS infection where aciclovir is the standard. (Source: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection)
source_refs: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

explanation.summary: Neonatal HSV with CNS or disseminated disease requires IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 21 days, with end-of-therapy repeat CSF PCR and ophthalmology review. Oral aciclovir is inadequate as initial therapy. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates. After completion of IV therapy, suppressive oral aciclovir is given for 6 months.
key_points: Neonatal HSV CNS disease needs IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg q8h for 21 days
Oral aciclovir is inadequate as primary therapy for neonatal HSV
Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates due to bilirubin displacement
explanation.pearls: After IV therapy, neonates receive suppressive oral aciclovir 300 mg/m2 three times daily for 6 months to reduce neurodevelopmental morbidity and recurrent skin disease.

sources.label: ASID: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection

stem: A 9-month-old previously well infant is brought to a regional ED with 3 days of coryza and 1 day of increasing cough and noisy breathing. He has not been feeding well today and his nappies are dry over the past 8 hours. He has had no apnoeas reported by his mother and is alert when stimulated. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and is up to date with vaccinations. His chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and mild expiratory wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.6 degrees Celsius, HR 158, RR 64, SpO2 90% on room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Moderate intercostal and subcostal recession, nasal flaring; cool peripheries; chest with widespread crackles and wheeze; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care viral PCR positive for respiratory syncytial virus; capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit, commence humidified low-flow nasal cannula oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 92 percent, support feeding with small frequent volumes or nasogastric feeds as needed, and reassess hourly
options.rationale: AU guidance targets SpO2 of at least 90 percent (not 92 percent); the higher threshold prolongs admission without outcome benefit and misstates AU policy. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes and intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg six hourly as the first-line therapy for moderate bronchiolitis in this child today
options.rationale: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; supportive care is the mainstay. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with parental safety-net advice, oral paracetamol 15 mg/kg six hourly and review with the GP in 24 hours if symptoms have not improved at all by then with rest
options.rationale: Hypoxia, dehydration and moderate work of breathing meet admission criteria; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily and order a chest X-ray as the first-line management for moderate bronchiolitis in this previously well 9-month-old infant today
options.rationale: Antibiotics and chest X-ray are not routinely indicated in straightforward viral bronchiolitis; supportive care is the mainstay. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit, commence humidified nasal cannula oxygen to keep SpO2 of at least 90 percent, support hydration with small frequent feeds or nasogastric top-ups, and reassess hourly
options.rationale: AU and RCH guidance for moderate bronchiolitis with hypoxia (SpO2 under 92 percent) and feeding difficulty is admission, oxygen to keep SpO2 of at least 90 percent, and feeding support; no routine antibiotics, bronchodilators or steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months. Admission is indicated for SpO2 under 92 percent on room air, moderate or severe work of breathing, feeding under 50 percent of usual, dehydration, apnoeas or risk factors such as ex-prematurity. Treatment is supportive: oxygen to maintain SpO2 of at least 90 percent, small frequent feeds or NG hydration, and humidified high-flow if escalation is needed. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and chest X-rays are not routine.
key_points: Admit if SpO2 under 92 percent or moderate-severe work of breathing or feeding under 50 percent of usual
Oxygen target is SpO2 of at least 90 percent, not higher, in stable bronchiolitis
No routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics or chest X-rays
explanation.pearls: Oxygen saturation target of at least 90 percent (not 92 percent) is the AU paediatric bronchiolitis admission threshold; aiming higher prolongs admission without outcome benefit.

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury in a non-mobile infant
stem: A 5-month-old girl is brought to ED by her mother after being noticed to have multiple bruises in different stages of healing. She is not yet rolling or crawling. Chest radiograph performed for an unrelated cough shows a healing posterior rib fracture. There is no documented family history of bleeding disorders or osteogenesis imperfecta. The history of injury offered is vague and changes between caregivers. Other siblings are unwell with no clear medical cause documented.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 132, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Multiple bruises over trunk and limbs in different stages of healing, frenal tear noted on upper lip examination, anterior fontanelle full
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 2.6 g/L, ALT 28 U/L; calcium and ALP within reference range; CXR shows healing posterior rib fracture

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with verbal safety advice for the parents, with a GP review in 4 weeks for general well-child check and no further specialist or child protection involvement initiated at this time
options.rationale: The combination of bruising in a non-mobile infant, frenal tear, sentinel posterior rib fracture and inconsistent history mandates inpatient evaluation, safeguarding referral and mandatory reporting. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury; AIFS mandatory reporting)

options.text: Arrange GP follow-up in 6 weeks for review of the bruises and the healing rib fracture, with no specific paediatric or child protection involvement requested before that GP review
options.rationale: Delayed outpatient review fails the safeguarding threshold; sentinel injuries demand same-day inpatient evaluation. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury)

options.text: Treat the rib fracture conservatively with simple analgesia and discharge home with no further investigation, no consultation with child protection services, and no follow-up at any later date
options.rationale: Posterior rib fractures in non-mobile infants carry a very high specificity for inflicted injury and require comprehensive workup with safeguarding. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury)

options.text: Telephone parents to clarify the history of the injury and arrange a home visit by a community nurse in 24 hours, with no immediate inpatient workup, safeguarding referral or mandatory report submitted
options.rationale: Reliance on caregiver-reclarification in a sentinel-injury picture risks ongoing harm; mandatory reporting and inpatient workup are required. (Source: AIFS mandatory reporting)

options.text: Admit for full skeletal survey, fundoscopy, head imaging and coagulation profile to exclude mimics, plus urgent paediatric and child protection team consultations and a mandatory report to statutory services
options.rationale: Suspected non-accidental injury in a non-mobile infant requires inpatient comprehensive evaluation (skeletal survey, fundoscopy, neuroimaging, coagulation and bone profile to exclude mimics), child protection consultation and statutory mandatory reporting. (Source: RCH CPG: suspected non-accidental injury; AIFS mandatory reporting)

explanation.summary: Sentinel injuries (bruises in a non-mobile infant, frenal tears, posterior rib fractures) carry high specificity for inflicted injury and trigger inpatient comprehensive evaluation. Workup excludes mimics (coagulopathy, osteogenesis imperfecta, metabolic bone disease) and documents the pattern (skeletal survey under 2 years, neuroimaging, fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhage when intracranial findings or under 2 years). All Australian states mandate reporting suspected child abuse by medical practitioners. Child protection and social work involvement, multidisciplinary case management and safe disposition planning follow.
key_points: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is highly suspicious for inflicted injury until proven otherwise
Posterior rib fractures in infants have high specificity for inflicted injury
Mandatory reporting by medical practitioners applies in all Australian states and territories
explanation.pearls: TEN-4 FACES rule: bruises in non-mobile infants under 4 months, or torso, ear or neck bruises in infants under 4 years, are sentinel injuries warranting safeguarding workup until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media without severe features in a well child over 24 months
stem: A 26-month-old child presents with 24 hours of left ear pain and unsettled sleep, with a temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius. He is feeding well and is alert. There is no history of recurrent ear infection and no perforation or otorrhoea. Father asks whether antibiotics are needed today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, RR 24, T 38.2, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mildly bulging erythematous left tympanic membrane with intact light reflex; right ear normal; no mastoid tenderness; no rash

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days starting at this visit today
options.rationale: First-line antibiotics are reserved for under 6 months, severe systemic illness, perforation with discharge, bilateral disease in under 2 year olds, or failure of watchful waiting at 48 hours. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 3 days starting at this visit today
options.rationale: Macrolides are not first-line for acute otitis media in Australia; if antibiotics are indicated, amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)

options.text: Regular paracetamol with safety-netting and planned clinical review at 48 hours
options.rationale: AU practice supports a watch and wait approach with adequate analgesia for non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months without high-risk features. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Same-day ENT referral for myringotomy with grommet insertion under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for recurrent or chronic otitis media with effusion and hearing impact, not an uncomplicated first presentation. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media)

options.text: Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops twice daily for 7 days with home review
options.rationale: Topical ear antibiotics treat otitis externa or chronic suppurative otitis media with perforation, not acute otitis media with an intact tympanic membrane. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: acute otitis media)

explanation.summary: Australian practice supports watchful waiting with analgesia for non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months who are systemically well. Antibiotics are reserved for children under 6 months, severe systemic illness, perforation with otorrhoea, bilateral disease in under 2 year olds, or failure to improve at 48 hours. First-line if needed is amoxicillin; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or cefuroxime is used in true penicillin allergy. Recurrent acute otitis media (three episodes in 6 months or four in 12 months) prompts ENT referral for grommet assessment.
key_points: Watch and wait with analgesia suits non-severe acute otitis media in children over 24 months
Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days is first-line when antibiotics are indicated
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, infants under 6 months, and severe illness skip the wait
explanation.pearls: Adequate paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4 to 6 hours combined with ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours controls otalgia in the first 48 hours better than antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Mild to moderate croup disposition and treatment selection
stem: A 2-year-old boy presents in the early hours of the morning with a 1 day coryzal illness followed by a sudden onset barking cough and noisy breathing. He has a mild intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest, mild chest wall recession on excitement, and settles when held by his mother. He is taking oral fluids. There are no drooling, dysphagia, or unvaccinated immunisation status concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 97% room air, T 37.8
data_table.Examination: Hoarse voice, barking cough, mild inspiratory stridor at rest, mild recession on crying, equal air entry, no foreign body history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for suspected bacterial tracheitis with a chest X-ray to confirm
options.rationale: Bacterial tracheitis presents with high fever, toxicity and copious tracheal secretions; this child has a typical croup pattern and antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL and admit to the paediatric high dependency unit overnight for continuous monitoring of airway
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe or life-threatening croup with persistent stridor at rest; this child has mild croup that settles when held. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

options.text: Single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, observe until stridor at rest settles and oral intake is reliable, then discharge with safety-net advice
options.rationale: The RCH Melbourne Croup CPG uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup, reserving 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) for severe or life-threatening disease. Post-dexamethasone observation is tied to clinical resolution rather than a fixed time clock; the 3-hour rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

options.text: Cool mist humidification therapy and discharge home with parental reassurance and no medication for this distressing nocturnal symptom
options.rationale: Humidification has not been shown to alter the course of croup; the RCH CPG recommends oral dexamethasone for all severities including mild. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

options.text: Urgent ENT review with anaesthetic team on standby for fibreoptic laryngoscopy to exclude any structural airway pathology
options.rationale: Airway instrumentation risks complete obstruction and is not indicated for typical viral croup; the RCH pathway uses oral dexamethasone alone for mild disease. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: The RCH Melbourne Croup CPG uses oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg) is reserved for severe or life-threatening disease where nebulised adrenaline is also given. Post-dexamethasone observation is tied to clinical resolution (stridor at rest settled, oral intake reliable) rather than a fixed time clock; the 3-hour observation rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only.
key_points: RCH dex dose: 0.15 mg/kg for mild/moderate; 0.6 mg/kg for severe/life-threatening only
Post-dex observation tied to clinical resolution, not a fixed 4-hour wait
3-hour rule applies after nebulised adrenaline only
Nebulised adrenaline reserved for severe or life-threatening croup
explanation.pearls: The dexamethasone peak effect is at 1 to 2 hours; reassess airway and feeding before discharge.

subtopic_detail: Acute asthma exacerbation in a 5 year old: oral prednisolone course
stem: A 5-year-old girl with a known diagnosis of asthma presents with 2 days of cough and wheeze after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She has used her salbutamol metered dose inhaler with spacer 4 hourly at home without sustained relief. She is talking in short phrases, with mild intercostal recession. She has been given salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer in the department with a partial response.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 38, SpO2 94% room air, T 37.2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, mild subcostal recession, no cyanosis, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in addition to ongoing bronchodilator therapy?

options.text: Nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms every 20 minutes for the first hour
options.rationale: Ipratropium is added to severe exacerbations in the first hour, not as the next single step in a moderate exacerbation with a partial salbutamol response. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg as a single dose given over 20 minutes now
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium is reserved for severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroids. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Inhaled fluticasone propionate 125 micrograms twice daily as preventer initiation
options.rationale: Preventer initiation is a planned outpatient decision; it does not treat the acute exacerbation. (Source: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days as adjunctive cover
options.rationale: Most paediatric asthma exacerbations are viral and antibiotics offer no benefit without focal pneumonia or signs of bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days starting at this presentation
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days is standard AU practice for acute asthma exacerbations of moderate or greater severity in children. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

explanation.summary: Acute asthma in school-aged children is graded mild, moderate, severe, or critical based on speech, work of breathing, oxygen saturation, and conscious state. Salbutamol via spacer is the cornerstone of bronchodilator delivery in children. Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days is added in moderate or greater exacerbations and reduces relapse. Severe disease may require ipratropium, intravenous magnesium sulfate, intravenous aminophylline, or intravenous salbutamol with paediatric intensive care input.
key_points: Salbutamol via spacer beats nebuliser for delivery and side effects in mild to moderate disease
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days suits moderate exacerbations from age 1 year
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes is reserved for severe disease
explanation.pearls: Spacer delivered salbutamol gives 6 puffs for a child under 6 years and 12 puffs for older children, repeated every 20 minutes for the first hour in moderate exacerbations.

sources.label: National Asthma Council: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: First febrile UTI in young girl: imaging algorithm
stem: An 18-month-old girl is admitted with a first episode of fever to 39 degrees Celsius and vomiting. A clean catch urine culture grows greater than 10 to the 8 colony forming units per litre of Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She responds to intravenous gentamicin with defervescence by 36 hours and switches to oral trimethoprim to complete a 7 day course. Family history is negative for renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 30, T 38.4 on day 2, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well perfused, soft non-tender abdomen, no flank mass, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: CRP peak 96 mg/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, urine culture E. coli >10^8 CFU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further imaging plan after clinical recovery?

options.text: Urgent micturating cystourethrogram during the admission to exclude grade V vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: Routine MCUG is no longer recommended after a single uncomplicated UTI; it is selected for atypical illness or abnormal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks of the acute illness with further imaging guided by findings
options.rationale: AU practice for a first febrile UTI in a child under 2 years is a renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks, with MCUG or DMSA reserved for atypical features or abnormal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: DMSA renal scintigraphy at 6 weeks regardless of ultrasound findings to look for cortical scarring
options.rationale: DMSA is reserved for recurrent or atypical UTI or abnormal ultrasound, not routine for a single uncomplicated infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to map the urinary tract
options.rationale: CT involves unnecessary radiation in young children and is not part of routine UTI follow up. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: No imaging is required; arrange continuous low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis for 12 months
options.rationale: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis without imaging is no longer recommended after a single uncomplicated febrile UTI. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric guidance for a first febrile urinary tract infection in a child under 2 years uses renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks as the screening investigation, looking for hydronephrosis, posterior urethral valves, duplex systems, or other structural abnormality. MCUG and DMSA are second-line and reserved for atypical UTI (non-Escherichia coli organism, septic illness, failure to respond within 48 hours, or abnormal voiding) or an abnormal ultrasound. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is no longer recommended in the absence of high-grade reflux or other anatomical risk.
key_points: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks is first-line after a first febrile UTI in a child under 2 years
Atypical illness or abnormal ultrasound triggers MCUG or DMSA
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is not supported by current evidence
explanation.pearls: An atypical UTI is one with seriously ill child, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, non-Escherichia coli organism, or failure to respond within 48 hours, and prompts additional imaging.

sources.label: NICE NG224: Urinary tract infection in under 16s

subtopic_detail: Functional constipation in a preschool child: disimpaction and maintenance
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with a 4 month history of infrequent hard stools, with bowel actions every 4 to 5 days and visible straining. There is intermittent soiling between bowel actions. Toilet training started at 30 months without success. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable left iliac fossa mass that is faecal in character. Anal examination shows no fissures or perianal disease. There are no red flag features for organic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Apyrexial, HR 100, RR 22, BP 92/58
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa, normal external anus, no fissure, normal sacral spine
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated based on history and examination

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Plain abdominal radiograph today to quantify faecal loading and guide laxative dosing
options.rationale: Abdominal radiography correlates poorly with clinical faecal loading and adds radiation without changing management. (Source: NICE CG99: Constipation in children)

options.text: Glycerol suppository now and review the family in 6 weeks without further laxative use
options.rationale: Rectal interventions are second-line for non-responders; oral macrogol disimpaction is preferred and acceptable to children. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Disimpaction with oral macrogol over 3 to 7 days then a daily maintenance osmotic laxative
options.rationale: AU practice for functional constipation with faecal loading begins with oral macrogol disimpaction then transitions to a maintenance osmotic laxative for several months. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Referral to paediatric gastroenterology for rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium, failure to thrive, and an empty rectum; this presentation is functional. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Increased dietary fibre and water intake alone with planned follow up in 3 months
options.rationale: Dietary advice alone is inadequate with established faecal loading and soiling; pharmacological disimpaction is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation in preschool children commonly presents with infrequent hard stools, withholding behaviours, and overflow soiling. Australian and UK practice favours oral macrogol (polyethylene glycol) for both disimpaction and maintenance, starting with escalating doses for 3 to 7 days, then a single daily maintenance dose for several months and slow weaning. Toilet training with positive routines, soft stool maintenance, and parental education are central. Red flag features (delayed meconium, ribbon stools, perianal disease, abnormal neurology, failure to thrive) warrant gastroenterology review.
key_points: Oral macrogol disimpaction over 3 to 7 days then maintenance is first-line
Soiling between hard stools usually reflects overflow from impaction, not behaviour
Maintenance laxative is continued for months with slow weaning, not stopped at first improvement
explanation.pearls: Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes is dosed at 1 to 1.5 g/kg daily for disimpaction in divided doses and 0.4 to 0.8 g/kg daily for maintenance in preschool children.

subtopic_detail: Eczema herpeticum recognition in a child with atopic dermatitis
stem: A 4-year-old girl with moderate atopic dermatitis presents with a 36 hour history of a worsening rash on her face and neck, fevers, and pain on touching the lesions. Examination shows clustered punched-out monomorphic erosions with yellow crusting overlying eczematous skin on her cheeks, neck, and upper trunk. She has not used new topical products and is currently on mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment for flares.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, T 38.6, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Clustered punched-out monomorphic erosions with crust on cheeks, neck, upper trunk; eczematous background; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Skin swab for viral PCR taken at triage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous aciclovir with paediatric infectious diseases and ophthalmology involvement
options.rationale: Eczema herpeticum is a dermatological emergency requiring intravenous aciclovir, with ophthalmology review if any periocular involvement to prevent corneal disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

options.text: Up-titrate topical mometasone furoate to twice daily across all involved sites for 7 days
options.rationale: Potent topical steroids alone do not treat herpes simplex infection and may worsen disseminated viral disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Atopic eczema)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily for impetiginised eczema as outpatient management
options.rationale: Impetigo gives honey crust but lacks the monomorphic punched-out vesicular erosions of eczema herpeticum and would not be treated alone. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.text: Wet wrap therapy with diluted topical steroid alone and review at the eczema clinic in 1 week
options.rationale: Wet wraps over active herpes simplex virus may spread infection and delay needed antiviral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Atopic eczema)

options.text: Oral valaciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days and discharge home with safety netting
options.rationale: Severe eczema herpeticum with systemic features or facial involvement warrants intravenous aciclovir not oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema herpeticum)

explanation.summary: Eczema herpeticum is herpes simplex virus infection complicating atopic dermatitis, presenting with clustered monomorphic punched-out vesiculo-erosions, often with fever and lymphadenopathy. It is a dermatological emergency in children because of the risk of disseminated viral disease, bacterial superinfection, and keratoconjunctivitis. Intravenous aciclovir is started promptly while viral PCR confirms the diagnosis, with ophthalmology review for periocular disease. Bacterial superinfection is treated with appropriate antibiotics and topical steroids resume only once the viral infection is controlled.
key_points: Monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever in an eczematous child point to eczema herpeticum
Intravenous aciclovir, ophthalmology, and infectious diseases input are warranted for facial or severe disease
Topical steroids alone or wet wraps over active disease can worsen viral spread
explanation.pearls: Periocular eczema herpeticum requires same-day ophthalmology review because herpes simplex keratitis can cause permanent corneal scarring and vision loss.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with excess cow milk intake
stem: A 22-month-old boy is referred by his maternal child health nurse for pallor and decreased activity over the past 2 months. He drinks approximately 1 litre of full cream cow milk daily and is a fussy eater. Family is Australian-born without known haemoglobinopathy. He has tongue pallor and a soft systolic flow murmur. His parents are otherwise reassured by his behaviour and growth which is at the 25th centile for weight and 50th centile for height.

data_table.Examination: Pallor of tongue and conjunctivae, soft systolic flow murmur at left sternal edge, no organomegaly, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 19 pg, ferritin 8 micrograms/L, CRP 3 mg/L, WCC and platelets normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion today as first-line because oral iron is poorly tolerated
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance of oral iron, or severe symptomatic anaemia not responding to oral therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months and reduce cow milk to under 500 mL daily
options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers is treated with oral iron with dietary advice to limit cow milk and increase iron-rich foods. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Packed red cell transfusion of 10 mL/kg over 4 hours and admit for further evaluation
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise; this child has stable haemodynamics. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Haemoglobin electrophoresis and bone marrow biopsy now to exclude thalassaemia and aplasia
options.rationale: Microcytosis with low ferritin in a milk-drinking toddler is iron deficiency until proven otherwise; further workup waits on therapeutic response. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Increased dietary iron-rich foods alone with repeat full blood count in 3 months
options.rationale: Established anaemia with ferritin 8 micrograms/L will not respond to diet alone in clinically meaningful time. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in early childhood is a common nutritional disorder in Australia, particularly in milk-drinking toddlers and those with restricted diets. Diagnostic criteria are microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin (below 12 micrograms/L) in the absence of inflammation. Treatment is oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months with dietary modification to limit cow milk to under 500 mL daily and introduce iron-rich foods. Haemoglobin should rise by 10 g/L within 4 weeks; failure of response prompts evaluation for malabsorption, ongoing losses, or alternative diagnoses.
key_points: Ferritin under 12 micrograms/L without inflammation confirms iron deficiency in children
Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months is first-line in stable iron deficiency anaemia
Cow milk over 500 mL daily after 12 months impairs iron status and is a key target for dietary advice
explanation.pearls: Repeat haemoglobin at 4 weeks of oral iron should rise by at least 10 g/L; a flatter response prompts review for adherence, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption such as coeliac disease.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: paediatric iron deficiency

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease beyond day 10 with persistent fever
stem: A 3-year-old boy is admitted on day 11 of illness with persistent fever to 39.5 degrees Celsius despite a 5 day course of empirical amoxicillin. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, a polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy of 2.5 cm. There is no extremity desquamation yet. Echocardiography shows a left anterior descending coronary artery z-score of 2.6.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, cracked fissured lips, polymorphous trunk rash, 2.5 cm right cervical node, no rash desquamation
data_table.Investigations: CRP 168 mg/L, ESR 88 mm/h, ALT 78 U/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L, Hb 96 g/L, albumin 27 g/L, urine WCC raised, blood cultures negative; echo LAD z-score 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: AU paediatric practice treats Kawasaki disease, including late-presenting and incomplete cases with coronary changes, with IVIG and antiplatelet aspirin to reduce coronary risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as primary monotherapy
options.rationale: Steroids are an adjunct in primary refractory or high-risk disease, not the sole initial treatment in Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six hourly for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
