options.rationale: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome causes flaccid bullae and skin tenderness, not non-purulent conjunctivitis and coronary changes. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.text: Subcutaneous infliximab loading dose 5 mg/kg today as primary refractory disease treatment
options.rationale: TNF-alpha blockers are reserved for IVIG-refractory disease as second or third line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Symptomatic care with paracetamol and ibuprofen with echocardiography review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Delayed treatment of Kawasaki disease beyond day 10 still benefits from IVIG when coronary or inflammatory markers persist. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Incomplete Kawasaki disease can be diagnosed when fewer than 4 of the principal clinical features are present alongside fever for at least 5 days, supported by laboratory criteria (elevated CRP/ESR, anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, raised ALT, sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis after day 7) or coronary changes on echocardiography. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin remains indicated even beyond day 10 when fever persists or coronary changes are evident. High-risk features (young age, low albumin, elevated CRP, hyponatraemia, coronary involvement) may prompt addition of corticosteroids or infliximab in tertiary centres. Echocardiography is repeated at 2 and 6 weeks.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is diagnosed by laboratory criteria or coronary abnormalities supporting prolonged fever with under 4 principal features
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin is the standard treatment, even after day 10 when inflammation or coronary changes persist
Adjunct steroids or infliximab apply to high-risk or refractory disease
explanation.pearls: A coronary artery z-score of 2.5 or greater on echocardiography is enough to confirm incomplete Kawasaki disease and mandate IVIG, regardless of how many classical criteria are met.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis with proteinuria: renal involvement assessment
stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with palpable purpura distributed over her buttocks and lower legs, with bilateral ankle swelling and intermittent colicky abdominal pain over the past 5 days. The rash followed a viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. She has not had macroscopic haematuria. Her parents ask about the next step in monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor surfaces of lower legs, bilateral ankle synovitis, soft non-tender abdomen, no scrotal swelling, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis dipstick blood 2+ protein 3+; urine protein creatinine ratio 280 mg/mmol; creatinine 52 micromol/L; albumin 32 g/L; platelets 320 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days followed by oral mycophenolate mofetil
options.rationale: Pulsed steroids and mycophenolate apply to crescentic nephritis after biopsy confirmation, not first-line outpatient escalation. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline)

options.text: Discharge with oral analgesia and review with the general practitioner in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Significant proteinuria is the dominant determinant of long-term renal outcome and requires specialist assessment, not routine general practitioner review. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Empirical oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days as post-streptococcal cover
options.rationale: HSP nephritis is immune complex disease, not infection; routine antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Admit for paediatric nephrology review and start oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Significant proteinuria with HSP (urine PCR over 250 mg/mmol) warrants nephrology referral and consideration of corticosteroid therapy with biopsy for nephrotic-range disease or persistent abnormality. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound today to exclude obstructive uropathy as the cause of proteinuria
options.rationale: HSP nephritis is parenchymal glomerular disease; ultrasound has no role in screening for it in this setting. (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein purpura)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the commonest childhood vasculitis and presents with palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. Long-term outcome is dominated by renal disease; about 1 in 3 children develop nephritis ranging from microscopic haematuria to nephrotic-nephritic syndrome. AU practice screens with serial urinalysis and urine protein:creatinine ratio for 6 months from onset, with paediatric nephrology referral for persistent proteinuria over 100 to 250 mg/mmol, hypertension, deteriorating function, or nephrotic features. Steroids reduce arthralgia and abdominal pain but their role in altering long-term renal outcome remains debated and they are reserved for selected cases by specialists.
key_points: Significant proteinuria (urine PCR over 250 mg/mmol) in HSP prompts nephrology review
Serial urinalysis and BP measurement are continued for 6 months from onset
Steroids are considered for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement rather than routinely
explanation.pearls: Renal biopsy is considered for HSP children with persistent nephrotic syndrome, deteriorating renal function, or persistent proteinuria over 100 mg/mmol beyond 4 to 6 weeks of conservative management.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis failing high flow nasal cannula: escalation decision
stem: A 4-month-old former 38 week infant has been admitted with RSV bronchiolitis. She has been on humidified high flow nasal cannula oxygen 2 L/kg/min at FiO2 0.5 for the past 4 hours. She remains tachypnoeic with marked subcostal recessions, intermittent grunting, and rising work of breathing. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, pCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. She is becoming less responsive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 78 with intermittent apnoeas, SpO2 88% on HFNC FiO2 0.5, T 38.0
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession, intermittent grunting, head bobbing, drowsy, reduced air entry bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Capillary gas pH 7.22 pCO2 70 mmHg HCO3 25 mmol/L lactate 1.4 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation without focal consolidation; RSV PCR positive

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Escalate to paediatric intensive care for non-invasive ventilation and intubation readiness
options.rationale: Rising CO2, respiratory acidosis, exhaustion, and apnoea on maximal HFNC are indications for ICU escalation with CPAP or intubation in infant bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised hypertonic saline 3% every 4 hours to improve mucus clearance and oxygenation
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not recommended for routine acute care in bronchiolitis and does not reverse impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer hourly for 3 hours
options.rationale: Salbutamol and corticosteroids are not effective in viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for secondary bacterial pneumonia coverage
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis without a focal consolidation or strong evidence of bacterial superinfection. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue current HFNC settings and observe for another 4 hours before considering escalation
options.rationale: Continued observation in the face of rising CO2 and exhaustion delays definitive ventilatory support and risks decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the leading cause of infant hospital admission in Australia and is managed with supportive care including nasal suction, hydration, and supplemental oxygen. High-flow nasal cannula is used for moderate disease, with thresholds for escalation that include rising CO2, persistent hypoxia despite maximal HFNC, apnoea, or exhaustion. Continuous positive airway pressure or intubation are delivered in paediatric intensive care for failure to respond to HFNC. Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and corticosteroids are not recommended for routine bronchiolitis.
key_points: HFNC failure includes rising CO2, exhaustion, apnoea, or persistent hypoxia at maximum settings
CPAP and intubation are the next steps in paediatric intensive care
Bronchodilators and steroids are not effective in viral bronchiolitis under 12 months
explanation.pearls: An infant on maximal HFNC with rising CO2 above 60 mmHg, falling pH below 7.25, exhaustion, or recurrent apnoea needs ICU escalation rather than further HFNC titration.

subtopic_detail: Day 4 neonatal jaundice approaching exchange threshold
stem:
A term male infant on day 4 of life is brought to the special care nursery with progressive jaundice. He was born at 39 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3.4 kg, now 3.1 kg. Mother is blood group O Rh positive and the infant is A Rh positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. He is breastfeeding only with reduced wet nappies.

The serum bilirubin has risen by 11 micromol/L per hour over the past 6 hours and is now 460 micromol/L; the exchange threshold for this infant is 480 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 56, T 36.8, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Cephalad jaundice extending to soles, sleepy but rousable, mild dehydration, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Total SBR 460 micromol/L (exchange threshold 480), conjugated 18 micromol/L, Hb 152 g/L, DAT positive, reticulocytes 8%, weight loss 9% from birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue single phototherapy with breastfeeding support and repeat bilirubin in 6 hours
options.rationale: Single phototherapy is inadequate when bilirubin is within 30 micromol/L of the exchange threshold and rising rapidly with positive DAT. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Immediate single volume exchange transfusion without trial of intensive phototherapy first
options.rationale: Intensive phototherapy with IVIG often averts the need for exchange when bilirubin is within range of the exchange threshold and not yet exceeded. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Cease breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to formula to exclude breast milk jaundice diagnosis
options.rationale: Cessation of breastfeeding is not the management of an acutely rising haemolytic jaundice at threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Intensive phototherapy on three sides with IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and prepare for exchange
options.rationale: Rising bilirubin near the exchange threshold with haemolytic disease is managed with intensive phototherapy, IVIG to reduce haemolysis, and exchange transfusion preparation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Phenobarbital 5 mg/kg twice daily to induce hepatic glucuronidation as bridging therapy
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is not standard acute therapy for haemolytic neonatal jaundice in current Australian neonatal practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice approaching the exchange transfusion threshold in haemolytic disease is a neonatal emergency. Australian guidance recommends intensive phototherapy on multiple sides, intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg) for confirmed haemolytic disease when bilirubin remains within 30 to 50 micromol/L of the exchange threshold or rises rapidly, adequate hydration including possible intravenous fluids, and exchange transfusion preparation. Exchange transfusion replaces the infant blood volume twice, removing bilirubin, antibody, and sensitised red cells. Long-term sequelae of acute bilirubin encephalopathy include athetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities.
key_points: Intensive phototherapy, IVIG and exchange preparation are the response to bilirubin near threshold in haemolytic disease
DAT positive ABO or Rh incompatibility increases haemolytic load and the rate of bilirubin rise
Exchange transfusion thresholds depend on gestation, postnatal age, and risk factors
explanation.pearls: Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg reduces the need for exchange transfusion in haemolytic disease of the newborn when bilirubin is within 30 to 50 micromol/L of the exchange threshold.

subtopic_detail: Complicated pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion management
stem: A 6-year-old boy was admitted 3 days ago with right lower lobe community acquired pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg six hourly. He has had persistent fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, increasing right-sided chest pain, and rising oxygen requirement. Repeat chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound shows 4 cm depth of fluid with internal septations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 38, T 39.1, SpO2 92% on 2 L/min via nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry and stony dull percussion right base, splinting on inspiration, no shift of trachea
data_table.Investigations: CRP 220 mg/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L; ultrasound right effusion 4 cm depth with internal septations; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Diagnostic pleural tap only with ongoing intravenous benzylpenicillin and no indwelling drain
options.rationale: Simple diagnostic tap is inadequate to drain a 4 cm septated empyema and leaves the infection undrained. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Continue benzylpenicillin monotherapy and reassess clinical state in 48 hours without drainage
options.rationale: Persistent fever and rising oxygen requirement with a septated effusion are indications for drainage and broader cover, not continued observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Refer to cardiothoracic surgery for primary video-assisted thoracoscopic decortication today
options.rationale: VATS is reserved for failure of chest drain with intrapleural fibrinolytic in Australian paediatric practice, not first-line for an unoperated septated effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Switch to broader spectrum antibiotics with intrapleural fibrinolytic delivered chest drain
options.rationale: Septated paediatric parapneumonic effusion failing antibiotics is treated with broader cover plus image-guided chest drain and intrapleural fibrinolytic per AU practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

options.text: Oral switch to amoxicillin clavulanate 25 mg/kg three times daily and discharge home today
options.rationale: Oral switch is inappropriate in a child with rising oxygen requirement, persistent sepsis features, and an undrained septated effusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Paediatric parapneumonic effusion progresses through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organising stages. Empyema (frank pus, positive culture, or pH less than 7.2) and septated effusion failing initial antibiotics are managed by broader spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes plus image-guided chest drainage with intrapleural fibrinolytic. Most children avoid surgical decortication; video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is reserved for failure of medical and drain-based therapy. Antibiotics typically continue for at least 2 to 4 weeks total with oral step-down once clinically improving.
key_points: Septated effusion failing antibiotics requires drainage and broader spectrum cover
Intrapleural fibrinolytic via chest drain is the AU paediatric step before VATS
Total antibiotic duration is at least 2 to 4 weeks with oral step-down after clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: Intrapleural urokinase via chest drain twice daily for 3 days clears most paediatric septated parapneumonic effusions without recourse to VATS decortication.

sources.label: BTS Guideline: pleural infection in children

subtopic_detail: Pertussis treatment in a young unvaccinated infant
stem: A 7-week-old infant presents with three weeks of progressive cough, now with paroxysms and post-tussive vomiting and one brief cyanotic episode. The infant has had no scheduled vaccines because the family delayed the 6-week visit. The mother had a non-productive cough for 4 weeks during the third trimester and did not receive an antenatal pertussis booster. The infant is feeding two-thirds of normal volumes and has no apnoeic pauses on monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, RR 44, T 37.2, SpO2 96% room air with brief desaturation to 88% during paroxysm
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, chest clear between paroxysms, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for Bordetella pertussis; chest x-ray shows perihilar streakiness without focal consolidation; FBC WCC 28 with lymphocytosis 18

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate antimicrobial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days as an outpatient with telephone review
options.rationale: Amoxicillin does not eradicate Bordetella pertussis from the nasopharynx and does not reduce transmission. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: pertussis)

options.text: Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days plus household post-exposure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Infants under 6 months warrant admission for monitoring of apnoea and cyanosis; azithromycin reduces transmission and is the preferred macrolide under 1 month and remains first-line up to 6 months. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: pertussis)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days as an outpatient referral
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a second-line option only when macrolides are contraindicated; it is also unsafe in infants under 2 months due to kernicterus risk. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 4 hours plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days
options.rationale: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids have not demonstrated benefit in pertussis and may delay recognition of deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting only; antibiotics offer no benefit after 21 days of cough in any age group
options.rationale: Under 6 months, treatment is recommended up to 6 weeks after cough onset because of higher complication and transmission risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Pertussis)

explanation.summary: Pertussis in an unvaccinated infant under 6 months requires admission for apnoea and cyanosis monitoring and macrolide therapy to reduce transmission. Azithromycin is preferred under 1 month due to the pyloric stenosis signal with erythromycin and remains first-line through 6 months. Antibiotics shorten infectivity but do not abort the paroxysmal phase once established. Household contacts including the index parent should receive post-exposure prophylaxis with the same macrolide course.
key_points: Admit infants under 6 months with confirmed pertussis for cardiorespiratory monitoring
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days is the first-line macrolide for treatment and prophylaxis
Treat up to 6 weeks after cough onset in young infants and start contact prophylaxis simultaneously
explanation.pearls: Pertussis paroxysms peak at week 2-4 and persist for 6-10 weeks; once the cough is established antibiotics will not shorten symptoms but they will cut transmission by about 5 days.

subtopic_detail: Measles recognition in an unvaccinated traveller-returned child
stem: A 4-year-old returns to the emergency department two days after presenting with fever and cough. She returned 10 days ago from a 6-week visit to family in Indonesia and has no record of MMR vaccination. Today her fever persists with a new descending maculopapular rash starting on the forehead. There is no contact with strawberry tongue, parotitis, or known varicella.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 26, T 39.4, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Confluent erythematous maculopapular rash on face and upper trunk; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; white spots on buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars; pharynx mildly injected; chest clear; no joint swelling

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next public health action?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol, school exclusion for 5 days, and routine MMR catch-up at the general practitioner next week
options.rationale: Measles is a notifiable urgent disease and discharge home without isolation risks community transmission, including to vulnerable contacts. (Source: NSW Health: Measles Control Guideline)

options.text: Reassure parents the rash is roseola, advise antipyretics, and review at the general practitioner if persistent at 72 hours from rash onset
options.rationale: Roseola features defervescence preceding rash in toddlers under 3 and does not include conjunctivitis or buccal enanthem. (Source: RCH CPG: Rash - Viral Exanthems)

options.text: Admit for intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours assuming early scarlet fever pending throat swab confirmation
options.rationale: Scarlet fever features a sandpaper-rough rash, strawberry tongue, and circumoral pallor; antibiotics are not warranted here. (Source: RCH CPG: Scarlet Fever)

options.text: Isolate in a negative-pressure room, notify the public health unit by phone today, and send measles IgM with throat and urine PCR
options.rationale: Koplik spots, fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and travel exposure in an unvaccinated child meet a measles clinical case; airborne isolation and phone-notification within 24 hours are mandated. (Source: CDNA SoNG: Measles)

options.text: Order varicella PCR from a vesicular fluid swab and start oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days empirically
options.rationale: Varicella presents with pruritic vesicles on an erythematous base in successive crops, not a confluent maculopapular descending rash. (Source: RCH CPG: Chickenpox)

explanation.summary: Measles is suspected in an unvaccinated returned traveller with the prodromal triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, plus pathognomonic Koplik spots and a descending rash. Phone notification of the local public health unit and airborne isolation are immediate priorities. Confirmatory testing is measles IgM serology together with throat and urine PCR. Post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR within 72 hours of exposure or NHIG within 6 days is offered to susceptible contacts identified by contact tracing.
key_points: Koplik spots plus fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and descending rash define a clinical measles case
Negative-pressure isolation and same-day phone notification are mandatory
Confirm with measles IgM plus throat or nasopharyngeal and urine PCR
explanation.pearls: Measles infectivity spans 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset; contacts within that window need urgent susceptibility checks regardless of age.

stem: A 14-month-old is brought for review because the parents have noticed an inward turning of the right eye when she looks at distant objects, present consistently for the past month. There is no family history of amblyopia. She was born at term and otherwise tracks objects normally at close range. Photographs show the asymmetry from 8 months of age.

data_table.Examination: Right convergent strabismus with corneal light reflex displaced to the lateral limbus on the right; red reflex symmetric and present bilaterally; no leukocoria; cover test reveals refixation movement of the right eye; visual fields by confrontation grossly intact

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that intermittent infantile strabismus typically resolves and review at the 18-month general practitioner check
options.rationale: Strabismus persisting beyond 4 months of age is abnormal and risks irreversible amblyopia without prompt assessment. (Source: RANZCO: Vision Screening Position Statement)

options.text: Prescribe occlusion patching of the left eye for 2 hours daily for 8 weeks then arrange optometry review
options.rationale: Patching is a treatment for amblyopia after orthoptic and refractive assessment, not a primary care first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric ophthalmologist within 4 weeks for cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic assessment
options.rationale: Constant unilateral strabismus persisting past 4 months requires paediatric ophthalmology assessment within 4 weeks to prevent amblyopia and exclude organic causes including retinoblastoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits before specialist referral is considered
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is not first-line without focal neurology or other red flags; ophthalmology review prioritises refraction and red reflex assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

options.text: Order a B-scan ultrasound of the right globe via the general practitioner pathway to exclude posterior segment pathology
options.rationale: Targeted imaging of the globe is determined by the ophthalmologist after clinical examination and is not a primary care ordering pathway. (Source: RANZCO: Vision Screening Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Persistent unilateral strabismus after 4 months of age is a referral indication to paediatric ophthalmology. The differential includes refractive error, anisometropia, and rarely retinoblastoma if the red reflex is abnormal or leukocoria is present. A symmetric red reflex on examination reduces but does not exclude retinoblastoma and prompt cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic measurements within 4 weeks are essential to start amblyopia therapy. Amblyopia rapidly becomes refractory after 7 years of age, so timely diagnosis matters.
key_points: Any constant strabismus past 4 months of age needs ophthalmology referral
Symmetric red reflex does not exclude retinoblastoma but lowers immediate concern
Cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic assessment within 4 weeks are the diagnostic basis
explanation.pearls: Pseudostrabismus from a wide nasal bridge mimics esotropia but the corneal light reflex remains central in both eyes; if displaced, refer.

stem: A 7-year-old is brought to the general practice with 2 weeks of scalp itch, and the mother has identified live head lice and eggs on combing. The child attends mainstream school and lives with two siblings without scalp itch. There is no recent overseas travel, no eczema, and the scalp is intact without bacterial superinfection.

data_table.Examination: Multiple eggs cemented to hair shafts within 1 cm of the scalp; two live lice identified on combing; no excoriation, no impetigo, no occipital lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Wet combing with conditioner every 4 days for 2 weeks until no live lice are seen on three consecutive combings
options.rationale: Wet combing with conditioner is the first-line and most cost-effective approach in Australian primary care; it is also safe in pregnancy and infants. (Source: RACGP: Head Lice Management)

options.text: Topical permethrin 1% lotion applied to dry hair for 10 minutes then rinsed, repeated weekly for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Permethrin is an option but Australian resistance rates are substantial and prolonged 6-weekly repetition is excessive. (Source: AMH: Pediculosis)

options.text: Oral ivermectin 200 microgram per kilogram as a single dose with rinse-out repeat at 8 days
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is reserved for treatment-refractory or institutional outbreaks, not as first-line in a routine case. (Source: AMH: Pediculosis)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days to clear lice and prevent impetiginisation
options.rationale: Antibiotics treat secondary bacterial superinfection only; they have no role in routine pediculosis without impetigo. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

options.text: Shave the head completely under general practitioner sedation and apply topical malathion 0.5% for 12 hours overnight
options.rationale: Head-shaving is not recommended and offers no benefit over evidence-based combing or topical therapies. (Source: RACGP: Head Lice Management)

explanation.summary: Pediculosis capitis in Australian primary care is managed first with wet combing using copious conditioner every 4 days until no live lice are detected on three consecutive sessions. Pyrethroid-based topicals are next-line given growing pyrethroid resistance. School exclusion is not required once treatment has started. Household members are checked but not treated empirically unless they harbour live lice.
key_points: Wet combing with conditioner is first-line and safe in any age
Treat only contacts with active live lice, not all household members empirically
School attendance is permitted once active treatment has commenced
explanation.pearls: Eggs more than 1 cm from the scalp are usually non-viable; presence alone does not equal active infestation.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: skin and soft tissue

stem: An 11-month-old presents with 18 hours of episodic inconsolable crying lasting 10 minutes every hour, drawing up his legs and now lying lethargic between episodes. Today there was one stool with red mucoid blood. He vomited twice with the second containing bile-stained material. He had a recent viral illness 5 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 38, T 37.6, SpO2 98%, BP 86/52, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable; right upper quadrant sausage-shaped mass palpable; bowel sounds reduced; perianal inspection shows redcurrant material on the nappy
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care ultrasound by emergency consultant shows a target sign at the hepatic flexure with poor colour Doppler signal in the inner loop

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat clinical observation for 4 hours with oral rehydration before re-examining for ongoing concerns
options.rationale: Hemodynamic instability and the classic triad with mass make urgent intervention the priority; delay risks ischaemic perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient lower limb venous Doppler study and surgical clinic review the next morning before deciding on reduction
options.rationale: There is no clinical indication for vascular imaging; the reduced colour Doppler signal in the loop indicates compromised bowel perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic exploration with manual reduction without further imaging or trial of pneumatic reduction
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated when pneumatic reduction fails or peritonitis or perforation is suspected; absence of those findings favours image-guided reduction first. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Transfuse 10 mL/kg packed red cells over 30 minutes for ongoing redcurrant rectal bleeding before imaging review
options.rationale: Empiric transfusion is not warranted without haemoglobin documentation and ongoing significant blood loss; volume resuscitation precedes transfusion decisions. (Source: NBA: Paediatric Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg balanced crystalloid and proceed to fluoroscopic air enema reduction with surgical and theatre standby
options.rationale: Stabilise circulation then pneumatic reduction by an experienced radiologist with surgical backup is the standard of care for uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception without peritonitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in a toddler with the classic triad of episodic colicky pain, redcurrant stool, and palpable mass needs rapid resuscitation and pneumatic reduction with theatre standby. Ultrasound demonstrates a target sign with reduced internal colour Doppler when bowel viability is at risk. Image-guided air enema is successful in 70-90% of cases, with surgical reduction reserved for peritonitis, perforation, or failed enema. A pathological lead point should be considered in atypical age groups outside 3 months to 3 years.
key_points: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg crystalloid before reduction
Air enema is first-line if no peritonitis or perforation
Surgical standby is essential because of perforation risk during pneumatic reduction
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after successful pneumatic reduction is about 10% in the first 24 hours; observe overnight before discharge.

subtopic_detail: Pre-operative correction in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
stem: A 5-week-old first-born male presents with 2 weeks of progressively forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed and visible peristalsis across the upper abdomen. He has lost 6% of his birth weight. An ultrasound by the on-call radiologist confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with a pyloric muscle thickness of 4.2 mm and channel length of 18 mm. Paediatric surgery has accepted him for pyloromyotomy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 42, T 36.8, SpO2 99%, capillary refill 3 seconds, anterior fontanelle mildly depressed
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.52, pCO2 50, HCO3 38, Na 132, K 3.0, Cl 92, glucose 4.1, creatinine 38

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step before theatre?

options.text: Proceed directly to theatre today as the procedure is brief and any electrolyte derangement will correct intraoperatively
options.rationale: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis predisposes to post-operative apnoea and arrhythmia; correction precedes anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus then maintenance with 4% dextrose and 0.18% sodium chloride until theatre
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluids should not be used; 0.18% saline-dextrose worsens hyponatraemia and is no longer Australian standard maintenance. (Source: RCH CPG: Intravenous Fluids)

options.text: Resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% then maintenance sodium chloride 0.45% with 5% dextrose and potassium chloride 20 mmol/L before theatre
options.rationale: Targets bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L; potassium replacement guards against post-operative apnoea and arrhythmia, and resuscitation precedes pyloromyotomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Replace the fluid deficit with oral electrolyte solution by feeding cup over 24 hours then proceed to surgery once tolerating feeds
options.rationale: Persistent gastric outlet obstruction precludes oral correction; ongoing vomiting will worsen alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric Stenosis)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg slowly to partially correct the metabolic alkalosis before theatre transfer
options.rationale: The metabolic alkalosis is driven by chloride and potassium depletion; bicarbonate worsens the alkalosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Acid-Base Disturbances)

explanation.summary: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is associated with hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and chloride loss. Pre-operative correction with isotonic saline resuscitation followed by 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose and potassium chloride 20 mmol/L is standard. Targets are chloride above 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L, and potassium above 3.5 mmol/L. Surgery is delayed until these targets are met to prevent post-anaesthetic apnoea.
key_points: Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% then maintenance saline-dextrose plus potassium
Delay surgery until chloride above 100 mmol/L and bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Failure to correct alkalosis before anaesthesia is the major preventable cause of post-pyloromyotomy apnoea.

subtopic_detail: Suspected inhaled foreign body in a toddler
stem: A 22-month-old presents 6 hours after a sudden coughing fit while eating peanuts during a family barbecue. The choking episode resolved spontaneously but he is now persistently coughing and his mother says his breathing sounds different. He has no preceding upper respiratory tract symptoms, no fevers, no eczema, and no prior wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 42, T 37.0, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild intercostal recession, unilateral monophonic wheeze right side, decreased air entry on the right, no stridor at rest, no drooling, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung with mediastinal shift to the left on expiratory film

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for three doses then reassess for viral-induced wheeze before further imaging
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not relieve mechanical airway obstruction and delays definitive airway clearance, with risk of mucus plugging and dislodgement. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia by the on-call paediatric otolaryngology service today
options.rationale: A witnessed choking event with persistent unilateral signs and obstructive emphysema on imaging is diagnostic and warrants same-day rigid bronchoscopy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

options.text: Perform five back blows and five chest thrusts now in the emergency department then observe in the short-stay unit
options.rationale: Back blows are reserved for the actively choking child unable to cough; this child has air movement and forced manoeuvres risk dislodging the object into the trachea. (Source: ANZCOR: Paediatric Basic Life Support)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days plus inhaled corticosteroid maintenance, with general practitioner review in 1 week
options.rationale: Steroids treat airway inflammation in asthma exacerbations and do not address mechanical obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Asthma)

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting after a normal inspiratory chest x-ray report and return if symptoms worsen overnight
options.rationale: Inspiratory films are commonly normal; the expiratory film here already shows mediastinal shift and the clinical scenario is diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Aspiration)

explanation.summary: Inhaled foreign body presents with sudden choking, persistent unilateral wheeze, and decreased air entry on the affected side. Expiratory or decubitus chest x-ray shows obstructive hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away from the affected side. Same-day rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice. Salbutamol and steroids do not relieve mechanical obstruction and may delay definitive airway clearance.
key_points: Choking with persistent unilateral signs is rigid bronchoscopy until proven otherwise
Decubitus or expiratory films reveal obstructive emphysema even when inspiratory films appear normal
Bronchodilators and steroids do not relieve mechanical obstruction
explanation.pearls: Peanuts cause acute lipoid pneumonia if retained; do not delay bronchoscopy waiting for normalisation of breath sounds.

subtopic_detail: Salter-Harris distal tibial fracture in a child
stem: A 12-year-old presents 90 minutes after twisting her right ankle on a trampoline. She heard a pop and could not bear weight to walk to the car. There is no head strike, no other limb injury. She has a previously normal contralateral ankle and no bleeding disorder. The ankle is now swollen with localised tenderness over the medial malleolus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 16, T 36.6, BP 110/72, capillary refill less than 2 seconds in the toes, sensation intact
data_table.Examination: Marked swelling around the medial malleolus, point tenderness over the distal tibial physis, unable to bear weight for four steps in the department, neurovascular status intact distally
data_table.Investigations: Ankle radiograph shows a vertical fracture line through the distal tibial epiphysis extending into the physis without metaphyseal involvement; mortise widening 1 mm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a removable below-knee splint, allow weight-bearing as tolerated, and arrange general practitioner review in 1 week without specialist referral
options.rationale: A Salter-Harris III intra-articular fracture risks growth disturbance and articular incongruity if reduction is inadequate; specialist input is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

options.text: Apply a full below-knee fibreglass cast and discharge with crutches and orthopaedic outpatient appointment within 6 weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient delay over 6 weeks risks malunion and growth arrest; intra-articular incongruity warrants earlier orthopaedic input. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

options.text: Discharge with a tubular bandage and crutches plus advice to return only if pain or swelling persists beyond 7 days
options.rationale: This is a confirmed intra-articular fracture, not a soft tissue sprain, and tubular bandaging is inadequate immobilisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

options.text: Apply a backslab and arrange same-day orthopaedic review for consideration of computed tomography and reduction of the intra-articular fracture
options.rationale: Salter-Harris III patterns require computed tomography to characterise displacement and possible operative fixation; backslab and same-day orthopaedic review are standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the ankle from the emergency department and review the patient in 48 hours
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is not first-line for an acute Salter-Harris fracture; computed tomography defines bony anatomy more practically. (Source: RCH CPG: Ankle Fractures)

explanation.summary: A vertical epiphyseal fracture extending to the physis without metaphyseal involvement is a Salter-Harris III pattern. These intra-articular fractures need computed tomography to define displacement and orthopaedic review for possible operative fixation. Initial management is a well-padded backslab with neurovascular checks. Long-term follow-up screens for growth arrest at the affected physis.
key_points: Salter-Harris III involves the epiphysis and physis without crossing the metaphysis
Computed tomography defines articular displacement and informs operative planning
Same-day orthopaedic review is required for intra-articular paediatric fractures
explanation.pearls: Growth arrest risk after Salter-Harris III is around 10-20%; counsel families about possible angular deformity at follow-up.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric Fracture Management

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis in high-risk ALL induction
stem: An 8-year-old has been diagnosed with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with a presenting white cell count of 88 x10^9/L and bulky cervical adenopathy. The paediatric oncology team plan induction chemotherapy commencing within 24 hours. Pre-chemotherapy bloods show baseline uric acid 0.62 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, potassium 4.6, phosphate 1.9 mmol/L, calcium 2.18 mmol/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 1450 U/L.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral 3 cm cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin, splenomegaly 5 cm, no respiratory compromise, no tumour lysis-related arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: G6PD assay pending and not yet returned from referral laboratory; weight 26 kg; eGFR estimated 76 mL/min/1.73 m2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate tumour lysis prophylaxis to commence now?

options.text: Hyperhydrate at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid without potassium plus oral allopurinol 100 mg/m2 three times daily, holding rasburicase pending G6PD
options.rationale: Rasburicase causes severe haemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; until the assay returns, hyperhydration plus allopurinol is appropriate and rasburicase is reserved if the assay is normal or hyperuricaemia escalates. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

options.text: Hyperhydrate at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid plus alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to maintain urine pH 7.0 to 7.5 throughout induction
options.rationale: Alkalinisation increases calcium phosphate precipitation and is no longer recommended once allopurinol or rasburicase are available. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

options.text: Commence intravenous rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg once daily for 5 days now and proceed to chemotherapy induction the morning after the first dose
options.rationale: Rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; testing should not be bypassed in elective induction. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

options.text: Restrict fluids to two-thirds maintenance to prevent volume overload and start oral allopurinol 100 mg/m2 once daily with daily renal function and electrolyte review
options.rationale: Fluid restriction worsens tumour lysis nephropathy; hyperhydration with at least 3 L/m2/day is essential. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

options.text: Initiate intermittent haemodialysis prophylactically from the start of chemotherapy to clear uric acid and prevent acute kidney injury during induction
options.rationale: Renal replacement therapy is reserved for established acute kidney injury, refractory hyperkalaemia, or severe hyperphosphataemia, not as routine prophylaxis. (Source: eviQ: Paediatric ALL Tumour Lysis)

explanation.summary: High-risk paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia carries substantial tumour lysis syndrome risk. Prophylaxis is hyperhydration at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid without potassium, plus allopurinol. Rasburicase is reserved for high-risk patients with rising or established hyperuricaemia, but only after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency has been excluded due to fatal haemolysis risk. Routine alkalinisation is no longer recommended. Renal replacement therapy is reserved for established complications such as refractory hyperkalaemia, severe hyperphosphataemia, or oligo-anuric acute kidney injury.
key_points: Hyperhydration at 3 L/m2/day plus allopurinol is the routine prophylactic platform
Rasburicase is held until glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is excluded
Avoid alkalinisation; it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation
explanation.pearls: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and pregnancy; sample for assay before any first dose even if the result will take days to return.

stem: An 8-month-old previously well infant is brought to ED in winter with 3 days of coryza, cough and worsening work of breathing. He has been feeding only one-third of normal and his last wet nappy was 6 hours ago. He has had two doses of low-flow oxygen at 1 L/min but remains tachypnoeic with subcostal recession. His parents have not yet given him any nebulised medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 68, SpO2 92% on 1 L/min nasal cannulae, T 38.0°C
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze and fine crackles, alert, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab: RSV positive; CXR not performed; cap gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg HCO3 25

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal cannula flow to 3 L/min and continue current observations with oral feeds
options.rationale: Standard low-flow cannulae above 2 L/min in infants is not better tolerated and does not provide positive pressure; HFNC is the next escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for three doses and reassess
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not benefit infants with bronchiolitis (under 12 months) and is not recommended in AU CPGs. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent over 15 minutes and reassess work of breathing
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline has not shown consistent benefit in bronchiolitis and is not part of AU first-line management. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg daily for 3 days and cease nasal oxygen
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and stopping oxygen at SpO2 92 percent risks deterioration. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min with continuous monitoring on ward
options.rationale: PARIS trial criteria are met (SpO2 under 92 percent on standard oxygen or persistent work of breathing); AU practice escalates to HFNC at 2 L/kg/min with reassessment at 1 hour. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis; PARIS trial)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in infants under 12 months with viral coryzal prodrome progressing to wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress. AU first-line is supportive care with feeding support and minimal-handling oxygen for SpO2 under 92 percent. The PARIS trial established HFNC at 2 L/kg/min as an effective rescue once standard cannulae fail, halving CPAP/intubation rates. Salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline and chest physio are NOT recommended; they neither shorten admission nor reduce escalation.
key_points: Diagnose clinically; CXR rarely needed.
Oxygen for SpO2 under 92 percent; minimal handling.
HFNC 2 L/kg/min for failure of standard oxygen (PARIS).
Salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline NOT routine.
Watch for apnoea in babies under 6 weeks or ex-preterm.
explanation.pearls: Failure of HFNC at 1 hour (HR not falling, RR not falling, SpO2 not improving) is a strong predictor of CPAP escalation - assess all three trajectories at the 60 minute mark rather than relying on absolute values alone.

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the GP with 6 months of infrequent hard stools, soiling episodes most days and abdominal pain. She passes stool once every 4 to 5 days with straining and screaming. She started day-care 8 months ago and reduced fluid intake notably around that time. Her parents have tried prune juice and increased fibre without sustained improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: Weight 14 kg (50th centile), height 95 cm (50th centile), well-appearing afebrile child
data_table.Examination: Soft non-distended abdomen with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa; perianal exam: no fissures or anal abnormalities; growth following centile
data_table.Investigations: None at this stage; no red flags (no failure to thrive, no delayed meconium, normal spine and lower limb examination)

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate now?

options.text: Commence oral macrogol 3350 (Movicol Junior) escalating disimpaction regimen over 7 days
options.rationale: AU first-line for paediatric faecal impaction is escalating macrogol 3350 disimpaction over up to 7 days followed by maintenance dosing; safe and well tolerated. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Continue dietary measures (increased fluid, fibre, pear/prune juice) and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Diet alone does not clear established faecal impaction; pharmacological disimpaction is required first. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Administer phosphate enemas daily for 3 days then commence oral lactulose maintenance
options.rationale: Phosphate enemas in toddlers carry risks of hyperphosphataemia and rectal trauma; oral macrogol is preferred when feasible. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer for manual disimpaction under general anaesthetic and surgical opinion within a fortnight
options.rationale: Manual disimpaction under GA is reserved for failure of medical disimpaction or anatomical concerns; not first-line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Order anorectal manometry and barium enema to exclude underlying Hirschsprung disease today
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium and failure to thrive; functional constipation does not warrant manometry without red flags. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation accounts for over 90 percent of childhood constipation; behavioural and dietary triggers (toilet training, daycare, low fluid intake) and pain-avoidance withholding are typical. Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for red flags (delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal lower limb or spine examination, gross perianal pathology). Treatment is structured: disimpaction (oral macrogol over 7 days), then maintenance (macrogol daily for at least 3 to 6 months), behavioural training (timed toileting) and family education.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis; investigations only for red flags.
Macrogol 3350 disimpaction over up to 7 days.
Maintenance macrogol for 3 to 6 months minimum.
Aim 1 soft stool daily with no soiling.
Red flags: delayed meconium, FTT, lumbosacral signs, anal anomaly.
explanation.pearls: Soiling (encopresis) is a sign of overflow incontinence around a faecal mass, NOT diarrhoea or behavioural defiance; ceasing maintenance laxatives too early is the commonest cause of relapse - taper over weeks rather than stopping abruptly.

stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to ED at 2 am with a 6-hour history of barking cough and noisy breathing that started after a coryzal illness. He is alert and consolable in his mother's lap. His parents have given paracetamol 2 hours ago for fever. He has no previous admissions and no chronic respiratory conditions.

data_table.Examination: Audible stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, no cyanosis; speaks in short sentences when settled; chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis; Westley croup score 4 (moderate)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses with continuous SpO2 monitoring
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not treat the upper-airway oedema of croup; it is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg with intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as cover
options.rationale: IV steroids offer no advantage over oral in mild to moderate croup and antibiotics treat bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis, not viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with ICU bed booked for likely escalation overnight
options.rationale: Adrenaline is added for SEVERE croup (Westley >= 8 or marked distress); moderate croup with rest stridor responds first to oral dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for at least 2 hours in the department
options.rationale: Moderate croup with stridor at rest is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg plus observation; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe distress. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Reassure parents, recommend cool mist humidifier at home and discharge with safety netting
options.rationale: Stridor at rest indicates moderate croup needing steroid and observation; cool mist has no evidence of benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a clinical diagnosis in children 6 months to 6 years with a viral prodrome, barking cough and inspiratory stridor (usually parainfluenza). Westley score stratifies mild (0 to 2), moderate (3 to 5), severe (6 to 11) and impending respiratory failure (>= 12). Oral dexamethasone benefits all severities. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides bridging vasoconstriction in severe disease; rebound at 2 hours mandates observation. Antibiotics, salbutamol and humidifiers do not improve outcomes.
key_points: Westley score 3 to 5 = moderate (stridor at rest, mild recession).
Dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg PO single dose.
Adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL nebulised for severe (Westley >= 6).
Observe at least 4 hours after adrenaline due to rebound.
Antibiotics, salbutamol, humidifiers NOT indicated.
explanation.pearls: Sudden deterioration in an apparently moderate croup with high fever, drooling and inability to lie down should prompt suspicion of bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis - avoid attempts at IV access or oral examination until anaesthetic-led airway support is at hand.

stem: A 4-year-old non-Indigenous, otherwise well boy presents with 18 hours of right ear pain following a viral URTI. He has had no previous episodes of otitis media and is up to date with immunisations including 13vPCV. His parents are happy to follow a 'wait and see' approach if it is safe and want to know how to monitor him.

data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane: bulging, erythematous, no perforation, no discharge; left tympanic membrane normal; not toxic, alert, playful
data_table.Investigations: None indicated; clinical diagnosis of acute otitis media (right)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus regular analgesia at home
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with adequate analgesia is preferred for non-severe AOM in non-Indigenous children over 2 years with no high-risk features. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: AOM)

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for 3 days as a single short parenteral course
options.rationale: Parenteral ceftriaxone is reserved for AOM with severe systemic illness, complications, or oral failure; not appropriate first-line in a well child. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen and fill antibiotic script only if no improvement at 48 hours
options.rationale: AU eTG endorses safety-net or delayed antibiotic prescribing in non-Indigenous children over 2 with non-severe AOM; analgesia first plus filled script only if no improvement in 48 hours. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: AOM)

options.text: Topical otic ciprofloxacin 0.3 percent drops twice daily for 7 days with no oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics are for perforated AOM or otitis externa; the intact tympanic membrane here makes them inappropriate. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Refer urgently for myringotomy and grommet insertion within the next fortnight as outpatient
options.rationale: Grommets are considered for recurrent AOM (>= 3 episodes in 6 months or 4 in a year); a single episode does not warrant surgical referral. (Source: RCH CPG: AOM)

explanation.summary: Acute otitis media is one of the commonest paediatric infections. AU guidance (eTG, RCH) supports watchful waiting with adequate analgesia in non-Indigenous children over 2 with non-severe AOM (no toxicity, no high fever, no severe pain) because most resolve spontaneously and treatment risks (rash, antibiotic resistance, diarrhoea) outweigh small benefits. Antibiotics are indicated for: under 2 years bilateral, Indigenous children, severe symptoms or systemic illness, recurrent or complicated AOM. First-line antibiotic is amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS for 5 days (Indigenous: 7 days).
key_points: Watchful waiting with analgesia first-line for non-Indigenous over 2.
Antibiotic: amoxicillin 15 mg/kg TDS 5 days (Indigenous: 7 days).
Indications for immediate antibiotics: under 2 bilateral, Indigenous, severe symptoms, complication.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children: treat all AOM with antibiotics.
Grommet referral for recurrent disease or persistent effusion with hearing impairment.
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children have a 4-fold higher rate of chronic suppurative otitis media and warrant antibiotics for every episode of AOM with longer treatment duration; routine watchful waiting does not apply.

stem: A 10-week-old formula-fed infant is brought to the GP with 5 weeks of frequent posseting, recurrent crying with feeds and now 2 weeks of streaks of fresh blood in stools. The crying is worst during and after feeds. She is otherwise alert; weight gain has dropped from the 50th to the 25th centile. There is no family history of atopy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 36, T 36.7°C, well-perfused infant
data_table.Examination: Mild eczema on cheeks, abdomen soft non-distended, normal anal exam, mild fissure not seen; weight tracking off centile downwards
data_table.Investigations: Stool: blood streaks visible; no infection symptoms; clinical exam otherwise normal

lead_in: Which initial management strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Commence omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily and continue current formula with anti-reflux thickening
options.rationale: PPIs do not treat CMPA and rectal bleeding with off-centile weight is not explained by simple reflux; protein elimination is first-line. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

options.text: Switch to a soy-based infant formula for 4 weeks then reintroduce cow's milk gradually
options.rationale: Soy formula is not recommended for infants under 6 months due to cross-reactivity in around 14 percent of CMPA and high phytoestrogen load. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

options.text: Trial of extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks with paediatric dietitian input
options.rationale: Non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy presents with reflux, irritability and rectal bleeding; AU first-line is eHF trial for 2 to 4 weeks; soy formula avoided in infants under 6 months. (Source: ASCIA cow's milk allergy 2023)

options.text: Refer urgently for paediatric colonoscopy to investigate the lower gastrointestinal bleeding now
options.rationale: Infant proctocolitis from CMPA is the commonest cause of small-volume rectal bleeding in this age; colonoscopy is reserved for ongoing bleeding despite elimination diet. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

options.text: Add probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri drops and review symptoms after 6 weeks of therapy
options.rationale: Probiotics may help colic but do not treat allergic proctocolitis; protein elimination is first-line for blood in stools. (Source: ASCIA 2023)

explanation.summary: Cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) is the commonest food allergy in infancy. Non-IgE-mediated CMPA (the proctocolitis form) presents with reflux, crying and small-volume rectal bleeding in well-appearing infants. Diagnosis is by elimination trial: extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks, with soy avoided under 6 months due to cross-reactivity and phytoestrogen load. Around 10 percent require amino-acid formula; reintroduction at 9 to 12 months using the AU milk ladder confirms tolerance. Most infants outgrow CMPA by age 3 to 5 years.
key_points: Non-IgE CMPA: reflux, crying, rectal bleeding, well-appearing infant.
First-line: extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks.
Avoid soy formula under 6 months age.
Amino-acid formula for severe or eHF non-responders (around 10 percent).
Reintroduce via milk ladder at 9 to 12 months.
explanation.pearls: Breastfeeding mothers of infants with CMPA can usually continue to breastfeed - the maternal cow's milk protein elimination diet (no dairy, no soy) plus a calcium supplement is preferred over weaning to specialised formula.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cow's milk protein allergy

stem: A 5-week-old male infant is brought to ED with fever measured at 38.6 degrees Celsius at home and again on arrival. He was born at term by normal vaginal birth with no maternal GBS risk factors and has been feeding normally until today. He has fed less in the last 6 hours. He appears alert in the parents' arms but is mildly tachypnoeic without distress.

data_table.Examination: Alert, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft; no focal infection; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Not yet done; needs evaluation per RCH SBI guideline

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate plan?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and safety-net advice with paediatric review in 24 hours
options.rationale: All febrile infants under 3 months require full septic workup; outpatient management of fever in this age group is not safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

options.text: Take blood and urine cultures, lumbar puncture and commence IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
options.rationale: AU first-line in fever under 6 weeks is full septic screen (FBC, CRP, blood culture, urine catheter sample, LP) plus empirical IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending cultures. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant; eTG)

options.text: Take blood cultures and CRP only and admit for 24 hours of observation without antibiotics
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are required in fever under 6 weeks even when the infant appears well; the consequences of missed bacterial meningitis are catastrophic. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

options.text: Perform urine bag sample only and commence oral amoxicillin awaiting outpatient review tomorrow
options.rationale: Urine bag samples have high contamination rates and oral antibiotics are inadequate; catheter or suprapubic urine plus IV antibiotics are required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

options.text: Administer intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg single dose and discharge home for review
options.rationale: Single-dose IM ceftriaxone is not adequate empirical therapy in suspected neonatal sepsis under 6 weeks; admission for IV combination therapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile infant)

explanation.summary: Fever in infants under 3 months carries a 7 to 12 percent risk of serious bacterial infection (UTI most common, then bacteraemia, then meningitis), with poor predictive value of clinical appearance. AU first-line is full septic screen (FBC, CRP, blood culture, catheter or SPA urine, lumbar puncture in under 6 weeks) plus empirical antibiotics. Under 6 weeks: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; 6 weeks to 3 months: cefotaxime or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin. CSF PCR for HSV is added if seizures, hepatitis, or maternal genital herpes.
key_points: All under 3 months with fever >= 38 degrees: septic workup + admission.
Under 6 weeks: full septic screen including LP; benzylpenicillin + gentamicin IV.
6 weeks to 3 months: blood + urine + selective LP per risk; IV antibiotics.
Catheter or SPA urine, NOT bag samples.
Add IV aciclovir if HSV risk factors (seizures, transaminitis, maternal HSV).
explanation.pearls: A 'fever-of-unknown-source' infant under 90 days with a positive urine culture still needs a normal CSF sample before stopping presumptive meningitis cover - around 5 percent of febrile UTIs in this age have concomitant meningitis.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is admitted with 6 days of fever to 39.5 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, an erythematous polymorphous trunk rash and induration of the hands but no significant cervical lymphadenopathy. Screening for streptococcal infection and respiratory viruses has been negative. The team is uncertain whether he meets criteria for definite Kawasaki disease.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, no exudate, polymorphous rash, dorsal hand induration; no cervical lymphadenopathy >= 1.5 cm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 525 x10^9/L, WCC 16 (neutrophils 12), CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 84 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis sterile pyuria; echo: small proximal LAD dilation (Z+2.1)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and reassess at 24 hours before further treatment
options.rationale: Sustained fever over 5 days with three principal features and supportive labs plus coronary dilation already meets incomplete Kawasaki criteria; delaying IVIG increases aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017; RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

options.text: Administer IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus high-dose aspirin and arrange paediatric cardiology
options.rationale: Incomplete KD with fever >= 5 days plus 3 features plus supportive labs (CRP, neutrophilia, anaemia, thrombocytosis, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia) and coronary dilation justifies IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin to reduce aneurysm risk. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017; RCH CPG)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as primary therapy and withhold IVIG until day 10
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are added (KAICA-style) for high-risk KD or IVIG-refractory disease; they are not primary therapy alone in standard initial care. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017)

options.text: Defer all treatment until thrombocytosis exceeds 600 x10^9/L and skin desquamation appears
options.rationale: Thrombocytosis and desquamation typically appear in week 2 to 3; waiting risks aneurysm formation - IVIG within 10 days reduces incidence from 25 percent to under 5 percent. (Source: AHA Kawasaki 2017)

options.text: Treat as scarlet fever with intravenous benzylpenicillin and reassess after 48 hours
options.rationale: Negative streptococcal screen and the clinical phenotype (conjunctivitis, mucositis, hand induration) plus coronary changes make Kawasaki the working diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis with a strong predilection for coronary arteries. Classic diagnosis: fever >= 5 days plus 4 of 5 features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucositis, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete KD = fever >= 5 days plus 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs (CRP >= 30, ESR >= 40, plus albumin under 30, anaemia, ALT raised, platelets >= 450 after 7 days, WCC >= 15, sterile pyuria) and/or coronary changes on echo. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever reduces coronary aneurysm risk five-fold; aspirin is added for anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet effect.
key_points: Classic KD: fever >= 5 days plus 4 of 5 features.
Incomplete KD: 2 to 3 features plus supportive labs or coronary changes.
Treat within 10 days: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin.
Supportive labs: CRP, ESR, neutrophilia, anaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7.
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks and 6 weeks to monitor coronaries.
explanation.pearls: An infant under 6 months with prolonged fever and irritability without classical KD features still warrants echocardiography because around 80 percent of KD-related coronary aneurysms in this age group present as incomplete or 'atypical' disease.

stem: A 6-year-old girl with focal epilepsy on valproate is brought to ED actively seizing. Paramedics gave IM midazolam 5 mg en route at 8 minutes and IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg on arrival at 18 minutes, but generalised tonic-clonic activity has continued. It is now 28 minutes of continuous seizure. The team is preparing the second-line agent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 32 (ongoing seizure), SpO2 93% on 6 L oxygen mask, T 37.2°C, BSL 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ongoing generalised tonic-clonic activity, eyes deviated upwards, pupils 4 mm equal; secured airway, IV access x 2
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.22, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 19, lactate 5.8, Na 138, K 4.0, Mg 0.84, Ca 2.32

lead_in: Which second-line anticonvulsant is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading at 1 mg/kg/min with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Phenytoin remains an acceptable option but carries higher cardiotoxicity and infusion-site risks; AU paediatric practice increasingly prefers levetiracetam. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Additional intravenous midazolam 0.15 mg/kg bolus then continuous infusion at 0.1 mg/kg/h
options.rationale: Further benzodiazepine after two failed doses increases respiratory depression without controlling seizure; second-line anticonvulsant is the correct step. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

options.text: Intravenous sodium valproate 40 mg/kg load over 10 minutes given her existing valproate use
options.rationale: Valproate is an option but not preferred when the patient is already on regular valproate (risk of overshoot toxicity); levetiracetam or phenytoin is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG)

options.text: Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg loading dose over 5 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: ConSEPT and EcLiPSE trials showed levetiracetam equivalent to phenytoin for paediatric status epilepticus and it has a more favourable side-effect profile, making it AU first-line second-line in many centres. (Source: ConSEPT/EcLiPSE; ANZICS paediatric)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation and propofol infusion as primary management without anticonvulsant loading
options.rationale: Refractory status requires anaesthetic agents AFTER a second-line anticonvulsant has been loaded; jumping to thiopentone/propofol is a third-line step. (Source: RCH CPG: Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Paediatric convulsive status epilepticus follows a tiered approach: 0 to 5 minutes assess airway, oxygen, IV access; 5 to 20 minutes first benzodiazepine (IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg or buccal 0.3 mg/kg); 20 to 40 minutes second benzodiazepine if still seizing; 30 to 40 minutes second-line anticonvulsant (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg). Refractory status (> 40 minutes) requires intubation and a third-line agent (thiopentone, midazolam infusion or propofol) in PICU. Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and pyridoxine deficiency must be excluded.
key_points: Two benzodiazepines then second-line anticonvulsant.
Second-line equivalence: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg.
Levetiracetam preferred in AU paediatric centres for safety.
Refractory status (> 40 min) = intubate + anaesthetic agent in PICU.
Exclude reversible causes: glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, pyridoxine, drugs.
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy presents under 18 months with apparently medication-refractory status; a single trial of pyridoxine 100 mg IV during ongoing seizures is diagnostic and therapeutic if there is rapid termination of seizure activity within minutes.

stem: A 9-year-old girl admitted with severe DKA (pH 7.05, BSL 32, ketones 5.6) was rehydrated with 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 5 mL/kg/h plus an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/h. Five hours into treatment she develops new-onset confusion and a fronto-occipital headache. Her parents report she 'doesn't recognise them' and she has had one episode of vomiting in the last 30 minutes. The bedside nurse notes that her BP has risen from 110/64 to 138/86 and her heart rate has fallen from 124 to 78.

data_table.Examination: Pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no focal weakness, bilateral plantar flexion responses; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L, ketones 3.2, pH 7.20 (improving), Na 140, K 4.1, corrected Na rising from 134 to 140

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Continue current fluid and insulin rates as her acidosis is improving and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration) plus altered mental status during DKA treatment is presumed cerebral oedema requiring immediate action. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA; ISPAD 2022)

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate to 0.1 unit/kg/h to reduce hyperglycaemia more aggressively
options.rationale: Increasing insulin worsens cerebral oedema by accelerating osmotic shifts; the priority is treating raised ICP. (Source: ISPAD DKA 2022)

options.text: Halve the fluid rate, give hypertonic saline 3 percent 3 mL/kg over 10 minutes and elevate head
options.rationale: Suspected cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA is treated with immediate fluid reduction and hypertonic 3 percent saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg (or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg) plus 30 degree head-up positioning. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA; ISPAD 2022)

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg bolus to correct the residual acidosis quickly
options.rationale: Bicarbonate worsens cerebral oedema risk and is not indicated in paediatric DKA except for severe hyperkalaemia with cardiac compromise. (Source: ISPAD DKA 2022)

options.text: Perform urgent CT brain before any intervention to confirm cerebral oedema is the cause now
options.rationale: Cerebral oedema in DKA is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must precede imaging; delays for CT worsen outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates 0.5 to 1 percent of paediatric DKA and accounts for the majority of DKA mortality. Risk factors: under 5 years, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis (pH under 7.1), elevated urea, low pCO2, high-volume fluid administration in first 4 hours, bicarbonate use. Warning signs: headache, altered mental state, Cushing triad, focal neurology, falling sodium during treatment. Treatment is immediate hypertonic saline 3 percent (2.5 to 5 mL/kg) OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg, halving fluid rate, 30 degree head-up. CT after stabilisation.
key_points: Cerebral oedema in 0.5 to 1 percent of paeds DKA; majority of DKA mortality.
Cushing triad + altered mental state = clinical diagnosis.
Treatment: hypertonic 3 percent NaCl 2.5 to 5 mL/kg OR mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg.
Halve fluid rate, elevate head 30 degrees, secure airway if GCS drops.
Risk factors: under 5, new-onset, pH under 7.1, raised urea, low pCO2.
explanation.pearls: Failure of serum sodium to rise as glucose falls (Hillier corrected sodium not increasing) during DKA treatment is the single best biochemical warning of impending cerebral oedema and warrants slowing fluid rate even before clinical features appear.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic 3 weeks after diagnosis with Henoch-Schonlein purpura (now IgA vasculitis) following a URTI. He had palpable purpura over both lower limbs and buttocks plus right ankle arthritis. The rash and joint symptoms have resolved. He has no abdominal pain, no haematuria visible and his BP at this visit is 102/68. His parents ask what the follow-up plan should be.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/68 (50th centile for age and height), HR 88, T 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Fading petechiae on lower legs, full range of joint movement, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis at diagnosis: 2+ blood, no protein; serum creatinine 38 micromol/L; albumin 38 g/L; today's urinalysis: 1+ blood, no protein

lead_in: Which monitoring plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Discharge from follow-up as rash has resolved and renal involvement appears self-limited
