options.rationale: Up to 50 percent of HSP nephritis appears in the first 3 months and a small fraction progresses to CKD; weekly to fortnightly urinalysis and BP monitoring for 6 months is required. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023; RCH CPG)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks to prevent late nephritis as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not prevent late nephritis in HSP; they are reserved for severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, or biopsy-proven nephritis. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)

options.text: Weekly urinalysis plus BP for 6 weeks then monthly for 6 months and nephrology referral if abnormal
options.rationale: AU and KHA-CARI guidance is weekly urinalysis and BP for 4 to 6 weeks, then monthly to 6 months, referring if persistent proteinuria, declining renal function or hypertension develops. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023; RCH CPG)

options.text: Arrange immediate renal biopsy to assess crescentic disease prior to immunosuppressive therapy
options.rationale: Renal biopsy is reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria, declining GFR, or persistent abnormal urinalysis - none currently present. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)

options.text: Single urinalysis and BP check at 12 months as he is now asymptomatic and well-appearing
options.rationale: Late-presenting nephritis would be missed by such infrequent monitoring; 6 months of structured surveillance is standard. (Source: KHA-CARI HSP 2023)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis (formerly HSP) is the commonest small-vessel vasculitis in children, presenting with palpable purpura, arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, and IgA nephritis. Renal involvement appears in around 40 percent (mostly within 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months after diagnosis); 1 to 2 percent progress to CKD. AU monitoring is weekly urinalysis (dipstick) and BP for 4 to 6 weeks, monthly to 6 months. Refer if persistent proteinuria, declining renal function, hypertension, or nephrotic features. Corticosteroids treat severe abdominal pain or scrotal involvement but do not prevent late nephritis.
key_points: Renal involvement in around 40 percent; 1 to 2 percent CKD.
Monitor weekly urinalysis + BP for 4 to 6 weeks, monthly to 6 months.
Refer for persistent proteinuria, declining GFR, hypertension, nephrosis.
Steroids treat severe pain/scrotal, NOT for renal prevention.
Renal biopsy if nephrotic, declining GFR, or persistent abnormalities.
explanation.pearls: Intussusception complicates around 2 percent of paediatric HSP and is typically ileo-ileal (not ileo-colic) - air enema may miss it; consider ultrasound first in any HSP child with severe abdominal pain regardless of stool patterns.

stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with 36 hours of right eye swelling that began after a URTI. The swelling has progressed and she now reports double vision when looking to the left. She has not been able to fully open the right eye since this morning. There is no history of trauma or insect bite. She is up to date with immunisations including Hib.

data_table.Examination: Right eye: marked periorbital erythema and oedema, proptosis 4 mm by exophthalmometer, painful restricted eye movements (failure to abduct), diplopia on left gaze; visual acuity 6/9 right, 6/6 left
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14, CRP 168 mg/L; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral cephalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with planned emergency department review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and diplopia are post-septal (orbital) cellulitis until proved otherwise; oral monotherapy is inadequate. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol eye drops with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics treat conjunctivitis; established orbital infection requires parenteral antibiotics and imaging. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Admit for urgent CT of orbits and sinuses and commence IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin
options.rationale: Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis is suggested by proptosis, painful EOM, diplopia or visual loss; AU first-line is urgent CT and IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin plus ENT and ophthalmology review. (Source: eTG; RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Discharge home with daily GP review and structured safety-netting advice on deterioration
options.rationale: Orbital cellulitis can progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis or vision loss within hours; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

options.text: Perform emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis prior to any imaging or antibiotic
options.rationale: Canthotomy is for orbital compartment syndrome (retrobulbar haemorrhage), not orbital cellulitis; imaging guides surgical drainage if a subperiosteal abscess is present. (Source: RCH CPG)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

explanation.summary: Periorbital (pre-septal) cellulitis is anterior to the orbital septum, presenting with eyelid erythema and oedema, normal eye movements, no proptosis, no visual loss. Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis - typically a complication of acute ethmoiditis - presents with the additional findings of proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, diplopia and visual changes. Orbital cellulitis demands urgent CT of orbits and paranasal sinuses, IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin (covering S. pyogenes, S. aureus and sinus organisms), ophthalmology and ENT involvement, and surgical drainage if a subperiosteal abscess is large or visual function declines.
key_points: Pre-septal: eyelid erythema, normal eye movements - oral antibiotics OK.
Post-septal: proptosis, EOM restriction, diplopia, vision change - emergency.
Workup: CT orbits and sinuses with contrast.
AU antibiotics: IV ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin (paeds dosing).
Surgical drainage for medium-large subperiosteal abscess or visual decline.
explanation.pearls: Visual acuity, pupillary reactions and colour vision (red desaturation test) are the most sensitive bedside markers of optic nerve compromise in orbital cellulitis - re-check them every hour during the first 24 hours of treatment to detect occult deterioration.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis

stem: A breastfed term male newborn (gestation 39+2 weeks, birthweight 3.4 kg) is reviewed on day 4 with visible jaundice noted by the midwife at home visit. He is feeding 8 times daily and producing 5 to 6 wet nappies. His mother is blood group O Rh-positive; cord blood and DAT are negative. He has had no previous transcutaneous bilirubin recorded. He is alert and feeding actively in the clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 138, RR 42; alert, well-perfused, weight 3.28 kg (-3.5 percent from birth)
data_table.Examination: Jaundice to chest and proximal limbs, soft fontanelle, no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae, normal Moro and tone
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 320 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 8 micromol/L (well under 20 percent), Hb 168 g/L, retics 2.5 percent, blood film normal

lead_in: Which management is most appropriate?

options.text: Admit for phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and review bilirubin in 6 hours
options.rationale: Bilirubin above the AU phototherapy line at 96 hours requires admission for phototherapy with continued breastfeeding plus a 6-hour repeat bilirubin to assess response. (Source: ANZ neonatal jaundice consensus 2024)

options.text: Reassure parents and review with repeat transcutaneous bilirubin in 48 hours
options.rationale: Total bilirubin 320 micromol/L at 96 hours in a term low-risk infant exceeds the AU phototherapy line; outpatient deferral risks kernicterus. (Source: ANZ neonatal jaundice consensus 2024; RWH paediatric jaundice)

options.text: Cease breastfeeding and switch to formula for 48 hours to confirm breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: Routine cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended; AU first-line is phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and lactation support. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)

options.text: Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion as bilirubin exceeds the exchange threshold today
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion threshold at 96 hours in a low-risk term infant is around 430 to 450 micromol/L; 320 is in the phototherapy not exchange range. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)

options.text: Commence oral phenobarbitone 5 mg/kg/day to induce bilirubin conjugation enzymes safely
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is not standard for neonatal jaundice; phototherapy is first-line and rapidly effective. (Source: ANZ consensus 2024)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management in AU uses age-specific phototherapy and exchange transfusion nomograms (eg KEMH/RWH/ANZ consensus 2024). Risk factors raise the action threshold lower: under 38 weeks, haemolysis (positive DAT, ABO/Rh mismatch, G6PD), sepsis, hypoalbuminaemia. Phototherapy is given with eye protection, breastfeeding continued (or expressed milk if too sleepy to feed), with 6-hourly bilirubin once treatment commences. Stop phototherapy when bilirubin falls 50 micromol/L below the line. Direct bilirubin over 20 percent of total prompts conjugated-hyperbilirubinaemia workup (biliary atresia, sepsis, metabolic).
key_points: Use age-specific phototherapy and exchange nomograms.
Lower threshold for risk factors: prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, hypoalbuminaemia.
Continue breastfeeding during phototherapy; eye protection.
Recheck bilirubin at 6 hours then 6 to 12 hourly to confirm response.
Conjugated fraction > 20 percent of total = workup for cholestasis.
explanation.pearls: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at any age beyond day 14 in a term infant is biliary atresia until proved otherwise - delay in Kasai portoenterostomy beyond 60 days of life roughly halves the chance of long-term liver-graft-free survival.

stem: You are the ED RMO seeing an 8-month-old infant brought in by her mother for worsening breathing. She has had 3 days of coryza and cough. Today the mother reports feeding has dropped to about 50% of usual volume and the last wet nappy was three hours ago. The infant is alert but distressed.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 62, SpO2 92% room air, HR 158, T 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, fine bilateral crackles, no wheeze, mucous membranes tacky
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for inpatient observation with supplemental oxygen as needed and paced nasogastric feeds
options.rationale: Sustained SpO2 below 92% on room air, RR over 60, and feeding under 50% of normal meet RCH admission criteria for moderate bronchiolitis; supportive oxygen and paced feeds are first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial inhaled salbutamol via spacer and formally reassess work of breathing after twenty minutes
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in typical viral bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months and are not recommended. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer a single oral prednisolone dose and observe in the emergency department for one hour
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids confer no benefit in acute bronchiolitis and are not used routinely. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home with written safety netting and a planned GP review the following morning
options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe with reduced feeding, reduced wet nappies, and borderline oxygenation, which together indicate moderate severity requiring admission. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with a planned repeat dose at thirty minutes if needed
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not routinely recommended and does not change admission rates or length of stay. (Source: RCH CPG Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric practice classifies bronchiolitis severity by oxygenation, respiratory effort, feeding, and hydration. Moderate severity meets admission criteria. Supportive care with oxygen and paced feeds is first-line; bronchodilators, steroids, and nebulised adrenaline are not recommended for typical viral bronchiolitis under 12 months. The discriminator here is recognising that feeding under 50% combined with borderline SpO2 mandates admission.
key_points: RCH admission triggers include SpO2 under 92%, RR over 60, feeds under half, or apnoeas
Bronchodilators, steroids, and adrenaline are not routinely indicated under 12 months
Paced NG feeds preserve hydration without increasing aspiration risk
explanation.pearls: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses SpO2 below 92% as the supplemental oxygen threshold; do not start oxygen at higher saturations as it prolongs admission.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 10-month-old boy admitted overnight with first febrile UTI. Urine grew E. coli sensitive to cefalexin. He responded to IV ceftriaxone within 24 hours and has been afebrile for 48 hours. He is now feeding well, hydrated, and ready for discharge on oral cefalexin to complete the course. The parents ask about follow-up imaging.

data_table.Examination: Well, no abdominal mass, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture E. coli sensitive to cefalexin; bedside renal tract ultrasound during admission was normal
data_table.Medications: Oral cefalexin to complete a total 10-day course

lead_in: What further imaging or investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan at three months to assess for renal scarring after the first febrile UTI
options.rationale: DMSA is recommended after atypical or recurrent UTIs, not after a first uncomplicated febrile UTI with normal ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram in the next four weeks to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
options.rationale: MCUG is reserved for atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or abnormal ultrasound findings, not for a first uncomplicated UTI that responded promptly. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: No further imaging is required as the renal tract ultrasound during admission was normal
options.rationale: For a first febrile UTI under 24 months with prompt response to first-line therapy and a normal ultrasound, no further imaging is required. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Commence trimethoprim antibiotic prophylaxis until two years of age as routine secondary prevention
options.rationale: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a single uncomplicated UTI is not recommended due to limited benefit and resistance. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

options.text: Repeat a urine culture at the end of the antibiotic course to confirm microbiological cure
options.rationale: Test of cure is not required if the child is clinically well at the end of therapy. (Source: RCH CPG UTI)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance from RCH stratifies post-UTI imaging by atypia and recurrence. A first febrile UTI in a child under 24 months who responds promptly and has a normal renal ultrasound needs no further imaging. MCUG and DMSA are reserved for atypical features or recurrence. The distractors test over-investigation patterns common in inherited NICE-derived practice.
key_points: Renal tract ultrasound during admission is standard for febrile UTI under 24 months
Atypical features include non-E coli organism, poor response by 48 hours, abdominal mass, or sepsis
Prophylaxis is not first-line after a single uncomplicated UTI
explanation.pearls: RCH UTI pathway: ultrasound during admission for under-24-months febrile UTI; MCUG only if atypical or recurrent or ultrasound abnormal.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: UTI in children

stem: You are the PICU registrar caring for an 8-year-old girl 6 hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis. She has received 10 mL/kg saline bolus and is on maintenance fluids with insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hr. Her GCS was 15 on arrival. The nurse calls because the patient is now harder to rouse and complains of a headache, with her father noting she is unusually irritable when stimulated.

data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils 3 mm reactive, no focal neurology, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18 (was 7.04), bicarbonate 14 (was 6), glucose 14 mmol/L, sodium 138, potassium 3.6
data_table.Medications: Insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hr; saline 0.9% with potassium replacement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch from saline to compound sodium lactate solution and continue the current insulin infusion rate while monitoring closely
options.rationale: Changing crystalloid type does not treat cerebral oedema; osmotherapy is the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion entirely because hypoglycaemia is the most likely cause of the decreased conscious state in this clinical context
options.rationale: Glucose is 14 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia is excluded; stopping insulin would worsen ketosis without addressing cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

options.text: Increase the fluid replacement rate to correct presumed ongoing dehydration and add a further isotonic saline bolus over thirty minutes
options.rationale: Aggressive rehydration in established cerebral oedema worsens intracranial pressure and contradicts current PICU guidance. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT brain before any treatment to confirm the diagnosis of cerebral oedema and exclude alternative intracranial pathology
options.rationale: Delaying osmotherapy for imaging worsens outcomes; treatment must precede imaging if cerebral oedema is clinically suspected. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

options.text: Administer hypertonic saline or mannitol immediately and halve the maintenance fluid rate while obtaining urgent neuroimaging only after stabilisation
options.rationale: Bradycardia with rising blood pressure, falling GCS, and headache in a child being treated for DKA is cerebral oedema; treatment with osmotherapy and fluid reduction must precede imaging. (Source: RCH CPG DKA)

explanation.summary: Paediatric DKA cerebral oedema typically presents 4 to 12 hours into treatment with bradycardia, rising BP, falling GCS, and headache. Recognition is clinical and treatment must precede imaging. Hypertonic 3% saline (2.5 to 5 mL/kg) or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg is first-line, with fluid rate reduction. Mortality remains 20 to 25% even with prompt treatment.
key_points: Cushing triad (bradycardia, hypertension, falling GCS) in DKA equals cerebral oedema until proven otherwise
Hypertonic saline 3% at 2.5 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg is first-line osmotherapy
Imaging follows stabilisation, not the other way around
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for paediatric DKA cerebral oedema include younger age, severe acidosis, low pCO2, and rapid sodium correction; ISPAD recommends limiting initial bolus to 10 to 20 mL/kg in 1 to 2 hours.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines DKA

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-month-old boy with 6 days of fever, irritability, and limited oral intake. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, and BCG site erythema, with no rash, no lymphadenopathy, and no peripheral changes. He has been treated empirically with oral antibiotics by the GP without improvement.

data_table.Examination: Conjunctival injection without exudate, dry cracked lips, BCG site erythema, no rash, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78, platelets 540 x10^9/L, ALT 88, albumin 28, urine WCC raised without bacteriuria, sodium 132

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and review tomorrow if no improvement, as classic criteria require five clinical features and have not yet been met
options.rationale: Waiting risks coronary aneurysm formation; supplementary laboratory criteria allow earlier diagnosis under 6 months when clinical features are sparse. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

options.text: Arrange echocardiography and commence IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin based on the supplementary laboratory criteria for incomplete disease
options.rationale: Persistent fever beyond 5 days with 2 clinical features plus supportive labs (CRP raised, platelets raised, low albumin, low sodium, raised ALT, sterile pyuria) meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria for treatment and urgent echocardiography. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

options.text: Change empiric antibiotics to IV ceftriaxone for occult bacterial sepsis after a full septic workup including lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Sterile pyuria, raised ALT, and low albumin in this pattern point to inflammatory rather than infectious aetiology in the prolonged fever picture. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

options.text: Arrange outpatient rheumatology review next week and commence oral prednisolone empirically for systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
options.rationale: sJIA requires quotidian fever pattern and evanescent rash, neither of which is present, and outpatient deferral risks aneurysms. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

options.text: Trial high-dose ibuprofen for presumed viral inflammation and reassess clinical features over the next forty-eight hours of observation
options.rationale: Delay risks coronary aneurysm; ibuprofen does not address the underlying vasculitis or replace IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Infants under 6 months frequently present with incomplete Kawasaki disease, with fewer than 4 of the 5 classic clinical features. The AHA 2017 algorithm allows treatment based on prolonged fever plus 2 clinical features and supplementary labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, plus 3 of: platelets over 450, low albumin, low sodium, raised ALT, sterile pyuria, WCC over 15). Early IVIG within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%. Echocardiography is mandatory at diagnosis.
key_points: Under 6 months age group has highest aneurysm risk despite often atypical presentation
AHA supplementary lab criteria allow earlier intervention in incomplete disease
IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk substantially
explanation.pearls: BCG site reactivation is highly specific for Kawasaki disease in vaccinated infants; it is not in classical criteria but strongly supports the diagnosis.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to ED to see a 4-month-old infant brought in with episodes of unusual pallor and apparent fatigue over 12 hours. The parents describe two episodes of inconsolable crying lasting around 10 minutes followed by limpness, with no fever or vomiting. The child has had one normal stool today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 44, T 36.9, SpO2 99%, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Pale, drowsy between episodes, abdomen soft with palpable fullness in right upper quadrant, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8, FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: CT abdomen with intravenous contrast to fully characterise abdominal pathology and assess for an underlying lead point causing the presentation
options.rationale: Ionising radiation in infants is avoided when ultrasound is diagnostic; CT has no first-line role for intussusception. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Three-view abdominal radiograph series to assess for free air and characterise any bowel obstruction before further imaging is arranged
options.rationale: Plain films may show non-specific signs but cannot reliably confirm or exclude intussusception; ultrasound is preferred first-line. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: EEG to evaluate for atypical seizure activity given the recurrent episodes of decreased responsiveness reported by the parents over twelve hours
options.rationale: The pattern of inconsolable crying followed by limpness with a palpable mass is classic for intussusception, not seizure activity. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound to assess for a target sign with paediatric surgical consult booked in parallel
options.rationale: Pallor, intermittent inconsolable crying, lethargy, and a palpable mass in a 4-month-old strongly suggest intussusception; ultrasound is the first-line investigation with high sensitivity. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

options.text: Lumbar puncture to exclude occult central nervous system infection causing the lethargy and unusual behaviour observed at home this morning
options.rationale: Without fever, irritability between episodes, or meningism, LP is not the priority and the clinical pattern is surgical. (Source: RCH CPG Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Intussusception classically presents at 3 months to 3 years with paroxysmal crying, drawing up of legs, pallor, lethargy between episodes, and a palpable sausage-shaped mass. Stool changes (redcurrant jelly) are late findings; their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. Ultrasound is highly sensitive and specific. Hydrostatic or pneumatic reduction is first-line management with surgery for failed reduction or perforation.
key_points: Lethargy between episodes is an under-recognised but specific feature in young infants
Ultrasound has sensitivity over 97% and is first-line
Air or contrast enema reduction is therapeutic in most cases without need for surgery
explanation.pearls: Pure lethargy in an infant can be the dominant presentation of intussusception, sometimes mistaken for sepsis or neurological illness; consider ultrasound when no clear cause is found.

stem: You are the ED RMO managing a previously well 3-year-old girl presenting with 24 hours of fever and progressive lethargy. She has mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill, and cool peripheries. An IV line is in. The senior nurse is preparing fluids while you prepare to give broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 78/40, RR 42, SpO2 96% room air, T 39.6, capillary refill 5 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mottled cool peripheries, drowsy but rousable, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, glucose 5.2, FBC and cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Administer a 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus of balanced crystalloid over 5 to 10 minutes with reassessment after each bolus
options.rationale: Current Australian and Surviving Sepsis paediatric guidance favours smaller boluses (10 to 20 mL/kg) with frequent reassessment to avoid fluid overload after the FEAST trial findings. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Administer a 40 mL/kg bolus of normal saline over the first ten minutes prior to any reassessment of haemodynamics or perfusion markers
options.rationale: Large rapid boluses without reassessment risk pulmonary oedema and worse mortality in resource-rich settings as well; paediatric guidance is smaller incremental boluses. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Start a peripheral noradrenaline infusion immediately as first-line haemodynamic support before any further crystalloid resuscitation is given
options.rationale: Vasopressors are second-line after initial crystalloid bolus and reassessment; immediate vasopressor in cold shock is not standard. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Commence packed red blood cell transfusion as initial volume resuscitation while awaiting the full blood count and group and screen results
options.rationale: Blood is not first-line volume; crystalloid is unless there is documented haemorrhage or low haemoglobin requiring transfusion. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

options.text: Administer 5% albumin 20 mL/kg as the preferred crystalloid alternative for septic shock fluid resuscitation in paediatric practice
options.rationale: Albumin is not preferred first-line; balanced crystalloid is recommended and albumin reserved for refractory shock if used at all. (Source: RCH CPG Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric sepsis fluid resuscitation in Australia uses 10 to 20 mL/kg boluses of balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte 148 or Hartmann's preferred over normal saline) with reassessment after each bolus. The FEAST trial showed harm from aggressive fluid boluses in African children with sepsis and informs cautious incremental dosing. Antibiotics within 1 hour and vasoactive support if perfusion does not improve after 40 to 60 mL/kg total are the next steps.
key_points: 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus then reassess, not 40 to 60 mL/kg blindly
Balanced crystalloid preferred over normal saline
Antibiotics within the first hour; vasopressors after 40 to 60 mL/kg if not responding
explanation.pearls: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2020 paediatric update recommends starting vasopressors via peripheral access if not responding after 40 to 60 mL/kg crystalloid rather than delaying for central access.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12-year-old girl in clinic after a third episode of syncope while swimming in cold water at school carnivals. Each episode involved sudden loss of consciousness with rapid recovery. Her ECG at rest shows a QTc of 488 ms calculated using the Bazett formula. Her paternal grandfather died suddenly aged 32 of unknown cause while swimming.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 sinus, BP 108/64
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Resting ECG QTc 488 ms (Bazett), no arrhythmia on Holter; electrolytes including magnesium normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Commence flecainide as antiarrhythmic prophylaxis pending genetic confirmation while continuing routine sport participation as tolerated by the patient
options.rationale: Flecainide is not first-line for LQTS and can prolong QT further; sport restriction is part of LQT1 management until confirmed. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

options.text: Commence metoprolol succinate at a paediatric dose and reassess in three months with repeat resting ECG to evaluate the effect on QTc and clinical symptoms
options.rationale: Selective beta1 blockers like metoprolol are inferior to nadolol and propranolol in LQTS and not first-line for paediatric patients with high-risk features. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

options.text: Implant a single-chamber ICD as primary prevention given the family history and three syncopal episodes despite a normal Holter recording
options.rationale: Beta-blockers and lifestyle changes are first-line; ICD is reserved for breakthrough events on therapy or aborted cardiac arrest, not initial management. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

options.text: Commence a non-selective beta-blocker such as nadolol or propranolol with referral for genetic testing and family cascade screening
options.rationale: Suspected LQT1 with swimming-triggered syncope and prolonged QTc plus family history requires beta-blockade (nadolol or propranolol preferred) and genetic confirmation with family screening. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange a tilt-table test to confirm vasovagal syncope as the likely diagnosis based on the recurrent self-limiting episodes
options.rationale: Exertion or swimming-triggered syncope with prolonged QTc and family sudden death is not vasovagal; further LQTS evaluation is required. (Source: HRS Inherited Arrhythmia Statement)

explanation.summary: Swimming-triggered syncope is the signature presentation of LQT1, which accounts for around 30 to 35% of LQTS. A QTc above 480 ms in a symptomatic patient plus family sudden death is diagnostic by Schwartz score. Non-selective beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol) are first-line; selective agents are inferior. ICD is reserved for breakthrough events or aborted cardiac arrest. Genetic testing guides family cascade screening.
key_points: LQT1 triggers: exercise and swimming; LQT2: auditory stimuli, postpartum; LQT3: rest and sleep
Nadolol and propranolol superior to selective beta-blockers in LQTS
ICD for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope on optimal beta-blockade
explanation.pearls: QTc above 480 ms with unexplained syncope scores 3 on Schwartz criteria; combined with family sudden death under 30, this triggers LQTS workup even without genetic confirmation.

sources.label: CSANZ Genetic Heart Disease Position Statement

stem: You are the PICU registrar receiving a 6-day-old breastfed boy retrieved from a regional centre with progressive lethargy and refusal to feed since day 4. He has had two brief tonic-clonic events. The infant is now obtunded. Bedside glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. The retrieval team has sent off a metabolic screen and ammonia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188, RR 70, T 36.4, SpO2 98% on minimal oxygen
data_table.Examination: Obtunded, hypotonic, no focal neurology, no dysmorphic features, normal newborn examination at birth
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.2, lactate 1.8, venous pH 7.49, bicarbonate 22, ammonia 540 micromol/L, anion gap 14, urine ketones negative
data_table.Medications: Nil; standard newborn vitamin K and hepatitis B at birth

lead_in: Which finding most strongly directs initial management?

options.text: Hypoglycaemia requiring high-rate dextrose infusion at 8 mg/kg/min with concurrent insulin to facilitate intracellular potassium shift
options.rationale: Glucose is 4.2 mmol/L, not low; insulin would be inappropriate and dangerous in this context. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

options.text: Hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis directing urgent referral for haemofiltration and a urea cycle defect pathway
options.rationale: Marked hyperammonaemia (over 200 micromol/L) with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis in a previously well neonate after milk feeds points to a urea cycle defect; haemofiltration is the definitive ammonia-lowering treatment alongside protein restriction and ammonia scavengers. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

options.text: Metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap and ketosis pointing toward organic acidaemia requiring sodium bicarbonate and biotin empirically
options.rationale: Anion gap is 14 and pH is alkalotic with absent ketones, which excludes organic acidaemia as the primary problem. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

options.text: Raised lactate suggesting mitochondrial disease and requiring high-dose thiamine, riboflavin, and coenzyme Q10 prior to further imaging
options.rationale: Lactate is 1.8 mmol/L which is within normal limits and does not support mitochondrial disease as the primary diagnosis. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

options.text: Normal newborn examination history excluding inborn error of metabolism and directing toward neonatal sepsis pathway and empiric antibiotics
options.rationale: Many inborn errors present after milk feeds are established with a symptom-free interval after birth; normal initial examination does not exclude them. (Source: ANZSIEM Hyperammonaemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Symptom-free interval followed by lethargy and encephalopathy after milk feeds in a neonate signals an inborn error of metabolism. Urea cycle defects classically cause hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis; organic acidaemias cause metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap and ketosis. Ammonia above 200 in a neonate is a haemofiltration indication. Stop protein, give 10% dextrose to suppress catabolism, and give ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate, arginine).
key_points: Symptom-free interval after birth then encephalopathy with milk feeds suggests urea cycle defect
Urea cycle defect: respiratory alkalosis, absent ketosis; organic acidaemia: metabolic acidosis with ketosis
Ammonia over 200 micromol/L in a neonate is a haemofiltration trigger
explanation.pearls: Boys with X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency typically present in the first week with this picture; carrier mothers may have a history of protein aversion or postpartum psychiatric symptoms.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-week-old previously well term male infant brought in by parents with 24 hours of fever, irritability, and reduced feeding (taking about half his usual volume). He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. There is no rash, no recent travel, and immunisations are up to date. ED has obtained a catheter urine specimen which is positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 178, RR 52, SpO2 98% RA, cap refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Alert when held; wet nappies reduced; no rash; chest clear; abdomen soft, no mass; suprapubic non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4, neutrophils 13.2, Hb 110, CRP 84, Na 138, K 4.6, Cr 28; urine: nitrites +, leuk +++, blood +, microscopy WCC >100/mcL; blood and urine cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days with GP review within 48 hours arranged
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inappropriate for febrile UTI under 3 months of age; the bacteraemia risk is too high. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin and IV benzylpenicillin with renal tract ultrasound during admission
options.rationale: Infants under 3 months with febrile UTI require admission and parenteral antibiotics; empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) is standard, and renal tract ultrasound is recommended during first febrile UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and arrange micturating cystourethrogram during this admission
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved for late-onset neonatal sepsis or proven resistant organisms; MCUG is not first-line imaging after a first febrile UTI under current Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg three times daily with paediatric review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotic monotherapy is not acceptable for febrile UTI under 3 months irrespective of agent due to bacteraemia and meningitis risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Discharge home awaiting urine culture sensitivities and start antibiotics if a pathogen grows
options.rationale: Awaiting cultures before treating any febrile infant under 3 months with positive urine dipstick risks progression to urosepsis and meningitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Febrile UTI in infants under 3 months is treated as serious bacterial infection until proven otherwise: admission, parenteral antibiotics, blood and urine cultures, and consideration of lumbar puncture if clinically unwell or under 4 weeks. Empirical IV gentamicin plus benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) is the standard Australian regimen, with oral switch when stable and afebrile typically after 2 to 4 days. Renal tract ultrasound is recommended after a first febrile UTI under 6 months to identify obstruction or significant abnormality. MCUG is reserved for recurrent UTI, atypical organism, or abnormal ultrasound. DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months assesses cortical scarring when indicated. E. coli accounts for over 80% of paediatric UTIs.
key_points: Under 3 months febrile UTI: admit, IV antibiotics, blood + urine cultures
Empirical IV gentamicin + benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin
Renal tract ultrasound after first febrile UTI under 6 months
MCUG only if recurrent, atypical, or abnormal USS
Catheter or SPA urine specimen preferred under 2 years
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin once-daily at 7.5 mg/kg in neonates and infants is preferred to divided dosing in Australian paediatric practice because of superior peak-to-MIC bactericidal activity and reduced nephrotoxicity.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 2-year-old girl in ED with a 1-day history of barking cough and stridor. She had a coryzal prodrome 2 days ago. At triage she had inspiratory stridor at rest with mild chest wall retractions, and was given a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg 30 minutes ago. On reassessment she now has inspiratory stridor at rest with marked sternal recession, looks distressed, and is reluctant to drink. She is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest, marked sternal recession, mild tracheal tug, no drooling, no cyanosis, alert but distressed, air entry symmetrical with no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging needed at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg (5 mL of 1:1000) with continued close monitoring in resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Stridor at rest with marked sternal recession indicates severe croup not yet responding to dexamethasone; nebulised adrenaline gives rapid (within 30 minutes) symptomatic relief and is indicated for moderate-severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Repeat oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg now and reassess clinical severity in a further 60 minutes
options.rationale: Dexamethasone takes 1 to 2 hours for effect; repeating it now does not provide rapid relief and the child needs immediate intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Heated humidified oxygen by mask at 6 L/min and reassess clinical severity in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Cochrane evidence shows no benefit of humidified air for croup; oxygen is given only if SpO2 is low, which is not the case here. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Urgent lateral neck radiograph to exclude foreign body or epiglottitis before further treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is not indicated in classic croup and risks deterioration if the child is distressed; clinical severity scoring guides management. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via spacer with budesonide and clinical reassessment in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Salbutamol does not treat upper airway obstruction; nebulised budesonide is an alternative steroid but oral dexamethasone has already been given. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup severity is graded as mild (stridor only with agitation, no recession), moderate (stridor at rest with mild-moderate recession), severe (stridor at rest with marked recession or distress, or hypoxia or altered mental state). All grades receive oral dexamethasone 0.15 to 0.6 mg/kg (single dose). Moderate to severe croup additionally receives nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 (or 0.5 mL/kg, max 5 mL), which acts within 30 minutes. Adrenaline effect lasts 1 to 2 hours; child must be observed for rebound. Disposition depends on response: home if mild and steroid effect achieved, observation for 4 hours post-adrenaline, admission for ongoing stridor at rest. Avoid distressing the child (no IV, no imaging unless essential).
key_points: Severity: mild (stridor with agitation), moderate (stridor at rest), severe (marked recession, hypoxia)
All grades: oral dexamethasone 0.15-0.6 mg/kg single dose
Moderate-severe: add nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000
Adrenaline acts within 30 minutes, effect 1-2 hours
Avoid distressing investigations
explanation.pearls: Nebulised L-adrenaline (1:1000) at 5 mL is equivalent in efficacy to racemic adrenaline 2.25% at 0.5 mL, and is the standard formulation in Australian paediatric ED; rebound stridor at 1 to 2 hours mandates 4-hour observation post-dose.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in ED at 02:30 reviewing a previously well 13-year-old boy with sudden onset severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 4 hours ago. He has vomited twice. He denies trauma, dysuria, or recent illness. He has not previously been sexually active. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and exquisitely tender; the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. The right side is unremarkable. Urinalysis is clear.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum erythematous, swollen, left testis high-riding with horizontal lie, exquisite tenderness, absent cremasteric reflex; right side normal; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: nil; FBC and EUC sent
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g PO 1 hour ago in ED

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent scrotal Doppler ultrasound to assess testicular blood flow before any surgical referral
options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive treatment and risks loss of the testis; with classic clinical findings, theatre takes priority over imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Empirical oral ceftriaxone and doxycycline for presumed epididymo-orchitis with urology review
options.rationale: Epididymitis usually has gradual onset, positive cremasteric reflex, and abnormal urinalysis; this presentation is classic torsion. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral orchidopexy by urology this hour
options.rationale: Time from onset to detorsion determines testicular salvage (about 90% salvage if under 6 hours, falling to under 10% by 24 hours); classic clinical features mandate theatre without delay for imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Attempt manual detorsion in ED rotating the left testis medially and admit for observation overnight
options.rationale: Manual detorsion (open-book, lateral rotation) may be a bridging measure where surgery is delayed, but does not replace urgent theatre; rotation direction is lateral, not medial, in most cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

options.text: Admit under paediatrics for analgesia and elevation, with urology review on the morning round
options.rationale: Delay beyond 6 hours dramatically reduces testicular salvage; deferring urology assessment is a sentinel error. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute scrotum)

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency where time to detorsion determines salvage. Classic features are sudden severe scrotal pain (often waking from sleep), vomiting, high-riding testis with horizontal lie, and absent cremasteric reflex. Salvage rates are around 90% if surgery occurs within 6 hours, falling to under 10% beyond 24 hours. When clinical suspicion is high, the patient goes directly to theatre; ultrasound is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty and must not delay surgery. Surgical exploration includes detorsion, viability assessment, and bilateral orchidopexy because the underlying bell-clapper deformity is bilateral. Differential includes epididymitis (gradual, urinary symptoms), torsion of appendix testis (blue dot sign, less severe), and incarcerated hernia.
key_points: Salvage ~90% if surgery <6 hours, <10% by 24 hours
Classic: sudden pain, vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
Do not delay theatre for ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high
Bilateral orchidopexy (bell-clapper is bilateral)
Differential: epididymitis (gradual, urinary symptoms), torsion of appendix testis
explanation.pearls: Absent cremasteric reflex has about 99% sensitivity for testicular torsion in adolescent boys, making it the single most useful bedside finding when paired with sudden severe pain.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9-month-old boy with 6 days of fever to 39.5, marked irritability, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, and a polymorphous truncal rash. He has no cervical lymphadenopathy, no oral changes, and no extremity changes yet. Mucosal swabs and blood cultures are pending. Initial bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised CRP, mild anaemia, hyponatraemia, low albumin, and elevated ALT. Echocardiogram performed by paediatric cardiology shows borderline left anterior descending coronary dilation (Z score 2.3).

data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, polymorphous truncal rash, irritable; no lymphadenopathy, no oral or hand or foot changes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19, neutrophils 14, Hb 96, plt 540, CRP 162, ESR 78, Na 130, ALT 88, albumin 28; urinalysis: sterile pyuria; echocardiogram: LAD Z score 2.3, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue supportive care and antipyretics; reassess at day 10 of fever to apply Kawasaki criteria
options.rationale: Awaiting full criteria delays treatment beyond day 10 and increases coronary aneurysm risk; incomplete Kawasaki with coronary changes is treated as Kawasaki. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for empirical sepsis with paediatric infectious diseases consultation
options.rationale: Septic workup is reasonable but ceftriaxone alone does not address the most likely diagnosis; coronary changes on echo support incomplete Kawasaki. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as first-line treatment of incomplete Kawasaki
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for IVIG resistance or as IVIG-adjunct in high-risk; it is not first-line in standard practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours with high-dose oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day divided
options.rationale: Infants under 1 year with prolonged fever, supportive lab features (raised CRP, sterile pyuria, hyponatraemia, low albumin, raised ALT) and coronary changes meet incomplete Kawasaki criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from about 25% to under 5%. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease; AHA Kawasaki Statement)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily monotherapy and repeat echocardiogram in 7 days for review
options.rationale: Oral steroid monotherapy is not standard initial therapy; IVIG remains the first-line agent with proven coronary protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Classic Kawasaki disease requires fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki applies when fewer criteria are met, especially in infants under 1 year and children over 8 (highest aneurysm risk groups). The AHA algorithm allows treatment when fever and 2 to 3 criteria coexist with elevated CRP/ESR plus supportive features (anaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, leukocytosis, sterile pyuria) OR coronary abnormalities on echo (Z score >=2.5 or dilation). IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to under 5%. Aspirin is reduced to antiplatelet dose after fever resolution.
key_points: Classic: fever >=5 days + 4 of 5 (CRASH and burn - Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands/feet)
Incomplete: fewer criteria but suggestive labs or coronary findings
IVIG 2 g/kg + high-dose aspirin within 10 days reduces aneurysm rate 25% to <5%
Infants <1 year highest aneurysm risk - lower threshold to treat
Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks
explanation.pearls: Coronary artery Z score >=2.5 on echocardiogram in a febrile child with under 4 classic criteria is sufficient to diagnose incomplete Kawasaki and commit to IVIG, regardless of inflammatory markers.

stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to postnatal ward at 90 minutes of life to review a term male infant born by elective LSCS to a 32-year-old G2P1 with insulin-treated type 1 diabetes. Birth weight is 4350 g (>97th centile). Maternal HbA1c at 36 weeks was 7.4%. The infant was placed skin-to-skin and breastfed at 30 minutes. Routine BSL screening at 90 minutes is 1.6 mmol/L (taken before the second feed). The infant is alert with normal tone, no jitteriness, no apnoea, and a normal cry.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 (axillary), HR 142, RR 50, SpO2 98% RA
data_table.Examination: Term appearance, large for gestational age, alert, normal tone, no jitteriness, no apnoea, plethoric but not cyanotic
data_table.Investigations: Bedside BSL 1.6 mmol/L; cord gases at delivery normal; no further bloods yet
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding only and recheck BSL prior to the next scheduled feed in 3 hours
options.rationale: BSL 1.6 in an at-risk asymptomatic infant requires active intervention; awaiting another feed risks symptomatic hypoglycaemia and neurological injury. (Source: ANZCOR Neonatal Resuscitation; RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give a single bolus of 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg intravenously and continue routine ward observations afterwards
options.rationale: IV bolus dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL persistently <1.2 despite feeds and gel; first-line in asymptomatic at-risk infant is dextrose gel. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day infusion via cannula and admit to neonatal nursery
options.rationale: IV dextrose is reserved for symptomatic, severe (<1.2), or refractory hypoglycaemia after dextrose gel and feed; this asymptomatic infant should have buccal gel first. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon 100 mcg/kg single dose with continued breastfeeding and observation
options.rationale: Glucagon is reserved for severe persistent hypoglycaemia where IV access is delayed; infants of diabetic mothers have depleted glycogen stores and respond unreliably. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Administer 40% buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg with immediate top-up feed and recheck BSL in 30 minutes
options.rationale: For asymptomatic at-risk neonatal hypoglycaemia in the first 48 hours, 40% buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) plus feed is the preferred Australian first-line intervention, with BSL recheck in 30 minutes; this avoids separation and IV access. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia; ANZNN)

explanation.summary: Infants at risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia (LGA, IDM, SGA, preterm) are screened with bedside BSL from 90 minutes of life and before feeds for 12 to 24 hours. Operational threshold for action is BSL <2.6 mmol/L in the first 48 hours. For asymptomatic at-risk infants, 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa followed by feed is first-line; this Australian Sugar Babies protocol increases breastfeeding success and reduces NICU admissions. Recheck BSL at 30 minutes. IV 10% dextrose at 60 to 80 mL/kg/day is reserved for symptomatic infants, BSL <1.2, or BSL not responsive to gel and feeds. Symptomatic infants (jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, lethargy) require immediate IV dextrose 2 mL/kg of 10% then maintenance infusion. Critical sample (insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ammonia, lactate) is taken before treatment when persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours raises concern for hyperinsulinism.
key_points: Operational threshold BSL <2.6 in first 48 hours for at-risk infants
Asymptomatic: 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg + feed, recheck 30 min
Symptomatic or BSL <1.2: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus + infusion
Critical sample if persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours
IDM: hyperinsulinism, depleted glycogen, vulnerable >48 hours
explanation.pearls: The Sugar Babies trial showed buccal 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg reduced NICU admission for neonatal hypoglycaemia by approximately 50% compared with feeds alone, and is the basis for Australian first-line use.

stem: You are the paediatric nephrology registrar reviewing an 8-year-old boy 6 weeks after a clinical diagnosis of Henoch-Schönlein purpura (palpable purpura, polyarthralgia, mild abdominal pain) which has otherwise resolved. He was managed conservatively at first presentation. Today his palpable purpura has cleared. Routine urinalysis shows persistent proteinuria and microscopic haematuria. Spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 280 mg/mmol (heavily nephrotic range). Serum albumin is 22 g/L. eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m2 (mildly reduced). He is normotensive. Complement and ANA are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 (50th centile for age and height), HR 88
data_table.Examination: Mild periorbital and ankle oedema, purpura resolved, abdomen soft, joints non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: protein +++, blood ++; UPCR 280 mg/mmol; albumin 22 g/L; eGFR 78; C3 normal, C4 normal, ANA negative, anti-dsDNA negative; hep B/C and ASOT negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and recheck urinalysis and renal function in 6 months as HSP nephritis usually self-resolves
options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia carries a high risk of progression and demands biopsy to grade severity, not watchful waiting. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases; KHA-CARI)

options.text: Empirical oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks then taper, without histological confirmation now
options.rationale: Empirical steroids without histology in nephrotic HSP may undertreat crescentic disease and overtreat mild lesions; biopsy guides immunosuppression intensity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

options.text: Renal biopsy now to grade nephritis severity and guide immunosuppressive therapy choice
options.rationale: HSP nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, or impaired GFR persisting beyond 4 weeks is an indication for renal biopsy to assess for crescents (ISKDC grading) and direct therapy intensity; isolated microscopic haematuria does not require biopsy. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases; RCH CPG: HSP)

options.text: Commence ACE inhibitor monotherapy (enalapril) with monthly urinalysis and BP monitoring at GP
options.rationale: ACE inhibitor is appropriate adjunct for ongoing proteinuria but does not replace biopsy and immunosuppression decision in nephrotic-range disease. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

options.text: Plasmapheresis with IV pulse methylprednisolone now and admit under nephrology for cyclophosphamide
options.rationale: Plasmapheresis and cyclophosphamide are reserved for biopsy-proven crescentic disease (typically >50% crescents) with rapidly progressive renal failure; this stable presentation requires histology first. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases)

explanation.summary: HSP nephritis affects 20 to 50% of children with HSP and is the main determinant of long-term outcome. Most cases (isolated microscopic haematuria or low-grade proteinuria) resolve without specific treatment, but persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypertension, or impaired GFR carry significant risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (about 5 to 10% develop ESKD over 20 years). Renal biopsy is indicated for nephrotic syndrome, persistent proteinuria after 4 weeks of UPCR >50 mg/mmol, raised creatinine, or hypertension. ISKDC grading by percentage crescents drives therapy: low grade (no crescents) receives ACE inhibitor; moderate (under 50%) receives oral prednisolone; severe (over 50% crescents) requires IV methylprednisolone, cyclophosphamide or MMF, and plasmapheresis in selected cases. All children with HSP need urinalysis surveillance for 6 months minimum.
key_points: HSP nephritis: main determinant of long-term outcome
Biopsy indication: nephrotic, persistent UPCR >50, raised Cr, HTN
ISKDC grade by crescents directs therapy intensity
ACE inhibitor adjunctively for proteinuria reduction
Surveillance urinalysis 6 months minimum after HSP
explanation.pearls: Crescent involvement of >50% of glomeruli on biopsy (ISKDC grade IV to V) in HSP nephritis carries about 25% risk of ESKD by 20 years and triggers aggressive immunosuppression including pulse methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide.

stem: You are the paediatric oncology registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a 3-week history of progressive abdominal distension, intermittent low-grade fever, weight loss, and bone pain in both legs causing limping. Examination shows a 10 cm firm abdominal mass crossing the midline. She has periorbital ecchymosis bilaterally. There is no haematuria. BP is 90th centile for age. Urinary VMA and HVA are markedly elevated. MIBG scan is being arranged. Bone marrow aspirate is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68 (90th centile), HR 124, T 37.8, RR 24, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: 10 cm firm irregular abdominal mass crossing midline, bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus on prolonged ocular pursuit, tender shins bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84, plt 198, WCC 12, LDH 1240, urinary VMA and HVA markedly elevated; MRI abdomen: 10 cm adrenal mass crossing midline encasing aorta

lead_in: Which feature most strongly differentiates this presentation from Wilms tumour?

options.text: Presence of a firm palpable abdominal mass detected on routine paediatric abdominal examination today
options.rationale: Abdominal mass is the classical presentation of BOTH Wilms tumour and neuroblastoma; it does not discriminate between them on its own. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

options.text: Hypertension within the 90th centile range for age detected on routine ward observations today
options.rationale: Both Wilms (renin) and neuroblastoma (catecholamines) can cause hypertension; this feature alone does not discriminate. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

options.text: Mass crossing the abdominal midline with encasement of the aorta on the most recent MRI scan
options.rationale: Crossing the midline favours neuroblastoma but is not absolutely specific; vascular encasement also occurs in advanced Wilms. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

options.text: Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) with opsoclonus and bone pain from skeletal metastasis
options.rationale: Periorbital ecchymosis from orbital metastases, opsoclonus-myoclonus paraneoplastic syndrome, and lytic bone metastases are hallmark neuroblastoma features that do not occur with Wilms; metastasis to bone, marrow, orbit, and skin is typical of neuroblastoma stage M. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

options.text: Markedly elevated urinary catecholamine metabolite levels (VMA and HVA) detected on urine testing
options.rationale: Urinary VMA and HVA are highly specific for neuroblastoma but the stem question asks about clinical features that differentiate; the orbital and bone disease pattern is more clinically discriminating. (Source: COG Neuroblastoma Risk Stratification)

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour are the two commonest paediatric solid abdominal malignancies. Neuroblastoma (median age 2 years) arises from neural crest, typically adrenal but can be any sympathetic chain site; it crosses midline, encases vessels, and metastasises to bone marrow, cortical bone, orbits, skin, and liver, with pathognomonic raccoon eyes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and Horner syndrome. Wilms tumour (median age 3 to 4) arises from kidney, displaces structures, rarely crosses midline, and metastasises to lung and liver; associated with WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash syndromes. Urinary VMA and HVA are elevated in over 90% of neuroblastomas; staging includes MIBG and bilateral bone marrow biopsy; INRG risk stratification (age, MYCN amplification, ploidy, histology, stage) drives therapy intensity from observation through surgery, chemotherapy, autologous SCT, and anti-GD2 immunotherapy.
key_points: Neuroblastoma: neural crest, crosses midline, encases vessels, bone/marrow/orbit metastases
Wilms: renal, displaces, rarely crosses midline, lung/liver metastases
Neuroblastoma paraneoplastic: opsoclonus-myoclonus, racoon eyes, Horner
Urinary VMA/HVA elevated in >90% of neuroblastomas
INRG risk stratification drives treatment intensity
explanation.pearls: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome occurs in 2 to 3% of children with neuroblastoma, often signalling lower-stage tumour with paradoxically worse neurological outcome; immunotherapy with rituximab is increasingly used for the paraneoplastic component.

stem: You are the paediatric immunology registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy referred by GP with 8 documented episodes over the past 6 months of fever to 40, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis with negative throat swabs, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Episodes last 4 days at a time and recur every 3 to 4 weeks with clockwork regularity. Between episodes he is entirely well. Growth is on the 50th centile. Family history is negative for periodic fevers. Genetic testing for MEFV, TNFRSF1A, MVK, and NLRP3 has returned negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Between episodes: afebrile, normal vitals
data_table.Examination: During episode: aphthous stomatitis, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymphadenopathy; between episodes: examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: During episode: CRP 120, neutrophilia, normal ferritin; between episodes: CRP <5, normal FBC; throat swabs negative on all episodes; genetic panel for FMF (MEFV), TRAPS (TNFRSF1A), HIDS (MVK), CAPS (NLRP3) all negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical daily oral colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily as prophylaxis against further episodes of fever
options.rationale: Colchicine is the treatment for familial Mediterranean fever which has been excluded genetically; PFAPA responds variably to colchicine but it is not first-line. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

options.text: Continuous oral cimetidine 20 mg/kg/day for 6 months as prophylaxis against further febrile attacks
options.rationale: Cimetidine has small case-series support for PFAPA prophylaxis but is not first-line; steroids at onset have the most robust evidence and immediate effect. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) 2 mg/kg daily during each acute febrile episode now
options.rationale: Anakinra is reserved for refractory PFAPA or biopsy-proven monogenic syndromes (CAPS, HIDS); it is not first-line and is not appropriate before trial of oral steroids. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

options.text: Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as definitive treatment of recurrent fever
options.rationale: Tonsillectomy is curative in 70 to 90% but is reserved for steroid-responsive PFAPA refractory to medical therapy or significantly affecting quality of life; trial of steroids comes first. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

options.text: Single oral dose of prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg at fever onset to abort each PFAPA episode promptly
options.rationale: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis, cervical Adenitis) responds dramatically to a single oral steroid dose at fever onset (response within hours); this is both diagnostic and therapeutic; first-line per Eurofever and Australian paediatric immunology practice. (Source: Eurofever PFAPA Guideline)

explanation.summary: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis, cervical Adenitis) is the commonest paediatric autoinflammatory syndrome, presenting between ages 2 and 5 with clockwork-regular febrile episodes lasting 3 to 6 days at 3 to 8 week intervals. Diagnosis is clinical after exclusion of monogenic periodic fevers (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS, CAPS) by genetic testing when family history suggests, and after exclusion of cyclic neutropenia by serial neutrophil counts. Pathognomonic feature is dramatic and rapid response to a single oral dose of prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg at fever onset, which aborts the episode within hours but may shorten intervals between episodes. Other options include cimetidine prophylaxis, colchicine, anakinra (refractory cases), or tonsillectomy (70 to 90% remission). Children grow out of PFAPA by adolescence in most cases. PFAPA does not cause amyloidosis or organ damage, unlike untreated FMF.
key_points: PFAPA: commonest paediatric autoinflammatory, ages 2-5
Clockwork fevers, exclude monogenic syndromes (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS, CAPS) genetically
Single oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg aborts episode within hours
Tonsillectomy curative in 70-90% if refractory
Resolves by adolescence in most cases without sequelae
explanation.pearls: Steroid response in PFAPA is so brisk and reproducible that resolution of fever within 4 hours of a single oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg dose is considered confirmatory of the diagnosis when other periodic fever syndromes have been excluded.

subtopic_detail: Urea cycle disorder - hyperammonaemia emergency management
stem: A 3-day-old term male infant presents with progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting since yesterday. He was born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with a normal birth weight and was breastfeeding well until 36 hours ago. On examination he is tachypnoeic, hypotonic, and minimally responsive to stimulation. A generalised tonic seizure occurs during assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 55, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 480 micromol/L (ref <50), venous pH 7.52, pCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, anion gap 12 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate with haemodialysis referral
options.rationale: Ammonia >400 micromol/L with respiratory alkalosis (not metabolic acidosis) and normal anion gap is characteristic of a urea cycle disorder. Nitrogen scavenger therapy reduces ammonia via alternative nitrogen excretion pathways, and haemodialysis is the most effective clearance method at this critical level. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

options.text: IV dextrose 10% bolus with insulin infusion and bicarbonate correction
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose is used in organic acidaemias with ketoacidosis to promote anabolism. This infant has respiratory alkalosis with a normal anion gap, not metabolic acidosis, making organic acidaemia unlikely. (Source: ASIEM: Acute Metabolic Emergencies)

options.text: High-dose oral carnitine supplementation with dietary protein restriction
options.rationale: Carnitine supplementation is first-line for fatty acid oxidation disorders and secondary carnitine deficiency in organic acidaemias. It does not address the enzymatic defect in urea cycle disorders and will not lower ammonia at this critical level. (Source: ASIEM: Acute Metabolic Emergencies)

options.text: Emergent exchange transfusion with fresh frozen plasma replacement
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is inefficient at removing ammonia compared to haemodialysis. It does not provide the sustained clearance required when ammonia exceeds 400 micromol/L and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

options.text: IV biotin 10 mg loading dose with empiric thiamine and riboflavin
options.rationale: Biotin is specific treatment for biotinidase deficiency and holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency, which present with metabolic acidosis and organic aciduria rather than the respiratory alkalosis pattern seen here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hyperammonaemia)

explanation.summary: Urea cycle disorders are the most common cause of severe hyperammonaemia in neonates presenting after the first 24 hours. The hallmark is respiratory alkalosis due to direct ammonia stimulation of the brainstem respiratory centre, distinguishing them from organic acidaemias which present with metabolic acidosis. OTC deficiency is the most common UCD and is X-linked. Emergency management requires cessation of protein, high caloric intake via IV dextrose, nitrogen scavenger therapy, and haemodialysis when ammonia exceeds 400 micromol/L.
key_points: Respiratory alkalosis with severe hyperammonaemia in a neonate strongly suggests a urea cycle disorder
Nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, phenylbutyrate) provide alternative pathways for nitrogen excretion bypassing the urea cycle
Haemodialysis is preferred over peritoneal dialysis or exchange transfusion for rapid ammonia clearance above 400 micromol/L
OTC deficiency is X-linked and the most common urea cycle disorder
explanation.pearls: Plasma amino acids showing elevated glutamine with low citrulline localise the defect to OTC or CPS1; urinary orotic acid is elevated in OTC deficiency but normal in CPS1 deficiency, providing definitive biochemical discrimination.

subtopic_detail: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn - iNO initiation
stem: A term neonate born through thick meconium-stained liquor develops progressive respiratory distress within the first 6 hours. Despite surfactant administration and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation with FiO2 1.0, hypoxaemia persists. Echocardiography confirms right-to-left shunting at the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale with a tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity consistent with suprasystemic pulmonary pressures. Structurally normal heart confirmed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, pre-ductal SpO2 82%, post-ductal SpO2 68%, MAP 42 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Oxygenation index 28, pH 7.28, pCO2 48 mmHg, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, chest X-ray showing bilateral patchy opacification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence IV milrinone infusion for right ventricular afterload reduction
options.rationale: IV milrinone is a useful adjunct in PPHN for its inotropic and pulmonary vasodilatory properties, but it is not the first-line pulmonary vasodilator. Inhaled nitric oxide should be trialled first given the OI >25, as it provides selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

options.text: Initiate inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm with serial oxygenation index monitoring
options.rationale: With an OI of 28 and confirmed PPHN on echocardiography, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) at 20 ppm is the first-line selective pulmonary vasodilator. ECMO referral is generally considered when OI exceeds 40 despite iNO, making iNO the appropriate next escalation step at this OI. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

options.text: Arrange emergent venoarterial ECMO transfer without further medical therapy
options.rationale: ECMO is generally considered when OI exceeds 40 despite optimal medical management including iNO. At an OI of 28, medical optimisation with iNO should be attempted first, as many neonates respond and avoid the significant risks of ECMO. (Source: ANZICS: Neonatal ECMO Guidelines)

options.text: Commence IV prostacyclin infusion with invasive haemodynamic monitoring
options.rationale: IV prostacyclin (epoprostenol) causes non-selective vasodilation including systemic hypotension and is generally reserved as a second-line agent when iNO is unavailable or ineffective. Its systemic effects make it less suitable as first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

options.text: Switch to conventional ventilation with permissive hypercapnia strategy
options.rationale: De-escalating from HFOV to conventional ventilation in worsening PPHN is counterproductive. HFOV optimises lung recruitment and oxygenation. Permissive hypercapnia may worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction as acidosis exacerbates PPHN. (Source: RCH CPG: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension)

explanation.summary: PPHN occurs when pulmonary vascular resistance fails to decrease after birth, causing right-to-left shunting and severe hypoxaemia. Meconium aspiration syndrome is a common cause. The oxygenation index (OI = MAP x FiO2 x 100 / PaO2) guides escalation: iNO is initiated when OI exceeds 25, and ECMO referral is considered when OI exceeds 40 despite iNO. A pre-ductal to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 10% is characteristic.
key_points: Oxygenation index >25 is the threshold for initiating iNO in PPHN
ECMO referral is considered when OI exceeds 40 despite optimal medical management
Pre-ductal to post-ductal SpO2 difference >10% is characteristic of right-to-left ductal shunting
iNO provides selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension
explanation.pearls: iNO should be weaned gradually once sustained improvement is achieved; abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension with acute deterioration within minutes.

subtopic_detail: Turner syndrome - initial cardiac and renal workup
stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred for short stature. She is tracking below the 1st centile for height with a height velocity of 3.5 cm/year. Her mid-parental height predicts the 35th centile. On examination she has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a low posterior hairline, and mild cubitus valgus. Karyotype confirms 45,X.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 105/65 mmHg (right arm), height 107 cm (<1st centile), weight 20 kg (10th centile)
data_table.Investigations: TSH 3.2 mIU/L (ref 0.5-5.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (ref 10-25), coeliac serology negative, IGF-1 low-normal for age

lead_in: Which investigation is the highest priority to arrange next?

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian morphology and uterine presence
options.rationale: While pelvic ultrasound is part of the Turner syndrome workup, gonadal assessment is not urgent at age 7 as puberty has not yet commenced. Cardiac assessment takes priority given the risk of life-threatening structural anomalies such as bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

options.text: Growth hormone stimulation testing before considering GH therapy
options.rationale: Growth hormone therapy in Turner syndrome is approved without the need for stimulation testing. Turner syndrome itself is an indication for GH therapy regardless of GH status. However, cardiac evaluation should precede initiation of any therapy. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

options.text: Echocardiography to screen for bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation
options.rationale: Cardiovascular anomalies occur in 25-45% of Turner syndrome patients. Bicuspid aortic valve (up to 30%) and coarctation of the aorta (up to 12%) are the most significant, carrying risks of aortic dissection and endocarditis. Echocardiography is the highest-priority investigation at diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

options.text: Renal ultrasound to assess for horseshoe kidney and collecting system anomalies
options.rationale: Renal anomalies (horseshoe kidney, duplicated collecting systems) occur in approximately 30% of Turner syndrome patients. Renal ultrasound is important and should be performed, but cardiac screening takes priority given the potentially life-threatening nature of undetected cardiac anomalies. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group)

options.text: Audiometry to screen for sensorineural and conductive hearing loss
options.rationale: Hearing loss is common in Turner syndrome, affecting up to 60% of patients.
